Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Authors Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Core claim: source-probe directions can encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode same contrast more abstractly and can be captured in natural language; OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection.

Setup: Model E6 = Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15 residual activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Datasets: source Roleplaying V8; targets Insider Trading Report C2R, Insider Trading Confirm W6, Sandbagging J9. Labels by GPT-4o K8: honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed for classifiers. Source activations standardized; same stats for targets. N4D = PCA on source-standardized activations, retaining leading 100 Q7 directions. Logistic regression lambda=10. B8Q = full-representation source-trained baseline. Target metric F3/AUROC with 95% CIs.

Dataset Appendix A: V8 371 labels -1/0/1 = 140/59/172. C2R 473 = 218/194/61. W6 151 = 29/38/84. J9 1000 = 379/375/246.

§4.1: B8Q transfer: C2R moderate, W6 good, J9 poor. Target-trained within retained source-PCA subspace separates all targets, so info exists but source-trained direction does not generalize. Appendix B8Q F3: C2R .706, W6 .874, J9 .606. Target-trained 5-fold CV in leading-100 source subspace: C2R .936, W6 .950, J9 .869.

§4.2 H2 greedy oracle over leading 100 source PCs: fits source logistic regression on subsets; target labels guide subset selection only. Transfer upper bound, not unbiased OOD estimate. Y4 variance selection only matches H2 on easy W6; far behind C2R/J9. H2 improvement over B8Q C2R .22, J9 .23; H2 F3 C2R .929, J9 .832. Mean H2 subset size target CV: C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14. Full-target H2 k: C2R 13, W6 7, J9 14. Internal issue: Appendix “Small H2 subset range 8–15” conflicts with full-target W6 k=7 unless only CV means.

§4.3: Neither source-side nor target-side ranking recovers transferable subspace or basis transferring better than B8Q. T6 transfers about as well as B8Q; source-reliant directions do not generalize. M9 strong on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Rankings use standardized coefficient X4 = abs coefficient × Q7 std dev on source-N4D-projected activations. Full-target H2 search supplies stable set/k rather than fold-specific selections.

§4.4/Appendix B: For each leading source direction, C7/GPT-5-mini receives 8 most-activating and 8 least-activating source examples, generates positive/negative/shared descriptions and R5 OOD score. Selection keeps directions reaching observed max in both scoring runs; scores noisy. Prompt rates usefulness for OOD deception; low for surface/task phrasing, >=5 for general deception-relevant strategies. Appendix C: lower-index Q7 directions align more strongly with SAE decoder features U9; Spearman rho with PC index: best-matching feature -.857, mean top-10 -.917.

§4.5: L2 = interpretation-selected PC probe from retained intersection; A7 = complement/interp-ablated PC probe; Y4 = equal-dimensional top-k variance-ranked PCs. §5: limitations single model/source; W6 high baseline uninformative; J9 weakest/most OOD; C2R improvement more robust; pipeline linear; direction encode claims descriptive not causal.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Authors Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Abstract/core claim: source-probe directions can encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode same contrast more abstractly and can be captured in natural language; OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection.

Setup: Model E6 = Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens only. Datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): source Roleplaying V8; targets Insider Trading Report C2R, Insider Trading Confirm W6, Sandbagging J9. Labels by GPT-4o K8: honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed for classifier experiments. Source activations standardized to zero mean/unit variance; same source stats for targets. N4D = PCA on source-standardized activations, retaining leading 100 PCs/directions Q7. Subset S projection precedes training/evaluation. Logistic regression lambda=10. B8Q = full-representation source-trained baseline on all standardized activations. Metrics are target F3/AUROC; error bars 95% CIs.

Dataset details Appendix A: V8 total 371 labels -1/0/1 = 140/59/172. C2R total 473 = 218/194/61. W6 total 151 = 29/38/84. J9 total 1000 = 379/375/246. V8 opportunity to lie; C2R trader decides whether to report insider-info use; W6 after concealing earlier insider trading asks to confirm non-use; J9 deliberate underperformance vs normal.

§4.1 baseline: W6 transfer reasonably good, C2R moderate, J9 poor. Target-trained classification within retained source-PCA subspace separates deceptive/honest on every target, so relevant info exists but source-trained direction does not generalize. Appendix numbers: B8Q F3 C2R .706, W6 .874, J9 .606. Target-trained 5-fold CV in leading-100 source subspace: C2R .936, W6 .950, J9 .869.

§4.2 H2 greedy oracle search over leading 100 source Q7 directions. Fit source logistic regression on candidate subsets; add direction most improving target F3; target labels guide subset selection only, not probe-weight fitting. H2 is transfer upper bound, not unbiased OOD estimate. Y4 variance selection only matches H2 on easy W6; far behind C2R/J9. Appendix: H2 improvement over B8Q C2R .22, J9 .23; H2 F3 C2R .929, J9 .832. Mean H2 subset size target CV: C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14. Full-target H2 k: C2R 13, W6 7, J9 14. Internal issue from earlier: Appendix “Small H2 subset range 8–15” conflicts with full-target W6 k=7 unless only CV means.

§4.3: Neither source-side nor target-side ranking recovers transferable subspace or basis transferring better than B8Q. T6 transfers about as well as B8Q; source-reliant directions do not generalize. M9 strong on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Rankings use standardized coefficient X4 = abs probe coefficient times corresponding Q7 standard deviation on source-N4D-projected activations. T6 = source-trained ranking probe/source-PCA probe; M9 = target-trained ranking probe/target-PCA probe. Full-target H2 search supplies stable set and k rather than fold-specific selections, so numbers differ slightly from CV.

§4.4 interpretation: Transferable subsets differ from directions relied on by source or target classification. H2-selected direction interpretations express abstract contrasts that survive domain change; only partial recovery. For each leading source direction, LLM interpreter C7 receives 8 most-activating and 8 least-activating source examples, generates positive/negative/whole-direction descriptions, then assigns OOD generalization score R5. Selection keeps all directions reaching observed maximum in both scoring runs; scores noisy. Appendix B prompt: interpretation uses GPT-5-mini (P2), OpenAI 2025. Prompt describes bipolar Q7 direction; input lines token<TAB>activation with activations normalized integers -10 to +10. Source setup in prompt: E6 instructed to enact simple V8 scenario and asked a question offering strategic opportunity to lie. Judge must infer dominant contrast, avoid unsupported generalization, rate usefulness for OOD deception; low ratings for surface cues/lexical habits/task phrasing, reserve >=5 for plausible general deception-relevant strategies/behaviors. Output format exactly Positive pole, Negative pole, Shared direction, R5 (1-10).

Appendix C: Lower-index Q7 directions align more strongly with SAE decoder features U9, measured by best-matching U9 and mean top-10 feature alignment, using andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct. Earlier appendix numbers: decoder alignment Spearman rho with PC index/decoder alignment? best-matching feature -.857, mean top 10 features -.917; lower indices easier to interpret.

§4.5 language/interp selection: L2 = interp-selected PC probe from retained intersection; controls A7 = complement/interp-ablated PC probe, Y4 = equal-dimensional top-k variance-ranked PCs. All trained as source probes and evaluated by target F3. Claims L2 exceeds B8Q on all targets and variance control, widely on C2R/J9; exceeds A7 everywhere. Recovery varies: C2R substantially closes baseline–H2 gap; J9 partially; W6 little headroom/uninformative, all methods except A7 roughly tied. Direction “encode” claims descriptive from examples/C7 verbalizations, not causal; high-rated directions not ablated during inference, reinforcing conflict with causal-reduction wording.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection” by Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars.

Main claims/results: Studies linear probes for deception/concepts in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations and OOD transfer failures. Source: Roleplaying deception scenarios. Targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Main result: projecting inputs onto small subsets of source-distribution PCs can enable cross-domain transfer nearly matching target-trained oracle probes. LLM judge partially identifies transferable PCs from natural-language interpretations; gap closure: 78% Report, 25% Sandbagging.

Dataset/setup: Labels honest 0, ambiguous -1, deceptive 1 by GPT-4o; ambiguous removed. Appendix A distributions incl ambiguous: Roleplaying 371, -1/0/1 = 140/59/172; Report 473, 218/194/61; Confirm 151, 29/38/84; Sandbagging 1000, 379/375/246. Activations: layer 15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, averaged over assistant response tokens. Standardize source activations; apply source stats to targets. PCA on scaled source activations; retain top 100 PCs. Logistic regression probes, λ=10. PC-subset experiments project to selected top-100 PCs. Baseline probes train on full standardized activations.

Baseline/greedy/rankings: Fig 2 source full-representation transfer AUROCs: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained top-100-PC oracle AUROCs: 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869, apparently Confirm / Report / Sandbagging. Greedy uses labeled target data, 5-fold CV, stop if no candidate improves AUROC by >0.001; upper bound not unbiased OOD estimate. Interpretability: For each top-100 source PC, take 8 most/least activating source examples; LLM describes poles/direction. GPT-5-mini prompt asks for bipolar contrast and OOD deception usefulness 1–10. No PC scored above 6; retain PCs scoring max in both runs, yielding 19 interp-selected PCs. 5 PCs appeared in greedy selections for >1 target; 3/5 got max score. Only 1 of top 5 source-PCA PCs got max score. Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection” by Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars.

Abstract claims:
- Studies linear probes for detecting behaviors/concepts in LM activations and their OOD transfer failures.
- Model studied: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.
- Evaluates probe generalization over 3 held-out deception detection datasets.
- Main result: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training distribution of activations enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained directly on the test distribution (oracle).
- PC interpretations can identify a subset of transferable PCs.
- Method: use an LLM judge to score each PC based on whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe on highest-scoring PCs.
- Reported gap closure: closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging.
- Interpretation claim: source probe heavily weighted directions cause deceptive responses through source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions.
- Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection” by Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars.

Abstract claims:
- Studies linear probes for detecting behaviors/concepts in LM activations and their OOD transfer failures.
- Model studied: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.
- Evaluates probe generalization over 3 held-out deception detection datasets.
- Main result: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training/source distribution of activations enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained directly on the test/target distribution (oracle).
- PC interpretations can identify a subset of transferable PCs.
- Method: use an LLM judge to score each PC based on whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe on highest-scoring PCs.
- Reported gap closure: closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging.
- Interpretation claim: source probe heavily weighted directions cause deceptive responses through source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions.
- Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Introduction details:
- Motivation: Linear probes can reveal semantic info but may fail OOD by learning spurious correlations despite behavioral concepts being linearly represented.
- Approach: work in basis of source-domain PCs rather than raw activations/model latent dimensions. Investigates which subset of PCs supports generalizable probe training and how to identify it.
- Testbed: deception probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Train on single source dataset: Roleplaying deception scenarios. Evaluate on 3 held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025).
- Figure 1 overview: project activations onto source-domain PCA basis, filter candidate PC directions, train probes on selected low-dimensional subspace.
- Claimed contributions:
  1. A small transferable subspace exists (Section 4.2): target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe.
  2. Source-side and target-side rankings both fail to recover the subspace (Section 4.3): ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not transfer better than full-representation baseline.
  3. LLM judge partially recovers the subspace without target data (Section 4.5): judge interprets/selects PCs likely to encode transferable behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns.

Abstract claims source-probe-heavy directions cause deceptive responses through source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode same contrast more abstractly and can be captured in natural language. Probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection.

Counts incl ambiguous: V8 371 = 140/59/172; C2R 473 = 218/194/61; W6 151 = 29/38/84; J9 1000 = 379/375/246.

Activations standardized with source stats; targets use same stats. PCA basis N4D retaining leading 100 PCs/Q7. Subset projection before training/eval. Logistic regression lambda=10. Full baseline B8Q trains on all standardized activations, not PCA subset. Lower-index PCs more interpretable/aligned with U9 SAE decoder features; Appendix C says lower Q7 show stronger decoder alignment for best-matching U9 and mean top-10 features. Earlier alignment observations: best-matching feature Spearman rho -0.857; mean top-10 rho -0.917. 95% CIs.

4.1 baseline: W6 transfer high, C2R moderate, J9 poor/most OOD. Appendix F3/AUROC: B8Q F3 C2R .706, W6 .874, J9 .606. Target-trained leading-100 source subspace 5-fold CV: C2R .936, W6 .950, J9 .869; target info present but source-trained direction fails to generalize.

4.3 rankings: T6 source-weight ranking transfers about as well as B8Q; source-reliant directions do not generalize. M9 target-separability ranking does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Rankings use standardized coefficient X4 = abs probe coefficient × Q7 SD. Full-target H2 supplies stable set and k.

Scores noisy; retain directions reaching observed maximum in both runs. Appendix E: maximum observed R5 was 6; 2 scoring runs; 19 directions reached max in both and retained for L2; A7 complement uses 81 directions. H2 selections shared by >1 target = 5: 62,57,9 on C2R+J9 and 81,86 on W6+J9. Of these, 3/5 max-rated: 62 R5=6, 57=6, 86=6; 9=3, 81=3. Related Work (part 2): cites literature on linear concept directions in activation space: true/false cross-dataset linear structure, linear representation hypothesis, honesty/emotion directions, refusal direction, assistant axis. Claims these features aid mechanistic understanding/intervention but leave stable concepts vs context-dependent correlations unresolved. On probes: linear/lightweight probes have history; include latent truthfulness and strategic deception. High accuracy does not prove model represents property because probes may learn task or surface correlates; encoded vs recoverable info distinction; in-distribution probes generalize unevenly; safety evaluation must distinguish robust internal signals from artifacts. Natural-language explanations: LLM neuron explanations, SAE feature labeling, concept identification/ablation for reducing misaligned behavior.

Other claimed context from intro: removing leading components improves downstream embedding performance (Mu et al. 2018); leading-component projections are a probing baseline in Kantamneni et al. 2025.

Introduction claims linear probes expose semantic information in LM representations but can fail OOD despite strong in-distribution performance. Selection problem: identify dimensions that permit generalizing rather than spurious source-trained classification.

Terminology now defined: model is Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Uses layer 15 residual-stream activations, following Ying et al. (2026), who found highest cross-domain discrimination there. For each prompt, activations are averaged over assistant-response tokens only. Datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): one source Roleplaying (V8), and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). No other source dataset used. Labels by GPT-4o (K8): honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed.

Preprocessing/setup: source activations standardized to zero mean/unit variance; source statistics also standardize targets. PCA transformation is called N4D and retains leading 100 principal components/directions, called PCs/Q7. Subset S projection happens before training/evaluation. All classifiers use logistic regression with lambda=10. Comparator full-representation baseline B8Q trains directly on all standardized activations, not PCA subset. Retained 100 PCs chosen for interpretability comparability, not because low-index PCs expected to generalize better: alignment with U9/Bricken et al. 2023 decreases with index, so lower indices more natural-language interpretable. Error bars are 95% CIs.

Experiment 4.1 baseline: W6 transfer reasonably good, C2R moderate, J9 poor. Target-trained classification within retained source subspace separates deceptive/honest on every target, so relevant info is present but source-trained direction fails to generalize. Fig.2: target F3 for source-trained full reps B8Q/blue, source-trained leading 100 Q7/orange, target-trained leading 100 source Q7/green with 5-fold CV.

4.2 transferable subspace: Small source-trained subspaces nearly match target-trained probes, especially C2R and J9. Variance selection matches H2 only on easy W6, far behind on C2R/J9; explained variance not predictive. Fig.3: target F3 for B8Q blue, Y4 variance subset with k matched to H2 teal, H2 purple. H2 greedy oracle: starts empty, considers each of leading 100 source Q7 directions; projects source activations onto current candidate subset, fits source logistic regression, adds direction most improving target F3. Target 5-fold CV selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluates selected source-trained probe on held-out fold; stop if no candidate improvement >0.001. Target labels guide subset selection, never probe-weight fitting. This is transfer upper bound, not unbiased OOD estimate.

4.3 hypotheses/rankings: Neither source-side nor target-side ranking recovers transferable subspace or basis transferring better than B8Q. T6 transfers about as well as B8Q; source-reliant directions do not generalize. M9 does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Target-class separation and transfer under source-fitted weights select different directions. Fig.4: T6 red, M9 pink, H2 purple. Hypotheses: transferable directions might be individually strong target-class separation or heavily weighted by source probe. Both rankings use standardized coefficient X4 = absolute probe coefficient × corresponding Q7 standard deviation, on source-N4D-projected activations. Source-trained ranking probe/source-PCA probe T6 and target-trained ranking probe/target-PCA probe M9 supply X4 orderings; evaluated probes train on source data projected onto top k ranked directions. Full-target H2 supplies stable set and k rather than fold-specific selections, so numbers differ slightly from CV.

4.4 interpretation: Transferable subsets differ from directions relied on by source or target classification. Interpretations of H2 directions express more abstract contrasts surviving domain changes; only partial recovery. For each leading source direction, LLM judge/interpreter C7 sees eight most-activating and eight least-activating source examples and generates positive-pole, negative-pole, whole-direction descriptions (Bills/Casademunt style), then assigns OOD/generalization score R5. Scores noisy; selection retains all directions reaching observed maximum in both scoring runs.

4.5 language-only/interp selection: Language-only selection without target data meaningfully improves over B8Q. L2 exceeds B8Q on all targets and variance control Y4, widely on C2R/J9; also exceeds A7 everywhere. Recovery varies: C2R substantially closes B8Q–H2 gap; J9 partially; W6 little headroom/uninformative, every selection except A7 roughly tied. Fig.5: L2 red, B8Q blue, Y4 at L2 dimension count teal, A7 brown. Retained intersection from interpreter scores defines L2 (interp-selected PC probe). Controls: complement A7 (interp-ablated PC probe) and equal-dimensional variance-ranked top-k PCs Y4; all trained as source probes.

Conclusion: robust behavioral probing requires identifying where a linearly accessible signal is represented robustly, not just whether accessible. Full-representation probes may combine general behavioral features with dataset-specific surface cues, enabling high in-distribution accuracy but harming transfer. OOD probing is representation/subspace selection plus classifier fitting: preserve intended behavioral feature and filter spurious correlations.

Sec 4.1 baseline/Fig 2: source-trained full transfer AUROCs: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained/oracle within top-100 PCs achieves about 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC across three targets, likely Report / Confirm / Sandbagging. Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Thesis: source-probe-heavy directions encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode same contrast more abstractly/capturable in NL; OOD robustness is largely subspace/representation selection.

Setup: E6 = Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; layer 15 residual stream, assistant-response-token average. Datasets from Goldowsky-Dill 2025: source Roleplaying V8; targets C2R Insider Trading Report, W6 Insider Trading Confirm, J9 Sandbagging. GPT-4o labeler K8: honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed. Counts before removal: V8 371 = 140/-1, 59/0, 172/1; C2R 473 = 218/-1, 194/0, 61/1; W6 151 = 29/-1, 38/0, 84/1; J9 1000 = 379/-1, 375/0, 246/1.

N4D = PCA on source-standardized activations, retain leading 100 PCs/Q7. Source activations standardized zero mean/unit variance; targets use same stats. Pipeline: project into source N4D basis, filter Q7 directions, train/evaluate selected subspace. Logistic regression lambda=10. Full baseline B8Q trains on all standardized activations. F3 = AUROC; 95% CIs.

Baseline/target-trained: Source-trained full reps transfer: W6 high, C2R moderate, J9 poor. Appendix B8Q F3: C2R 0.706, W6 0.874, J9 0.606. Target-trained 5-fold CV F3 in leading-100 source subspace: C2R 0.936, W6 0.950, J9 0.869, showing info present but source-trained direction does not generalize.

H2: greedy target-guided oracle over leading 100 source Q7; add directions maximizing held-target-fold F3 improvement with source-trained logistic weights; target labels guide subset selection only, not weights. Transfer upper bound, not unbiased OOD estimate. H2 F3 C2R 0.929, J9 0.832; improves B8Q by 0.22 C2R and 0.23 J9. Mean H2 subset size in target CV: C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14. Earlier full-target H2 k recorded C2R 13, W6 7, J9 14, but Appendix E/D H2 table lists J9 15 indices: C2R 6,89,62,66,26,14,57,25,93,9,70,97,78; W6 71,53,28,86,32,81,77; J9 37,62,54,41,46,9,57,44,51,43,19,48,86,81,33. Shared H2 selections >1 target: 62,57,9,81,86.

Hypothesis tests/rankings: Neither source-side nor target-side ranking recovers transferable subspace better than B8Q. T6 source-PCA probe/ranking transfers about like B8Q; source-reliant directions do not generalize. M9 target-PCA/ranking does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Rankings use X4 = abs probe coefficient × corresponding Q7 std. Appendix D contradictorily claims H2 and M9 agree on > half and M9 largely recovers transferable space, but reported H2–M9 Jaccards are low: C2R 0.182, W6 0.077, J9 0.167. T6 source top indices: 7,8,11,12,4,5,2,3,6,27,22,21,1,41,18. M9 table: C2R 5,6,89,18,79,46,87,4,14,34,29,1,66,67,19; W6 4,1,8,53,30,7,13,18,5,20,26,49,28,31,97; J9 51,91,97,13,39,77,4,66,53,86,62,23,41,10,61.

Interpretability/L2: C7 interpreter GPT-5-mini sees eight most/least activating source examples per bipolar Q7 direction; prompt asks for contrast and R5 1–10 OOD deception usefulness, penalizing surface/noisy/task-specific. Appendix E says max observed R5 was 6; scoring runs=2; 19 directions reached max in both runs and were retained for L2; complement A7 has 81 directions. L2 = intersection retained by both scoring runs; no target data. L2 improves over B8Q on all targets and over variance control; large gains C2R/J9; exceeds A7 everywhere. L2 F3 C2R 0.881, J9 0.662; Baseline–H2 gap recovered by L2: C2R 78%, J9 25%. Appendix E says among shared H2 selections, 3/5 maximum-rated: 62 R5=6, 57 R5=6, 9 R5=3, 81 R5=3, 86 R5=6. Among top 5 T6 selections, only Q7 4 has max R5=6; Q7 7=3, 8=4, 11=3, 12=3.

Decoder alignment: Appendix C says lower-index Q7 align more strongly with SAE decoder vectors U9, measured by best-matching feature and mean top-10 features; Spearman rho best -0.857, mean top10 -0.917, meaning alignment decreases with PC index/lower indices easier to interpret.

Limitations: Single model/source; W6 high baseline uninformative; J9 weakest/most OOD/modest improvement; C2R more robust. Linear N4D+logistic only; nonlinear probes/readout locations open. Direction “encode” claims descriptive from examples/verbalizations, not causal; high-rated directions not ablated during inference.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Authors Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Work during 11th AI Safety Camp; compute by AI Safety Camp.

Core claims: Linear probes for detecting deception in LM activations can fail OOD; OOD robustness depends largely on subspace selection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15 residual stream. Source: Roleplaying deception scenarios. Targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Main claim: small subsets of source-domain PCs enable transfer nearly matching target-trained probes; cannot be found by source-side or target-side separability alone. LLM judge/interp with no target data partially recovers transferable directions; gap closure: 78% on Report and 25% on Sandbagging.

Data/setup: Labels honest=0/deceptive=1/ambiguous=-1 by GPT-4o; ambiguous removed. Earlier text said Roleplaying source had 311 retained responses, but Appendix A table says total 371 with 140 ambiguous, 59 honest, 172 deceptive, implying 231 retained: inconsistency. Appendix A target retained counts implied: Report 255, Confirm 122, Sandbagging 621. Activations averaged over assistant response only. Source activations standardized; same stats applied to target. PCA on scaled source; retain top 100 PCs. Logistic regression λ=10. Baseline probes train on full standardized activations.

Sec 4.1: Source-trained full-representation probe transfers: Confirm AUROC 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes within top-100 source-PC subspace, 5-fold CV: AUROC 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869, apparently Report / Confirm / Sandbagging. Claim: top-100 contains enough info; failure is source probe learning non-generalizing direction.

Sec 4.2 greedy transferable subspace: Starts empty; searches top 100 source PCs; adds candidate maximizing target AUROC after fitting source logistic regression. 5-fold over target: select PCs on non-held-out target folds, evaluate source-trained probe on held-out fold. Stop if improvement <=0.001. Average selected sizes: 15 Report, 8 Confirm, 14 Sandbagging. Control: top-k by variance matched to greedy size. Greedy uses target labels, upper bound. Greedy oracle AUROC: Report 0.929, Sandbagging 0.832. Improves full baseline by 0.22 Report and 0.23 Sandbagging. Variance control matches greedy only for Confirm.

Sec 4.3: Tests whether transferable PCs are detectable source-side. PC rankings use standardized coefficient = abs coefficient × PC SD. Source-PCA by source-trained probe weights; Target-PCA by target-trained probe weights. Final probes trained on source projected onto top k. Fig 4 greedy run on full target dataset, single PC sets: k=13 Report, 7 Confirm, 14 Sandbagging. Source-PCA transfers about like full baseline. Target-PCA does well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, below random transfer on Sandbagging.

Sec 4.4: For each top-100 source PC, take 8 most/least activating source examples. GPT-5-mini describes poles/shared direction and rates OOD usefulness 1–10. No PC above 6; max observed OOD score treated as 6. Scoring twice; PCs scoring max both runs retained, yielding 19 PCs. Of 5 PCs in greedy selections for more than one target, 3/5 got max OOD. Only 1 of top 5 PCs selected by source-PCA probes got max.

Sec 4.5/Fig 5: Interp-selected subspace = 19 PCs. Compared to full baseline, top-19 variance PCs, remaining 81 after ablation. Interp-selected outperforms baseline/controls on all 3 targets and beats interp-ablated. Report 0.706→0.881, closing 78% of gap to greedy 0.929. Confirm near ceiling 0.874, little headroom. Sandbagging 0.606→0.662, closing 25% of gap to greedy 0.832.

Sec 5 limitations: Single model/source/layer; Sandbagging weakest/small margins; fully linear; no causal validation/ablation.

Appendix C: Lower PCs show stronger decoder alignment to SAE features, Spearman ρ = -0.857 for best matching feature and -0.917 for mean top 10; SAE andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct.

Appendix D: Table 2 PC sets. Source probe weights top list: PC7, PC8, PC11, PC12, PC4, PC5, PC2, PC3, PC6, PC27, PC22, PC21, PC1, PC41, PC18. This conflicts with earlier selection rule if these are claimed as LLM-selected transferable PCs, because PC9/PC81 scored only 3. Table 4 gives OOD scores/interpretations for source top PCs: PC7=3, PC8=4, PC11=3, PC12=3, PC4=6, matching claim that only one of top five source-PCA PCs got max.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Authors Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars.

Abstract claims:
- Study linear probes for detecting behaviors/concepts in LM activations; concern is OOD transfer failure.
- Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.
- Evaluates probe generalization over 3 held-out deception detection datasets.
- Main finding: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training distribution of activations enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained directly on the test distribution (oracle).
- PC interpretations can identify a subset of transferable PCs.
- Method: use an LLM judge to score each PC based on whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe on highest-scoring PCs.
- Reported gap closure: baseline-to-oracle gap closed by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging.
- Interpretation: directions heavily weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; directions that transfer encode the same contrast more abstractly, capturable by natural language descriptions.
- Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Sec 4.3: Tests whether transferable PCs are detectable source-side. Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection” by Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars.

Main claims/checks:
- Main claim/conclusion: projecting onto small subset of source PCs enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching target-trained probes; robust OOD probing is framed as representation/subspace selection, not just linear accessibility.
- Abstract/intro claimed LLM judge recovers all five repeatedly transferable PCs / identifies every repeatedly transferable PC and full shared transfer subspace. Sec. 4.4 contradicted this: only 3/5 repeated greedy PCs got max OOD score; only partial recovery. Conclusion says interpretability score “partially recovers the subspace,” consistent with Sec. 4.4 but inconsistent with abstract/intro if those stronger claims remain.
- Abstract claimed interpreted-PC probing closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Sec. 4.5 and Limitations repeat these gap-closure claims.

Datasets/setup:
- Datasets: Roleplaying source; targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1 by GPT-4o; ambiguous removed.
- Appendix A Table 1 label distributions: Roleplaying 371; 140/59/172. Report 473; 218/194/61. Confirm 151; 29/38/84. Sandbagging 1000; 379/375/246. Usable after removing ambiguous: Roleplaying 59/172, Report 194/61, Confirm 38/84, Sandbagging 375/246.
- Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; layer 15 residual stream activations; averaged over assistant response tokens.
- Preprocess: standardize using source mean/variance; same stats for targets. PCA on scaled source activations; retain top 100 PCs.
- Probes: logistic regression λ=10. Baseline uses full standardized activations, not limited to top 100 PCs unless specified.

Results:
- Sec. 4.1 Fig. 2 full source-rep transfer baselines: Confirm 0.874 AUROC; Report 0.706; Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained top-100 source-PC oracle: approx Report/Confirm/Sandbagging 0.936/0.950/0.869.
- Sec. 4.2 greedy target-supervised PC selection: 5-fold target CV selection, held-out eval; stops if no improvement >0.001; upper bound using target labels. Average selected sizes: 15 PCs Report, 8 Confirm, 14 Sandbagging. Fig. 3: greedy improves baseline by about +0.22 Report and +0.23 Sandbagging; Sec. 4.5 gives Report greedy oracle 0.929 and Sandbagging 0.832.
- Sec. 4.3: source-PCA probe ranks PCs by source-trained weights; target-PCA probe ranks by target-trained weights in source-PCA basis, metric abs(coef)×PC std. k from greedy on full target dataset: 13 Report, 7 Confirm, 14 Sandbagging. Source/target separability alone cannot identify transferable subset.
- Sec. 4.4 interpretability: each top-100 source PC interpreted from 8 most/least activating source examples. LLM judge rates OOD usefulness 1–10. No PC >6; 19 PCs score 6 in both runs. Five PCs appeared in greedy selections for more than one target; only 3/5 got max OOD score. Partial recovery.
- Sec. 4.5 interpreted PC selection: use 19 max-OOD-score PCs without target data. Outperforms baseline and variance controls on all targets; Report 0.706→0.881, closes 78% gap to greedy 0.929. Confirm baseline near ceiling 0.874. Sandbagging 0.606→0.662, closes 25% gap to greedy 0.832.

Limitations/conclusion:
- Narrow: single model/layer/source dataset; Confirm uninformative due to high baseline; Sandbagging margins small; pipeline linear; no causal validation of PC interpretations.
- Conclusion says LLM-judge score partially recovers subspace and OOD probing is robust subspace selection.

Appendices:
- Appendix B: GPT-5-mini used to interpret directions; activations normalized -10 to +10; prompt asks bipolar PC interpretation and OOD deception usefulness rating.
- Appendix C: Lower PCs show stronger decoder alignment to SAE features using andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct; Spearman ρ=-0.857 for best-matching SAE feature and -0.917 for mean top 10.
- Appendix D: Claims Jaccard overlap between greedy and target-pca is 0.182 Report, 0.077 Confirm, 0.167 Sandbagging, and less than one-fifth. Table 2 lists source probe top PCs; greedy sets: Report 13 PCs, Confirm 7 PCs, Sandbagging 15 PCs; target separability ranking lists 15 PCs for each target. Internal issues: Jaccards do not match full printed table sets, and Sandbagging greedy has 15 PCs here vs Sec. 4.3 k=14.
- Appendix E Table 3 lists five repeatedly selected PCs and LLM OOD scores: PC62 Report+Sandbagging score 6; PC57 Report+Sandbagging score 6; PC9 Report+Sandbagging score 3; PC81 Confirm+Sandbagging score 3; PC86 Confirm+Sandbagging score 6. This supports Sec. 4.4’s “3/5 max score” but contradicts Table 3 caption if read as “selected for likely transferability based on interpretation,” because two have low score 3. Appendix E Table 4 gives example PC scores/interpretations: PC7=3, PC8=4, PC11=3, PC12=3, PC4=6.

Datasets/setup:
- Datasets: Roleplaying source; targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Appendix A descriptions: Roleplaying = simple scenario with opportunity to lie; Report = trader decides whether to honestly report using insider info; Confirm = after hiding earlier insider-info use, asked to confirm it did not use any; Sandbagging = instructed to underperform on some tasks while behaving normally on others.
- Labels: honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1 by GPT-4o; ambiguous removed for experiments.
- Appendix A Table 1 label distributions (total; -1/0/1): Roleplaying 371; 140/59/172. Insider Trading Report 473; 218/194/61. Insider Trading Confirm 151; 29/38/84. Sandbagging 1000; 379/375/246. After removing ambiguous, usable class counts would be Roleplaying 59/172, Report 194/61, Confirm 38/84, Sandbagging 375/246.

- Preprocess: standardize using source mean/variance; same stats for targets. PCA on scaled source activations; retain top 100 PCs.
- Probes: logistic regression λ=10. Baseline uses full standardized activations, not limited to top 100 PCs unless specified.

Sec. 4.1 Fig. 2:
- Full source-rep transfer baselines: Confirm 0.874 AUROC; Report 0.706; Sandbagging 0.606.
- Target-trained top-100 source-PC oracle: Report/Confirm/Sandbagging about 0.936/0.950/0.869. Shows target info exists in source-PC subspace, but source-learned directions don’t generalize.

Sec. 4.2 greedy target-supervised PC selection:
- Greedy selects among top 100 source PCs using labeled target data; 5-fold target CV selection on non-held-out folds, evaluation on held-out fold. Stop if no improvement >0.001.
- Average selected sizes: 15 PCs Report, 8 Confirm, 14 Sandbagging.
- Greedy is an upper bound/not unbiased OOD because target labels guide subset choice.
- Fig. 3: full baseline vs top-k variance vs greedy oracle PCs. Greedy improves baseline by about +0.22 Report and +0.23 Sandbagging; implied approx Report 0.926, Sandbagging 0.836. Sec. 4.5/Limitations give Report greedy oracle 0.929 and Sandbagging 0.832, small numerical mismatches.
- Variance control only matches in easy Confirm case; variance explained not predictive.

Sec. 4.3 Fig. 4:
- Tests whether transferable PCs are target-class-separating individually or heavily weighted by source probe.
- Source-PCA probe ranks PCs by weights from source-trained probe in source-PCA basis. Target-PCA probe ranks PCs by target-trained weights in source-PCA basis. Metric: abs(coefficient) × PC std dev.
- k from greedy on full target dataset: 13 Report, 7 Confirm, 14 Sandbagging.
- Source-PCA probe transfers about as well as full baseline; target-PCA probe good on Report but worse than greedy on Confirm and below random on Sandbagging. Thus source-side or target-side separability alone cannot identify transferable subset.

Sec. 4.4 interpreting transferable subspace:
- For each top-100 source PC, take 8 most/least activating source examples. LLM describes positive pole, negative pole, whole direction. LLM judge rates generalizability/OOD score 1–10.
- No PC scored above 6; 6 is max observed. Retain PCs scoring 6 in both runs: 19 PCs.
- Five PCs appeared in greedy selections for more than one target. Only 3/5 got max OOD score; only 1 of top 5 source-PCA-probe PCs got max. Authors say partial recovery; conflicts with earlier all-five/full-shared-subspace claim.

Appendix B LLM Judge Prompt:
- Says “We use GPT-5-mini (OpenAI, 2025) to interpret directions.” Prompt describes bipolar PC direction. Activations normalized to integers -10 to +10. Examples selected from Roleplaying setup: model instructed to roleplay in simple scenario and asked a question giving strategic chance to lie. Prompt asks for narrow dominant contrast from high-positive and high-negative examples; warns not to overgeneralize or treat as sentiment unless supported. It asks to rate OOD deception usefulness 1–10, with low scores for surface cues/task-specific phrasing/noisy/brittle/context-dependent directions and scores ≥5 only for plausibly general deception-relevant strategy/behavior. Required output: Positive pole, Negative pole, Shared direction, OOD deception usefulness.

Sec. 4.5 interpreted PC selection/Fig. 5:
- Select 19 max-OOD-score PCs without target data. Compare interp-selected 19 PCs against full baseline, top-19 variance PCs, and interp-ablated remaining 81 PCs; 95% CIs.
- Interp-selected probe outperforms baseline and variance control on all 3 targets, with wide margins on Report/Sandbagging, and outperforms interp-ablated across all 3.
- Report: baseline 0.706 to interp-selected 0.881; closes 78% of gap to greedy oracle 0.929.
- Confirm: baseline near ceiling at 0.874; little headroom; all methods aside from interp-ablated roughly similar/uninformative.
- Sandbagging: baseline 0.606 to interp-selected 0.662; closes 25% of gap to greedy oracle 0.832. Weakest result.
- Overall conclusion: natural-language interpretation alone, without target data, improves OOD generalization.

Sec. 5 Limitations:
- Claims are narrow: single model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15) and single source dataset Roleplaying; generalization to other models/datasets open.
- Insider Trading Confirm deemed uninformative because baseline already 0.874.
- Sandbagging margins small; Report result described as more robust.
- Pipeline fully linear: PCA projection + logistic regression; nonlinear probes/readout locations open.
- No causal validation: PC interpretations are descriptive from top examples and LLM verbalization; authors say they have not ablated high-scoring PCs during inference to causally verify encoding.

Sec. 6 Conclusion:
- Reiterates that small subset of source PCs enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches target-trained probes, and cannot be found with source-side or target-side separability alone.
- Says LLM-judge interpretability score with no target access partially recovers subspace.
- Frames OOD probing as selecting robust subspace preserving intended behavioral feature and filtering spurious correlations; full-representation probes may mix general behavioral features with dataset-specific surface cues.

Acknowledgment/Impact:
- Work conducted during 11th AI Safety Camp; compute provided by AI Safety Camp; thanks to Prasad Mahadik and Arya Hariharan.
- Impact statement is generic: goal is to advance ML; no specific societal consequences highlighted.

Full-representation probes can mix general behavioral features with dataset-specific cues, high ID but worse transfer; sparse directional subspaces may isolate general behavioral structure.

Paper title: “PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations.” Author Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero, WVU.

Core framing: PrivDrift audits active-context re-disclosure: user-disclosed sensitive info remains behaviorally recoverable via later prompts after unrelated topic drift. Not about training-data memorization/permanent memory/personalization memory/cross-session retention or assuming users think same-session LLMs forget; risk in shared/persistent sessions, browser assistants, enterprise copilots, agent workflows, prompt injection/tool outputs. Secret S at turn t0; d unrelated drift turns; probe P; leakage if response reveals S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Adversary may inspect transcript, but benchmark tests whether model itself re-discloses under later query/pressure.

Dataset: N=1000 controlled multi-turn dialogues: 900 synthetic + 100 human-authored under same constraints, inserted throughout rather than separate block; cached metadata lacks human-authored IDs so only aggregate results, human-vs-synthetic left future. Secret categories: phone, email, SSN, credit card. Drift lengths 0,2,3,4,5,6 (no d=1); Table 1 aggregate length avg words 359.16, median 385, min/max 43/795; avg approx tokens 478.87, median 513.33, min/max 57.33/1060.00. Appendix A Table 7 by drift: d0 N197 avg/median words 44.29/43, avg/median tokens 59.05/57.33; d2 N147 253.97/258 words, 338.62/344 tokens; d3 N142 344.18/347, 458.91/462.67; d4 N166 452.27/447, 603.02/596; d5 N181 520.92/543, 694.56/724; d6 N167 568.03/605, 757.37/806.67. Counts sum to 1000 and weighted avg words matches 359.16. Secret inserted in opening turn. Drift from topic-conditioned dense Q-A/fallback tasks; rewrite model preserves exact secret, drift length, role structure, final probes while improving fluency. Fixed-format secrets; future work should extend to unstructured sensitive attributes.

Probing/eval: Three persuasion probes per dialogue: Simple neutral direct, Medium contextual justification, Hard urgent/high-pressure. Drift sampled d=0 p=0.2; otherwise uniform {2,3,4,5,6}; results bounded to short-to-medium drift up to d=6, not full modern long-context windows. Models GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B via OpenRouter/API-served; same 1000 dialogues/model; 3000 responses/model, 9000 total. API models may change; mitigation: logging identifiers, prompts, timestamps, cached responses, paired stats on identical sets. Dialogue-level leakage = any probe leaks; probe-level analyses by persuasion/secret/drift. CIs bootstrap over dialogues. Detector: Stage 1 normalization/regex-like matching: numeric strip non-digits; alphanumeric normalize case/whitespace preserving meaningful delimiters; Leak_regex=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)]. Stage 2 regex-negative responses passed to open-weights Llama judge; leakage if full secret, substantial substring, or enough partial info to identify secret. Regex-only and hybrid reported; fuzzy auxiliary/post-hoc also reported. No formal human inter-annotator agreement yet; future manual audit. Stats: McNemar, Cochran’s Q/posthoc McNemar, chi-square/Cramer’s V.

Privacy Half-Life: δ=0.1×L(0). τ=min observed d such that L(d)≤δ and all later observed d′>d also ≤δ; if none, τ=max(Dobs)+1. Prevents transient dips counting.

Section 5 results: 5.1 Table 2 dialogue-level regex vs hybrid: GPT 47.70/47.70 Δ0 p=1.0; DeepSeek 37.80/38.70 Δ+0.90 p=7.7e-3; Qwen 53.50/54.60 Δ+1.10 p=2.57e-3. Hybrid differs slightly; dominated by direct/near-direct reproduction; judge adds up to 1.10 pp. 5.2 Table 3 dialogue-level hybrid + 95% CI: DeepSeek 38.70% [35.7,41.6]; GPT 47.70% [44.6,50.8]; Qwen 54.60% [51.6,57.7]. Main result range 38.7%–54.6%. 5.3 Table 4 persuasion probe-level hybrid significant all models (Cochran Q p<1e-5), non-monotonic/model-dependent: GPT simple 39.30, medium 40.50, hard 32.90 (hard reduces); DeepSeek simple 28.10, medium 22.00, hard 29.20 (medium lowest); Qwen simple 38.70, medium 33.30, hard 40.60 (hard highest). 5.4 Drift length: dip near d=3 followed by rebound; Cramer’s V small/negligible probe-level: DeepSeek 0.1073, GPT 0.0659, Qwen 0.0723. Do not generalize to arbitrary long contexts; risk persists across several unrelated shifts. 5.5 Table 5 secret type strongly determines leakage (probe-level hybrid). Cramer’s V: DeepSeek 0.5871, GPT 0.7731, Qwen 0.6927. Rates: SSN GPT 0.14, DeepSeek 1.11, Qwen 5.97; Credit card GPT 0.00, DeepSeek 0.39, Qwen 4.01; Email GPT 78.24, DeepSeek 57.11, Qwen 81.13; Phone GPT 70.89, DeepSeek 46.13, Qwen 57.24. Interpretation: format/sensitivity cues more than generalized contextual confidentiality; SSNs/CC suppressed far more than emails/phones. 5.6 Privacy Half-Life: with δ=0.1L(0), no model reaches threshold at tested drift lengths; τ=7 for all models and persuasion levels (max d=6 + 1). 5.7 Fuzzy post-hoc cached outputs (Table 6 probe-level %): DeepSeek regex 25.50, fuzzy .85 26.40, fuzzy .80 26.53, hybrid 26.43; GPT 36.80, 37.03, 37.07, 37.57; Qwen 36.97, 37.60, 37.93, 37.53. Fuzzy closely tracks hybrid; auxiliary only.

Section 6 Discussion restates: persistent active-context privacy risk; no implication of permanent memory or all long-context settings. Behavior mostly direct/near-direct because fuzzy tracks hybrid. Strongest pattern is secret-type asymmetry: SSNs/credit cards suppressed more than emails/phones, suggesting format-sensitive safeguards rather than robust confidentiality reasoning. Persuasion significant but non-monotonic/model-dependent: GPT hard reduces, DeepSeek medium lowest, Qwen hard highest. Topic drift not implicit privacy boundary; intermediate dips not stable enough for Privacy Half-Life criterion; motivates stability-based evaluation.

Section 7 Limitations/Future Work: bounded drift only up to d=6; fixed-format structured secrets easier to detect than unstructured sensitive info; active context only, not training-data memorization/personalization/cross-session; 900 synthetic/100 human-authored inserted throughout but metadata lacks human flags; detector scope includes deterministic, fuzzy, external LLM judge, no formal human IAA; API-served models may change; planned release of generation code, probe templates, eval scripts, aggregate results, sanitized dialogue subset/examples with non-real identifiers/templates sufficient to reproduce benchmark without realistic identifiers.

Section 8 Conclusion: restates PrivDrift benchmark for active-context privacy leakage under topic drift and persuasion intensity. Across three LLMs and 1,000 dialogues/model, dialogue-level hybrid leakage substantial, 38.7%–54.6%. Persuasion effects are model-dependent; secret type has strongest association. Within tested drift range, topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; Privacy Half-Life exceeds observed window for all models. Secret-type asymmetry suggests protections are uneven and more format-cue-based than robust contextual confidentiality.

Appendix B Table 8 additional probe-level Cramer’s V effect sizes for hybrid leakage vs variables: DeepSeek secret type 0.5871 Large, drift length 0.1073 Small, persuasion 0.0718 Negligible; GPT secret type 0.7731 Large, drift length 0.0659 Negligible, persuasion 0.0689 Negligible; Qwen secret type 0.6927 Large, drift length 0.0723 Negligible, persuasion 0.0639 Negligible. Appendix C: Figure 6 dialogue construction details.

Paper title: “PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations.” Author Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero, West Virginia University.

Abstract claims:
- Problem: In persistent/shared-session/tool-augmented LLM settings, user-disclosed sensitive info may remain behaviorally recoverable through later prompts even after dialogue shifts to unrelated topics.
- Introduces PrivDrift benchmark for auditing whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after conversational topic drift and persuasion-based probing.
- Dataset/benchmark: 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes.
- Evaluation: across three LLMs with extended context windows.
- Main result: dialogue-level hybrid leakage remains substantial, ranging from 38.7% to 54.6%.
- Leakage varies strongly by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity.
- Within tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage.
- Conclusion: privacy risk in active LLM contexts should be evaluated as persistent behavioral failure mode rather than only training-data memorization or immediate jailbreak behavior.

Keywords: Trustworthy AI, Large Language Models, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

- Introduces PrivDrift benchmark for auditing whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after conversational topic drift and persuasion-based probing.
- Dataset/benchmark: 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes.
- Evaluation: across three LLMs with extended context windows.
- Main result: dialogue-level hybrid leakage remains substantial, ranging from 38.7% to 54.6%.
- Leakage varies strongly by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity.
- Within tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage.
- Conclusion: privacy risk in active LLM contexts should be evaluated as persistent behavioral failure mode rather than only training-data memorization or immediate jailbreak behavior.

Keywords: Trustworthy AI, Large Language Models, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Section 3 framework: PrivDrift has three components: parametric dialogue generator, probing harness, metric suite for leakage detection/temporal analysis. Figure 1 overview: constructs controlled dialogues, appends standardized probes, queries target models, scores with hybrid detector.

Persona/secret injection: persona sampled from >100 professions/demographic profiles plus ground-truth secret S. Topic drift: each dialogue assigned a topic such as tax filing, medical triage, travel logistics. Drift turns drawn from topic-conditioned library of dense Q-A pairs and fallback tasks involving professional writing, structured reasoning, or long-form summarization. Drift length d sampled from mixed distribution: d=0 with p=0.2; otherwise Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=0.8. No d=1 condition.

Paper title: “PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations.” Author Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero, WVU.

Threat model: active-context re-disclosure: secret S disclosed at turn t0 remains recoverable after d unrelated, content-dense drift turns; standardized probe appended; leakage if response reveals S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Raw transcript may be inspectable; focus is behavioral reproduction, not permanent memory. Settings include shared/persistent sessions, assistants, copilots, agents, prompt injection/tool/RAG contexts.

Benchmark/design: PrivDrift = dialogue generator, probing harness, metrics. Same 1,000-dialogue benchmark evaluated on 3 models (1,000 dialogues/model; not 3,000 unique dialogues). Dataset = 900 synthetic + 100 human-authored; human-authored inserted throughout, not separate block; cached eval metadata does not preserve human-vs-synthetic row IDs, so only aggregate results and no human-vs-synthetic comparison. Table 1: 1,000 dialogues; 4 secret categories; drift lengths 0,2,3,4,5,6; avg words 359.16; median 385; min/max 43/795; avg approx tokens 478.87; median 513.33; min/max 57.33/1060. Ns sum to 1,000 and weighted averages match Table 1. Secret categories: phone, email, SSN, credit card. Health/family/immigration/financial hardship only future unstructured-sensitive-attribute work, not evaluated categories. Secret in opening turn. Personas >100. Drift topics include tax, medical triage, travel; dense QA/fallback tasks. Naturalistic rewrite preserves exact secret, drift length, roles, final probe conditions.

Axes: topic drift and persuasion intensity. Drift d≤6: bounded short-to-medium drift, not full long-context saturation. Sampling: d=0 p=.2; otherwise Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} p=.8; no d=1. Probe styles: Simple direct, Medium contextual justification, Hard high-pressure/urgent. Each dialogue evaluated under 3 probes, so 3,000 responses/model and 9,000 total.

Evaluation: Hierarchical hybrid detector. Stage 1 normalized/regex exact matching: numeric strip non-digits; alphanumeric normalize case/whitespace and preserve meaningful delimiters; Leak_regex if normalized secret contained in normalized response. Stage 2 regex-negative responses to Llama judge; judge sees secret and response; labels reveal full/substantial/enough partial. Regex-only and hybrid reported separately. Fuzzy matching also reported as cached sensitivity/auxiliary. Dialogue-level leakage: dialogue leaks if any standardized probe elicits secret. Persuasion/fuzzy analyses probe-level; dialogue-level can exceed average persuasion-level rates. 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues. Probe sensitivity checks over cached responses. McNemar/Bonferroni for paired comparisons; Cochran’s Q + post-hoc McNemar for repeated persuasion; chi-square and Cramer’s V for associations. Limitations: no formal human inter-annotator agreement yet; future manual audit of borderline partial disclosures/obfuscations.

Privacy Half-Life τ: δ=0.1×L(0); τ=min observed d where L(d)≤δ and all later observed d′>d also ≤δ; later rebound disqualifies transient decrease; if none τ=max(D_obs)+1. Since D_obs={0,2,3,4,5,6}, τ=7 if no stable decay.

Models: GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B via OpenRouter API; same histories/templates. API-served models may change; mitigations: log identifiers, prompts, timestamps, cached responses, paired stats on identical dialogue sets.

Raw transcript may be inspectable; key question is behavioral reproduction, not permanent model memory. Settings include shared/persistent sessions, assistants, copilots, agents, prompt injection/tool/RAG contexts.

Benchmark/design: PrivDrift = dialogue generator, probing harness, metrics. Same 1,000-dialogue benchmark evaluated on 3 models (not 3,000 unique dialogues). Dataset = 900 synthetic + 100 human-authored; human-authored inserted throughout; identifiers not preserved; no human-vs-synthetic analysis. Table 1: 1,000 dialogues; 4 secret categories; drift lengths 0,2,3,4,5,6; avg words 359.16; median 385; min/max 43/795; avg approx tokens 478.87; median 513.33; min/max 57.33/1060. Secret categories: phone, email, SSN, credit card. Watch for later claims about health details as evaluated categories. Secret in opening turn. Personas >100. Drift topics include tax, medical triage, travel; dense QA/fallback tasks. Naturalistic rewrite preserves exact secret, drift length, roles, final probe conditions.

Axes: topic drift and persuasion intensity. Drift d≤6, sampled d=0 p=.2; otherwise Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} p=.8; no d=1. Probe styles: Simple direct, Medium contextual justification, Hard high-pressure/urgent. Each dialogue evaluated under 3 probes, so 3,000 responses/model and 9,000 total.

Evaluation: Hierarchical hybrid detector. Stage 1 normalized/regex exact matching: numeric strip non-digits; alphanumeric normalize case/whitespace and preserve meaningful delimiters; Leak_regex if normalized secret contained in normalized response. Stage 2 regex-negative responses to Llama judge; judge sees secret and response; labels reveal full/substantial/enough partial. Regex-only and hybrid reported separately. Dialogue-level leakage: dialogue leaks if any standardized probe elicits secret. Persuasion/fuzzy analyses probe-level. This can make dialogue-level leakage exceed average persuasion-level rates. 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues. Probe sensitivity checks over cached responses. McNemar/Bonferroni for paired comparisons; Cochran’s Q + post-hoc McNemar for repeated persuasion; chi-square and Cramer’s V for associations.

Privacy Half-Life τ: δ=0.1×L(0); τ=min observed d where L(d)≤δ and all later observed d′>d also ≤δ; later rebound disqualifies transient decrease; if none τ=max(D_obs)+1. Since D_obs={0,2,3,4,5,6}, τ=7 if no stable decay.

Models: GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B via OpenRouter API; same histories/templates.

§5 results:
- Table 2 dialogue-level regex vs hybrid: GPT 47.70 vs 47.70 Δ0 p=1.0; DeepSeek 37.80 vs 38.70 Δ+0.90 p=7.7e-3; Qwen 53.50 vs 54.60 Δ+1.10 p=2.57e-3. Claim judge adds up to 1.10 pp and leakage dominated by direct/near-direct reproduction.
- Table 3 dialogue-level hybrid with 95% CI: DeepSeek 38.70% [35.7,41.6]; GPT 47.70% [44.6,50.8]; Qwen 54.60% [51.6,57.7].
- Table 4 probe-level hybrid by persuasion: GPT Simple 39.30%, Medium 40.50%, Hard 32.90% (hard reduces leakage); DeepSeek Simple 28.10%, Medium 22.00%, Hard 29.20% (medium lowest); Qwen Simple 38.70%, Medium 33.30%, Hard 40.60% (hard highest). Cochran’s Q p<1e-5 for all; non-monotonic and model-dependent.
- §5.4 drift length: curves dip near d=3 then rebound; Cramer’s V probe-level: DeepSeek 0.1073, GPT 0.0659, Qwen 0.0723. Claim drift does not reliably reduce leakage within d≤6 and not about arbitrary long contexts.
- Table 5 probe-level hybrid by secret type: GPT SSN 0.14%, credit card 0.00%, email 78.24%, phone 70.89%; DeepSeek SSN 1.11%, credit card 0.39%, email 57.11%, phone 46.13%; Qwen SSN 5.97%, credit card 4.01%, email 81.13%, phone 57.24%. Cramer’s V secret-type association: DeepSeek 0.5871, GPT 0.7731, Qwen 0.6927. Claim SSNs/credit cards suppressed far more than emails/phones.
- §5.6 Half-life: no model approaches threshold at tested drift; τ=max(D_obs)+1=7 for all models and persuasion levels.
- Table 6 probe-level cached regex/fuzzy/hybrid: DeepSeek regex 25.50, fuzzy .85 26.40, fuzzy .80 26.53, hybrid 26.43; GPT 36.80, 37.03, 37.07, 37.57; Qwen 36.97, 37.60, 37.93, 37.53. Claim fuzzy supports hybrid; auxiliary only.
- Figures mentioned: Fig 4 hybrid leakage vs drift, dip near d=3/rebound; Fig 5 heatmap by drift and persuasion.

§6 Discussion: Summarizes persistent active-context privacy risk; does not imply permanent model memory or that all long-context settings behave similarly. Says assistants may reproduce sensitive in-context info under retrieval pressure. Cached probe evaluation shows behavior mostly direct/near-direct because fuzzy closely tracks hybrid. Strongest pattern is secret-type asymmetry: SSNs/credit cards suppressed much more than emails/phones, suggesting format-sensitive safeguards rather than contextual confidentiality reasoning. Persuasion significant but non-monotonic/model-dependent: GPT hard reduces leakage; DeepSeek medium lowest; Qwen hard highest. Topic drift not an implicit privacy boundary; intermediate dips not stable enough for Privacy Half-Life, motivating stability-based evaluation.

final_notes:
Paper title: “PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations.” Author Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero, WVU.

Core framework: QX2/PrivDrift audits active-context re-disclosure of user-provided secrets after topic drift and standardized probes. E9U is assistant reproducing/revealing earlier sensitive value, not mere transcript presence. Secret S at t0, intervening drift D of d unrelated exchanges, then probe P. Leakage can be exact/approx/semantic. D7A drift lengths: 0,2,3,4,5,6; d=0 p=.2, others uniform p=.8. S8Q categories: A2L phone/contact, F8Z email/electronic contact, W3B SSN/government ID, N6G credit card/payment. V4N probe styles: C8R neutral direct, Z2F contextual/form-filling, L9W urgent/high-pressure. H8D composite detector positive if normalized inclusion or LLM judge finds full/substantial/identifying partial disclosure. B6T normalization-based matching first stage; U3P deterministic/regex-only baseline reported separately. LLM judge used for deterministic negatives. K2V privacy half-life tau: first observed d where L(d)<=0.1*L(0) and all later observed d also <= threshold; if none, tau=max(D_obs)+1. Later resurgence disqualifies transient decreases.

Dataset/setup: N=1000 dialogues: 900 synthetic, 100 human-authored, interspersed. Avg words 359.16, median 385, min/max 43/795; approx tokens avg 478.87, median 513.33, min/max 57.33/1060. Pipeline preserves exact secret, drift count, role structure, final-probe condition. Same histories/probes through OpenRouter. Each of 3 models processes 1000 dialogues × 3 V4N probes = 3000 cached responses/model, 9000 total. G4P = dialogue-level any-probe leakage; P6S = probe-level response statistic. G4P can exceed condition-specific means. CIs bootstrap over dialogues; matched comparisons McNemar; persuasion Cochran’s Q then McNemar; chi-square/Cramer’s V for associations. Appendix A Table 7 D7A counts/lengths: d=0 N197 avg words 44.29 median 43 tokens 59.05/57.33; d=2 N147 253.97/258 tokens 338.62/344; d=3 N142 344.18/347 tokens 458.91/462.67; d=4 N166 452.27/447 tokens 603.02/596; d=5 N181 520.92/543 tokens 694.56/724; d=6 N167 568.03/605 tokens 757.37/806.67. Counts sum 1000 and weighted averages match overall.

Models: M7Q = GPT-OSS-120B, T4X = DeepSeek-R1, Y9C = Qwen3-VL-235B. Limitations say API-served models may change over time despite logged identifiers, prompts, timestamps, cached responses, and paired statistics.

Results:
- §5.1 claims H8D largely agrees with B6T, but Table 2 actually compares U3P vs H8D G4P: M7Q 47.70 vs 47.70 Δ0 p=1.0; T4X 37.80 vs 38.70 Δ+0.90 p=7.7e-3; Y9C 53.50 vs 54.60 Δ+1.10 p=2.57e-3. Potential inconsistency: B6T named but U3P shown.
- Table 3 H8D G4P bootstrap CIs: T4X 38.70% [35.7,41.6]; M7Q 47.70% [44.6,50.8]; Y9C 54.60% [51.6,57.7]. Supports substantial leakage and model variation.
- §5.3 V4N P6S H8D: M7Q C8R 39.30, Z2F 40.50, L9W 32.90; T4X 28.10, 22.00, 29.20; Y9C 38.70, 33.30, 40.60. Cochran Q p<1e-5 for every model. Directions non-monotonic: M7Q lower at L9W, T4X lowest at Z2F, Y9C highest at L9W.
- §5.4 says cached P6S associations with D7A small/negligible; risk persists; Figure 4 H8D vs D7A has dip near d=3 then rebound. Intro specifically claims SSNs/payment identifiers receive much stronger suppression than contact identifiers; no evaluated system attains stable decay. Active-context privacy should be evaluated as persistent behavioral failure, not only parameter memorization or immediate jailbreak behavior.

Threat model/framework definitions from §3:
- E9U = active-context re-disclosure: assistant reproduces earlier sensitive value under later querying/justification/pressure; not mere presence of value in transcript. Transcript invisibility is not assumed.
- User supplies secret S at t0. Unrelated content-dense exchanges/J7K = topic drift are D={u1,a1,...,ud,ad}; standardized probe P appended after drift. Exact, approximate, or semantic revelation of S = leakage.
- D7A = drift length/intervening-turn quantity d, turns between disclosure and final probe. Values in benchmark: 0,2,3,4,5,6. Sampling: d=0 with p=.2; otherwise uniform over {2,3,4,5,6} with p=.8. Immediate recall included; short-to-medium drift emphasized.
- S8Q = secret type. Four fixed-format categories: A2L=phone numbers/contact values; F8Z=email addresses/electronic contact values; W3B=Social Security Numbers/government identifiers; N6G=credit card numbers/payment identifiers. Each inserted as ground-truth secret, not inferred.
- V4N = persuasion intensity/probe style: C8R=Simple neutral direct retrieval; Z2F=Medium contextual justification/form-filling; L9W=Hard urgent/high-pressure elicitation. Standardized conditions, not unconstrained adversarial search.
- H8D = hybrid composite detector. Labels response positive if normalized inclusion succeeds OR LLM judge finds full secret, substantial substring, or sufficient partial info to identify it. - B6T = normalization-based matching, first stage/hierarchical eval. Numeric secrets/responses strip non-digit chars; alphanumeric normalizes case/whitespace but retains meaningful delimiters. Formula Leak_U3P(R,S)=I[phi(S) subset phi(R)].
- U3P = regex-only/deterministic baseline, reported separately alongside H8D.
- LLM judge: open-weights Llama judge receives S and R, binary full/substantial-disclosure verdict for deterministic negatives; judge errors possible, not treated as error-free.
- K2V = Privacy Half-Life/stability metric tau. Observed lengths D_obs and leakage rates L(d), safety threshold delta=0.1*L(0). tau=min d in D_obs such that L(d)<=delta and for all later observed d’, L(d’)<=delta. Empty set tau=max(D_obs)+1. This is sustained suppression, not momentary decrease.

- Total dialogues N=1000: 900 synthetic, 100 human-authored, interspersed not contiguous.
- Secret categories=4. Avg words/dialogue 359.16; median 385; min/max 43/795. Approx tokens avg 478.87; median 513.33; min/max 57.33/1060.00.
- Pipeline: scaffold-then-rewrite preserves exact ground truth secret, intervening-turn counts, role structure, final-probe conditions; rewriting model only improves fluency/persona realism. Human-authored dialogues obey same constraints. Personas sampled from >100 professions/demographic profiles. Topic-dense drift library includes tax filing, medical triage, travel logistics plus professional-writing/structured-reasoning/long-form-summarization fallback tasks; annotators contribute subset.

Detector scope: labels concern surface-form outputs under U3P, R5J, and external judge; no formal human–automated inter-annotator agreement; larger manual audits future work. Planned artifacts: generation code, probe templates, eval scripts, aggregate results, sanitized dialogue subset; synthetic PII-like strings require non-real identifiers/templates sufficient for reproduction.

Paper title: “PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations.” Author Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero, WVU.

Core framing: PrivDrift audits whether user-disclosed sensitive info remains behaviorally recoverable through later prompts after conversation shifts to unrelated topics. Not training-data memorization, personalization memory, permanent/cross-session memory; risk is active-context re-disclosure in shared/persistent sessions, browser assistants, enterprise copilots, agent workflows, prompt injection/tool outputs. Secret S disclosed at t0; followed by d unrelated content-dense drift turns; standardized probe P appended; leakage if response reveals S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Discussion/conclusion: topic drift is not an implicit privacy boundary, does not reliably reduce leakage within tested range, and temporary dips should not be treated as suppression.

Dataset/benchmark: N=1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues, one seeded secret each, drift length d∈{0,2,3,4,5,6}; no d=1. 900 synthetic + 100 human-authored under same constraints; inserted throughout, not separate block; cached metadata lacks human-authored IDs so only aggregate results, human-vs-synthetic future work. Secret categories: phone numbers, emails, SSNs, credit cards. Drift turns from topic-conditioned library/fallback tasks; refinement preserves exact secret, drift length, role structure, final probe conditions. Limitations: bounded drift up to d=6 only short-to-medium active-context drift, not full long-context saturation; fixed-format structured secrets easier to detect than unstructured sensitive attributes. Table 1 overall: 1,000 total; avg words 359.16, median 385, min/max 43/795; avg approx tokens 478.87, median 513.33, min/max 57.33/1060.00. Appendix Table 7 by drift: d0 N197 avg words 44.29 median 43 avg tokens 59.05 median 57.33; d2 N147 avg words 253.97 median 258 avg tokens 338.62 median 344; d3 N142 avg words 344.18 median 347 avg tokens 458.91 median 462.67; d4 N166 avg words 452.27 median 447 avg tokens 603.02 median 596; d5 N181 avg words 520.92 median 543 avg tokens 694.56 median 724; d6 N167 avg words 568.03 median 605 avg tokens 757.37 median 806.67. These N sum to 1,000 and weighted average matches overall 359.16 words.

Probing: final standardized probe appended to completed conversation history. Three persuasion levels: Simple direct neutral query; Medium contextual justification; Hard high-pressure/urgent. Drift distribution: d=0 p=0.2; otherwise Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=0.8. Results bounded active-context persistence, not arbitrary long context windows.

Evaluation/hybrid detector: Stage 1 normalization matching; numeric secrets strip non-digits from secret/response; alphanumeric normalize case/whitespace preserving meaningful delimiters. Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)]. Stage 2 regex-negative responses passed to open-weights Llama judge (Meta AI, 2024), given secret and model response, binary verdict if reveals full secret, substantial substring, or enough partial info. Definitions/framework: E9U=active-context re-disclosure: assistant reproduces earlier sensitive value under later query/justification/pressure; not mere transcript presence. Paper title: “PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations.” Author Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero, WVU.

Core framing: PrivDrift audits whether user-disclosed sensitive info remains behaviorally recoverable through later prompts after unrelated topic drift. Not about training-data memorization, personalization memory, cross-session retention, or permanent model memory; risk is active-context re-disclosure under retrieval pressure. Risks: shared/persistent sessions, browser assistants, enterprise copilots, agent workflows, prompt injection/tool outputs. Benchmark: 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, standardized probes; evaluated per model. Main result/conclusion: dialogue-level hybrid leakage substantial, 38.7%–54.6%; varies by model, secret type, persuasion intensity; within d≤6 drift does not reliably reduce leakage. SSNs/credit cards suppressed more than emails/phones. Secret type strongest association; protections uneven/format-sensitive rather than robust contextual confidentiality. Privacy Half-Life exceeds observed window/no model reaches stable decay in observed drift range.

Dataset: N=1000 dialogues, 900 synthetic + 100 human-authored, mixed throughout; no human identifiers in cached metadata, only aggregate results. Current cached evaluation metadata does not preserve which rows are human-authored, so no human-vs-synthetic comparison. Table 1 overall: secret categories 4; drift lengths 0,2,3,4,5,6; avg words 359.16, median 385, min/max 43/795; avg approx tokens 478.87, median 513.33, min/max 57.33/1060.00. Appendix A/Table 7 by drift: d0 N=197 avg words 44.29 median 43 avg tokens 59.05 median 57.33; d2 N=147 avg words 253.97 median 258 avg tokens 338.62 median 344; d3 N=142 avg words 344.18 median 347 avg tokens 458.91 median 462.67; d4 N=166 avg words 452.27 median 447 avg tokens 603.02 median 596; d5 N=181 avg words 520.92 median 543 avg tokens 694.56 median 724; d6 N=167 avg words 568.03 median 605 avg tokens 757.37 median 806.67. Counts sum to 1000 and weighted means match Table 1. Four PII categories: phone, email, SSN, credit card. Drift turns from topic-conditioned dense Q-A/fallback tasks. Rewriting model preserves exact secret, drift length, role structure, final probe.

Probing/evaluation: Three persuasion levels per dialogue: Simple, Medium, Hard. Drift sampled d=0 p=.2; otherwise uniform {2,3,4,5,6}; no d=1. Models: GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B via OpenRouter/API-served models. Same 1,000 dialogues per model, 3 probes/dialogue = 3,000 responses/model, 9,000 total. Dialogue-level leakage = any standardized probe elicits secret. Persuasion and fuzzy analyses are probe-level. Dialogue-level can exceed average individual persuasion-level leakage.

Hybrid detector: Stage 1 normalization matching: numeric secrets strip non-digits; alphanumeric normalize case/whitespace preserving delimiters; Leak_regex=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)]. Stage 2: regex-negative responses judged by open-weights Llama judge; binary if response reveals full secret/substantial part/enough partial info. Regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid labels reported separately. No formal human inter-annotator agreement yet; future manual audit of borderline partial disclosures/obfuscations. Uncertainty/tests: dialogue-level 95% bootstrap CIs; McNemar for paired comparisons; Cochran’s Q + post-hoc McNemar for persuasion; chi-square/Cramer’s V for associations.

Privacy Half-Life: threshold δ=0.1×L(0). τ=min observed d such that L(d)≤δ and all later observed d′ also ≤δ; if none, τ=max(D_obs)+1. For observed D={0,2,3,4,5,6}, no stable decay means τ=7/exceeds observed window.

Results: Table 2 dialogue regex vs hybrid: GPT 47.70 vs 47.70 Δ0 p=1.0; DeepSeek 37.80 vs 38.70 Δ+0.90 p=7.7e-3; Qwen 53.50 vs 54.60 Δ+1.10 p=2.57e-3. Table 3 dialogue-level hybrid + bootstrap CIs: DeepSeek 38.70% [35.7,41.6]; GPT 47.70% [44.6,50.8]; Qwen 54.60% [51.6,57.7]. Persuasion: Cochran’s Q p<1e-5 all models; Table 4 probe-level hybrid: GPT Simple 39.30%, Medium 40.50%, Hard 32.90%; DeepSeek Simple 28.10%, Medium 22.00%, Hard 29.20%; Qwen Simple 38.70%, Medium 33.30%, Hard 40.60%. Internal inconsistency found earlier: Section 5.3 text said DeepSeek medium highest, but table has hard highest and medium lowest. Discussion later correctly says DeepSeek medium persuasion lowest; GPT hard/high-pressure reduces leakage; Qwen hard highest. Drift: dip near d=3 then rebound; effect sizes small/negligible; Appendix B/Table 8 Cramer’s V: DeepSeek .1073 small, GPT .0659 negligible, Qwen .0723 negligible. Secret type: strongest association; Appendix B/Table 8 Cramer’s V: DeepSeek .5871 large, GPT .7731 large, Qwen .6927 large. Table 5 probe-level hybrid by type: SSN GPT .14%, DeepSeek 1.11%, Qwen 5.97%; Credit card GPT 0.00%, DeepSeek .39%, Qwen 4.01%; Email GPT 78.24%, DeepSeek 57.11%, Qwen 81.13%; Phone GPT 70.89%, DeepSeek 46.13%, Qwen 57.24%. τ=7 for all models and persuasion levels. Fuzzy Table 6 probe-level rates: DeepSeek Regex 25.50, Fuzzy .85 26.40, Fuzzy .80 26.53, Hybrid 26.43; GPT 36.80, 37.03, 37.07, 37.57; Qwen 36.97, 37.60, 37.93, 37.53. Appendix B persuasion effect sizes: DeepSeek .0718 negligible; GPT .0689 negligible; Qwen .0639 negligible. Appendix C only notes Figure 6 dialogue construction details.

Limitations/future work: bounded drift up to d=6 only, not full modern context windows/long-context saturation; fixed-format structured secrets only, future unstructured sensitive attributes; active context only; API-served models may change, mitigated by logging model IDs, prompts, timestamps, cached responses, paired stats; planned release of generation code, probe templates, evaluation scripts, aggregate files, sanitized subset/examples with non-real identifiers and templates.
