errors.claim: “Archive verification establishes one environment across all 1,320 confirmatory cells”
errors.evidence: Earlier methods described the same count as discovery cells: “Realised objectives 6, discovery cells 1320, specs 15,840.”
errors.explanation: The paper previously labels the 1,320 cells as discovery cells, whereas this section calls them confirmatory cells. If discovery and confirmatory cells are distinct phases, this is an internal inconsistency in the status of the 1,320-cell set.

errors.claim: “Another checks every manuscript numeric token against stored-result derivations.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record manuscript numeric inconsistencies, e.g. “Table 1 text said ‘Across factor-four binnings: 0.70 to 0.77,’ but factor-four threshold range is .7232–.7448; .7018/.7719 are equal-thirds/deciles.” Also §7.5 text said A6N degeneracy occurs “above 1,000 edges” while the table shows it at 1,000 and above.
errors.explanation: A claim that every numeric token is checked against stored derivations conflicts with previously observed manuscript numeric claims that do not match the corresponding tables/results.

grade.reason: Reviewer error 3 directly identifies that the text's claim that the loosest tolerance permits filing contradicts Table 5 which shows π*=0.4109 (below the 0.80 threshold) and marks those combinations as not filable.

errors.claim: “A specification is a tuple of analytic choices $s=(o,a,d,m,\tau,P,r,g)$ ...”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Pre-registered multiverse/crossed grid over seven analytic axes of circuit discovery.” The tuple in this part lists eight analytic choices: objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, evaluation metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, and granularity.
errors.explanation: The paper previously described the design as crossing seven analytic axes, but the formal specification here defines eight analytic-choice axes. Unless one of these is not intended to count as an axis, the counts conflict.

errors.claim: “Seven discovery objectives, seven ablation operators, four corruption distributions nested within the five operators that read them, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants, five seeds: 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 specifications as pre-registered.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record: “Main numbers: 15,840 pre-registered specifications; 7,561 produced a claim.”
errors.explanation: This part says the pre-registered grid had 18,480 specifications, later reduced to a realised grid of 15,840 after one objective failed. Earlier parts characterized 15,840 itself as the pre-registered specification count, which conflicts with the current distinction between pre-registered and realised specifications.

errors.claim: “At the median circuit size of 200 edges the analytic random line k/(2|E|-k) gives 0.031, so the random baseline already exceeds 3% overlap.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record the graph size as “|E|=32,491.” Using the formula quoted in this part gives 200/(2×32,491−200)=200/64,782≈0.0031, not 0.031. The same paragraph’s 500-edge example, 500/(2|E|-500)≈0.008, is consistent with |E|=32,491.
errors.explanation: The stated value for the 200-edge random Jaccard baseline is off by a factor of 10 and conflicts with the paper’s own graph size and formula.

errors.claim: “The null is degenerate above 1,000 edges, where a uniform draw touches all 156 components and can produce only one claim.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 shows the null has already collapsed at exactly size 1,000: “1,000 | 380 | ... | Null F 0.0000 | Null classes 1”. The caption also says: “at and above 1,000 edges.”
errors.explanation: The text says the degeneration occurs above 1,000 edges, but the table and caption show it occurs at 1,000 edges as well.

errors.claim: “A second script checks that every numeric token in this manuscript matches a value derived from the stored results.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Earlier numeric error: at median size 200, k/(2|E|−k)≈.0031, not stated .031.”
errors.explanation: The manuscript contains at least one numeric token that is arithmetically inconsistent with its own stated quantities, so the claim that every numeric token matches derived values is contradicted by the paper’s earlier text.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Explanation Multipity: Circuit-Level Interpretability”; subtitle/claim: “Evidence Does Not Survive Defensible Analytic Variation.” Author Ajay Pravin Mahale, 12 Aug 2026.

Regulatory framing: EU AI Act/Regulation 2024/1689 high-risk providers technical documentation. Intro quotes Annex IV 2(b), 2(e), Art. 86(1), from consolidated text amended by Reg. 2026/1744. Claim map: φ_overseer keyed by dominant layer band, size class, ranked input segment; φ_affected leads with input segment. Three granularities.

Premise/design: audit value requires analysts to reach compatible conclusions. Mechanistic interpretability/circuit discovery as candidate filing content. Same system/tool, different defensible settings. Specification tuple eight choices: objective o, ablation a, corruption d, metric m, size threshold τ, prompt P, seed r, granularity g; method also says seven discovery axes, with granularity for claim mapping/specs.

Scope/model/task: GPT-2 small, IOI only; no scaling claim. GPT-2 graph factorised Q/K/V inputs, |E|=32,491. Circuits touch 144 attention heads + 12 MLPs=156 components.

Grid: seven objectives, seven ablations, four corruptions nested within five ablations, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompts, five seeds. 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 specs pre-registered; one objective fails all 220 cells due runtime MSE vs integral target, unrepaired. Paper title: “Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability”; subtitle/claim: “Evidence Does Not Survive Defensible Analytic Variation.” Author Ajay Pravin Mahale, date 12 Aug 2026.

Abstract key claims to track:
- Context: EU AI Act requires providers of high-risk systems to file technical documentation describing how system reaches decisions. Mechanistic interpretability, especially circuit discovery, is framed as source of such evidence.
- Research question: whether evidence survives when “two competent analysts, the same system, the same tool, different defensible settings.”
- Design: pre-registered crossed grid of seven analytic axes; every level taken from a published implementation. Each discovered circuit mapped through a deterministic claim map to a structured Annex IV statement.
- Scope/model/task: GPT-2 small and indirect object identification (IOI) task. Study covers one model and one task; scaling untested.

Paper title: “Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability”; subtitle/claim: “Evidence Does Not Survive Defensible Analytic Variation.” Author Ajay Pravin Mahale, date 12 Aug 2026.

Regulatory framing: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 high-risk providers must file technical documentation. Intro quotes Annex IV point 2(b): “general logic of the AI system and of the algorithms”; point 2(e): “assessment of the technical measures needed to facilitate the interpretation of the outputs”; Article 86(1): right to “clear and meaningful explanations…” for certain automated decisions. Quotes from consolidated text as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, CELEX 02024R1689-20260727, read 11 Aug 2026. Claim map has two addressees: φ_overseer built on Annex IV 2(e), 3, and Article 14(4)(c), keyed by dominant layer band, size class, ranked input segment; φ_affected built on Article 86(1), leading with input segment. Three granularities are nested; finer claims refine rather than contradict coarser.

Premise: audit value requires two auditors/analysts to reach compatible/same conclusions. Mechanistic interpretability, especially circuit discovery, is candidate technical content for filings. If same system/tool yields incompatible filings under defensible settings, evidence is not filable. Research question/design: whether evidence survives when “two competent analysts, same system, same tool, different defensible settings.” Earlier paper says pre-registered multiverse/crossed grid over seven analytic axes; Part 4 formalism defines specification tuple with eight analytic choices/axes: objective o, ablation a, corruption distribution d, evaluation metric m, size threshold τ, prompt variant P, seed r, granularity g. Every level of every axis from published implementation, none invented.

Scope/model/task: GPT-2 small and indirect object identification (IOI) task. One model, one task; scaling untested. Section 3 reiterates “nothing at all about scale.” Part 6 says choice is for comparability with non-identifiability/faithfulness literature at this scale; edge count makes size-matched random baseline meaningful.

Grid/method details from Part 6: seven discovery objectives, seven ablation operators, four corruption distributions nested within five operators that read them, four metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants, five seeds. It states 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 specifications as pre-registered; corruption nested because two ablation operators do not read corrupt distribution. Discovery uses edge attribution patching family and integrated edge gradients in Miller et al. library; lineage Conmy et al.; corruptions from Wang et al. One objective fails: all 220 cells raise runtime error from mean squared error against integral target inside library code; failure set exactly that arm by digest; not repaired. Realised grid six objectives, 1,320 cells, 15,840 specifications. Note possible inconsistency with earlier “15,840 pre-registered specifications.”

Pre-registration: analysis plan committed/tagged before confirmatory sweep, both abstracts drafted in advance; deviations append-only with dates and before/after affected result seen. Statistics: no p-values across specs; grid not independent sample. Bootstrap resamples specifications, not pairs, B=10,000, because F and J-bar are U-statistics over dependent pairs. Intervals quantify uncertainty given grid only.

Claim map φ fixed in pre-registration, deterministic code, published, not LLM-generated. Size bins from committed calibration rule, not chosen to maximize flip rate. Table 1 size-binning sensitivity: committed F=0.7316; thresholds ×0.5 F=0.7448; ×0.8 0.7435; ×0.9 0.7394; ×1.1 0.7289; ×1.25 0.7314; ×1.5 0.7308; ×2 0.7232; equal thirds 0.7018; deciles 0.7719; no size term (COARSE) 0.5733. Text says committed bins not maximum; four alternatives higher, including halving thresholds; across factor-four binnings range 0.70–0.77.

Main numbers: earlier notes/parts say 15,840 pre-registered specifications; 7,561 produced a claim. Derived statement flips across 73.2% of specification pairs, 95% CI 0.725–0.738. Part 4 gives observed flip rate 0.7316. Modal claim 41.1% of space. Filability criterion: evidence filable at tolerance α iff π* ≥ 1−α; evidence fails at every plausible tolerance. Claim instability F = 1 − [Σc nc(nc−1)]/[N(N−1)], unbiased Gini–Simpson/probability two draws without replacement differ; modal share π* = maxc nc/N. Within-group F weights pairs equally and reduces to Eq. 2 when G empty. With nine observed claim classes, ceiling F≤0.8889; observed 0.7316 is 82.3% of ceiling.

Part 6 exclusions/table: threshold rule admits no circuit for 8,279 of 15,840 realised specifications, discard rate 52.3%, uneven by metric and disclosed before lock. Surviving pool 52% comprehensiveness vs 25% by design. Table 2: comprehensiveness kept 3,947 discarded 13 rate .003; KL divergence kept 1,467 discarded 2,493 rate .630; logit difference kept 1,270 discarded 2,690 rate .679; sufficiency kept 877 discarded 3,083 rate .779. Kept total 7,561, discarded 8,279.

Formalism/model graph: circuit discovery returns C(s)⊆E. GPT-2 small factorised graph separate Q/K/V inputs, |E|=32,491. Circuits touch 144 attention heads and 12 MLPs=156 total. Circuit instability D=1−|Ci∩Cj|/|Ci∪Cj|; J-bar mean Jaccard similarity over unordered pairs.

Controls: instability survives. Standardising evaluation metric leaves flip 59.4%. Removing circuit size from claim and holding it fixed leaves 27.1% flip, CI 0.255–0.286. At fixed circuit size discovered circuits more stable than size-matched random null: 0.2746 vs 0.4230.

Mechanism/function claims: structurally near-disjoint, median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%; functionally uncorrelated kappa about 0.015/0.0146. Functional instability 0.3972 pooled, 0.4777 smallest circuits. Paper denies filings differ despite same mechanisms or same mechanism described differently. Seeds are evaluation-set variability, not nondeterminism. Non-claims: no better method, not worthless, not random, no scale claim.

errors.claim: “At the median circuit size of 200 edges the analytic random line k/(2|E|-k) gives 0.031, so the random baseline already exceeds 3% overlap.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record the graph size as “|E|=32,491.” Using the formula quoted in this part gives 200/(2×32,491−200)=200/64,782≈0.0031, not 0.031. The same paragraph’s 500-edge example, 500/(2|E|-500)≈0.008, is consistent with |E|=32,491.
errors.explanation: The stated value for the 200-edge random Jaccard baseline is off by a factor of 10 and conflicts with the paper’s own graph size and formula.

errors.claim: “A second script checks that every numeric token in this manuscript matches a value derived from the stored results.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Earlier numeric error: at median size 200, k/(2|E|−k)≈.0031, not stated .031.”
errors.explanation: The manuscript contains at least one numeric token that is arithmetically inconsistent with its own stated quantities, so the claim that every numeric token matches derived values is contradicted by the paper’s earlier text.

grade.reason: Review item 3 points out the analytic formula k/(2|E|-k) with k=200 and |E|=32,491 gives ≈0.0031 (0.31%), not 0.031 (3.1%), which is the planted error.

errors.claim: “A specification is s=(o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g), respectively discovery objective, ablation operator, corruption distribution, evaluation metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, granularity. Every axis level comes from a published implementation...”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record the paper’s related-work/method framing as: “this paper expands single-axis finding into ‘seven-axis regulatory propagation’; ... Need later design to have seven axes.”
errors.explanation: The formalism defines eight specification axes, not seven. Unless one listed element is not intended as an axis, this conflicts with the earlier claim that the design/propagation is seven-axis.

errors.claim: “Across factor-four binnings | 0.70 to 0.77”
errors.evidence: The factor-four threshold binnings shown are all thresholds ×0.5 through ×2, with F values 0.7448, 0.7435, 0.7394, 0.7289, 0.7314, 0.7308, and 0.7232.
errors.explanation: Those rows range from 0.7232 to 0.7448, not 0.70 to 0.77. The 0.70 and 0.77 endpoints appear to come from “equal thirds” and “deciles,” which are not factor-four threshold binnings.

errors.claim: “A6N samples the full edge population with R=1,000 null multiverses; its degeneracy occurs above 1,000 edges.”
errors.evidence: The same section says “A6N collapses at and above 1,000 edges,” and Table 7 shows A6N F = 0.0000 and A6N classes = 1 already at size 1,000, as well as at 2,000, 5,000, and 10,000.
errors.explanation: If degeneracy means collapse to one class / F=0, the table shows it occurs at 1,000 edges, not only above 1,000 edges.

errors.claim: “Thus 2,692 of 7,561 specifications contribute no flips; instability lives entirely below 2,000 edges.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 reports for size 2,000: n = 312, Discovered F = 0.5714, Classes = 3.
errors.explanation: The discovered circuits still show instability at exactly 2,000 edges. Therefore it is not true that instability lives entirely below 2,000 edges, unless ‘below’ is being used imprecisely to include 2,000.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Explanation Multipity: Circuit-Level Interpretability”. Main claim: circuit-derived regulatory evidence fails Y3W across plausible conformity tolerances; competent analysts using same system/tool get incompatible statements; standardisation/size controls do not remove failure; structural and functional disagreement rule out same-mechanism rewording; no scale claim beyond GPT-2 small/IOI. Legal basis: EU AI Act/Reg. 2024/1689 Annex IV 2(b), 2(e), Art 86(1), consolidated text amended by Reg. 2026/1744. Audit commissioning requires two auditors to reach same conclusion. No improved discovery method proposed. Discussion says interpretability evidence not worthless; evidentiary weight measurable cheaply relative to circuit sweep.

Earlier potential inconsistency: related work said “seven-axis regulatory propagation,” but formalism defines 8-axis spec s=(o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g). Q7V graph |E|=32,491; 144 heads + 12 MLPs=156 components. F=unbiased Gini–Simpson pair claim disagreement; F ceiling for 9 classes=.8889.

Y3W protocol: for filed claim c, declare S defensible analytic axes/levels with citations; declare deterministic published code φ (not LLM); compute π*=max_c n_c/N over S and F; evidence passes Y3W at tolerance α iff π*≥1−α; report π*, F, discard rate per axis level, and within-group decomposition of every pooled statistic. Filing unable to state π* is asserted, not audited. Implementability only needs declared space and measured agreement, not adjudication of analytic correctness.

Method: Q7V=GPT-2 small; task Z4K=IOI. Grid: 7 objectives, 7 operators, 4 corruptions nested within 5 operators, 4 metrics, 3 thresholds, 2 prompt variants, 5 seeds. Per objective 22 op/corruption combos; 1,540 discovery cells; 18,480 specs. One objective failed due MSE/integral target runtime error: 220 cells excluded. Realised: 6 objectives, 1,320 cells, 15,840 specs. Discard/no-circuit 8,279 (52.3%); kept 7,561. Metric retention: T9V 3,947 kept/13 discarded; H2W 1,467/2,493; N6C 1,270/2,690; U4J 877/3,083. Bootstrap resamples specifications, B=10,000; no spec-level p-values.

Part 5 G7U committed bins F=.7316; threshold ×0.5 .7448; ×0.8 .7435; ×0.9 .7394; ×1.1 .7289; ×1.25 .7314; ×1.5 .7308; ×2 .7232; equal thirds .7018; deciles .7719; no size term/E7R .5733. Earlier issue: text “Across factor-four binnings: 0.70 to 0.77” conflicts with ×0.5–×2 range .7232–.7448; .7018/.7719 are equal-thirds/deciles. D9P maps Annex IV 2(e), 3 and Art 14(4)(c), ordered by dominant layer band, size class, ranked input segment. L3X maps Art 86(1), input segment/right of decision subject. Granularities E7R/K8Z/V2H constructed so refinement cannot contradict coarser statement. φ deterministic code, not LLM.

Results: decision rules fixed 6 Aug 2026. Table 3: J6D J-bar=.1396 [.1377,.1418], premise holds; X4R F=.7316 [.7247,.7380], confirmed; Q2F decision “not separated from random null,” result separated with disjoint intervals, outcome rejected; Z8N functional gap F-(1-agreement)=.3344 [.3297,.3394], supported. Claim-producing specs 7,561; distinct circuits 3,218; all spec pairs 28,580,580. D quantiles: 1% .196, 25% .788, median .960, 75% .998. Table 6 residual F after standardising: metric .5939; ablation .7014; objective .7018; threshold .7070; corruption .7092; prompt .7232; seed .7307. REML log10 size structural variance: ablation-corruption 78.8%, residual 11.5%, ablation 4.4%, threshold 4.1%, metric .7%.

Table 7 sizes/n/discF/classes/A6NF/A6Nclasses: 10/2492/.4543/3/.7331/6; 20/489/.3380/4/.6622/3; 50/519/.4639/3/.7310/6; 100/242/.5792/3/.6584/3; 200/199/.5122/4/.6366/3; 500/236/.4258/3/.1421/3; 1000/380/.5133/3/0/1; 2000/312/.5714/3/0/1; 5000/625/0/1/0/1; 10000/2067/0/1/0/1.

Bootstrap invalid for tiny conditioning groups; unusable intervals replaced by point estimates/diagnostics.

Reproducibility: public timestamped commit tagged prereg-p1-confirmatory. Archive verification: one environment across all 1,320 confirmatory cells; content-addressed comparison recovers code commit, 22/22 files identical. Analysis needs no GPU. Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929-1958, “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting.” Dropout retains units with probability p during training; standard test uses unthinned net with outgoing weights scaled by p. Hidden p often 0.5; input closer to 1. SGD, momentum, annealed LR, L2; max-norm constrains incoming weights ||w||2≤c. Pretrained weights scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetuning.

Sec.6 datasets Table 1: MNIST 784, 60K/10K. SVHN 3072, 600K/26K. CIFAR-10/100 3072, 60K/10K. ImageNet ILSVRC-2012 dim 65536 (256×256 color), 1.2M/150K — internal arithmetic inconsistency: 256×256 color should be 196608 if color counted as for CIFAR/SVHN. TIMIT 2520, 1.1M frames/58K. Reuters 2000, 200K/200K. Alt Splicing 1014, 2932/733. Sec.6 says dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs no-dropout NNs.

MNIST/Table 2: ReLU 3×1024 no dropout 1.25; dropout+max-norm ReLU 3×1024 1.06, 3×2048 1.04, 2×4096 1.01, 2×8192 0.95; maxout dropout+max-norm 0.94. Pretrained: DBN+finetune 1.18; DBM+finetune 0.96; DBN+dropout 0.92; DBM+dropout 0.79, stated best for permutation-invariant MNIST. MNIST dropout uses p=0.5 hidden, p=0.8 input.

SVHN/Table 3: conv+maxpool 3.95; +dropout FC 3.02; stochastic pooling 2.80; +dropout all layers 2.55; maxout 2.47; human 2.0. CIFAR/Table 4 CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100: conv max pooling 15.60/43.48; stochastic pooling 15.13/42.51; Snoek 14.98/–; dropout FC 14.32/41.26; dropout all layers 12.61/37.20; maxout 11.68/38.57. ImageNet Table 5 ILSVRC-2010: Conv Net+dropout 37.5/17.0 top1/top5. Table 6 ILSVRC-2012: Conv Net+dropout val 40.7/18.2; Avg 5 Conv Nets+dropout val 38.1/16.4, test top-5 16.4; standard features about 26% top-5.

TIMIT/Table 7 phone error: NN 6 layers 23.4; Dropout NN 6 layers 21.8; DBN-pretrained NN 4/6/8 layers 22.7/22.4/20.7; mcRBM-DBN 5 layers 20.5; DBN-pretrained NN 4 + dropout 19.7; 8 + dropout 19.7. Internal inconsistency: text says 8-layer error reduces from 20.5 to 19.7, but table says 8-layer baseline is 20.7; 20.5 is 5-layer mcRBM-DBN. Reuters: best no-dropout NN 31.05%, dropout 29.62%. Alternative Splicing/Table 8 Code Quality bits: NN early stopping 440; Regression PCA 463; SVM PCA 487; NN dropout 567; Bayesian NN 623.

Sec.6.5 regularizers MNIST 784-1024-1024-2048-10 ReLU. Table 9 error %: L2 1.62; L2+L1 near end 1.60; L2+KL sparsity 1.55; Max-norm 1.35; Dropout+L2 1.25; Dropout+Max-norm 1.05.

Sec.7: dropout autoencoder features more meaningful; dropout activations sparser. Dropout-rate experiment fixed 784-2048-2048-2048-10 no input dropout: error flat 0.4≤p≤0.8, rises near p=1; keeping pn constant improves small-p, p≈0.6 best, default 0.5 close. Dataset size: no gain for MNIST subsets 100/500; gain increases then declines. Sec.7.5: MC averaging at test around k=50 matches weight scaling; more samples slightly better but within 1 SD.

Sec.8 Dropout RBMs: RBM joint P(h,v)=1/Z exp(vᵀWh+aᵀh+bᵀv), so a hidden bias, b visible bias. Dropout RBM adds rj~Bernoulli(p), dropped hidden units constrained hj=0. Sec.8.1 internal error: conditionals swap biases, hidden σ(bj+ΣiWijvi), visible σ(ai+ΣjWijhj), conflicting with joint. Dropout RBM features coarser; fewer dead units; activations much sparser without extra sparsity regularizer.

Sec.9 Marginalizing Dropout: linear regression with input dropout marginalized objective ||y-pXw||2+p(1-p)||Γw||2, Γ=(diag XᵀX)^1/2; with w̃=pw gives ||y-Xw̃||2+((1-p)/p)||Γw̃||2. Logistic/deep exact closed form hard. Table 10 Bernoulli vs Gaussian dropout: MNIST 2×1024, 1.08±0.04 vs 0.95±0.04; CIFAR-10 3 conv + 2 FC, 12.6±0.1 vs 12.5±0.1. Gaussian σ=sqrt((1-p)/p).

Sec.10: Gaussian dropout multiplies activations by N(1,σ²); no test scaling since expectation unchanged. Bernoulli can equivalently use multiplier 1/p w.p. p, 0 otherwise at training and no test scaling; variance (1-p)/p. Table 10 suggests Gaussian slightly better.

Heuristics: if n units optimal standard, use at least n/p for dropout; 10–100× standard LR, momentum 0.95–0.99; max-norm c 3–4; hidden p typically 0.5–0.8, real-valued inputs p=0.8.

Appendix B.3 says CIFAR-10/100 have 50K train/10K test, conflicting with earlier Table 1 60K/10K; uses 5K validation then recombine, GCN per color channel + ZCA; same architecture/dropout rates as SVHN except smaller input-layer learning rates, plus translations/flips/rotations. TIMIT appendix: Kaldi log-filter banks; 21-frame windows; no speaker-dependent ops; inputs mean centered/unit variance; p=0.8 input, 0.5 hidden; max-norm c=4 for nonpretrained dropout nets, momentum .95, LR .1 decay; DBN pretraining with CD-1 RBMs, Gaussian RBM variance fixed 1; dropout DBN finetune LR about .01; max-norm did not improve DBN finetuning. Reuters appendix: RCV1 >800K docs/103 classes; subset 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocab, 50 categories, exactly one class/document, equal train/test; dropout improved all tried architectures but less than image/speech due to large data. Alt Splicing appendix: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue types from 27 mouse tissues; target 4 softmax units, each 3 states inc/exc/nc; Code Quality defined from target probabilities, predictions, and average target; two-layer dropout net 1024 each, p=0.5 hidden, p=0.7 input, max-norm with high decaying LRs; 5-fold average as Xiong et al.

Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929-1958, “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting.” Dropout randomly drops units/connections during training, sampling thinned nets; test approximates averaging with unthinned net using W_test=pW. Alternative: scale retained activations by 1/p during training, no test scaling. Hidden p often 0.5; input closer to 1. SGD/minibatches; unused params zero gradient. Momentum, LR annealing, L2 helpful. Dropout+max-norm+large decaying LR+high momentum boosts. Pretrained weights scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetune; smaller finetune LRs.

Datasets Table 1: MNIST 784 60K/10K; SVHN 3072 600K/26K; CIFAR 3072 60K/10K; ImageNet ILSVRC-2012 65536 “256×256 color,” 1.2M/150K (internal arithmetic inconsistency: color 256×256 should be 196608); TIMIT 2520 1.1M/58K; Reuters 2000 200K/200K; Alt Splicing 1014 2932/733. Appendix B.3 says CIFAR-10/100 have 50K training and 10K test each, conflicting with Table 1’s CIFAR 60K training.

Key results: MNIST Table 2 best DBM+dropout finetune 0.79; dropout+max-norm Maxout 0.94; spatial/augmentation can do better. SVHN Table 3: dropout all layers 2.55, maxout 2.47, human 2.0. CIFAR Table 4: CIFAR-10/100 errors dropout all layers 12.61/37.20, maxout 11.68/38.57. ImageNet: ILSVRC-2010 Conv Net+dropout 37.5/17.0 top1/top5; ILSVRC-2012 avg 5 Conv Nets+dropout val 38.1/16.4, test top-5 16.4. TIMIT Table 7 core phone error: NN 23.4; dropout NN 21.8; DBN 4/6/8 22.7/22.4/20.7; mcRBM-DBN 20.5; DBN+dropout 4 and 8 both 19.7. Internal inconsistency: text says 8-layer reduces from 20.5 to 19.7, but table’s 8-layer baseline is 20.7. Reuters: best NN no dropout 31.05%, dropout 29.62%. Alternative Splicing Table 8 Code Quality: NN early stopping 440; Regression PCA 463; SVM PCA 487; NN dropout 567; Bayesian NN 623. Internal inconsistency: paragraph says dropout “outperforms all other methods,” but Bayesian is higher.

Regularizer comparison MNIST Table 9, 784-1024-1024-2048-10 ReLUs: L2 1.62; L2+L1 late 1.60; L2+KL 1.55; Max-norm 1.35; Dropout+L2 1.25; Dropout+Max-norm 1.05. Model combination usually improves ML performance. For large neural nets, averaging outputs of many separately trained nets is prohibitively expensive. Section 2 motivation: analogy to sexual reproduction. Although asexual reproduction might preserve co-adapted gene sets and seem better for individual fitness, sexual reproduction may select for gene “mix-ability,” forcing genes to work well with random partners and reducing complex co-adaptations. Similarly, dropout forces each hidden unit to work with a random sample of other units, making features robust/useful on their own or with few collaborators. It should not simply lead to many copies of hidden units; replica codes are poor for noisy channels. Second analogy: conspiracies—many small conspiracies are more robust than one large one, especially under non-stationary conditions. Complex co-adaptations can fit training data but fail on novel test data more than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

Previous work (Sec. 3): Dropout can be interpreted as regularizing by adding noise to hidden units. Denoising Autoencoders add noise to input units and train to reconstruct noise-free input. Authors say dropout extends this by applying noise effectively to hidden layers, interpreting it as model averaging, and using noise for supervised learning and other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAEs typically work best with 5% noise; with dropout’s test-time weight scaling authors can use higher noise: often optimal to drop 20% of input units and 50% of hidden units. Dropout is stochastic regularization minimizing loss under a noise distribution/expected loss. Deterministic counterparts can be obtained by marginalizing noise; paper will show analytic marginalization in simple cases. Related: van der Maaten et al. deterministic regularizers for exponential-family noise including “blankout noise,” but only input noise/no hidden layers; Wang and Manning speed up dropout by marginalizing dropout noise; Chen et al. marginalization for DAEs. Adversarial dropping work (Globerson & Roweis; Dekel et al.) fixes max units dropped and minimizes loss against adversary, but also lacks hidden units.

Sec. 4 formal model: Network has L hidden layers, l indexes hidden layers; y^(0)=x input. Standard feed-forward: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)), for l=0,…,L−1; f e.g. sigmoid 1/(1+exp(−x)). Dropout feed-forward: for layer l, sample r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p), form thinned output \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l) elementwise, then z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) \tilde y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). r^(l) entries independent, prob p of 1. Applied at each layer; amounts to sampling a sub-network. During learning, derivatives of loss are backpropagated through the sampled sub-network.

Dropout alone improves, but dropout + max-norm + large decaying learning rates + high momentum gives significant boost; max-norm permits huge LR without weights blowing up; dropout noise helps exploration; decaying LR settles.

Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929-1958, “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting.” Abstract claims dropout prevents co-adaptation by randomly dropping units/connections during training, samples exponentially many thinned nets; at test approximate averaging with one unthinned net using smaller weights; improves over other regularization methods on vision, speech, document classification, computational biology, many benchmarks.

Dropout definition: dropping hidden and visible units temporarily removes unit and incoming/outgoing connections. Each unit retained independently with probability p, often 0.5; input retention usually closer to 1. n units => 2^n thinned nets sharing weights; each training case samples new thinned net. Test approximation: use unthinned net, scale trained weights by retention probability p, W_test^(l)=pW^(l), making expected dropout output match test output.

Motivation/related work: dropout adds noise to hidden units, extends denoising/noise regularization ideas; DAEs often use 5% input noise, dropout often drops 20% inputs and 50% hidden. Prior work mostly input noise/no hidden/adversarial dropping.

Sec. 4 formal model: Standard feed-forward y^(0)=x; z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). Dropout: r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then compute next layer using \tilde y. Independent masks; backprop through sampled subnetwork.

Sec. 5.1 training: SGD/minibatches, each case samples thinned net; gradients averaged, unused params get zero. Momentum, annealed LR, L2 useful. Max-norm regularization constrains incoming weight vector ||w||_2≤c; dropout + max-norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives boost.

Sec. 5.2 pretraining: Dropout can finetune pretrained RBM/AE/DBM nets; pretraining unchanged. Pretrained weights scaled up by 1/p so expected output with dropout equals pretraining output. Use smaller finetuning LRs to preserve pretrained info; dropout finetuning can improve.

Sec. 6 datasets/claim: Experiments on MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing. Claim dropout improved generalization on all listed datasets vs non-dropout neural nets. Table 1 dataset overview: MNIST vision 784, 60K train/10K test; SVHN vision 3072, 600K/26K; CIFAR-10/100 vision 3072, 60K/10K; ImageNet ILSVRC-2012 vision listed as 65536 “256×256 color,” 1.2M/150K (internal arithmetic issue: color 256×256 should be 196608, not 65536); TIMIT speech 2520 (120-dim, 21 frames), 1.1M frames/58K frames; Reuters-RCV1 text 2000, 200K/200K; Alternative Splicing genetics 1014, 2932/733.

Sec. 6.1 image datasets: MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet. States models achieving state-of-art on all use dropout.

MNIST Table 2/results: Standard NN logistic 2 layers 800 units 1.60%; Gaussian SVM 1.40%; Dropout NN logistic 3×1024 1.35%; Dropout ReLU 3×1024 1.25%; Dropout+max-norm ReLU 3×1024 1.06%; 3×2048 1.04%; 2×4096 1.01%; 2×8192 0.95%; Dropout+max-norm Maxout Goodfellow 2 layers (5×240) 0.94%; DBN+finetune logistic 500-500-2000 1.18%; DBM+finetune 0.96%; DBN+dropout finetune 0.92%; DBM+dropout finetune 0.79. Text says permutation-invariant non-dropout/no-unsup-pretraining NN about 1.60; dropout reduces to 1.35; ReLU to 1.25; max-norm 1.06; bigger nets better, 2 layers 8192 gets 0.95 with >65M params on 60K data, no early stopping needed. Goodfellow maxout improves to 0.94. All dropout nets use p=0.5 hidden, p=0.8 input. DBM-pretrained dropout nets 0.79, best reported for permutation-invariant setting; better possible using 2-D spatial info and data augmentation. Figure 4 begins: robustness tested with many architectures keeping hyperparameters including p fixed; same architectures with/without dropout show separate clusters; dropout much lower test errors.

Sec. 6.1 image datasets says state-of-art models on all use dropout.

On CIFAR-100 dropout reduces 43.48→37.20, called huge improvement.

Logistic/deep no closed form. Bernoulli vs Gaussian Table 10: MNIST Bernoulli 1.08±0.04, Gaussian 0.95±0.04; CIFAR-10 Bernoulli 12.6±0.1, Gaussian 12.5±0.1. Gaussian dropout multiply activations by N(1,σ²), σ²=(1-p)/p.

Conclusion/current part: dropout improves across object/digit/speech/document/biology; claims methods with dropout achieve state-of-art on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST. Dropout RBMs developed; desirable empirical properties. Drawback: dropout nets typically take 2–3× longer than same architecture standard net because noisy updates/random architectures; trade-off overfitting vs training time; marginalizing dropout can produce expectation regularizer (linear regression modified L2); speeding up future work. Appendix heuristics: because only pn units retained in expectation and co-adaptations inhibited, if n units optimal for standard net, dropout net should have at least n/p units. Dropout nets often need 10–100× standard-net LR and momentum 0.95–0.99. Max-norm c typically 3–4. Hidden p typical 0.5–0.8; real-valued inputs p≈0.8; smaller p needs larger n and can underfit/slows training, large p may insufficiently regularize.

Appendix B details: MNIST 60K train/10K test; hold out 10K train for validation, tune so best validation after 1M updates, then combine validation+train and train 1M. Architectures Fig 4 all combinations 2/3/4 layers and 1024/2048 units = six; all architectures incl Table 2 use hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8, final momentum 0.95, max-norm c=2. Also tried 2/3-layer 4096/8192; 2-layer improved as in Table 2; 3-layer worse unless more dropout but not better than 2-layer. SVHN: approx 600K train/26K test; validation 6000 from standard+extra, RGB zero mean/unit variance; best net 3 conv layers 96/128/256 5×5 stride1, each maxpool 3×3 stride2, then two FC 2048 ReLUs; dropout retain probs input→conv→FC p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5), max-norm c=4, momentum 0.95; did not recombine validation for final training.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines dropout training as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), and says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\). Earlier notes also record that the paper described weight scaling as an approximation to model averaging, not an exact equality.
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)] \ne f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). The equality would hold for the preactivation/weighted input, or for linear activations, but not for every hidden unit’s output under the stated general nonlinear model.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p, matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier §4 equations in notes define unit output as nonlinear: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z), and dropout uses \tilde y=r*y before applying f. Notes also record that the earlier claim that expected hidden-unit output under deletion equals test-time output conflicts with the nonlinear f equations; equality only holds generally for preactivations/linear cases.
errors.explanation: Multiplying incoming weights by 1/p makes the expected preactivation match the pretrained preactivation, but with nonlinear f it does not generally make the expected unit output match the pretrained output.

errors.claim: K9D (ILSVRC-2012) dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image has 256 × 256 × 3 = 196608 input values, not 65536.
errors.explanation: The numeric dimensionality conflicts with the parenthetical description in the same table: 65536 corresponds to 256 × 256 grayscale, not color.

errors.claim: “L8J substitution further reduces error (Goodfellow et al., 2013)” for J3V and W6R.
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports “Conv Net + max pooling + QX2 in all layers” as 12.61 on J3V and 37.20 on W6R, while “Conv Net + L8J” is 11.68 on J3V and 38.57 on W6R.
errors.explanation: L8J reduces J3V error relative to QX2 in all layers, but increases W6R error from 37.20 to 38.57. The prose summary overstates the result if it applies to both collections.

errors.claim: “Prose comparison | 8-layer net | Pre-QX2 error 20.5%”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7” and “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010) | 20.5.”
errors.explanation: The 20.5% pre-dropout error belongs to the 5-layer mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN, not the 8-layer G6W-pretrained NN. The 8-layer baseline in the table is 20.7%, so calling 20.5% the 8-layer net’s pre-QX2 error is inconsistent.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L distribution is defined just above as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), with parameters θ={W,a,b}. Thus a is the hidden-unit bias vector and b is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the stated joint distribution, the hidden conditional should use hidden bias a_j, and the visible conditional should use visible bias b_i. The displayed conditionals swap a and b, and even use b_j for hidden units and a_i for visible units, conflicting with the model definition.

errors.claim: “QX2 methods achieve state of the art on A2F, K9D, W6R and H4Z, with considerable improvement to standard neural nets on other collections.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Vision claim SOTA models on all five vision collections use dropout.” The five vision collections listed earlier were H4Z/MNIST, A2F/SVHN, J3V/CIFAR-10, W6R/CIFAR-100, and K9D/ImageNet.
errors.explanation: The conclusion lists only four datasets as state-of-the-art and appears to put the remaining collections, including J3V/CIFAR-10, in the weaker category of merely improving standard neural nets. This conflicts with the earlier claim that dropout was used in state-of-the-art models on all five vision collections.

errors.claim: “For a task whose optimal standard-net layer has n hidden units, a good QX2 layer should contain at least n/p units. Removing units reduces capacity: only pn units remain in expectation...”
errors.evidence: If the QX2 layer contains “n/p units,” then with retention probability p the expected number retained is p·(n/p)=n, not pn.
errors.explanation: The paragraph defines n as the optimal standard-net layer size and then recommends n/p units for the dropout layer. Under that recommendation, the expected retained units are n; the statement “only pn units remain” is inconsistent unless n is silently redefined as the dropout-layer size.

errors.claim: “Each collection contains 50,000 training and 10,000 test images” for J3V and W6R.
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 1 notes: “CIFAR-10/100 J3V/W6R 3072 table says 60K/10K.”
errors.explanation: This part says the J3V/W6R training set size is 50,000, while the earlier dataset table was recorded as saying 60,000 training examples for the same collections.

final_notes:
Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958. Main claims: dropout/QX2 temporarily removes random units/connections during training, samples exponentially many shared-weight thinned networks, and uses one unthinned weight-scaled net at test to approximate model averaging. Gates r~Bernoulli(p), output r*y; test W_test=pW. Visible/hidden units can be removed. Typical hidden p earlier 0.5; input ~0.8. Dropout approximates equally weighted geometric mean of predictions. Internal issue: paper equates expected hidden-unit output under dropout with reduced-weight output despite nonlinear activations; equality only linear/preactivation.

Learning: boosted by high momentum, large decaying learning rates, max-norm/V9C ||w||<=c. Each minibatch example samples own thinned net; unused params zero gradient. Pretraining: finetune pretrained nets with dropout using smaller LR; before dropout finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p to preserve expected preactivation/input.

§6 results: Table 1 datasets: MNIST/H4Z 784 60K/10K; SVHN/A2F 3072 600K/26K; CIFAR-10/100 J3V/W6R 3072 table says 60K/10K; ImageNet/K9D table says 65536 (256×256 color), 1.2M/150K — internal inconsistency because 256×256 color=196608; TIMIT/N8Q 2520 1.1M/58K; Reuters/M5X 2000 200K/200K; Alt Splicing/Z7P 1014 2932/733. Vision claim SOTA models on all five vision collections use dropout. MNIST Table 2 best DBM+dropout finetuning 0.79. SVHN Table 3 best +L8J 2.47, Human 2.0. CIFAR Table 4: +QX2 all layers 12.61/37.20; +L8J 11.68/38.57. Internal error: prose says L8J further reduces error, but on CIFAR-100/W6R worse than QX2 all layers. ImageNet: convnet+dropout won ILSVRC-2012; Table 6 avg 5 ConvNets+QX2 val 38.1/16.4, test top5 16.4. TIMIT Table 7: NN 23.4; dropout NN 21.8; pretrained 4/6/8 layers 22.7/22.4/20.7; mcRBM-pretrained 5 layers 20.5; pretrained 4/8 layers+dropout both 19.7. Internal error: prose says 8-layer pre-dropout error 20.5%, table gives 20.7. Reuters: best NN without QX2 31.05%, with QX2 29.62%. Alternative Splicing Table 8: NN early stopping 440; Regression PCA 463; SVM PCA 487; NN+QX2 567; Bayesian NN 623 (C4Y bits higher better). §6.5 Table 9 MNIST regularizers: Y5F 1.62; +O3U 1.60; +KL sparsity 1.55; V9C 1.35; QX2+Y5F 1.25; QX2+V9C 1.05.

§7 salient features: autoencoders 256 F3N on MNIST/H4Z: no QX2 features not meaningful/co-adapted; hidden QX2 p=0.5 learns localized edges/strokes/spots. Sparsity: no dropout mean activations ~2.0, dropout ~0.7. Rate: low p underfits fixed architecture; error flat p=0.4–0.8, rises near p=1. Low p=0.1 fixed arch 2.7%, fixed expected retained width 1.7%; best p near 0.6; usual 0.5 close. Dataset size: smallest MNIST subsets no improvement; gain first increases then decreases. X9M vs T6R: sample averaging reaches T6R around k≈50 and then slightly better within one SD; T6R fairly good approximation.

§8 B8T/dropout RBM-like U2L: ordinary U2L joint exp(v^TWh+a^Th+b^Tv)/Z, so a=hidden biases, b=visible biases. B8T adds r_j~Bernoulli(p), h_j=0 if dropped. Internal error §8.1: hidden/visible conditionals swap biases, using sigma(b_j+Σ_i W_ij v_i) for hidden and sigma(a_i+Σ_j W_ij h_j) for visible, contradicting joint. Learning CD-1 sampling r per case. B8T features coarser than U2L, fewer dead units; sparser representations.

§9 Marginalizing QX2: linear regression input retention p marginalized objective E_R||y-(R*X)w||² = ||y-pXw||²+p(1-p)||Γw||², Γ=(diag X^TX)^1/2. With w~=pw equivalent ||y-Xw~||²+((1-p)/p)||Γw~||². Logistic/deep nets: closed form hard; Wang & Manning approximate logistic marginalization; assumptions weaken with layers.

§10 Gaussian noise: Bernoulli/P7V vs Gaussian/D4K inverted representation. Table 10: H4Z P7V 1.08±0.04, D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V P7V 12.6±0.1, D4K 12.5±0.1; 10 seeds. P7V p: H4Z hidden 0.5 input 0.8; J3V (0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5). D4K σ=sqrt((1-p)/p). Inverted dropout multiplier 1/p w.p. p else 0, mean 1 variance (1-p)/p, no test scaling; equivalent to standard with rescaled LR/init.

§11 Conclusion: says QX2 SOTA on A2F, K9D, W6R, H4Z and improves standard nets on other collections; internal issue vs earlier vision summary claiming SOTA/dropout on all five incl J3V. Training typically 2–3× standard.

Appendix A: A.1 says for optimal standard-net layer n, QX2 layer at least n/p units; internal issue same paragraph says “only pn units remain” though n/p width retains n expected. A.2 QX2 LR 10–100× standard; momentum 0.95–0.99. A.3 V9C c typical 3–4. A.4 p=1 no dropout; hidden typical 0.5–0.8; real inputs incl images/speech 0.8; input optimum closer to 1 than 0.5.

Appendix B: B.1 H4Z: 10K validation held out; endpoint 1M updates; sweep 2/3/4 layers, widths 1024/2048; hidden p=0.5 input p=0.8; momentum 0.95; V9C c=2; regularizer architecture 784-1024-1024-2048-10; data-size sets 100,500,1K,5K,10K,50K; fixed-width rate arch 784-2048-2048-2048-10 no input corruption; fixed expected widths pn=256 first two hidden, pn=512 last. Additional 2-layer nets improve; 3-layer slightly worse. X9M samples k thinned nets per test case, averages predictions, k→∞ true model average. B.2 A2F: validation 6000 = standard 400/class + additional 200/class; conv filters 96/128/256, 5×5, stride 1, maxpool 3×3 stride2; two FC 2048; F3N; p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5), c=4, momentum 0.95. B.3 J3V/W6R: says each has 50K training/10K test, conflicting with Table 1 notes 60K/10K; 5K validation, then combined train/val; preprocessing global contrast norm per image/color channel then ZCA; architecture/retention match A2F, input LR smaller. B.4 N8Q: 680 speakers, 8 dialects, 10 sentences; Kaldi log-filter banks, monophone forced alignment/frame labels; consecutive windows predict central frame, no speaker-dependent ops, mean-centered unit-variance inputs. Settings: 21 consecutive frames/window; input p=0.8, hidden p=0.5; V9C c=4; momentum 0.95; high LR 0.1 decays as ε0(1+t/T)^-1; G6W/U2L pretraining CD-1 with Gaussian-U2L input variance fixed to 1; best QX2 G6W-finetuning LR ~0.01; adding V9C during G6W finetuning no improvement. B.5 M5X: full Reuters corpus >800K docs, 103 tree classes; used subset 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocab, 50 disjoint categories, exactly one per doc; equal train/test splits giving >200K training examples. B.6 Z7P: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, four tissue types from 27 mouse tissues; four target softmax units, one per tissue, states inc/exc/nc; C4Y formula sums target p log(q/bar p), bar p averaged over i,t. Settings: QX2 hidden units on 1000s scale vs Bayesian network few tens; trained QX2 two layers of 1024; hidden p=0.5, input p=0.7; V9C and high decaying LRs; results averaged over same 5 folds as Xiong et al. (2011).

Introduction details: With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is presented as best regularization for a fixed-sized model. Dropout is proposed as a cheaper approximation to an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models’ predictions. An n-unit network represents 2^n possible thinned networks while retaining only O(n^2) or fewer parameters via weight sharing. For every presentation of each training case a new thinned member is sampled/trained, so each particular member is trained rarely if ever. Multilayer nonlinear hidden representations can learn complicated relationships but limited-data sampling noise can create relationships present in train but absent in genuine test data, even from same distribution. Prior/standard responses: early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 and L2 penalties; these constrain parameters rather than averaging every parameter setting.

Model combination: usually improves performance, but training/output averaging of many large nets is expensive; diversity requires different architectures or data, hyperparameters are architecture-specific/difficult, training is computationally costly, data requirements may preclude subset training, and inference may be infeasible for rapid response. Practical dropout inference rule is weight scaling: use one unthinned network rather than explicitly evaluating exponentially many members. More expensive alternative: Monte-Carlo model averaging of sampled thinned members’ predictions. Claim: weight scaling/dropout gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularization methods across varied classification problems. Dropout extends beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models including Boltzmann Machines; Restricted Boltzmann Machines can have Dropout RBM form with shared parameters.

§2 Motivation: Analogy to sexual reproduction. Asexual reproduction preserves successful co-adapted gene sets and might seem superior for individual-fitness optimization; sexual recombination breaks complex co-adaptations, yet advanced organisms evolved sexually. Livnat et al. account: long-run selection may favor gene “mix-ability” over individual fitness; genes working with random partners are robust; lack of guaranteed partner sets encourages individually useful/simple collaborations; reducing complex co-adaptations helps useful new genes spread. Dropout-trained hidden units similarly face random partners, encouraging independently useful robust features rather than reliance on other hidden units to fix mistakes, though units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating each hidden unit many times is poor robustness, analogous to replica codes for noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: ten five-person conspiracies likely more robust than one fifty-person conspiracy; large complex co-adaptations can work under unchanged/rehearsed training conditions but fail under non-stationary/novel test conditions more easily than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

An n-unit net represents 2^n thinned nets but only O(n^2) or fewer parameters. Each training case presentation samples/trains a new thinned network, so any particular member rarely/never trained. Hidden representations can overfit sampling noise. Prior regularizers include early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1/L2; they constrain parameters rather than average settings.

Model combination: improves performance but many large nets are expensive; diversity needs different architectures/data; hyperparameters hard; training/inference costly; data may preclude subsets. Practical dropout inference: weight scaling in one unthinned net instead of evaluating exponentially many members. Alternative: Monte Carlo model averaging of sampled thinned nets. Claim: dropout/weight scaling gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied classification problems. Dropout extends beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models including RBMs/Dropout RBM.

Figure 1: standard net with two hidden layers vs dropout thinned net with crossed-out units and removed incoming/outgoing connections.

§2 Motivation: Analogy to sexual reproduction. Asexual reproduction preserves successful co-adapted gene sets and might seem superior for individual-fitness optimization; sexual recombination breaks complex co-adaptations, yet advanced organisms evolved sexually. Livnat et al. account: long-run selection may favor gene “mix-ability” over individual fitness; genes working with random partners are robust; lack of guaranteed partner sets encourages individually useful/simple collaborations; reducing complex co-adaptations helps useful new genes spread. Dropout-trained hidden units similarly face random partners, encouraging independently useful robust features rather than reliance on other hidden units to fix mistakes, though units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating each hidden unit many times is poor robustness, analogous to replica codes for noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: ten five-person conspiracies likely more robust than one fifty-person conspiracy; large complex co-adaptations can work under unchanged/rehearsed training conditions but fail under non-stationary/novel test conditions more easily than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

§3 Related work: Dropout interpreted as adding noise to hidden-unit states, extending denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010), which used input corruption and clean-input reconstruction. Claimed extensions over DAEs: effective hidden-layer corruption, model-averaging interpretation, supervised and unsupervised use, applicability to other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann machines. Test-time weight scaling permits higher noise than usually best for DAEs. Table: typical best DAE noise 5%; dropout often optimal input-unit removal 20%; dropout often optimal hidden-unit removal 50%. Stochastic minimization under noise distribution minimizes expected loss; adversarial alternatives (Globerson & Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010) let adversary choose removals subject to fixed max number rather than probability distribution and have no hidden units. Analytically marginalizing dropout gives deterministic regularizers in simple cases. Exponential-family input-noise regularizers including dropout/“blankout noise” studied by van der Maaten et al. (2013), limited to models without hidden layers. Chen et al. (2012) examined marginalization for denoising autoencoders; Wang & Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate dropout.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines dropout training as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), and says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\). Earlier notes also record that the paper described weight scaling as an approximation to model averaging, not an exact equality.
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)] \ne f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). The equality would hold for the preactivation/weighted input, or for linear activations, but not for every hidden unit’s output under the stated general nonlinear model.

§2 Motivation: Sexual reproduction analogy. Random partners discourage complex co-adaptations and encourage robust, individually useful hidden units. Replication is poor robustness; multiple simple co-adaptations generalize better than large fragile ones.

Apply at every layer to sample subnetwork; backprop derivatives through that subnetwork. Hidden and visible/input units can both be removed. At inference no units removed and W_test^(l)=p W^(l); Figure 2 says training unit present with probability p and weights w, testing unit always present with outgoing weights pw; Figure 3 contrasts standard vs gated/dropout computation. Opening sentence of this part claimed expected hidden-unit output under training deletion distribution equals test-time output under reduced weights, but this conflicts with nonlinear f equations and with earlier approximation wording; equality only applies to preactivation/linear case generally. Retention choices independent with common p in simplest construction; validation can choose p; usual default close to optimal across many tasks/networks; optimal input retention generally nearer complete retention.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p, matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier §4 equations in notes define unit output as nonlinear: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z), and dropout uses \tilde y=r*y before applying f. Notes also record that the earlier claim that expected hidden-unit output under deletion equals test-time output conflicts with the nonlinear f equations; equality only holds generally for preactivations/linear cases.
errors.explanation: Multiplying incoming weights by 1/p makes the expected preactivation match the pretrained preactivation, but with nonlinear f it does not generally make the expected unit output match the pretrained output.

§5 Learning Dropout Nets: Dropout alone gives significant gains; combining with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and incoming-weight constraint/max-norm regularization gives further boost. errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L distribution is defined just above as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), with parameters θ={W,a,b}. Thus a is the hidden-unit bias vector and b is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the stated joint distribution, the hidden conditional should use hidden bias a_j, and the visible conditional should use visible bias b_i. The displayed conditionals swap a and b, and even use b_j for hidden units and a_i for visible units, conflicting with the model definition.

Low p=0.1 fixed arch 2.7%, fixed expected retained width 1.7%; best p near 0.6; usual 0.5 close. Dataset size: smallest MNIST subsets no improvement; gain first increases then decreases. X9M vs T6R: sample averaging reaches T6R around k≈50 and then slightly better within one SD; T6R fairly good approximation.

§8 B8T/dropout RBM-like U2L: ordinary U2L joint exp(v^TWh+a^Th+b^Tv)/Z, so a=hidden biases, b=visible biases. B8T adds r_j~Bernoulli(p), enforces h_j=0 if dropped; conditional on r ordinary U2L with removed hidden units. Internal error §8.1: hidden/visible conditionals swap biases, using sigma(b_j+Σ_i W_ij v_i) for hidden and sigma(a_i+Σ_j W_ij h_j) for visible, contradicting joint. Learning uses CD-1 sampling r per case. B8T features coarser than U2L, fewer dead units; sparser representations.

§9 Marginalizing QX2: linear regression input retention p marginalized objective E_R||y-(R*X)w||² = ||y-pXw||²+p(1-p)||Γw||², Γ=(diag X^TX)^1/2. With w~=pw equivalent ||y-Xw~||²+((1-p)/p)||Γw~||². Logistic/deep nets: closed form hard; Wang & Manning approximate logistic marginalization; assumptions weaken with layers.

§10 Multiplicative Gaussian Noise: compares Bernoulli dropout/P7V with Gaussian dropout/D4K matched on mean/variance using inverted representation. Table 10 classification error: H4Z 2 layers 1024 each P7V 1.08±0.04, D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V 3 conv+2 FC P7V 12.6±0.1, D4K 12.5±0.1; 10 seeds. P7V p: H4Z hidden 0.5 input 0.8; J3V layers (0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5). D4K σ=sqrt((1-p)/p). Gaussian multiplier r'~N(1,σ²); for σ=1 equivalent h_i+h_i r, r~N(0,1). §11 Conclusion: says large-model construction repeatedly samples/trains smaller submodels; U2L fits and B8T has desirable empirical properties. Says training typically 2–3× as long as standard network; noise/stochastic architectures major cause; gradients not those of final inference architecture; stronger QX2 trades more training time for less overfitting. Noise marginalization gives expectation-equivalent regularizer; linear regression gives modified Y5F; more complicated equivalents unclear; accelerating QX2 future work.

errors.claim: “For a task whose optimal standard-net layer has n hidden units, a good QX2 layer should contain at least n/p units. Removing units reduces capacity: only pn units remain in expectation...”
errors.evidence: If the QX2 layer contains “n/p units,” then with retention probability p the expected number retained is p·(n/p)=n, not pn.
errors.explanation: The paragraph defines n as the optimal standard-net layer size and then recommends n/p units for the dropout layer. errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines nonlinear activations as admissible, including the sigmoid, and defines training output as y_i^(l+1)=f(w_i^(l+1) \tilde y^l + b_i^(l+1)) with Bernoulli gates, while test-time uses W_test^(l)=p W^(l).
errors.explanation: With a nonlinear f such as the sigmoid, E[f(w(r*y)+b)] is generally not equal to f(p w y+b). The formulas support equality of expected preactivation/input contribution under scaling, not equality of expected hidden-unit output.

errors.claim: K9D (ILSVRC-2012) dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: The same table lists “A2F” and “J3V/W6R” as “3072 (32 × 32 color),” which counts three color channels: 32 × 32 × 3 = 3072. But 256 × 256 color would be 256 × 256 × 3 = 196608, not 65536.
errors.explanation: Within the table, color-image dimensionality is counted using RGB channels for 32×32 images, so the K9D entry is inconsistent with that convention and with its own “color” description.

errors.claim: “QX2 in fully connected layers improves it, extension to every layer improves it further, and L8J substitution further reduces error …”
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports for W6R: “Conv Net + max pooling + QX2 in all layers” = 37.20, but “Conv Net + L8J” = 38.57.
errors.explanation: If the statement is meant to summarize both J3V and W6R, L8J does not further reduce W6R error relative to dropout in all layers; it is worse. It only further reduces the J3V error, from 12.61 to 11.68.

errors.claim: Prose comparison: “8-layer net” pre-QX2 error = 20.5%.
errors.location: this part, N8Q prose comparison table
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” as 20.7%, while 20.5% belongs to “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010).”
errors.explanation: The stated pre-dropout error for the 8-layer net uses the value of a different 5-layer mcRBM-G6W model, not the 8-layer G6W-pretrained model shown in the table.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: Earlier in the same model definition, the joint distribution is defined as exp( v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v ), so a is the hidden-unit bias vector and b is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: The conditional distributions swap the bias symbols: hidden conditional should use the hidden bias a_j, and visible conditional should use the visible bias b_i. As written, b_j is indexed over hidden units and a_i over visible units, conflicting with the joint distribution’s definitions.

errors.claim: "Each collection contains 50,000 training and 10,000 test images" for J3V and W6R.
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from Table 1: "Datasets: ... CIFAR 3072 color 60K/10K".
errors.explanation: The earlier dataset summary recorded CIFAR as having 60K training examples and 10K test examples, but Appendix B.3 says CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 each have 50K training and 10K test images.

final_notes:
Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958, “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting.” Aliases: QX2/P7V=dropout/Bernoulli dropout, D4K=Gaussian dropout, V9C=max-norm, E5Q=DBM, G6W=DBN, F3N=ReLUs, L8J=maxout, H4Z=MNIST, N8Q=TIMIT, J3V=CIFAR-10, W6R=CIFAR-100, A2F=SVHN, K9D=ImageNet, M5X=Reuters, Z7P=Alternative Splicing, B8T=dropout RBM, T6R=standard test-time weight scaling, X9M=MC averaging.

Core: Dropout randomly removes units/connections during training, samples shared-parameter thinned nets; test usually uses unthinned net with scaled weights pW approximating averaging/geometric mean; MC averaging alternative. Internal issue: text claimed expected hidden-unit output under deletion equals test-time output under reduced weights, but nonlinear f only preserves expected preactivation/input contribution generally. Training masks r~Bernoulli(p); unused params get zero gradient. Combines with high momentum, large decaying LR, max-norm. Max-norm projects incoming hidden-unit vector ||w||2<=c. For pretrained nets before dropout finetuning, weights multiplied by 1/p so expected output under random removal matches pretraining output.

§6/Table 1: Claims dropout improves generalization over non-dropout NNs on every tested dataset. Datasets recorded: MNIST 784 60K/10K; SVHN 3072 color 600K/26K; CIFAR 3072 color 60K/10K; ImageNet 65536 (256×256 color) 1.2M/150K; TIMIT 2520 1.1M/58K; Reuters 2000 200K/200K; Alt Splicing 1014 2932/733. Internal issues: ImageNet dimension/color inconsistent with RGB counting; Appendix B.3 says CIFAR-10/100 each contain 50K training and 10K test images, conflicting with earlier CIFAR 60K/10K if that was train/test.

Results: MNIST Table 2 errors: standard NN 1.60, dropout logistic 1.35, dropout ReLU 1.25, dropout+maxnorm ReLU 0.95, dropout+maxnorm maxout 0.94, DBN+dropout 0.92, DBM+dropout 0.79. SVHN Table 3: conv+dropout FC 3.02, +dropout all layers 2.55, conv+maxout 2.47, human 2.0. CIFAR Table 4: dropout FC 14.32/41.26, dropout all layers 12.61/37.20, maxout 11.68/38.57. Internal issue: prose says maxout further reduces error on both CIFAR datasets, but CIFAR-100 maxout 38.57 worse than dropout-all-layers 37.20. ImageNet: ILSVRC-2010 conv+dropout 37.5/17.0 vs baselines 47.1/28.2 and 45.7/25.7. ILSVRC-2012 avg 5 conv+dropout val 38.1/16.4, test top5 16.4; standard ~26% top5. TIMIT Table 7 phone errors: NN 6-layer 23.4; dropout NN 6-layer 21.8; DBN-pretrained 4/6/8-layer 22.7/22.4/20.7; mcRBM-DBN 5-layer 20.5; DBN-pretrained 4-layer+dropout 19.7; 8-layer+dropout 19.7. Internal issue: prose says 8-layer pre-dropout error 20.5%, but table gives 20.7; 20.5 is 5-layer mcRBM-DBN. Reuters: best NN error 31.05 without dropout, 29.62 with. Alt Splicing Table 8 bits higher better: NN early stopping 440; regression PCA 463; SVM PCA 487; NN+dropout 567; Bayesian NN 623. §6.5 MNIST regularizers Table 9 error: Y5F 1.62; Y5F+O3U 1.60; Y5F+KL 1.55; max-norm 1.35; dropout+Y5F 1.25; dropout+max-norm 1.05.

§7: Dropout autoencoders on MNIST learn localized meaningful features, induce sparsity; best retention p≈0.5–0.6; MC averaging ~weight-scaling by k=50, slightly better within 1 SD.

§8 dropout RBM: mixture of exponentially many hidden-subset RBMs. Joint exp(v^TWh+a^T h+b^T v), so a hidden bias, b visible bias. Internal issue: conditional equations swap biases. MNIST features coarser, fewer dead units, much sparser activations.

§9: Linear regression marginalization objective gives modified weight decay ((1-p)/p)||Γw~||². Logistic/deep exact marginalization hard.

§10: Gaussian dropout may work as well/slightly better than Bernoulli with matched mean/variance. Table 10: MNIST P7V 1.08±0.04 vs D4K 0.95±0.04; CIFAR-10 P7V 12.6±0.1 vs D4K 12.5±0.1. Bernoulli settings: MNIST hidden .5 input .8; CIFAR p=(.9,.75,.75,.5,.5,.5). Gaussian σ=sqrt((1-p)/p), no test-time scaling in inverted representation.

§11/Appendix A: Claims dropout achieves SOTA on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST; training typically 2–3× standard net. Practical guide: tune extensively; dropout layer at least n/p units if standard optimal has n; LR 10–100× standard, momentum 0.95–0.99, max-norm c 3–4, hidden p 0.5–0.8 default 0.5, real inputs/images/speech p≈0.8.

Appendix B: B.1 MNIST: 10K validation held out, hyperparams by validation, then train+validation combined to same 1M update endpoint. Sweep depths 2/3/4, widths 1024/2048, hidden p=.5 input p=.8, momentum .95, max-norm c=2. B.2 SVHN: training count approximate; validation 6000 = 400/class standard + 200/class additional; RGB normalized; no benefit contrast norm/ZCA; arch 3 conv 96/128/256 5×5, maxpool, two FC 2048, p=(.9,.75,.75,.5,.5,.5), max-norm c=4. B.3 CIFAR: 50K train/10K test; validation 5K; GCN+ZCA; arch/retention match SVHN. B.4 TIMIT: 680 speakers/8 dialects; 21-frame windows, input p=.8, hidden p=.5, max-norm c=4, momentum .95, high LR .1 decay, DBN pretrain RBMs CD-1, Gaussian RBM input variance fixed 1, best dropout DBN finetune LR ~.01; max-norm during DBN finetuning no improvement. B.5 Reuters: full >800K docs/103 tree classes; used subset 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocab, 50 disjoint categories, single label, equal train/test >200K train. B.6 Alt Splicing: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue types; 4 target softmaxes/one per tissue, states inc/exc/nc; metric C4Y sums p log(q/bar p), higher better; dropout net two layers 1024, hidden p=.5 input p=.7, max-norm+high decaying LR, 5 folds as Xiong et al.

§2 Motivation: Uses analogy to sexual reproduction. Asexual reproduction preserves successful co-adapted gene sets, so might seem better for individual-fitness optimization; sexual recombination breaks complex co-adaptations, yet most advanced organisms evolved sexually. Livnat et al. (2010) account: long-run selection may prioritize gene mix-ability/robustness with random partner gene sets over individual fitness; discourages large fragile co-adaptations and helps useful genes spread. Dropout/QX2 similarly makes hidden units work with randomly selected partners, favoring independently useful robust features rather than reliance on other hidden units to fix mistakes; units in same layer still learn different functions. Replicating each hidden unit many times is poor robustness solution, analogous to replica codes for noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: ten five-person conspiracies more likely to cause havoc than one fifty-person conspiracy; stationary/rehearsed conditions let large conspiracies work, but nonstationarity favors smaller conspiracies. Complex co-adaptations can fit training data yet fail on novel test data more readily than multiple simpler co-adaptations achieving same result.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines nonlinear activations as admissible, including the sigmoid, and defines training output as y_i^(l+1)=f(w_i^(l+1) \tilde y^l + b_i^(l+1)) with Bernoulli gates, while test-time uses W_test^(l)=p W^(l).
errors.explanation: With a nonlinear f such as the sigmoid, E[f(w(r*y)+b)] is generally not equal to f(p w y+b). The formulas support equality of expected preactivation/input contribution under scaling, not equality of expected hidden-unit output.

§5 Learning Dropout/QX2 Nets. §5.1 Backprop: Dropout alone gives significant gains; combining with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and incoming-weight constraint/max-norm regularization gives further boost. SGD differs from standard training only by per-case sampled thinned net: each mini-batch case forward/backprops through its own sampled net; gradients averaged; unused parameter gets zero contribution from that case. Momentum, annealed learning rates, and Y5F remain useful. Max-norm constraint for incoming hidden-unit weight vector w: ||w||_2 <= c; if w leaves radius-c ball, project back to surface. c tuned on validation.

§5.2 Unsupervised Pretraining: Smaller finetuning learning rates preserve useful pretrained info and improve final generalization relative to finetuning without dropout; learning rates comparable to best random-init rates erased pretrained info in initial experiments. Pretraining itself unchanged. Before dropout finetuning, pretrained weights multiplied by 1/p so expected random-removal output matches pretraining output. Aliases: QX2=dropout, V9C=max-norm regularization/incoming-weight constraint, E5Q=Deep Boltzmann Machines, U2L=stacked? likely RBMs, G6W=DBN, F3N=ReLUs, L8J=maxout. H4Z=MNIST, N8Q=TIMIT, J3V=CIFAR-10, W6R=CIFAR-100, A2F=SVHN, K9D=ImageNet/ILSVRC-2012, M5X=Reuters-RCV1, Z7P=Alternative Splicing.

Abstract/Intro: Dropout temporarily removes randomly selected units/connections during training, inhibits co-adaptation, samples exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. Test-time uses one unthinned network with reduced/scaled weights to approximate averaged predictions of thinned nets; alternative Monte Carlo averaging. Claims large reductions in overfitting and improved supervised vision, speech, document classification, computational biology; state-of-art on many benchmarks. Dropout approximates equally weighted geometric mean of predictions of exponentially many learned parameter-sharing models. n-unit network represents 2^n thinned networks with O(n^2) or fewer params; newly sampled thinned net per presentation, so any specific thinned net trained rarely/never. Existing regularizers constrain params; dropout averages over parameter settings. Extends to graphical models incl. Boltzmann Machines/RBMs.

§2 Motivation: Sexual reproduction analogy; dropout forces hidden units to work with random partners, robust independently useful features; same-layer units can still learn different functions. Replicating hidden units is poor robustness solution. Conspiracy analogy: small conspiracies generalize better than one large one.

§3 Related Work: Noise in hidden-unit states as regularizer, extending denoising autoencoders. Dropout contributions vs DAEs: hidden-layer corruption, model-averaging interpretation, supervised/unsupervised use, neuron-based architectures incl. Boltzmann Machines. Weight scaling/model averaging allows higher noise than usually best for DAEs. Table: DAE typical best noise 5%; dropout often optimal input-unit removal 20%; hidden-unit removal 50%. Stochastic minimization under noise distribution minimizes expected loss. Analytical/marginalized dropout in simple cases; prior blankout-noise work limited to no hidden layers.

§4 Model Description: Feed-forward net: y^(0)=x; standard z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Dropout: r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), independent, ~y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l); z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)~y^l+b_i^(l+1); y_i=f(z_i). Apply at every layer to sample subnetwork; backprop through subnetwork; hidden and visible units can be removed. Inference: no units removed and W_test^(l)=p W^(l). Fig. 2: train unit present with prob p, outgoing weights w; test unit always present, outgoing weights pw. Internal issue already noted: opening claim says expected hidden-unit output under training deletion equals actual test-time output under reduced weights, but formulas with nonlinear f only make expected preactivation/input contribution equal, not output generally.

§5 Learning Dropout/QX2 Nets. §5.1 Backprop: Dropout alone gives significant gains; combining with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and incoming-weight constraint/max-norm regularization gives further boost. Max-norm also usually improves deep-net SGD without dropout; previously used in collaborative filtering. Optimization account: max-norm permits huge learning rates inside fixed-radius weight ball without explosion; dropout noise explores difficult regions; decaying rates reduce exploratory steps toward minimum. SGD differs from standard training only by per-case sampled thinned net: each mini-batch case forward/backprops through its own sampled net; gradients averaged; unused parameter gets zero contribution from that case. Momentum, annealed learning rates, and Y5F remain useful. Max-norm: incoming hidden-unit weight vector ||w||_2 <= c; project to radius-c ball if exceeded; c tuned on validation.

§5.2 Unsupervised Pretraining: Smaller finetuning learning rates preserve pretrained info and improve final generalization vs finetuning without dropout; learning rates comparable to best random-init rates erased pretrained info in initial experiments. Pretraining unchanged. Before dropout finetuning, pretrained weights multiplied by 1/p so expected random-removal output matches pretraining output. Unlabeled data via pretraining can significantly improve over random init in some cases, with pretraining followed by backprop finetuning using stacked U2L, autoencoders, or E5Q; all admit this finetuning procedure.

§6 Experimental Results: Claims generalization improved over non-dropout NNs on every tested data set; domains: object classification, digits, speech, documents, computational biology. Table 1 dataset overview: H4Z 784 60K/10K; A2F 3072 color 600K/26K; J3V/W6R 3072 color 60K/10K; K9D 65536 (256×256 color) 1.2M/150K; N8Q 2520 1.1M frames/58K; M5X 2000 200K/200K; Z7P 1014 2932/733. Internal issue found: K9D dimension/color inconsistent with table’s RGB counting.

§6.1 Image Data: Claims state of art on all five vision collections use dropout.
§6.1.1 H4Z/MNIST: Dropout improves over best permutation-invariant NNs without dropout/pretraining; ReLUs improve further; max-norm further; larger nets help; maxout helps. Dropout prevents overfitting in largest network without early stopping. Pretrained nets improve too: DBN/G6W and DBM/E5Q, with E5Q+dropout best reported permutation-invariant result. Spatial info and distortions can do better on other collections. Table 2 errors: standard NN logistic 2×800 1.60; SVM Gaussian 1.40; dropout logistic 3×1024 1.35; dropout ReLU 1.25; +maxnorm ReLU 3×1024 1.06; 3×2048 1.04; 2×4096 1.01; 2×8192 0.95; dropout+maxnorm maxout 2 layers (5×240) 0.94; DBN finetune 1.18; DBM finetune 0.96; DBN+dropout finetune 0.92; DBM+dropout finetune 0.79. Fig 4: fixed hyperparameters including retention probability across architectures; dropout/non-dropout curves form separated clusters; improvement large without architecture-specific tuning.
§6.1.2 A2F/SVHN opening: Conv nets best; adding dropout to fully connected layers improves, adding to convolutional layers improves further, maxout additional gains. Despite few conv parameters suggesting little overfit, lower-layer corruption supplies noisy inputs preventing higher FC layers overfitting.
