§7 salient features: In 256-ReLU single-hidden-layer MNIST autoencoders with similar reconstruction errors, no-dropout first-layer features are not meaningful/co-adapted; dropout p=0.5 features detect localized edges, strokes, spots. Dropout breaks co-adaptations by making specific partners unreliable. Sparsity: dropout induces sparse hidden activations without sparsity regularizer. In test mini-batch histograms, no-dropout mean activations mostly near 2.0 with large off-zero activation mass and many highly active units; dropout means around 0.7, sharp zero peak, very few highly active units. Retention-rate experiment: fixed architecture underfits at low p; test error decreases, flat for 0.4≤p≤0.8, rises near p=1. At p=0.1, fixed architecture error 2.7%, fixed expected retained width pn error 1.7%; best p close to 0.6, default 0.5 close to optimal. Dataset-size experiment on MNIST subsets: two smallest training sizes show no dropout improvement; gain rises then falls as data increase, with sweet spot where enough data prevents noisy memorization but not enough to eliminate overfitting. Test-time averaging comparison: MC/sample averaging becomes as good as weight-scaling around k=50 and slightly better within 1 SD; weight scaling is described as fairly good approximation to true model average.

errors.evidence: Earlier in the same model definition, the joint distribution is defined as exp( v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v ), so a is the hidden-unit bias vector and b is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: The conditional distributions swap the bias symbols: hidden conditional should use the hidden bias a_j, and visible conditional should use the visible bias b_i. As written, b_j is indexed over hidden units and a_i over visible units, conflicting with the joint distribution’s definitions.

DAEs usually best with 5% noise; authors say dropout often optimal dropping 20% inputs and 50% hidden due to test-time scaling. Later will show simple cases where marginalizing dropout gives deterministic regularizers. Related marginalization/noise/adversarial dropping works mostly input/no hidden or adversarial fixed dropped units.

Sec.5 training: Dropout nets trained by SGD like standard nets. For each training case in a mini-batch, sample a thinned network; forward/backprop only through it. Max-norm constrains incoming weights at each hidden unit to ||w||2≤c; if exceeds, project onto ball radius c. grade.reason: The reviewer shows the paper itself lists 31.05% and 29.62%, whose relative reduction is ≈4.6%, contradicting the claimed 14.3% reduction.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines dropout training as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), and says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\). Earlier notes also record that the paper described weight scaling as an approximation to model averaging, not an exact equality.
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)] \ne f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). The equality would hold for the preactivation/weighted input, or for linear activations, but not for every hidden unit’s output under the stated general nonlinear model.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p, matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier §4 equations in notes define unit output as nonlinear: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z), and dropout uses \tilde y=r*y before applying f. Notes also record that the earlier claim that expected hidden-unit output under deletion equals test-time output conflicts with the nonlinear f equations; equality only holds generally for preactivations/linear cases.
errors.explanation: Multiplying incoming weights by 1/p makes the expected preactivation match the pretrained preactivation, but with nonlinear f it does not generally make the expected unit output match the pretrained output.

errors.claim: K9D (ILSVRC-2012) dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image has 256 × 256 × 3 = 196608 input values, not 65536.
errors.explanation: The numeric dimensionality conflicts with the parenthetical description in the same table: 65536 corresponds to 256 × 256 grayscale, not color.

errors.claim: “L8J substitution further reduces error (Goodfellow et al., 2013)” for J3V and W6R.
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports “Conv Net + max pooling + QX2 in all layers” as 12.61 on J3V and 37.20 on W6R, while “Conv Net + L8J” is 11.68 on J3V and 38.57 on W6R.
errors.explanation: L8J reduces J3V error relative to QX2 in all layers, but increases W6R error from 37.20 to 38.57. The prose summary overstates the result if it applies to both collections.

errors.claim: “Prose comparison | 8-layer net | 20.5%”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7” and “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010) | 20.5.”
errors.explanation: The 20.5% pre-QX2 error belongs to the 5-layer mcRBM-G6W-pretrained net, not the 8-layer G6W-pretrained net. The 8-layer pre-QX2 error in the same table is 20.7%.

errors.claim: “Bag-of-words document classification on a subset of M5X improves with QX2 by a 14.3% relative reduction”
errors.evidence: The same part gives “Without QX2 | 31.05%” and “With QX2 | 29.62%.”
errors.explanation: The absolute reduction is 1.43 percentage points, which is about 4.6% relative to 31.05%, not 14.3%.

errors.claim: “QX2 substantially improves standard neural nets and exceeds every other method.”
errors.evidence: The same paragraph says “Bayesian neural nets outperform QX2 on Z7P,” and Table 8 reports “Neural Network with QX2 | 567” versus “Bayesian Neural Network | 623,” with higher values preferred.
errors.explanation: QX2 does not exceed every other method because the Bayesian neural network has a higher C4Y score than QX2.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\, \sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L distribution was defined just above with exponent “\(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+ \mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+ \mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\),” so \(\mathbf a\) is the hidden bias vector and \(\mathbf b\) is the visible bias vector.
errors.explanation: The hidden conditional should use the hidden bias \(a_j\), not the visible bias \(b_j\). This also creates a dimensional inconsistency because \(b\) has one component per visible unit, not per hidden unit.

errors.claim: “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: The model exponent defines “\(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+ \mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\),” making \(\mathbf b\) the visible bias vector and \(\mathbf a\) the hidden bias vector.
errors.explanation: The visible conditional should use the visible bias \(b_i\), not the hidden bias \(a_i\). The conditional equations swap the roles of \(a\) and \(b\) relative to the model definition.

errors.claim: “Each collection contains 50,000 training and 10,000 test images” for J3V and W6R.
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 1 was recorded as: “J3V/W6R=CIFAR-10/100 3072, table says 60K/10K.”
errors.explanation: The appendix says the CIFAR datasets have 50K training images, while the earlier table was noted as giving 60K training images. These training-set counts conflict within the paper.

final_notes:
Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958. Dropout/QX2 randomly removes units/connections during training, samples shared-weight thinned nets, and uses one unthinned weight-scaled net at test time. Test W_test=pW. Typical hidden retention earlier stated 0.5; appendix says hidden typical 0.5–0.8/default 0.5; input often ~0.8 for real-valued images/speech and closer to 1 than 0.5. Claims dropout approximates equally weighted geometric mean/model averaging. Internal issue: sometimes equates expected hidden output under dropout with reduced-weight output despite nonlinear activations; equality only for preactivation/linear case.

Learning: high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and max-norm/V9C constraint help. Practical guide: dropout nets need tuning; if optimal standard layer has n hidden units, good dropout layer should contain at least n/p units. Dropout LR typically 10–100× standard-net optimum; standard momentum 0.9, dropout ~0.95–0.99. V9C typical c=3–4. Pretraining with dropout: use smaller LRs; before dropout finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p.

§6 claim: dropout improves generalization over non-dropout neural nets on every tested dataset. Table 1: H4Z/MNIST 784, 60K/10K; A2F/SVHN 3072, 600K/26K; J3V/W6R=CIFAR-10/100 3072, table says 60K/10K; K9D/ImageNet says 65536 (256×256 color), 1.2M/150K — internal inconsistency since 256×256 color is 196608; N8Q/TIMIT 2520, 1.1M/58K; M5X/Reuters 2000, 200K/200K; Z7P/Alternative Splicing 1014, 2932/733. Appendix B.3 says J3V/W6R each contain 50,000 train/10,000 test images, contradicting Table 1’s 60K/10K.

Vision: §6.1 says SOTA models on all five image datasets use dropout. MNIST Table 2: best permutation-invariant DBM+dropout 0.79; DBN+dropout 0.92; dropout+V9C maxout 0.94; dropout+V9C ReLU 0.95–1.06; dropout ReLU 1.25; no-drop standard NN 1.60. SVHN Table 3: ConvNet max-pool 3.95; +QX2 FC 3.02; +QX2 all layers 2.55; +L8J 2.47; human 2.0. CIFAR Table 4: +QX2 all layers 12.61/37.20; +L8J 11.68/38.57. Internal error: prose says L8J further reduces error, but on W6R it is worse than QX2 all layers. ImageNet: ILSVRC-2010 ConvNet+QX2 37.5 top1/17.0 top5. ILSVRC-2012 avg 5 ConvNets+QX2 val 38.1/16.4, test top5 16.4.

N8Q/TIMIT Table 7: NN 6 layers 23.4; QX2 NN 6 layers 21.8; G6W-pretrained 4/6/8 layers 22.7/22.4/20.7; mcRBM-G6W-pretrained 5 layers 20.5; G6W-pretrained 4 + QX2 19.7; 8 + QX2 19.7. Internal error: prose says 8-layer pre-QX2 error 20.5, but table gives 20.7 and 20.5 is 5-layer mcRBM.

M5X/Reuters: text says QX2 gives 14.3% relative reduction, but table says 31.05% to 29.62%, a 1.43-point/4.6% relative reduction. B.5: full corpus >800,000 documents, 103 tree-arranged classes; used subset 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocab, 50 disjoint categories, one category/document, equal train/test splits (>200,000 training examples).

Z7P Table 8 C4Y bits, higher preferred: early-stop NN 440; Regression PCA 463; SVM PCA 487; NN+QX2 567; Bayesian NN 623. Internal error: text says QX2 “exceeds every other method,” contradicted by Bayesian NN 623>567; same section says Bayesian nets outperform QX2/SOTA. B.6: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue types from 27 mouse tissues; each input has 4 target softmax units (one/tissue), each with states inc/exc/nc. C4Y sums target p log(q/bar p). QX2 hidden scale 1000s; Bayesian-network hidden scale a few tens; trained QX2 network 2 layers ×1024 units, hidden p=.5, input p=.7, V9C and high decaying LR, same 5 folds as Xiong et al. 2011.

§6.5 H4Z regularizer Table 9: Y5F 1.62; Y5F+O3U 1.60; Y5F+KL 1.55; V9C 1.35; QX2+Y5F 1.25; QX2+V9C 1.05 lowest. §7: dropout autoencoders learn meaningful edges/strokes/spots and sparser activations. Retention Fig9 H4Z flat 0.4≤p≤0.8; p=0.1 gives 2.7% fixed vs 1.7% pn fixed; best near p=0.6. Dataset-size: no QX2 improvement for two smallest subsets; gain rises then falls. X9M vs T6R: finite-sample averaging matches T6R around k=50 and slightly better within 1 SD.

§8 B8T/dropout RBM: mixture of shared-weight RBMs with hidden subset sampled by retention vector r. Exponent v^TWh + a^T h + b^T v, so a=hidden biases, b=visible biases; g forces h_j=0 if r_j=0. Internal error in §8.1: conditional equations swap biases, using b_j for hidden conditional and a_i for visible conditional. CD-1 used; each mini-batch case has different r. B8T p=0.5 features coarser/sparser than ordinary RBM.

§9: linear regression marginalized dropout objective = ||y-pXw||²+p(1-p)||Γw||²; with w~=pw, penalty ((1-p)/p)||Γw~||². §10: Gaussian noise Table 10 H4Z P7V 1.08±.04, D4K .95±.04; J3V P7V 12.6±.1, D4K 12.5±.1. In inverted representation Bernoulli mean 1 var (1-p)/p; Gaussian N(1,σ²), σ=sqrt((1-p)/p); no test-time T6R. §11: claims QX2 achieves SOTA on A2F, K9D, W6R, H4Z; considerable improvements elsewhere; training typically 2–3× standard.

Appendix B: H4Z validation 10K; endpoint 1M updates; depths 2/3/4, widths 1024/2048, p hidden .5/input .8, momentum .95, V9C c=2. A2F validation 6000, conv filters 96/128/256, FC 2048/2048, p=(.9,.75,.75,.5,.5,.5), c=4, momentum .95. J3V/W6R preprocessing GCN+ZCA; architecture/retention match A2F; smaller input LRs. N8Q: 680 speakers, 8 dialects, 10 sentences; Kaldi log-filter banks; monophone alignment; no speaker-dependent ops; mean-centered/unit-variance inputs. N8Q settings: 21 consecutive frames/window, input p=.8, hidden p=.5, V9C c=4, momentum .95, high LR .1, decay ε0(1+t/T)^−1, G6W pretraining U2L CD-1, Gaussian-U2L input variance fixed 1, best QX2 G6W-finetuning LR about .01; V9C during G6W finetuning no improvement, smaller LR important.

Introduction details: With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is presented as best regularization for a fixed-sized model. Dropout is proposed as a cheaper approximation to an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models’ predictions. An n-unit network represents 2^n possible thinned networks while retaining only O(n^2) or fewer parameters via weight sharing. For every presentation of each training case a new thinned member is sampled/trained, so each particular member is trained rarely if ever. Multilayer nonlinear hidden representations can learn complicated relationships but limited-data sampling noise can create relationships present in train but absent in genuine test data, even from same distribution. Prior/standard responses: early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 and L2 penalties; these constrain parameters rather than averaging every parameter setting.

Model combination: usually improves performance, but training/output averaging of many large nets is expensive; diversity requires different architectures or data, hyperparameters are architecture-specific/difficult, training is computationally costly, data requirements may preclude subset training, and inference may be infeasible for rapid response. Practical dropout inference rule is weight scaling: use one unthinned network rather than explicitly evaluating exponentially many members. More expensive alternative: Monte-Carlo model averaging of sampled thinned members’ predictions. Claim: weight scaling/dropout gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularization methods across varied classification problems. Dropout extends beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models including Boltzmann Machines; Restricted Boltzmann Machines can have Dropout RBM form with shared parameters.

Introduction: With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is best regularization for fixed model. Dropout is cheaper approximation to equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned parameter-sharing models’ predictions. An n-unit net represents 2^n thinned nets but only O(n^2) or fewer parameters. Each training case presentation samples/trains a new thinned network, so any particular member rarely/never trained. Hidden representations can overfit sampling noise. Prior regularizers include early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1/L2; they constrain parameters rather than average settings.

Model combination: improves performance but many large nets are expensive; diversity needs different architectures/data; hyperparameters hard; training/inference costly; data may preclude subsets. Practical dropout inference: weight scaling in one unthinned net instead of evaluating exponentially many members. Alternative: Monte Carlo model averaging of sampled thinned nets. Claim: dropout/weight scaling gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied classification problems. Dropout extends beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models including RBMs/Dropout RBM.

Figure 1: standard net with two hidden layers vs dropout thinned net with crossed-out units and removed incoming/outgoing connections.

§2 Motivation: Analogy to sexual reproduction. Asexual reproduction preserves successful co-adapted gene sets and might seem superior for individual-fitness optimization; sexual recombination breaks complex co-adaptations, yet advanced organisms evolved sexually. Livnat et al. account: long-run selection may favor gene “mix-ability” over individual fitness; genes working with random partners are robust; lack of guaranteed partner sets encourages individually useful/simple collaborations; reducing complex co-adaptations helps useful new genes spread. Dropout-trained hidden units similarly face random partners, encouraging independently useful robust features rather than reliance on other hidden units to fix mistakes, though units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating each hidden unit many times is poor robustness, analogous to replica codes for noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: ten five-person conspiracies likely more robust than one fifty-person conspiracy; large complex co-adaptations can work under unchanged/rehearsed training conditions but fail under non-stationary/novel test conditions more easily than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

Abstract/main claims: Dropout temporarily removes randomly selected units/connections during training to reduce co-adaptation; samples exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. Introduction: With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is best regularization for fixed model. Dropout is cheaper approximation to equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned parameter-sharing models’ predictions. An n-unit net represents 2^n thinned nets but only O(n^2) or fewer parameters. Each training case presentation samples/trains a new thinned network, so any particular member rarely/never trained. Hidden representations can overfit sampling noise. Prior regularizers include early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1/L2; they constrain parameters rather than average settings.

Model combination: improves performance but many large nets are expensive; diversity needs different architectures/data; hyperparameters hard; training/inference costly; data may preclude subsets. Practical dropout inference: weight scaling in one unthinned net instead of evaluating exponentially many members. Alternative: Monte Carlo model averaging of sampled thinned nets. Claim: dropout/weight scaling gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied classification problems. Dropout extends beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models including RBMs/Dropout RBM.

Figure 1: standard net with two hidden layers vs dropout thinned net with crossed-out units and removed incoming/outgoing connections.

§2 Motivation: Analogy to sexual reproduction. Asexual reproduction preserves successful co-adapted gene sets and might seem superior for individual-fitness optimization; sexual recombination breaks complex co-adaptations, yet advanced organisms evolved sexually. Livnat et al. account: long-run selection may favor gene “mix-ability” over individual fitness; genes working with random partners are robust; lack of guaranteed partner sets encourages individually useful/simple collaborations; reducing complex co-adaptations helps useful new genes spread. Dropout-trained hidden units similarly face random partners, encouraging independently useful robust features rather than reliance on other hidden units to fix mistakes, though units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating each hidden unit many times is poor robustness, analogous to replica codes for noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: ten five-person conspiracies likely more robust than one fifty-person conspiracy; large complex co-adaptations can work under unchanged/rehearsed training conditions but fail under non-stationary/novel test conditions more easily than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

§3 Related work: Dropout interpreted as adding noise to hidden-unit states, extending denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010), which used input corruption and clean-input reconstruction. Claimed extensions over DAEs: effective hidden-layer corruption, model-averaging interpretation, supervised and unsupervised use, applicability to other neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann machines. Test-time weight scaling permits higher noise than usually best for DAEs. Table: typical best DAE noise 5%; dropout often optimal input-unit removal 20%; dropout often optimal hidden-unit removal 50%. Stochastic minimization under noise distribution minimizes expected loss; adversarial alternatives (Globerson & Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010) let adversary choose removals subject to fixed max number rather than probability distribution and have no hidden units. Analytically marginalizing dropout gives deterministic regularizers in simple cases. Exponential-family input-noise regularizers including dropout/“blankout noise” studied by van der Maaten et al. (2013), limited to models without hidden layers. Chen et al. (2012) examined marginalization for denoising autoencoders; Wang & Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to accelerate dropout.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines dropout training as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), and says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\). Earlier notes also record that the paper described weight scaling as an approximation to model averaging, not an exact equality.
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)] \ne f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). The equality would hold for the preactivation/weighted input, or for linear activations, but not for every hidden unit’s output under the stated general nonlinear model.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\, \sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L distribution was defined just above with exponent “\(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+ \mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+ \mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\),” so \(\mathbf a\) is the hidden bias vector and \(\mathbf b\) is the visible bias vector.
errors.explanation: The hidden conditional should use the hidden bias \(a_j\), not the visible bias \(b_j\). This also creates a dimensional inconsistency because \(b\) has one component per visible unit, not per hidden unit.

errors.claim: “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: The model exponent defines “\(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+ \mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\),” making \(\mathbf b\) the visible bias vector and \(\mathbf a\) the hidden bias vector.
errors.explanation: The visible conditional should use the visible bias \(b_i\), not the hidden bias \(a_i\). The conditional equations swap the roles of \(a\) and \(b\) relative to the model definition.

final_notes:
Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929-1958, “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting.” Dropout retains units with probability p during training; standard test uses unthinned net with outgoing weights scaled by p. Hidden p often 0.5; input closer to 1. SGD/momentum/annealed LR/L2; max-norm incoming weights ||w||2≤c. Pretrained weights scaled by 1/p before dropout finetuning.

Datasets Table 1: MNIST 784, 60K/10K. SVHN 3072, 600K/26K. CIFAR-10/100 3072, 60K/10K. ImageNet ILSVRC-2012 dim 65536 (256×256 color), 1.2M/150K — internal arithmetic inconsistency: 256×256 color should be 196608 if color counted as for CIFAR/SVHN. TIMIT 2520, 1.1M frames/58K. Reuters 2000, 200K/200K. Alt Splicing 1014, 2932/733. Sec.6 says dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs no-dropout NNs.

MNIST/Table 2: ReLU 3×1024 no dropout 1.25; dropout+max-norm ReLU 3×1024 1.06, 3×2048 1.04, 2×4096 1.01, 2×8192 0.95; maxout dropout+max-norm 0.94. Pretrained: DBN+finetune 1.18; DBM+finetune 0.96; DBN+dropout 0.92; DBM+dropout 0.79, stated best for permutation-invariant MNIST. MNIST dropout p=0.5 hidden, p=0.8 input. Appendix B.1: MNIST says 60K train/10K test, held out 10K validation, tuned so best validation after 1M updates, then “combined” and trained on “all 55,000 images” for 1M updates — internal inconsistency because should be 60K. Fig.4 architectures: 2/3/4 layers with 1024/2048 units = six; p=0.5 hidden, p=0.8 input, momentum .95, max-norm c=2. Tried 2/3 layer nets with 4096/8192; 2-layer improved, 3-layer worse; more dropout helped but not enough.

SVHN/Table 3: conv+maxpool 3.95; +dropout FC 3.02; stochastic pooling 2.80; +dropout all layers 2.55; maxout 2.47; human 2.0. App B.2: ~600K train/26K test; validation 6000; RGB zero mean/unit variance; best arch 3 conv 96/128/256 5×5 stride1, each followed by 3×3 maxpool stride2, then two FC 2048; ReLU; dropout all layers p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5); max-norm c=4, momentum .95; no recombine validation.

CIFAR/Table 4 CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100: conv max pooling 15.60/43.48; stochastic pooling 15.13/42.51; Snoek 14.98/–; dropout FC 14.32/41.26; dropout all layers 12.61/37.20; maxout 11.68/38.57. Appendix B.3 says CIFAR-10/100 have 50K train/10K test, conflicting with earlier Table 1 60K/10K. Uses 5K validation, then combines like MNIST. Preprocessing: per-image per-channel GCN, then ZCA whitening; when translating/reflecting, rotate back after ZCA? Network architecture/dropout rates same as SVHN except smaller input-layer learning rates.

ImageNet Table 5 ILSVRC-2010: Conv Net+dropout 37.5/17.0 top1/top5. Table 6 ILSVRC-2012: Conv Net+dropout val 40.7/18.2; Avg 5 Conv Nets+dropout val 38.1/16.4, test top-5 16.4; standard features about 26% top-5.

TIMIT/Table 7 phone error: NN 6 layers 23.4; Dropout NN 6 layers 21.8; DBN-pretrained NN 4/6/8 layers 22.7/22.4/20.7; mcRBM-DBN 5 layers 20.5; DBN-pretrained NN 4 + dropout 19.7; 8 + dropout 19.7. Internal inconsistency: text says 8-layer error reduces from 20.5 to 19.7, but table says 8-layer baseline is 20.7; 20.5 is 5-layer mcRBM-DBN. App B.4: Kaldi log-filter banks, monophone forced alignment, 21-frame windows, no speaker-dependent ops, mean centered/unit variance. p=0.8 input, 0.5 hidden; max-norm c=4 all layers; momentum .95, LR .1 decay. DBN pretraining RBMs CD-1, Gaussian RBM variance fixed 1; DBN+dropout finetune LR about .01; max-norm no improvement.

Reuters: best no-dropout NN 31.05%, dropout 29.62%. App B.5: RCV1 >800K docs, 103 classes hierarchy; subset 402,738 articles, vocab 2000, 50 categories, each doc one class; equal train/test split; dropout improved all tried architectures, modest due to large dataset >200K training examples.

Alternative Splicing/Table 8 Code Quality bits: NN early stopping 440; Regression PCA 463; SVM PCA 487; NN dropout 567; Bayesian NN 623. App B.6: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue types; each input target has 4 softmax units (one/tissue), each 3 states inc/exc/nc; metric Code Quality; two-layer dropout net 1024 each layer, p=0.5 hidden, p=0.7 input, max-norm and high decaying LRs; averaged over same 5 folds as Xiong et al.

Sec.6.5 regularizers MNIST 784-1024-1024-2048-10 ReLU. Table 9 error %: L2 1.62; L2+L1 near end 1.60; L2+KL sparsity 1.55; Max-norm 1.35; Dropout+L2 1.25; Dropout+Max-norm 1.05.

Sec.7: dropout autoencoder features more meaningful; dropout activations sparser. Dropout-rate fixed 784-2048-2048-2048-10 no input dropout: error flat 0.4≤p≤0.8, rises near p=1; keeping pn constant improves small-p, p≈0.6 best. Dataset size: no gain for MNIST subsets 100/500; gain increases then declines. MC averaging at test around k=50 matches weight scaling; more samples slightly better within 1 SD.

Sec.8 Dropout RBMs: RBM joint P(h,v)=1/Z exp(vᵀWh+aᵀh+bᵀv), so a hidden bias, b visible bias. Dropout RBM adds rj~Bernoulli(p), dropped hidden hj=0. Sec.8.1 internal error: conditionals swap biases, hidden σ(bj+ΣiWijvi), visible σ(ai+ΣjWijhj), conflicting with joint. Dropout RBM features coarser; fewer dead units; activations sparser.

Sec.9/10: marginalized linear regression objective ||y-pXw||2+p(1-p)||Γw||2; with w̃=pw gives ||y-Xw̃||2+((1-p)/p)||Γw̃||2. Gaussian dropout multiplies by N(1,σ²); no test scaling; Bernoulli alternative multiplier 1/p w.p. p, 0 otherwise; variance (1-p)/p. Table 10 Bernoulli vs Gaussian: MNIST 1.08±0.04 vs 0.95±0.04; CIFAR-10 12.6±0.1 vs 12.5±0.1.

Conclusion/App A: dropout improved many domains; dropout methods achieve SOTA on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST; training usually 2–3× longer. Heuristics: if n units optimal for standard net use at least n/p dropout. Use 10–100× standard LR, momentum .95–.99; max-norm c typically 3–4. Hidden p typically 0.5–0.8; real-valued inputs typical p=0.8.

Thinned networks: Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network consisting of units that survived dropout (Figure 1b). A net with n units can be seen as a collection of 2^n possible thinned networks. Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned models is infeasible. Instead use a single neural net without dropout, with scaled-down trained weights. Section 2 motivation details: Uses analogy to sexual reproduction (Livnat et al. 2010). Asexual reproduction might seem better for preserving co-adapted genes, but sexual reproduction may select for “mix-ability”/robustness: genes must work with random partners and not rely on large fixed co-adapted sets. Similarly, each hidden unit trained with dropout must work with a randomly chosen sample of other units, learn useful features on its own or with few others, and not rely on others to correct mistakes. Hidden units within a layer should still learn different things. Authors reject robustness by making many copies of each hidden unit as poor, analogous to replica codes being poor for noisy channels. Second analogy: successful conspiracies—ten conspiracies of five people likely better under non-stationary conditions than one conspiracy requiring fifty people; complex co-adaptations can fit training data but fail on novel test data more than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

Intro/dropout definition: Deep nets overfit with limited data; dropout approximates equally weighted geometric mean/model averaging of exponentially many learned models sharing parameters. Dropping out hidden and visible units means temporarily removing unit and incoming/outgoing connections. Each unit retained independently with probability p; p tunable or 0.5 often near optimal for hidden units; input retention usually closer to 1. Applying dropout samples a thinned network. A net with n units has 2^n thinned networks; shared weights keep parameters O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned network; explicit averaging infeasible. Test uses no-dropout net with outgoing weights scaled by retention probability p, intended to match expected training-time hidden output and combine 2^n networks. Fig. 2: training unit present with probability p and outgoing weights w; test always present with outgoing weights pw.

Motivation: Sexual reproduction analogy: dropout selects hidden units/features that work with random partners (“mix-ability”) rather than complex co-adapted sets; units should still learn different things. Replica-code-like copying is rejected. Conspiracy analogy: multiple small co-adaptations may generalize better than one large fragile co-adaptation.

Related work: Dropout as stochastic regularization/noise. Denoising autoencoders add noise to inputs and reconstruct clean input; paper claims to extend by applying dropout/noise in hidden layers, interpreting as model averaging, applying to supervised learning, and to neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAEs typically best with 5% noise; authors say test-time weight scaling permits much higher noise: often optimal to drop 20% of inputs and 50% of hidden units. Deterministic counterpart obtained by marginalizing dropout noise: paper will show simple cases where dropout analytically marginalizes to deterministic regularizers. Related: van der Maaten et al. (2013) deterministic regularizers for exponential-family noise including “blankout” dropout, only inputs/no hidden layers; Wang & Manning (2013) speed up dropout by marginalizing noise; Chen et al. (2012) marginalization for denoising autoencoders. Also adversarial unit dropping by Globerson & Roweis/Dekel et al.: loss minimized when adversary picks units to drop with max number fixed; no hidden-unit models.

Formal model (Sec.4): Neural network with L hidden layers; l indexes hidden layers. y(0)=x input. z(l) inputs into layer l, y(l) outputs; W(l), b(l) weights/biases. Standard feedforward for l=0,...,L-1: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)), e.g. sigmoid f(x)=1/(1+exp(-x)). Dropout feedforward: sample r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p), form thinned outputs \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l) elementwise, then z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) \tilde y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). For any layer l, r^(l) independent Bernoulli variables with probability p of 1; sample/multiply outputs to create thinned outputs, used as next layer input. Applied at each layer, sampling a sub-network. Learning backpropagates derivatives through sampled sub-network. Test time scales weights as W_test^(l)=p W^(l) and uses resulting network without dropout.

Dropout definition/formal model: Dropping hidden/visible units means temporarily removing unit and incoming/outgoing connections. Each unit retained independently with probability p (hidden p=0.5 often near optimal; input retention closer to 1). Net with n units has 2^n thinned networks. Training samples new thinned network per case. Test: no-dropout network with W_test^(l)=p W^(l), matching expected training-time hidden output. Formal: y(0)=x; standard z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Dropout samples r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), uses \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l) into next layer; backprop through sampled subnetwork.

Motivation/related work: Dropout encourages features that work with random partners (“mix-ability”), not fragile co-adaptations. Related to stochastic regularization/noise and denoising autoencoders, but extends noise/dropout to hidden layers, supervised learning, model averaging, Boltzmann machines. DAEs usually best with 5% noise; authors say dropout often optimal dropping 20% inputs and 50% hidden due to test-time scaling. Later will show simple cases where marginalizing dropout gives deterministic regularizers. Related marginalization/noise/adversarial dropping works mostly input/no hidden or adversarial fixed dropped units.

Sec.5 training: Dropout nets trained by SGD like standard nets. For each training case in a mini-batch, sample a thinned network; forward/backprop only through it. Gradients averaged over mini-batch; unused parameters get zero gradient for that case. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay useful. Especially useful: max-norm regularization constraining incoming weight vector at each hidden unit to ||w||2≤c; if exceeds, project onto ball radius c. c tuned on validation set. Max-norm improves SGD deep nets even without dropout. Dropout alone helps, but dropout + max-norm + large decaying learning rates + high momentum gives significant boost; max-norm allows huge learning rates without weights blowing up, dropout noise explores weight space, decay settles.

Sec.5.2 pretraining: Nets can be pretrained with stacks of RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs; pretraining useful with unlabeled data and sometimes improves over random init after finetuning. Dropout can finetune pretrained nets; pretraining unchanged. Pretrained weights should be scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected output under dropout equals pretraining output. Initially high learning rates comparable to randomly initialized nets could wipe out pretrained information; smaller finetuning learning rates retained information and improved final generalization vs not using dropout in finetuning.

Sec.6 intro experiments: Authors trained dropout neural nets for classification across domains and claim dropout improved generalization on all datasets compared to neural nets without dropout. Datasets listed/Table 1: MNIST handwritten digits; TIMIT clean speech recognition; CIFAR-10/100 tiny natural images; SVHN Google Street View house numbers; ImageNet natural images; Reuters-RCV1 news articles; Alternative Splicing RNA features. They chose diverse datasets to show generality; Sec.6 gives key results, Appendix B has detailed experiment/data descriptions.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines dropout training as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), and says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\). Earlier notes also record that the paper described weight scaling as an approximation to model averaging, not an exact equality.
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)] \ne f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). The equality would hold for the preactivation/weighted input, or for linear activations, but not for every hidden unit’s output under the stated general nonlinear model.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p, matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier §4 equations in notes define unit output as nonlinear: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z), and dropout uses \tilde y=r*y before applying f. Notes also record that the earlier claim that expected hidden-unit output under deletion equals test-time output conflicts with the nonlinear f equations; equality only holds generally for preactivations/linear cases.
errors.explanation: Multiplying incoming weights by 1/p makes the expected preactivation match the pretrained preactivation, but with nonlinear f it does not generally make the expected unit output match the pretrained output.

errors.claim: K9D (ILSVRC-2012) dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image has 256 × 256 × 3 = 196608 input values, not 65536.
errors.explanation: The numeric dimensionality conflicts with the parenthetical description in the same table: 65536 corresponds to 256 × 256 grayscale, not color.

errors.claim: “L8J substitution further reduces error (Goodfellow et al., 2013)” for J3V and W6R.
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports “Conv Net + max pooling + QX2 in all layers” as 12.61 on J3V and 37.20 on W6R, while “Conv Net + L8J” is 11.68 on J3V and 38.57 on W6R.
errors.explanation: L8J reduces J3V error relative to QX2 in all layers, but increases W6R error from 37.20 to 38.57. The prose summary overstates the result if it applies to both collections.

errors.claim: “Prose comparison | 8-layer net | Pre-QX2 error 20.5%”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7” and “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010) | 20.5.”
errors.explanation: The 20.5% pre-dropout error belongs to the 5-layer mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN, not the 8-layer G6W-pretrained NN. The 8-layer baseline in the table is 20.7%, so calling 20.5% the 8-layer net’s pre-QX2 error is inconsistent.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L distribution is defined just above as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), with parameters θ={W,a,b}. Thus a is the hidden-unit bias vector and b is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the stated joint distribution, the hidden conditional should use hidden bias a_j, and the visible conditional should use visible bias b_i. The displayed conditionals swap a and b, and even use b_j for hidden units and a_i for visible units, conflicting with the model definition.

errors.claim: “QX2 methods achieve state of the art on A2F, K9D, W6R and H4Z, with considerable improvement to standard neural nets on other collections.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Vision claim SOTA models on all five vision collections use dropout.” The five vision collections listed earlier were H4Z/MNIST, A2F/SVHN, J3V/CIFAR-10, W6R/CIFAR-100, and K9D/ImageNet.
errors.explanation: The conclusion lists only four datasets as state-of-the-art and appears to put the remaining collections, including J3V/CIFAR-10, in the weaker category of merely improving standard neural nets. This conflicts with the earlier claim that dropout was used in state-of-the-art models on all five vision collections.

errors.claim: “For a task whose optimal standard-net layer has n hidden units, a good QX2 layer should contain at least n/p units. Removing units reduces capacity: only pn units remain in expectation...”
errors.evidence: If the QX2 layer contains “n/p units,” then with retention probability p the expected number retained is p·(n/p)=n, not pn.
errors.explanation: The paragraph defines n as the optimal standard-net layer size and then recommends n/p units for the dropout layer. Under that recommendation, the expected retained units are n; the statement “only pn units remain” is inconsistent unless n is silently redefined as the dropout-layer size.

errors.evidence: This same section says “Held-out training images for validation | 10,000,” and earlier Table 1 recorded H4Z/MNIST as “784 60K/10K.”
errors.explanation: If H4Z has 60,000 training images and 10,000 are held out for validation, combining validation and training should use 60,000 images, not 55,000. The 55,000 figure also does not align with holding out 10,000 images from the recorded 60K training set.

final_notes:
Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958. Main claims: dropout/QX2 temporarily removes randomly selected units/connections during training, samples exponentially many shared-weight thinned networks, and uses one unthinned weight-scaled network at test time to approximate model averaging. Gates r~Bernoulli(p), output r*y; test no removals and W_test=pW. Typical hidden retention 0.5; input ~0.8. Dropout approximates equally weighted geometric mean of predictions. Internal issue: paper equates expected hidden-unit output under dropout with reduced-weight output despite nonlinear activations; equality only linear/preactivation.

Learning: gains boosted by high momentum, large decaying learning rates, max-norm/V9C ||w||<=c. Each minibatch example samples own thinned net; unused parameters get zero gradient. Pretraining: finetune pretrained nets with dropout using smaller learning rates; before dropout finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p to preserve expected preactivation/input.

§6 results: Table 1 datasets: H4Z/MNIST 784 60K/10K; A2F/SVHN 3072 600K/26K; J3V/W6R CIFAR-10/100 3072 table says 60K/10K; K9D/ImageNet table says 65536 (256×256 color), 1.2M/150K — internal inconsistency because 256×256 color=196608; N8Q/TIMIT 2520 1.1M/58K; M5X/Reuters 2000 200K/200K; Z7P Alt Splicing 1014 2932/733. Vision claim SOTA models on all five vision collections use dropout. MNIST Table 2 best DBM+dropout finetuning 0.79. SVHN Table 3 best +L8J 2.47, Human 2.0. CIFAR Table 4: +QX2 all layers 12.61/37.20; +L8J 11.68/38.57. Internal error: prose says L8J further reduces error, but on W6R it is worse than QX2 all layers. Introduction details: With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is presented as best regularization for a fixed-sized model. Dropout is proposed as a cheaper approximation to an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models’ predictions. An n-unit network represents 2^n possible thinned networks while retaining only O(n^2) or fewer parameters via weight sharing. Practical dropout inference rule is weight scaling: use one unthinned network rather than explicitly evaluating exponentially many members. §2 Motivation: Analogy to sexual reproduction. Asexual reproduction preserves successful co-adapted gene sets and might seem superior for individual-fitness optimization; sexual recombination breaks complex co-adaptations, yet advanced organisms evolved sexually. Livnat et al. account: long-run selection may favor gene “mix-ability” over individual fitness; genes working with random partners are robust; lack of guaranteed partner sets encourages individually useful/simple collaborations; reducing complex co-adaptations helps useful new genes spread. Dropout-trained hidden units similarly face random partners, encouraging independently useful robust features rather than reliance on other hidden units to fix mistakes, though units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating each hidden unit many times is poor robustness, analogous to replica codes for noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: ten five-person conspiracies likely more robust than one fifty-person conspiracy; large complex co-adaptations can work under unchanged/rehearsed training conditions but fail under non-stationary/novel test conditions more easily than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines dropout training as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), and says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\). Earlier notes also record that the paper described weight scaling as an approximation to model averaging, not an exact equality.
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)] \ne f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). The equality would hold for the preactivation/weighted input, or for linear activations, but not for every hidden unit’s output under the stated general nonlinear model.

§2 Motivation: Sexual reproduction analogy; random partners discourage complex co-adaptations and encourage robust, individually useful hidden units.

§3 Related work: Dropout as adding noise to hidden-unit states; extends denoising autoencoders by hidden-layer corruption, model-averaging interpretation, supervised/unsupervised use, applicability beyond feed-forward nets. Test-time weight scaling permits higher noise than DAEs. Typical best DAE noise 5%; dropout often optimal input removal 20%; hidden removal 50%. Stochastic minimization under noise distribution vs adversarial deletion. Marginalizing dropout gives deterministic regularizers in simple cases.

§4 Model Description: Network has L hidden layers; y^(0)=x; ordinary z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z), f can be sigmoid. Dropout: independent Bernoulli gates r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), thinned outputs \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then z_i=w_i \tilde y^l+b_i and y_i=f(z). Apply at every layer; backprop through sampled subnetwork. Hidden and visible/input units can both be removed. Inference: no units removed and W_test^(l)=p W^(l); Fig.2 says training unit present with probability p and weights w, testing always present with outgoing weights pw. Retention choices independent with common p in simplest construction; validation can choose p; usual default close to optimal; optimal input retention generally nearer complete retention. Internal issue noted: claims equating expected hidden-unit output under dropout with test-time/reduced-weight output conflict with nonlinear f; equality generally only for preactivation/linear case.

§5 Learning Dropout Nets: Dropout alone gives significant gains; combining with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and incoming-weight constraint/max-norm regularization gives further boost. Max-norm usually also improves deep-net SGD without dropout; previously used for collaborative filtering. Optimization account: fixed-radius weight ball permits huge learning rates without explosion; dropout noise explores hard-to-reach regions; decaying rates take progressively shorter steps ending at a minimum. SGD differs from standard nets only by per-case sampled thinned network: each mini-batch case gets its own forward/backward sampled network; parameter gradients averaged; unused parameter for a case contributes zero gradient. Momentum, annealed rates and max-norm remain useful. Incoming hidden-unit weight vector constrained ||w||_2 <= c; if outside radius-c ball, project back to surface; c tuned on validation.

§5.2 Unsupervised pretraining: Smaller finetuning learning rates preserve pretrained information and improve final generalization relative to finetuning without dropout; rates comparable to best random-initialized-net rates erased pretrained info in initial experiments. Pretraining itself unchanged. Before dropout finetuning, pretrained weights multiplied by 1/p so expected preactivation/input under random removal matches pretraining; text says expected unit output matches, but that conflicts with nonlinear-output equations. Unlabeled-data pretraining can improve over random init in some cases; pretraining methods include stacked RBMs, autoencoders, and DBMs, followed by dropout backprop finetuning.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L distribution is defined just above as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), with parameters θ={W,a,b}. Thus a is the hidden-unit bias vector and b is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the stated joint distribution, the hidden conditional should use hidden bias a_j, and the visible conditional should use visible bias b_i. The displayed conditionals swap a and b, and even use b_j for hidden units and a_i for visible units, conflicting with the model definition.

errors.claim: “For a task whose optimal standard-net layer has n hidden units, a good QX2 layer should contain at least n/p units. Removing units reduces capacity: only pn units remain in expectation...”

errors.explanation: The paragraph defines n as the optimal standard-net layer size and then recommends n/p units for the dropout layer. Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958. Main claims: dropout/QX2 temporarily removes randomly selected units/connections during training, samples exponentially many shared-weight thinned networks, and uses one unthinned weight-scaled network at test time to approximate model averaging. Gates r~Bernoulli(p), output r*y; test no removals and W_test=pW. Typical hidden retention earlier 0.5; input ~0.8. Dropout approximates equally weighted geometric mean of predictions. Internal issue: paper equates expected hidden-unit output under dropout with reduced-weight output despite nonlinear activations; equality only linear/preactivation.

Learning: gains boosted by high momentum, large decaying learning rates, max-norm/V9C ||w||<=c. Each minibatch example samples own thinned net; unused parameters get zero gradient. Pretraining: finetune pretrained nets with dropout using smaller learning rates; before dropout finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p to preserve expected preactivation/input.

§6 results: Table 1 datasets: H4Z/MNIST 784 60K/10K; A2F/SVHN 3072 600K/26K; J3V/W6R CIFAR-10/100 3072 table says 60K/10K; K9D/ImageNet table says 65536 (256×256 color), 1.2M/150K — internal inconsistency because 256×256 color=196608; N8Q/TIMIT 2520 1.1M/58K; M5X/Reuters 2000 200K/200K; Z7P Alt Splicing 1014 2932/733. Vision claim SOTA models on all five vision collections use dropout. MNIST Table 2 best DBM+dropout finetuning 0.79. SVHN Table 3 best +L8J 2.47, Human 2.0. CIFAR Table 4: +QX2 all layers 12.61/37.20; +L8J 11.68/38.57. Internal error: prose says L8J further reduces error, but on W6R it is worse than QX2 all layers. ImageNet Table 6 avg 5 ConvNets+QX2 val 38.1/16.4, test top5 16.4. TIMIT Table 7: NN 23.4; dropout NN 21.8; pretrained 4/6/8 layers 22.7/22.4/20.7; mcRBM-pretrained 5 layers 20.5; pretrained 4/8 layers+dropout both 19.7. Internal error: prose says 8-layer pre-dropout 20.5%, table gives 20.7. Reuters: best NN without QX2 31.05%, with QX2 29.62%. Alt Splicing Table 8: NN early stopping 440; Regression PCA 463; SVM PCA 487; NN+QX2 567; Bayesian NN 623 (C4Y bits higher better). §6.5 Table 9 regularizers: Y5F 1.62; +O3U 1.60; +KL sparsity 1.55; V9C 1.35; QX2+Y5F 1.25; QX2+V9C 1.05.

Low p=0.1 fixed arch 2.7%, fixed expected retained width 1.7%; best p near 0.6. Dataset size: smallest MNIST subsets no improvement; gain first increases then decreases. errors.claim: “The weights obtained from pretraining should be scaled up by a factor of 1/(1-p). This makes sure that for each unit, the expected output from it under random dropout will be the same as the output during pretraining.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Each unit retained independently with probability p”; “Fig. 2: training unit present with probability p”; “Dropout feedforward: sample r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p)” and “Test time scales weights as W_test^(l)=p W^(l).”
errors.explanation: Given the paper’s own definition that p is the retention probability, dropout reduces expected outgoing contribution by a factor p. To preserve pretraining outputs under dropout, weights would need scaling by 1/p, not 1/(1-p). The stated factor is inconsistent with the earlier definition of p unless p were the drop probability, which the paper says it is not.

final_notes:
Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929-1958, “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting.” Dropout randomly drops units/connections during training; samples exponentially many thinned nets; at test uses unthinned net with outgoing weights scaled by retention probability p. p=0.5 often hidden, input closer to 1. Prevents co-adaptations; approximates model averaging/geometric mean. DAEs often best with 5% noise; dropout can use higher noise (e.g. 20% inputs, 50% hidden). Training: SGD with thinned net per case; unused params zero. Momentum, annealed LR, L2 useful. Max-norm constrains incoming weights ||w||₂≤c. Dropout+max-norm+large decaying LR+high momentum helps.

Known internal issues: (1) Unsupervised pretraining section said pretrained weights “should be scaled up by 1/(1-p)” to match pretraining output, but with p as retention probability and test scaling p, preserving expectation seems to require 1/p. (2) Sec.6 intro claimed dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs neural nets without dropout, but Alternative Splicing Table 8 has NN dropout Code Quality 567 below Bayesian NN 623, and paragraph saying dropout “outperforms all other methods” is also contradicted by Bayesian NN. (3) Table 1 says CIFAR-10/100 have 60K train/10K test; Appendix B.3 says 50K train/10K test. (4) TIMIT text says 8-layer error reduces from 20.5 to 19.7, but Table 7 says 8-layer baseline 20.7; 20.5 is 5-layer mcRBM-DBN. (5) Dropout RBM joint defines a hidden bias and b visible bias, but conditional formulas use b_j for hidden and a_i for visible.

Dataset/Table notes: Table 1: MNIST 784 60K/10K; SVHN 3072 600K/26K; CIFAR-10/100 3072 60K/10K (conflicts with App. B.3 50K/10K); ImageNet 65536 1.2M/150K; TIMIT 2520 1.1M/58K; Reuters 2000 200K/200K; Alt Splicing 1014 2932/733. MNIST best permutation-invariant DBM+dropout 0.79. SVHN CNN dropout all layers 2.55, FC only 3.02, maxout 2.47. CIFAR-10 dropout all layers 12.61 vs baseline 15.60; maxout 11.68. CIFAR-100 dropout all layers 37.20 vs baseline 43.48; maxout 38.57. ImageNet ILSVRC-2010 Table 5: Conv Net+dropout 37.5/17.0 vs prior 47.1/28.2, 45.7/25.7. ILSVRC-2012: Avg 5 Conv Nets+dropout val 38.1/16.4 and test top-5 16.4; won ILSVRC-2012.

TIMIT Table 7 phone error: NN 6 layers 23.4; Dropout NN 6 layers 21.8; DBN-pretrained 4/6/8 layers 22.7/22.4/20.7; mcRBM-DBN 5 layers 20.5; DBN-pretrained+dropout 4 and 8 layers both 19.7. Reuters: best NN no dropout 31.05%, dropout 29.62%. Alternative Splicing Table 8 Code Quality: NN early stopping 440, Regression PCA 463, SVM PCA 487, NN dropout 567, Bayesian NN 623.

Regularizers on MNIST Table 9, 784-1024-1024-2048-10 ReLUs: L2 1.62; L2+L1 1.60; L2+KL sparsity 1.55; Max-norm 1.35; Dropout+L2 1.25; Dropout+Max-norm 1.05. Sec.7: MNIST autoencoders 256 ReLUs; hidden dropout p=0.5 yields more meaningful/sparse features. Fixed 2048x3 no input dropout error flat for p=0.4–0.8; fixed expected retained units p≈0.6 best, p=0.5 close. No improvement for 100/500 examples; gain increases then declines. MC test averaging around k=50 as good as weight scaling; after that MC slightly better within 1 SD.

Sec.9: Marginalizing dropout for linear regression with input retention p gives ||y-pXw||²+p(1-p)||Γw||²; reparam gives ||y-Xw~||²+((1-p)/p)||Γw~||². Table 10 Gaussian vs Bernoulli dropout: MNIST 0.95±0.04 vs 1.08±0.04; CIFAR-10 12.5±0.1 vs 12.6±0.1. Gaussian multiplier N(1,σ²), σ²=(1-p)/p, no test scaling.

Appendix practical: if n hidden units optimal for standard net, use at least n/p for dropout. Dropout often needs 10–100x LR; momentum 0.95–0.99; max-norm c typical 3–4. Hidden p typical 0.5–0.8; real-valued inputs typical 0.8.

Appendix details: MNIST held out 10K validation then recombined; hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8, momentum 0.95, c=2. SVHN: ~600K/26K, validation 6000, RGB standardized; best arch 3 conv (96/128/256, 5x5 stride 1, maxpool 3x3 stride 2) + two 2048 FC ReLU; dropout p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5); c=4; momentum 0.95. CIFAR App. B.3: 50K train/10K test; 5K validation then recombine; contrast norm per image/channel then ZCA; architecture/dropout rates same as SVHN except smaller input-layer learning rates; fragment mentions rotating it back. TIMIT App. B.4: Kaldi log-filter banks, monophone forced alignment; 21-frame windows; no speaker-dependent ops; mean centered/unit variance; input p=0.8 hidden p=0.5; c=4 for dropout NNs; momentum 0.95 LR 0.1 decay ε0(1+t/T)^−1; DBN RBMs CD-1; Gaussian RBM variance fixed 1; DBN+dropout finetune best LR about 0.01 and max-norm did not help. Reuters App. B.5: RCV1 >800K docs/103 classes; subset 402,738 docs, vocab 2000, 50 classes, one class/doc; equal train/test; dropout improved all architectures but less than image/speech due large data. Alternative Splicing App. B.6: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue types from 27 mouse tissues; targets are 4 softmax units, each 3 states inc/exc/nc; metric Code Quality sum p log(q/pbar); two-layer dropout net 1024 each, hidden p=0.5 input p=0.7, max-norm/high decaying LR; averaged over same 5 folds as Xiong et al.

Section 2 motivation details: Uses analogy to sexual reproduction (Livnat et al. 2010). Asexual reproduction might seem better for preserving co-adapted genes, but sexual reproduction may select for “mix-ability”/robustness: genes must work with random partners and not rely on large fixed co-adapted sets. Similarly, each hidden unit trained with dropout must work with a randomly chosen sample of other units, learn useful features on its own or with few others, and not rely on others to correct mistakes. Hidden units within a layer should still learn different things. Authors reject robustness by making many copies of each hidden unit as poor, analogous to replica codes being poor for noisy channels. Second analogy: successful conspiracies—ten conspiracies of five people likely better under non-stationary conditions than one conspiracy requiring fifty people; complex co-adaptations can fit training data but fail on novel test data more than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

Fig. 2: training unit present with probability p and outgoing weights w; test always present with outgoing weights pw.

Motivation: Sexual reproduction analogy: dropout selects hidden units/features that work with random partners (“mix-ability”) rather than complex co-adapted sets; units should still learn different things. Replica-code-like copying is rejected. Conspiracy analogy: multiple small co-adaptations may generalize better than one large fragile co-adaptation.

Related work: Dropout as stochastic regularization/noise. Denoising autoencoders add noise to inputs and reconstruct clean input; paper claims to extend by applying dropout/noise in hidden layers, interpreting as model averaging, applying to supervised learning, and to neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAEs typically best with 5% noise; authors say test-time weight scaling permits much higher noise: often optimal to drop 20% of inputs and 50% of hidden units. Deterministic counterpart obtained by marginalizing dropout noise: paper will show simple cases where dropout analytically marginalizes to deterministic regularizers. Related: van der Maaten et al. (2013) deterministic regularizers for exponential-family noise including “blankout” dropout, only inputs/no hidden layers; Wang & Manning (2013) speed up dropout by marginalizing noise; Chen et al. (2012) marginalization for denoising autoencoders. Also adversarial unit dropping by Globerson & Roweis/Dekel et al.: loss minimized when adversary picks units to drop with max number fixed; no hidden-unit models.

Formal model (Sec.4): Neural network with L hidden layers; l indexes hidden layers. y(0)=x input. z(l) inputs into layer l, y(l) outputs; W(l), b(l) weights/biases. Standard feedforward for l=0,...,L-1: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)), e.g. sigmoid f(x)=1/(1+exp(-x)). Dropout feedforward: sample r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p), form thinned outputs \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l) elementwise, then z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) \tilde y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). For any layer l, r^(l) independent Bernoulli variables with probability p of 1; sample/multiply outputs to create thinned outputs, used as next layer input. Applied at each layer, sampling a sub-network. Learning backpropagates derivatives through sampled sub-network. Test time scales weights as W_test^(l)=p W^(l) and uses resulting network without dropout.

steps.notes_before:
Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929-1958, “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” by Srivastava et al. Abstract claims dropout randomly drops units/connections during training to prevent co-adaptation; training samples exponentially many thinned networks; test approximates averaging predictions using one unthinned network with smaller weights; significantly reduces overfitting vs other regularizers; improves vision, speech, document classification, computational biology; obtains state-of-the-art on many benchmarks.

Intro/dropout definition: Dropout approximates equally weighted geometric mean/model averaging of exponentially many learned models sharing parameters. Dropping hidden/visible units means temporarily removing unit and incoming/outgoing connections. Each unit retained independently with probability p; p tunable, 0.5 often near optimal for hidden units; input retention usually closer to 1. Net with n units has 2^n thinned networks. Each training case samples a new thinned network. Test uses no-dropout net with outgoing weights scaled by retention probability p, to match expected training-time hidden output and combine 2^n networks. Fig. 2: training unit present with probability p and outgoing weights w; test always present with outgoing weights pw.

Motivation/related work: Dropout selects units/features that work with random partners (“mix-ability”), avoiding fragile co-adaptations. Related to stochastic regularization/noise, denoising autoencoders, marginalizing dropout noise, adversarial feature deletion. DAEs typically best with 5% noise; authors say test-time weight scaling permits much higher noise: often drop 20% inputs and 50% hidden units. Will show simple cases where dropout marginalizes to deterministic regularizers.

Formal model (Sec.4): Neural net with L hidden layers, y(0)=x. Standard feedforward: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). Dropout: sample r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p), create thinned outputs \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then feed forward using \tilde y. r variables independent with probability p of 1. Learning backpropagates through sampled sub-network. Test scales weights as W_test^(l)=p W^(l) and uses no dropout.

Sec.5.1 training: Dropout nets trained by SGD like standard nets, except each training case in a mini-batch samples a thinned network by dropping units. Forward/backprop only on that thinned network. Gradients averaged over mini-batch; unused parameters get zero gradient for that case. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay useful. Max-norm regularization especially useful: constrain incoming weight vector at each hidden unit to ||w||_2 ≤ c by projecting onto ball radius c when exceeded; c selected by validation. Max-norm improves SGD deep nets even without dropout. Dropout alone helps, but dropout + max-norm + large decaying learning rates + high momentum gives significant boost; justification: max-norm allows huge learning rates without weights blowing up, dropout noise explores weight space, decayed LR settles into minimum.

Sec.5.2 unsupervised pretraining: Nets can be pretrained with RBM stacks, autoencoders, DBMs; pretraining uses unlabeled data and can improve finetuning. Dropout can finetune pretrained nets; pretraining procedure unchanged. Part claims pretrained weights “should be scaled up by 1/(1-p)” so expected output under dropout matches pretraining output. This conflicts with earlier p=retention probability; preserving expected outgoing contribution would suggest 1/p, not 1/(1-p). Authors say stochastic dropout initially wiped pretrained info when finetuning LRs comparable to best LRs for random init, but with smaller LRs pretrained information retained and final generalization improved vs finetuning without dropout.

Table 1 gives dataset descriptions. Datasets listed: MNIST handwritten digits; TIMIT clean speech recognition; CIFAR-10/100 tiny natural images; SVHN house-number images; ImageNet natural images; Reuters-RCV1 newswire articles; Alternative Splicing RNA features for gene splicing prediction. Purpose: show dropout is general, not domain-specific. Key results in Sec.6; more detailed descriptions in Appendix B.

Structure ahead: Sec.6 experiments vs regularization/model combination; Sec.7 analysis/hyperparameters; Sec.8 Dropout RBM; Sec.9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A practical guide; Appendix B experiment details.

grade.reason: The first reported error directly identifies the incorrect 1/(1-p) scaling and correctly explains that retention p reduces expected contribution, so the correct reciprocal is 1/p.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines dropout training as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), and says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\). Earlier notes also record that the paper described weight scaling as an approximation to model averaging, not an exact equality.
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)] \ne f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). The equality would hold for the preactivation/weighted input, or for linear activations, but not for every hidden unit’s output under the stated general nonlinear model.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by \(1/(1-p)\), matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from §4: “independent Bernoulli gates \(r_j^{(l)}\sim Bernoulli(p)\)” and “Figure 2 says training unit present with probability \(p\) and weights \(w\), testing unit always present with outgoing weights \(pw\).”
errors.explanation: The paper previously defined \(p\) as the retention/presence probability, so dropout reduces the expected incoming signal by a factor of \(p\). To match a pretrained network’s expected output during dropout finetuning, weights would need scaling by \(1/p\), not \(1/(1-p)\).

errors.claim: “K9D (ILSVRC-2012) | Vision | 65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: The same table treats color images as having three channels: “A2F | Vision | 3072 (32 × 32 color)” and “J3V/W6R | Vision | 3072 (32 × 32 color),” where 32×32×3 = 3072. But 256×256 color would be 256×256×3 = 196608, not 65536.
errors.explanation: Within the table’s own dimensionality convention, the K9D dimensionality is inconsistent with the stated image size and color format.

errors.claim: “...extension to every layer improves it further, and L8J substitution further reduces error...”
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports for W6R: “Conv Net + max pooling + QX2 in all layers” = 37.20, while “Conv Net + L8J” = 38.57.
errors.explanation: If the statement is meant to summarize both J3V and W6R, it conflicts with the table: L8J reduces J3V error from 12.61 to 11.68, but increases W6R error from 37.20 to 38.57.

errors.claim: Prose comparison: “8-layer net” has “Pre-QX2 error” of 20.5%.
errors.location: this part, table immediately after Table 7
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” as 20.7%, while 20.5% is listed for “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010).”
errors.explanation: The 20.5% pre-QX2 error belongs to a 5-layer mcRBM-G6W-pretrained net, not the 8-layer G6W-pretrained net. If the prose comparison is for the 8-layer net, it conflicts with Table 7.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right).” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: The model was defined immediately above with exponent “\(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\)”, so \(\mathbf a\) is the hidden-unit bias vector and \(\mathbf b\) is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the stated joint distribution, the hidden conditional should use the hidden bias \(a_j\), and the visible conditional should use the visible bias \(b_i\). The displayed conditionals swap the bias symbols, creating an internal inconsistency.

errors.claim: “For a task whose optimal standard-net layer has n hidden units, a good QX2 layer should contain at least n/p units… only pn units remain in expectation.”
errors.evidence: The same paragraph says the QX2 layer should contain “at least n/p units” and the retention probability is p.
errors.explanation: If the dropout/QX2 layer has n/p units and each is retained with probability p, the expected number retained is p·(n/p)=n, not pn. The “only pn units remain” statement is inconsistent with the paragraph’s own sizing heuristic unless n has silently changed meaning.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958. Main defs: dropout randomly removes units/connections during training; p is retention probability; r~Bernoulli(p). Test uses full net with weights scaled by p to approximate averaging thinned nets. Earlier internal issues: §4 opening claimed expected hidden output under deletion equals reduced-weight test output, conflicting with nonlinear activations except linear/preactivation case. §5.2 says pretrained weights multiplied by 1/(1-p) to match random removal, but with p=retention should be 1/p. Table1: ImageNet dimension 65536 conflicts with “256×256 color” convention (should include ×3). §8.1 RBM conditionals swap visible/hidden biases relative to joint.

Training: per-case masks; unused params get zero gradient. Dropout helps; high momentum, large decaying LR, max-norm ||w||2<=c help. §6 data: improvement over non-dropout neural nets on all tested data. Vision: MNIST Table2 best DBN+dropout 0.79; SAE+dropout 0.92; dropout/max-norm NN down to 0.95; maxout 0.94. SVHN Table3 best ConvNet+maxout 2.47, +dropout all layers 2.55, human 2.0. §7: Dropout autoencoder features more meaningful; sparse hidden activations mean ~0.7 vs no dropout ~2.0. §11 conclusion: dropout samples/trains smaller submodels from overfittable large model; state of art on several datasets/tasks; training 2–3× standard net. Appendix A practical guide: QX2=dropout-like, V9C=max-norm. B.3 CIFAR-10/100: 50k train/10k test, 5k validation; GCN/channel then ZCA; arch/retention match SVHN. B.4 TIMIT: 680 speakers, 8 dialects, 10 sentences; Kaldi log-filter banks; monophone labels; 21-frame windows; input p=.8, hidden p=.5, max-norm c=4, momentum .95, LR .1 decay; pretraining U2L CD-1, Gaussian-U2L input variance fixed 1; best QX2 finetune LR about .01; max-norm during finetuning no improvement. Abstract claims: Large parameter-rich deep neural nets overfit; test-time combining independently trained large models is slow/obstructed. Dropout temporarily removes randomly selected units and their connections during training, inhibits excessive co-adaptation, and samples exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. A single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of these networks. Keywords: neural networks, regularization, model combination, deep learning.

Introduction details: With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is presented as best regularization for a fixed-sized model. Dropout is proposed as a cheaper approximation to an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models’ predictions. An n-unit network represents 2^n possible thinned networks while retaining only O(n^2) or fewer parameters via weight sharing. For every presentation of each training case a new thinned member is sampled/trained, so each particular member is trained rarely if ever. Multilayer nonlinear hidden representations can learn complicated relationships but limited-data sampling noise can create relationships present in train but absent in genuine test data, even from same distribution. Prior/standard responses: early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 and L2 penalties; these constrain parameters rather than averaging every parameter setting.

Model combination: usually improves performance, but training/output averaging of many large nets is expensive; diversity requires different architectures or data, hyperparameters are architecture-specific/difficult, training is computationally costly, data requirements may preclude subset training, and inference may be infeasible for rapid response. Practical dropout inference rule is weight scaling: use one unthinned network rather than explicitly evaluating exponentially many members. More expensive alternative: Monte-Carlo model averaging of sampled thinned members’ predictions. Claim: weight scaling/dropout gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularization methods across varied classification problems. Dropout extends beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models including Boltzmann Machines; Restricted Boltzmann Machines can have Dropout RBM form with shared parameters.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines dropout training as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), and says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\). Earlier notes also record that the paper described weight scaling as an approximation to model averaging, not an exact equality.
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)] \ne f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). The equality would hold for the preactivation/weighted input, or for linear activations, but not for every hidden unit’s output under the stated general nonlinear model.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by \(1/(1-p)\), matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”

errors.explanation: The paper previously defined \(p\) as the retention/presence probability, so dropout reduces the expected incoming signal by a factor of \(p\). To match a pretrained network’s expected output during dropout finetuning, weights would need scaling by \(1/p\), not \(1/(1-p)\).

errors.claim: “P(hj = 1|rj, v) = 1(rj = 1) σ(bj + Σi Wij vi)” and “P(vi = 1|h) = σ(ai + Σj Wij hj)”
