final_notes:
Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929-1958, “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting.” Dropout randomly drops units during training; original retaining prob p and test full net with outgoing weights scaled by p. Inverted dropout: retained activations ×1/p during training, no test scaling. Hidden p=0.5 often optimal; input p closer to 1. Dropout discourages co-adaptations/encourages robust mixable features.

Training: SGD with sampled thinned net; backprop only through retained units. Momentum, annealed LR, L2 useful. Max-norm constrains incoming weights ||w||≤c. Dropout+max-norm+large decaying LR/high momentum gives gains. Pretraining can be followed by dropout finetuning; pretrained weights scaled up by 1/p first.

Sec.6 claims dropout improves generalization on all datasets vs standard NNs. Datasets: MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, TIMIT, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing. ImageNet table listed 65536 “256×256 color” despite color-channel dimensionality issue.

MNIST/Table 2: Standard NN logistic 2×800 1.60%; dropout logistic 3×1024 1.35; dropout ReLU 3×1024 1.25; dropout+max-norm ReLU 3×1024 1.06; 3×2048 1.04; 2×4096 1.01; 2×8192 0.95; maxout 0.94; DBN+dropout 0.92; DBM+dropout 0.79, claimed best permutation-invariant MNIST. Internal error: text says maxout “worsened” to 0.94 though table improves over 0.95. Fig.4/B.1: all combinations of 2,3,4 hidden layers with 1024 or 2048 units = 6 architectures; MNIST uses p=0.5 hidden, p=0.8 input, final momentum 0.95, max-norm c=2. MNIST protocol: 60k train/10k test; hold out 10k validation for hyperparams, then recombine and train 1M updates. 2/3-layer nets with 4096/8192 tried; 2-layer improved as Table 2, 3-layer slightly worse unless more dropout but still not better.

SVHN/Table 3: ConvNet+max-pooling 3.95; +dropout FC 3.02; stochastic pooling 2.80; +dropout all layers 2.55; maxout 2.47; human 2.0. B.2: ~600k train/26k test; validation 6000 (400/class standard + 200/class extra); RGB normalized zero mean/unit variance; no contrast norm/ZCA benefit. Best architecture: conv layers 96/128/256 filters, 5×5 stride 1; each followed by 3×3 max pool stride 2; two FC layers 2048; ReLU. Dropout all layers p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5) input→conv→FC; max-norm c=4; momentum .95. Validation not recombined; report smallest validation error.

CIFAR/Table 4 CIFAR-10/100: ConvNet max pooling 15.60/43.48; stochastic pooling 15.13/42.51; Snoek 14.98/–; +dropout FC 14.32/41.26; +dropout all layers 12.61/37.20; maxout 11.68/38.57. No augmentation except input dropout; also describes translation/rotation augmentation with architecture/dropout same as SVHN except smaller input-layer learning rates. B.3: CIFAR 50k train/10k test, 32×32 color, 10/100 classes; 5k validation then recombined like MNIST; preprocessing global contrast normalization per image/channel then ZCA whitening.

ImageNet: ILSVRC-2010 Table 5 top1/top5: Sparse Coding 47.1/28.2; SIFT+Fisher 45.7/25.7; ConvNet+dropout 37.5/17.0. ILSVRC-2012 Table 6: feature systems test top5 27.3/26.2; ConvNet+dropout val 40.7/18.2; average 5 ConvNets+dropout val 38.1/16.4, test top5 16.4. Text: convnets+dropout won ILSVRC-2012.

TIMIT/Table 7 phone error: NN 6 layers 23.4; Dropout NN 6 layers 21.8; DBN-pretrained 4/6/8 layers 22.7/22.4/20.7; mcRBM-DBN 5 layers 20.5; DBN 4 + dropout 19.7; DBN 8 + dropout 19.7. Internal error: text says 8-layer error reduces from 20.5 to 19.7, but 8-layer baseline is 20.7; 20.5 is 5-layer mcRBM. B.4: Kaldi log-filter banks; monophone forced alignment; 21-frame windows, predict central frame; no speaker-dependent ops; inputs mean-centered/unit variance. Similarly, each hidden unit trained with dropout must work with a randomly chosen sample of other units, learn useful features on its own or with few others, and not rely on others to correct mistakes. Second analogy: successful conspiracies—ten conspiracies of five people likely better under non-stationary conditions than one conspiracy requiring fifty people; complex co-adaptations can fit training data but fail on novel test data more than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

Related work: Dropout as stochastic regularization/noise. Denoising autoencoders add noise to inputs and reconstruct clean input; paper claims to extend by applying dropout/noise in hidden layers, interpreting as model averaging, applying to supervised learning, and to neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAEs typically best with 5% noise; authors say test-time weight scaling permits much higher noise: often optimal to drop 20% of inputs and 50% of hidden units. Formal model (Sec.4): Neural network with L hidden layers; l indexes hidden layers. y(0)=x input. z(l) inputs into layer l, y(l) outputs; W(l), b(l) weights/biases. For any layer l, r^(l) independent Bernoulli variables with probability p of 1; sample/multiply outputs to create thinned outputs, used as next layer input. Applied at each layer, sampling a sub-network. Learning backpropagates derivatives through sampled sub-network. steps.notes_before:
Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929-1958, “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” by Srivastava et al. Abstract/intro claims dropout randomly drops units/connections during training to prevent co-adaptation; samples thinned networks sharing weights; test approximates averaging with unthinned net with outgoing weights scaled by retention probability p. Claims improves vision, speech, document classification, computational biology; SOTA on many benchmarks.

Dropout definition/formal model: Dropping hidden/visible units temporarily removes unit and incoming/outgoing connections. Each unit retained independently with probability p (hidden p=0.5 often near optimal; input retention closer to 1). Net with n units has 2^n thinned networks. Training samples new thinned network per case. Test uses no-dropout network with W_test^(l)=p W^(l), matching expected training hidden output. Formal: y(0)=x; standard z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Dropout samples r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), uses \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l) into next layer; backprop through sampled subnetwork.

Motivation/related work: Encourages features that work with random partners (“mix-ability”), not fragile co-adaptations. Related to stochastic regularization/noise/DAEs, but extends to hidden layers, supervised learning, model averaging, Boltzmann machines. DAEs usually best with 5% noise; dropout often optimal dropping 20% inputs/50% hidden due to test-time scaling. Related marginalization/noise/adversarial dropping works mostly input/no hidden or adversarial fixed dropped units.

Sec.5 training: Dropout nets trained by SGD. For each training case in mini-batch, sample thinned net; forward/backprop only through it. Gradients averaged; unused params get zero gradient for that case. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 useful. Max-norm regularization constrains incoming weight vector at each hidden unit to ||w||2≤c; project if exceeds. Dropout alone helps, but dropout+max-norm+large decaying learning rates+high momentum gives big boost.

Sec.5.2 pretraining: Nets can be pretrained with RBMs/autoencoders/DBMs; dropout can finetune pretrained nets; pretraining unchanged. Pretrained weights should be scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected dropout output equals pretraining output. Smaller finetuning learning rates retained pretrained information and improved final generalization vs no dropout finetuning.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines dropout training as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), and says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\). Earlier notes also record that the paper described weight scaling as an approximation to model averaging, not an exact equality.
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)] \ne f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). The equality would hold for the preactivation/weighted input, or for linear activations, but not for every hidden unit’s output under the stated general nonlinear model.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p, matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier §4 equations in notes define unit output as nonlinear: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z), and dropout uses \tilde y=r*y before applying f. Notes also record that the earlier claim that expected hidden-unit output under deletion equals test-time output conflicts with the nonlinear f equations; equality only holds generally for preactivations/linear cases.
errors.explanation: Multiplying incoming weights by 1/p makes the expected preactivation match the pretrained preactivation, but with nonlinear f it does not generally make the expected unit output match the pretrained output.

errors.claim: “K9D (ILSVRC-2012) | Vision | 65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image has 256 × 256 × 3 = 196,608 dimensions, not 65,536; 65,536 equals 256 × 256 for a single-channel image.
errors.explanation: The dimensionality entry conflicts with the parenthetical description “256 × 256 color.”

errors.claim: “substitution of another activation class (L8J: maxout) worsens them”
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports “QX2 NN + V9C | F3N | 2 layers, 8192 units | 0.95” and then “QX2 NN + V9C (Goodfellow et al., 2013) | L8J | 2 layers, (5 × 240) units | 0.94.”
errors.explanation: Since lower error is better, the maxout/L8J result improves on 0.95 rather than worsening it.

errors.claim: “Prose comparison | 8-layer net | 20.5%” / the prose comparison gives the pre-QX2 error for the 8-layer net as 20.5%.
errors.location: this part, Table 7/prose comparison for N8Q
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7” and “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010) | 20.5.”
errors.explanation: The 20.5% value belongs to the 5-layer mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN, not the 8-layer G6W-pretrained NN. The 8-layer pre-QX2 error in the table is 20.7%.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L energy just above is defined as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), so a is the hidden-unit bias vector and b is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the model definition, the hidden conditional should use the hidden bias a_j, not b_j. This is also dimensionally inconsistent because b indexes visible units, not hidden units.

errors.claim: “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L energy is exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), so b is the visible-unit bias vector and a is the hidden-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the stated energy, the visible conditional should use the visible bias b_i, not a_i. This contradicts the parameter roles defined in the same subsection.

final_notes:
Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958. Authors: Srivastava et al.

Core definitions/claims: Dropout randomly removes units/connections during training, samples exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned nets, reduces co-adaptation. Test-time uses one unthinned net with outgoing weights scaled by retention probability p, approximating averaging/geometric mean. Hidden and visible/input units can be dropped; gates independent Bernoulli with common p. Main claim: dropout/weight scaling gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied classification tasks. Internal issue noted: paper sometimes equates expected nonlinear hidden-unit output under dropout with reduced-weight output, generally false except for preactivations/linear units.

Training (§5): Dropout alone helps; high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and max-norm incoming-weight constraint help further. SGD samples different thinned net per case; gradients averaged; unused parameters get zero contribution. Max-norm projects incoming hidden-unit weights to ||w||₂≤c. For pretraining, pretrained weights multiplied by 1/p before dropout finetuning to match expected preactivation, though nonlinear-output expectation phrasing is inconsistent. Dropout training typically takes 2–3× as long as standard same architecture.

§6 experiments: datasets MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, TIMIT, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing. Internal arithmetic issue: ImageNet listed as 65536 “256×256 color,” conflicting with 256×256×3=196608. §6 says dropout improves over non-dropout neural nets on every tested dataset; state-of-art models on all five vision collections use dropout; conclusion says state of art on four named/anonymized datasets.

MNIST: Table 2 best errors include dropout+max-norm ReLU 0.95, maxout 0.94, DBN+dropout 0.92, DBM?+dropout 0.79. Internal error: prose says maxout worsens but table shows 0.94 vs previous 0.95. Appendix B.1: 10k validation held out, 1M updates endpoint, hidden p=0.5/input p=0.8, momentum 0.95, max-norm c=2. Retention comparison no input corruption; fixed expected widths pn=256 first two hidden, pn=512 last. MC averages k thinned nets per test case.

SVHN: Table 3 conv+maxpool 3.95; +dropout FC 3.02; stochastic pooling 2.80; +dropout all layers 2.55; +maxout 2.47. Appendix: validation 400/class standard + 200/class extra = 6000; architecture 3 conv layers 96/128/256, max-pool after each, two FC 2048; retentions (0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5); max-norm c=4; momentum 0.95.

CIFAR: CIFAR-10 dropout FC 14.32, all layers 12.61, maxout 11.68; CIFAR-100 dropout FC 41.26, all layers 37.20, maxout 38.57 (maxout worse than all-layer dropout). Appendix: 50k train/10k test; 5k validation then combined validation/training; global contrast normalization and ZCA; architecture/retentions match SVHN.

ImageNet: ConvNet+dropout won ILSVRC-2012; ILSVRC-2010 ConvNet+dropout 37.5/17.0 top1/top5; 2012 avg 5 ConvNets+dropout test top5 16.4.

TIMIT: Table 7: NN 6 layers 23.4; dropout NN 6 layers 21.8; G6W-pretrained NN 4/6/8 layers 22.7/22.4/20.7; mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN 5 layers 20.5; G6W-pretrained NN 4+dropout 19.7; 8+dropout 19.7. Internal error: prose says 8-layer pre-dropout error 20.5, table gives 20.7. Appendix: 680 speakers, 8 dialects, 10 sentences each; Kaldi log-filter banks; monophone labels; no speaker-dependent operations; inputs mean-centered/unit-variance. TIMIT settings: 21 consecutive frames/window, input p=0.8, hidden p=0.5, max-norm/V9C c=4 all layers, momentum 0.95, high LR 0.1 with decay ε0(1+t/T)^-1; G6W pretraining = U2L CD-1; Gaussian-U2L input variance fixed 1; best QX2 G6W-finetuning LR about 0.01; adding V9C during G6W finetuning gave no improvement.

Reuters/M5X: best NN without dropout 31.05%, with dropout 29.62%. Full corpus >800k docs, 103 tree classes; subset 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocab, 50 disjoint categories, one category per document; equal train/test splits give >200k training examples.

Alternative Splicing/Z7P: Code Quality bits higher better: NN early stopping 440; Regression PCA 463; SVM PCA 487; NN dropout 567; Bayesian NN 623. Data: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue types from 27 mouse tissues. Four target softmax units, one per tissue; states inc/exc/nc. C4Y sums p log(q/bar p). QX2 NN has two 1024-unit layers; hidden p=0.5, input p=0.7; V9C + high decaying learning rates; averaged over same 5 folds as Xiong et al. QX2 hidden scale 1000s, Bayesian-network hidden scale few tens.

Standard regularizers MNIST Table 9: plain NN 1.62; early stopping 1.60; KL-sparsity 1.55; weight decay 1.35; dropout+plain 1.25; dropout+weight decay 1.05.

§7: Autoencoder MNIST dropout p=0.5 yields edge/stroke/spot detectors; sparse activations no-dropout mean ~2.0, dropout ~0.7. Retention error flat 0.4≤p≤0.8, rises near p=1; fixed-width p=0.1 error 2.7%, fixed expected retained width 1.7%; best near p=0.6. Dataset-size: no improvement on two smallest subsets; gain increases then decreases. MC averaging about as good around k=50, then slightly better within one SD.

§8 Dropout RBM-like model: hidden retention r, dropped h_j=0, CD-1. Internal error §8.1: energy has a^T h + b^T v, so hidden conditional should use a_j and visible conditional b_i, but text swaps them. Dropout RBM features coarser/fewer dead units/sparser.

§9 linear marginalization gives objective ||y-Xw~||² + ((1-p)/p)||Γw~||². §10 Gaussian dropout: match σ²=(1-p)/p; no test scaling; Gaussian works as well or better. Appendix A: dropout nets need tuning; layer at least n/p units; high LRs 10–100× standard, momentum 0.95–0.99, max-norm c 3–4; hidden p 0.5–0.8; real-valued inputs often 0.8; input optimum closer to 1 than 0.5.

An n-unit net represents 2^n thinned nets but only O(n^2) or fewer parameters. Each training case samples/trains a new thinned network, so any member rarely/never trained. Practical dropout inference: weight scaling in one unthinned net rather than evaluating exponentially many members; alternative Monte Carlo model averaging. Claim: dropout/weight scaling gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied classification problems. Dropout extends to graphical models including RBMs/Dropout RBM.

§2 Motivation: Sexual reproduction analogy. Random partners discourage complex co-adaptations and encourage robust, individually useful hidden units. Replication is poor robustness; multiple simple co-adaptations generalize better than large fragile ones.

§3 Related work: Dropout as adding noise to hidden-unit states; extends denoising autoencoders by hidden-layer corruption, model-averaging interpretation, supervised/unsupervised use, applicability beyond feed-forward nets. Test-time weight scaling permits higher noise than DAEs. Typical best DAE noise 5%; dropout often optimal input removal 20%; hidden removal 50%. Stochastic minimization under noise distribution vs adversarial deletion. Marginalizing dropout gives deterministic regularizers in simple cases; prior work includes blankout noise/marginalized DAEs.

Apply at every layer to sample subnetwork; backprop derivatives through that subnetwork. Hidden and visible/input units can both be removed. Opening sentence of this part claimed expected hidden-unit output under training deletion distribution equals test-time output under reduced weights, but this conflicts with nonlinear f equations and with earlier approximation wording; equality only applies to preactivation/linear case generally. Retention choices independent with common p in simplest construction; validation can choose p; usual default close to optimal across many tasks/networks; optimal input retention generally nearer complete retention.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L energy just above is defined as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), so a is the hidden-unit bias vector and b is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the model definition, the hidden conditional should use the hidden bias a_j, not b_j. This is also dimensionally inconsistent because b indexes visible units, not hidden units.

errors.claim: “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L energy is exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), so b is the visible-unit bias vector and a is the hidden-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the stated energy, the visible conditional should use the visible bias b_i, not a_i. This contradicts the parameter roles defined in the same subsection.

final_notes:
Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929-1958, “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting.” Dropout randomly drops units/connections during training; each presentation samples thinned net; test approximates averaging using unthinned net with outgoing weights scaled by retention p. Alternative inverted dropout: scale retained activations by 1/p during training and no test-time scaling. Hidden p often 0.5; input closer to 1, e.g. 0.8 real-valued. Training uses SGD, momentum, annealed LR, L2; max-norm constrains incoming weights ||w||2≤c. Pretrained weights scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetuning.

Sec.6 datasets/Table 1: MNIST 784, train 60K/test 10K; SVHN 3072, 600K/26K; CIFAR-10/100 3072, train 60K/test 10K; ImageNet ILSVRC-2012 dim 65536 (256×256 color), train 1.2M/test 150K; TIMIT 2520, 1.1M/58K; Reuters 2000, 200K/200K; Alternative Splicing 1014, 2932/733. Internal errors: ImageNet 256×256 color should be 196608 if counted as for CIFAR/SVHN; Appendix B.3 says CIFAR-10/100 have 50K training/test 10K, conflicting with Table 1’s 60K train. Sec.6 says dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs no-dropout neural nets.

MNIST/Table 2: dropout results include logistic 3×1024 1.35; ReLU 3×1024 1.25; dropout+max-norm ReLU 3×1024 1.06, 3×2048 1.04, 2×4096 1.01, 2×8192 0.95; maxout dropout+max-norm 0.94. Pretrained: DBN+finetune 1.18; DBM+finetune 0.96; DBN+dropout 0.92; DBM+dropout 0.79. DBM-pretrained dropout 0.79% best permutation-invariant MNIST. Appendix B.1: MNIST 60K train/10K test, held out 10K train for validation, tuned so best validation after 1M updates, then recombined validation+training and trained 1M updates. For Fig.4 architectures all 2/3/4-layer with 1024/2048 units (6 total); for all incl Table 2 used hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8, final momentum 0.95, max-norm c=2. 2/3-layer 4096/8192 tested; 2-layer improved as Table 2; 3-layer worse than 2-layer at same dropout, more dropout helped but not enough.

SVHN/Table 3: best dropout CNN: 3 conv+maxpool then 2 FC, dropout all layers p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5), max-norm. Errors: conv+maxpool 3.95; +dropout FC 3.02; stochastic pooling 2.80; +dropout all layers 2.55; maxout 2.47; human 2.0. Appendix B.2: approx 600K train/26K test; validation 6000 = 400/class standard + 200/class extra; RGB pixels normalized zero mean/unit variance; no benefit from contrast norm/ZCA. Best architecture conv filters 96/128/256, 5×5 stride1, maxpool 3×3 stride2; FC 2048,2048; ReLU; p as above; max-norm c=4, momentum .95; did not recombine validation due to large training set, reported model with smallest validation error.

CIFAR Table 4 errors CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100: conv maxpool 15.60/43.48; stochastic pooling 15.13/42.51; Snoek 14.98/–; dropout FC 14.32/41.26; dropout all layers 12.61/37.20; maxout 11.68/38.57. Appendix B.3: says CIFAR-10/100 have 50K train/10K test each, 10/100 categories, 32×32 color; used 5K train for validation then recombined like MNIST; preprocessing global contrast normalization per image/channel then ZCA whitening; augment by translations/reflections and rotations, then rotate back; architecture/dropout same as SVHN except smaller input-layer learning rates.

ImageNet: Table 5 ILSVRC-2010 test: Sparse Coding 47.1/28.2; SIFT+Fisher 45.7/25.7; Conv Net+dropout 37.5/17.0. Table 6 ILSVRC-2012: Conv Net+dropout val 40.7/18.2; Avg 5 Conv Nets+dropout val 38.1/16.4, test top-5 16.4.

TIMIT/Table 7 PER: NN 6 layers 23.4; Dropout NN 6 layers 21.8; DBN-pretrained NN 4/6/8 layers 22.7/22.4/20.7; mcRBM-DBN-pretrained NN 5 layers 20.5; DBN-pretrained 4+dropout 19.7; DBN-pretrained 8+dropout 19.7. Internal inconsistency: text says 8-layer error reduces from 20.5 to 19.7, but table says 8-layer baseline is 20.7; 20.5 is 5-layer mcRBM-DBN. Appendix B.4: Kaldi log-filter banks; 21-frame windows predict central frame; no speaker-dependent operations; inputs mean-centered/unit variance; dropout p=0.8 input, 0.5 hidden; max-norm c=4 all layers; momentum .95, LR .1 with decay ε0(1+t/T)^−1; DBN RBMs CD-1, Gaussian visible variance fixed 1; DBN finetune with dropout needed smaller LR ~.01; max-norm did not help.

Reuters: 50 disjoint topics. Best NN without dropout 31.05%; with dropout 29.62%. Appendix B.5: RCV1 has >800K docs, 103 hierarchical classes; subset 402,738 articles, vocab 2000 words, 50 categories, exactly one class per doc, equal train/test; dropout improved classification across many architectures but less than image/speech, perhaps because >200K training examples.

Alternative Splicing/Table 8: Code Quality = negative KL divergence / higher better. Results: NN early stopping 440; Regression PCA 463; SVM PCA 487; NN dropout 567; Bayesian NN 623. Internal inconsistency: text says Bayesian NNs perform worse than dropout/dropout outperforms all other methods, but table/metric show Bayesian NN better. Appendix B.6: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue types from 27 mouse tissues; target has 4 softmax units (one/tissue), each 3 states inc/exc/nc; metric sums p_i,t^s log(q_t^s(r_i)/pbar^s); two-layer dropout net 1024 each; p=0.5 hidden, 0.7 input; max-norm/high decaying LR; averaged over same 5 folds as Xiong et al.

Sec.6.5/Table 9 MNIST regularizers same ReLU 784-1024-1024-2048-10: L2 1.62; L2+L1 late 1.60; L2+KL-sparsity 1.55; Max-norm 1.35; Dropout+L2 1.25; Dropout+Max-norm 1.05. Sec.7: autoencoders similar reconstruction, dropout features more meaningful/sparse. Retaining p on MNIST fixed 784-2048-2048-2048-10 no input dropout: p too small underfits, 0.4–0.8 flat, p=1 worse. Keeping pn constant small p much better than fixed-n; best ~0.6. Dataset size: no gain for 100/500, gain increases then declines. MC averaging ~k=50 equals weight scaling; after that MC slightly better within 1 SD.

Sec.8 Dropout RBMs. RBM energy implies P(h,v)=1/Z exp(vᵀWh+aᵀh+bᵀv), so a hidden biases, b visible biases. Internal inconsistency: Sec.8.1 conditionals swap biases, using bj for P(hj=1|rj,v) and ai for P(vi=1|h). Sec.9 marginal dropout linear regression gives ridge-like penalty p(1-p)||Γw||²; absorbed p penalty ((1-p)/p)||Γw~||². Sec.10 Gaussian dropout: MNIST 2×1024 Bernoulli 1.08±0.04, Gaussian 0.95±0.04; CIFAR-10 Bernoulli 12.6±0.1, Gaussian 12.5±0.1; Gaussian r′~N(1,σ²), σ²=(1-p)/p matches inverted Bernoulli.

Conclusion: dropout improved object/digit/speech/document/biology tasks; claims state-of-art on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST; dropout training 2–3× slower. Appendix heuristics: dropout layer at least n/p units if standard optimal n; LR often 10–100× standard, momentum .95–.99; max-norm c 3–4; hidden p .5–.8; real inputs p .8.

Dropout prevents overfitting and efficiently approximates combining exponentially many different neural network architectures.

Thinned networks: Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network consisting of units that survived dropout (Figure 1b). A net with n units can be seen as a collection of 2^n possible thinned networks. These share weights, so total parameters remain O(n^2) or less. For each presentation of each training case, a new thinned network is sampled and trained; each thinned network is trained very rarely, if at all.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned models is infeasible. Instead use a single neural net without dropout, with scaled-down trained weights. If a unit is retained with probability p during training, its outgoing weights are multiplied by p at test time (Figure 2). The paper claims this ensures that for any hidden unit the expected output under training-time dropout distribution is the same as actual output at test time. By this scaling, 2^n shared-weight networks can be combined into one test-time network. Authors claim training with dropout plus this approximate averaging gives significantly lower generalization error across many classification problems than other regularization methods.

Abstract claims: dropout randomly drops units/connections during training to prevent co-adaptation; training samples exponentially many thinned networks; test approximates averaging predictions using one unthinned network with smaller weights; significantly reduces overfitting and improves over other regularizers; improves supervised learning in vision, speech recognition, document classification, computational biology; obtains state-of-the-art on many benchmarks.

Intro/motivation: Deep nets with multiple nonlinear hidden layers are expressive but overfit with limited data; regularization includes early stopping, L1/L2, soft weight sharing. Bayesian model averaging is gold standard but expensive. Authors aim to approximate an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions of exponentially many learned models sharing parameters. Averaging many separately trained large nets is too expensive, and diversity usually requires different architectures/training data.

Dropout definition/claims: “Dropping out” units (hidden and visible) means temporarily removing a unit and all incoming/outgoing connections. Units are dropped randomly. Simplest: each unit retained independently with probability p; p can be tuned or set to 0.5, close to optimal for many networks/tasks. For input units, optimal retention probability usually closer to 1 than 0.5. Dropout prevents overfitting and efficiently approximates combining exponentially many architectures.

Thinned networks/test-time: Applying dropout samples a thinned network of surviving units. A net with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks; shared weights keep parameters O(n^2) or less. For each presentation of each training case, a new thinned network is sampled/trained; each thinned network is trained rarely if at all. Explicit averaging over thinned models infeasible. Instead use one no-dropout net with weights scaled down: if a unit retained with probability p during training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test time. Claimed to make expected training-time output of any hidden unit equal actual test-time output and combine 2^n shared-weight networks into one test-time network.

Figures/structure: Fig. 1 standard net with 2 hidden layers and example thinned net. Fig. 2 training unit present with probability p and outgoing weights w; test always present with outgoing weights pw. Structure: Sec.2 motivation; Sec.3 previous work; Sec.4 formal model; Sec.5 training algorithm; Sec.6 experiments across domains vs regularization/model combination; Sec.7 analysis/hyperparameters; Sec.8 Dropout RBM; Sec.9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A practical guide.

Extension: Dropout can apply beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models such as Boltzmann Machines. Introduces dropout RBM and compares with standard RBM; experiments reportedly show dropout RBMs better in certain respects.

Section 2 motivation details: Uses analogy to sexual reproduction (Livnat et al. 2010). Asexual reproduction might seem better for preserving co-adapted genes, but sexual reproduction may select for “mix-ability”/robustness: genes must work with random partners and not rely on large fixed co-adapted sets. Similarly, each hidden unit trained with dropout must work with a randomly chosen sample of other units, learn useful features on its own or with few others, and not rely on others to correct mistakes. Hidden units within a layer should still learn different things. Authors reject robustness by making many copies of each hidden unit as poor, analogous to replica codes being poor for noisy channels. Second analogy: successful conspiracies—ten conspiracies of five people likely better under non-stationary conditions than one conspiracy requiring fifty people; complex co-adaptations can fit training data but fail on novel test data more than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

Start of Sec.3 Related Work: Dropout can be interpreted as regularizing a neural net by adding noise to hidden units. Adding noise to unit states was previously used in Denoising Autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010), where noise ... [continues].

Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929-1958, “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” by Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov. Abstract claims dropout randomly drops units/connections during training to prevent co-adaptation; training samples exponentially many thinned networks; test approximates averaging predictions using one unthinned network with smaller weights; significantly reduces overfitting vs other regularizers; improves supervised learning in vision, speech recognition, document classification, computational biology; obtains state-of-the-art on many benchmarks.

Intro/dropout definition: Deep nets overfit with limited data; dropout approximates equally weighted geometric mean/model averaging of exponentially many learned models sharing parameters. Dropping out hidden and visible units means temporarily removing unit and incoming/outgoing connections. Each unit retained independently with probability p; p tunable or 0.5 often near optimal for hidden units; input retention usually closer to 1. Applying dropout samples a thinned network. A net with n units has 2^n thinned networks; shared weights keep parameters O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned network; explicit averaging infeasible. Test uses no-dropout net with outgoing weights scaled by retention probability p, intended to match expected training-time hidden output and combine 2^n networks. Fig. 2: training unit present with probability p and outgoing weights w; test always present with outgoing weights pw.

Motivation: Sexual reproduction analogy: dropout selects hidden units/features that work with random partners (“mix-ability”) rather than complex co-adapted sets; units should still learn different things. Replica-code-like copying is rejected. Conspiracy analogy: multiple small co-adaptations may generalize better than one large fragile co-adaptation.

Related work: Dropout as stochastic regularization/noise. Denoising autoencoders add noise to inputs and reconstruct clean input; paper claims to extend by applying dropout/noise in hidden layers, interpreting as model averaging, applying to supervised learning, and to neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAEs typically best with 5% noise; authors say test-time weight scaling permits much higher noise: often optimal to drop 20% of inputs and 50% of hidden units. Deterministic counterpart obtained by marginalizing dropout noise: paper will show simple cases where dropout analytically marginalizes to deterministic regularizers. Related: van der Maaten et al. (2013) deterministic regularizers for exponential-family noise including “blankout” dropout, only inputs/no hidden layers; Wang & Manning (2013) speed up dropout by marginalizing noise; Chen et al. (2012) marginalization for denoising autoencoders. Also adversarial unit dropping by Globerson & Roweis/Dekel et al.: loss minimized when adversary picks units to drop with max number fixed; no hidden-unit models.

Formal model (Sec.4): Neural network with L hidden layers; l indexes hidden layers. y(0)=x input. z(l) inputs into layer l, y(l) outputs; W(l), b(l) weights/biases. Standard feedforward for l=0,...,L-1: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)), e.g. sigmoid f(x)=1/(1+exp(-x)). Dropout feedforward: sample r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p), form thinned outputs \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l) elementwise, then z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) \tilde y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). For any layer l, r^(l) independent Bernoulli variables with probability p of 1; sample/multiply outputs to create thinned outputs, used as next layer input. Applied at each layer, sampling a sub-network. Learning backpropagates derivatives through sampled sub-network. Test time scales weights as W_test^(l)=p W^(l) and uses resulting network without dropout.

Dropout can extend to graphical models/Boltzmann Machines; dropout RBM compared with standard RBM and reportedly better in certain respects.

Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929-1958, “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” by Srivastava et al. Abstract/intro claims dropout randomly drops units/connections during training to prevent co-adaptation; each presentation samples a thinned network from exponentially many sharing weights; test approximates averaging predictions using one unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by retention probability p. Significantly reduces overfitting and improves vision, speech recognition, document classification, computational biology; obtains SOTA on many benchmarks.

Dropout definition/formal model: Dropping hidden/visible units means temporarily removing unit and incoming/outgoing connections. Each unit retained independently with probability p (hidden p=0.5 often near optimal; input retention closer to 1). Net with n units has 2^n thinned networks. Training samples new thinned network per case. Test: no-dropout network with W_test^(l)=p W^(l), matching expected training-time hidden output. Formal: y(0)=x; standard z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Dropout samples r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), uses \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l) into next layer; backprop through sampled subnetwork.

Motivation/related work: Dropout encourages features that work with random partners (“mix-ability”), not fragile co-adaptations. Related to stochastic regularization/noise and denoising autoencoders, but extends noise/dropout to hidden layers, supervised learning, model averaging, Boltzmann machines. DAEs usually best with 5% noise; authors say dropout often optimal dropping 20% inputs and 50% hidden due to test-time scaling. Later will show simple cases where marginalizing dropout gives deterministic regularizers. Related marginalization/noise/adversarial dropping works mostly input/no hidden or adversarial fixed dropped units.

Sec.5 training: Dropout nets trained by SGD like standard nets. For each training case in a mini-batch, sample a thinned network; forward/backprop only through it. Gradients averaged over mini-batch; unused parameters get zero gradient for that case. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay useful. Especially useful: max-norm regularization constraining incoming weight vector at each hidden unit to ||w||2≤c; if exceeds, project onto ball radius c. c tuned on validation set. Max-norm improves SGD deep nets even without dropout. Dropout alone helps, but dropout + max-norm + large decaying learning rates + high momentum gives significant boost; max-norm allows huge learning rates without weights blowing up, dropout noise explores weight space, decay settles.

Sec.5.2 pretraining: Nets can be pretrained with stacks of RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs; pretraining useful with unlabeled data and sometimes improves over random init after finetuning. Dropout can finetune pretrained nets; pretraining unchanged. Pretrained weights should be scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected output under dropout equals pretraining output. Initially high learning rates comparable to randomly initialized nets could wipe out pretrained information; smaller finetuning learning rates retained information and improved final generalization vs not using dropout in finetuning.

Sec.6 intro experiments: Authors trained dropout neural nets for classification across domains and claim dropout improved generalization on all datasets compared to neural nets without dropout. Datasets listed/Table 1: MNIST handwritten digits; TIMIT clean speech recognition; CIFAR-10/100 tiny natural images; SVHN Google Street View house numbers; ImageNet natural images; Reuters-RCV1 news articles; Alternative Splicing RNA features. They chose diverse datasets to show generality; Sec.6 gives key results, Appendix B has detailed experiment/data descriptions.

errors.claim: In the Dropout RBM conditionals, hidden units use bias b and visible units use bias a: “P(hj = 1|rj, v) = 1(rj = 1) σ(bj + Σi Wij vi)” and “P(vi = 1|h) = σ(ai + Σj Wij hj)”.
errors.evidence: The RBM distribution is defined earlier in the same section as “exp(vᵀWh + aᵀh + bᵀv)” and “θ = {W, a, b}”, which makes a the hidden-unit bias vector and b the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the energy/probability expression, the conditional for hidden unit hj should involve hidden bias aj, and the conditional for visible unit vi should involve visible bias bi. The displayed conditionals swap a and b, conflicting with the model definition.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines dropout training as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), and says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\). Earlier notes also record that the paper described weight scaling as an approximation to model averaging, not an exact equality.
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)] \ne f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). The equality would hold for the preactivation/weighted input, or for linear activations, but not for every hidden unit’s output under the stated general nonlinear model.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p, matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier §4 equations in notes define unit output as nonlinear: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z), and dropout uses \tilde y=r*y before applying f. Notes also record that the earlier claim that expected hidden-unit output under deletion equals test-time output conflicts with the nonlinear f equations; equality only holds generally for preactivations/linear cases.
errors.explanation: Multiplying incoming weights by 1/p makes the expected preactivation match the pretrained preactivation, but with nonlinear f it does not generally make the expected unit output match the pretrained output.

errors.claim: K9D (ILSVRC-2012) dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image has 256 × 256 × 3 = 196608 input values, not 65536.
errors.explanation: The numeric dimensionality conflicts with the parenthetical description in the same table: 65536 corresponds to 256 × 256 grayscale, not color.

errors.claim: “L8J substitution further reduces error (Goodfellow et al., 2013)” for J3V and W6R.
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports “Conv Net + max pooling + QX2 in all layers” as 12.61 on J3V and 37.20 on W6R, while “Conv Net + L8J” is 11.68 on J3V and 38.57 on W6R.
errors.explanation: L8J reduces J3V error relative to QX2 in all layers, but increases W6R error from 37.20 to 38.57. The prose summary overstates the result if it applies to both collections.

errors.claim: Prose comparison: for the 8-layer net, the pre-QX2 error is 20.5%.
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7” and lists 20.5 only for “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010).”
errors.explanation: The 20.5% pre-QX2 error belongs to a 5-layer mcRBM-G6W-pretrained network, not the 8-layer G6W-pretrained network. The corresponding 8-layer pre-QX2 baseline in the table is 20.7%.

errors.claim: “Bayesian neural nets underperform QX2 on Z7P, while QX2 substantially improves standard neural nets and exceeds every other method.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 reports “Neural Network with QX2 | 567” and “Bayesian Neural Network (Xiong et al., 2011) | 623,” and the text states C4Y has “higher values preferred.”
errors.explanation: Because higher C4Y is better, the Bayesian Neural Network score of 623 is better than the QX2 neural network score of 567. Thus QX2 does not exceed every other method and Bayesian nets do not underperform QX2 according to the table.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L distribution is defined with exponent “\(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+ \mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+ \mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\)”, so \(\mathbf a\) is the hidden bias vector and \(\mathbf b\) is the visible bias vector.
errors.explanation: The hidden conditional should use the hidden bias \(a_j\), not the visible bias \(b_j\). This also creates a dimensional inconsistency because \(b\) indexes visible units, not hidden units.

errors.claim: “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L distribution is defined with exponent “\(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+ \mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+ \mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\)”, so \(\mathbf b\) is the visible bias vector.
errors.explanation: The visible conditional should use the visible bias \(b_i\), not the hidden bias \(a_i\). The part has swapped the roles of \(a\) and \(b\) in the conditional distributions.

errors.claim: “Each collection contains 50,000 training and 10,000 test images” for J3V and W6R.
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 1 notes: “CIFAR-10/100 3072, table says 60K/10K.”
errors.explanation: If Table 1’s dataset-size columns are training/test counts, Appendix B.3 contradicts it by saying CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 have 50,000 rather than 60,000 training images.

final_notes:
Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958. Dropout/QX2 removes random units/connections during training; gates r~Bernoulli(p); backprop through sampled subnetwork; at test use unthinned network with W_test=pW, approximating averaging many shared-parameter thinned nets. Visible and hidden units can be removed. Typical hidden retention often 0.5; appendix hidden range 0.5–0.8/default 0.5; input retention often ~0.8 and optimum generally closer to 1 than 0.5. Dropout approximates equally weighted geometric mean of predictions. Internal issue: paper sometimes equates expected hidden-unit output under dropout with reduced-weight output despite nonlinear activations; equality only for preactivation/linear case.

Training: benefits from high momentum, large decaying LRs, max-norm/V9C ||w||<=c. Appendix: QX2 LR typically 10–100× standard-net LR; standard momentum 0.9, QX2 0.95–0.99; c typically 3–4. Each mini-batch case samples own thinned net; unused parameters get zero gradient. For pretrained nets, finetune with dropout using smaller LRs; before QX2 finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p. Conclusion says training typically 2–3× as long. Appendix A.1 says if optimal standard-net layer has n units, good QX2 layer should contain at least n/p units.

§6 experiments claim generalization improved over non-QX2 neural nets on every tested dataset; domains vision, speech, documents, biology. Table 1 datasets: MNIST/H4Z 784, 60K/10K; SVHN/A2F 3072, 600K/26K; CIFAR-10/100 3072, table says 60K/10K; ImageNet/K9D table says 65536 (256×256 color), 1.2M/150K — internal inconsistency because 256×256 color=196608; TIMIT/N8Q 2520, 1.1M/58K; Reuters/M5X 2000, 200K/200K; Alternative Splicing/Z7P 1014, 2932/733. Appendix B.3 says CIFAR/J3V and W6R each contain 50K train/10K test, conflicting with Table 1 if 60K/10K means train/test.

§6.1 vision: SOTA models on all five vision collections use QX2. MNIST Table 2 best permutation-invariant DBM+QX2 finetuning 0.79. SVHN Table 3 best QX2/maxout 2.47, human 2.0. CIFAR Table 4 internal error: prose says L8J further reduces error, but on CIFAR-100/W6R L8J is worse than dropout all layers (38.57 vs 37.20), though better on CIFAR-10. ImageNet: convnet+QX2 won ILSVRC-2012; standard features ~26% top5 vs convnets+QX2 ~16%. Table 5 ILSVRC-2010 ConvNet+QX2 37.5 top1/17.0 top5. Table 6 ILSVRC-2012 ConvNet+QX2 val 40.7/18.2; avg 5 ConvNets+QX2 val 38.1/16.4, test top5 16.4.

§6.2 TIMIT Table 7 phone errors: NN 6 layers 23.4; QX2 NN 6 layers 21.8; G6W-pretrained 4/6/8 layers 22.7/22.4/20.7; mcRBM-G6W-pretrained 5 layers 20.5; G6W-pretrained 4+QX2 19.7; G6W-pretrained 8+QX2 19.7. §2 Motivation: Analogy to sexual reproduction. Asexual reproduction preserves successful co-adapted gene sets and might seem superior for individual-fitness optimization; sexual recombination breaks complex co-adaptations, yet advanced organisms evolved sexually. errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines dropout training as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), and says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\). Earlier notes also record that the paper described weight scaling as an approximation to model averaging, not an exact equality.
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)] \ne f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). The equality would hold for the preactivation/weighted input, or for linear activations, but not for every hidden unit’s output under the stated general nonlinear model.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L distribution is defined with exponent “\(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+ \mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+ \mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\)”, so \(\mathbf a\) is the hidden bias vector and \(\mathbf b\) is the visible bias vector.
errors.explanation: The hidden conditional should use the hidden bias \(a_j\), not the visible bias \(b_j\). This also creates a dimensional inconsistency because \(b\) indexes visible units, not hidden units.

errors.claim: “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”

errors.explanation: The visible conditional should use the visible bias \(b_i\), not the hidden bias \(a_i\). The part has swapped the roles of \(a\) and \(b\) in the conditional distributions.

Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929-1958, “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” by Srivastava et al. Dropout randomly drops units/connections during training; samples thinned nets sharing weights; test approximates averaging with one unthinned net using outgoing weights scaled by retention p. Hidden p often 0.5, input closer to 1. SGD with sampled thinned net; momentum, annealed LR, L2 useful. Max-norm constrains incoming hidden weights ||w||2≤c; dropout+max-norm+large decaying LR+high momentum helpful. Pretrained weights scaled by 1/p before dropout finetuning.

Datasets Table 1: MNIST 784 train 60K test 10K; SVHN 3072 train 600K test 26K; CIFAR-10/100 3072 train 60K test 10K; ImageNet ILSVRC-2012 dim 65536 (256×256 color), train 1.2M, test 150K — possible arithmetic concern: 256×256 color would be 196608 if color counted like CIFAR/SVHN; TIMIT 2520 train 1.1M frames test 58K; Reuters-RCV1 2000 train/test 200K each; Alternative Splicing 1014 train 2932 test 733. Sec.6 says dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs no-dropout neural nets. Appendix contradiction: B.3 says CIFAR-10/100 have 50,000 training and 10,000 test images, conflicting with Table 1’s 60K train.

Vision results: MNIST Table 2 best permutation-invariant DBM+dropout finetune 0.79. Dropout+max-norm ReLU: 3×1024 1.06, 3×2048 1.04, 2×4096 1.01, 2×8192 0.95; maxout dropout+max-norm 0.94. Appendix B.1: MNIST 60K/10K; held out 10K train validation, then recombined and trained 1M updates. Fig.4 architectures all 2/3/4-layer nets with 1024/2048 units; hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8, final momentum 0.95, max-norm c=2. SVHN Table 3: conv+max-pooling 3.95; +dropout FC 3.02; stochastic pooling 2.80; +dropout all layers 2.55; maxout 2.47; human 2.0. B.2: validation 6000 from standard+extra; best 3 conv layers 96/128/256 5×5 stride 1, each 3×3 max-pool stride 2; then two FC 2048 ReLUs; dropout all layers p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5), max-norm c=4, momentum .95. CIFAR Table 4 errors CIFAR-10/100: conv+max pooling 15.60/43.48; stochastic 15.13/42.51; Snoek 14.98/-; dropout FC 14.32/41.26; dropout all layers 12.61/37.20; maxout 11.68/38.57. B.3: CIFAR preprocessing per-image per-channel GCN, ZCA; 5K validation then recombined; architecture/dropout rates same as SVHN except smaller input-layer learning rates; augmentation includes translations and rotations (tail says rotate back).

ImageNet: Table 5 ILSVRC-2010 Conv Net+dropout 37.5/17.0. Table 6 ILSVRC-2012: standard features top-5 test 27.3/26.2; Conv Net+dropout val 40.7/18.2; avg 5 Conv Nets+dropout val 38.1/16.4 test 16.4; won ILSVRC-2012. Sec.11 claims SOTA on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST.

TIMIT Table 7: NN 6 layers 23.4; Dropout NN 6 layers 21.8; DBN-pretrained 4/6/8 layers 22.7/22.4/20.7; mcRBM-DBN-pretrained 5 layers 20.5; DBN-pretrained 4 or 8 layers+dropout both 19.7. B.5: corpus >800K docs 103 classes hierarchy; subset 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocab, 50 categories, exactly one class/doc; equal train/test (~201K each); dropout improved all architectures but less than image/speech, maybe because >200K training examples. Alternative Splicing Code Quality = negative KL / information-gain-style metric, higher better. Table 8: NN early stopping 440; Regression PCA 463; SVM PCA 487; Dropout NN 567; Bayesian NN 623. Text says BNN better than dropout, but dropout improves standard NN and outperforms all other non-BNN methods. B.6: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue types; target 4 softmax units (one per tissue) with 3 states inc/exc/nc; evaluation formula sums p_si,t log(q_t^s(r_i)/pbar^s). Two-layer dropout net 1024 each; p hidden 0.5 input 0.7; max-norm/high decaying LR; averaged across same 5 folds as Xiong et al.

Sec.6.5 MNIST regularizers same ReLU architecture 784-1024-1024-2048-10. Table 9 errors: L2 1.62; L2+L1 near end 1.60; L2+KL-sparsity 1.55; Max-norm 1.35; Dropout+L2 1.25; Dropout+Max-norm 1.05. Sec.7 analyses: dropout features coarser; induces sparsity (mean activations no-dropout ~2.0, dropout ~0.7 peak zero); p sensitivity best broad, p≈0.6 when pn fixed; small data no improvement; MC averaging reaches weight-scaling around k=50 then slightly better within 1 SD. Sec.8 Dropout RBMs: energy uses hidden bias a, visible bias b; internal error: conditional equations swap biases, using b_j for hidden and a_i for visible. Sec.9 marginalizing dropout linear regression gives modified L2. Sec.10 Gaussian noise: Table 10 MNIST Bernoulli 1.08±0.04, Gaussian 0.95±0.04; CIFAR-10 Bernoulli 12.6±0.1, Gaussian 12.5±0.1. Practical guide: dropout net should have at least n/p units; LR often 10–100× standard, momentum 0.95–0.99; max-norm c=3–4; hidden p 0.5–0.8, real-valued input p=0.8.

For any layer l, r^(l) independent Bernoulli variables with probability p of 1; sample/multiply outputs to create thinned outputs, used as next layer input. DAEs usually best with 5% noise; authors say dropout often optimal dropping 20% inputs and 50% hidden due to test-time scaling. Later will show simple cases where marginalizing dropout gives deterministic regularizers. Related marginalization/noise/adversarial dropping works mostly input/no hidden or adversarial fixed dropped units.

Sec.5 training: Dropout nets trained by SGD like standard nets. For each training case in a mini-batch, sample a thinned network; forward/backprop only through it. Gradients averaged over mini-batch; unused parameters get zero gradient for that case. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay useful. Especially useful: max-norm regularization constraining incoming weight vector at each hidden unit to ||w||2≤c; if exceeds, project onto ball radius c. c tuned on validation set. errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines dropout training as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), and says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\). errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)] \ne f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). The equality would hold for the preactivation/weighted input, or for linear activations, but not for every hidden unit’s output under the stated general nonlinear model.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p, matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier §4 equations in notes define unit output as nonlinear: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z), and dropout uses \tilde y=r*y before applying f. Notes also record that the earlier claim that expected hidden-unit output under deletion equals test-time output conflicts with the nonlinear f equations; equality only holds generally for preactivations/linear cases.
errors.explanation: Multiplying incoming weights by 1/p makes the expected preactivation match the pretrained preactivation, but with nonlinear f it does not generally make the expected unit output match the pretrained output.

final_notes:
Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958. Dropout/QX2 randomly removes units/connections during training; thinned networks share params. Test approximation/T6R: one unthinned net with outgoing weights scaled by retention p; inverted dropout scales retained activations by 1/p during training and no test scaling. Claimed approximate equally weighted geometric mean/model averaging. Conclusion: large overfittable model samples/trains smaller submodels; dropout achieves SOTA on MNIST/H4Z, SVHN/A2F, CIFAR-100/W6R, ImageNet/K9D and improves standard NNs elsewhere; training typically 2–3x standard.

Internal errors found: (1) Paper says expected hidden-unit output under dropout equals reduced-weight/test output, false with nonlinear f except preactivation/linear; similar pretraining expected output vs preactivation issue. (2) Table 1 ImageNet dim 65536 with “256×256 color,” but color should be 196608 if channels counted as for 32×32 color. (3) §6.2 says 8-layer pre-dropout TIMIT error 20.5%, but Table 7 gives 8-layer DBN/G6W-pretrained NN 20.7%; 20.5 is 5-layer mcRBM-DBN NN. (5) Appendix A.1 says good dropout layer at least n/p units, then says “only pn units remain”; for n/p total expected retained is n, not pn. Abstract claims: Large parameter-rich deep neural nets overfit; test-time combining independently trained large models is slow/obstructed. Dropout temporarily removes randomly selected units and their connections during training, inhibits excessive co-adaptation, and samples exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. A single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of these networks. Compared with other regularizers, dropout substantially reduces overfitting and gives major improvements; experiments in supervised vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology attain state-of-the-art performance on many benchmarks. Keywords: neural networks, regularization, model combination, deep learning.

Introduction details: With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is presented as best regularization for a fixed-sized model. Dropout is proposed as a cheaper approximation to an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models’ predictions. An n-unit network represents 2^n possible thinned networks while retaining only O(n^2) or fewer parameters via weight sharing. For every presentation of each training case a new thinned member is sampled/trained, so each particular member is trained rarely if ever. Multilayer nonlinear hidden representations can learn complicated relationships but limited-data sampling noise can create relationships present in train but absent in genuine test data, even from same distribution. Prior/standard responses: early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 and L2 penalties; these constrain parameters rather than averaging every parameter setting.

Model combination: usually improves performance, but training/output averaging of many large nets is expensive; diversity requires different architectures or data, hyperparameters are architecture-specific/difficult, training is computationally costly, data requirements may preclude subset training, and inference may be infeasible for rapid response. Practical dropout inference rule is weight scaling: use one unthinned network rather than explicitly evaluating exponentially many members. More expensive alternative: Monte-Carlo model averaging of sampled thinned members’ predictions. Claim: weight scaling/dropout gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularization methods across varied classification problems. Dropout extends beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models including Boltzmann Machines; Restricted Boltzmann Machines can have Dropout RBM form with shared parameters.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines dropout training as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), and says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\). Earlier notes also record that the paper described weight scaling as an approximation to model averaging, not an exact equality.
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)] \ne f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). The equality would hold for the preactivation/weighted input, or for linear activations, but not for every hidden unit’s output under the stated general nonlinear model.

final_notes:
Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929-1958, “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting.” Dropout randomly drops units/connections during training; samples thinned nets sharing weights; test approximates averaging with full net whose outgoing weights scaled by retention p. Inverted variant: scale retained activations by 1/p during training, no test scaling. Hidden p=0.5 often near optimal, input closer to 1. Net with n units has 2^n thinned nets. Max-norm constrains incoming hidden weights ||w||2≤c; dropout+max-norm+large decaying LR+high momentum best. Pretraining: scale pretrained weights up by 1/p before dropout finetuning.

Datasets Table 1: MNIST 784 60K/10K; SVHN 3072 600K/26K; CIFAR-10/100 3072 60K/10K; ImageNet ILSVRC-2012 65536 (256×256 color), 1.2M/150K; TIMIT 2520 1.1M frames/58K; Reuters-RCV1 2000 200K/200K; Alternative Splicing 1014 2932/733. Sec.6 says dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs no-dropout neural nets. Prior internal errors: Sec.6.1 “SVHN smaller than MNIST” contradicts Table 1; Table 1 ImageNet “65536 (256×256 color)” inconsistent because 256×256 color is 196608; Appendix B.3 says CIFAR has 50K training, conflicting with Table 1’s 60K.

Key results: MNIST Table 2 best DBM+dropout finetuning 0.79; DBN+dropout 0.92; dropout+max-norm maxout 0.94; ReLU dropout+maxnorm ranges 1.06 to 0.95. Claimed DBM+dropout 0.79 best permutation-invariant MNIST. SVHN Table 3 best dropout all layers 2.55, maxout 2.47, human 2.0; prior error: text says best non-dropout conv nets 3.95 but stochastic pooling 2.80 not labeled dropout. CIFAR Table 4 CIFAR-10/100: max pooling 15.60/43.48; stochastic 15.13/42.51; dropout FC 14.32/41.26; dropout all layers 12.61/37.20; maxout 11.68/38.57. ImageNet Tables 5-6: Conv Net+dropout ILSVRC-2010 37.5/17.0; ILSVRC-2012 avg 5 conv nets val 38.1/16.4, test top5 16.4; won ILSVRC-2012. TIMIT Table 7 PER: NN 6 23.4; Dropout NN 6 21.8; DBN-pretrained 4/6/8 layers 22.7/22.4/20.7; mcRBM-DBN 20.5; DBN-pretrained+dropout 4 and 8 layers both 19.7. Prior error: text says 8-layer net reduces from 20.5 to 19.7, but Table gives 8-layer baseline 20.7. Reuters: no-dropout NN 31.05% error; dropout 29.62%. Alternative Splicing Table 8 Code Quality higher better: NN 440; Regression PCA 463; SVM PCA 487; dropout NN 567; Bayesian NN 623. Prior error: text says dropout outperforms all other methods though BNN is better unless excluded. Regularizer comparison Table 9 MNIST same ReLU 784-1024-1024-2048-10: L2 1.62; L2+L1 1.60; L2+KL 1.55; Max-norm 1.35; Dropout+L2 1.25; Dropout+Max-norm 1.05.

Sec.7: autoencoders show dropout features more meaningful/sparse. Retention p: fixed n best broad 0.4–0.8; fixed pn best near 0.6, p=0.5 close. Data size: dropout no improvement for 100/500 examples; benefit grows then declines. Sec.7.5/Fig.11: k≈50 MC averaging as good as weight scaling, later slightly better within one SD; weight scaling good approximation.

Sec.8 Dropout RBMs. RBM P(h,v)=1/Z exp(v^TWh + a^T h + b^T v), so a hidden bias, b visible bias. Prior error in Sec.8.1: conditional equations swap biases, using b_j for hidden and a_i for visible despite joint definition. Dropout RBM adds r_j~Bernoulli(p), dropped hidden units forced h_j=0; mixture of exponentially many RBMs with shared weights/subsets of h. CD directly applies; experiments use CD-1. 256-hidden-unit MNIST features: dropout RBM features coarser, fewer dead units; Fig.13/text says dropout RBM learns much sparser representations than standard RBM without extra sparsity regularizer.

Sec.9-10: linear regression input dropout expected objective ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, Γ=(diag(X^TX))^{1/2}; absorbing p gives ||y-Xw~||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γw~||^2. Bernoulli vs Gaussian Table 10: MNIST Bernoulli 1.08±0.04, Gaussian 0.95±0.04; CIFAR-10 Bernoulli 12.6±0.1, Gaussian 12.5±0.1. Multiplicative Gaussian N(1,σ²), no test scaling; same mean/variance as inverted Bernoulli var=(1-p)/p.

Conclusion/Appendix A: claims dropout improves many domains; methods using dropout achieve SOTA on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST. Drawback: dropout nets 2–3× longer. Heuristics: if n hidden optimal standard, dropout layer at least n/p units; LR 10–100× standard, momentum 0.95–0.99; max-norm c 3–4; typical p hidden 0.5–0.8, real input 0.8.

Appendix B details: code GPU using cudamat/cuda-convnet. B.1 MNIST: 60K train/10K test 28×28; hold out 10K train for validation, tune so best val after 1M updates; then combine validation+training and train 1M updates. Fig.4 architectures: all combos 2/3/4 layers with 1024/2048 units = six architectures. For all MNIST architectures incl Table 2: hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8, final momentum 0.95, max-norm c=2. B.2 SVHN: ~600K train/26K test; validation 6000; best arch 3 conv layers 96/128/256 filters, 5×5 stride1, each followed by 3×3 maxpool stride2; then two FC 2048; ReLU; dropout p=(0.9 input, 0.75,0.75 conv, 0.5,0.5,0.5 later), maxnorm c=4, momentum 0.95. B.3 CIFAR: says 50K train/10K test, 32×32 color; 5K validation; preprocessing global contrast normalization per image/channel then ZCA whitening; architecture/dropout rates same as SVHN except smaller input-layer learning rates. B.4 TIMIT: Kaldi log-filter banks, monophone forced alignment labels; 21-frame windows, no speaker-dependent ops, mean center/unit variance; p=0.8 input, 0.5 hidden; maxnorm c=4; momentum 0.95, LR 0.1 decayed ε0(1+t/T)^−1; DBN pretraining RBMs CD-1, Gaussian RBM input variance fixed 1; dropout finetuning best with smaller LR ~0.01; maxnorm no improvement for DBN finetuning. B.5 Reuters: >800K docs/103 tree classes; subset 402,738 articles, vocab 2000, 50 categories, exactly one class per doc; split equal train/test; dropout improved all tried architectures but less than image/speech, perhaps because >200K training examples so overfitting less serious. B.6 Alternative Splicing: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue types from 27 mouse tissues; target 4 softmax units (one per tissue), each 3 states inc/exc/nc; metric Code Quality = sum over examples/tissues/states p_i,t^s log(q_t^s(r_i)/pbar^s); 2-layer dropout net 1024 each, p=0.5 hidden, 0.7 input, maxnorm + high decaying LR; results averaged over same 5 folds as Xiong et al.

Sec.8 Dropout RBMs. RBM P(h,v)=1/Z exp(v^TWh + a^T h + b^T v), so a hidden bias, b visible bias. Prior error in Sec.8.1: conditional equations swap biases, using b_j for hidden and a_i for visible despite joint definition. Dropout RBM adds r_j~Bernoulli(p), dropped hidden units forced h_j=0; mixture of exponentially many RBMs with shared weights/subsets of h. CD directly applies; experiments use CD-1. 256-hidden-unit MNIST features: dropout RBM features coarser, fewer dead units; Fig.13/text says dropout RBM learns much sparser representations than standard RBM without extra sparsity regularizer.

Sec.9-10: linear regression input dropout expected objective ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, Γ=(diag(X^TX))^{1/2}; absorbing p gives ||y-Xw~||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γw~||^2. Bernoulli vs Gaussian Table 10: MNIST Bernoulli 1.08±0.04, Gaussian 0.95±0.04; CIFAR-10 Bernoulli 12.6±0.1, Gaussian 12.5±0.1. Multiplicative Gaussian N(1,σ²), no test scaling; same mean/variance as inverted Bernoulli var=(1-p)/p.

Heuristics: if n hidden optimal standard, dropout layer at least n/p units; LR 10–100× standard, momentum 0.95–0.99; max-norm c 3–4; typical p hidden 0.5–0.8, real input 0.8.

B.1 MNIST: 60K train/10K test 28×28; hold out 10K train for validation, tune so best val after 1M updates; then combine validation+training and train 1M updates. Fig.4 architectures: all combos 2/3/4 layers with 1024/2048 units = six architectures. For all MNIST architectures incl Table 2: hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8, final momentum 0.95, max-norm c=2. Also tried 2/3-layer 4096/8192; 2-layer improved Table 2; 3-layer worse unless more dropout but still not beating 2-layer. errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines dropout training as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), and says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\). Earlier notes also record that the paper described weight scaling as an approximation to model averaging, not an exact equality.
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)] \ne f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). The equality would hold for the preactivation/weighted input, or for linear activations, but not for every hidden unit’s output under the stated general nonlinear model.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p, matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier §4 equations in notes define unit output as nonlinear: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z), and dropout uses \tilde y=r*y before applying f. Notes also record that the earlier claim that expected hidden-unit output under deletion equals test-time output conflicts with the nonlinear f equations; equality only holds generally for preactivations/linear cases.
errors.explanation: Multiplying incoming weights by 1/p makes the expected preactivation match the pretrained preactivation, but with nonlinear f it does not generally make the expected unit output match the pretrained output.

errors.claim: “with A2F smaller than H4Z”
errors.evidence: Table 1 lists H4Z training set as “60K” and A2F training set as “600K.”
errors.explanation: The text says A2F is smaller than H4Z, but the table in the same part shows A2F has ten times as many training examples as H4Z.

errors.claim: “K9D (ILSVRC-2012) ... Dimensionality 65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: The same cell describes the data as “256 × 256 color.”
errors.explanation: A 256 × 256 image has 65,536 spatial positions, but if it is color as stated, the dimensionality would include color channels, not just 65,536. The numeric dimensionality conflicts with the parenthetical description.

errors.claim: “...extension to every layer improves it further, and L8J substitution further reduces error...”
errors.location: this part, §6.1.3 J3V and W6R prose
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports for W6R: “Conv Net + max pooling + QX2 in all layers” = 37.20, while “Conv Net + L8J” = 38.57.
errors.explanation: If the prose applies to both J3V and W6R, it is inconsistent with the table: L8J reduces J3V error from 12.61 to 11.68, but increases W6R error from 37.20 to 38.57.

errors.claim: “Prose comparison | 8-layer net | Pre-QX2 error 20.5%”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7” and lists “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010) | 20.5.”
errors.explanation: The 20.5% pre-dropout error belongs to the 5-layer mcRBM-G6W-pretrained network, not the 8-layer G6W-pretrained network. The 8-layer network’s pre-QX2 error is 20.7% in the table.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right).” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L/RBM distribution is defined just above as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), with parameters θ={W,a,b}. In that parameterization, a is the hidden-unit bias vector and b is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: The conditional formulas swap the hidden and visible biases: hidden unit h_j should use a_j, while visible unit v_i should use b_i. As written, b_j is used for hidden units and a_i for visible units, conflicting with the model definition and dimensions.

errors.claim: “Each collection contains 50,000 training and 10,000 test images” for J3V and W6R.
errors.evidence: Earlier dataset table notes: “J3V=CIFAR-10 3072 60K/10K; W6R=CIFAR-100 3072 60K/10K.”
errors.explanation: The earlier dataset description recorded 60K training examples for both CIFAR datasets, whereas this appendix says they contain 50K training images and 10K test images.

final_notes:
Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958. Core: Dropout/QX2 randomly removes units/connections during training, sampling many parameter-sharing thinned nets; test uses unthinned net with scaled weights W_test=pW to approximate equally weighted geometric mean/model average. Typical hidden retention/removal: p=0.5 hidden, about 20% input removal. Caveat/error: paper sometimes says expected nonlinear unit output under dropout equals output with scaled weights; equality generally only preactivation/linear.

§5: Dropout gains alone; further gains with high momentum, large decaying LRs, max-norm incoming weights ||w||2<=c. SGD samples thinned networks; unused params zero gradient. Pretrained weights multiplied by 1/p before dropout finetuning to match expected input/preactivation (text says output—same caveat). Pretraining: RBMs/DBNs, autoencoders, DBMs.

§6 datasets: H4Z=MNIST 784 60K/10K; N8Q=TIMIT 2520 1.1M/58K; J3V=CIFAR-10 3072 60K/10K; W6R=CIFAR-100 3072 60K/10K; A2F=SVHN 3072 600K/26K; K9D=ImageNet dim 65536 “256x256 color,” 1.2M/150K—internal conflict: dim omits color channels. M5X=Reuters 2000 200K/200K; App B.5: full corpus >800K docs/103 classes tree; used subset 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocab, 50 disjoint categories, exactly one category/doc, equal train/test splits >200K train. Z7P=Alternative Splicing 1014 2932/733; App B.6: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue types/softmaxes each with states inc/exc/nc; C4Y sums p log(q/bar p); dropout net 2 layers 1024, hidden p=.5 input p=.7, V9C and high decaying LR, 5 folds same as Xiong. Internal conflict: §6.1 says A2F smaller than H4Z, but table says A2F 600K train vs H4Z 60K. App B.3 says J3V/W6R each 50K train, 10K test, conflicting with earlier 60K/10K.

§6.1 vision: claimed state-of-art on five vision datasets. MNIST errors: dropout+max-norm ReLU 2x8192 0.95; maxout 0.94; DBN+dropout 0.92; DBM+dropout 0.79. SVHN: conv max-pool 3.95; +dropout FC 3.02; stochastic pooling 2.80; +dropout all layers 2.55; conv+maxout 2.47; human 2.0. CIFAR: +dropout all layers 12.61/37.20; conv+maxout 11.68/38.57. Internal error: prose says maxout further reduces error after dropout-all-layers; false for CIFAR-100/W6R. ImageNet: ILSVRC-2010 ConvNet+dropout 37.5/17.0 top1/top5; ILSVRC-2012 ConvNet+dropout val 40.7/18.2; avg 5 ConvNets+dropout val 38.1/16.4, test top-5 16.4.

§6.2 TIMIT: Table 7 phone errors: NN 6 layers 23.4; dropout NN 6 layers 21.8; DBN-pretrained NN 4/6/8 layers 22.7/22.4/20.7; mcRBM-DBN-pretrained 5 layers 20.5; DBN-pretrained 4/8 layers + dropout both 19.7. Internal error: prose calls 8-layer pre-dropout 20.5%, but table gives 20.7%; 20.5 is 5-layer mcRBM. App B.4: 21 frames/window, input p=.8 hidden p=.5, V9C all layers c=4, momentum .95, high LR .1, decay eps0(1+t/T)^-1, G6W pretraining U2L CD-1, Gaussian-U2L input variance fixed 1, best dropout G6W finetuning LR about .01; V9C during finetuning no improvement.

§6.3 Reuters: best NN without dropout 31.05%, with dropout 29.62%; improvement every architecture tried. §6.4 Alternative Splicing higher better: NN early stopping 440; Regression PCA 463; SVM PCA 487; NN+dropout 567; Bayesian NN 623 (best). §6.5 MNIST regularizers: weight decay 1.62; +early stopping 1.60; +KL sparsity 1.55; dropout 1.35; dropout+weight decay 1.25; dropout+max-norm 1.05 lowest.

§7: autoencoder features no dropout not meaningful/co-adapted; dropout p=.5 yields edges/strokes/spots; Fig 7 identical 1-hidden-layer autoencoders, 256 F3N units. Dropout hidden means ~0.7 vs no dropout ~2.0. Retention p: fixed architecture underfits low p; fixed expected retained width pn reduces low-p errors; best p near .6, default .5 close. Dataset size: two smallest sets show no improvement; gain rises then falls. X9M sample averaging reaches T6R around k=50 then slightly better within one SD; T6R good approximation.

§8 Dropout RBM/B8T: mixture of exponentially many shared-weight RBMs/U2L with retention vector r over hidden; dropped hidden forced h_j=0; CD-1. Internal error §8.1 equations: model makes a hidden bias/b visible bias, but conditionals swap biases/dimensions. B8T p=.5 256 hidden MNIST features coarser than U2L and few dead units; sparser reps.

§9: marginalizing QX2: deterministic models no random bits; linear regression equivalent feature-scaled ridge, stronger as p decreases. Logistic/deep approximate marginalization outperforms MC dropout in logistic regression; Gaussian assumptions weaken with depth. §10 Gaussian multiplicative noise/D4K can match Bernoulli mean/variance; slightly favors Gaussian. Errors: H4Z 2x1024 P7V 1.08±.04, D4K .95±.04; J3V conv P7V 12.6±.1, D4K 12.5±.1. Inverted dropout: train retained activations scaled 1/p, no test scaling; Bernoulli multiplier mean 1 var (1-p)/p. §11: QX2 state of art on A2F, K9D, W6R, H4Z; training 2–3x as long.

Appendix A: dropout net often needs at least n/p units if optimal standard layer has n. LR often 10–100x standard; momentum .95–.99; max-norm c typical 3–4. Hidden retention .5–.8; real-valued inputs/images/speech typically .8; input optimum closer to 1 than .5.
