Introduction details: With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is presented as best regularization for a fixed-sized model. Dropout is proposed as a cheaper approximation to an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models’ predictions. An n-unit network represents 2^n possible thinned networks while retaining only O(n^2) or fewer parameters via weight sharing. For every presentation of each training case a new thinned member is sampled/trained, so each particular member is trained rarely if ever. Prior/standard responses: early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 and L2 penalties; these constrain parameters rather than averaging every parameter setting.

Model combination: usually improves performance, but training/output averaging of many large nets is expensive; diversity requires different architectures or data, hyperparameters are architecture-specific/difficult, training is computationally costly, data requirements may preclude subset training, and inference may be infeasible for rapid response. Practical dropout inference rule is weight scaling: use one unthinned network rather than explicitly evaluating exponentially many members. More expensive alternative: Monte-Carlo model averaging of sampled thinned members’ predictions. Claim: weight scaling/dropout gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularization methods across varied classification problems. Dropout extends beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models including Boltzmann Machines; Restricted Boltzmann Machines can have Dropout RBM form with shared parameters.

§2 Motivation: Analogy to sexual reproduction. Asexual reproduction preserves successful co-adapted gene sets and might seem superior for individual-fitness optimization; sexual recombination breaks complex co-adaptations, yet advanced organisms evolved sexually. Livnat et al. account: long-run selection may favor gene “mix-ability” over individual fitness; genes working with random partners are robust; lack of guaranteed partner sets encourages individually useful/simple collaborations; reducing complex co-adaptations helps useful new genes spread. Dropout-trained hidden units similarly face random partners, encouraging independently useful robust features rather than reliance on other hidden units to fix mistakes, though units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating each hidden unit many times is poor robustness, analogous to replica codes for noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: ten five-person conspiracies likely more robust than one fifty-person conspiracy; large complex co-adaptations can work under unchanged/rehearsed training conditions but fail under non-stationary/novel test conditions more easily than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right).” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L/RBM distribution is defined just above as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), with parameters θ={W,a,b}. In that parameterization, a is the hidden-unit bias vector and b is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: The conditional formulas swap the hidden and visible biases: hidden unit h_j should use a_j, while visible unit v_i should use b_i. As written, b_j is used for hidden units and a_i for visible units, conflicting with the model definition and dimensions.

Part 2 adds motivation: Bayesian model averaging is a gold standard, weighting models by posterior probability, but is computationally expensive; authors aim to approximate an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions of exponentially many learned models sharing parameters. Model combination nearly always improves ML; averaging many separately trained large neural nets is prohibitively expensive, especially because diversity usually requires different architectures or training data, and test-time use of many large nets can be infeasible.

Dropout definition: “dropping out” units (hidden and visible) means temporarily removing a unit and all incoming/outgoing connections. Which units are dropped is random. Simplest case: each unit retained independently with fixed probability p; p can be tuned on validation set or set to 0.5, said close to optimal for many networks/tasks. For input units, optimal retention probability is usually closer to 1 than to 0.5.

Dropout claims here: prevents overfitting and efficiently approximates combining exponentially many different neural network architectures. Figure 2: At training time, a unit is present with probability p and has outgoing weights w; at test time it is always present and weights are multiplied by p. Caption claims output at test time is the same as expected output at training time.

Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929-1958, “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” by Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov. Abstract claims: deep nets overfit; dropout randomly drops units and connections during training to prevent co-adaptation; training samples from exponentially many thinned networks; at test time approximate averaging predictions of all thinned networks by using one unthinned network with smaller weights; significantly reduces overfitting and improves over other regularizers; improves supervised learning in vision, speech recognition, document classification, computational biology; obtains state-of-the-art on many benchmark datasets.

Introduction/motivation: Deep nets with multiple nonlinear hidden layers are expressive but overfit with limited data; regularization methods include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, soft weight sharing. Bayesian model averaging is described as a gold standard, weighting models by posterior probability, but computationally expensive. Authors aim to approximate an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions of exponentially many learned models sharing parameters. Model combination nearly always improves ML; averaging many separately trained large neural nets is prohibitively expensive, especially because diversity usually requires different architectures or training data, and test-time use of many large nets can be infeasible.

Dropout definition/claims: “Dropping out” units (hidden and visible) means temporarily removing a unit and all incoming/outgoing connections. Which units are dropped is random. Simplest case: each unit retained independently with fixed probability p; p can be tuned on validation set or set to 0.5, said close to optimal for many networks/tasks. For input units, optimal retention probability is usually closer to 1 than to 0.5. Dropout prevents overfitting and efficiently approximates combining exponentially many different neural network architectures.

Thinned networks: Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network consisting of units that survived dropout (Figure 1b). A net with n units can be seen as a collection of 2^n possible thinned networks. These share weights, so total parameters remain O(n^2) or less. For each presentation of each training case, a new thinned network is sampled and trained; each thinned network is trained very rarely, if at all.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned models is infeasible. Instead use a single neural net without dropout, with scaled-down trained weights. If a unit is retained with probability p during training, its outgoing weights are multiplied by p at test time (Figure 2). The paper claims this ensures that for any hidden unit the expected output under training-time dropout distribution is the same as actual output at test time. By this scaling, 2^n shared-weight networks can be combined into one test-time network. Authors claim training with dropout plus this approximate averaging gives significantly lower generalization error across many classification problems than other regularization methods.

Figures/structure: Figure 1 illustrates a standard neural net with 2 hidden layers and an example thinned net after dropout, with crossed units dropped. Figure 2: at training time, a unit is present with probability p and has outgoing weights w; at test time it is always present and weights are multiplied by p; caption/part claims output at test time equals expected output at training time. Paper structure stated: Sec. 2 motivation; Sec. 3 previous work; Sec. 4 formal dropout model; Sec. 5 training algorithm; Sec. 6 experimental results across domains comparing with other regularization/model combination; Sec. 7 analyzes dropout effects and hyperparameter interactions; Sec. 8 Dropout RBM; Sec. 9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A practical guide and detailed hyperparameter considerations.

Extension beyond feed-forward nets: Dropout can be applied more generally to graphical models such as Boltzmann Machines. Paper introduces dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine and compares it with standard RBM; experiments reportedly show dropout RBMs are better than standard RBMs in certain respects.

Section 2 motivation details: Uses analogy to sexual reproduction (Livnat et al. 2010). Asexual reproduction might seem better for preserving co-adapted genes, but sexual reproduction may select for “mix-ability”/robustness: genes must work with random partners and not rely on large fixed co-adapted sets. Similarly, each hidden unit trained with dropout must work with a randomly chosen sample of other units, learn useful features on its own or with few others, and not rely on others to correct mistakes. Hidden units within a layer should still learn different things. Authors reject robustness by making many copies of each hidden unit as poor, analogous to replica codes being poor for noisy channels. Second analogy: successful conspiracies—ten conspiracies of five people likely better under non-stationary conditions than one conspiracy requiring fifty people; complex co-adaptations can fit training data but fail on novel test data more than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

Start of Sec.3 Related Work: Dropout can be interpreted as regularizing a neural net by adding noise to hidden units. Adding noise to unit states was previously used in Denoising Autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010), where noise ... [continues].

Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929-1958, “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” by Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov. Abstract claims dropout randomly drops units/connections during training to prevent co-adaptation; training samples exponentially many thinned networks; test approximates averaging predictions using one unthinned network with smaller weights; significantly reduces overfitting vs other regularizers; improves supervised learning in vision, speech recognition, document classification, computational biology; obtains state-of-the-art on many benchmarks.

Intro/dropout definition: Deep nets overfit with limited data; dropout approximates equally weighted geometric mean/model averaging of exponentially many learned models sharing parameters. Dropping out hidden and visible units means temporarily removing unit and incoming/outgoing connections. Each unit retained independently with probability p; p tunable or 0.5 often near optimal for hidden units; input retention usually closer to 1. Applying dropout samples a thinned network. A net with n units has 2^n thinned networks; shared weights keep parameters O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned network; explicit averaging infeasible. Test uses no-dropout net with outgoing weights scaled by retention probability p, intended to match expected training-time hidden output and combine 2^n networks. Fig. 2: training unit present with probability p and outgoing weights w; test always present with outgoing weights pw.

Motivation: Sexual reproduction analogy: dropout selects hidden units/features that work with random partners (“mix-ability”) rather than complex co-adapted sets; units should still learn different things. Replica-code-like copying is rejected. Conspiracy analogy: multiple small co-adaptations may generalize better than one large fragile co-adaptation.

Related work: Dropout as stochastic regularization/noise. Denoising autoencoders add noise to inputs and reconstruct clean input; paper claims to extend by applying dropout/noise in hidden layers, interpreting as model averaging, applying to supervised learning, and to neuron-based architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAEs typically best with 5% noise; authors say test-time weight scaling permits much higher noise: often optimal to drop 20% of inputs and 50% of hidden units. Deterministic counterpart obtained by marginalizing dropout noise: paper will show simple cases where dropout analytically marginalizes to deterministic regularizers. Related: van der Maaten et al. (2013) deterministic regularizers for exponential-family noise including “blankout” dropout, only inputs/no hidden layers; Wang & Manning (2013) speed up dropout by marginalizing noise; Chen et al. (2012) marginalization for denoising autoencoders. Also adversarial unit dropping by Globerson & Roweis/Dekel et al.: loss minimized when adversary picks units to drop with max number fixed; no hidden-unit models.

Formal model (Sec.4): Neural network with L hidden layers; l indexes hidden layers. y(0)=x input. z(l) inputs into layer l, y(l) outputs; W(l), b(l) weights/biases. Standard feedforward for l=0,...,L-1: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)), e.g. sigmoid f(x)=1/(1+exp(-x)). Dropout feedforward: sample r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p), form thinned outputs \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l) elementwise, then z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) \tilde y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). For any layer l, r^(l) independent Bernoulli variables with probability p of 1; sample/multiply outputs to create thinned outputs, used as next layer input. Applied at each layer, sampling a sub-network. Learning backpropagates derivatives through sampled sub-network. Test time scales weights as W_test^(l)=p W^(l) and uses resulting network without dropout.

Structure ahead: Sec.5 training algorithm; Sec.6 experiments across domains vs regularization/model combination; Sec.7 analysis/hyperparameters; Sec.8 Dropout RBM; Sec.9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A practical guide. Dropout can extend to graphical models/Boltzmann Machines; dropout RBM compared with standard RBM and reportedly better in certain respects.

Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929-1958, “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” by Srivastava et al. Abstract/intro claims dropout randomly drops units/connections during training to prevent co-adaptation; each presentation samples a thinned network from exponentially many sharing weights; test approximates averaging predictions using one unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by retention probability p. Significantly reduces overfitting and improves vision, speech recognition, document classification, computational biology; obtains SOTA on many benchmarks.

Dropout definition/formal model: Dropping hidden/visible units means temporarily removing unit and incoming/outgoing connections. Each unit retained independently with probability p (hidden p=0.5 often near optimal; input retention closer to 1). Net with n units has 2^n thinned networks. Training samples new thinned network per case. Test: no-dropout network with W_test^(l)=p W^(l), matching expected training-time hidden output. Formal: y(0)=x; standard z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Dropout samples r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), uses \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l) into next layer; backprop through sampled subnetwork.

Motivation/related work: Dropout encourages features that work with random partners (“mix-ability”), not fragile co-adaptations. Related to stochastic regularization/noise and denoising autoencoders, but extends noise/dropout to hidden layers, supervised learning, model averaging, Boltzmann machines. DAEs usually best with 5% noise; authors say dropout often optimal dropping 20% inputs and 50% hidden due to test-time scaling. Later will show simple cases where marginalizing dropout gives deterministic regularizers. Related marginalization/noise/adversarial dropping works mostly input/no hidden or adversarial fixed dropped units.

Sec.5 training: Dropout nets trained by SGD like standard nets. For each training case in a mini-batch, sample a thinned network; forward/backprop only through it. Gradients averaged over mini-batch; unused parameters get zero gradient for that case. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay useful. Especially useful: max-norm regularization constraining incoming weight vector at each hidden unit to ||w||2≤c; if exceeds, project onto ball radius c. c tuned on validation set. Max-norm improves SGD deep nets even without dropout. Dropout alone helps, but dropout + max-norm + large decaying learning rates + high momentum gives significant boost; max-norm allows huge learning rates without weights blowing up, dropout noise explores weight space, decay settles.

Sec.5.2 pretraining: Nets can be pretrained with stacks of RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs; pretraining useful with unlabeled data and sometimes improves over random init after finetuning. Dropout can finetune pretrained nets; pretraining unchanged. Pretrained weights should be scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected output under dropout equals pretraining output. Initially high learning rates comparable to randomly initialized nets could wipe out pretrained information; smaller finetuning learning rates retained information and improved final generalization vs not using dropout in finetuning.

Sec.6 intro experiments: Authors trained dropout neural nets for classification across domains and claim dropout improved generalization on all datasets compared to neural nets without dropout. Datasets listed/Table 1: MNIST handwritten digits; TIMIT clean speech recognition; CIFAR-10/100 tiny natural images; SVHN Google Street View house numbers; ImageNet natural images; Reuters-RCV1 news articles; Alternative Splicing RNA features. They chose diverse datasets to show generality; Sec.6 gives key results, Appendix B has detailed experiment/data descriptions.

Structure ahead: Sec.6 experiments vs regularization/model combination; Sec.7 analysis/hyperparameters; Sec.8 Dropout RBM; Sec.9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A practical guide; Appendix B detailed experiments. Dropout can extend to graphical/Boltzmann models; dropout RBM compared to standard RBM.

errors.claim: “We tried many network architectures and found that dropout gave improvements in classification accuracy over all of them.”
errors.evidence: Notes: Reuters results were “best no-dropout NN 31.05%, dropout 29.62%,” but the Conclusion has an internal error saying “Reuters standard NNs did better without dropout,” contradicting those numbers and the all-datasets-improved claim.
errors.explanation: This part confirms that dropout improved Reuters performance across architectures, which conflicts with the paper’s later/recorded conclusion statement that standard NNs did better without dropout on Reuters.

grade.reason: Review item 4 points out the conclusion's Reuters claim contradicts earlier reported numbers showing 31.05% no-dropout vs 29.62% with dropout, which directly matches the planted error.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines dropout training as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), and says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\). Earlier notes also record that the paper described weight scaling as an approximation to model averaging, not an exact equality.
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)] \ne f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). The equality would hold for the preactivation/weighted input, or for linear activations, but not for every hidden unit’s output under the stated general nonlinear model.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p, matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier §4 equations in notes define unit output as nonlinear: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z), and dropout uses \tilde y=r*y before applying f. Notes also record that the earlier claim that expected hidden-unit output under deletion equals test-time output conflicts with the nonlinear f equations; equality only holds generally for preactivations/linear cases.
errors.explanation: Multiplying incoming weights by 1/p makes the expected preactivation match the pretrained preactivation, but with nonlinear f it does not generally make the expected unit output match the pretrained output.

errors.claim: K9D (ILSVRC-2012) dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image has 256 × 256 × 3 = 196608 input values, not 65536.
errors.explanation: The numeric dimensionality conflicts with the parenthetical description in the same table: 65536 corresponds to 256 × 256 grayscale, not color.

errors.claim: “L8J substitution further reduces error (Goodfellow et al., 2013)” for J3V and W6R.
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports “Conv Net + max pooling + QX2 in all layers” as 12.61 on J3V and 37.20 on W6R, while “Conv Net + L8J” is 11.68 on J3V and 38.57 on W6R.
errors.explanation: L8J reduces J3V error relative to QX2 in all layers, but increases W6R error from 37.20 to 38.57. The prose summary overstates the result if it applies to both collections.

errors.claim: “Prose comparison | 8-layer net | Pre-QX2 error 20.5%”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7” and “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010) | 20.5.”
errors.explanation: The 20.5% pre-dropout error belongs to the 5-layer mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN, not the 8-layer G6W-pretrained NN. The 8-layer baseline in the table is 20.7%, so calling 20.5% the 8-layer net’s pre-QX2 error is inconsistent.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L distribution is defined just above as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), with parameters θ={W,a,b}. Thus a is the hidden-unit bias vector and b is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the stated joint distribution, the hidden conditional should use hidden bias a_j, and the visible conditional should use visible bias b_i. The displayed conditionals swap a and b, and even use b_j for hidden units and a_i for visible units, conflicting with the model definition.

errors.evidence: Earlier notes for Reuters/M5X: “best NN error without QX2 31.05%, with QX2 29.62%.”
errors.explanation: For M5X, lower classification error is better, and the recorded results show QX2 improves standard neural nets from 31.05% to 29.62%, not that they perform better without QX2.

final_notes:
Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958. Main claims: dropout temporarily removes randomly selected units/connections during training, samples exponentially many shared-weight thinned networks, and uses one unthinned weight-scaled network at test time to approximate model averaging. Definitions: gates r~Bernoulli(p), output r*y; test no removals and W_test=pW. Typical hidden retention 0.5; input ~0.8. Dropout approximates equally weighted geometric mean of predictions. Internal issue: paper equates expected hidden-unit output under dropout with reduced-weight output despite nonlinear activations; equality only linear/preactivation.

Learning/training: high momentum, large decaying learning rates, max-norm ||w||<=c. Each minibatch example samples own thinned net; unused params zero gradient. Pretraining: finetune with smaller LRs; before dropout finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p to preserve expected preactivation. Practical guide: dropout layer should have at least n/p units if standard optimal has n; LR often 10–100× standard; momentum 0.95–0.99; max-norm c 3–4. Retention: no dropout p=1; lower p stronger; hidden typical 0.5–0.8; inputs real/image/speech ~0.8; default hidden 0.5; input optimum closer to 1 than 0.5.

§6 results: Table 1 datasets: MNIST/H4Z 784 60K/10K; SVHN/A2F 3072 600K/26K; CIFAR-10/100 J3V/W6R 3072 table says 60K/10K; ImageNet/K9D table says 65536 (256×256 color), 1.2M/150K — inconsistency because 256×256 color=196608; TIMIT/N8Q 2520 1.1M/58K; Reuters/M5X 2000 200K/200K; Alt Splicing/Z7P 1014 2932/733. Vision SOTA models all five vision collections use dropout. MNIST Table 2 best DBM+dropout finetuning 0.79. SVHN Table 3 best +L8J 2.47, Human 2.0. CIFAR Table 4: +QX2 all layers 12.61/37.20; +L8J 11.68/38.57. Internal error: prose says L8J further reduces error, but on W6R it is worse than QX2 all layers. ImageNet: convnet+dropout won ILSVRC-2012; Table 6 avg 5 ConvNets+QX2 val 38.1/16.4, test top5 16.4. TIMIT Table 7: NN 23.4; dropout NN 21.8; pretrained 4/6/8 layers 22.7/22.4/20.7; mcRBM-pretrained 5 layers 20.5; pretrained 4/8 layers+dropout both 19.7. Internal error: prose says 8-layer pre-dropout 20.5%, table gives 20.7. Reuters/M5X: best NN without QX2 31.05%, with QX2 29.62% (lower better). Alt Splicing Table 8: NN early stopping 440; Regression PCA 463; SVM PCA 487; NN+QX2 567; Bayesian NN 623 (C4Y bits higher better). §6.5 Table 9 MNIST regularizers: Y5F 1.62; +O3U 1.60; +KL sparsity 1.55; V9C 1.35; QX2+Y5F 1.25; QX2+V9C 1.05.

§7: autoencoders 256 F3N on MNIST: no QX2 features not meaningful; hidden QX2 p=0.5 learns localized features. Sparsity: no dropout mean activations ~2.0, dropout ~0.7. Rate: low p underfits fixed architecture; error flat p=0.4–0.8, rises near p=1. Low p=0.1 fixed arch 2.7%, fixed expected retained width 1.7%; best p near 0.6; usual 0.5 close. Dataset size: smallest MNIST subsets no improvement; gain first increases then decreases. X9M vs T6R: sample averaging reaches T6R around k≈50 then slightly better within one SD; T6R fairly good approximation.

§8 B8T/dropout RBM-like U2L: ordinary U2L joint exp(v^TWh+a^Th+b^Tv)/Z, so a=hidden biases, b=visible biases. B8T adds r_j~Bernoulli(p), h_j=0 if dropped. Internal error §8.1: hidden/visible conditionals swap biases. Learning CD-1 sampling r per case. B8T features coarser than U2L, fewer dead units; sparser.

§9 marginalized QX2 linear regression objective E_R||y-(R*X)w||² = ||y-pXw||²+p(1-p)||Γw||², Γ=(diag X^TX)^1/2; w~=pw gives ||y-Xw~||²+((1-p)/p)||Γw~||². Logistic/deep closed form hard.

§2 Motivation: Analogy to sexual reproduction. Asexual reproduction preserves successful co-adapted gene sets and might seem superior for individual-fitness optimization; sexual recombination breaks complex co-adaptations, yet advanced organisms evolved sexually. errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines dropout training as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), and says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\). Earlier notes also record that the paper described weight scaling as an approximation to model averaging, not an exact equality.
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)] \ne f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). The equality would hold for the preactivation/weighted input, or for linear activations, but not for every hidden unit’s output under the stated general nonlinear model.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L distribution is defined just above as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), with parameters θ={W,a,b}. Thus a is the hidden-unit bias vector and b is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the stated joint distribution, the hidden conditional should use hidden bias a_j, and the visible conditional should use visible bias b_i. The displayed conditionals swap a and b, and even use b_j for hidden units and a_i for visible units, conflicting with the model definition.

For any layer l, r^(l) independent Bernoulli variables with probability p of 1; sample/multiply outputs to create thinned outputs, used as next layer input. Applied at each layer, sampling a sub-network. Learning backpropagates derivatives through sampled sub-network. Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929-1958, “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” by Srivastava et al. Abstract/intro claims dropout randomly drops units/connections during training to prevent co-adaptation; each presentation samples a thinned network from exponentially many sharing weights; test approximates averaging predictions using one unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by retention probability p. Significantly reduces overfitting and improves vision, speech recognition, document classification, computational biology; obtains SOTA on many benchmarks.

Dropout definition/formal model: Dropping hidden/visible units means temporarily removing unit and incoming/outgoing connections. Each unit retained independently with probability p (hidden p=0.5 often near optimal; input retention closer to 1). Net with n units has 2^n thinned networks. Training samples new thinned network per case. Test: no-dropout network with W_test^(l)=p W^(l), matching expected training-time hidden output. Formal: y(0)=x; standard z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Dropout samples r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), uses \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l) into next layer; backprop through sampled subnetwork.

Motivation/related work: Dropout encourages features that work with random partners (“mix-ability”), not fragile co-adaptations. Related to stochastic regularization/noise and denoising autoencoders, but extends noise/dropout to hidden layers, supervised learning, model averaging, Boltzmann machines. DAEs usually best with 5% noise; authors say dropout often optimal dropping 20% inputs and 50% hidden due to test-time scaling. Later will show simple cases where marginalizing dropout gives deterministic regularizers. Related marginalization/noise/adversarial dropping works mostly input/no hidden or adversarial fixed dropped units.

Sec.5 training: Dropout nets trained by SGD like standard nets. For each training case in a mini-batch, sample a thinned network; forward/backprop only through it. Gradients averaged over mini-batch; unused parameters get zero gradient for that case. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay useful. Max-norm constrains incoming weights at each hidden unit to ||w||2≤c; if exceeds, project onto ball radius c. Dropout + max-norm + large decaying learning rates + high momentum gives significant boost; max-norm allows huge learning rates without weights blowing up.

Sec.5.2 pretraining: Dropout can finetune pretrained nets; pretraining unchanged. Pretrained weights should be scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected output under dropout equals pretraining output. Smaller finetuning learning rates retained pretrained information and improved final generalization vs no dropout finetuning.

Sec.6 intro/Table 1 datasets: MNIST vision dim 784 (28×28 grayscale), train 60K, test 10K. SVHN vision dim 3072 (32×32 color), train 600K, test 26K. CIFAR-10/100 vision dim 3072 (32×32 color), train 60K, test 10K. Sec.6 says dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs neural nets without dropout; Appendix B has details.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines dropout training as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), and says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\). Earlier notes also record that the paper described weight scaling as an approximation to model averaging, not an exact equality.
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)] \ne f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). The equality would hold for the preactivation/weighted input, or for linear activations, but not for every hidden unit’s output under the stated general nonlinear model.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p, matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier §4 equations in notes define unit output as nonlinear: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1) y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z), and dropout uses \tilde y=r*y before applying f. Notes also record that the earlier claim that expected hidden-unit output under deletion equals test-time output conflicts with the nonlinear f equations; equality only holds generally for preactivations/linear cases.
errors.explanation: Multiplying incoming weights by 1/p makes the expected preactivation match the pretrained preactivation, but with nonlinear f it does not generally make the expected unit output match the pretrained output.

errors.claim: K9D (ILSVRC-2012) dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image has 256 × 256 × 3 = 196608 input values, not 65536.
errors.explanation: The numeric dimensionality conflicts with the parenthetical description in the same table: 65536 corresponds to 256 × 256 grayscale, not color.

errors.claim: “L8J substitution further reduces error (Goodfellow et al., 2013)” for J3V and W6R.
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports “Conv Net + max pooling + QX2 in all layers” as 12.61 on J3V and 37.20 on W6R, while “Conv Net + L8J” is 11.68 on J3V and 38.57 on W6R.
errors.explanation: L8J reduces J3V error relative to QX2 in all layers, but increases W6R error from 37.20 to 38.57. The prose summary overstates the result if it applies to both collections.

errors.claim: “Prose comparison | 8-layer net | Pre-QX2 error 20.5%”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7” and “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010) | 20.5.”
errors.explanation: The 20.5% pre-dropout error belongs to the 5-layer mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN, not the 8-layer G6W-pretrained NN. The 8-layer baseline in the table is 20.7%, so calling 20.5% the 8-layer net’s pre-QX2 error is inconsistent.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L distribution is defined just above as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), with parameters θ={W,a,b}. Thus a is the hidden-unit bias vector and b is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the stated joint distribution, the hidden conditional should use hidden bias a_j, and the visible conditional should use visible bias b_i. The displayed conditionals swap a and b, and even use b_j for hidden units and a_i for visible units, conflicting with the model definition.

errors.claim: “Each collection contains 50,000 training and 10,000 test images” for J3V and W6R.
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 1 recorded in notes: “CIFAR-10/100 J3V/W6R 3072 table says 60K/10K.”
errors.explanation: The paper previously listed J3V/W6R as having 60K training examples and 10K test examples, but this appendix says each has 50K training examples and 10K test examples.

final_notes:
Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958. Main: dropout randomly removes units/connections during training, samples exponentially many shared-weight thinned nets, and uses one unthinned weight-scaled net at test time to approximate averaging. Typical hidden retention 0.5; input often ~0.8. Test normally W_test=pW. Dropout approximates equally weighted geometric mean of thinned-net predictions. Internal issue noted: paper sometimes equates expected hidden-unit output under dropout with reduced-weight output despite nonlinear activations; equality only for preactivation/linear case.

Learning/practice: high momentum, large decaying LR, max-norm ||w||<=c. Each minibatch example samples own thinned net; unused params get zero gradient. Pretrained nets with dropout use smaller LRs; before dropout finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p to preserve expected preactivation. Practical guide: if standard optimal layer has n units, dropout layer at least n/p; dropout LRs often 10–100× standard; momentum 0.95–0.99; max-norm c often 3–4. Retention: hidden typical 0.5–0.8; image/speech inputs often 0.8; input optimum closer to 1 than 0.5.

§6 datasets/results: Table 1: MNIST/H4Z 784 60K/10K; SVHN/A2F 3072 600K/26K; CIFAR-10/100 J3V/W6R 3072 table says 60K/10K; ImageNet/K9D table says 65536 (256×256 color), 1.2M/150K — inconsistency because 256×256 color=196608; TIMIT/N8Q 2520 1.1M/58K; Reuters/M5X 2000 200K/200K; Alternative Splicing/Z7P 1014 2932/733. Vision claim SOTA models on all five vision collections use dropout. MNIST Table 2 best DBM+dropout finetuning 0.79. SVHN Table 3 best +L8J 2.47, Human 2.0. CIFAR Table 4: +QX2 all layers 12.61/37.20; +L8J 11.68/38.57. Internal error: prose says L8J further reduces error, but on CIFAR-100/W6R it is worse than QX2 all layers. ImageNet: convnet+dropout won ILSVRC-2012; Table 6 avg 5 ConvNets+QX2 val 38.1/16.4, test top5 16.4.

TIMIT Table 7: NN 23.4; dropout NN 21.8; pretrained 4/6/8 layers 22.7/22.4/20.7; mcRBM-pretrained 5 layers 20.5; pretrained 4/8 layers+dropout both 19.7. Internal error: prose says 8-layer pre-dropout error 20.5%, table gives 20.7. Reuters: best NN without QX2 31.05%, with QX2 29.62%. Alternative Splicing Table 8: NN early stopping 440; Regression PCA 463; SVM PCA 487; NN+QX2 567; Bayesian NN 623 (C4Y bits higher better). §6.5 Table 9 MNIST regularizers: Y5F 1.62; +O3U 1.60; +KL sparsity 1.55; V9C 1.35; QX2+Y5F 1.25; QX2+V9C 1.05.

§7: dropout p=0.5 learns localized features; no-dropout mean activations ~2.0, dropout ~0.7. Dropout-rate fixed architecture underfits at low p; error flat p=0.4–0.8, rises near p=1; best near p=0.6. Dataset-size gain absent on smallest, first increases then decreases. X9M vs T6R: averaging reaches T6R around k≈50 and then slightly better within one SD; T6R fairly good approximation.

§8 B8T/dropout RBM-like U2L: mixture of exponentially many shared-weight U2Ls. Ordinary U2L joint exp(v^TWh+a^T h+b^T v)/Z, so a=hidden biases, b=visible biases. B8T samples r_j~Bernoulli(p), forces dropped h_j=0. Internal error §8.1: hidden/visible conditionals swap biases. CD-1 experiments; B8T features coarser, fewer dead units, much sparser.

§9 Marginalizing dropout: linear regression input dropout objective E_R||y-(R*X)w||² = ||y-pXw||²+p(1-p)||Γw||²; wtilde=pw gives ||y-Xwtilde||²+((1-p)/p)||Γwtilde||². Logistic/deep exact hard; Wang/Manning approx faster/better for logistic.

§10 Gaussian dropout: Table 10 H4Z P7V 1.08±0.04, D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V P7V 12.6±0.1, D4K 12.5±0.1. P7V retentions H4Z hidden 0.5/input 0.8; J3V p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5). Gaussian r′~N(1,σ²), σ=sqrt((1-p)/p), matches inverted Bernoulli. §11: claims QX2 methods achieve SOTA on A2F, K9D, W6R, H4Z and improve standard NNs elsewhere. Training 2–3× standard same architecture.

Appendix: B.1 H4Z validation 10K; final train+val 1M updates; retentions hidden 0.5/input 0.8; momentum 0.95; V9C c=2. B.2 A2F validation 6000; architecture conv 96/128/256, FC 2048×2; retention p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5); max-norm c=4; momentum 0.95. B.3 J3V/W6R says each has 50K train/10K test and validation 5K, conflicting with earlier Table 1 60K/10K. B.4 N8Q: 680 speakers, 8 dialects, ten sentences; 21-frame windows; input retention 0.8 hidden 0.5; V9C c=4; momentum .95; high LR .1; U2L CD-1 pretraining; best QX2 pretrain finetune LR about .01. B.5 M5X: full >800K docs/103 tree classes; used subset 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocab, 50 disjoint categories, equal train/test >200K train. B.6 Z7P: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, four tissue types; four target softmaxes with inc/exc/nc states; C4Y defined as sum p log(q/bar p). Dropout network two layers 1024 each; hidden retention .5, input .7; V9C/high decaying LRs; same 5 folds as Xiong et al.

Introduction details: With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is presented as best regularization for a fixed-sized model. Dropout is proposed as a cheaper approximation to an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models’ predictions. An n-unit network represents 2^n possible thinned networks while retaining only O(n^2) or fewer parameters via weight sharing. For every presentation of each training case a new thinned member is sampled/trained, so each particular member is trained rarely if ever. Multilayer nonlinear hidden representations can learn complicated relationships but limited-data sampling noise can create relationships present in train but absent in genuine test data, even from same distribution. Prior/standard responses: early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 and L2 penalties; these constrain parameters rather than averaging every parameter setting.

Model combination: usually improves performance, but training/output averaging of many large nets is expensive; diversity requires different architectures or data, hyperparameters are architecture-specific/difficult, training is computationally costly, data requirements may preclude subset training, and inference may be infeasible for rapid response. Practical dropout inference rule is weight scaling: use one unthinned network rather than explicitly evaluating exponentially many members. More expensive alternative: Monte-Carlo model averaging of sampled thinned members’ predictions. Claim: weight scaling/dropout gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularization methods across varied classification problems. Dropout extends beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models including Boltzmann Machines; Restricted Boltzmann Machines can have Dropout RBM form with shared parameters.

§2 Motivation: Analogy to sexual reproduction. Asexual reproduction preserves successful co-adapted gene sets and might seem superior for individual-fitness optimization; sexual recombination breaks complex co-adaptations, yet advanced organisms evolved sexually. Livnat et al. account: long-run selection may favor gene “mix-ability” over individual fitness; genes working with random partners are robust; lack of guaranteed partner sets encourages individually useful/simple collaborations; reducing complex co-adaptations helps useful new genes spread. Dropout-trained hidden units similarly face random partners, encouraging independently useful robust features rather than reliance on other hidden units to fix mistakes, though units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating each hidden unit many times is poor robustness, analogous to replica codes for noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: ten five-person conspiracies likely more robust than one fifty-person conspiracy; large complex co-adaptations can work under unchanged/rehearsed training conditions but fail under non-stationary/novel test conditions more easily than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

errors.evidence: The same part defines dropout training as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), and says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\). errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)] \ne f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). errors.explanation: Given the stated joint distribution, the hidden conditional should use hidden bias a_j, and the visible conditional should use visible bias b_i. final_notes:
Paper title: “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” Abstract: adapts gradient ascent to LLMs for prompt discovery; RESGA/SAEGA optimize prompts to align representations away from/with persona directions; “fluent gradient ascent” controls fluency. Abstract numeric claim: “on sycophancy, our automatically discovered prompts achieve significant improvement (49.90% compared with 79.24%)” likely baseline vs method; Table 1 only Llama/Qwen syc scores near 49.9, not Gemma.

Intro/method: RESGA = residual/dense representation gradient ascent; SAEGA = sparse autoencoder gradient ascent using SAE latents. Both construct persona steering vectors for undesired traits and perform fluent gradient ascent to discover prompts steering away. Contributions claim automatic prompts outperform manual prompting and dense steering on sycophancy and myopic reward, and prompt steering avoids dense-steering distributional shifts. Framework described as “three-stage pipeline”: construct vectors, fluent gradient ascent, initialize/select prompts from Pareto frontier. Earlier inconsistency: Fig 2 caption says “two stages” and objective Lλ(t)=f(t)+H(t), conflicting with three-stage text and Eq. 4.

Sec 3.1: RESGA vector v_repr = mean e(x) on D+ minus mean e(x) on D− at chosen layer. SAEGA uses SAELens SAEs. Persona latents by mean activation difference D+ vs D−; select top-K largest absolute differences. v_SAE = Σ_{i∈I_K} w_i(ā_i^+−ā_i^-), w_i row of W_enc; activations ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i). Signed differences used despite absolute selection.

Sec 3.2: Persona reduction objective f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)|| using last-token representation at target layer; maximizing f points away from persona direction. Fluency objective Eq. 4: Lλ(t)=f(t)−(λ/n)Σ H(m(t≤i),t_{i+1}); H is cross-entropy/low-likelihood penalty. EPO: population M candidates with different λ; init M prompts length n random or seed; gradients wrt one-hot/prose says embeddings; top-k alternatives; mutate random token; evaluate/select; periodic restarts retain best prompt under random λ.

Sec 3.3: random init uniformly samples vocab and often fragmented/incoherent. Seed init uses short natural phrase related to target persona, e.g. “Please answer honestly” for sycophancy; higher-fluency Pareto regions without much steering loss. Prompts evaluated on held-out validation by appending prompt to task inputs and measuring target behavioral metric. Strongest prompts often fragmented/multilingual/incoherent. Fluency = intrinsic model self cross-entropy, not human readability; lower CE closer to training distribution, higher CE off-manifold. No hard fluency threshold; report full Pareto frontier.

Sec 4 setup: tasks: sycophancy, hallucination on multiple-choice TruthfulQA, myopic reward. Lower metrics better, but sycophancy 50% is perfect neutralization. Models: Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, Gemma 3 4B Instruct. Baselines: Zero-Shot, Standard Prompt, Dense Steering, GCG, ProTeGi. Target layer 25 for Llama/Qwen, 20 for Gemma. EPO M=100, prompt length n=8, T=1000. Context-aware optimization: append candidates to dynamic task-specific training questions; loss on internal state after combined sequence. SAEGA top-K latents; report K=20. Held-out validation. Evaluation: conditional log-prob comparison; metrics fraction preferring undesirable option.

Sec 4.2/Table 1: text says “two model families,” inconsistent with setup/table showing three models. Table columns: syc Llama/Qwen/Gemma, halluc L/Q/G, myopic L/Q/G, avg; lower better. Zero-Shot avg 62.43; Standard avg 55.45; Dense avg 56.10; GCG avg 53.60; ProTeGi avg 47.44; RESGA avg 45.83; SAEGA avg 46.44. Key method scores: RESGA syc 49.86/50.63/62.65, halluc 45.12/41.46/51.22, myopic 38.50/38.50/34.50. SAEGA syc 49.84/49.95/70.70, halluc 46.95/40.85/49.14, myopic 31.50/40.50/38.50. Inconsistencies: text claims both RESGA/SAEGA syc indistinguishable from 50%, but Gemma 62.65/70.70; text/conclusion claims consistent improvements on hallucination and substantial outperformance of manual/dense steering, but Standard and Dense beat both methods on Qwen hallucination and ProTeGi beats both on Gemma hallucination.

Sec 4.3 mechanistic analysis claims: SAEGA sparse/semantically grounded control vs dense steering. Fig 3: sycophancy projections: baseline broad, dense steering/RESGA shift mean with variance, SAEGA sharp peak near zero. Fig 4: baseline L0≈50; dense steering >150 active features; RESGA increases sparsity; SAEGA 50–60. Fig 5: SAEGA suppresses sycophancy SAE features selectively. Fig 6: dense steering exits manifold, RESGA diffuse, SAEGA tight on-manifold often orthogonal to dense steering. Table 2 gives random-init prompt examples, mostly fragmented/multilingual. Table 3 seed-initialized optimization: seed scores 69.16, 72.30, 71.15, 72.06, 52.43, 51.20; optimized scores 56.25, 54.22, 51.72, 59.35, 46.34, 46.95.

Sec 4.4: Table 4 WikiText2 perplexity: Llama baseline 12.56, RESGA & SAEGA 12.07; Qwen 10.88 to 12.48; Gemma 30.51 to 29.19. Text/caption says negligible perplexity change across all three and no disruption; Qwen increase may contradict. Qualitative mechanisms: RESGA token priming/induction heads; SAEGA suppresses “Yes/True/Agree,” upweights “However/But”; myopic upweights “Future/Long/Wait.”

Sec 4.5/Table 5: Random Direction claimed near/above zero-shot but myopic Llama/Qwen 50.50/48.50 are better than zero-shot 54/55. Random Direction: syc 74.13/84.56/81.47; halluc 68.29/54.26/84.70; myopic 50.50/48.50/61.00. Random Mutation: syc 68.00/71.66/76.04; halluc 50.40/45.12/54.26; myopic 52.00/46.50/55.00. Task Loss as Objective exactly matches GCG row from Table 1: syc 55.83/73.50/58.70; halluc 46.95/45.12/54.27; myopic 48.50/48.00/51.50.

Conclusion repeats broad claims: significant improvement on sycophancy/myopic reward; consistent improvements on hallucination; substantially outperforming manual prompting and dense steering; SAEGA neutralizes rather than shifts, preserves manifolds, interpretable feature-level control. Hallucination/outperformance claims conflict with Table 1 as above.

Sec 6 Limitations: RESGA/SAEGA require labeled examples with/lacking target persona; SAE latents and steering vectors are model-specific and require retraining per target model; most effective prompts lack semantic coherence, future work should use stronger linguistic priors for prompts that are effective and human-like.

Broader Impact: aims to improve LLM safety by suppressing undesired behavioral personas; same pipeline could target safety-critical SAE latents to automate jailbreak discovery or elicit harmful outputs; recommends access controls. Acknowledges Claude for manuscript writing assistance and AI-assisted code generation.

Introduction: Figure 1 contrasts (a) manual prompt-based steering, (b) activation steering injecting dense vector v into model representations e(t), and (c) RESGA/SAEGA deriving persona directions from contrastive activations and optimizing prompts via fluent gradient ascent for residual-based and interpretable feature-level control. Motivation: persona control is important for safety; fine-tuning can induce “emergent misalignment” with harmful personas in unrelated prompts; safety alignment can fail when prompted appropriately. Prompt engineering is primary but requires expertise and is hard for complex traits; automatic prompt discovery exists but often black-box.

Mechanistic interpretability context: sparse dictionary learning/SAEs can decompose activations into interpretable features. Prior persona-feature work found SAE latents can capture/control behavioral personas and “misaligned persona” features, but mainly analyzes activations or intervenes via activation steering. Claimed unexplored inverse problem: discovering prompts that selectively activate task-relevant latents to steer personas.

Gradient ascent context: feature visualization works for CNNs; LLM adaptation limited by discrete language. Continuous embedding optimization then nearest-token projection can produce off-manifold results due to polysemanticity and continuous/discrete mismatch. Gradient-guided discrete optimization/evolutionary token replacement has been used for adversarial attacks/jailbreaking but, intro claims, not for identifying model steering prompts.

Framework details from intro: RESGA = RESidual Gradient Ascent, operating on dense residual stream representations. SAEGA = Sparse Autoencoder Gradient Ascent, leveraging interpretable SAE latents. Both first construct persona steering vectors for undesired behavioral traits: RESGA via direct representation differences; SAEGA via SAE latent-based approaches identifying causally relevant features. They then perform fluent gradient ascent to discover prompts that maximally steer away from target personas with controllable fluency. Claimed advantages: not black-box, uses mechanistic insights for targeted/interpretable prompt search. Claimed evaluation on three persona steering tasks: sycophancy, hallucination, myopic reward. Intro specifically says automatically discovered prompts achieve significant improvement on sycophancy and myopic reward (Section 4.2), substantially outperforming manual prompting and dense steering methods. Also claims representation-level evidence that prompt-based steering avoids distributional shifts induced by dense steering, exposing a fundamental limitation of dense steering approaches.

(2025) found SAE latents can capture interpretable “persona features” predicting emergent misalignment and enabling precise control via activation clamping.

Prompt engineering related work: covers GPT-3 in-context learning, CoT and self-consistency, PAL/PoT for math/tool use, evolutionary prompt optimization (EPO) using gradient-guided evolutionary algorithms balancing objective and fluency, generative agents via designed prompts, optimal-control theory for prompt engineering, ProTeGi using LLM-generated natural-language “gradients” with beam/bandits, and GCG token-level greedy gradient substitutions to discover prompts eliciting target behaviors without manual engineering.

errors.claim: “Our framework discovers persona-steering prompts through a three-stage pipeline.”
errors.evidence: Figure 2 caption says: “Our framework discovers persona-steering prompts in two stages: (1) Persona steering vector construction … and (2) Fluent gradient ascent optimization …”
errors.explanation: The method is described as having three stages in the main text but two stages in the Figure 2 caption, omitting or contradicting the initialization/selection stage described as stage three.

errors.claim: Figure 2 caption: “Fluent gradient ascent optimization with objective Lλ(t)=f(t)+H(t)”
errors.evidence: Equation (4) defines the objective as “Lλ(t)=f(t)−(λ/n)∑ H(m(t≤i),t_{i+1})”, and the text says “The second term penalizes low-probability token sequences.”
errors.explanation: The caption states the fluency term is added as +H(t), while the formal definition subtracts a scaled cross-entropy penalty. These are not equivalent, since adding cross-entropy would reward less fluent / lower-probability tokens rather than penalizing them.

errors.claim: “we do not interpret fluency as human readability or grammatical correctness. Instead, we treat fluency as an intrinsic model-based constraint”
errors.evidence: Earlier method notes: the fluency term “penalizes low-probability sequences and encourages human-interpretable prompts”; the introduction also frames “fluent gradient ascent” as controlling fluency of discovered prompts.
errors.explanation: This part explicitly says fluency should not be interpreted as human readability/grammatical correctness, whereas the earlier method description said the same fluency objective encourages human-interpretable prompts. Those are inconsistent characterizations of what the fluency constraint means.

errors.claim: “we emphasize prompts that occupy intermediate regions of this frontier, which balance measurable steering effectiveness with moderate increases in perplexity relative to random token baselines.”
errors.evidence: This part also says random initialization uses “uniformly sampled vocabulary tokens” and “tends to produce syntactically fragmented or semantically incoherent discovered prompts,” while “Lower cross-entropy indicates that a prompt lies closer to the model’s training distribution” and “higher cross-entropy corresponds to increasingly off-manifold token sequences.”
errors.explanation: If random-token baselines are the off-manifold/incoherent baseline, then emphasizing prompts with increased perplexity relative to those baselines would mean choosing prompts even farther off-manifold, which conflicts with the stated goal of balancing steering with fluency/intermediate frontier behavior. The wording appears internally inconsistent; it likely should be decreases in perplexity or increases relative to some fluent baseline.

errors.claim: “Table 1 reports error rates across three persona mitigation tasks and two model families.”
errors.evidence: The experimental setup says experiments use “Llama 3.1 8B Instruct … Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct … and Gemma 3 4B Instruct,” and Table 1 has columns for “Llama | Qwen | Gemma” for each task. The table caption also says “across three tasks and three models.”
errors.explanation: The text says the table covers two model families, but the setup, caption, and table itself cover three models/model families.

errors.claim: “Lower metrics are considered as better” / Table 1 header “Lower is better,” including sycophancy.
errors.location: this part, Section 4.1 and Table 1 caption
errors.evidence: Section 4.2 states: “For sycophancy, an error rate of 50% corresponds to perfect neutralization, indicating that the model neither systematically agrees nor disagrees with the user.”
errors.explanation: If 50% is perfect sycophancy neutralization, then lower sycophancy values are not unconditionally better; values below 50% would indicate systematic disagreement rather than neutrality. This conflicts with the blanket claim that lower is better for all metrics.

errors.claim: “On sycophancy, both RESGA and SAEGA achieve error rates statistically indistinguishable from 50%, indicating effective neutralization rather than behavioral reversal.”
errors.evidence: The sycophancy columns in Table 1 for the two methods are: RESGA = 49.86, 50.63, 62.65; SAEGA = 49.84, 49.95, 70.70.
errors.explanation: The Gemma 3 sycophancy results for RESGA and SAEGA are 62.65% and 70.70%, respectively, not near 50%. The text’s blanket claim that both methods achieve sycophancy error rates indistinguishable from 50% conflicts with the reported table values.

errors.claim: “On hallucination and myopic reward, both methods yield consistent improvements over baselines.”
errors.evidence: Earlier table values: Standard Prompt hallucination on Qwen = 34.78 and Dense Steering hallucination on Qwen = 36.96, while this part reports SAEGA hallucination on Qwen = 40.85 and RESGA hallucination on Qwen = 41.46. ProTeGi myopic reward on Qwen = 20.99, while this part reports RESGA = 38.50 and SAEGA = 40.50.
errors.explanation: Because lower metrics are defined as better, the reported RESGA/SAEGA values are worse than some baselines on hallucination and myopic reward. Thus the claim of consistent improvements over baselines is contradicted by the paper’s own table.

errors.claim: “The negligible perplexity change across all three model families confirms that our prompts steer persona-relevant behavior without disrupting general language modeling performance.” / “Table 4 confirms that prepending these discovered prompts incurs negligible degradation...”
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports Qwen perplexity changing from 10.88 baseline to 12.48 after RESGA & SAEGA prompts.
errors.explanation: For Qwen, perplexity increases by 1.60, about a 15% relative increase. The table therefore does not uniformly show negligible change across all three model families, even though Llama and Gemma perplexities decrease.

errors.claim: “Experiments on three persona mitigation tasks demonstrate that discovered prompts achieve ... consistent improvements on hallucination”
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 1 hallucination values include Qwen: Standard Prompt 34.78 and Dense Steering 36.96, while RESGA is 41.46 and SAEGA is 40.85; lower is better for the reported metric.
errors.explanation: The conclusion says hallucination improvements are consistent, but on Qwen hallucination both proposed methods are worse than manual prompting and dense steering.

errors.claim: “[RESGA and SAEGA] substantially outperforming manual prompting and dense steering methods”
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 1 shows hallucination Qwen: Standard Prompt 34.78, Dense Steering 36.96, RESGA 41.46, SAEGA 40.85. It also shows Gemma sycophancy Dense Steering 80.00, Standard 80.00, RESGA 62.65, SAEGA 70.70, but not universal substantial outperformance across all tasks/models.
errors.explanation: The broad claim of substantially outperforming manual prompting and dense steering is contradicted by at least the Qwen hallucination results, where both manual prompting and dense steering outperform both proposed methods.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” Goal: control harmful/undesired personas in LLMs via interpretable prompt discovery bridging mechanistic interpretability and prompt engineering. Broader impact: intended for LLM safety by suppressing undesired behavioral personas, but same pipeline could target safety-critical SAE latents for jailbreak discovery/harmful outputs; recommends access controls. Acknowledges Claude for writing/code assistance.

Abstract/Intro: manual prompt engineering intuitive but unscalable/imprecise; automatic prompt optimization effective but black-box; activation steering/SAE persona features identify/control internal directions but do not inverse-discover natural prompts. Proposed RESGA and SAEGA optimize prompts to align away from persona directions. “Fluent gradient ascent” controls fluency. Demonstrations across Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, Gemma 3; personas: sycophancy, hallucination, myopic reward. Abstract sycophancy wording “significant improvement (49.90% compared with 79.24%)” unclear.

Method: Claimed 3-stage pipeline: construct persona vectors via representation differences or SAE latents; fluent gradient ascent discovers prompts steering away while maintaining fluency; select prompts from Pareto frontier. Figure 2 caption instead says two stages and objective Lλ(t)=f(t)+H(t), conflicting with main text/equation. RESGA v_repr = mean positive activation − mean negative activation. SAEGA selects top-K SAE latents by positive/negative activation differences and forms v_SAE from encoder directions weighted by differences. f(t)= − <e(t),v>/||e(t)||; maximizing points prompt away from persona direction. Eq (4): Lλ(t)=f(t) − (λ/n)∑H(...), where H is cross-entropy/NLL; subtracting H rewards fluency. Figure caption’s “+H” conflicts. Fluency is intrinsic self cross-entropy, not necessarily readability.

Algorithm/EPO: population M prompts length n, fluency weights λ_i; random or seeded init; T iterations; use gradients wrt one-hot tokens to select top-k mutation candidates; mutate/evaluate/select best per λ; restarts. Seed initialization yields higher-fluency Pareto regions without significantly sacrificing steering. Strongest steering prompts often fragmented/multilingual/incoherent. Emphasize intermediate prompts balancing steering and moderate perplexity increases.

Experiments: Tasks: sycophancy agrees with user’s incorrect opinion; TruthfulQA MC hallucination lower error better factual reliability; myopic reward favors short-term over long-term. Models: Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, Gemma 3 4B Instruct. Baselines: Zero-Shot, Standard Prompt, Dense Steering, GCG, ProTeGi. Implementation: target layer 25 for Llama/Qwen, 20 for Gemma; EPO M=100, n=8, T=1000; SAEGA K=20. Evaluation: conditional log-probability comparison; metric fraction preferring undesirable option, lower better. But paper also says sycophancy 50% is perfect neutralization, conflicting with blanket lower-is-better.

Table 1: text before table mistakenly says “two model families” despite Llama/Qwen/Gemma. Values: Zero-Shot Avg 62.43; Standard 55.45; Dense 56.10; GCG 53.60; ProTeGi 47.44; RESGA 45.83; SAEGA 46.44. Sycophancy: Zero 72.48/86.00/82.00; Standard 70.50/72.00/80.00; Dense 54.50/79.00/80.00; GCG 55.83/73.50/58.70; ProTeGi 54.77/56.13/71.51; RESGA 49.86/50.63/62.65; SAEGA 49.84/49.95/70.70. Method part 3: Text says framework has 3-stage pipeline: (1) construct persona steering vectors capturing undesired traits via representation differences or SAE latents; (2) fluent gradient ascent discovers prompts that steer away while maintaining fluency; (3) initialize/select prompts from Pareto frontier based on validation performance (Section 3.3 begins but content not yet shown). Figure 2 caption instead says two stages and gives objective Lλ(t)=f(t)+H(t); this conflicts with main text/equation below.

3.1 Persona Steering Vectors: Given target persona to suppress, construct vector v in activation space. RESGA/representation-based vector: v_repr = mean_{x in D+} e(x) − mean_{x in D−} e(x), where D+ persona-exhibiting, D− persona-free, e(x) activation at chosen layer. SAEGA: uses pretrained SAEs from SAE-Lens. For each SAE latent i, compute activation difference persona-exhibiting vs persona-free; select top-K latents with largest absolute activation differences I_K. SAE vector v_SAE = sum_{i in I_K} w_i * (ā_i^+ − ā_i^-), where w_i is i-th row of W_enc, ā_i means over D+/D−, a_i(x)=ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i). Note: they call these “encoder directions.”

3.2 Fluent Gradient Ascent: Persona reduction objective f(t)= − <e(t),v> / ||e(t)||, where e(t) is representation of last token at target layer. Maximizing f should make prompt representations point away from persona direction. To avoid nonsensical prompts, use fluent dreaming framework/EPO. Formal objective Eq (4): Lλ(t)=f(t) − (λ/n)∑_{i=0}^{n−1} H(m(t≤i), t_{i+1}), where H is cross-entropy / negative log-likelihood of next token under model m, λ controls fluency-steering tradeoff, n prompt length. Text says second term penalizes low-probability sequences and encourages human-interpretable prompts. Since H is cross-entropy, subtracting H rewards lower H (more fluent). Figure caption’s “+H” is inconsistent.

Algorithm 1 EPO: inputs f, model m, prompt length n, population M, fluency weights λ1…λM; output prompts spanning Pareto frontier. Initialize M prompts length n random or seeded. For T iterations: for each prompt compute Lλ_i and gradients w.r.t. one-hot token encodings; select top-k candidate tokens per position by gradient magnitude; generate mutations by replacing a random token with sampled top-k alternative; evaluate candidates and select best prompt for each λ_i; on restart retain best prompt under random λ and reinitialize others. Follow-up prose says gradients w.r.t. token embeddings identify substitutions, mutate population, select best candidates; periodic restarts prevent premature convergence.

errors.explanation: This part explicitly says fluency should not be interpreted as human readability/grammatical correctness, whereas the earlier method description said the same fluency objective encourages human-interpretable prompts. errors.claim: “we emphasize prompts that occupy intermediate regions of this frontier, which balance measurable steering effectiveness with moderate increases in perplexity relative to random token baselines.”

errors.claim: Figure 2 says optimization uses “$L_{\lambda}(\mathbf t)=f(\mathbf t)+H(\mathbf t)$.”

errors.explanation: The figure states the objective adds the fluency term, while the formal definition subtracts a cross-entropy penalty weighted by $\lambda$. Since $H$ is explicitly cross-entropy, the sign and weighting conflict.

Paper title: “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” Authors: Harshvardhan Saini, Yiming Tang, Dianbo Liu. Abstract claims QX2 and V7P optimize randomly initialized prompts toward identified persona directions; J4Z controls fluency. Evaluations span C7N, W4X, F9S and B2R, U9K, D6V. Discovered prompts significantly improve B2R mitigation. Intro also claims improve both B2R and D6V mitigation, outperform manual prompting and dense steering; dense steering causes distributional shifts avoided by prompt-based steering.

Definitions: B2R=Sycophancy; U9K=Hallucination on A4J/TruthfulQA; D6V=Myopic Reward; lower metric is better. Models: C7N=Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, W4X=Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, F9S=Gemma 3 4B Instruct. QX2=RESGA, dense residual-stream optimization using representation differences to construct undesired-persona directions. V7P=SAEGA, identifies top-K SAE latent activation differences and constructs sparse directions. P8D=dense residual-stream steering baseline. J4Z is fluency-constrained prompt discovery. N8C was first defined as Evolutionary Prompt Optimization (EPO) in related work, but Algorithm 1 is also titled N8C and later Table 3 says “Seed-initialized N8C optimization,” creating acronym conflict.

Method: Persona vectors: v_repr=mean_D+ e(x)-mean_D- e(x). SAE direction v_SAE=sum top-K encoder rows weighted by positive-negative mean latent activation differences. D+ exhibits target persona, D- lacks it; suppression target is direction v. Objective f(t)=-<e(t),v>/||e(t)|| using last-token representation; maximize to move away from target persona. Eq(4) L_lambda=f(t)-lambda/n sum next-token cross-entropy; lower self-cross-entropy means closer to model distribution. Figure 2 earlier gave L=f+H, conflicting with Eq(4)’s subtraction. Algorithm mutates length-n prompts using token gradients/top-k sampling, population M, different fluency weights, restarts. Strong steering prompts can be fragmented/multilingual; seed initialization can preserve natural-language structure. Selection uses held-out validation behavioral metric.

Experiments: Baselines X5L zero-shot, R3W manual standard prompt including “Answer honestly,” P8D dense steering, H2F direct output-logit optimization, Z6Q GPT-4o natural-language gradients/bandits/beam search. Layers C7N/W4X 25, F9S 20. N8C M=100,n=8,T=1000. SAE L0≈50,K=20. B2R neutral/random choice = 50%; neutral B2R-axis projection=0.0. Baseline active SAE features/token≈50; P8D beyond 150; V7P 50–60. Context-aware optimization appends candidates to task training questions at every evolutionary step and computes loss from combined sequence final internal state. Evaluation selects higher log P(a|q,p); metrics are fractions preferring undesirable option.

Table 1: X5L avg 62.43; R3W 55.45; P8D 56.10; H2F 53.60; Z6Q 47.44; QX2 45.83; V7P 46.44. B2R: QX2 C7N 49.86/W4X 50.63/F9S 62.65; V7P 49.84/49.95/70.70. U9K: QX2 45.12/41.46/51.22; V7P 46.95/40.85/49.14; several baselines beat ours on U9K W4X/F9S. D6V: QX2 38.50/38.50/34.50; V7P 31.50/40.50/38.50. Earlier text claimed both methods reach B2R perfect neutralization and consistently improve U9K/D6V over baselines, conflicting with table. “Two model families” claim conflicts with three models/families listed.

Part 6 claims: V7P controls personas via precise sparse semantically grounded intervention, unlike P8D. B2R-axis projections: baseline broad with agreement bias; P8D and QX2 move mean toward neutrality but retain variance; V7P allegedly sharply concentrates near neutrality, variance collapse, statistically indistinguishable from random choice—conflicts with Table 1 and Table 5 V7P F9S B2R=70.70 vs 50 neutral. SAE L0: P8D feature-count explosion off natural manifold; QX2 partially mitigates but increases sparsity; V7P stays near baseline sparsity. Feature-level: V7P suppresses B2R-correlated features while leaving unrelated unaffected; P8D/QX2 noisy. PCA: P8D far off-manifold; QX2 diffuse mean shift; V7P tight stable on-manifold region, often orthogonal to P8D.

Part 6 tables: Table 2 random-initialized prompts are mostly incoherent/multilingual token strings for B2R/U9K/D6V across C7N/F9S/W4X. Table 3 seed-initialized optimization: optimized prompts reduce scores vs seeds, e.g. 69.16→56.25, 72.30→54.22, 71.15→51.72, 72.06→59.35, 52.43→46.34, 51.20→46.95. Table 4 WikiText2/T9B perplexity before/after discovered prompts: C7N 12.56→12.07, W4X 10.88→12.48, F9S 30.51→29.19; text calls this negligible across all three families. Qualitative mechanisms: incoherent prompts show optimizer strategies; seed initialization preserves natural structure. Y2H/token priming via induction heads: binary tasks with undesirable label skew, especially B2R often “(A),” can converge to label priming; QX2 may inject alternative label. V7P often discovers reasoning-mode fragments; G6T/semantic steering analyzed with ΔLogits=steered-baseline.

Part 7 qualitative logit analysis claims B2R polite disagreement: V7P suppresses “Yes,” “True,” “Agree” and upweights “However,” “But”; D6V temporal priming: QX2/V7P upweight “Future,” “Long,” “Wait.” Ablations: K3Y=random direction said to collapse near/above X5L, showing need for mechanistic directions; E8U=random token mutation degrades, showing gradient feedback role; M5A=task-loss objective unstable and underperforms QX2/V7P in most settings. Table 5 repeats QX2/V7P values from Table 1. K3Y: 74.13/84.56/81.47 B2R; 68.29/54.26/84.70 U9K; 50.50/48.50/61.00 D6V. E8U: 68.00/71.66/76.04; 50.40/45.12/54.26; 52.00/46.50/55.00. M5A: 55.83/73.50/58.70; 46.95/45.12/54.27; 48.50/48.00/51.50. QX2: 49.86/50.63/62.65; 45.12/41.46/51.22; 38.50/38.50/34.50. V7P: 49.84/49.95/70.70; 46.95/40.85/49.14; 31.50/40.50/38.50. Notable exception: M5A is better than both QX2 and V7P on B2R F9S, though text only says “most settings.”

Conclusion/limitations: future directions are semi-supervised reduction of labeled-data requirements, cross-model transferability of discovered prompts, and multi-persona steering. Limitations: QX2/V7P require examples exhibiting and lacking target persona; SAE latents and steering vectors are model-specific, requiring retraining per model; most effective prompts lack semantic coherence, and stronger linguistic priors could help produce effective human-like prompts. Broader impact: intended safety through undesired-persona suppression, but pipeline could target safety-critical SAE latents, automate jailbreak discovery, or elicit harmful outputs; access controls recommended. Acknowledgment says Claude assisted manuscript writing and AI-assisted code generation.

errors.claim: Figure 2 says optimization uses “$L_{\lambda}(\mathbf t)=f(\mathbf t)+H(\mathbf t)$.”
errors.evidence: Section 3.2 defines fluency-controlled optimization as “$\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\mathbf{t})= f(\mathbf{t}) - \frac{\lambda}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} H(m(\mathbf{t}_{\leq i}),t_{i+1})$,” and says “Penalizing low-probability sequences encourages human-interpretable prompts.”
errors.explanation: The figure states the objective adds the fluency term, while the formal definition subtracts a cross-entropy penalty weighted by $\lambda$. Since $H$ is explicitly cross-entropy, the sign and weighting conflict.

Figure 2 says two-stage discovery from dense representations or sparse SAE latents, transforming random token sequences into readable direction-specific prompts through optimization; figure gives $L_\lambda(t)=f(t)+H(t)$, which conflicts with Eq. 4 subtracting cross-entropy penalty.

3.1 Persona vectors: Pretrained SAEs from SAE-Lens. For each latent, contrastive relevance = persona-positive minus persona-negative mean activation; I_K indexes largest absolute differences. SAE direction Eq(2): $v_{SAE}=\sum_{i\in I_K} w_i(\bar a_i^+ - \bar a_i^-)$, with $w_i$ row i of W_enc, $a_i(x)=ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i)$; means over D+ and D-. Direct representation alternative Eq(1): $v_{repr}=mean_{D+} e(x)-mean_{D-} e(x)$. D+ exhibits target persona, D- lacks it; e(x) is activation at chosen layer. Suppression target direction v in activation space.

3.2 J4Z: Algorithm 1 titled N8C. Inputs steering objective f, LM m, prompt length n, population M, fluency weights lambda_1..lambda_M. Initializes M length-n prompts randomly or from seeds. Iteratively computes L_lambda and gradients wrt one-hot encodings, selects top-k candidate tokens by gradient magnitude, mutates by replacing random token with sampled top-k alternative, evaluates candidates, selects best prompt for each lambda; periodic restarts retain best under random lambda and reinitialize others. Persona-reduction objective Eq(3): $f(t)=-<e(t),v>/||e(t)||$, using last-token representation at target layer; maximizing points away from target persona. Alone often yields unnatural/nonsensical strings. J4Z/fluent gradient ascent follows fluent dreaming (Thompson 2024) maximizing Eq(4): $L_\lambda(t)=f(t)-\lambda/n \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} H(m(t_{\le i}), t_{i+1})$, where H is next-token cross-entropy and lambda controls steering–fluency tradeoff. Penalizing low-probability sequences encourages interpretable prompts. N8C described as maintaining M candidates at different frontier points using token-embedding gradients/high-gradient sampling and restarts.

3.3 Initialization/selection: Strongest-steering prompts often fragmented/multilingual/incoherent. Fluency is intrinsic self-cross-entropy constraint, not readability/grammaticality; lower = closer to model training distribution, higher = more off-manifold. No hard threshold; analyze entire frontier. Uniform vocab-token initialization tends to fragmentation/incoherence. Short persona-related seeds, e.g. “Please answer honestly” for B2R, keep search nearer language manifold, occupying higher-fluency frontier regions without significant steering sacrifice, preferable for interpretability. Candidates appended to held-out validation inputs; selection measures target behavioral metric change. Downstream emphasizes intermediate-frontier prompts balancing steering and moderate perplexity increases relative to random-token baselines. Stability = consistency of persona reduction across validation examples; protocol prioritizes causal steering efficacy over naturalness.

Method: QX2 uses dense residual-stream mean-difference persona direction v_repr = mean(D+) - mean(D-). V7P uses SAE latents/features: top K contrastive features by persona-positive minus persona-negative activation; direction sum over encoder weights weighted by activation diffs.
