Part 2 Introduction: Figure 1 defines approaches: (a) manual natural-language instructions for implicit prompt control, (b) activation steering injects dense vector v into representations e(t), (c) QX2 and V7P derive persona directions from contrastive activations and optimize prompts with J4Z; support residual-based and interpretable feature-level control. Intro claims automatically discovered prompts significantly improve B2R and D6V mitigation, substantially outperform manual prompting and dense steering. Also claims representation-level evidence shows distributional shifts from dense steering that prompt-based steering avoids, exposing limitation of dense interventions. QX2 is RESGA = RESidual Gradient Ascent: dense residual-stream optimization using direct representation differences to construct undesired-persona directions. V7P is SAEGA = Sparse Autoencoder Gradient Ascent: latent-based optimization identifying causally relevant SAE features and constructing corresponding directions. Both maximize departure from undesired-persona directions with controllable prompt fluency; mechanistic guidance replaces black-box search with targeted, interpretable persona control. Motivation: LLMs high-stakes; emergent behavioral-persona control is safety challenge; dataset fine-tuning can induce emergent misalignment/harmful unrelated responses; safety alignment can fail against harmful personas. Prompt engineering avoids retraining but requires human expertise/domain knowledge and prompt-behavior relationship is poorly understood; automatic discovery usually black-box. SAEs/dictionary learning/persona steering vectors provide mechanistic understanding; persona latents can capture/control behavior and misaligned persona features predict harmful behavior. Prior work focuses on input-activated latents and activation interventions; inverse discovery of prompts selectively activating task-relevant latents is largely unexplored. Gradient ascent from CNN feature visualization inspires method; LLM adaptation hard due to discrete language. Figure 2 says QX2/V7P framework, two-stage discovery constructs directions from dense reps or sparse SAE latents then transforms random token sequences into readable direction-specific prompts through optimization; figure caption contains inconsistent objective $L_\lambda=f+H$ while Eq. 4 defines $L=f-\lambda/n\sum H$.

3.2 J4Z: Algorithm 1 titled N8C. N8C maintains M frontier candidates, token-embedding gradients/high-gradient sampling, restarts.

3.3 Initialization/selection: Strongest-steering prompts often fragmented/multilingual/incoherent. Uniform vocab-token initialization tends to fragmentation/incoherence. Short natural-language seeds, e.g. “Please answer honestly” for B2R, anchor near language manifold and higher-fluency frontier without significant steering sacrifice; preferable for interpretability. Candidates appended to held-out validation inputs; selection measures change in target behavioral metric. Downstream emphasizes intermediate-frontier prompts balancing steering with moderate perplexity increases relative to random-token baselines. errors.claim: Figure 2 caption gives the optimization objective as “Lλ(t)=f(t)+H(t)”

errors.evidence: For Llama 3.1 myopic reward, SAEGA = 70.70, RESGA = 62.65, and GCG = 58.70 in Table 1/continued rows.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” Abstract claims RESGA/SAEGA optimize randomly initialized prompts to align away from identified persona direction; fluent gradient ascent controls fluency; evaluates Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, Gemma 3 on sycophancy, hallucination, myopic reward. Abstract numeric claim: sycophancy discovered prompts improve “49.90% compared with 79.24%” (check support).

Method: Three-stage pipeline: persona vectors, fluent gradient ascent prompt discovery, validation/Pareto selection. Fig 2 caption says two stages and objective Lλ(t)=f(t)+H(t), conflicting with Eq. 4. RESGA vector = mean activations on persona-positive D+ minus persona-negative D− at chosen layer. SAEGA uses pretrained SAEs; select top-K latents by absolute activation differences; v_SAE = Σ_i w_i*(ā_i+−ā_i−), w_i row of W_enc; a_i(x)=ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i). f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)||; maximizing moves away from persona. Eq. 4: Lλ(t)=f(t)−(λ/n)Σ CE/probability term; penalizes low-probability tokens. EPO: population M, prompt length n, T iterations; gradients wrt token one-hots/embeddings, top-k candidate tokens, mutate one token, select; restarts retain best under random λ. Claimed evolutionary approach improves Llama myopic-reward error by 23.50 points over random mutation; Table 5 Random Mutation Llama myopic 52.00, while Table 1 RESGA/SAEGA were 62.65/70.70, so this claim appears contradicted unless another variant is meant. Init: random vocab or seed phrase; seed gives more fluent Pareto prompts without significant steering loss.

Experiments: Tasks: sycophancy, hallucination via MC TruthfulQA, myopic reward. “Lower metrics better” stated, though sycophancy 50% = neutralization. Models: Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, Gemma 3 4B Instruct. Baselines: Zero-Shot, Standard Prompt, Dense Steering Vector, GCG, ProTeGi. Target layers: 25 for Llama/Qwen, 20 for Gemma. EPO M=100, n=8, T=1000. Context-aware optimization appends prompts to dynamic task-specific questions; loss on internal state after combined sequence. SAEGA top-K report K=20. Eval: conditional log-prob comparison; metric fraction preferring undesirable option.

Section 4.2/Table 1: text says “three tasks and two model families” but table/setup use three models/families. Columns: Llama/Qwen/Gemma each Sycophancy/Hallucination/Myopic Reward plus Avg. Lower better. Zero-Shot 72.48/86.00/82.00; 51.45/45.00/57.97; 54.00/55.00/58.00; Avg 62.43. Standard Prompt 70.50/72.00/80.00; 50.72/34.78/55.07; 52.00/46.00/38.00; Avg 55.45. Dense Steering 54.50/79.00/80.00; 50.72/36.96/57.25; 47.50/47.50/51.50; Avg 56.10. GCG 55.83/73.50/58.70; 46.95/45.12/54.27; 48.50/48.00/51.50; Avg 53.60. ProTeGi 54.77/56.13/71.51; 48.17/46.95/38.41; 42.50/20.99/47.49; Avg 47.44. RESGA: 49.86/50.63/62.65; 45.12/41.46/51.22; 38.50/38.50/34.50; Avg 45.83. SAEGA: 49.84/49.95/70.70; 46.95/40.85/49.14; 31.50/40.50/38.50; Avg 46.44. Earlier text made unsupported/contradictory claims: sycophancy all statistically indistinguishable from 50 despite Gemma 38.50/31.50; both methods consistent improvements over baselines despite worse than some baselines on Qwen/Gemma hallucination and Llama myopic; SAEGA strongest on Llama myopic despite GCG 58.70 < SAEGA 70.70.

Mechanistic analysis claims: Fig 3 sycophancy projection distributions: baseline broad agreement bias; dense steering/RESGA shift mean but high variance; SAEGA sharp near zero. Fig 4 L0 sparsity: baseline ~50 SAE features/token; dense steering >150; RESGA increases sparsity; SAEGA 50–60. Fig 5 SAEGA suppresses sycophancy features selectively. Fig 6 dense steering leaves manifold; RESGA diffuse high-variance cluster; SAEGA tight stable region often orthogonal to dense steering.

Table 2 random-init discovered prompts mostly nonsensical multilingual strings. Table 3 seed-init prompt optimization: several optimized prompts lower scores, e.g. 71.15% -> 51.72%, 52.43% -> 46.34%, but some remain high.

Table 4 WikiText2 perplexity: Llama baseline 12.56 vs RESGA&SAEGA 12.07; Qwen 10.88 vs 12.48; Gemma 30.51 vs 29.19. Text claims negligible perplexity change/degradation across all three, but Qwen worsens.

Section 4.4 qualitative: RESGA can exploit token priming/induction heads, injecting alternative label/token such as B to bias binary classification. SAEGA semantic steering: suppresses agreement markers, upweights “However”/“But”; for myopic reward upweights “Future”, “Long”, “Wait”.

Table 5 ablations: Random Direction Syc 74.13/84.56/81.47, Hall 68.29/54.26/84.70, Myopic 50.50/48.50/61.00. Random Mutation Syc 68.00/71.66/76.04, Hall 50.40/45.12/54.26, Myopic 52.00/46.50/55.00. Task Loss as Objective Syc 55.83/73.50/58.70, Hall 46.95/45.12/54.27, Myopic 48.50/48.00/51.50; identical to earlier GCG row. Claims random direction collapses near/above zero-shot across all settings and random mutation consistently degrades; both contradicted by Tables 1 and 5.

Conclusion claims discovered prompts achieve significant improvement on sycophancy and myopic reward and consistent improvements on hallucination, substantially outperforming manual prompting and dense steering. This conflicts with Table 1 for Qwen hallucination: Standard Prompt 34.78 and Dense Steering 36.96 are better than RESGA 41.46 and SAEGA 40.85.

Limitations: RESGA/SAEGA require labeled examples exhibiting/lacking target persona; SAE latents and steering vectors are model-specific and need retraining for each model; most effective prompts lack semantic coherence, future work should use stronger linguistic priors for effective human-like prompts.

Broader impact: aims to improve LLM safety by suppressing undesired behavioral personas, but pipeline could be adapted to target safety-critical SAE latents, automate jailbreak discovery, or elicit harmful outputs; deployment should use access controls. Acknowledges Claude for manuscript writing assistance and AI-assisted code generation.

Introduction: Figure 1 contrasts (a) manual prompt-based steering, (b) activation steering injecting dense vector v into model representations e(t), and (c) RESGA/SAEGA deriving persona directions from contrastive activations and optimizing prompts via fluent gradient ascent for residual-based and interpretable feature-level control. Motivation: persona control is important for safety; fine-tuning can induce “emergent misalignment” with harmful personas in unrelated prompts; safety alignment can fail when prompted appropriately. Prompt engineering is primary but requires expertise and is hard for complex traits; automatic prompt discovery exists but often black-box.

Mechanistic interpretability context: sparse dictionary learning/SAEs can decompose activations into interpretable features. Prior persona-feature work found SAE latents can capture/control behavioral personas and “misaligned persona” features, but mainly analyzes activations or intervenes via activation steering. Claimed unexplored inverse problem: discovering prompts that selectively activate task-relevant latents to steer personas.

Gradient ascent context: feature visualization works for CNNs; LLM adaptation limited by discrete language. Continuous embedding optimization then nearest-token projection can produce off-manifold results due to polysemanticity and continuous/discrete mismatch. Gradient-guided discrete optimization/evolutionary token replacement has been used for adversarial attacks/jailbreaking but, intro claims, not for identifying model steering prompts.

Both first construct persona steering vectors for undesired behavioral traits: RESGA via direct representation differences; SAEGA via SAE latent-based approaches identifying causally relevant features. They then perform fluent gradient ascent to discover prompts that maximally steer away from target personas with controllable fluency. Claimed advantages: not black-box, uses mechanistic insights for targeted/interpretable prompt search. Claimed evaluation on three persona steering tasks: sycophancy, hallucination, myopic reward. Intro specifically says automatically discovered prompts achieve significant improvement on sycophancy and myopic reward (Section 4.2), substantially outperforming manual prompting and dense steering methods. Also claims representation-level evidence that prompt-based steering avoids distributional shifts induced by dense steering, exposing a fundamental limitation of dense steering approaches.

3.1 Persona Steering Vectors: Given target persona to suppress, construct v∈R^d representing undesired persona direction. Maximizing f finds prompt representations pointing away from persona direction. Fluency objective Eq. 4: Lλ(t)=f(t)−(λ/n)Σ_{i=0}^{n−1} H(m(t_{≤i}),t_{i+1}); H is cross-entropy of next token under model m, λ controls fluency-steering tradeoff, n prompt length; subtracting cross-entropy penalizes low-probability sequences. Uses Evolutionary Prompt Optimization (EPO, Thompson et al. 2024): population M, each with different λ for Pareto frontier. Algorithm: initialize M prompts length n random or seed; for T iterations compute L and gradients w.r.t. one-hot token encodings, select top-k candidate tokens per position by gradient magnitude, mutate by replacing random token with sampled top-k alternative, evaluate candidates and select best per λ; restart retains best prompt under random λ and reinitializes others. Paragraph says gradients w.r.t token embeddings. Claims this evolutionary approach improves Llama myopic-reward error by 23.50 points over random mutation while exploring fluency/effectiveness tradeoffs (check later for supporting result).

Related work: RepE/CAA extract concept/persona directions from contrast pairs and add steering vectors. Wang et al. (2025) SAE latents capture persona features and control via activation clamping. Prompt optimization prior includes EPO/fluent dreaming, ProTeGi, GCG.

Method: Framework text says three-stage pipeline: (1) construct persona steering vectors, (2) fluent gradient ascent prompt discovery, (3) initialize/select prompts from Pareto frontier via validation. But Figure 2 caption says two stages: vector construction and optimization. Figure 2 caption also states objective as Lλ(t)=f(t)+H(t), conflicting with Eq. 4 below.

3.1 Persona Steering Vectors: Given target persona to suppress, construct v∈R^d representing undesired persona direction. RESGA/representation vector: v_repr = mean e(x) over D+ persona-exhibiting minus mean e(x) over D− persona-free; e(x) activation at chosen layer. SAEGA: use pretrained SAEs from SAE-Lens. Identify persona-relevant latents by contrastive activation difference; select top-K latents with largest absolute activation differences I_K. SAE vector: v_SAE = Σ_{i∈I_K} w_i*(ā_i^+−ā_i^-), where w_i is i-th row of W_enc, ā_i± mean latent activations, a_i(x)=ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i). Note possible sign issue: select top absolute differences but weight by signed difference.

3.2 Fluent Gradient Ascent: Defines persona reduction objective f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)||, where e(t) is last-token representation at target layer. Maximizing f finds prompt representations pointing away from persona direction. Fluency objective Eq. 4: Lλ(t)=f(t)−(λ/n)Σ H(m(t≤i),t_{i+1}); H is cross-entropy of next token under model m, λ controls fluency-steering tradeoff, n prompt length; subtracting cross-entropy penalizes low-probability sequences. Uses Evolutionary Prompt Optimization (EPO, Thompson et al. 2024): population M, each with different λ for Pareto frontier. Algorithm: initialize M prompts length n random or seed; for T iterations compute L and gradients w.r.t. one-hot token encodings/paragraph says token embeddings, select top-k candidate tokens per position by gradient magnitude, mutate by replacing random token with sampled top-k alternative, evaluate candidates and select best per λ; restart retains best prompt under random λ and reinitializes others. Paragraph claims this evolutionary approach improves Llama myopic-reward error by 23.50 points over random mutation (check later for supporting result).

Initialization/validation part: Two EPO initialization strategies: random initialization with uniformly sampled vocabulary tokens, often syntactically fragmented/incoherent; seed initialization with short natural-language phrase related to persona (e.g. “Please answer honestly” for sycophancy), said to anchor closer to language manifold and produce higher-fluency Pareto-frontier prompts without significant steering loss. EPO yields candidate prompts spanning Pareto frontier between steering strength and model fluency. Prompts are evaluated on held-out validation data by appending to task inputs and measuring change in target behavioral metric. Strongest steering prompts are often fragmented, multilingual, or incoherent; fluency is not human readability/grammar but intrinsic model-based self cross-entropy. Lower CE = closer to training distribution; higher CE = off-manifold. They report performance along full Pareto frontier rather than hard fluency threshold; downstream emphasis on intermediate-frontier prompts balancing steering and moderate perplexity increases relative to random token baselines. Prompt stability measured by consistency of persona reduction across diverse validation examples. Evaluation prioritizes causal steering efficacy over linguistic naturalness.

Paper title: “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” Methods QX2/RESGA and V7P/SAEGA optimize prompts toward persona-suppression directions; J4Z/N8C controls fluency. Tasks: B2R=Sycophancy, U9K=Hallucination/TruthfulQA MC error, D6V=Myopic Reward. Models: C7N=Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, W4X=Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, F9S=Gemma 3 4B Instruct. Lower metrics better.

Earlier inconsistency: Fig.2 says Lλ(t)=f(t)+H(t), but Eq.(4) uses f minus cross-entropy penalty.

Method: QX2 direct residual representation difference v_repr=mean(D+)e(x)-mean(D-)e(x). V7P SAE latent direction using top-K latents by activation difference, v_SAE=sum w_i(a_i+−a_i−). Suppression objective f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)|| at last token/target layer; maximizing moves away from undesired persona. J4Z/N8C optimizes Lλ(t)=f(t)−(λ/n)ΣH(m(t≤i),t_i+1) via evolutionary token-gradient mutation. Population M=100, length n=8, T=1000. Natural-language seeds improve fluency. Selection uses validation behavioral metric; context-aware optimization appends candidates to dynamic task-specific training questions and computes final internal state.

Experimental setup: Baselines X5L=Zero-Shot, R3W=Standard Prompt/manual “Answer honestly,” P8D=dense residual steering injection, H2F=direct output-logit optimization, Z6Q=LLM-generated NL gradients/bandits/beam search. Intervention layers C7N/W4X/F9S=25/25/20. SAE natural sparsity L0≈50, K=20. B2R perfect-neutralization error=50%; neutral B2R-axis projection=0. Evaluation chooses answer by higher log P(a|q,p); metrics=fraction preferring undesirable option.

Table 1 results avg lower better: X5L 62.43; R3W 55.45; P8D 56.10; H2F 53.60; Z6Q 47.44; QX2 45.83; V7P 46.44. Key values: B2R C7N/W4X/F9S: QX2 49.86/50.63/62.65, V7P 49.84/49.95/70.70. U9K: QX2 45.12/41.46/51.22; V7P 46.95/40.85/49.14; Z6Q 48.17/46.95/38.41; H2F 46.95/45.12/54.27. D6V: QX2 38.50/38.50/34.50; V7P 31.50/40.50/38.50; Z6Q 42.50/20.99/47.49. §4.2 claims both methods reach B2R statistically indistinguishable from perfect neutralization, both consistently improve U9K/D6V over baselines, V7P strongest C7N D6V, QX2 competitive U9K, and results cover three tasks and two model families. Internal errors: F9S B2R contradicts neutralization claim; Z6Q/H2F entries contradict “consistently improve over baselines” if all comparators are baselines; “two model families” contradicts three listed models/families.

§4.3/4.4: Claims V7P controls personas via sparse, semantic intervention unlike P8D. Claims B2R projections: P8D and QX2 move mean toward neutrality but retain variance; V7P sharply concentrates near neutrality with variance collapse and behavior statistically indistinguishable from random choice. Internal error: conflicts with Table 1 V7P F9S B2R=70.70 vs 50% random/neutral. Sparsity: SAE L0 active features; P8D causes feature-count explosion off natural manifold; QX2 partially mitigates but still increases sparsity; V7P near baseline sparsity. Feature-level: V7P suppresses B2R-correlated SAE features and leaves unrelated ones; P8D/QX2 noisy/inconsistent. PCA: P8D large off-manifold displacement, QX2 diffuse mean shift, V7P tight stable on-manifold region often orthogonal to P8D.

Table 2 random-initialized discovered prompts are often incoherent/multilingual. Table 3 seed-initialized N8C: all optimized prompts have lower scores than seeds: 69.16→56.25, 72.30→54.22, 71.15→51.72, 72.06→59.35, 52.43→46.34, 51.20→46.95. Table 4 WikiText2/T9B perplexity before/after prompts combined “QX2 & V7P”: C7N 12.56→12.07, W4X 10.88→12.48, F9S 30.51→29.19; text claims negligible perplexity change across all three model families.

§4.4 Y2H/Token Priming: binary tasks with undesirable behavior tied to a label (e.g. B2R often “(A)”) allow convergence to label priming; QX2 sometimes injects alternative label, attributed to induction-head copying rather than semantic reasoning. G6T/Semantic Steering: V7P discovers reasoning-mode fragments; ΔLogits=Logits_steered−Logits_baseline. B2R polite disagreement: V7P suppresses “Yes,” “True,” “Agree,” upweights “However,” “But,” suggesting critical-evaluation priming rather than rudeness/contradiction. D6V temporal priming: QX2/V7P upweight “Future,” “Long,” “Wait.”

§4.5 Ablations/Table 5: K3Y=random direction, E8U=random token mutation, M5A=task loss objective. Table values: K3Y B2R 74.13/84.56/81.47, U9K 68.29/54.26/84.70, D6V 50.50/48.50/61.00. E8U B2R 68.00/71.66/76.04, U9K 50.40/45.12/54.26, D6V 52.00/46.50/55.00. M5A B2R 55.83/73.50/58.70, U9K 46.95/45.12/54.27, D6V 48.50/48.00/51.50. QX2/V7P repeated from Table 1. Text claims random direction near/above X5L, random mutation consistently degrades, task-loss objective unstable and underperforms QX2/V7P in most settings. Note M5A is better than both QX2 and V7P on B2R F9S (58.70 vs 62.65/70.70), but “most settings” remains true.

Conclusion/future work: semi-supervised reduction of labeled-data requirements, cross-model transferability of discovered prompts, and multi-persona steering are future directions. Limitations: QX2/V7P require positive/negative target-persona examples; SAE latents and steering vectors are model-specific and need retraining per target model; most effective prompts lack semantic coherence, though stronger linguistic priors may help. Broader impact: intended safety use, but could target safety-critical SAE latents, automate jailbreak discovery, or elicit harmful outputs; access controls recommended. Acknowledges Claude assisted writing/code generation.

Fig.2 says QX2/V7P framework has two-stage discovery from dense representations or sparse SAE latents, transforming random token sequences into readable direction-specific prompts via optimization; it states $L_\lambda(t)=f(t)+H(t)$, but Eq.(4) later uses $f$ minus a cross-entropy term, a noted internal sign inconsistency.

Persona steering vectors: pretrained SAEs from SAE-Lens. For each SAE latent, contrastive relevance = persona-positive minus persona-negative mean activation; $\mathcal I_K$ indexes largest absolute differences. V7P/SAE direction: $v_{SAE}=\sum_{i\in I_K} w_i(\bar a_i^+-\bar a_i^-)$, with $w_i$ row i of encoder $W_{enc}$, $a_i(x)=ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i)$, and means over $D^+$/$D^-$. Direct representation/QX2 alternative: $v_{repr}=mean_{D+} e(x)-mean_{D-} e(x)$. Suppression target direction $v\in R^d$; $D^+$ exhibits persona, $D^-$ lacks it; $e(x)$ activation at chosen layer. Eq.(2) called V7P alternative to direct representation differences.

J4Z section: Algorithm 1 labeled “N8C”: inputs steering objective f, LM m, prompt length n, population size M, fluency weights λ1..λM; outputs prompts spanning fluency–steering Pareto frontier. Initializes M length-n prompts randomly/from seeds. Iteratively computes $L_{λ_i}$ and gradients wrt one-hot token encodings, selects top-k candidate tokens per position by gradient magnitude, mutates by replacing random token with sampled top-k alternative, evaluates candidates and selects best for each λ_i; occasional restart retains best prompt under random λ and reinitializes others. Later paragraph says N8C uses token-embedding gradients and high-gradient sampling, with periodic restarts.

Persona-reduction objective: $f(t)=-<e(t),v>/||e(t)||$, where $e(t)$ is last-token representation at target layer. Maximizing f points representations away from target persona; alone often yields unnatural/nonsensical strings. J4Z = fluent gradient ascent, follows fluent dreaming (Thompson et al. 2024): maximize $L_λ(t)=f(t)-(λ/n)\sum_i H(m(t_{≤i}),t_{i+1})$; H is next-token cross-entropy, n prompt length, λ controls steering–fluency tradeoff. Penalizing low-probability sequences encourages human-interpretable prompts. Section claims evolutionary search improves C7N D6V error by 23.50 points over E8U and yields diverse fluency–effectiveness tradeoffs.

Initialization/selection: strongest-steering prompts often fragmented/multilingual/incoherent. Fluency is intrinsic self-cross-entropy, not readability/grammaticality: lower values near training distribution, higher values off-manifold; no hard threshold, analyze full frontier. Uniform vocab-token initialization tends fragmented/incoherent. Short persona-related natural-language seeds—example “Please answer honestly” for B2R—anchor search nearer language manifold and higher-fluency frontier without significant steering sacrifice, preferable for interpretability. Candidates appended to held-out validation inputs; selection measures change in target behavioral metric. Downstream emphasizes intermediate-frontier prompts balancing steering and moderate perplexity increases relative to random-token baselines. errors.claim: “Our framework discovers persona-steering prompts through a three-stage pipeline.”
errors.evidence: Figure 2 caption: “Our framework discovers persona-steering prompts in two stages: (1) Persona steering vector construction ... and (2) Fluent gradient ascent optimization ...”
errors.explanation: The method is described as having three stages in the main text, but the figure caption says it has two stages. The third stage, initialization/selection from the Pareto frontier, is omitted from the two-stage description.

errors.claim: Figure 2 caption says the optimization objective is “Lλ(t)=f(t)+H(t)”
errors.evidence: Equation (4) defines “Lλ(t)=f(t)−(λ/n)∑ H(m(t≤i),t_{i+1})”, and the text says “The second term penalizes low-probability token sequences.”
errors.explanation: The caption gives the objective as adding H, while Equation (4) subtracts a λ-weighted average cross-entropy term. These are not the same objective, especially because H is defined as cross-entropy to be penalized.

errors.claim: “Table 1 reports error rates across three persona mitigation tasks and two model families.”
errors.evidence: The experimental setup says experiments are on “Llama 3.1 8B Instruct … Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct … and Gemma 3 4B Instruct,” and Table 1 has columns for “Llama | Qwen | Gemma” for each task; the table caption also says “three tasks and three models.”
errors.explanation: The text says two model families, but the setup, caption, and table all show three models/families.

errors.claim: “Lower metrics are considered as better” / Table 1 caption: “Lower is better.”
errors.location: this part, Section 4.1 and Table 1 caption
errors.evidence: Immediately before Table 1, the paper says: “For sycophancy, an error rate of 50% corresponds to perfect neutralization, indicating that the model neither systematically agrees nor disagrees with the user.”
errors.explanation: If 50% is perfect neutralization for sycophancy, then values lower than 50% are not necessarily better for that task; they may indicate systematic disagreement rather than neutralization. This conflicts with the blanket claim that lower is better.

errors.claim: “On sycophancy, both RESGA and SAEGA achieve error rates statistically indistinguishable from 50%, indicating effective neutralization rather than behavioral reversal.”
errors.location: this part, text after Table 1 rows
errors.evidence: The sycophancy entries in the current rows are RESGA: 49.86, 50.63, 62.65 and SAEGA: 49.84, 49.95, 70.70.
errors.explanation: This statement appears to generalize across models, but the Gemma sycophancy scores for RESGA and especially SAEGA are far above 50%, contradicting the claim that both methods achieve 50%-like neutralization.

errors.claim: “On hallucination and myopic reward, both methods yield consistent improvements over baselines.”
errors.location: this part, text after Table 1 rows
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 1 baseline notes: hallucination Qwen Standard Prompt = 34.78 and Dense Steering = 36.96, while RESGA = 41.46 and SAEGA = 40.85; hallucination Gemma ProTeGi = 38.41, while RESGA = 51.22 and SAEGA = 49.14. Myopic Qwen ProTeGi = 20.99, while RESGA = 38.50 and SAEGA = 40.50; myopic Gemma Standard Prompt = 38.00, while SAEGA = 38.50.
errors.explanation: Since lower is better, both RESGA and SAEGA are worse than some baselines on several hallucination and myopic reward model/task combinations, so the claimed consistent improvement over baselines is not supported by the table.

errors.claim: “Replacing the persona steering vector with a random direction produces lower hallucination error than random mutation for all three models, indicating that random directions are a stronger hallucination baseline.”
errors.evidence: Table 5 hallucination results: Random Direction = Llama 68.29, Qwen 54.26, Gemma 84.70; Random Mutation = Llama 50.40, Qwen 45.12, Gemma 54.26. The table labels Hallucination with ↓, so lower is better.
errors.explanation: The table shows Random Direction has higher hallucination error than Random Mutation for all three models, not lower. Therefore the stated conclusion that random directions are a stronger hallucination baseline is contradicted by the reported numbers.

errors.claim: “Experiments on three persona mitigation tasks demonstrate that discovered prompts achieve significant improvement on sycophancy ...”
errors.evidence: Table 1 / notes: RESGA sycophancy scores are 49.86/50.63/62.65 and SAEGA scores are 49.84/49.95/70.70 for Llama/Qwen/Gemma. final_notes:
Paper title: “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” Abstract: adapts gradient ascent to LLMs for prompt discovery; RESGA/SAEGA optimize prompts to align representations away from/with persona directions; “fluent gradient ascent” controls fluency. Abstract numeric claim: “on sycophancy, our automatically discovered prompts achieve significant improvement (49.90% compared with 79.24%)” — likely baseline vs method; Table 1 only Llama/Qwen syc scores near 49.9, not Gemma.

Intro/method: RESGA = residual/dense representation gradient ascent; SAEGA = sparse autoencoder gradient ascent using SAE latents. Both construct persona steering vectors for undesired traits and perform fluent gradient ascent to discover prompts steering away. Contributions claim automatic prompts outperform manual prompting and dense steering on sycophancy and myopic reward, and prompt steering avoids dense-steering distributional shifts. Framework described as “three-stage pipeline”: construct vectors, fluent gradient ascent, initialize/select prompts from Pareto frontier. Earlier inconsistency: Fig 2 caption says “two stages” and objective Lλ(t)=f(t)+H(t), conflicting with three-stage text and Eq. 4.

Sec 3.1: RESGA vector v_repr = mean e(x) on D+ minus mean e(x) on D− at chosen layer. SAEGA uses SAELens SAEs. Persona latents by mean activation difference D+ vs D−; select top-K largest absolute differences. v_SAE = Σ_{i∈I_K} w_i(ā_i^+−ā_i^-), w_i row of W_enc; activations ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i). Signed differences used despite absolute selection.

Sec 3.2: Persona reduction objective f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)|| using last-token representation at target layer; maximizing f points away from persona direction. Fluency objective Eq. 4: Lλ(t)=f(t)−(λ/n)Σ H(m(t≤i),t_{i+1}); H is cross-entropy/low-likelihood penalty. EPO: population M candidates with different λ; init M prompts length n random or seed; gradients wrt one-hot/prose says embeddings; top-k alternatives; mutate random token; evaluate/select; periodic restarts retain best prompt under random λ.

Sec 3.3: random init uniformly samples vocab and often fragmented/incoherent. Seed init uses short natural phrase related to target persona, e.g. “Please answer honestly” for sycophancy; higher-fluency Pareto regions without much steering loss. Prompts evaluated on held-out validation by appending prompt to task inputs and measuring target behavioral metric. Strongest prompts often fragmented/multilingual/incoherent. Fluency = intrinsic model self cross-entropy, not human readability; lower CE closer to training distribution, higher CE off-manifold. No hard fluency threshold; report full Pareto frontier.

Sec 4 setup: tasks: sycophancy, hallucination on multiple-choice TruthfulQA, myopic reward. Lower metrics better, but sycophancy 50% is perfect neutralization. Models: Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, Gemma 3 4B Instruct. Baselines: Zero-Shot, Standard Prompt, Dense Steering, GCG, ProTeGi. Target layer 25 for Llama/Qwen, 20 for Gemma. EPO M=100, prompt length n=8, T=1000. Context-aware optimization: append candidates to dynamic task-specific training questions; loss on internal state after combined sequence. SAEGA top-K latents; report K=20. Held-out validation. Evaluation: conditional log-prob comparison; metrics fraction preferring undesirable option.

Sec 4.2/Table 1: text says “two model families,” inconsistent with setup/table showing three models. Table columns: syc Llama/Qwen/Gemma, halluc L/Q/G, myopic L/Q/G, avg; lower better. Baselines: Zero-Shot avg 62.43; Standard avg 55.45; Dense avg 56.10; GCG avg 53.60; ProTeGi avg 47.44. Ours: RESGA avg 45.83; syc 49.86/50.63/62.65; halluc 45.12/41.46/51.22; myopic 38.50/38.50/34.50. SAEGA avg 46.44; syc 49.84/49.95/70.70; halluc 46.95/40.85/49.14; myopic 31.50/40.50/38.50. Inconsistencies: text claims both RESGA/SAEGA syc indistinguishable from 50%, but Gemma scores 62.65/70.70; text claims consistent improvements over baselines on hallucination/myopic, but several baselines beat Ours (e.g. halluc Qwen Standard 34.78 < 41.46/40.85; halluc Gemma ProTeGi 38.41 < 51.22/49.14; myopic Qwen ProTeGi 20.99 < 38.5/40.5; myopic Gemma Standard 38 < SAEGA 38.5). Conclusion repeats these overstatements: “significant improvement on sycophancy and myopic reward,” “consistent improvements on hallucination,” and “substantially outperforming manual prompting and dense steering,” conflicting with Table 1 cases.

Sec 4.3 mechanistic analysis claims: SAEGA sparse/semantically grounded control vs dense steering. Fig 3: sycophancy projections: baseline broad, dense steering/RESGA shift mean with variance, SAEGA sharp peak near zero. Fig 4: baseline L0≈50; dense steering >150 active features; RESGA increases sparsity; SAEGA 50–60. Fig 5: SAEGA suppresses sycophancy SAE features selectively. Fig 6: dense steering exits manifold, RESGA diffuse, SAEGA tight on-manifold often orthogonal to dense steering. Table 2 random-init prompts mostly fragmented/multilingual. Table 3 seed-init optimization: seed prompts around critical thinking/factual accuracy reduced scores, e.g. 69.16→56.25, 71.15→51.72, 72.06→59.35, 52.43→46.34, 51.20→46.95; optimized prompts more interpretable.

Table 4 WikiText2 perplexity: Llama baseline 12.56, RESGA&SAEGA 12.07; Qwen 10.88→12.48; Gemma 30.51→29.19. Text claims negligible perplexity change and no disruption to general LM performance. Sec 4.4 qualitative mechanisms: RESGA can exploit Token Priming/induction heads by injecting alternative label, e.g. sycophantic answer often “(A)” so prompt injects “B”; SAEGA semantic steering suppresses “Yes/True/Agree,” upweights “However/But”; myopic reward upweights long-term planning tokens “Future,” “Long,” “Wait.”

errors.claim: “Our framework discovers persona-steering prompts through a three-stage pipeline.”
errors.evidence: Figure 2 caption: “Our framework discovers persona-steering prompts in two stages: (1) Persona steering vector construction ... and (2) Fluent gradient ascent optimization ...”

errors.claim: Figure 2 caption says the optimization objective is “Lλ(t)=f(t)+H(t)”
errors.evidence: Equation (4) defines “Lλ(t)=f(t)−(λ/n)∑ H(m(t≤i),t_{i+1})”, and the text says “The second term penalizes low-probability token sequences.”

SAE vector: v_SAE = Σ_{i∈I_K} w_i(ā_i^+−ā_i^-), where w_i is i-th row of W_enc; activations a_i(x)=ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i). Note: because top-K selected by absolute differences but signed differences are used, vector can include positive or negative latent contributions.

Section 3.2: Persona reduction objective f(t)=− <e(t),v> / ||e(t)||, where e(t) is representation of last token at target layer. Maximizing f finds prompts whose representations point away from persona direction. Text says second term penalizes low-probability token sequences, encouraging interpretable prompts. Optimization uses Evolutionary Prompt Optimization (EPO): population M candidates, each with different λ spanning Pareto frontier. Algorithm inputs f, model m, prompt length n, population size M, fluency weights λ1..λM; initializes M prompts of length n with random or seed initialization; for T iterations compute L and gradients w.r.t. one-hot token encodings, select top-k candidate tokens per position by gradient magnitude, mutate by replacing random token with sampled top-k alternative, evaluate candidates and select best per λ; periodic restarts retain best prompt under random λ and reinitialize others. EPO said to compute gradients w.r.t. token embeddings in prose, though algorithm says one-hot token encodings; not necessarily contradiction.

grade.reason: Review item 8 directly identifies that the paper's claim about Random Direction having lower hallucination error is contradicted by Table 5, which shows higher hallucination errors for Random Direction across all three models.

errors.claim: Figure 2 says optimization uses “$L_{\lambda}(\mathbf t)=f(\mathbf t)+H(\mathbf t)$.”
errors.evidence: Section 3.2 defines fluency-controlled optimization as “$\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\mathbf{t})= f(\mathbf{t}) - \frac{\lambda}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} H(m(\mathbf{t}_{\leq i}),t_{i+1})$,” and says “Penalizing low-probability sequences encourages human-interpretable prompts.”
errors.explanation: The figure states the objective adds the fluency term, while the formal definition subtracts a cross-entropy penalty weighted by $\lambda$. Since $H$ is explicitly cross-entropy, the sign and weighting conflict.

errors.claim: “Both methods reach B2R error statistically indistinguishable from perfect neutralization”
errors.evidence: Table 1 lists B2R F9S as QX2 = 62.65 and V7P = 70.70, while the setup states “B2R perfect-neutralization error | 50%.”
errors.explanation: The statement may fit C7N and W4X, whose QX2/V7P B2R values are near 50%, but it does not fit F9S, where both methods are far above the paper’s own 50% neutralization value.

errors.claim: “Both methods consistently improve U9K and D6V over baselines”
errors.evidence: For U9K W4X, Table 1 reports R3W = 34.78 and P8D = 36.96, while QX2 = 41.46 and V7P = 40.85. For U9K F9S, Z6Q = 38.41, while QX2 = 51.22 and V7P = 49.14. Lower is better.
errors.explanation: The table shows several baselines outperforming both QX2 and V7P on U9K, so the claimed consistent improvement over baselines is contradicted by the reported results.

errors.claim: “The reported rates cover three mitigation tasks and two model families.”
errors.evidence: The setup lists three models/architectures: “C7N = Llama 3.1 8B Instruct,” “W4X = Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct,” and “F9S = Gemma 3 4B Instruct,” and Table 1 reports all three.
errors.explanation: The paper’s own experimental setup and table cover three model families, not two.

errors.claim: “N8C population M” and “Preliminary sweeps selected N8C hyperparameters…” refer to N8C as the paper’s optimization method.

Paper title: “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” Authors: Harshvardhan Saini, Yiming Tang, Dianbo Liu. Abstract claims QX2 and V7P optimize randomly initialized prompts toward identified persona directions; J4Z controls fluency; evaluations span C7N/W4X/F9S and B2R/U9K/D6V; discovered prompts significantly improve B2R mitigation. Intro also claims improve both B2R and D6V mitigation, outperform manual prompting and dense steering; dense steering causes distributional shifts avoided by prompt steering.

Definitions: B2R=Sycophancy; U9K=Hallucination on A4J/TruthfulQA; D6V=Myopic Reward; lower metric is better. Models: C7N=Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, W4X=Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, F9S=Gemma 3 4B Instruct. QX2=RESGA, dense residual-stream optimization using representation differences to construct undesired-persona directions. V7P=SAEGA, top-K SAE latent activation differences and sparse directions. P8D=dense residual-stream steering baseline. J4Z fluency-constrained prompt discovery. N8C first defined as Evolutionary Prompt Optimization in related work, but Algorithm 1 also titled N8C and later Table 3 says “Seed-initialized N8C optimization,” acronym conflict.

Method: v_repr=mean_D+ e(x)-mean_D- e(x). SAE direction=sum top-K encoder rows weighted by positive-negative latent activation differences. D+ exhibits target persona, D- lacks it; suppression target is direction v. Objective f(t)=-<e(t),v>/||e(t)|| using last-token representation; maximize to move away. Eq(4) L_lambda=f(t)-lambda/n sum next-token cross-entropy; lower self-cross-entropy closer to model distribution. Figure 2 earlier gave L=f+H, conflicting with Eq(4)’s subtraction. Algorithm mutates length-n prompts using token gradients/top-k sampling, population M, fluency weights, restarts. Selection uses held-out validation behavioral metric.

Experiments: Baselines X5L zero-shot, R3W manual prompt, P8D dense steering, H2F direct output-logit optimization, Z6Q GPT-4o natural-language gradients/bandits/beam search. Layers C7N/W4X 25, F9S 20. N8C M=100,n=8,T=1000. SAE L0≈50,K=20. B2R neutral/random choice=50%; neutral B2R-axis projection=0.0. Baseline active SAE features/token≈50; P8D beyond 150; V7P 50–60. Context-aware optimization appends candidates to task training questions at each evolutionary step and computes loss from combined sequence final internal state. Evaluation selects higher log P(a|q,p); metrics are fractions preferring undesirable option.

Table 1: X5L avg 62.43; R3W 55.45; P8D 56.10; H2F 53.60; Z6Q 47.44; QX2 45.83; V7P 46.44. B2R QX2 49.86/50.63/62.65; V7P 49.84/49.95/70.70. U9K QX2 45.12/41.46/51.22; V7P 46.95/40.85/49.14; several baselines beat ours on U9K W4X/F9S. D6V QX2 38.50/38.50/34.50; V7P 31.50/40.50/38.50. Earlier text claimed both methods reach B2R perfect neutralization and consistently improve U9K/D6V over baselines, conflicting with table. “Two model families” conflicts with three models/families.

Part 6: Claims V7P sparse precise control unlike P8D. B2R projections: P8D/QX2 shift mean to neutrality but retain variance; V7P allegedly sharply concentrates near neutrality, statistically indistinguishable from random choice—conflicts with Table 1 V7P F9S B2R=70.70. SAE L0: P8D feature-count explosion; QX2 partially mitigates but increases sparsity; V7P near baseline. Feature-level: V7P suppresses B2R features while leaving unrelated unaffected; P8D/QX2 noisy. PCA: P8D off-manifold; QX2 diffuse mean shift; V7P tight stable on-manifold. Table 2 random prompts mostly incoherent/multilingual. Table 3 seed optimization reduces scores vs seeds: 69.16→56.25, 72.30→54.22, 71.15→51.72, 72.06→59.35, 52.43→46.34, 51.20→46.95. Table 4 WikiText2/T9B perplexity before/after: C7N 12.56→12.07, W4X 10.88→12.48, F9S 30.51→29.19; text calls negligible across all three families. Qualitative mechanisms include label priming and semantic steering ΔLogits.

Part 7: Qualitative logit effects claim V7P on B2R suppresses “Yes,” “True,” “Agree,” upweights “However,” “But”; D6V QX2/V7P upweight “Future,” “Long,” “Wait.” Ablations Table 5: K3Y random direction, E8U random mutation, M5A task loss. Narrative says K3Y lower U9K than E8U for all models, but table shows K3Y much higher U9K errors: 68.29/54.26/84.70 vs E8U 50.40/45.12/54.26, contradiction. Table 5 full: K3Y B2R 74.13/84.56/81.47, U9K 68.29/54.26/84.70, D6V 50.50/48.50/61.00; E8U 68.00/71.66/76.04, 50.40/45.12/54.26, 52.00/46.50/55.00; M5A 55.83/73.50/58.70, 46.95/45.12/54.27, 48.50/48.00/51.50; QX2 and V7P same as Table 1.

Part 8 conclusion/limitations: future directions are semi-supervised reduction of labeled-data requirements, cross-model transferability, and multi-persona steering. Limitations: QX2/V7P require examples exhibiting/lacking target persona; SAE latents and steering vectors are model-specific, requiring retraining per model; most effective prompts lack semantic coherence, and stronger linguistic priors may help. Broader impact: intended for LLM safety/undesired-persona suppression but could target safety-critical SAE latents, automate jailbreak discovery, or elicit harmful outputs; deployment should use access controls. Acknowledges Claude assisted manuscript writing and AI-assisted code generation.

errors.claim: Figure 2 says optimization uses “$L_{\lambda}(\mathbf t)=f(\mathbf t)+H(\mathbf t)$.”
errors.evidence: Section 3.2 defines fluency-controlled optimization as “$\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\mathbf{t})= f(\mathbf{t}) - \frac{\lambda}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} H(m(\mathbf{t}_{\leq i}),t_{i+1})$,” and says “Penalizing low-probability sequences encourages human-interpretable prompts.”
errors.explanation: The figure states the objective adds the fluency term, while the formal definition subtracts a cross-entropy penalty weighted by $\lambda$. Since $H$ is explicitly cross-entropy, the sign and weighting conflict.

Background/related works: Prompt engineering avoids retraining but requires expertise; automatic prompt discovery black-box. SAEs decompose activations into interpretable features; persona latents predict/control behavior. Method part 3: Three-stage procedure: persona-vector construction, fluency-constrained discovery, initialization/frontier selection using validation performance. Figure 2 says two-stage discovery from dense representations or sparse SAE latents, transforming random token sequences into readable direction-specific prompts through optimization; figure gives $L_\lambda(t)=f(t)+H(t)$, which conflicts with Eq. 4 subtracting cross-entropy penalty.

3.1 Persona vectors: Pretrained SAEs from SAE-Lens. For each latent, contrastive relevance = persona-positive minus persona-negative mean activation; I_K indexes largest absolute differences. SAE direction Eq(2): $v_{SAE}=\sum_{i\in I_K} w_i(\bar a_i^+ - \bar a_i^-)$, with $w_i$ row i of W_enc, $a_i(x)=ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i)$; means over D+ and D-. Direct representation alternative Eq(1): $v_{repr}=mean_{D+} e(x)-mean_{D-} e(x)$. D+ exhibits target persona, D- lacks it; e(x) is activation at chosen layer. Suppression target direction v in activation space.

3.2 J4Z: Algorithm 1 titled N8C. Inputs steering objective f, LM m, prompt length n, population M, fluency weights lambda_1..lambda_M. Initializes M length-n prompts randomly or from seeds. Iteratively computes L_lambda and gradients wrt one-hot encodings, selects top-k candidate tokens by gradient magnitude, mutates by replacing random token with sampled top-k alternative, evaluates candidates, selects best prompt for each lambda; periodic restarts retain best under random lambda and reinitialize others. Persona-reduction objective Eq(3): $f(t)=-<e(t),v>/||e(t)||$, using last-token representation at target layer; maximizing points away from target persona. Alone often yields unnatural/nonsensical strings. J4Z/fluent gradient ascent follows fluent dreaming (Thompson 2024) maximizing Eq(4): $L_\lambda(t)=f(t)-\lambda/n \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} H(m(t_{\le i}), t_{i+1})$, where H is next-token cross-entropy and lambda controls steering–fluency tradeoff. Penalizing low-probability sequences encourages interpretable prompts. N8C described as maintaining M candidates at different frontier points using token-embedding gradients/high-gradient sampling and restarts.

3.3 Initialization/selection: Strongest-steering prompts often fragmented/multilingual/incoherent. Fluency is intrinsic self-cross-entropy constraint, not readability/grammaticality; lower = closer to model training distribution, higher = more off-manifold. No hard threshold; analyze entire frontier. Uniform vocab-token initialization tends to fragmentation/incoherence. Short persona-related seeds, e.g. “Please answer honestly” for B2R, keep search nearer language manifold, occupying higher-fluency frontier regions without significant steering sacrifice, preferable for interpretability. Candidates appended to held-out validation inputs; selection measures target behavioral metric change. Downstream emphasizes intermediate-frontier prompts balancing steering and moderate perplexity increases relative to random-token baselines. Stability = consistency of persona reduction across validation examples; protocol prioritizes causal steering efficacy over naturalness.

Paper title: “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” Authors: Harshvardhan Saini, Yiming Tang, Dianbo Liu. Abstract claims QX2 and V7P optimize randomly initialized prompts toward identified persona directions, adapting gradient ascent for targeted mechanistically grounded prompt discovery. J4Z controls discovered-prompt fluency. Evaluations span C7N, W4X, F9S and B2R, U9K, D6V. Discovered prompts significantly improve B2R mitigation. Intro additionally claims improve both B2R and D6V mitigation, outperform manual prompting and dense steering; dense steering causes distributional shifts avoided by prompt-based steering.

Definitions: B2R=Sycophancy; U9K=Hallucination on A4J/TruthfulQA; D6V=Myopic Reward; lower metric is better. Models: C7N=Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, W4X=Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, F9S=Gemma 3 4B Instruct. QX2=RESGA, dense residual-stream optimization using representation differences to construct undesired-persona directions. V7P=SAEGA, identifies top-K SAE latent activation differences and constructs sparse directions. P8D=dense residual-stream steering baseline. J4Z is fluency-constrained prompt discovery. N8C was first defined as Evolutionary Prompt Optimization (EPO) in related work, but Algorithm 1 is also titled N8C and later Table 3 says “Seed-initialized N8C optimization,” creating acronym conflict.

Method: Persona vectors: v_repr=mean_D+ e(x)-mean_D- e(x). SAE direction v_SAE=sum top-K encoder rows weighted by positive-negative mean latent activation differences. D+ exhibits target persona, D- lacks it; suppression target is direction v. Objective f(t)=-<e(t),v>/||e(t)|| using last-token representation; maximize to move away from target persona. Eq(4) L_lambda=f(t)-lambda/n sum next-token cross-entropy; lower self-cross-entropy means closer to model distribution. Figure 2 earlier gave L=f+H, conflicting with Eq(4)’s subtraction. Algorithm mutates length-n prompts using token gradients/top-k sampling, population M, different fluency weights, restarts. Strong steering prompts can be fragmented/multilingual; seed initialization can preserve natural-language structure. Selection uses held-out validation behavioral metric.

Experiments: Baselines X5L zero-shot, R3W manual standard prompt including “Answer honestly,” P8D dense steering, H2F direct output-logit optimization, Z6Q GPT-4o natural-language gradients/bandits/beam search. Layers C7N/W4X 25, F9S 20. N8C M=100,n=8,T=1000. SAE L0≈50,K=20. B2R neutral/random choice = 50%; neutral B2R-axis projection=0.0. Baseline active SAE features/token≈50; P8D beyond 150; V7P 50–60. Context-aware optimization appends candidates to task training questions at every evolutionary step and computes loss from combined sequence final internal state. Evaluation selects higher log P(a|q,p); metrics are fractions preferring undesirable option.

Table 1: X5L avg 62.43; R3W 55.45; P8D 56.10; H2F 53.60; Z6Q 47.44; QX2 45.83; V7P 46.44. B2R: QX2 C7N 49.86/W4X 50.63/F9S 62.65; V7P 49.84/49.95/70.70. Earlier text claimed both methods reach B2R perfect neutralization and consistently improve U9K/D6V over baselines, conflicting with table. “Two model families” claim conflicts with three models/families listed.

Part 6 claims: V7P controls personas via precise sparse semantically grounded intervention, unlike P8D. B2R-axis projections: baseline broad with agreement bias; P8D and QX2 move mean toward neutrality but retain variance; V7P allegedly sharply concentrates near neutrality, variance collapse, statistically indistinguishable from random choice—conflicts with Table 1 V7P F9S B2R=70.70 vs 50 neutral. Table 3 seed-initialized optimization: optimized prompts reduce scores vs seeds, e.g. 69.16→56.25, 72.30→54.22, 71.15→51.72, 72.06→59.35, 52.43→46.34, 51.20→46.95. Y2H/token priming via induction heads: binary tasks with undesirable label skew, especially B2R often “(A),” can converge to label priming; QX2 may inject alternative label. errors.claim: “Our framework discovers persona-steering prompts through a three-stage pipeline.”

errors.explanation: The caption gives the objective as adding H, while Equation (4) subtracts a λ-weighted average cross-entropy term. These are not the same objective, especially because H is defined as cross-entropy to be penalized.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” Abstract: adapts gradient ascent to LLMs for targeted prompt discovery; RESGA and SAEGA optimize prompts to align representations away from/with persona directions; “fluent gradient ascent” controls fluency. Abstract numeric claim: “on sycophancy, our automatically discovered prompts achieve significant improvement (49.90% compared with 79.24%)” likely baseline vs method.

Intro/method: RESGA = residual/dense representation gradient ascent; SAEGA = sparse autoencoder gradient ascent using SAE latents. Pipeline described as three stages: construct persona steering vectors; fluent gradient ascent to discover prompts steering away while maintaining fluency; select prompts from Pareto frontier based on validation. Internal inconsistency: Fig. 2 caption says “two stages” and objective Lλ(t)=f(t)+H(t), conflicting with three-stage text and Eq. 4.

Sec. 3.1: RESGA vector v_repr = mean e(x) on D+ minus mean e(x) on D− at chosen layer. SAEGA uses SAELens SAEs. Persona latents selected by top-K largest absolute mean activation differences; v_SAE = Σ w_i(ā_i^+−ā_i^-), with signed differences despite absolute selection.

Sec. 3.2: Persona reduction objective f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)|| using last-token representation at target layer; maximizing points away from persona direction. Fluency objective Eq. 4: Lλ(t)=f(t)−(λ/n)Σ H(m(t≤i),t_{i+1}). EPO: population with different λ; length n prompts; gradients wrt one-hot/embeddings; top-k alternatives; mutate one random token; evaluate/select; periodic restarts.

Sec. 3.3: random init often fragmented/incoherent. Seed init uses short natural-language phrase related to persona, e.g. “Please answer honestly”; improves fluency/Pareto region. Prompts evaluated on held-out validation by appending to task inputs and measuring behavioral metric. Strongest steering prompts often fragmented/multilingual/incoherent. Fluency = model self cross-entropy, not human readability; no hard threshold.

Sec. 4 setup: Tasks: sycophancy, hallucination on MC TruthfulQA, myopic reward. Lower metrics better; sycophancy 50% described as perfect neutralization. Models: Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, Gemma 3 4B Instruct. Baselines: Zero-Shot, Standard Prompt, Dense Steering Vector, GCG, ProTeGi. Layers: 25 for Llama/Qwen, 20 for Gemma. EPO M=100, length n=8, T=1000. Evaluation by conditional log-prob comparison; metric = fraction preferring undesirable option. Inconsistency: Sec. 4.2 text says Table 1 across “two model families,” but setup/table show three models.

Table 1 baselines: Zero-Shot avg 62.43; syc Llama/Qwen/Gemma 72.48/86.00/82.00; halluc 51.45/45.00/57.97; myopic 54/55/58. Standard Prompt avg 55.45; syc 70.50/72/80; halluc 50.72/34.78/55.07; myopic 52/46/38. Dense Steering avg 56.10; syc 54.50/79/80; halluc 50.72/36.96/57.25; myopic 47.5/47.5/51.5. GCG avg 53.60; syc 55.83/73.50/58.70; halluc 46.95/45.12/54.27; myopic 48.5/48/51.5. ProTeGi avg 47.44; syc 54.77/56.13/71.51; halluc 48.17/46.95/38.41; myopic 42.50/20.99/47.49.

Table 1 ours: RESGA avg 45.83; syc Llama/Qwen/Gemma 49.86/50.63/62.65; halluc 45.12/41.46/51.22; myopic 38.50/38.50/34.50. SAEGA avg 46.44; syc 49.84/49.95/70.70; halluc 46.95/40.85/49.14; myopic 31.50/40.50/38.50. Inconsistencies: text says both RESGA/SAEGA sycophancy statistically indistinguishable from 50%, but Gemma values 62.65 and 70.70 are not near 50. Text/conclusion says both methods consistently improve on hallucination/myopic and substantially outperform manual prompting/dense steering, contradicted by Qwen hallucination vs Standard Prompt/Dense Steering and myopic Qwen vs ProTeGi.

Mechanistic analysis claims: Fig. 3 sycophancy-axis projections: baseline broad agreement bias; Dense/RESGA shift mean but retain variance; SAEGA sharp near zero, instance-wise neutrality/random-choice behavior. SAEGA Gemma sycophancy 70.70 undermines blanket neutralization claim. Fig. 4 SAE L0: baseline ~50 active features/token; dense steering >150; RESGA increases sparsity; SAEGA 50–60 preserves manifold. Fig. 5: SAEGA selectively suppresses sycophancy features; dense/RESGA noisy. Fig. 6: dense exits manifold; RESGA diffuse; SAEGA tight stable subspace often orthogonal to dense direction.

Table 2 random-init prompt examples mostly fragmented/multilingual/incoherent. Table 3 seed-initialized examples improve metrics: 69.16→56.25, 72.30→54.22, 71.15→51.72, 72.06→59.35, 52.43→46.34, 51.20→46.95.

Table 4 WikiText2 perplexity: Baseline vs RESGA & SAEGA: Llama 12.56→12.07, Qwen 10.88→12.48, Gemma 30.51→29.19. Inconsistency: caption/Sec. 4.4 says negligible perplexity change/degradation across all three, but Qwen increases ~15%.

Sec. 4.4 qualitative: Token Priming via induction heads; some RESGA prompts inject alternative label/token B. Semantic Steering via Vocabulary Shift: SAEGA suppresses agreement markers and upweights pivots; RESGA/SAEGA upweight long-term tokens for myopic reward.

Sec. 4.5/Table 5 ablations: Random Direction syc 74.13/84.56/81.47; halluc 68.29/54.26/84.70; myopic 50.50/48.50/61.00. Random Mutation syc 68.00/71.66/76.04; halluc 50.40/45.12/54.26; myopic 52.00/46.50/55.00. Task Loss as Objective syc 55.83/73.50/58.70; halluc 46.95/45.12/54.27; myopic 48.50/48.00/51.50. Inconsistency: text says Random Direction collapses to near/above zero-shot across all tasks/models, but myopic Random Direction beats zero-shot for Llama/Qwen. Task Loss row exactly matches earlier GCG row values.

Conclusion claims framework bridges MI and prompt discovery; RESGA/SAEGA via persona vectors and evolutionary gradient ascent; significant improvement on sycophancy and myopic reward and consistent hallucination improvements; outperform manual/dense; SAEGA neutralizes behavior, preserves manifolds, interpretable feature control. Sec. 6 limitations: methods require labeled examples; SAE latents and steering vectors are model-specific and require retraining for each target model; most effective prompts often semantically incoherent. Broader impact: same pipeline could target safety-critical SAE latents to automate jailbreak discovery/harmful outputs; deployment needs access controls. Acknowledgment: Claude used for manuscript writing assistance and AI-assisted code generation.

Introduction: Figure 1 contrasts (a) manual prompt-based steering, (b) activation steering injecting dense vector v into model representations e(t), and (c) RESGA/SAEGA deriving persona directions from contrastive activations and optimizing prompts via fluent gradient ascent for residual-based and interpretable feature-level control. Motivation: persona control is important for safety; fine-tuning can induce “emergent misalignment” with harmful personas in unrelated prompts; safety alignment can fail when prompted appropriately. Prompt engineering is primary but requires expertise and is hard for complex traits; automatic prompt discovery exists but often black-box.

Mechanistic interpretability context: sparse dictionary learning/SAEs can decompose activations into interpretable features. Prior persona-feature work found SAE latents can capture/control behavioral personas and “misaligned persona” features, but mainly analyzes activations or intervenes via activation steering. Claimed unexplored inverse problem: discovering prompts that selectively activate task-relevant latents to steer personas.

Gradient ascent context: feature visualization works for CNNs; LLM adaptation limited by discrete language. Continuous embedding optimization then nearest-token projection can produce off-manifold results due to polysemanticity and continuous/discrete mismatch. Gradient-guided discrete optimization/evolutionary token replacement has been used for adversarial attacks/jailbreaking but, intro claims, not for identifying model steering prompts.

Framework details from intro: RESGA = RESidual Gradient Ascent, operating on dense residual stream representations. SAEGA = Sparse Autoencoder Gradient Ascent, leveraging interpretable SAE latents. Both first construct persona steering vectors for undesired behavioral traits: RESGA via direct representation differences; SAEGA via SAE latent-based approaches identifying causally relevant features. They then perform fluent gradient ascent to discover prompts that maximally steer away from target personas with controllable fluency. Claimed advantages: not black-box, uses mechanistic insights for targeted/interpretable prompt search. Claimed evaluation on three persona steering tasks: sycophancy, hallucination, myopic reward. grade.reason: None of the reported errors point out the specific contradiction in Table 5 showing SAEGA (31.50) beats RESGA (38.50) on Llama myopic reward, so the planted claim was not identified.

errors.claim: Figure 2 says optimization uses “$L_{\lambda}(\mathbf t)=f(\mathbf t)+H(\mathbf t)$.”
errors.evidence: Section 3.2 defines fluency-controlled optimization as “$\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\mathbf{t})= f(\mathbf{t}) - \frac{\lambda}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} H(m(\mathbf{t}_{\leq i}),t_{i+1})$,” and says “Penalizing low-probability sequences encourages human-interpretable prompts.”
errors.explanation: The figure states the objective adds the fluency term, while the formal definition subtracts a cross-entropy penalty weighted by $\lambda$. Since $H$ is explicitly cross-entropy, the sign and weighting conflict.

errors.claim: “Both methods reach B2R error statistically indistinguishable from perfect neutralization”
errors.evidence: Table 1 lists B2R F9S scores of 62.65 for QX2 and 70.70 for V7P, while §4.1/Table implementation states “B2R perfect-neutralization error | 50%.”
errors.explanation: The table shows that on F9S, both methods are well above the paper’s own 50% neutralization value, especially V7P at 70.70, so the blanket claim that both methods reach perfect-neutralization-level B2R error conflicts with the reported results.

errors.claim: “Both methods consistently improve U9K and D6V over baselines”
errors.evidence: In Table 1, U9K W4X: QX2 = 41.46 and V7P = 40.85, but R3W = 34.78 and P8D = 36.96 are lower/better. U9K F9S: QX2 = 51.22 and V7P = 49.14, but Z6Q = 38.41 is lower/better. D6V W4X: QX2 = 38.50 and V7P = 40.50, but Z6Q = 20.99 is lower/better.
errors.explanation: Because lower metrics are defined as better, the table contains multiple cases where one or both proposed methods are worse than one or more baselines. Thus the claim of consistent improvement over baselines is contradicted by the table.

errors.claim: “The reported rates cover three mitigation tasks and two model families.”
errors.evidence: §4.1 Models says evaluation uses C7N = Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, W4X = Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, and F9S = Gemma 3 4B Instruct; Table 1 reports all three.
errors.explanation: The setup and table describe three distinct model families/architectures, not two, so the statement that reported rates cover two model families is internally inconsistent.

errors.claim: “V7P instead sharply concentrates near neutrality: variance collapse enforces instance-wise neutrality and behavior statistically indistinguishable from random choice.”
errors.location: this part, Neutralization vs. Distributional Shifting
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 1 B2R results: V7P C7N 49.84, W4X 49.95, but F9S 70.70; notes also state B2R perfect neutralization/random choice error is 50%.
errors.explanation: The claim says V7P behavior is statistically indistinguishable from random choice, but for F9S on B2R V7P has 70.70% undesirable preference, far from the paper’s own 50% neutral/random-choice benchmark.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” Abstract claims QX2 and V7P optimize random prompts toward identified persona directions; J4Z controls discovered-prompt fluency. Evaluations span C7N, W4X, F9S and B2R, U9K, D6V. Abstract says discovered prompts significantly improve B2R mitigation. Intro additionally claims improve B2R and D6V mitigation, outperform manual prompting and dense steering; dense steering causes distributional shifts avoided by prompt steering.

Definitions: QX2 = RESGA/residual gradient ascent using dense residual-stream representation difference; V7P = SAEGA using top SAE latents; J4Z = fluency control; N8C = Evolutionary Prompt Optimization in related work but Algorithm 1 also titled N8C; Z6Q = ProTeGi; H2F = GCG; P8D = dense steering vector; X5L = zero-shot; R3W = standard/manual prompt. Y2H = Token Priming via induction heads; G6T = Semantic Steering/vocabulary shift; T9B = WikiText2.

Method: Three-stage procedure: persona-vector construction, fluency-constrained discovery, validation selection. Fig. 2 gives Lλ=f+H, conflicting with Eq. 4 subtracting cross-entropy penalty. Persona directions: direct Eq(1) v_repr=mean_D+ e(x)-mean_D- e(x); SAE Eq(2) v_SAE=sum_{i in I_K} w_i(mean a_i+ - mean a_i-), I_K largest absolute activation differences. Suppression objective Eq(3) f(t)=-<e(t),v>/||e(t)|| using last-token representation. J4Z Eq(4): Lλ=f(t)-λ/n sum CE; lower self-CE = more on-distribution. Algorithm initializes M length-n prompts randomly/from seeds, mutates high-gradient token alternatives, restarts, tracks fluency/steering frontier. Seed prompts like “Please answer honestly” for B2R can improve fluency without much steering loss. Candidates appended to held-out validation inputs; selection by target metric change.

Experiments §4.1: Tasks: B2R sycophancy, U9K TruthfulQA MC error, D6V myopic reward; lower better. Models: C7N=Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, W4X=Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, F9S=Gemma 3 4B Instruct; V7P uses SAE-Lens SAEs. Baselines: X5L, R3W “Answer honestly,” P8D residual injection, H2F direct output-logit optimization, Z6Q GPT-4o natural-language optimization. Implementation: layers C7N/W4X 25, F9S 20; N8C M=100, prompt length n=8, T=1000; SAE L0≈50; K=20; B2R perfect neutralization error 50%; neutral B2R-axis projection 0.0; baseline active SAE features/token ≈50; P8D active features >150; V7P 50–60. Context-aware optimization appends candidate prompts to dynamic task-specific training questions at every evolutionary step, using combined sequence final internal state. Evaluation metric is fraction preferring undesirable option.

§4.2 Table 1 results lower better Avg: X5L 62.43, R3W 55.45, P8D 56.10, H2F 53.60, Z6Q 47.44, QX2 45.83, V7P 46.44. B2R: QX2 C7N 49.86/W4X 50.63/F9S 62.65; V7P 49.84/49.95/70.70. U9K: QX2 45.12/41.46/51.22; V7P 46.95/40.85/49.14. D6V: QX2 38.50/38.50/34.50; V7P 31.50/40.50/38.50. Z6Q strong: U9K F9S 38.41 and D6V W4X 20.99. Internal errors found: §4.2 overclaims both methods reach B2R perfect neutralization despite F9S far above 50; overclaims consistent U9K/D6V improvement over baselines despite several baselines beating ours; says rates cover two model families despite three models/families listed.

§4.3/4.4: Mechanism analysis claims V7P sparse semantically grounded intervention vs P8D global interference. Claims B2R-axis projections: P8D/QX2 move mean toward neutrality but retain variance; V7P variance collapse near neutrality, instance-wise neutral/random behavior—conflicts with V7P B2R F9S 70.70. Claims SAE L0: P8D feature-count explosion off manifold, QX2 partial, V7P near baseline sparsity. Claims feature-level V7P suppresses B2R-relevant features and avoids unrelated activation; PCA: P8D off-manifold, QX2 diffuse high variance, V7P tight on-manifold region often orthogonal to P8D.

Table 2 gives random-initialized discovered prompts, mostly incoherent, for QX2/V7P across tasks/models. Table 3 seed-initialized N8C: six seed prompts score 69.16,72.30,71.15,72.06,52.43,51.20%; optimized scores 56.25,54.22,51.72,59.35,46.34,46.95%, all lower than seeds. Method part 3: Three-stage procedure: persona-vector construction, fluency-constrained discovery, initialization/frontier selection using validation performance. Figure 2 says two-stage discovery from dense representations or sparse SAE latents, transforming random token sequences into readable direction-specific prompts through optimization; figure gives $L_\lambda(t)=f(t)+H(t)$, which conflicts with Eq. 4 subtracting cross-entropy penalty.

3.1 Persona vectors: Pretrained SAEs from SAE-Lens. For each latent, contrastive relevance = persona-positive minus persona-negative mean activation; I_K indexes largest absolute differences. SAE direction Eq(2): $v_{SAE}=\sum_{i\in I_K} w_i(\bar a_i^+ - \bar a_i^-)$, with $w_i$ row i of W_enc, $a_i(x)=ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i)$; means over D+ and D-. Direct representation alternative Eq(1): $v_{repr}=mean_{D+} e(x)-mean_{D-} e(x)$. D+ exhibits target persona, D- lacks it; e(x) is activation at chosen layer. Suppression target direction v in activation space.

3.2 J4Z: Algorithm 1 titled N8C. Inputs steering objective f, LM m, prompt length n, population M, fluency weights lambda_1..lambda_M. Initializes M length-n prompts randomly or from seeds. Iteratively computes L_lambda and gradients wrt one-hot encodings, selects top-k candidate tokens by gradient magnitude, mutates by replacing random token with sampled top-k alternative, evaluates candidates, selects best prompt for each lambda; periodic restarts retain best under random lambda and reinitialize others. Persona-reduction objective Eq(3): $f(t)=-<e(t),v>/||e(t)||$, using last-token representation at target layer; maximizing points away from target persona. Alone often yields unnatural/nonsensical strings. J4Z/fluent gradient ascent follows fluent dreaming (Thompson 2024) maximizing Eq(4): $L_\lambda(t)=f(t)-\lambda/n \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} H(m(t_{\le i}), t_{i+1})$, where H is next-token cross-entropy and lambda controls steering–fluency tradeoff. Penalizing low-probability sequences encourages interpretable prompts. N8C described as maintaining M candidates at different frontier points using token-embedding gradients/high-gradient sampling and restarts.

3.3 Initialization/selection: Strongest-steering prompts often fragmented/multilingual/incoherent. Fluency is intrinsic self-cross-entropy constraint, not readability/grammaticality; lower = closer to model training distribution, higher = more off-manifold. No hard threshold; analyze entire frontier. Uniform vocab-token initialization tends to fragmentation/incoherence. Short persona-related seeds, e.g. “Please answer honestly” for B2R, keep search nearer language manifold, occupying higher-fluency frontier regions without significant steering sacrifice, preferable for interpretability. Candidates appended to held-out validation inputs; selection measures target behavioral metric change. Downstream emphasizes intermediate-frontier prompts balancing steering and moderate perplexity increases relative to random-token baselines. Stability = consistency of persona reduction across validation examples; protocol prioritizes causal steering efficacy over naturalness.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” Framework: RESGA/SAEGA use gradient ascent to optimize prompts aligned away from identified persona directions; fluent gradient ascent controls fluency. Tasks: sycophancy, hallucination, myopic reward. Models: Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, Gemma 3 4B Instruct. Abstract claim: sycophancy significant improvement “49.90% compared with 79.24%” likely baseline/method wording to check.

Intro/method inconsistencies already noted: method says three-stage pipeline, Fig 2 caption says two stages. Fig 2 objective L_lambda(t)=f(t)+H(t) conflicts with Eq. 4 L_lambda(t)=f(t)-(lambda/n)sum CE/NLL H. v_repr = mean_D+ e(x)-mean_D- e(x). SAEGA selects top-K latents by largest absolute activation differences; v_SAE=sum selected encoder rows weighted by activation difference. Persona reduction f(t)= -<e(t),v>/||e(t)||; maximize to point away from persona. EPO M=100, prompt length n=8, T=1000, gradients wrt token one-hots/embeddings, mutations from top-k gradient candidates, restarts. Seed prompts can improve fluency. Fluency = self cross-entropy; no hard threshold.

Experiments: lower metrics better, but sycophancy 50% is perfect neutralization. Baselines: Zero-Shot, Standard Prompt, Dense Steering Vector, GCG, ProTeGi. Layers: Llama/Qwen 25, Gemma 20. Context-aware optimization appends prompts to training questions. SAEGA top-K, reports K=20. Section 4.2 says “two model families,” conflicting with three models/table.

Table 1: Zero-Shot syc 72.48/86.00/82.00; halluc 51.45/45.00/57.97; myopic 54.00/55.00/58.00; Avg 62.43. Standard Prompt syc 70.50/72.00/80.00; halluc 50.72/34.78/55.07; myopic 52.00/46.00/38.00; Avg 55.45. Dense Steering syc 54.50/79.00/80.00; halluc 50.72/36.96/57.25; myopic 47.50/47.50/51.50; Avg 56.10. GCG syc 55.83/73.50/58.70; halluc 46.95/45.12/54.27; myopic 48.50/48.00/51.50; Avg 53.60. ProTeGi syc 54.77/56.13/71.51; halluc 48.17/46.95/38.41; myopic 42.50/20.99/47.49; Avg 47.44. Ours: RESGA syc 49.86/50.63/62.65; halluc 45.12/41.46/51.22; myopic 38.50/38.50/34.50; Avg 45.83. SAEGA syc 49.84/49.95/70.70; halluc 46.95/40.85/49.14; myopic 31.50/40.50/38.50; Avg 46.44. Text claims sycophancy both methods statistically indistinguishable from 50, but Gemma 62.65/70.70 contradict. Text/conclusion claims hallucination consistent improvements, contradicted by Qwen/Gemma baselines outperforming ours. Myopic improvement not uniform: Qwen ProTeGi 20.99 beats ours; Gemma Standard 38.00 beats SAEGA 38.50. Conclusion also claims substantial outperformance over manual prompting/dense steering, but Standard/Dense are better on Qwen hallucination and Standard beats SAEGA on Gemma myopic.

Mechanistic analysis claims: SAEGA sparse/semantically grounded, not global interference. Fig 3 sycophancy projections: SAEGA sharp peak near zero. Fig 4 L0: baseline ~50 features/token; dense steering >150; RESGA increases sparsity somewhat; SAEGA 50–60. Fig 5: SAEGA suppresses causally relevant sycophancy SAE features, leaves unrelated unaffected. Fig 6: dense exits manifold; RESGA diffuse; SAEGA tight stable region often orthogonal to dense direction. Table 2 has mostly nonsensical random-initialized prompts. Table 3 seed examples include optimized prompts lowering scores, some nonsensical.

Table 4 WikiText2 perplexity: Llama 12.56 baseline vs 12.07 RESGA&SAEGA; Qwen 10.88 vs 12.48; Gemma 30.51 vs 29.19. Caption/text claims negligible change across all three; Qwen increase conflicts. Qualitative mechanisms: RESGA can exploit token priming/induction heads by injecting alternative label token B where sycophantic answer often A; SAEGA suppresses agreement markers/upweights “However”/“But”; myopic reward upweights long-term tokens “Future,” “Long,” “Wait.”

Table 5 ablations: Random Direction syc 74.13/84.56/81.47; halluc 68.29/54.26/84.70; myopic 50.50/48.50/61.00. Random Mutation syc 68.00/71.66/76.04; halluc 50.40/45.12/54.26; myopic 52.00/46.50/55.00. Task Loss as Objective syc 55.83/73.50/58.70; halluc 46.95/45.12/54.27; myopic 48.50/48.00/51.50; identical to GCG row in Table 1. Section claims Random Direction collapses to near/above zero-shot across all tasks/models, contradicted by several below-zero-shot values, esp myopic Llama/Qwen.

Conclusion: reiterates framework, claims experiments show significant sycophancy/myopic reward improvement, consistent hallucination improvement, and substantial outperformance over manual/dense steering; this conflicts with Table 1 as above. Also says mechanistic analysis reveals SAEGA neutralizes rather than shifts behavior, preserves manifolds, feature-level control.

Limitations: require labeled positive/negative persona examples; SAE latents/steering vectors are model-specific and need retraining per model; most effective prompts are not semantically coherent, future work should add linguistic priors for human-like prompts. Broader impact: pipeline aims to suppress undesired personas but could target safety-critical SAE latents to automate jailbreak discovery/ harmful outputs; deployment should have access controls. Acknowledgment: Claude used for manuscript writing assistance and AI-assisted code generation.
