Method Section 3: opening says framework has three-stage pipeline: (1) construct persona steering vectors using representation differences or SAE latent approaches; (2) use fluent gradient ascent to discover prompts that steer away from target persona while maintaining fluency; (3) initialize and select effective prompts from Pareto frontier based on validation performance. But Figure 2 caption says framework has two stages: vector construction and fluent gradient ascent optimization, creating a possible internal inconsistency. Figure 2 also states objective as L_lambda(t)=f(t)+H(t), inconsistent with Eq. 4 below.

Section 3.1: Persona steering vector v in R^d represents direction of undesired persona. Representation-based steering: v_repr = mean_{D+} e(x) - mean_{D-} e(x), where D+ exhibits target persona, D- persona-free, e(x) activation at chosen layer. SAEGA: uses pretrained SAEs from SAE-Lens. For each SAE latent i, relevance = difference in mean activation on persona-exhibiting vs persona-free; select top-K latents with largest absolute activation differences I_K. SAE steering vector uses encoder directions: v_SAE = sum_{i in I_K} w_i * (a_i^+bar - a_i^-bar), where w_i is i-th row of W_enc, a_i(x)=ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i).

Section 3.2: Given v, discover prompts steering away from target persona. Persona reduction objective f(t)= - <e(t),v> / ||e(t)||, where e(t) is representation of last token at target layer. Maximizing f finds prompts whose representations point away from persona direction. Fluency objective Eq. 4: L_lambda(t)= f(t) - (lambda/n) sum_{i=0}^{n-1} H(m(t_<=i), t_{i+1}); H is cross-entropy/negative log likelihood of next token under model m; lambda controls fluency-steering tradeoff; second term penalizes low-probability sequences, encouraging interpretable prompts. Optimization uses Evolutionary Prompt Optimization (EPO, Thompson et al. 2024), maintaining M candidate prompts, each targeting a Pareto point for a fluency weight lambda_i. Algorithm inputs f, m, length n, population M, lambdas. It initializes M prompts with random or seed initialization; for T iterations compute L and gradients w.r.t. one-hot token encodings, select top-k candidate tokens per position by gradient magnitude, mutate by replacing random token with sampled top-k alternative, evaluate candidates and select best prompt for each lambda_i; at restart, retain best under random lambda and reinitialize others. Text after algorithm says gradients w.r.t token embeddings identify substitutions; periodic restarts prevent premature convergence; output diverse prompts varying fluency/effectiveness.

Method Section 3: opening says framework has three-stage pipeline: (1) construct persona steering vectors using representation differences or SAE latent approaches; (2) use fluent gradient ascent to discover prompts that steer away from target persona while maintaining fluency; (3) initialize and select effective prompts from Pareto frontier based on validation performance. But Figure 2 caption says framework has two stages: vector construction and fluent gradient ascent optimization, possible internal inconsistency. Figure 2 also states objective as L_lambda(t)=f(t)+H(t), inconsistent with Eq. 4.

Section 3.1: Persona steering vector v in R^d represents direction of undesired persona. Representation-based steering: v_repr = mean_{D+} e(x) - mean_{D-} e(x), where D+ exhibits target persona, D- persona-free, e(x) activation at chosen layer. SAEGA: uses pretrained SAEs from SAE-Lens. For each SAE latent i, relevance = difference in mean activation on persona-exhibiting vs persona-free; select top-K latents with largest absolute activation differences I_K. SAE steering vector uses encoder directions: v_SAE = sum_{i in I_K} w_i * (a_i^+bar - a_i^-bar), where w_i is i-th row of W_enc, a_i(x)=ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i).

Section 3.2: Given v, discover prompts steering away from target persona. Persona reduction objective f(t)= - <e(t),v> / ||e(t)||, where e(t) is representation of last token at target layer. Maximizing f finds prompts whose representations point away from persona direction. Fluency objective Eq. 4: L_lambda(t)= f(t) - (lambda/n) sum H(m(t_<=i), t_{i+1}); H is cross-entropy/negative log likelihood of next token under model m; lambda controls fluency-steering tradeoff; second term penalizes low-probability sequences, encouraging interpretable prompts. Optimization uses Evolutionary Prompt Optimization (EPO, Thompson et al. 2024), maintaining M candidate prompts, each targeting a Pareto point for a fluency weight lambda_i. Algorithm inputs f, m, length n, population M, lambdas. It initializes M prompts with random or seed initialization; for T iterations compute L and gradients w.r.t. one-hot token encodings, select top-k candidate tokens per position by gradient magnitude, mutate by replacing random token with sampled top-k alternative, evaluate candidates and select best prompt for each lambda_i; at restart, retain best under random lambda and reinitialize others. Text after algorithm says gradients w.r.t token embeddings identify substitutions; periodic restarts prevent premature convergence; output diverse prompts varying fluency/effectiveness.

Current part adds initialization/evaluation protocol. Two EPO initialization strategies: random initialization uniformly sampled vocabulary tokens, often syntactically fragmented/semantically incoherent; seed initialization uses short natural-language phrase related to target persona (e.g., “Please answer honestly” for sycophancy), anchoring near language manifold. Claims seed-initialized prompts occupy higher-fluency Pareto regions without significantly sacrificing steering effectiveness, preferable for interpretability. EPO yields candidate prompts along Pareto frontier between steering strength and LM fluency. Prompts evaluated on held-out validation data by appending to task inputs and measuring change in target behavioral metric. Strongest steering prompts often fragmented, multilingual, or incoherent. They explicitly do not equate fluency with human readability/grammar; fluency is intrinsic model-based self cross-entropy. Lower CE = closer to training distribution; higher CE = off-manifold. No hard fluency threshold; report/analyze full Pareto frontier. Downstream emphasis on intermediate frontier regions balancing steering with moderate perplexity increases relative to random token baselines. Prompt stability assessed by consistency of reducing target persona across diverse validation examples, to avoid narrow degenerate solutions. Evaluation prioritizes causal steering efficacy over linguistic naturalness.

Paper title: “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” Authors: Harshvardhan Saini, Yiming Tang, Dianbo Liu. Abstract/intro claims QX2/RESGA and V7P/SAEGA optimize prompts toward mechanistically identified persona directions; J4Z controls fluency; evaluated on C7N, W4X, F9S and B2R, U9K, D6V; discovered prompts significantly improve B2R and D6V mitigation and outperform manual prompting/dense steering. Intro claims dense steering causes distributional shifts avoided by prompt-based steering.

Definitions/methods: QX2 = RESGA = residual gradient ascent using dense residual representation differences. V7P = SAEGA = sparse autoencoder gradient ascent using causally relevant SAE features. J4Z = fluent gradient ascent/fluency-controlled prompt optimization. N8C introduced as Evolutionary Prompt Optimization (EPO), gradient-guided evolutionary search balancing objective and fluency, but Algorithm 1 is labelled “N8C.” Z6Q = ProTeGi; H2F = GCG. P8D = Dense Steering Vector/residual-stream injection baseline; §4.1/§4.3 say P8D causes active-feature/L0 explosion beyond 150 vs V7P 50–60 and natural/baseline ≈50, so P8D is less sparse/more disruptive.

Three-stage procedure: persona-vector construction, fluency-constrained discovery, and initialization/frontier selection using validation performance. Figure 2 caption says two-stage discovery constructs directions from dense representations or sparse SAE latents, then transforms random token sequences into readable direction-specific prompts through optimization with Lλ(t)=f(t)+H(t), conflicting with Eq. 4 sign if H is ordinary cross-entropy.

Persona vectors: SAE latent relevance = persona-positive mean activation minus persona-negative mean activation; IK indexes largest absolute differences. V7P vector: v_SAE = Σ_{i∈IK} w_i*(ā_i^+−ā_i^−), w_i row i of W_enc, a_i(x)=ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i). QX2: v_repr = mean_{D+}e(x)−mean_{D−}e(x). Persona-reduction objective f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)||; maximizing f moves away from persona.

J4Z/N8C: initializes M length-n prompts randomly or from seeds. Iteratively uses Lλ and gradients wrt one-hot tokens, top-k mutations, evaluates/selects per λ; periodic restart. Eq. 4: Lλ(t)=f(t)−(λ/n)ΣH(m(t≤i),t_{i+1}); H is next-token cross-entropy; penalizes low-probability sequences. Fluency = self-cross-entropy, lower closer to training distribution. Natural-language seeds anchor search. Candidates appended to held-out validation inputs; selected by target behavioral metric.

Experiments: B2R=Sycophancy (Perez), U9K=Hallucination/factual reliability multiple-choice error on A4J=TruthfulQA, D6V=Myopic Reward (Perez). Lower better. Models: C7N=Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, W4X=Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, F9S=Gemma 3 4B Instruct. V7P uses SAE-Lens. Baselines X5L zero-shot, R3W manual, P8D dense steering, H2F direct output-logit optimization, Z6Q GPT-4o LLM gradients/bandits/beam search. Implementation: layers C7N/W4X 25, F9S 20; N8C M=100, prompt length 8, T=1000; K=20; neutral B2R=50%; natural SAE L0≈50; P8D active features >150, V7P 50–60. Evaluation: log P(a|q,p), choose higher-prob answer; metrics fraction preferring undesirable option.

§4.2/Table 1: claim both methods reach B2R error statistically indistinguishable from perfect neutralization conflicts for F9S: QX2 B2R F9S 62.65, V7P 70.70 vs neutral 50%. Also claims three tasks/two model families, but setup/table have three model families. Table 1 averages: X5L 62.43; R3W 55.45; P8D 56.10; H2F 53.60; Z6Q 47.44; QX2 45.83; V7P 46.44. QX2 B2R 49.86/50.63/62.65; V7P B2R 49.84/49.95/70.70. U9K QX2 45.12/41.46/51.22; V7P 46.95/40.85/49.14. D6V QX2 38.50/38.50/34.50; V7P 31.50/40.50/38.50.

§4.3/4.4 mechanisms: claims V7P differs qualitatively from P8D by sparse, semantically grounded intervention. B2R projections: P8D/QX2 move mean toward neutrality but retain variance; V7P concentrates near neutrality/statistically random—again conflicts with F9S B2R 70.70. SAE L0: P8D unnatural feature-count explosion, QX2 partial mitigation but increases sparsity, V7P near baseline. Feature-level: V7P suppresses B2R-correlated features and avoids unrelated/spurious activation; P8D/QX2 noisy/inconsistent. PCA: P8D large off-manifold displacement; QX2 diffuse mean shift; V7P tight stable on-manifold region often orthogonal to P8D.

Table 2 lists random-initialized discovered prompts, many incoherent/multilingual; Table 3 seed-initialized N8C shows optimized prompts reduce score vs seeds (e.g. 69.16→56.25, 52.43→46.34). Table 4 T9B WikiText2 perplexity baseline vs QX2&V7P: C7N 12.56→12.07, W4X 10.88→12.48, F9S 30.51→29.19; text calls changes negligible and says general LM performance not disrupted. Qualitative mechanisms: incoherent prompts reflect optimizer token-probability strategies; seeds preserve natural-language structure. Y2H/token priming via induction heads: binary tasks with undesirable behavior associated with label, B2R often “(A),” can converge to label priming, especially QX2 injecting alternative label; injected “B” boosts generation by in-context copying. G6T/semantic steering: V7P often finds reasoning-mode fragments rather than simple token forcing; uses ΔLogits = steered−baseline to characterize vocabulary shift. For B2R polite disagreement V7P suppresses “Yes,” “True,” “Agree” and upweights “However,” “But”; for D6V QX2/V7P upweight “Future,” “Long,” “Wait.”

§4.5/Table 5 ablations: K3Y=random direction, E8U=random mutation, M5A=task loss objective. Claims K3Y collapses to near/above X5L across tasks/models; E8U consistently degrades; M5A unstable and underperforms QX2/V7P in most settings. Table 5 values: K3Y B2R 74.13/84.56/81.47; U9K 68.29/54.26/84.70; D6V 50.50/48.50/61.00. E8U B2R 68.00/71.66/76.04; U9K 50.40/45.12/54.26; D6V 52.00/46.50/55.00. M5A B2R 55.83/73.50/58.70; U9K 46.95/45.12/54.27; D6V 48.50/48.00/51.50. QX2/V7P same as Table 1.

Conclusion/limitations: future work = semi-supervised reduction of labeled data requirements, cross-model prompt transferability, multi-persona steering. Limitations: QX2/V7P require positive/negative persona examples; SAE latents/steering vectors are model-specific and require retraining per target model; most effective prompts lack semantic coherence and stronger linguistic priors may yield effective human-like prompts. Broader impact: intended for safety/persona suppression but could target safety-critical latents, automate jailbreak discovery, or elicit harmful outputs; deployment needs access controls. Acknowledges Claude helped writing/code generation.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors: Berdoz, Billeter, Vonlanthen, Wattenhofer; ETH Zurich. Reproducibility: code/datasets released at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; training details/hyperparams in Appendix F; PCA details in E.5. Author contributions: Berdoz conceived/designed/led planning; Billeter contributed equally and led technical development; Vonlanthen advisor; Wattenhofer PI.

Core claim: train LLMs to produce profile-consistent political survey answers using structured reasoning and RL/GRPO from survey responses, evaluated on smartvote Swiss candidates, Wahl-O-Mat German parties, ANES U.S. respondents. Reasoning improves opinion modeling but does not eliminate bias.

Method: per-unit opinion alignment: given policy question q and persona/unit p, learn stance y. Output schema `<reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>`. Training data contains only final stances, no human reasoning. Reward = 0.25 format + 0.01 length + 1 correctness; format gives up to 4 tag points, length is -|L-L*|, correctness indicator. They say no explicit persona representation, only country label in prompt, and train one model per unit/profile. Optional SFT warm start uses synthetic CoT demonstrations.

Datasets: smartvote CH: 18 candidates, 6 parties x3, 60 policy items from 2023 Swiss elections, binary Yes/No, 48 train/12 test topic-stratified. WoM DE: 6 parties CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Linke, AfD; labels Yes/Neutral/No; train from Wahl-O-Mat 2021–2025; test EU&I 2024 30 items. ANES 2020 US: 21 respondents, 3 per 7-point ideology; 79 policy items recoded Yes/Neutral/No; 67 train/12 test. Groups Left/Center/Right in appendix.

Models/backbones: Llama 3.1 8B non-reasoning, Qwen3 8B and Magistral 24B reasoning-pretrained; 4-bit quantization for training. Baselines: random uniform; majority most frequent train option per unit; ICL same-topic train QA pairs; ORPO using Stammbach et al. hyperparams. §4.2 Methods inconsistency: says “three configurations” but names only GRPO and SFT+GRPO; Table 3 earlier also includes SFT. Synthetic SFT arguments: §4.2 says smartvote and ANES generated by Llama 3.1 70B; does not mention WoM despite Table 3 having SFT/SFT+GRPO for WoM.

Table 3: mean macro-F1 % ± std over 8 stochastic T=1 runs; per-unit macro-F1 then averaged across units. Random: smartvote 50, WoM/ANES 33.33. Majority: 37.43, 27.44, 22.98. SFT+GRPO key scores: Llama smartvote 66.88, WoM 52.53, ANES 40.66; Qwen3 65.11, 49.38, 38.44; Magistral 70.73, 53.21, 45.43. Magistral best overall. Llama SFT ANES 42.77 exceeds Llama SFT+GRPO 40.66; §4.3 acknowledges exception. Magistral GRPO ANES 43.79 > Magistral SFT 39.15, but SFT+GRPO best 45.43. ORPO poor on smartvote for Qwen/Magistral (~23).

§4.3: SFT+GRPO outperforms naive and SFT baselines across datasets except Llama 3.1 8B on ANES; highest score smartvote 70.73, ANES hardest 45.43. SFT+GRPO comparable/better than ICL on ANES and smartvote, outperforms ICL on WoM. Native reasoning support not consistently helpful: Llama 8B beats Qwen3 8B on WoM/ANES, Magistral 24B best overall. GRPO alone underperforms SFT+GRPO. Neutral classes lower performance; Neutral studied in §4.6; no-Neutral in E.1.

§4.4: agents generally make coherent arguments implying final answer; failures include illogical/hallucinated elements and uneven alignment by topic.

§4.5/Fig.3: ideology impacts learnability for Llama 3.1 8B SFT+GRPO. smartvote clear Left vs Center/Right gap. WoM and ANES similar but weaker; WoM Left and Center roughly equal, ANES lower. For Right group in smartvote and ANES, SFT outperforms all other methods on average, suggesting difficulty with right-wing profiles. Possible causes: known left-leaning LLM tendencies or Right profiles intrinsically harder; WoM Right stronger possibly due larger training sets (E.4). Earlier Fig.3 caption said SFT+GRPO typically best and all methods underperform center/right.

§4.6/Fig.4: Neutral reasoning hard on ANES, all Llama 3.1 8B SFT+GRPO. Recall worst on Neutral; Right, partly Center, have highest Neutral base rate. F1 and accuracy negatively correlated with Neutral base rate, significant 5%; regression E.3. Removing Neutral improves all groups and SFT+GRPO relative to ICL, but does not close Left–Right gap; Left–Center gap narrows. Alternative ANES recoding D/E.2 shows same negative correlation but nearly identical Center/Right performance, implying some artifact of recoding.

§4.7/Fig.2: smartvote representativity in PCA political space. Authors claim no overall left shift; agents shift toward center-right on left-right x-axis and toward center on conservative-liberal y-axis. Group-average distances: Right individuals become more left-wing; Left and Center become more right-wing and conservative. Earlier Fig.2 caption/description noted agents more centrist/conservative, average distortions more conservative/no clear left-right bias—possible tension with “center-right” wording.

§4.8/Fig.5-6: biased smartvote SFT data from Llama 3.3 70B progressive/conservative. Progressive-biased data strongly harms Right with inconsistent Left effects; conservative-biased data harms Left without consistently benefiting Right. Bias harms underrepresented perspective more than helps overrepresented; Right impaired more severely by adverse bias. Fig.6 PCA: biased data mostly shifts underrepresented groups, Right more strongly. Conservative-biased and default SFT displacement patterns highly similar, suggesting default centerward shift in Fig.2 may be mainly base model alignment, not SFT-data bias.

§4.9/Fig.7 and Discussion caption: synthetic/counterfactual smartvote positions by flipping/inverting every smartvote answer in train and test. Inversion roughly 180° rotation about origin in Fig.2 (E.6), converting e.g. right-wing to left-wing positions and left to right. Left candidates worsen after flipping, individually and on average. Right candidates improve, but still remain worse on average than original Left candidates; Left drops to roughly original Right level. Authors infer disparity is not purely model political bias; Right positions/right-like preference profiles may be intrinsically harder, or left-leaning profiles easier.

Discussion limitations: opinion learning limited by respondent noise so F1 near 1.0 unlikely; small numbers of individuals/parties because computationally intensive one-model-per-profile; scarce/short/non-comparable surveys. Future work: investigate political-group disparities and bias mitigation; replace per-agent training with single persona-conditioned model using compact representations; add confidence estimates; better questionnaires and uncertainty handling may mitigate Neutral difficulty.

Conclusion: says they train “persona-conditioned agents” on known opinions, in tension/conflict with earlier method saying no explicit persona representation is used and current setup is one model per profile, with persona-conditioned model only future work. Conclusion also says SFT+GRPO generally outperforms all baselines, Neutral remains challenging, and performance varies across political spectrum.

Ethics statement: warns opinion modeling has risks; uses anonymized survey data and public figures’ positions; says systematic ideological disparities with “consistent underperformance on center and right-wing profiles” and difficulty modeling Neutral. This overstates consistency: earlier results said WoM Left and Center roughly equal and WoM Right stronger, while smartvote had clearer Left vs Center/Right gap. Ethics cautions against real-world applications until fairness issues are resolved and suggests bias mitigation could enable digital-democracy applications.

Abstract claims: Opinion modeling captures individual/group political preferences, with applications such as digital democracies and shaping fairer/more popular policies. Introduction: Motivation is digital twins voting/representing opinions; challenge is faithfully representing human political diversity. Treat opinion formation as reasoning: agent writes short rationale and final choice; rewarded when choice matches respondent’s answer, teaching it to reason toward survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors: Frédéric Berdoz, Yann Billeter, Yann Vonlanthen, Roger Wattenhofer; ETH Zurich. Reproducibility: code/datasets released at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; training details/hyperparameters in Appendix F; PCA details in Section E.5. Author contributions: Berdoz conceived/designed/led planning/direction; Billeter contributed equally and led technical development/dataset collection/training/evaluation/analysis; Vonlanthen advised methodology/design; Wattenhofer supervised.

Core goal: individual-level political opinion alignment/simulation. Given policy question q and persona/unit p (respondent/party/candidate), learn p’s stance using known individual opinions, not demographic proxies. Preference-consistent modeling, not voting prediction.

Method: survey data D={(p_j,q_i,y*_{ij})}. Output schema `<reasoning>[justification]</reasoning><answer>[stance]</answer>`. Data have only final stances, no reasoning traces. GRPO trains traces/final answers. Reward: format reward 1 per correctly placed tag among four tags max 4; length reward R_length=-|L-L*|; correctness 1[y_i=y_i*]. Total alpha1=0.25, alpha2=0.01, alpha3=1. No explicit persona representation; train one model per unit, with country label in system prompt. Optional SFT uses CoT demonstrations. Methods had mismatch: says “three configurations” but lists GRPO and SFT+GRPO only; Table 3 includes SFT too.

Datasets/evaluation: smartvote CH: 2023 Swiss, 75 items/60 policy Q across 12 topics, 18 candidates, 4-point collapsed Yes/No, topic-stratified 48 train/12 test. WoM DE: official Wahl-O-Mat 2021–2025, six parties, Yes/Neutral/No; test EU&I 2024, 30 items recoded same. ANES 2020 US: 79 policy items after exclusions, recoded Yes/Neutral/No using conservative/aggressive schemes; default conservative. 67 train/12 test random split. Ideology analysis: 21 respondents, 3 per option on 7-point ideology. Political groups Left/Center/Right assigned to parties/ideologies.

Models/experiments: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B; Qwen/Magistral reasoning-pretrained, Llama non-reasoning. 4-bit quantization. Synthetic arguments for smartvote/ANES via Llama 3.1 70B for SFT. Biased SFT arguments later generated with Llama 3.3 70B. Baselines: random uniform; majority; ICL same-topic/random; ORPO.

Table 3: mean macro-F1 % over 8 runs at T=1.0, averaged per unit. Random: 50/33.33/33.33 smartvote/WoM/ANES. Majority: 37.43/27.44/22.98. Llama: ICL 55.97/28.17/23.2; ORPO 43.53/43.29/34.84; SFT 63.44/48.95/42.77; GRPO 55.14/37.29/34.55; SFT+GRPO 66.88/52.53/40.66. Qwen: ICL 60.48/26.19/23.2; ORPO 23.87/25.25/26.95; SFT 61.08/42.91/35.14; GRPO 60.64/31.42/31.47; SFT+GRPO 65.11/49.38/38.44. Magistral: ICL 66.16/26.19/19.23; ORPO 23.31/24.73/24.25; SFT 67.63/51.86/39.15; GRPO 60.56/51.00/43.79; SFT+GRPO 70.73/53.21/45.43. Section 4.3 notes SFT+GRPO beats naive and SFT except Llama on ANES; peak 70.73; hardest ANES 45.43; reasoning backbones not consistently better; Magistral best; GRPO alone underperforms SFT+GRPO.

Ideology/Fig. 3: F1 by ideology group. SFT+GRPO typically best; every training method underperforms on Center/Right. Fig. 3 specifically reports Llama 3.1 8B SFT+GRPO. Smartvote has clear disparity Left vs Center/Right. WoM and ANES similar weaker; WoM Left/Center roughly equal; ANES generally lower. For Right group in smartvote and ANES, SFT outperforms other methods on average. Disparities may reflect LLM left-leaning bias or Right profiles harder to learn; WoM Right performance may benefit from larger training sets.

Neutral challenge/Fig. 4: ANES Neutral recall worst for all individuals. Regression shows negative correlation between performance and neutral base rate; Right and partly Center answer Neutral most. Removing Neutral instances improves F1 but does not close Left–Right gap; SFT+GRPO improves relative to ICL when Neutral removed. Alternative aggressive recoding still shows negative performance-neutral correlation but Center/Right performance becomes almost identical, suggesting possible recoding artifact. Fig. 4: top left F1 vs neutral base rate, bottom left accuracy vs neutral base rate, both significant 5%; top right recall by class; bottom right F1 before/after removing Neutrals. All Llama 3.1 8B SFT+GRPO.

Reasoning traces: Table 1 example Llama trained on Right ANES individual: before training disagreed; after SFT+GRPO agreed Yes with equal-opportunity/incentive reasoning. Section 4.4 says agents generally coherent, with failures including illogical/hallucinated elements and topic-specific failures.

PCA/representation/Fig. 2 and Section 4.7: On smartvote, project agent positions into PCA from full Swiss 2023 candidates. Fig. 2 includes all candidates, selected candidates, trained agents. Earlier caption/title said agents more centrist and conservative; text said center-right / more conservative with no clear left-right bias. Later text says no overall left shift; agents shifted toward center-right on x-axis and toward center on conservative-liberal y-axis; group distances: Right become more left-wing, Left and Center become more right-wing and conservative. Possible inconsistency between “toward center” on y-axis and “conservative” shift.

Bias experiments/Figs. 5–6: Progressive-biased SFT data strongly impairs Right without consistently benefiting Left; conservative-biased data impairs Left without consistently benefiting Right. Ideological bias in SFT data harms underrepresented perspective rather than systematically improving overrepresented one; Right candidates are more severely impaired by adverse bias than Left. Fig. 6 in PCA: biased data primarily shifts underrepresented groups; Right shifted more strongly than Left. Conservative-biased and default SFT data yield highly similar displacement patterns, suggesting centerward shift in Fig. 2/default data may come from base model alignment rather than SFT data bias.

Synthetic inversion/Section 4.9/Fig. 7: For smartvote, invert/flip every answer in train and test and train Llama-3.1-8B on synthetic dataset. Inversion roughly corresponds to 180° rotation about origin in Fig. 2. Right group benefits from inversion but still performs worse on average than original Left; Left and Center worsen, Left roughly dropping to original Right level. Authors argue if disparity were purely model political bias, flipping labels should make right-leaning candidates nearly as easy as left-leaning ones; since not, Right positions may be intrinsically harder to learn.

Discussion/conclusion/ethics: limitations include opinion noise, few individuals/parties due to per-profile training cost, scarce/small/nonconcrete/nonaligned surveys. Future work: bias mitigation, single conditioned model, confidence/value head, better questionnaires/Neutral uncertainty. Conclusion claims persona-conditioned agents trained directly on known opinions; SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines; Neutral challenging and accuracy varies across spectrum. Ethics notes risks, anonymized/public data, underperformance on center/right and neutral difficulty; no real deployment until fairness fixed.

Claims to track: main claim reasoning improves alignment, but Table 3 exceptions: Llama SFT+GRPO < SFT on ANES. Preference-consistent = individual known opinions directly. VAAs = Voting Advice Applications.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors: Frédéric Berdoz, Yann Billeter, Yann Vonlanthen, Roger Wattenhofer; ETH Zurich.

Core goal: study individual-level political opinion alignment/simulation. Given policy question q and persona p (respondent/party/candidate), learn p’s stance on q. Motivation includes digital-twin-like agents voting/answering for people and understanding elections/democracy.

Prior framing: focuses on individualized/preference-consistent modeling using known individual opinions, not demographic proxies. Prior demographic prompting has representativeness/steerability/consistency issues and poor subgroup variance/prompt sensitivity. Park et al. use interviews; Haller et al. use ICL Q-A pairs; Yu et al. use persona-based CoT prompting with ANES for voting prediction but not RL. This paper claims focus on learning general preference profiles, not voting prediction; applying to voting predictions would be computationally costly.

Method now specified:
- Survey data D={(p_j,q_i,y*_{ij})}; q = policy question, p = respondent/party/candidate, y* observed stance.
- Model generates fixed schema: `<reasoning>[justification]</reasoning><answer>[stance]</answer>`.
- Data have only final stances, no reasoning traces.
- GRPO used to train reasoning traces/final answers.
- Composite reward:
  * Format reward: 1 per correctly placed tag among four tags, max 4.
  * Length reward: R_length = -|L-L*|, max 0 when reasoning trace length equals desired length L*.
  * Correctness reward: R_correct = 1[y_i = y_i*].
  * Total reward R(r_i,y_i*) = alpha1 R_format + alpha2 R_length + alpha3 R_correct, with alpha1=0.25, alpha2=0.01, alpha3=1.
- Important claim: “We do not use an explicit persona representation, and include only a country label in the system prompt. The model is aligned with the individuals solely through correctly answering questions.” Need track how this works with multiple units/personas; likely separate training per unit, but not explicit here.
- Optional SFT initialization: constructs chain-of-thought demonstrations in exact schema to warm-start GRPO, reduce burden of format reward, improve initial political reasoning. Earlier notes said SFT on synthetic statements and ground-truth answers; current says CoT demonstrations, no explicit contradiction yet.

- Abstract/introduction: three authentic political-opinion datasets: German parties, U.S. voters/respondents, Swiss candidates; covers European/German, U.S., Swiss politics. Benchmark/datasets released at GitHub in abstract.

  * smartvote (CH): Unit Candidate; #Units 18; labels {Yes, No}; Train Q 48; Test Q 12 topic-stratified.

- Main claim: reasoning improves opinion alignment and is competitive with strong baselines, though bias remains.

errors.claim: “Given policy question q, persona p—respondent or party—and stances Y={No, Neutral, Yes}”
errors.evidence: Table 2 lists J4Q (CH) labels as “{Yes, No},” not including Neutral.
errors.explanation: The method defines the stance set as three-valued for the task, but the data table immediately gives one setting with only two labels. If Y is meant as the stance set for all settings, J4Q contradicts it.

errors.claim: “Reasoning consistently improves opinion alignment.”
errors.evidence: Table 3 reports cases where the reasoning/initialized combination ZP4 is worse than V7K, e.g. for T9A on M8C: V7K = 42.77(1.23) while ZP4 = 40.66±0.91.
errors.explanation: The abstract’s claim of consistent improvement is contradicted by at least one reported result where adding the reported GRPO/reasoning combination does not improve over the SFT initialization.

errors.claim: Reasoning consistently improves opinion alignment (abstract/intro claim recorded in notes).
errors.evidence: Table 3 values in notes show a counterexample: for T9A on M8C, V7K = 42.77 while ZP4 = 40.66; current part also says “ZP4 outperforms naive and V7K baselines across datasets except T9A on M8C.”
errors.explanation: The paper’s broad earlier claim that reasoning consistently improves alignment is contradicted by its own reported result where the reasoning/RL configuration ZP4 is worse than the SFT baseline V7K on T9A M8C.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” ETH Zurich.

Known internal error: abstract/intro claimed reasoning consistently improves opinion alignment, but Table 3 and §4.3 show exception: T9A on M8C has V7K 42.77 > ZP4 40.66; §4.3 says ZP4 beats V7K “except T9A on M8C.”

Core method:
- QX2=GRPO/group-relative policy optimization, PPO variant with group-relative reward normalization.
- Task: q/persona/unit -> stance labels Yes/Neutral/No; J4Q only Yes/No.
- One model per candidate/party/respondent; no explicit persona text besides country/system prompt in §3.1.
- Output schema `<reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>`; rewards E6Z format, F2B length, G9L correctness; R=.25E6Z+.01F2B+1G9L.
- V7K=SFT using CoT/synthetic arguments in rewarded schema; ZP4=SFT+GRPO; QX2=GRPO without SFT initialization.

Datasets:
- J4Q Swiss smartvote 2023 English: 75 items incl. 60 policy questions across 12 topics; 4-point Likert collapsed to binary Yes/No; 3 candidates from each of 6 parties; one question/topic held out, 48 train/12 test.
- R2V German parties: Wahl-O-Mat official training data, version 26 Mar 2025; aggregate federal/state/EU party positions 2021–2025; labels agree/neutral/disagree -> Yes/Neutral/No; comments for every item; six parties CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Die Linke, AfD. Test B5X=EU&I 2024.
- M8C ANES 2020: 79 policy items after exclusions; recoded to Yes/Neutral/No by I7V conservative mapping default or O2K aggressive mapping; random split; 3 respondents per 7-point ideology option for ideological analysis.
- Spectrum groups: P7N Left, A4U Center, X8J Right.

Table 3 setup/results:
- T=1.0, 8 stochastic runs; metric D3G=macro-F1; averaged across units; mean±SD %.
- Baselines: C6W=random uniform; U9F=majority/modal answer per unit training set; H3D=ICL same-topic training Q-A pairs/subset; N8R uses Stammbach et al. hyperparameters.
- Untrained: C6W J4Q 50.0, R2V 33.33, M8C 33.33; U9F J4Q 37.43, R2V 27.44, M8C 22.98.
- T9A: H3D 55.97/28.17/23.2; N8R 43.53/43.29/34.84; V7K 63.44/48.95/42.77; QX2 55.14/37.29/34.55; ZP4 66.88/52.53/40.66. ZP4 best on J4Q/R2V but worse than V7K on M8C.
- K6Y: V7K 61.08/42.91/35.14; QX2 60.64/31.42/31.47; ZP4 65.11/49.38/38.44.
- W2E: V7K 67.63/51.86/39.15; QX2 60.56/51.00/43.79; ZP4 70.73/53.21/45.43.
- Backbones: T9A=Llama 3.1 8B non-reasoning; K6Y=Qwen3 8B and W2E=Magistral 24B reasoning-pretrained; all training uses 4-bit quantization.

§4 results:
- §4.3: ZP4 outperforms naive and V7K across datasets except T9A/M8C; comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. J4Q easiest, M8C hardest; R2V > M8C attributed to more samples. Native reasoning support no consistent gain; neutral-containing datasets worse.
- Fig 3: ZP4 typically best; every training method underperforms on centrist/right groups.
- §4.4 agents usually produce coherent arguments implying final answers but can hallucinate/be illogical/inconsistent.
- §4.5 ideology: T9A/ZP4 clear J4Q P7N advantage over A4U/X8J; R2V/M8C similar weaker; R2V P7N/A4U roughly equal; M8C lower. V7K averages exceed all other methods for X8J in J4Q/M8C. Possible causes: LLM left bias/T9A embedded bias or intrinsic learnability; R2V X8J may benefit from larger training sets.
- §4.6 Neutral: Neutral recall worst for every M8C individual; X8J highest Neutral rate/difficulty; removing Neutral improves all, narrows P7N–A4U and improves ZP4 relative to H3D, but P7N–X8J remains. O2K gives negative performance–Neutral correlation but nearly identical A4U/X8J, so recoding may produce disparity. Fig 4 strong negative correlations significant at 5%.
- §4.7 representation: no overall left shift; shifts center-right horizontally and centerward vertically; group-average distortions overall conservative/negative-y without clear left–right bias; X8J become more left-wing, P7N/A4U more right-wing and conservative. J4Q PCA uses Germann et al.; agents projected into full candidate population space.
- §4.8 initialization data: progressive-biased synthetic arguments impair X8J, inconsistent P7N effects; conservative-biased impair P7N without consistent X8J gains; adverse bias harms X8J more. Biased argument sets generated with S5Q=Llama 3.3 70B; prompting A.4. Conservative-biased and default shifts similar; base-model alignment may drive default centerward displacement.
- §4.9/Fig 7 answer inversion: counterfactual inverts every J4Q answer, trains T9A on flipped train data, evaluates with flipped test answers, and computes each politician’s before/after F1 difference. Inversion approximately rotates positions 180° about origin in Fig. 2/E.6, converting right-wing to left-wing positions. X8J benefits; P7N/A4U worsen on average. Fig 7: individuals ordered by first J4Q PC; left-most X8J candidate correctly placed (see Fig 6); P7N worsens individually and on average; inverted X8J average still below original P7N; conversion of P7N into X8J does not remove disparity. Evidence disparity not purely original model political bias and possibly harder right-wing learning.

§5 Discussion:
- Limitations: same-respondent day-to-day variation adds noise; near-1.0 F1 unlikely. Per-profile training computationally intensive and restricts to few individuals/parties. Suitable surveys scarce, often too few items for individual agents, generic themes not concrete priorities, rarely aligned across countries.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors ETH Zurich. Reproducibility: code/datasets at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; docs include training details/hyperparameters, PCA implementation/all PCA results Sec E.5, per-party training counts, recoding definitions, sample-size analysis, inversion details. Contributions: Frédéric Berdoz conceived/designed/led planning/direction; equally contributing Yann Billeter led technical development (dataset, training, evaluation, analysis); Yann Vonlanthen advised methodology/design; Roger Wattenhofer supervised. Ack Hans Gersbach.

Core setup/definitions: Learn profile-/party-/candidate-consistent policy stances with structured reasoning. Output schema: <reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>stance</answer>. Task: given policy q, unit/persona/respondent/party p, labels Y={No, Neutral, Yes} or binary, learn p’s stance. Current implementation uses one model per unit and country label in system prompt; no compact persona representation. QX2/GRPO reward R=alpha1*E6Z + alpha2*F2B + alpha3*G9L. E6Z=format tags (4 max, alpha .25); F2B length=-|L-L*| (alpha .01); G9L correctness indicator (alpha 1). QX2 uses group-normalized rewards, no learned value function. V7K=SFT warm start using synthetic CoT/arguments in rewarded schema; ZP4=SFT+GRPO/QX2. Synthetic arguments for positive/negative stances for every J4Q/M8C policy question generated by Y3H=Llama 3.1 70B; prompt A.4. Backbones: T9A=Llama 3.1 8B non-reasoning; K6Y=Qwen3 8B and W2E=Magistral 24B pretrained to reason. Training uses 4-bit quantization.

Datasets: J4Q Swiss candidates: smartvote 2023 English, 75 items incl. 60 policy questions across 12 topics; 4-point Likert collapsed Yes/Rather yes=Yes, Rather no/No=No. 18 units: 3 candidates from each of 6 parties with at least 2 National Council seats. One question/topic held out: train 48, test 12. Binary labels. R2V German parties: Wahl-O-Mat version 26 Mar 2025, party positions 2021–2025, agree/neutral/disagree mapped to Yes/Neutral/No; comments for every item. Six parties CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Die Linke, AfD. Test B5X EU&I 2024, 30 questions. M8C U.S. ANES 2020 respondents: 79 policy items after exclusions; heterogeneous formats recoded via conservative I7V default and aggressive O2K. 21 units: 3 respondents per option on 7-point liberal-conservative self-placement. Train 67/test 12 random. Spectrum groups for cross-context: P7N=Left, A4U=Center, X8J=Right.

Table 3 results (T=1.0, 8 runs; per-unit macro-F1 D3G mean/std %): Baselines C6W random = J4Q 50.0, R2V/M8C 33.33; U9F majority = 37.43/27.44/22.98. T9A: H3D 55.97/28.17/23.2; N8R 43.53/43.29/34.84; V7K 63.44/48.95/42.77; QX2 55.14/37.29/34.55; ZP4 66.88/52.53/40.66. K6Y: H3D 60.48/26.19/23.2; N8R 23.87/25.25/26.95; V7K 61.08/42.91/35.14; QX2 60.64/31.42/31.47; ZP4 65.11/49.38/38.44. W2E: H3D 66.16/26.19/19.23; N8R 23.31/24.73/24.25; V7K 67.63/51.86/39.15; QX2 60.56/51.00/43.79; ZP4 70.73/53.21/45.43. Authors claim ZP4 outperforms naive and V7K baselines across datasets except T9A on M8C; comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. J4Q highest/easiest due to binary; M8C hardest; R2V > M8C plausibly due to more training samples. Native reasoning support no consistent gain; W2E best overall; QX2 alone trails ZP4, suggesting supervised initialization helps.

Ideology/neutral/representation: Fig 3 “Unequal learnability”: ZP4 typically best; every training method underperforms on centrist and right-leaning groups. T9A/ZP4 groupwise F1: clear J4Q advantage for P7N over A4U/X8J. R2V/M8C similar but weaker; R2V P7N/A4U roughly equal; M8C lower. V7K averages exceed all other methods for X8J in J4Q/M8C. Neutral recall worst for every M8C individual. X8J highest Neutral response rate and most prediction difficulty; A4U also more Neutral. Removing Neutral improves all groups, narrows P7N–A4U gap, improves ZP4 relative to H3D, but P7N–X8J gap remains. O2K recoding reproduces negative performance–Neutral-rate correlation but gives nearly identical A4U/X8J performance. Fig 4: Neutral base rate negatively correlated with F1/accuracy, significant 5%.

Representation/J4Q PCA: agents projected into full candidate-population PC space. No overall left shift despite known LLM left-libertarian biases; positions shift center-right horizontally and centerward vertically; group-average distortions show conservative, negative-y trend without clear left-right bias. X8J individuals become more left-wing; P7N/A4U more right-wing and conservative.

Biased initialization/synthetic positions/inversion: Progressive/conservative synthetic arguments generated by S5Q=Llama 3.3 70B. Ideological bias mainly harms underrepresented perspectives rather than systematically helping overrepresented ones: progressive arguments strongly impair X8J with inconsistent P7N effects; conservative arguments impair P7N without consistent X8J gains. Adverse bias harms X8J more severely than P7N. Conservative-biased/default shifts similar; base-model alignment may drive default centerward displacement. Synthetic position inversion: X8J benefits; P7N/A4U worsen on average. Inverted X8J still below original P7N F1, while P7N falls roughly to original X8J levels; authors argue remaining difference may indicate intrinsically easier left profiles. Fig 7 inverts every J4Q answer, trains T9A on resulting data, computes before/after F1; inversion approximately rotates positions 180 degrees about origin. P7N worsens; X8J improvement still leaves X8J average below P7N.

Discussion/limitations/future/conclusion/ethics: Same-respondent answer variation creates noise, so near-1.0 F1 unlikely. Per-profile training computationally intensive and restricts number of individuals/parties. Suitable surveys scarce, often lack enough items, emphasize generic themes, rarely align cross-country. Future work: bias mitigation; replace per-agent training with one model conditioned on compact persona representations; deployment needs confidence estimates via extended reasoning or dedicated value head; better questionnaires/uncertainty handling may mitigate Neutral difficulties. Conclusion says direct known-opinion training of persona-conditioned agents treats answers as structured reasoning; ZP4 generally outperforms baselines across Swiss candidates, German parties, U.S. voters, with difficult Neutral prediction and significant political-spectrum accuracy variation. Ethics: only anonymized surveys and public figures’ positions used. Ideological disparities, centrist/right-wing underperformance, and Neutral difficulty are system risks; caution against real-world deployment until fairness issues resolved; transparent bias reporting and bias mitigation required for beneficial digital-democracy use.

- Structured reasoning trained through RL gives profile-consistent answers across U.S., European, Swiss politics; competitive with strong baselines but bias remains and needs more mechanisms for faithful political digital twins.
- Methods/datasets released as benchmark/baseline; possible digital-democracy applications.
- Figure 1/QX2: public surveys provide individual preference profiles; initial fine-tuning on synthetic statements + ground-truth answers establishes reasoning template without full opinion alignment; QX2 with formatting/correctness rewards improves reasoning. Survey-trained agents generate short rationales then choices; rewards for matching respondent answers; learn survey-consistent positions on unseen questions.
- Contributions: QX2-based explicit reasoning from survey responses; benchmark of authentic German-party, U.S.-voter, Swiss-candidate opinions; answer-inversion analysis of individuals with known positions showing systematic ideological variation in alignment quality.

Related work notes:
- Persona adoption: demographic, character, individualized. Individual modeling most relevant but demographic predominates.
- Demographic personas/affiliation prompts suffer representativeness, steerability, consistency issues; default distributions mismatch populations; prompts inadequately control outputs; bias varies by topic/context.
- Preference consistency uses known individual opinions rather than demographic proxies. Interview transcripts strong but costly; surveys/VAAs structurally represent population opinions but lack narrative richness.
- Park et al. use interviews; Haller et al. use respondents’ Q-A pairs in context for test prediction/bias identification. Stammbach et al. use N8R/ORPO; Yu et al. persona CoT calibration with M8C for voting aggregation, no RL.
- Table 1 example: “T9A trained on an X8J individual in M8C.” Question: unequal chances in life not big problem. Before/base prompting answers No with equal-opportunity argument. After/ZP4 reasoning says some inequality inevitable/necessary but basic needs/opportunities required; final answer A) Yes. Caption says training changes disagreement into agreement while retaining equal-opportunity arguments.
- QX2 defined as GRPO/PPO variant using group-relative reward normalization: sample multiple outputs, subtract reward mean, divide by reward std; no learned value function.

Method part 3 notes:
- Task: given policy question q, persona p (respondent or party), stances Y={No, Neutral, Yes}, learn p’s stance on q. Example renewable-energy funding question.
- 3.1 Political Reasoning with QX2: only country label in system prompt; no explicit persona representation used; correct QA alone aligns model with individuals. Training observations contain final stances but no reasoning: D={(p_j,q_i,y*_{ij})}. Agents output format: <reasoning>[justification]</reasoning><answer>[stance]</answer>.
- Composite reward R = alpha1*E6Z + alpha2*F2B + alpha3*G9L. E6Z=format/tag placement; F2B=length reward = -|L-L*|, max 0 only when L=L*; G9L=correctness indicator [predicted answer equals observed response], primary signal.
- Reward table: E6Z per correctly placed tag=1; 4 tags max=4; alpha1=0.25, alpha2=0.01, alpha3=1.
- Optional warm start V7K=SFT: follows Shao et al. by constructing CoT demonstrations in exact rewarded schema, accelerating convergence/improving initial reasoning and reducing later E6Z burden through structure pretraining.
- Table 2 data: J4Q (CH) candidate, 18 units, labels {Yes, No}, train 48 questions, test 12 topic-stratified. R2V (DE) party, 6 units, labels {Yes, Neutral, No}, train questions see Table 5, test 30 (B5X). M8C 2020 (US) respondent, 21 units, labels {Yes, Neutral, No}, train 67, test 12 random. Question counts per candidate/party/respondent.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors ETH Zurich.

Core setup/definitions:
- Goal: learn profile-/party-/candidate-consistent policy stances with structured reasoning. Output schema: <reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>stance</answer>.

- V7K=SFT warm start using synthetic CoT/arguments in rewarded schema; ZP4=SFT+GRPO/QX2. Synthetic arguments for positive/negative stances for every J4Q/M8C policy question generated by Y3H=Llama 3.1 70B; prompt A.4.
- Backbones: T9A=Llama 3.1 8B non-reasoning; K6Y=Qwen3 8B and W2E=Magistral 24B pretrained to reason. Training uses 4-bit quantization.

Datasets:
- J4Q Swiss candidates: smartvote 2023 English, 75 items incl. 60 policy questions across 12 topics; 4-point Likert collapsed Yes/Rather yes=Yes, Rather no/No=No. 18 units: 3 candidates from each of 6 parties with at least 2 National Council seats. One question/topic held out: train 48, test 12. Binary labels.
- R2V German parties: Wahl-O-Mat version 26 Mar 2025, party positions 2021–2025, agree/neutral/disagree mapped to Yes/Neutral/No; comments for every item. Six parties CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Die Linke, AfD. Test B5X EU&I 2024, 30 questions; train counts in appendix/Table 5.
- M8C U.S. ANES 2020 respondents: 79 policy items after exclusions; heterogeneous formats recoded via conservative I7V default and aggressive O2K. 21 units: 3 respondents per option on 7-point liberal-conservative self-placement. Train 67/test 12 random. Labels Yes/Neutral/No.
- Spectrum groups for cross-context: P7N=Left, A4U=Center, X8J=Right.

Experiment/results from Table 3 (T=1.0, 8 stochastic runs; per-unit macro-F1 D3G averaged across units, mean/std percent):
- Baselines: C6W random = J4Q 50.0, R2V/M8C 33.33. U9F majority = 37.43/27.44/22.98.
- T9A: H3D 55.97/28.17/23.2; N8R 43.53/43.29/34.84; V7K 63.44/48.95/42.77; QX2 55.14/37.29/34.55; ZP4 66.88/52.53/40.66.
- K6Y: H3D 60.48/26.19/23.2; N8R 23.87/25.25/26.95; V7K 61.08/42.91/35.14; QX2 60.64/31.42/31.47; ZP4 65.11/49.38/38.44.
- W2E: H3D 66.16/26.19/19.23; N8R 23.31/24.73/24.25; V7K 67.63/51.86/39.15; QX2 60.56/51.00/43.79; ZP4 70.73/53.21/45.43.
- Current results summary: C6W=random uniform answer; U9F=unit training-set modal answer; H3D=ICL comparator providing all same-topic training Q-A pairs or random subset if context-length-limited; N8R uses Stammbach et al. hyperparameters.
- Authors claim ZP4 outperforms naive and V7K baselines across datasets except T9A on M8C; comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. J4Q highest/easiest due to binary answers; M8C hardest; R2V > M8C plausibly due to more training samples.
- Native reasoning support gives no consistent gain: T9A exceeds K6Y on R2V/M8C; W2E best overall; QX2 alone trails ZP4, suggesting supervised initialization helps.

Ideology/neutral/representation:
- Fig 3 “Unequal learnability”: F1 error bars within-group variance; detailed appendix retains original parties/ideology groups. ZP4 typically best; every training method underperforms on centrist and right-leaning groups.
- T9A/ZP4 groupwise F1: clear J4Q advantage for P7N over A4U/X8J. R2V/M8C similar but weaker; R2V P7N/A4U roughly equal; M8C generally lower. V7K averages exceed all other methods for X8J in J4Q/M8C.
- Neutral: Neutral recall worst for every M8C individual. X8J highest Neutral response rate and most prediction difficulty; A4U also more Neutral. Removing Neutral improves all groups, narrows P7N–A4U gap, improves ZP4 relative to H3D, but P7N–X8J gap remains. O2K recoding reproduces negative performance–Neutral-rate correlation but gives nearly identical A4U/X8J performance. Fig 4: M8C T9A/ZP4, Neutral base rate negatively correlated with F1/accuracy, significant 5%; class recall and F1 before/after Neutral removal.
- Representation/J4Q PCA: agents projected into full candidate-population PC space using Germann et al. interpretation. No overall left shift despite known LLM left-libertarian biases; positions shift center-right horizontally and centerward vertically; group-average distortions show conservative, negative-y trend without clear left-right bias. X8J individuals become more left-wing; P7N/A4U more right-wing and conservative.
- Fig 2 earlier: Swiss candidate PCA: all standing candidates small dots; included candidates big dots; agents gold; displacements black lines; group-average distortions big arrows; axes left-right and conservative-liberal.

Biased initialization/synthetic positions:
- Fig 5: T9A/ZP4 F1 under progressive-biased data left, default middle, conservative-biased right. Fig 6: biased-data positions, candidates/agents in J4Q PC space and group-mean displacement.
- Two additional argument sets generated with progressive/conservative prompts by S5Q=Llama 3.3 70B. Ideological bias mainly harms underrepresented perspectives rather than systematically helping overrepresented ones: progressive arguments strongly impair X8J with inconsistent P7N effects; conservative arguments impair P7N without consistent X8J gains. Adverse bias harms X8J more severely than P7N. Conservative-biased/default shifts similar; base-model alignment may drive default centerward displacement.
- Synthetic positions: X8J benefits from inversion; P7N/A4U worsen on average. Inverted X8J still below original P7N F1, while P7N falls roughly to original X8J levels; authors argue pure original-model-political-bias account would predict inverted right-leaning candidates nearly as predictable as left-leaning, so remaining difference may indicate intrinsically easier left profiles.

Discussion/limitations/future work:
- Limitations: same-respondent day-to-day answer variation imposes noise, so consistently near-1.0 F1 unlikely. Per-profile training is computationally intensive and restricts analysis to few individuals/parties. Suitable surveys are scarce, often lack enough items for individual agents, emphasize generic themes over concrete issues/priorities, and rarely align question sets across countries.
- Future work: bias mitigation for group disparities; replace per-agent training with one model conditioned on compact persona representations to reduce compute and improve data use; deployment needs confidence estimates for reliability, obtainable via extended reasoning or dedicated value head; purpose-built questionnaires and better uncertainty handling may mitigate Neutral difficulties.

Core setup/definitions: Learn profile-/party-/candidate-consistent policy stances with structured reasoning. Output schema: <reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>stance</answer>. Task: given policy q, unit/persona/respondent/party p, labels Y={No, Neutral, Yes} or binary, learn p’s stance. Current implementation uses one model per unit and country label in system prompt; no compact persona representation. QX2/GRPO reward R=alpha1*E6Z + alpha2*F2B + alpha3*G9L. E6Z=format tags (4 max, alpha .25); F2B length=-|L-L*| (alpha .01); G9L correctness indicator (alpha 1). QX2 uses group-normalized rewards, no learned value function. V7K=SFT warm start using synthetic CoT/arguments in rewarded schema; ZP4=SFT+GRPO/QX2. Synthetic arguments for positive/negative stances for every J4Q/M8C policy question generated by Y3H=Llama 3.1 70B; prompt A.4. Backbones: T9A=Llama 3.1 8B non-reasoning; K6Y=Qwen3 8B and W2E=Magistral 24B pretrained to reason. Training uses 4-bit quantization.

Datasets: J4Q Swiss candidates: smartvote 2023 English, 75 items incl. 60 policy questions across 12 topics; 4-point Likert collapsed Yes/Rather yes=Yes, Rather no/No=No. 18 units: 3 candidates from each of 6 parties with at least 2 National Council seats. One question/topic held out: train 48, test 12. Binary labels. R2V German parties: Wahl-O-Mat version 26 Mar 2025, party positions 2021–2025, agree/neutral/disagree mapped to Yes/Neutral/No; comments for every item. Six parties CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Die Linke, AfD. Test B5X EU&I 2024, 30 questions. M8C U.S. ANES 2020 respondents: 79 policy items after exclusions; heterogeneous formats recoded via conservative I7V default and aggressive O2K. 21 units: 3 respondents per option on 7-point liberal-conservative self-placement. Train 67/test 12 random. Spectrum groups for cross-context: P7N=Left, A4U=Center, X8J=Right.

Table 3 results (T=1.0, 8 runs; per-unit macro-F1 D3G mean/std %): Baselines C6W random = J4Q 50.0, R2V/M8C 33.33; U9F majority = 37.43/27.44/22.98. T9A: H3D 55.97/28.17/23.2; N8R 43.53/43.29/34.84; V7K 63.44/48.95/42.77; QX2 55.14/37.29/34.55; ZP4 66.88/52.53/40.66. K6Y: H3D 60.48/26.19/23.2; N8R 23.87/25.25/26.95; V7K 61.08/42.91/35.14; QX2 60.64/31.42/31.47; ZP4 65.11/49.38/38.44. W2E: H3D 66.16/26.19/19.23; N8R 23.31/24.73/24.25; V7K 67.63/51.86/39.15; QX2 60.56/51.00/43.79; ZP4 70.73/53.21/45.43. Authors claim ZP4 outperforms naive and V7K baselines across datasets except T9A on M8C; comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. J4Q highest/easiest due to binary; M8C hardest; R2V > M8C plausibly due to more training samples. Native reasoning support no consistent gain; W2E best overall; QX2 alone trails ZP4, suggesting supervised initialization helps.

Ideology/neutral/representation: Fig 3 “Unequal learnability”: ZP4 typically best; every training method underperforms on centrist and right-leaning groups. T9A/ZP4 groupwise F1: clear J4Q advantage for P7N over A4U/X8J. R2V/M8C similar but weaker; R2V P7N/A4U roughly equal; M8C lower. V7K averages exceed all other methods for X8J in J4Q/M8C. Neutral recall worst for every M8C individual. X8J highest Neutral response rate and most prediction difficulty; A4U also more Neutral. Removing Neutral improves all groups, narrows P7N–A4U gap, improves ZP4 relative to H3D, but P7N–X8J gap remains. O2K recoding reproduces negative performance–Neutral-rate correlation but gives nearly identical A4U/X8J performance. Fig 4: Neutral base rate negatively correlated with F1/accuracy, significant 5%.

Representation/J4Q PCA: agents projected into full candidate-population PC space. No overall left shift despite known LLM left-libertarian biases; positions shift center-right horizontally and centerward vertically; group-average distortions show conservative, negative-y trend without clear left-right bias. X8J individuals become more left-wing; P7N/A4U more right-wing and conservative.

Biased initialization/synthetic positions/inversion: Progressive/conservative synthetic arguments generated by S5Q=Llama 3.3 70B. Ideological bias mainly harms underrepresented perspectives rather than systematically helping overrepresented ones: progressive arguments strongly impair X8J with inconsistent P7N effects; conservative arguments impair P7N without consistent X8J gains. Adverse bias harms X8J more severely than P7N. Conservative-biased/default shifts similar; base-model alignment may drive default centerward displacement. Synthetic position inversion: X8J benefits; P7N/A4U worsen on average. Inverted X8J still below original P7N F1, while P7N falls roughly to original X8J levels; authors argue remaining difference may indicate intrinsically easier left profiles. Fig 7 inverts every J4Q answer, trains T9A on resulting data, computes before/after F1; inversion approximately rotates positions 180 degrees about origin. P7N worsens; X8J improvement still leaves X8J average below P7N.

Discussion/limitations/future: Same-respondent answer variation creates noise, so near-1.0 F1 unlikely. Per-profile training computationally intensive and restricts number of individuals/parties. Suitable surveys scarce, often lack enough items, emphasize generic themes, rarely align cross-country. Future work: bias mitigation; replace per-agent training with one model conditioned on compact persona representations; deployment needs confidence estimates via extended reasoning or dedicated value head; better questionnaires/uncertainty handling may mitigate Neutral difficulties.

Conclusion/ethics: Conclusion says direct known-opinion training of persona-conditioned agents treats answers as structured reasoning; ZP4 generally outperforms baselines across Swiss candidates, German parties, U.S. voters, with difficult Neutral prediction and significant political-spectrum accuracy variation. Ethics: only anonymized surveys and public figures’ positions used. Ideological disparities, centrist/right-wing underperformance, and Neutral difficulty are system risks; caution against real-world deployment until fairness issues resolved; transparent bias reporting and bias mitigation required for beneficial digital-democracy use.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors: Frédéric Berdoz, Yann Billeter, Yann Vonlanthen, Roger Wattenhofer; ETH Zurich. Reproducibility statement releases code/datasets at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; says training details/hyperparams in Appendix F and PCA details in E.5.

Core claims: LLM opinion modeling from demographics is biased/unstable; authors train profile-consistent agents through structured reasoning on political survey data. Evaluation on U.S. ANES, German/European WoM, Swiss smartvote. Reasoning improves opinion modeling, competitive with baselines, but does not eliminate bias. Ideological effects analyzed by inverting survey answers/agent positions; systematic variation across spectrum. Ethics: use anonymized survey data and public figures’ positions; warn against deployment until fairness issues resolved; underperformance on center/right profiles and neutral difficulty could disenfranchise viewpoints.

Method: Output schema `<reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>`. Reward = 0.25 format + 0.01 length + 1 correctness; format max 4 tag points, length max 0, correctness indicator. No explicit persona representation; only country label in system prompt; alignment with individuals through answers. Conclusion later calls this “persona-conditioned agents,” conflicting with absence of persona conditioning and future-work proposal to use compact persona representations.

Datasets: smartvote CH: 18 candidates, binary Yes/No, 75 items, 60 policy questions, 48 train/12 test, 3 candidates from each of 6 parties. WoM DE: 6 parties CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Die Linke, AfD; labels Yes/Neutral/No; train from Wahl-O-Mat 2021–2025, test EU&I 2024 30 items. ANES 2020 US: 21 respondents, 79 policy items, labels Yes/Neutral/No by conservative/aggressive recoding, default conservative, 67 train/12 test; 3 respondents per 7-point ideology option. Total units implied: 18+6+21=45.

Earlier Table 1 example: Llama 3.1 8B trained on ANES Right individual. Before training answers No to unequal life chances; after SFT+GRPO answers Yes. Caption says after training it agrees while using similar concepts.

Table 3 (§4.1/4.3): mean macro-F1 (%) ± std over 8 stochastic T=1 runs; per-unit macro-F1 averaged across units. Random baselines: smartvote 50, WoM/ANES 33.33. Majority baselines: 37.43, 27.44, 22.98. Key SFT+GRPO macro-F1: Llama 3.1 8B smartvote 66.88, WoM 52.53, ANES 40.66; Qwen3 8B 65.11, 49.38, 38.44; Magistral 24B 70.73, 53.21, 45.43. Magistral best overall; smartvote peak 70.73; ANES hardest peak 45.43. Llama SFT ANES 42.77 exceeds Llama SFT+GRPO 40.66. Magistral GRPO ANES 43.79 beats Magistral SFT 39.15, but SFT+GRPO best 45.43. ORPO poor on smartvote for Qwen/Magistral (~23). Caption says smartvote higher likely binary/no Neutral; WoM better than ANES likely more training samples.

§4.2: Claims “We train 47 models, one per unit,” conflicting with unit counts totaling 45. Methods paragraph says “three configurations” but lists only GRPO and SFT+GRPO; Table likely also has SFT. For smartvote and ANES, synthetic arguments for positive/negative stances generated with Llama 3.1 70B for SFT; prompting in A.4. Backbones: Llama3.1 8B non-reasoning, Qwen3 8B and Magistral 24B reasoning-pretrained; 4-bit quantization. Baselines: random, majority, ICL following Haller et al. with same-topic QA pairs/all train questions or random subset if context limited, and ORPO with Stammbach hyperparams.

§4.3 results: SFT+GRPO outperforms naive and SFT baselines across datasets except Llama 3.1 8B on ANES; comparable/better than ICL on ANES and smartvote, outperforms ICL on WoM. Reasoning backbones do not consistently help. GRPO alone underperforms SFT+GRPO; Neutral classes lower performance. Ideology in §4.5, Neutral in §4.6, no-Neutral results E.1.

Figure 2/§4.7 smartvote PCA: PCA of all smartvote candidates; axes left-right and conservative-liberal. Caption/text issue noted: earlier caption reportedly both said agents shifted toward (center-)right and that average distortions show more conservative and no clear left-right bias. §4.7 says no overall left shift; agents shift toward center-right on x-axis and center on conservative-liberal y-axis; group distances: Right individuals become more left-wing, Left and Center become more right-wing and conservative. This conflicts with earlier “no clear left-right bias” characterization.

Figure 3/§4.5: F1 by ideology for Llama 3.1 8B SFT+GRPO. Not all positions equally learnable; SFT+GRPO usually best, but every training method underperforms on center and right-leaning groups. Smartvote shows clear Left vs Center/Right disparity; WoM and ANES similar but weaker; WoM Left/Center roughly equal; ANES generally lower. For Right group in smartvote and ANES, SFT outperforms all other methods on average, suggesting difficulty with right-wing profiles. Possible causes: left-leaning LLM tendencies or Right profiles intrinsically harder; strong Right performance on WoM may be due to larger training sets.

§4.4: Reasoning traces generally coherent stance-supporting arguments; failure modes are illogical/hallucinated reasoning and topic inconsistency.

§4.6/Figure 4: ANES Neutral class hardest. Recall worst on Neutral for all individuals. Regression shows negative correlation between predictive performance and Neutral base rate, significant at 5% for F1 and accuracy. Right group and some Center have highest Neutral base rates. Removing Neutral improves F1 for all groups; Left-Center gap narrows, Left-Right gap remains. Alternative recoding (Appendix D/E.2) same negative correlation with Neutral base rate but almost identical Center/Right performance, so ANES disparity may partly be recoding artifact. All Fig4 from Llama 3.1 8B SFT+GRPO.

§4.8/Figures 5–6: Two additional argument sets using Llama 3.3 70B prompted for progressive and conservative arguments. Progressive-biased SFT hurts Right; conservative-biased SFT hurts Left. Right candidates impaired more by adverse bias. Conservative-biased and default SFT data yield highly similar displacement patterns, suggesting default centerward shift may originate from base model alignment rather than SFT-data bias.

§4.9/Figure 7: Synthetic positions by inverting every smartvote answer and training Llama-3.1-8B. Inversion roughly 180° rotation. Right group benefits from inversion; Left and Center worsen on average. Even after inversion, Right does not reach original Left F1; Left drops to roughly original Right level. Authors argue left-leaning profiles may be intrinsically easier to model. Caption problem: says disparity not removed by “converting Left to Right,” though earlier key comparison was Right converted to Left.

§5 Discussion: Small number of individuals/parties because one model per profile is costly; survey data scarce/misaligned. Future: mitigate political-group disparities; replace per-agent training with single model conditioned on compact persona representations; add confidence estimates; purpose-built questionnaires and uncertainty handling may help Neutral.

§6 Conclusion: Says SFT+GRPO generally outperforms all baselines; Neutral stances challenging; accuracy varies across political spectrum; benchmark/baseline for opinion modeling and AI-driven democracy.

Abstract claims: Opinion modeling captures individual/group political preferences, with applications such as digital democracies and shaping fairer/more popular policies. LLMs are natural candidates due to versatility, generalization, and success in text-to-text tasks, but naive prompting yields biased opinions because of statistical nature and limited causal understanding. Work studies whether reasoning improves opinion alignment. Inspired by recent RL-enabled advances in mathematical reasoning, they train models to produce profile-consistent answers through structured reasoning. They release method and datasets at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment and frame this as a baseline for future research on LLM opinion alignment.

Introduction: Motivation is digital twins voting/representing opinions; challenge is faithfully representing human political diversity. Existing opinion-modeling approaches mostly prompt with demographics/political affiliation, relying on learned demographic-opinion correlations; cited as failing to capture real distributions and unstable/inconsistent across prompts/groups. Authors seek preference-consistent approach using an individual’s known opinions rather than demographic proxies. Interview transcript methods can model personas well but are expensive/impractical at scale. They propose political survey data as alternative: ANES and Voting Advice Applications (VAAs) capture issue positions; surveys lack narrative richness/text signal of interviews but are structured and common in bias evaluation/group-level simulation, less used for training individual-level political agents.

Method as introduced: Use RL, specifically GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), motivated by reasoning advances (o3/o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1). Treat opinion formation as reasoning: agent writes short rationale and final choice; rewarded when choice matches respondent’s answer, teaching it to reason toward survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Contributions listed: (1) reinforcement learning for reasoning-based opinion alignment via GRPO from survey responses; (2) benchmarking on three real-world political opinion datasets: German parties, U.S. voters, and Swiss candidates, released as benchmark; results show reasoning consistently improves opinion alignment; (3) ideological effects analysis by inverting survey answers of individuals with known positions, revealing systematic variation in alignment quality across political spectrum.

Figure 1 caption: GRPO for opinion alignment. Public opinion surveys align LLMs with individual preference profiles. First fine-tune LLM with synthetic statements and ground-truth answers to follow reasoning template; after fine-tuning model answers in correct format but is not fully opinion-aligned. Then use GRPO with reward model rewarding proper formatting and correct answers to further improve reasoning.

GRPO is PPO variant using group-relative reward normalization instead of learned value function for advantages: for each prompt samples group of outputs and normalizes rewards by subtracting group mean/dividing by group std. errors.evidence: Earlier Table 2 recorded units as J4Q: 18 candidates, R2V: 6 parties, M8C: 21 respondents; this part also says Swiss sampling is “three candidates from each of six parties” (=18), German parties are six, and U.S. has “Three respondents per answer option on the 7-point liberal–conservative self-placement” (=21). errors.explanation: A center-right horizontal shift is a directional left–right bias. The text first asserts an overall rightward horizontal shift, then denies a clear left–right bias.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors ETH Zurich.

Main claims:
- Abstract/intro/conclusion: reasoning/direct known-opinion training improves opinion alignment; survey-trained agents generate rationales then choices; rewards for matching respondents; learn survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Conclusion says ZP4 generally outperforms all baselines across Swiss candidates, German parties, U.S. voters, but Neutral prediction and political-spectrum accuracy variation remain.
- Naive prompting biased; structured reasoning trained with RL gives profile-consistent answers across U.S., European, Swiss politics; competitive with strong baselines but residual bias remains.
- Contributions: QX2-based explicit reasoning from survey responses; benchmark of German-party, U.S.-voter, Swiss-candidate opinions; answer-inversion analysis of individuals with known positions showing systematic ideological variation in alignment quality.
- Figure 1: SFT on synthetic statements + ground-truth answers establishes reasoning template without full opinion alignment; then QX2 with formatting/correctness rewards improves reasoning.

Methods/data:
- Task: Given policy question q, persona p, stances Y={No, Neutral, Yes}, learn p’s stance. J4Q labels only {Yes, No}.
- §3.1 QX2: only country label in system prompt; no explicit persona representation. Training observations D={(p_j,q_i,y*ij)}; final stances observed, reasoning not observed.
- Output schema: `<reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>`.
- Rewards: E6Z format tag placement; F2B length = -|L-L*|; G9L correctness = 1[y_i=y_i*]; R=α1E6Z+α2F2B+α3G9L. Reward table: E6Z max 4, α1=.25, α2=.01, α3=1.
- QX2 earlier defined as GRPO/group-relative normalization, PPO variant: sample multiple outputs per prompt, subtract mean reward, divide by reward std.
- V7K=SFT from synthetic CoT demos in rewarded schema; ZP4=SFT+GRPO. Synthetic arguments for positive/negative stances for every J4Q/M8C policy question generated by Y3H=Llama 3.1 70B; unclear how R2V V7K/ZP4 synthetic data are produced though Table 3 reports them.
- Datasets: J4Q Swiss candidates, 18 units, binary, train 48/test 12 topic-stratified; R2V German parties, 6 units, labels Yes/Neutral/No, B5X OOD test 30; M8C ANES 2020, 21 respondents, train 67/test 12 random. Spectrum groups P7N Left, A4U Center, X8J Right.
- Internal error: §4.2 says 47 models trained one per candidate/party/respondent, but units imply 18+6+21=45.

Results:
- Table 3: T=1.0, 8 stochastic runs, per-unit D3G=macro-F1 averaged across units; mean±SD percent.
- Baselines C6W random: J4Q 50.0, R2V 33.33, M8C 33.33; U9F majority: 37.43/27.44/22.98. H3D=ICL gives same-topic training Q/A before unseen question, random subset if context-limited. N8R uses Stammbach hyperparameters.
- Backbones: T9A=Llama 3.1 8B non-reasoning; K6Y=Qwen3 8B reasoning; W2E=Magistral 24B reasoning; 4-bit quantization.
- Table 3 pattern: ZP4 usually best. W2E ZP4: J4Q 70.73, R2V 53.21, M8C 45.43. W2E QX2: 60.56/51.00/43.79. T9A V7K beats T9A QX2 on all datasets. K6Y QX2 often weak except J4Q.
- §4.3 claims: ZP4 outperforms naive and V7K baselines across datasets except T9A on M8C; comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. J4Q higher than M8C/R2V due binary answers; R2V > M8C due more training. Native reasoning no consistent gain; W2E best overall; supervised init helps. Neutral-containing datasets worse.
- Ideology: ZP4 typically best; all training methods underperform on centrist/right groups. T9A/ZP4: J4Q P7N advantage over A4U/X8J; R2V/M8C similar weaker; R2V P7N/A4U roughly equal. V7K averages exceed all other methods for X8J in J4Q/M8C.
- Neutral: Neutral recall worst for every M8C individual. X8J highest Neutral response rate/difficulty; A4U also more Neutral. Removing Neutral improves all groups and narrows P7N–A4U, but P7N–X8J remains. O2K recoding reproduces negative F1–Neutral correlation but A4U/X8J nearly identical. Figure 4: Neutral base rate negatively correlated with F1/accuracy, significant 5%.
- Reasoning traces generally coherent; failures include illogical/hallucinated elements and topical inconsistency.
- Representation: §4.7 mixed wording: says no overall left shift, center-right horizontal and centerward vertical shifts, conservative negative-y trend without clear left-right bias; X8J become more left-wing, P7N/A4U more right-wing/conservative. Uses J4Q PC interpretation from Germann et al.; agents projected into full candidate-population PC space.
- Biased initialization: progressive arguments strongly impair X8J; conservative impair P7N; overrepresented groups not consistently helped; adverse bias harms X8J more. Progressive/conservative data generated by S5Q=Llama 3.3 70B. Conservative-biased and default data yield similar shifts; base-model alignment may drive default centerward displacement.
- Synthetic inversion: X8J benefits; P7N/A4U worsen. Inverted X8J still below original P7N; inverted P7N falls roughly to original X8J. Authors argue remaining gap suggests learnability differences beyond pure model political bias. Counterfactual inverts every J4Q answer, trains T9A on inverted train/test, computes before/after F1 difference; inversion approximately rotates positions 180° about origin in Fig. 2/Section E.6.

Discussion/ethics:
- Limitations: answer noise means near-1.0 F1 unlikely; per-profile training costly and restricts analysis; suitable surveys scarce. Future: bias mitigation; one model conditioned on compact personas; confidence estimates; better questionnaires/uncertainty handling may mitigate Neutral issues.
- Ethics: individual-opinion modeling has mis/disinformation/downstream risks; only anonymized surveys and public figures used. Ideological disparities, centrist/right-wing underperformance, and neutral difficulty are system risks; caution against real-world use until fairness resolved.

Reproducibility statement:
- Code/datasets URL: https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment
- Released docs include training details/hyperparameters, PCA implementation details/all PCA results Section E.5, per-party training counts, recoding definitions, training-sample-size analysis, inversion details.
- Author contributions: Frédéric Berdoz conceived/designed project and led planning/direction; equally contributing Yann Billeter led technical development, dataset collection, training, evaluation, analysis; Yann Vonlanthen advised methodology/design; Roger Wattenhofer supervised. Acknowledges Hans Gersbach.
