Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors: Berdoz, Billeter, Vonlanthen, Wattenhofer. Reproducibility: code/datasets released at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; training details/hyperparameters in Appendix F; PCA details in Section E.5. Contributions: Frédéric Berdoz conceived/designed project and led planning/direction; Yann Billeter contributed equally and led technical development/data/model/evaluation/analysis; Yann Vonlanthen advised; Roger Wattenhofer supervised. Acknowledgment to Hans Gersbach.

Core claim/conclusion: train per-profile/persona LLM agents to answer political survey questions consistently with known opinion profiles, using structured reasoning and RL/GRPO from answer correctness, no gold reasoning. Across Swiss candidates, German parties, and U.S. voters, SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines; Neutral remains challenging; performance varies by ideology. Work positioned as benchmark/baseline for systematic opinion modeling and early step toward representative AI-driven democracy. Code/data released.

Method: one model per unit/profile (candidate/party/respondent), no explicit persona except country label in system prompt. Output schema `<reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>`. Reward = 0.25 format + 0.01 length + 1 correctness; format max 4 points for tags; length negative distance from target length; correctness indicator. GRPO normalizes rewards within sampled group, no learned value function. Optional SFT before GRPO uses synthetic CoT demonstrations generated by larger LLM. Future work: replace per-agent training with one model conditioned on compact personas; add confidence estimates via reasoning scheme or value head.

Datasets: smartvote CH candidate unit: 18 candidates, binary Yes/No; 2023 elections; 75 items, 60 policy across 12 topics; Likert collapsed; 3 candidates from each of 6 parties; topic-stratified 48 train/12 test. WoM DE party unit: 6 parties CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Linke, AfD; Yes/Neutral/No; Wahl-O-Mat train (federal/state/EU 2021–2025), EU&I 2024 30-item test. ANES 2020 US respondent unit: 21 respondents sampled 3 per 7-point ideology; 79 policy items, recoded Yes/Neutral/No by conservative/aggressive schemes (default conservative); random 67 train/12 test. Political groups Left/Center/Right in appendix.

Experimental setup: Llama3.1 8B non-reasoning, Qwen3 8B and Magistral 24B reasoning-pretrained; 4-bit. Baselines: random, majority, ICL same-topic examples, ORPO. Methods text once says “three configurations” but lists only GRPO and SFT+GRPO; tables include SFT too.

Table 3: macro-F1 % ± std over 8 stochastic T=1 runs, per-unit averaged. Random: smartvote 50, WoM/ANES 33.33. Majority: 37.43/27.44/22.98. SFT+GRPO: Llama 66.88/52.53/40.66; Qwen 65.11/49.38/38.44; Magistral 70.73/53.21/45.43. Magistral best overall. Llama SFT ANES 42.77 > Llama SFT+GRPO 40.66. §4.3 says SFT+GRPO beats naive/SFT except Llama ANES; Llama beats Qwen on WoM/ANES; GRPO alone underperforms SFT+GRPO; Neutral lowers performance. Internal error: §4.3 says scores peak on ANES (45.43) and smartvote is hardest (70.73), but table shows smartvote highest/easiest and ANES lowest/hardest.

Reasoning quality: examples generally coherent but failures include illogical/hallucinated reasoning and topic mismatch. Table 1 shows Llama base disagreed with a right-wing ANES profile; after SFT+GRPO reasoning reframed inequality and answered profile-consistently.

Bias/ideology results: Fig 2 smartvote PCA axes left-right and conservative-liberal. Authors say unlike prior left-libertarian bias, no overall left shift; agents shift center-right on x and toward center/conservative on y. Group distances: Right individuals move leftward; Left and Center move rightward/conservative. Fig 3: F1 by ideology for Llama SFT+GRPO. Smartvote strong Left vs Center/Right disparity; WoM/ANES similar weaker. Right group in smartvote and ANES: SFT alone outperforms other methods on average, suggesting difficulty with right-wing profiles. WoM Right relatively strong, possibly larger training sets.

ANES Neutral (§4.6/Fig 4): Neutral recall worst. Negative significant correlation between predictive performance and Neutral base rate; Right and somewhat Center have more Neutral. Removing Neutral improves all groups and SFT+GRPO relative to ICL, narrows Left-Center gap but Left-Right remains. Alternative recoding keeps negative neutral-performance correlation but makes Center/Right nearly identical, so disparity partly recoding artifact.

Biased SFT (§4.8/Figs 5–6): progressive-biased synthetic arguments impair Right strongly; conservative-biased impair Left without consistently benefiting Right. Bias harms underrepresented perspectives; Right harmed more by adverse bias. Conservative-biased and default SFT produce similar displacement, suggesting default centerward shift may stem from base model alignment not SFT bias.

Synthetic inversion (§4.9/Fig 7): invert every smartvote answer in train/test; roughly 180° rotation in PCA. Left candidates become worse after flipping; Right candidates improve, but still average below original Left. Authors conclude disparity is not just original political bias; right positions may be harder / left-leaning preference profiles intrinsically easier.

Discussion/ethics: opinion labels noisy, F1 near 1 unlikely; few units because one model per profile is computationally intensive; data scarcity, few survey items, generic themes, and cross-country mismatch limit comparability. Future work: bias mitigation; single compact-persona conditioned model; confidence estimates/value head; questionnaires/uncertainty for Neutral. Ethics: mis/disinformation and democratic-representation risks; anonymized/public data; caution against deployment until fairness issues resolved, but possible future support for digital democracy/fairer policies.

Abstract claims: Opinion modeling captures individual/group political preferences, with applications such as digital democracies and shaping fairer/more popular policies. They propose political survey data as alternative: ANES and Voting Advice Applications (VAAs) capture issue positions; surveys lack narrative richness/text signal of interviews but are structured and common in bias evaluation/group-level simulation, less used for training individual-level political agents.

First fine-tune LLM with synthetic statements and ground-truth answers to follow reasoning template; after fine-tuning model answers in correct format but is not fully opinion-aligned. Then use GRPO with reward model rewarding proper formatting and correct answers to further improve reasoning.

Table 1 example: Llama 3.1 8B trained on an individual in the Right group in ANES. Question: “Do you agree that it is not really that big a problem if some people have more of a chance in life than others?” Before (prompting base model): answers “No” with equal-shot/fairness/level-playing-field argument. After SFT+GRPO: reasoning says inequality/opportunity differences are inevitable/necessary for incentives, focus on basic necessities/opportunities; final `<answer>A) Yes</answer>`. Caption says before training Llama disagreed; after training it agreed, and reasoning still appeals to similar “equal opportunity” arguments but frames them differently. Additional examples Appendix B.

Training LLMs to reason: CoT and “Let’s think step by step” improve accuracy; recent shift to training reasoning traces via search/RL. GRPO is PPO variant using group-relative reward normalization instead of learned value function for advantages: for each prompt samples group of outputs and normalizes rewards by subtracting group mean/dividing by group std. GRPO effective for math reasoning, achieving SOTA on benchmarks (Guo et al., 2025).

(2024) use interview transcripts and outperform demographic baselines but transcript availability limits; Haller et al. (2025) use in-context respondent QA pairs to predict test answers, focusing on bias identification rather than opinion modeling. Yu et al. Contributions: RL/GRPO for reasoning-based opinion alignment from survey responses; benchmark on German parties, U.S. voters, Swiss candidates; ideological effects analysis by inverting survey answers of individuals with known positions, finding systematic variation across political spectrum. errors.claim: “Performance varies by dataset: scores peak on ANES (45.43), while smartvote is hardest (70.73).”
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 3 notes: SFT+GRPO macro-F1 for Magistral 24B is smartvote 70.73, WoM 53.21, ANES 45.43; caption says smartvote scores higher than ANES/WoM likely due binary/no Neutral.
errors.explanation: The numbers themselves show the opposite of the sentence: 70.73 is the highest score and belongs to smartvote, while 45.43 is lower and belongs to ANES. Thus smartvote is not the hardest according to the reported table.

errors.claim: “We report results for three configurations: GRPO on the survey questions and answers, as well as SFT+GRPO.”
errors.evidence: The same sentence says there are three configurations but explicitly names only two: GRPO and SFT+GRPO. Later §4.3 says “SFT+GRPO outperforms naive and SFT baselines,” and earlier Table 3 notes include SFT results.
errors.explanation: The paper appears to omit SFT from the list while saying there are three configurations. This is internally inconsistent with the count and with later/table discussion of SFT.

errors.claim: Figure 2 caption says agents are “shifted towards the (center-)right,” but also says the average distortions show “no clear left-right bias.”
errors.evidence: Same caption: “we observe that our agents are shifted towards the (center-)right” and then “The average distortions ... show an overall trend towards more conservative (negative y) and no clear left-right bias.”

errors.evidence: Table 3 reports SFT+GRPO macro-F1 for Magistral as smartvote 70.73, WoM 53.21, ANES 45.43; notes state smartvote is highest/easiest and ANES lowest/hardest.

errors.evidence: Table 2 lists J4Q (CH) labels as “{Yes, No},” not including Neutral.
errors.explanation: The method defines the stance set as three-valued for the task, but the data table immediately gives one setting with only two labels. If Y is meant as the stance set for all settings, J4Q contradicts it.

errors.explanation: Calling M8C the highest-peaking dataset and J4Q the hardest contradicts both the reported table values and the immediately preceding explanation that J4Q scores are considerably higher/easier.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” ETH Zurich. Reproducibility: code/datasets at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; released docs include training details/hyperparameters, PCA implementation (all PCA: Sec E.5), per-party training counts, recoding definitions, training-sample-size analysis, inversion details. Author contributions: Frédéric Berdoz conceived/designed/project planning/research direction; Yann Billeter equally contributing led technical development, data, training/eval/analysis; Yann Vonlanthen methodology/design; Roger Wattenhofer PI. Acknowledges Hans Gersbach.

Internal error already found in Part 6: §4.3 says “M8C peaks highest and J4Q is hardest,” contradicting Table 3 and same paragraph: J4Q scores are highest/easier due to binary answers. Table peak: W2E/ZP4 J4Q 70.73, R2V 53.21, M8C 45.43; T9A/ZP4 J4Q 66.88, M8C 40.66.

Earlier abstract/intro claimed reasoning consistently improves opinion alignment. Table 3 counterexample: T9A M8C V7K 42.77 > ZP4 40.66; Part 6 acknowledges exception: “ZP4 outperforms naive and V7K baselines across datasets except T9A on M8C.” Conclusion says ZP4 “generally outperforms all baselines,” softer/not contradiction.

Methods/definitions: QX2 = GRPO/group-relative policy optimization, PPO variant with group-relative reward normalization. Task q, persona p, stances Y={No, Neutral, Yes}; J4Q only {Yes, No}. §3.1 only country label in system prompt; Part 5 clarified one model trained per candidate/party/respondent, so correct QA alone aligns model with individual/unit. Output schema `<reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>`; rewards E6Z format, F2B length, G9L correctness; R=.25E6Z+.01F2B+1G9L. V7K = SFT using synthetic arguments/CoT demos; ZP4=SFT+GRPO; QX2=GRPO without SFT. Synthetic arguments for J4Q/M8C generated by Y3H=Llama 3.1 70B; biased variants by S5Q=Llama 3.3 70B.

Datasets: J4Q Swiss smartvote 2023 English; 75 items incl 60 policy, 4-point Likert collapsed Yes/No; 3 candidates from each of 6 parties with ≥2 National Council seats; one question/topic held out; 48 train/12 test; PCA uses Germann et al. interpretation, projected into full candidate-population PC space. R2V German parties/Wahl-O-Mat; official training data v26 Mar 2025; federal/state/EU 2021–2025; labels agree/neutral/disagree to Yes/Neutral/No; comments for every item; parties CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Die Linke, AfD; test B5X=EU&I 2024. M8C ANES 2020; 79 policy items; recoded Yes/Neutral/No by I7V conservative or O2K aggressive mapping; random split; 3 respondents per answer option on 7-point ideology. Spectrum groups P7N Left, A4U Center, X8J Right.

Table 3: T=1.0, 8 stochastic runs; metric D3G=macro-F1 per unit then averaged, mean±SD %. Untrained C6W random/uniform: J4Q 50.0, R2V 33.33, M8C 33.33. U9F majority/modal: 37.43/27.44/22.98. H3D ICL supplies same-topic training QA pairs. N8R uses Stammbach et al. 2024 hyperparams. T9A=Llama 3.1 8B: H3D 55.97/28.17/23.2; N8R 43.53/43.29/34.84; V7K 63.44/48.95/42.77; QX2 55.14/37.29/34.55; ZP4 66.88/52.53/40.66. K6Y=Qwen3 8B: V7K 61.08/42.91/35.14; QX2 60.64/31.42/31.47; ZP4 65.11/49.38/38.44. W2E=Magistral 24B: V7K 67.63/51.86/39.15; QX2 60.56/51.00/43.79; ZP4 70.73/53.21/45.43. All training uses 4-bit quantization.

Results/claims: ZP4 generally best vs naive/V7K except T9A M8C; comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. Native reasoning support no consistent gain: T9A exceeds K6Y on R2V/M8C, W2E best overall, QX2 trails ZP4; supervised initialization improves dynamics. Neutral-containing datasets worse; Neutral includes uncertainty/social desirability/strategic non-commitment. Fig 3: within-group variance; ZP4 typically best; all methods underperform centrist/right. Reasoning generally coherent but may be illogical/hallucinated/inconsistent.

Ideology: T9A/ZP4 groupwise F1 clear J4Q P7N advantage over A4U/X8J; R2V/M8C similar weaker; R2V P7N/A4U roughly equal; M8C lower. V7K averages exceed all methods for X8J in J4Q/M8C. Neutral recall worst for every M8C individual; X8J highest Neutral rate and most difficulty; A4U also more Neutral. Removing Neutral improves all groups, narrows P7N–A4U, improves ZP4 vs H3D, P7N–X8J remains. O2K keeps negative performance–Neutral-rate correlation but gives nearly identical A4U/X8J. Fig 4: significant 5% negative correlations of M8C Neutral base rate with F1/accuracy.

Representation: no overall left shift; positions shift center-right horizontally and centerward vertically; group-average distortions conservative/negative-y without clear left-right bias. X8J agents become more left-wing; P7N/A4U more right-wing and conservative. Initialization bias: progressive args hurt X8J, inconsistent P7N effects; conservative hurt P7N without consistent X8J gains; adverse bias hurts X8J more. Conservative-biased/default shifts similar; base-model alignment may drive default centerward displacement. Synthetic inversion: flip every J4Q answer, train T9A on flipped train, evaluate flipped test; roughly rotates Fig 2 positions 180° including right-to-left conversion. P7N worsens, X8J improves but average remains below P7N; disparity not purely original-model political bias.

Discussion/conclusion/ethics: Limitations: same-respondent variation adds noise so near-1.0 F1 unlikely; per-profile training computationally intensive/few individuals; suitable surveys scarce. Future: bias mitigation; one model conditioned on compact persona; confidence estimates via extended reasoning/value head; purpose-built questionnaires and better uncertainty. Conclusion: direct known-opinion training treats answers as structured reasoning; ZP4 generally outperforms baselines across Swiss/German/U.S.; Neutral and spectrum variation difficult. Ethics: anonymized surveys/public figures; warns ideological disparities, centrist/right underperformance, Neutral difficulty; avoid real-world use until fairness resolved.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors: Berdoz, Billeter, Vonlanthen, Wattenhofer; ETH Zurich. Reproducibility statement releases code/datasets at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; says training details/hyperparameters in Appendix F and PCA details in Section E.5.

Core claim/conclusion: train LLM agents on known opinions to answer profile-consistent political survey items using structured reasoning and RL/GRPO. Across smartvote Swiss candidates, Wahl-O-Mat German parties, and ANES U.S. voters, SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines; Neutral stances remain hard; performance/accuracy uneven across political spectrum. Provides benchmark/baseline for systematic opinion modeling and possible representative AI-driven democracy.

Method: per-unit opinion alignment: given policy question q and persona/unit p, learn stance y. Output schema `<reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>`. Training data contains only final stances, no human reasoning. Reward = 0.25 format + 0.01 length + 1 correctness; format up to 4 tag points, length is -|L-L*|, correctness indicator. They say no explicit persona representation, only country label in prompt, and train one model per unit. Optional SFT warm start uses synthetic CoT demonstrations.

Datasets: smartvote CH: 18 candidates, 6 parties x3, 60 policy items from 2023 Swiss elections, binary Yes/No, 48 train/12 test topic-stratified. WoM DE: 6 parties CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Linke, AfD; Yes/Neutral/No; train Wahl-O-Mat 2021–2025; test EU&I 2024 30 items. ANES 2020 US: 21 respondents, 3 per 7-point ideology; 79 policy items recoded Yes/Neutral/No; 67 train/12 test. Groups Left/Center/Right in appendix.

Models/backbones: Llama 3.1 8B non-reasoning, Qwen3 8B and Magistral 24B reasoning-pretrained; 4-bit training. Baselines: random uniform; majority most frequent train option per unit; ICL with same-topic train QA pairs; ORPO. §4.2 inconsistency: says “three configurations” but names only GRPO and SFT+GRPO; Table 3 also includes SFT. Synthetic SFT: smartvote and ANES use Llama 3.1 70B generated arguments; no WoM mentioned though Table 3 has WoM SFT/SFT+GRPO.

Table 3: mean macro-F1 % ± std over 8 stochastic T=1 runs; per-unit macro-F1 averaged across units. Random baselines smartvote 50, WoM/ANES 33.33. Majority baselines 37.43, 27.44, 22.98. SFT+GRPO: Llama smartvote 66.88, WoM 52.53, ANES 40.66; Qwen3 65.11, 49.38, 38.44; Magistral 70.73, 53.21, 45.43. Magistral best overall. Llama SFT ANES 42.77 exceeds Llama SFT+GRPO 40.66; acknowledged. Magistral SFT+GRPO best ANES 45.43. ORPO poor on smartvote for Qwen/Magistral (~23).

§4.3: SFT+GRPO outperforms naive and SFT baselines across datasets except Llama on ANES; highest smartvote 70.73, ANES hardest 45.43. SFT+GRPO comparable/better than ICL on ANES/smartvote, better than ICL on WoM. Native reasoning support not consistently helpful: Llama beats Qwen3 on WoM/ANES; Magistral 24B best overall. GRPO alone underperforms SFT+GRPO. Neutral classes lower performance; studied in §4.6; no-Neutral in E.1.

§4.4: reasoning examples generally coherent but can be illogical/hallucinated; alignment may hold on one topic but not others.

Fig. 3 / ideology: earlier caption/summary said SFT+GRPO typically best and all methods underperform on center and right-leaning groups. Text says for Llama SFT+GRPO: smartvote has Center/Right advantage over Left; WoM Left and Center roughly equal; ANES generally lower. Also says for Right group in smartvote and ANES, SFT outperforms all other methods on average; right performance on WoM may benefit from larger training sets. Ethics statement later claims “consistent underperformance on center and right-wing profiles,” which conflicts with the mixed/nuanced Fig. 3 text.

§4.6/Fig. 4 ANES Neutral: Neutral recall worst for all individuals; Right group highest neutral base rate, Center somewhat high. Predictive performance negatively correlates with neutral base rate; significant at 5% for F1 and accuracy. Removing Neutral improves F1 for all groups but does not close Left–Right gap; Left–Center gap narrows. SFT+GRPO improves relative to ICL when Neutral removed. Alternative ANES recoding yields same negative correlation but almost identical Center/Right performance, suggesting artifact of recoding. All Fig. 4 results Llama 3.1 8B SFT+GRPO.

Fig. 2 / §4.7 smartvote PCA: caption/summary said agents more centrist and conservative; text said shifted center-right but also no clear left-right bias. Candidates’ and agents’ positions projected into first two PCs from all 2023 Swiss candidates. Despite known left-libertarian LLM biases, they claim no overall left shift; agents shifted toward center-right on x-axis and toward center on conservative-liberal y-axis. Group distances: Right individuals become more left-wing, while Left and Center become more right-wing and conservative.

§4.8/Figs. 5–6 biased SFT: additional progressive/conservative argument sets using Llama 3.3 70B. Progressive-biased SFT strongly hurts Right without consistent Left benefit; conservative-biased hurts Left without consistent Right improvement. Bias harms underrepresented perspective rather than improving overrepresented one. Right impaired more severely by adverse bias than Left. Conservative-biased and default SFT yield similar displacement patterns, suggesting default centerward shift may come from base model alignment rather than SFT bias.

§4.9 / Fig. 7 synthetic positions: invert every smartvote answer and train Llama-3.1-8B on inverted data. Inversion roughly 180° rotation in PCA, converting e.g. right-wing to left-wing positions. Original-data F1 plotted by smartvote PCA first component; arrows show F1 difference after train/test answers flipped. Right group benefits from inversion; Left and Center perform worse on average. Left candidates worse after flipping individually and on average. Even after inversion, Right does not reach original Left F1, while Left drops to roughly Right’s original level. Authors infer not purely original political bias; Left positions/profiles may be easier and Right/Center positions harder to learn. Fig. 7 caption notes left-most Right candidate is correctly placed (see Fig. 6).

Discussion limitations: opinion learning limited by noise; F1 near 1.0 unlikely. Small number of individuals/parties due to per-profile training computational cost; data scarcity; few surveys with enough concrete items; cross-country question sets rarely align. Future work: investigate political-group disparities/bias mitigation; replace per-agent training with single model conditioned on compact persona representations; add confidence estimates via reasoning scheme or value head; purpose-built questionnaires and uncertainty handling may mitigate Neutral-class difficulty.

Ethics: acknowledges risks in opinion modeling amid mis/disinformation; uses anonymized survey data and public figures’ positions; cautions against real-world applications until fairness issues resolved; says bias could disenfranchise viewpoints; suggests proper bias mitigation could support digital democracies/fairer popular policies. Author contributions: Frédéric Berdoz conceived/designed project and led planning/direction; Yann Billeter contributed equally and led technical development/data/model/evaluation/analysis; Yann Vonlanthen advised; Roger Wattenhofer supervised. Acknowledges Prof. Hans Gersbach.

Introduction: Motivation is digital twins voting/representing opinions; challenge is faithfully representing human political diversity. Existing opinion-modeling approaches mostly prompt with demographics/political affiliation, relying on learned demographic-opinion correlations; cited as failing to capture real distributions and unstable/inconsistent across prompts/groups. Authors seek preference-consistent approach using an individual’s known opinions rather than demographic proxies. Interview transcript methods can model personas well but are expensive/impractical at scale. They propose political survey data as alternative: ANES and Voting Advice Applications (VAAs) capture issue positions; surveys lack narrative richness/text signal of interviews but are structured and common in bias evaluation/group-level simulation, less used for training individual-level political agents.

Method as introduced: Use RL, specifically GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), motivated by reasoning advances (o3/o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1). Treat opinion formation as reasoning: agent writes short rationale and final choice; rewarded when choice matches respondent’s answer, teaching it to reason toward survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Contributions listed: (1) reinforcement learning for reasoning-based opinion alignment via GRPO from survey responses; (2) benchmarking on three real-world political opinion datasets: German parties, U.S. voters, and Swiss candidates, released as benchmark; results show reasoning consistently improves opinion alignment; (3) ideological effects analysis by inverting survey answers of individuals with known positions, revealing systematic variation in alignment quality across political spectrum.

Paper focuses on individualized personas, but literature mostly demographic. Demographic prompting uses political affiliation alone or with age/education/location; richer contexts include belief-network demonstrations; other work combines demographics with demonstrations or ORPO. Question: “Do you agree that it is not really that big a problem if some people have more of a chance in life than others?” Before (prompting base model): answers “No” with equal-shot/fairness/level-playing-field argument. After SFT+GRPO: reasoning says inequality/opportunity differences are inevitable/necessary for incentives, focus on basic necessities/opportunities; final `<answer>A) Yes</answer>`. Caption says before training Llama disagreed; after training it agreed, and reasoning still appeals to similar “equal opportunity” arguments but frames them differently. Additional examples Appendix B.

Training LLMs to reason: CoT and “Let’s think step by step” improve accuracy; recent shift to training reasoning traces via search/RL. GRPO is PPO variant using group-relative reward normalization instead of learned value function for advantages: for each prompt samples group of outputs and normalizes rewards by subtracting group mean/dividing by group std. GRPO effective for math reasoning, achieving SOTA on benchmarks (Guo et al., 2025).

They propose political survey data (ANES and Voting Advice Applications/VAAs) as structured alternative; surveys lack narrative richness/text signal but are common in bias evaluation/group simulation and less used for training individual-level political agents. Use RL, specifically GRPO. Treat opinion formation as reasoning: agent writes short rationale and final choice; rewarded when final choice matches respondent’s answer, teaching it to reason toward survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Figure 1: first fine-tune LLM with synthetic statements and ground-truth answers to follow reasoning template; after SFT model answers in correct format but not fully opinion-aligned. Then use GRPO with reward model rewarding proper formatting and correct answers. Contributions: (1) RL for reasoning-based opinion alignment via GRPO from survey responses; (2) benchmark on three real-world political opinion datasets: German parties, U.S. voters, Swiss candidates, released as benchmark; results show reasoning consistently improves opinion alignment; (3) ideological effects analysis by inverting survey answers of individuals with known positions, finding systematic variation in alignment quality across political spectrum.

Related work: Political opinion modeling requires LLMs to adopt political personas. Persona types: demographic, character, individualized. Paper focuses on individualized personas, but literature mostly demographic. Demographic prompting uses political affiliation alone or with age/education/location; richer contexts include belief-network demonstrations; other work combines demographics with demonstrations or ORPO. Limitations of demographic approaches from Santurkar et al.: representativeness (default distributions fail true populations), steerability (insufficient control), consistency (biases vary by topics/contexts). Models may approximate overall distributions but fail subgroup variance and are prompt-sensitive. Beyond demographics: Park et al. (2024) use interview transcripts and outperform demographic baselines but transcript availability limits; Haller et al. (2025) use in-context respondent QA pairs to predict test answers, focusing on bias identification rather than opinion modeling. Yu et al. (2025) propose persona-based CoT-inspired prompting combining demographic, ideological, and temporal factors calibrated using ANES; simulate individual respondents’ voting behavior and aggregate predictions. Unlike current paper, Yu et al. do not use RL and target voting predictions rather than learning general preference profiles. Current paper says its method could theoretically apply to voting prediction but computational cost of modeling representative sample size is currently prohibitive.

Table 1 example: Llama 3.1 8B trained on an individual in the Right group in ANES. Question: “Do you agree that it is not really that big a problem if some people have more of a chance in life than others?” Before prompting base model: answers “No” with equal-shot/fairness/level-playing-field argument. After SFT+GRPO: reasoning says inequality/opportunity differences are inevitable/necessary for incentives, focus on basic necessities/opportunities; final `<answer>A) Yes</answer>`. Caption says before training Llama disagreed; after training it agreed, and reasoning still appeals to similar “equal opportunity” arguments but frames them differently. Additional examples Appendix B.

Training LLMs to reason: CoT and “Let’s think step by step” improve accuracy; recent shift to training reasoning traces via search/RL. GRPO is PPO variant using group-relative reward normalization instead of learned value function for advantages: for each prompt samples group of outputs and normalizes rewards by subtracting group mean/dividing by group std. GRPO effective for math reasoning, achieving SOTA on benchmarks (Guo et al., 2025).

final_notes:
Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors ETH Zurich. Reproducibility: code/datasets at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; released docs include training/hyperparameters, PCA details (all PCA results Section E.5), per-party training counts, recoding definitions, training-sample-size analysis and inversion details.

Internal errors found:
1) Abstract/intro claimed reasoning “consistently” improves alignment, but Table 3/§4.3 show exception: T9A on M8C has V7K 42.77 > ZP4 40.66. §4.3 explicitly says ZP4 outperforms V7K “except T9A on M8C.”
2) Figure 3 summary claims ZP4 typically works best and every training method underperforms on centrist/right-leaning groups. But §4.5 says T9A/ZP4 on J4Q has clear A4U/X8J advantage over P7N.
3) Ethics statement repeats “consistent centrist/right-wing underperformance,” conflicting with §4.5: T9A/ZP4 on J4Q has A4U/X8J advantage over P7N, and R2V P7N/A4U roughly equal.

Methods/definitions:
- QX2 = GRPO/group-relative policy optimization, PPO variant with group-relative reward normalization.
- Output schema `<reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>`; rewards E6Z format, F2B length, G9L correctness; R=0.25E6Z+0.01F2B+1G9L.
- V7K = optional SFT initialization with synthetic CoT/arguments in rewarded schema. ZP4 = SFT + GRPO.
- H3D = contextual ICL comparator following Haller et al. (2025), gives question–answer pairs before unseen question, all same-topic training questions or random subset if context length limits.
- C6W = random uniform-answer selector. U9F = majority/modal answer from each unit’s training set. N8R uses Stammbach et al. (2024) hyperparameters.
- §3 task allowed labels {No, Neutral, Yes}, but J4Q labels only {Yes, No}.
- §3.1 said only country label in system prompt/no explicit persona; Part 5 clarified one model trained per candidate/party/respondent.

Datasets:
- J4Q Swiss smartvote 2023 English; 75 items incl. 60 policy questions/12 topics; 4-point Likert collapsed to Yes/No. Three candidates from each of six parties with ≥2 National Council seats. One question per topic held out, so 48 train/12 test.
- R2V German parties from Wahl-O-Mat official data, version 26 Mar 2025; federal/state/EU positions 2021–2025; labels agree/neutral/disagree to Yes/Neutral/No; comment per item. Six parties CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Die Linke, AfD. Test B5X = EU&I 2024 recoded same.
- M8C ANES 2020; 79 policy items after exclusions; recoded to Yes/Neutral/No by I7V conservative mapping, O2K aggressive alternative. Random split. Three respondents per answer option on 7-point liberal–conservative self-placement for ideology analysis.
- Spectrum groups: P7N Left, A4U Center, X8J Right.
- One model per candidate/party/respondent. Backbones: T9A=Llama 3.1 8B non-reasoning; K6Y=Qwen3 8B; W2E=Magistral 24B. Training experiments use 4-bit quantization.

Table 3 values/claims:
- Metric D3G=macro-F1 %, T=1.0, 8 stochastic runs, averaged across units.
- Untrained: C6W 50.0/33.33/33.33 for J4Q/R2V/M8C; U9F 37.43/27.44/22.98.
- T9A: H3D 55.97/28.17/23.2; N8R 43.53/43.29/34.84; V7K 63.44/48.95/42.77; QX2 55.14/37.29/34.55; ZP4 66.88/52.53/40.66.
- K6Y: V7K 61.08/42.91/35.14; QX2 60.64/31.42/31.47; ZP4 65.11/49.38/38.44.
- W2E: V7K 67.63/51.86/39.15; QX2 60.56/51.00/43.79; ZP4 70.73/53.21/45.43.
- §4.3 summary: ZP4 beats naive and V7K except T9A/M8C; comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V; J4Q highest, M8C hardest; R2V>M8C attributed to more training samples. Native reasoning support no consistent gain: T9A>K6Y on R2V/M8C, W2E best overall, QX2 alone trails ZP4.

Results by groups/neutral/ideology:
- §4.5: R2V/M8C patterns similar but weaker; R2V P7N/A4U roughly equal; M8C lower. V7K averages exceed all other methods for X8J in J4Q/M8C. Explanations include LLM left-leaning bias, T9A embedded biases, or intrinsic survey-signal learnability; strong R2V X8J may benefit from larger training sets.
- §4.6: Neutral recall worst for every M8C individual. X8J highest Neutral response rate and suffers most; A4U also more Neutral. Removing Neutral improves all groups, narrows P7N–A4U, improves ZP4 relative to H3D, but P7N–X8J differences remain. O2K gives similar negative Neutral-rate correlation but nearly identical A4U/X8J performance, so recoding may partly produce disparity. Figure 4: M8C T9A/ZP4 Neutral base rate negatively correlated with F1/accuracy, significant at 5%.

Representation/bias:
- Figure 2/§4.7: Swiss PCA agent positions; no overall left shift despite LLM left-libertarian bias literature. Positions shift center-right horizontally and centerward vertically; group-average distortions show conservative negative-y trend without clear left–right bias. X8J individuals become more left-wing; P7N/A4U more right-wing and conservative.
- §4.8: biased initialization data: progressive-biased data harms X8J; conservative-biased harms P7N; adverse bias harms X8J more. Conservative-biased and default data produce similar shifts; base model alignment may drive default centerward displacement.
- §4.9/Fig. 7 synthetic positions/answer inversion: counterfactual flips J4Q train/test answers. P7N worsens; X8J improves but average remains below P7N. Pure original-model-political-bias account insufficient; right-wing profiles may be intrinsically harder / left-leaning easier.

Discussion/conclusion/ethics:
- Limitations: answer variation imposes noise; per-profile training computationally intensive; scarce survey items/question alignment issues.
- Future work: bias mitigation, possible persona-conditioned single model, confidence estimates/value head, better questionnaires/uncertainty handling.
- Conclusion: “ZP4 generally outperforms all baselines,” difficult Neutral prediction and political-spectrum accuracy variation; benchmark as early step toward representative AI-driven democracy.
- Ethics: uses anonymized surveys/public figures; warns ideological disparities, neutral difficulty, and claimed centrist/right-wing underperformance are deployment risks; cautions against real-world applications until fairness issues resolved.
- Author contributions: Frédéric Berdoz conceived/designed project and led planning/direction; Yann Billeter equally contributing led technical development/dataset/training/evaluation/analysis; Yann Vonlanthen advised methodology/design; Roger Wattenhofer supervised.

Introduction claims/details:
- Opens with broad claim: “Reasoning consistently improves opinion alignment.” Survey-trained agents generate short rationales then choices; receive rewards for matching respondents’ answers; learn survey-consistent positions on unseen questions.
- Motivation from recent RL gains incl. o3/o4-mini and DeepSeek-R1.
- Goal/application: individual digital twins voting on every issue require accurate political-behavior simulation, useful for elections/policy/democracy.
- Existing LLM political discourse does not reliably represent human viewpoint diversity; demographic/affiliation prompts exploit correlations but miss distributions and are unstable.
- Preference consistency uses known individual opinions rather than demographic proxies. Interview transcripts can work but are costly/impractical at scale.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors: Berdoz, Billeter, Vonlanthen, Wattenhofer. Reproducibility statement releases code/datasets at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; training details/hyperparameters in Appendix F; PCA details in Section E.5. Author contributions: Berdoz conceived/designed/led planning/research direction; Yann Billeter contributed equally and led technical development (dataset collection, model training, evaluation, analysis); Yann Vonlanthen advised; Wattenhofer supervised.

Core claim: train LLMs to produce profile-consistent political survey answers using structured reasoning and RL/GRPO from survey responses, evaluated on smartvote Swiss candidates, Wahl-O-Mat German parties, ANES U.S. respondents. Reasoning improves opinion modeling but does not eliminate bias.

Method: per-unit opinion alignment: given policy question q and persona/unit p, learn stance y. Output schema `<reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>`. Training data contains only final stances, no human reasoning. Reward = 0.25 format + 0.01 length + 1 correctness; format gives up to 4 tag points, length is -|L-L*|, correctness indicator. They say no explicit persona representation, only country label in prompt, and train one model per unit (§4.2). Potential inconsistency: Conclusion calls these “persona-conditioned agents,” but method says no explicit persona conditioning/per-unit training; Discussion says persona-conditioned single model is future work.

Datasets: smartvote CH: 18 candidates, 6 parties x3, 60 policy items from 2023 Swiss elections, binary Yes/No, 48 train/12 test topic-stratified. WoM DE: 6 parties CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Linke, AfD; labels Yes/Neutral/No; train from Wahl-O-Mat 2021–2025; test EU&I 2024 30 items. ANES 2020 US: 21 respondents, 3 per 7-point ideology; 79 policy items recoded Yes/Neutral/No; 67 train/12 test. Groups Left/Center/Right in appendix.

Models/backbones: Llama 3.1 8B non-reasoning, Qwen3 8B and Magistral 24B reasoning-pretrained; 4-bit quantization for training. Baselines: random uniform; majority most frequent train option per unit; ICL same-topic train QA pairs; ORPO using Stammbach et al. hyperparams. §4.2 inconsistency: says “three configurations” but names only GRPO and SFT+GRPO; Table 3 also includes SFT. Synthetic SFT arguments: §4.2 says for smartvote and ANES generated by Llama 3.1 70B; does not mention WoM despite Table 3 having SFT/SFT+GRPO for WoM.

Table 3: mean macro-F1 % ± std over 8 stochastic T=1 runs; per-unit macro-F1 then average across units. Random: smartvote 50, WoM/ANES 33.33. Majority: 37.43, 27.44, 22.98. SFT+GRPO key scores: Llama smartvote 66.88, WoM 52.53, ANES 40.66; Qwen3 65.11, 49.38, 38.44; Magistral 70.73, 53.21, 45.43. Magistral best overall. Llama SFT ANES 42.77 exceeds Llama SFT+GRPO 40.66; §4.3 acknowledges exception. ORPO poor on smartvote for Qwen/Magistral (~23).

§4.3/Conclusion: SFT+GRPO generally outperforms naive and SFT baselines across datasets except Llama 3.1 8B on ANES; highest score smartvote 70.73, ANES hardest 45.43. SFT+GRPO comparable/better than ICL on ANES and smartvote, outperforms ICL on WoM. Native reasoning support not consistently helpful: Llama 8B beats Qwen3 8B on WoM/ANES, Magistral 24B best overall. GRPO alone underperforms SFT+GRPO. Neutral classes lower performance; Neutral studied in §4.6; no-Neutral in E.1. Conclusion says Neutral stances remain challenging and accuracy varies across political spectrum.

§4.4: reasoning examples generally coherent but with failures: illogical/hallucinated elements; agent may align on one topic but not others.

§4.5/Fig.3: ideology impacts learnability for Llama 3.1 8B SFT+GRPO. smartvote shows clear Left vs Center/Right gap. WoM and ANES similar but weaker; WoM Left and Center roughly equal, ANES generally lower. For Right group in smartvote and ANES, SFT outperforms all other methods on average, suggesting difficulty with right-wing profiles. Possible causes: known left-leaning LLM tendencies or Right profiles intrinsically harder; WoM Right stronger possibly due larger training sets (E.4). Earlier Fig.3 caption said SFT+GRPO typically best and all methods underperform center/right.

§4.6/Fig.4: Neutral reasoning is hard on ANES, all Llama 3.1 8B SFT+GRPO. Recall worst on Neutral class; Right, and partly Center, have highest Neutral base rate. F1 and accuracy negatively correlated with Neutral base rate, significant at 5%; regression E.3. Removing Neutral improves all groups and improves SFT+GRPO relative to ICL, but does not close Left–Right gap; Left–Center gap narrows. Alternative ANES recoding (Appendix D/E.2) shows same negative correlation but nearly identical Center/Right performance, implying artifact of recoding.

§4.7/Fig.2: smartvote representativity in PCA political space using full 2023 Swiss candidate PCs; included candidates and projected agent positions. Authors claim no overall left shift; instead agents shift toward center-right on left-right x-axis and toward center on conservative-liberal y-axis. Group-average distances: Right individuals become more left-wing; Left and Center become more right-wing and conservative. Earlier Fig.2 caption/description noted agents more centrist/conservative, average distortions more conservative/no clear left-right bias—possible tension with “center-right” wording.

§4.8/Fig.5: biased SFT data generated with Llama 3.3 70B progressive/conservative prompts affects Llama SFT+GRPO on smartvote. Progressive bias strongly impairs Right candidates with inconsistent Left effects; conservative bias impairs Left without consistently benefiting Right. Conclusion: ideological bias in SFT data harms underrepresented perspectives more than helping overrepresented ones. Internal inconsistency in §4.8: text says “Left candidates are impaired more severely by adverse bias than Right candidates,” but subsequent Fig.6 text/caption says, “Consistent/Similar to the F1 results,” Right candidates are affected more strongly than Left.

§4.8/Fig.6: biased data effects in PCA space. Biased data primarily shifts underrepresented groups; Right candidates said to be affected more strongly than Left in positional displacement. Conservative-biased and default SFT data produce similar displacement patterns, suggesting centerward shift in Fig.2 may come from base model alignment rather than SFT-data bias.

§4.9/Fig.7: synthetic smartvote positions by inverting every answer and training Llama-3.1-8B. Inversion roughly 180° rotation about origin in Fig.2 (E.6), e.g. right-wing positions become left-wing. Compute F1 difference before/after inversion. Right group benefits; Left and Center worsen on average. Even after inversion, Right does not reach original Left F1; Left drops to roughly original Right level. Authors infer if model political bias alone caused gap, flipping labels should make right-leaning candidates nearly as easy as left-leaning; since not, left-leaning preference profiles may be intrinsically easier to model.

§5 Discussion: Limitations: opinion learning limited by respondent noise; F1 near 1 unlikely; small number of individuals/parties due to computational intensity from training one model per profile; data scarce, surveys often too few items/generic, cross-country question sets rarely align. Future work: investigate political-group disparities and bias mitigation; replace per-agent training with a single model conditioned on compact persona representations; add confidence estimates via reasoning scheme or value head; purpose-built questionnaires and better uncertainty handling may mitigate Neutral-class difficulty.

Ethics: acknowledges opinion modeling risks amid mis/disinformation; uses anonymized survey data and public figures’ positions for privacy. States systematic performance disparities with consistent underperformance on center and right-wing profiles and difficulties modeling neutral positions. Warns against real-world applications until fairness issues resolved; suggests potential beneficial applications such as digital democracies with proper bias mitigation.

Synthetic SFT arguments: §4.2 says for smartvote and ANES generated by Llama 3.1 70B; does not mention WoM despite Table 3 having SFT/SFT+GRPO for WoM.

Table 3: mean macro-F1 % ± std over 8 stochastic T=1 runs; per-unit macro-F1 then average across units. Random: smartvote 50, WoM/ANES 33.33. Majority: 37.43, 27.44, 22.98. §4.3: SFT+GRPO outperforms naive and SFT baselines across datasets except Llama 3.1 8B on ANES; highest score smartvote 70.73, ANES hardest 45.43. §4.5/Fig.3: ideology impacts learnability for Llama 3.1 8B SFT+GRPO. smartvote shows clear Left vs Center/Right gap. Possible causes: known left-leaning LLM tendencies or Right profiles intrinsically harder; WoM Right stronger possibly due larger training sets (E.4). Earlier Fig.3 caption said SFT+GRPO typically best and all methods underperform center/right.

§4.6/Fig.4: Neutral reasoning is hard on ANES, all Llama 3.1 8B SFT+GRPO. Recall worst on Neutral class; Right, and partly Center, have highest Neutral base rate. Authors claim no overall left shift; instead agents shift toward center-right on left-right x-axis and toward center on conservative-liberal y-axis. Group-average distances: Right individuals become more left-wing; Left and Center become more right-wing and conservative. Earlier Fig.2 caption/description noted agents more centrist/conservative, average distortions more conservative/no clear left-right bias—potential tension with “center-right” wording.

§4.8/Fig.5: biased SFT data generated with Llama 3.3 70B progressive/conservative prompts affects Llama SFT+GRPO on smartvote. Progressive bias strongly impairs Right candidates with inconsistent Left effects; conservative bias impairs Left without consistently benefiting Right. Conclusion: ideological bias in SFT data harms underrepresented perspectives more than helping overrepresented ones. Internal inconsistency in §4.8: text says “Left candidates are impaired more severely by adverse bias than Right candidates,” but subsequent Fig.6 text/caption says, “Consistent/Similar to the F1 results,” Right candidates are affected more strongly than Left.

§4.8/Fig.6: biased data effects in PCA space. Biased data primarily shifts underrepresented groups; Right candidates said to be affected more strongly than Left in positional displacement. Conservative-biased and default SFT data produce similar displacement patterns, suggesting centerward shift in Fig.2 may come from base model alignment rather than SFT-data bias.

§4.9/Fig.7: synthetic smartvote positions by inverting every answer and training Llama-3.1-8B. Inversion roughly 180° rotation about origin in Fig.2 (E.6), e.g. right-wing positions become left-wing. Compute F1 difference before/after inversion. Right group benefits; Left and Center worsen on average. Even after inversion, Right does not reach original Left F1; Left drops to roughly original Right level. Authors infer if model political bias alone caused gap, flipping labels should make right-leaning candidates nearly as easy as left-leaning; since not, left-leaning preference profiles may be intrinsically easier to model. Current Discussion repeats Fig.7 caption: learning Right and Center harder than Left; arrows show F1 difference after flipping all train/test answers; Left candidates worse after flipping, Right improve but remain below Left on average; “as disparity is not removed by converting Left to Right,” Right positions may be harder to learn. Caption also says left-most Right candidate is correctly placed and refers to Fig.6.

§5 Discussion: Limitations: opinion learning limited by respondent noise; F1 near 1 unlikely; small number of individuals/parties due to computational intensity from training one model per profile; data scarce, surveys often too few items/generic, cross-country question sets rarely align. Future work: investigate political-group disparities and bias mitigation; replace per-agent training with a single model conditioned on compact persona representations; add confidence estimates via reasoning scheme or value head; purpose-built questionnaires and better uncertainty handling may mitigate Neutral-class difficulty.

errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “They say no explicit persona representation, only country label in prompt, and train one model per unit (§4.2).” Also Discussion future work proposes “replace per-agent training with a single model conditioned on compact persona representations.”
errors.explanation: The conclusion describes the agents as persona-conditioned, but the method previously stated that there is no explicit persona representation/conditioning; instead, a separate model is trained per individual/party. Persona conditioning is presented earlier as future work, not as the current setup.

grade.reason: The reviewer explicitly flags the sentence claiming Left candidates are more impaired and cites later text and Fig. 6 caption that state Right candidates are affected more strongly, matching the planted error and its contradicting evidence.

errors.claim: “Given policy question q, persona p—respondent or party—and stances Y={No, Neutral, Yes}”
errors.evidence: Table 2 lists J4Q (CH) labels as “{Yes, No},” not including Neutral.
errors.explanation: The method defines the stance set as three-valued for the task, but the data table immediately gives one setting with only two labels. If Y is meant as the stance set for all settings, J4Q contradicts it.

errors.claim: “Reasoning consistently improves opinion alignment.”

errors.explanation: The abstract’s claim of consistent improvement is contradicted by at least one reported result where adding the reported GRPO/reasoning combination does not improve over the SFT initialization.

errors.claim: Reasoning consistently improves opinion alignment / reasoning boosts opinion alignment consistently.
errors.evidence: This part states: “ZP4 outperforms naive and V7K baselines across datasets except T9A on M8C.” Earlier Table 3 values in the notes show T9A V7K M8C = 42.77 while T9A ZP4 M8C = 40.66.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors ETH Zurich. Reproducibility statement gives GitHub: https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; released docs include training details/hyperparameters, PCA implementation/all PCA results Section E.5, per-party training counts, recoding definitions, training-sample-size analysis, inversion details. Author contributions: Frédéric Berdoz conceived/designed project/led planning/direction; equally contributing Yann Billeter led technical development including dataset collection, training, evaluation, analysis; Yann Vonlanthen advised methodology/design; Roger Wattenhofer supervised. Acknowledges Prof. Dr. Hans Gersbach.

Key internal-error watch: Abstract/intro claimed reasoning consistently improves opinion alignment; §4.3 says “ZP4 outperforms naive and V7K baselines across datasets except T9A on M8C,” matching Table 3 where T9A V7K M8C 42.77 > ZP4 40.66. Thus any unqualified “consistently improves/outperforms all” is too strong unless phrased as “generally.”

Methods/definitions: QX2=GRPO/group-relative policy optimization, PPO variant with group-relative reward normalization. Rewards: E6Z format, F2B length, G9L correctness; R=α1E6Z+α2F2B+α3G9L with α1=.25, α2=.01, α3=1. Task: q, persona p, stances Y={No, Neutral, Yes}; J4Q labels only {Yes, No}. Output schema `<reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>`. V7K=SFT optional supervised initialization using CoT demos in rewarded schema; intended to speed convergence/reduce formatting burden/initialize political reasoning.

Datasets/setup/Table 3: Table 3: T=1.0, 8 stochastic runs; metric D3G=macro-F1 per unit, averaged across units; mean±SD percent. Methods: C6W=random uniform-answer selector; U9F=majority/modal answer from unit training set; H3D=ICL comparator using same-topic training Q–A pairs or random subset under context limits; N8R uses Stammbach et al. hyperparameters. Trained: V7K=SFT, QX2=GRPO, ZP4=SFT+GRPO. Table 3 values: C6W J4Q 50.0/R2V 33.33/M8C 33.33; U9F 37.43/27.44/22.98. T9A: H3D 55.97/28.17/23.2; N8R 43.53/43.29/34.84; V7K 63.44/48.95/42.77; QX2 55.14/37.29/34.55; ZP4 66.88/52.53/40.66. K6Y: V7K 61.08/42.91/35.14; QX2 60.64/31.42/31.47; ZP4 65.11/49.38/38.44. W2E: V7K 67.63/51.86/39.15; QX2 60.56/51.00/43.79; ZP4 70.73/53.21/45.43. §4.3: ZP4 beats naive and V7K except T9A/M8C; comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. J4Q easiest due binary no Neutral; M8C hardest; R2V>M8C attributed to more training samples. Native reasoning support not consistently beneficial: T9A>K6Y on R2V/M8C; W2E best overall; QX2 alone trails ZP4, so supervised init helps.

Datasets: R2V German parties: Wahl-O-Mat official training data version 26 Mar 2025; elections 2021–2025; Yes/Neutral/No; comments for every item; parties CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Die Linke, AfD; test B5X=EU&I 2024. M8C=ANES 2020 Time Series; 79 policy items after exclusions; recoded Yes/Neutral/No by I7V conservative mapping default or O2K aggressive mapping. Random split. Three respondents per option on 7-point liberal–conservative self-placement. J4Q=smartvote 2023 English; 75 items incl. 60 policy questions across 12 topics; 4-point Likert collapsed to Yes/No; three candidates from each of six parties with ≥2 National Council seats; one question/topic held out, 48 train/12 test. Spectrum groups P7N Left, A4U Center, X8J Right. One model per candidate/party/respondent. Backbones: T9A=Llama 3.1 8B non-reasoning; K6Y=Qwen3 8B; W2E=Magistral 24B; all training uses 4-bit quantization. Synthetic arguments for J4Q/M8C generated by Y3H=Llama 3.1 70B; biased argument sets by S5Q=Llama 3.3 70B.

Results/claims: Fig.3 “Unequal learnability”: F1 error bars within-group variance; appendix retains parties/ideology; ZP4 typically works best; every training method underperforms on centrist/right-leaning groups. §4.4: agents generally produce coherent arguments implying final answers; failures include illogical/hallucinated elements and topic-inconsistent individual matching. §4.5 ideology: T9A/ZP4 J4Q P7N clearly > A4U/X8J; R2V/M8C similar weaker; R2V P7N/A4U roughly equal; M8C lower. V7K averages exceed all other methods for X8J in J4Q/M8C. Strong R2V X8J may benefit from larger training sets. §4.6 Neutral: Neutral recall worst for every M8C individual. X8J highest Neutral response rate and most difficulty; A4U also more Neutral. Removing Neutral improves all groups, narrows P7N–A4U, improves ZP4 relative to H3D but P7N–X8J remains. O2K gives negative performance–Neutral-rate correlation but nearly identical A4U/X8J performance. Fig.4: test Neutral base rate vs F1/accuracy significant negative correlations at 5%. §4.7 representation: no overall left shift; positions shift center-right horizontally and centerward vertically; group-average distortions overall conservative/negative-y without clear left–right bias; X8J become more left-wing, P7N/A4U more right-wing and conservative. §4.8 initialization bias: progressive arguments impair X8J; conservative impair P7N; overrepresented groups not systematically helped; adverse bias harms P7N more severely than X8J. Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors: Berdoz, Billeter, Vonlanthen, Wattenhofer. Reproducibility: code/datasets released at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; training hyperparameters in Appendix F; PCA details in Section E.5. Author contributions: Frédéric Berdoz conceived/designed project and led planning/research direction; Yann Billeter contributed equally and led technical development including data/model/evaluation/analysis; Yann Vonlanthen advised on methodology/design; Roger Wattenhofer supervised.

Core claim/question: reasoning improves individual-level political opinion alignment in LLMs. Naive demographic/political-label prompting gives biased, unstable, correlation-driven opinions. Authors prefer individual known opinions from surveys/VAAs. Three datasets: German parties, U.S. voters, Swiss candidates. Contributions: GRPO-based RL with explicit reasoning; benchmark; ideological analysis, including answer inversion improving Right profiles but harming Left/Center. Conclusion says SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines, but uneven due to Neutral difficulty and political-spectrum variation.

Method: Given policy question q and persona p, learn p’s stance from survey responses only, no reasoning traces. Output schema: `<reasoning>[justification]</reasoning><answer>[stance]</answer>`. GRPO reward: format up to 4 tag points scaled .25; length .01; correctness +1. Optional SFT warm start uses constructed/synthetic CoT demos. No explicit persona representation; country label in system prompt; individual alignment from answering questions. GRPO samples groups and normalizes rewards by group mean/std, no value function.

Datasets/Table 2: smartvote CH: Candidate, 18 units, binary Yes/No, 48 train, 12 test topic-stratified. WoM DE: Party, 6 units, Yes/Neutral/No, train counts appendix/Table 5, 30 EU&I test. ANES US: Respondent, 21 units, Yes/Neutral/No, 67 train, 12 test random. Counts are questions per unit. WoM official Wahl-O-Mat 26 Mar 2025, federal/state/European elections 2021–2025; parties CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Linke, AfD; agree/neutral/disagree mapped Yes/Neutral/No; test EU&I 2024, 30 recoded items. ANES: 79 policy items excluding demographics/knowledge/candidate evals/thermometers; recoded conservative/aggressive, default conservative; ideology analysis uses 3 respondents per 7-point liberal-conservative option = 21. Swiss smartvote: English 2023 questionnaire; 75 total, 60 policy over 12 topics; 4-point collapsed Yes/No; 3 candidates from each of 6 parties with at least two National Council seats = 18; one question per topic held out = 12. Political groups Left/Center/Right.

Experimental setup: one model per unit; models Llama3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B; 4-bit training. Methods sentence earlier had inconsistency: said “three configurations” but named only GRPO and SFT+GRPO, while Table 3 includes SFT too. Synthetic arguments for smartvote/ANES generated by Llama 3.1 70B for SFT. Baselines: random, majority, ICL, ORPO.

Table 3 macro-F1 over 8 T=1 runs. Random: smartvote 50, WoM/ANES 33.33; majority 37.43/27.44/22.98. Key: Llama SFT+GRPO 66.88/52.53/40.66; Qwen SFT+GRPO 65.11/49.38/38.44; Magistral SFT+GRPO 70.73/53.21/45.43. SFT+GRPO best for smartvote/WoM all models and ANES only for Magistral; Llama ANES SFT 42.77 beats SFT+GRPO 40.66. Section 4.3 claims SFT+GRPO outperforms naive and SFT except Llama ANES; peak smartvote 70.73, ANES hardest 45.43; comparable/better than ICL on ANES/smartvote and beats ICL on WoM. Native reasoning does not consistently help; Magistral best overall. GRPO alone underperforms SFT+GRPO.

Fig. 3: F1 by ideology/groups for Llama. SFT+GRPO typically best, but all methods underperform on center/right. Clear smartvote disparity Left vs Center/Right; WoM and ANES similar but weaker; WoM Left and Center roughly equal; ANES lower. For Right group in smartvote and ANES, SFT outperforms all other methods on average, suggesting difficulty with right-wing profiles. Strong Right WoM performance may be aided by larger training sets (E.4).

Section 4.6/Fig. 4: ANES Neutral class hardest; recall worst for Neutral for all individuals. Right, and some Center, have highest Neutral base rate. Negative correlation between performance and Neutral base rate significant at 5% for F1 and accuracy. Removing Neutral test instances improves F1 for all groups but does not remove Left–Right gap; gap Left–Center narrows. SFT+GRPO improves relative to ICL when Neutral removed (E.1). Alternative ANES recoding (Appendix D/E.2) shows same negative correlation but nearly identical Center/Right performance, suggesting some artifact of recoding. All Fig. 4 results use Llama 3.1 8B SFT+GRPO.

Fig. 2 / Section 4.7: smartvote PCA politics space based on full set of 2023 Swiss candidates; axes x left-right, y conservative-liberal; agents shifted toward center-right on x-axis and center on y-axis; no overall left shift despite left-libertarian biases. Group-averaged distances: Right individuals become more left-wing, while Left and Center become more right-wing and conservative.

Fig. 5/6 and Section 4.8: biased SFT data tests impact of progressive/conservative arguments generated by Llama 3.3 70B. Llama SFT+GRPO on biased datasets: progressive bias strongly impairs Right without consistent Left benefit; conservative bias impairs Left without consistent Right benefit. Right candidates are more severely impaired by adverse bias. PCA shifts: biased data mainly shifts underrepresented groups, Right more strongly than Left. Conservative-biased and default SFT displacement patterns are highly similar, suggesting default centerward shift may come from base model alignment rather than SFT data bias.

Section 4.9/Fig. 7: synthetic positions by flipping/inverting every smartvote answer in train and test and training Llama-3.1-8B. Inversion roughly 180° rotation about origin in Fig. 2, converting e.g. right-wing positions into left-wing ones. F1 difference before/after inversion: original Right group benefits; Left and Center perform worse on average. After inversion, Right still does not reach original Left F1, while Left drops to roughly original Right level. Authors infer disparity is not purely base-model political bias; left-leaning preference profiles may be intrinsically easier / Right and Center positions harder to learn. Fig. 7 caption in Discussion: individuals ordered by first PCA component; left-most Right candidate correctly placed per Fig. 6; arrows show F1 changes after all answers flipped.

Discussion limitations/future work: opinion labels noisy, same respondent may answer differently, so F1 near 1.0 unlikely. Small number of individuals/parties because one model per profile is computationally intensive. Suitable surveys scarce, often too few items or too generic; question sets rarely align across countries, limiting comparability. Future work: investigate group disparities and bias mitigation; replace per-agent training with single model conditioned on compact persona representations; add confidence estimates via reasoning scheme or dedicated value head; purpose-built questionnaires and uncertainty handling may mitigate Neutral-class difficulty.

Ethics statement: acknowledges risks in opinion modeling amid misinformation/disinformation; uses anonymized survey data and public figures’ positions for privacy. Reiterates systematic disparities with underperformance on center/right profiles and neutral positions. Cautions against real-world applications until fairness issues are resolved; suggests potential societal benefits such as digital democracies only with proper bias mitigation.

LLMs are natural candidates due to versatility, generalization, and success in text-to-text tasks, but naive prompting yields biased opinions because of statistical nature and limited causal understanding. Work studies whether reasoning improves opinion alignment. Inspired by recent RL-enabled advances in mathematical reasoning, they train models to produce profile-consistent answers through structured reasoning. Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors: Frédéric Berdoz, Yann Billeter, Yann Vonlanthen, Roger Wattenhofer; ETH Zurich; emails {fberdoz, ybilleter, yvonlanthen, wattenhofer}@ethz.ch.

Abstract claims: Opinion modeling captures individual/group political preferences, with applications such as digital democracies and shaping fairer/more popular policies. LLMs are natural candidates due to versatility/generalization/text-to-text success, but naive prompting yields biased opinions due to statistical nature and limited causal understanding. Study asks whether reasoning improves opinion alignment. Inspired by RL-enabled math reasoning advances, they train models to produce profile-consistent answers through structured reasoning. Evaluation on three datasets covering U.S., European, and Swiss politics. Results: reasoning enhances opinion modeling and is competitive with strong baselines, but does not fully remove bias. They release method/datasets at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment and frame this as baseline for future LLM opinion alignment research.

Introduction details: Motivation is whether AI/digital twins could vote on behalf of people and faithfully reflect opinions. LLMs generate political discourse but often fail to reflect true diversity of human political viewpoints. Existing opinion modeling mostly prompts with demographics and political affiliations, relying on learned correlations; these methods fail to capture real opinion distributions and are unstable/inconsistent across prompts/demographic groups. Authors seek a preference-consistent approach using an individual’s known opinions rather than demographic proxies.

They argue interview-transcript persona modeling can perform strongly but is too costly to scale. Proposed alternative: political survey data, including American National Election Studies (ANES) and Voting Advice Applications (VAAs), which capture positions on political issues. Surveys lack narrative richness/textual signal but provide structured political opinions across populations. Surveys are common in bias evaluation and group simulation but not widely used for training individual-level political agents.

Method preview: Use RL, specifically GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), motivated by reasoning gains from models such as o3/o4-mini and DeepSeek-R1. Treat opinion formation as a reasoning problem: agent writes a short rationale plus final choice; reward is given when final choice matches respondent’s answer, teaching reasoning toward survey-consistent positions on unseen questions.

Stated contributions: (1) introduce GRPO-based reinforcement learning method encouraging explicit reasoning to improve opinion alignment from survey responses; (2) benchmark on three real-world political datasets/authentic political opinions: German parties, U.S. voters, and Swiss candidates; release them as benchmark; results show reasoning consistently improves opinion alignment; (3) analyze ideological effects by inverting survey answers of individuals with known positions, showing answer inversion improves Left profiles but harms Right profiles.

Figure 1 description: Public opinion surveys used to align LLMs with individual preference profiles. First LLM is fine-tuned with synthetic statements and ground-truth answers to follow a reasoning template. After fine-tuning model uses correct format but is not fully aligned. errors.claim: “X8J benefits from inversion; P7N/A4U worsen on average.”

final_notes:
Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” ETH Zurich.

Core method/results: structured reasoning trained via RL improves profile-consistent political answers across U.S./German/Swiss settings incl unseen questions, but bias remains. Agents generate rationales then choices; reward for matching respondent/party/candidate answers. Preference consistency uses known individual opinions, not demographic proxies. Output schema <reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>stance</answer>. Reward R=.25 E6Z + .01 F2B + 1 G9L; E6Z format max 4, F2B=-|L-L*|, G9L=1 if stance matches observed. V7K=SFT warm start using synthetic CoT demonstrations. QX2=GRPO/PPO-like RL with group-relative normalization. N8R=ORPO. ZP4=SFT+GRPO initialized combination. System prompt only country label.

Datasets: J4Q Swiss candidates: 18 units, train 48/test 12, binary Yes/No; smartvote 2023, 75 items incl 60 policy questions, 12 topics, 3 candidates from each of 6 parties. R2V German parties: 6 units, train official Wahl-O-Mat 2021–2025 / test 30 EU&I 2024 B5X, 3 labels. M8C US ANES 2020: 21 respondents, train 67/test 12, 3 labels; recoding I7V default conservative, O2K aggressive alternative. Spectrum groups: P7N=Left, A4U=Center, X8J=Right.

Table 3 macro-F1 %, T=1, 8 stochastic runs. Untrained baselines: C6W random J4Q 50/R2V 33.33/M8C 33.33; U9F majority 37.43/27.44/22.98. T9A: H3D 55.97/28.17/23.2; N8R 43.53/43.29/34.84; V7K 63.44/48.95/42.77; QX2 55.14/37.29/34.55; ZP4 66.88/52.53/40.66. K6Y: H3D 60.48/26.19/23.2; N8R 23.87/25.25/26.95; V7K 61.08/42.91/35.14; QX2 60.64/31.42/31.47; ZP4 65.11/49.38/38.44. W2E: H3D 66.16/26.19/19.23; N8R 23.31/24.73/24.25; V7K 67.63/51.86/39.15; QX2 60.56/51.00/43.79; ZP4 70.73/53.21/45.43. ZP4 best for J4Q/R2V all backbones; M8C exception: T9A V7K 42.77 > ZP4 40.66; W2E QX2 43.79 > W2E V7K but < ZP4 45.43.

Baselines: C6W=random uniform, U9F=unit training-set modal answer, H3D=ICL contextual comparator using same-topic train Q/A or random subset if context limits; N8R uses Stammbach et al. hyperparameters. Section 4.3 claims ZP4 outperforms naive and V7K except T9A on M8C; comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. J4Q highest, M8C hardest; R2V > M8C due more train samples. Native reasoning support no consistent gain: T9A>K6Y on R2V/M8C, W2E best overall, QX2 trails ZP4. Neutral-containing datasets worse.

Ideology: Figure 3 “Unequal learnability”; F1 error bars within-group variance; detailed appendix retains original parties/ideology groups. ZP4 typically best; every training method underperforms on centrist and right-leaning groups. T9A/ZP4 groupwise F1: J4Q P7N advantage over A4U/X8J; R2V/M8C similar weaker; R2V P7N/A4U roughly equal; M8C lower. V7K averages exceed all other methods for X8J in J4Q/M8C. Possible causes: LLM left tendencies, T9A biases, intrinsic survey-signal learnability. R2V X8J stronger perhaps larger training sets.

Neutral: For M8C, Neutral recall worst for every individual. X8J highest Neutral response rate and most prediction difficulty; A4U also more Neutral. Removing Neutral improves all groups, narrows P7N–A4U differences, improves ZP4 relative to H3D, but P7N–X8J gap remains. O2K reproduces negative performance–Neutral-rate correlation but nearly identical A4U/X8J, so recoding may partly produce disparity. Figure 4: M8C T9A/ZP4 regress Neutral base rate vs F1/accuracy; strong negative significant correlations at 5%; class recall and F1 before/after Neutral removal.

Representation: No overall left shift despite LLM left-libertarian bias; positions shift center-right horizontally and centerward vertically; group-average distortions show overall conservative, negative-y trend without clear left-right bias. X8J individuals become more left-wing; P7N/A4U more right-wing and conservative. J4Q PCA uses Germann et al. political interpretation; agents projected into full candidate population space.

Initialization data: Figure 5 compares T9A/ZP4 F1 under progressive-biased/default/conservative-biased data. Progressive arguments strongly impair X8J with inconsistent P7N effects; conservative arguments impair P7N without consistent X8J gains; adverse bias harms X8J more. Extra argument sets generated by S5Q=Llama 3.3 70B with progressive/conservative prompts. Positional effects agree: underrepresented groups shift most, X8J more than P7N. Conservative-biased and default shifts similar; base-model alignment may drive default centerward displacement. Figure 6 shows biased-data positions and group-mean displacement.

Synthetic positions/inversion: Counterfactual inverts every J4Q answer, trains T9A on flipped train data, and evaluates before/after F1 difference, apparently after flipping both training and test answers. Inversion approximately rotates positions 180° about origin in Fig. 2/Section E.6, converting right-wing to left-wing positions and vice versa. Figure 7: points show original F1; individuals ordered by first J4Q PC; left-most X8J candidate is correctly placed per Fig. 6. P7N worsens individually and on average; X8J improves but average remains below P7N. “Conversion of P7N into X8J does not remove disparity,” interpreted as evidence right-wing learning may be intrinsically harder.

Discussion/conclusion/ethics: Limitations/future: day-to-day respondent variation adds noise, near-1.0 F1 unlikely; per-profile training compute-intensive; suitable surveys scarce. Future: mitigate group disparities; one model conditioned on compact persona representations; confidence estimates via extended reasoning/value head; better questionnaires/uncertainty handling for Neutral. Conclusion: direct known-opinion training of persona-conditioned agents treats answers as structured reasoning; ZP4 generally outperforms baselines across Swiss/German/US, but Neutral prediction is difficult and political-spectrum accuracy varies. Ethics: only anonymized surveys and public figures’ positions used; ideological disparities, centrist/right-wing underperformance and neutral-position difficulty are system risks; authors caution against real-world use until fairness issues resolved and commit to transparent bias reporting.

Reproducibility/final matter: code and datasets released at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment. Documentation said to include training details/hyperparameters, PCA implementation and all PCA results in Section E.5, per-party training counts, recoding definitions, training-sample-size analysis, and inversion details. Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors ETH Zurich.

- LLMs can model individual/group political preferences, but naive prompting yields biased opinions due to statistical operation and limited causal understanding.
- Structured reasoning trained via RL improves profile-consistent answers across U.S., European/German, and Swiss politics, including unseen questions, while remaining competitive with strong baselines.
- Bias remains; additional mechanisms needed for faithful political digital twins.
- Methods/datasets released; possible digital-democracy application.
- “Reasoning consistently improves opinion alignment”: survey-trained agents generate short rationales then choices, rewarded for matching respondent answers.
- Preference consistency uses known individual opinions rather than demographic proxies; interview methods accurate but costly; surveys/VAAs offer scalable preference profiles.
- Contributions include QX2-based explicit reasoning from survey responses; benchmark of German-party, U.S.-voter, Swiss-candidate opinions; answer-inversion analysis: improves P7N profiles but harms X8J profiles.

Related work notes:
- Political personas: demographic, character, individualized; demographic dominates but has representativeness/steerability/consistency limitations.
- N8R = ORPO (odds ratio preference optimization) from Hong et al. (2024).
- Park et al. interviews outperform demographic baselines but limited by transcript availability. Haller et al. use respondents’ QA pairs in context to predict test questions, for bias identification rather than opinion modeling.
- Table 1 example: T9A trained on X8J individual in M8C; before base prompting says No/equal opportunity; after ZP4 reasoning says inequality/opportunity differences inevitable/necessary but basic opportunities matter, final A) Yes. Caption: training changes disagreement to agreement while retaining equal-opportunity arguments under different framing.
- QX2 = GRPO, PPO variant using group-relative reward normalization instead of learned value function; samples multiple outputs per prompt, subtracts reward mean/divides by std.
- Yu et al. persona-based CoT demographic/ideological/temporal prompting calibrated with M8C; no RL; target voting, not general preference profiles.

Method part 3 notes:
- Task: Given policy question q, persona p (respondent or party), stance labels Y={No, Neutral, Yes}, learn p’s stance on q. Example question: government funding for renewable energy.
- QX2 political reasoning: system prompt only contains country label; no explicit persona representation. Training observations D={(p_j,q_i,y*_{ij})}; final stances observed, no reasoning. Agents generate both reasoning and answer in exact schema: <reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>stance</answer>.
- Composite reward: E6Z format/tag placement; F2B length reward; G9L correctness/observed-response agreement. Correctness is primary. Formula: F2B=-|L-L*|, G9L=1[y_i=y_i*], R=alpha1 E6Z + alpha2 F2B + alpha3 G9L. E6Z: 1 per correctly placed tag, 4 tags max=4. F2B max 0 at L=L*. Weights: alpha1=.25, alpha2=.01, alpha3=1.
- Optional supervised warm start V7K=SFT constructs CoT demonstrations in exact rewarded schema (following Shao et al. 2024), to accelerate convergence, improve initial reasoning, reduce format burden, initialize political reasoning. Earlier Figure 1 described initial fine-tuning on synthetic statements and ground-truth answers establishing reasoning template without full opinion alignment.
- Table 2 datasets: J4Q (CH), unit Candidate, 18 units, labels {Yes, No}, train 48 questions, test 12 topic-stratified. Baselines: C6W=random uniform, U9F=unit training-set modal answer, H3D=ICL contextual comparator using same-topic train Q/A or random subset if context limits; N8R uses Stammbach et al. hyperparameters.
