§6.4 Claim 4 few-shot reproduced. Table 2 Flamingo targeted H2Q with shots: shot=0 V9D C8H .6095, Q7X .7708; shot=2 V9D .5730, Q7X .6635. Q7X > V9D on all listed shot=0 and shot=2 task metrics. Perturbations optimized 0-shot and evaluated 2-shot; context shifts make attacks harder, though T4B Q7X rises from .988 to .994.

§6.5.1 Noise Initialization B8N=CroPA+Init on BLIP-2. Text claims B8N consistently outperforms Q7X/V9D across every metric, but internal errors found: Table 3 has B8N below Q7X on unknown A7L/T4B, bomb G9M, very good T4B; Table 4 has B8N T4B .9342 below Q7X .9457. Table 3 C8H: unknown V9D .6095 Q7X .7708 B8N .8977; bomb .7560/.8433/.9260; I am sorry .7318/.7985/.9458; very good .7540/.8190/.8761; too late .7585/.8535/.9333. Table 4 BLIP-2 avg C8H: V9D .7104, Q7X .7958, E3W .370, B8N .9209. Current part adds Y2K target-text/learned-noise feature uptake for “Bomb”: Q7X 21.80, B8N 23.09.

§6.5.2 K3R/Image Augmentation: says unmodified Q7X does not yield effective universality; prompt-directed signals tied to originating image low-level features; weakens original K3R claim. Table 5 untargeted K3R H2Q, best over iterations: Base .3500/.4920/.4000/.5000/C8H .4355; J6T .6560/.7160/.5000/.9500/C8H .7055; U8G .4520/.7240/.5000/.5500/C8H .5565. Text says U8G believed to outperform J6T, but table shows J6T better overall and on most tasks (new error). Base peaks 1700 iters; J6T 1500; U8G 1600.

errors.claim: “Target-text choice strongly influences outcomes relative to input-image-specific features.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: Abstract claims “target semantics/frequency do not determine transferability.”
errors.explanation: The current statement attributes strong influence over outcomes to the target text, while the abstract-level claim says target semantics/frequency do not determine transferability. If “target-text choice” is being used to explain transfer outcomes, this conflicts with the earlier conclusion that target properties do not determine transferability.

steps.notes_before:
Paper title: “Revisiting CroPA: A Reproducibility Study and Enhancements for Cross-Prompt Adversarial Transferability in Vision-Language Models.” Studies/reproduces Luo et al. “An Image is Worth 1000 Lies.” Abstract claims Q7X/CroPA and superiority to existing baselines in N6Z validated; target semantics/frequency do not determine transferability; enhancements: initialization, common/shared perturbations across images, attention-directed loss; evaluation on Flamingo/OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, LLaVA; enhancements consistently increase adversarial effectiveness.

Definitions: F8V = Cross-Model Transferability; K3R = Cross-Image Transferability; N6Z = Cross-Prompt Transferability; Z4P = Universal Adversarial Perturbations. Tasks: A7L/VQA = VQAgeneral, T4B = VQAspecific, G9M = Classification, D5R = Captioning, C8H = Overall. H2Q = ASR. Earlier targeted success = exact target-text generation; untargeted success = departure from clean-image prediction. Internal inconsistency already found in §5.4: transfer evaluation defines success/H2Q as failure to generate correct output/ground truth, conflicting with earlier untargeted definition based on departure from clean prediction.

Related/scope: §2.3 says no credible benchmarks/baselines established for N6Z, but Yang et al. (2024) comparator E3W/CIA exists using gradient perturbations to inject target tokens, unlike Q7X competing-prompt optimization. Watch tension with superiority-to-baselines claims. §3 reproduction tests Claim 1 Q7X achieves N6Z across targets; Claim 2 best aggregate across prompt counts; Claim 3 converges to higher H2Q with iterations; Claim 4 outperforms baselines in few-shot. Extended scope includes F8V, K3R, other N6Z methods.

§4 Methodology: targeted objective min over visual perturbation sum_i L(f(xv+δv, xt^i), T); untargeted max discrepancy from clean. Baselines: R4K = Single-P, V9D = Multi-P. §4.3 evaluation discards prompt perturbations, uses only optimized image perturbation. Q7X/CroPA stated joint min-max: min_δv max_δt L(f(xv+δv, xt+δt),T), image-gradient descent and prompt-gradient ascent PGD, image updates N times per prompt update. Internal inconsistency found: Algorithm 1 initializes/updates x'_t^i but computes both gradients with unperturbed x_t^i and never uses x'_t^i in f.

§5: Opens by saying Q7X performs poorly on G9M/D5R and has limited F8V; S3D optimization raises single-model H2Q but constrains transferability. §5.4 threat models: F8V one image perturbation eliciting specified target text from multiple VLMs independent of prompt; K3R one pattern causing target text for any image/prompt; ε=16/255. But all N6Z/F8V transfer results use untargeted/non-targeted H2Q for between-model/image transfer. E3W excluded from transfer comparisons after negligible transfer.

§5 result claims: Q7X perturbation training on 50 images >6h, 48GB L40S, 95% VRAM. Initialization time/image 20–25s. Initialization aggregate accuracy gains 6–15%; targeted H2Q gains up to 15%. P2F aggregate targeted H2Q 96.85%. P2F increase over base Q7X inconsistently characterized: results 12.5%, discussion 13.5% (error found). P2F A7L +13%, D5R +28%. Value-guided F8V improvement: G9M 14%, D5R 21%. J6T aggregate K3R +approx 27%; U8G net over base K3R Q7X around 12%. §5.1 W5J = Noise Initialization via SDXL target-image feature alignment then S3D MSE to target vision feature. §5.2 P2F/CroPA+D-UAP/re-CroPA adds value-vector term; internal error found: Eq12 L_P2F = L_Q7X − λL_X9C while L_X9C is cosine distance from target, so minimizing maximizes distance. §5.3 U8G = CutMix; J6T = SCMix/common perturbation.

§6: Internal error found: says “Five state-of-the-art VLMs” but lists only OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, LLaVA. §6.1 Claim 1 reproduced: Flamingo/OpenFlamingo Q7X examples transfer across held-out prompts; Table 1 targeted H2Q on Flamingo. Q7X C8H by target: unknown .7708; I am sorry .7985; not sure .5033; very good .7020; too late .6920; metaphor .8680. Q7X underperforms on G9M/D5R for some targets. §6.2 Claim 2 reproduced: Q7X exceeds baselines at equal prompt counts; gains saturate; target unknown. §6.3 Claim 3 reproduced: taskwise convergence unstable; aggregate trend increasing; OpenFlamingo, target unknown.

§6.4 Claim 4 few-shot reproduced. Table 2 Flamingo targeted H2Q with shots: shot=0 V9D C8H .6095, Q7X .7708; shot=2 V9D .5730, Q7X .6635. Q7X > V9D on all listed shot=0 and shot=2 task metrics. Perturbations optimized 0-shot and evaluated 2-shot; context shifts make attacks harder, though T4B Q7X rises from .988 to .994.

§6.5.1 Noise Initialization B8N=CroPA+Init on BLIP-2. Text claims B8N consistently outperforms Q7X/V9D across every metric, but internal errors found: Table 3 has B8N below Q7X on unknown A7L/T4B, bomb G9M, very good T4B; Table 4 has B8N T4B .9342 below Q7X .9457. Table 3 C8H: unknown V9D .6095 Q7X .7708 B8N .8977; bomb .7560/.8433/.9260; I am sorry .7318/.7985/.9458; very good .7540/.8190/.8761; too late .7585/.8535/.9333. Table 4 BLIP-2 avg C8H: V9D .7104, Q7X .7958, E3W .370, B8N .9209. Y2K target-text/learned-noise feature uptake for “Bomb”: Q7X 21.80, B8N 23.09.

§6.5.2 K3R/Image Augmentation: says unmodified Q7X does not yield effective universality; prompt-directed signals tied to originating image low-level features; weakens original K3R claim. Table 5 untargeted K3R H2Q, best over iterations: Base .3500/.4920/.4000/.5000/C8H .4355; J6T .6560/.7160/.5000/.9500/C8H .7055; U8G .4520/.7240/.5000/.5500/C8H .5565. Text says U8G believed to outperform J6T, but table shows J6T better overall and on most tasks (error). Base peaks 1700 iters; J6T 1500; U8G 1600.

§6.5.3 P2F/X9C target value vectors for “Bomb”: Table 6 BLIP2 targeted H2Q: V9D C8H .75, Q7X .8433, E3W .4199, P2F .9685; P2F task values A7L .9420 T4B .9720 G9M .9790 D5R .9810. Table 7 OpenFlamingo: V9D C8H .7638, Q7X .8233, E3W .4380, P2F .9270; P2F task values .9000/.9520/.9500/.9060.

§6.5.4 F8V value guidance: claims significant improvement over vanilla Q7X, especially G9M/D5R, modest VQA gain; BLIP2 perturbations transfer passably to same-encoder InstructBLIP and fail to OpenFlamingo; training on Flamingo transfers insignificantly to other models. Table 8 cross-model tests: P2F beats Q7X and V9D in every listed setting/task. C8H P2F: BLIP2→InstructBLIP .6850, BLIP2→Flamingo .2335, BLIP2→LLaVA .5325; InstructBLIP→BLIP2 .4900, →LLaVA .3558, →Flamingo .1375; Flamingo→BLIP2 .1013, →InstructBLIP .0938, →LLaVA .1025. Current part says value vectors consistent across images and reflect encoder architecture/pretraining; target-text choice strongly influences outcomes relative to input-image-specific features. Potential conflict noted with abstract claim that target semantics/frequency do not determine transferability.

errors.claim: “Experiments across all evaluated benchmarks are described as significantly favoring semantic noise over Q7X and random-initialized baselines.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “§6.5.1 Noise Initialization B8N=CroPA+Init on BLIP-2. Text claims B8N consistently outperforms Q7X/V9D across every metric, but internal errors found: Table 3 has B8N below Q7X on unknown A7L/T4B, bomb G9M, very good T4B; Table 4 has B8N T4B .9342 below Q7X .9457.”
errors.explanation: The discussion’s blanket statement that semantic initialization is favored across all evaluated benchmarks conflicts with reported table entries where B8N/semantic initialization is worse than Q7X on several task metrics.

errors.claim: “Semantic anchoring raises H2Q without sacrificing N6Z.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Table 3 has B8N below Q7X on unknown A7L/T4B, bomb G9M, very good T4B; Table 4 has B8N T4B .9342 below Q7X .9457.”
errors.explanation: If semantic anchoring refers to the noise initialization results, the paper’s own tables show some N6Z/task H2Q values decrease relative to Q7X, so it is not true that H2Q is raised without any sacrifice.

errors.claim: “Computational scarcity repeatedly hindered the successful key-result replication...”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “§6.1 Claim 1 reproduced”; “§6.2 Claim 2 reproduced”; “§6.3 Claim 3 reproduced”; “§6.4 Claim 4 few-shot reproduced.”
errors.explanation: The limitations section suggests key-result replication was hindered or not fully successful, but the results section explicitly says the four main claims/key results were reproduced.

errors.claim: “Due to the relative novelty of this concept, no credible benchmarks/baselines have been established yet.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: Abstract says the study confirms CroPA’s superior cross-prompt transferability “vs baselines.” Introduction contribution says they reproduced the claim that “increasing number of prompts improves transferability but converges rapidly and baselines still do not surpass CroPA.”
errors.explanation: The paper has already described comparisons against baselines for CroPA/cross-prompt transferability, so claiming that no credible baselines have been established is inconsistent with its own earlier framing.

errors.claim: “we extend the scope of CroPA by investigating its efficacy in cross-model and cross-image contexts as well as compare it to other methods in cross-prompt transferability.”
errors.evidence: Earlier Related Works notes: Section 2.3 says “no credible benchmarks/baselines established yet due to novelty,” while also mentioning CIA as an additional comparison.
errors.explanation: This part presents comparison to other cross-prompt methods as part of the study scope, which conflicts with the earlier statement that no credible cross-prompt benchmarks/baselines had been established.

errors.claim: “Given that cross-prompt transferability represents a novel direction in adversarial machine learning, no established baselines exist in current literature.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Section 2.3 says ... Yang et al. (2024) CIA explores cross-prompt transferability via Context Injection Attack and is used as comparison.” Also Section 3 scope says they “compare to other cross-prompt methods.”
errors.explanation: The paper previously identifies an existing cross-prompt attack method from the literature, CIA, and says it is used as a comparison. That conflicts with the claim here that no established baselines exist in the current literature.

errors.claim: Compute gradient for adversarial prompt: g_t = ∇_{x_t} L(f(x'_v, x_t^i), T); Update with gradient ascent: x_t'^i = x_t'^i + α₂·sign(g_t)
errors.evidence: Earlier methodology described CroPA as using learnable prompt perturbations added to the prompt, with objective min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v, x_t+δ_t), T), and Figure 1 says δ_v and δ_t are elementwise added. Algorithm 1 also initializes x_t'^i as the adversarial prompt.
errors.explanation: The algorithm’s prompt gradient is computed on f(x'_v, x_t^i), the unperturbed prompt, while updating x_t'^i. This conflicts with the stated CroPA formulation where the perturbed prompt x_t+δ_t / x_t'^i should be part of the forward pass for the prompt adversary to compete with the image perturbation.

errors.claim: “we derive the initial perturbation by minimizing the following objective: δ_init = argmin... ||f_v(x+δ)-f_v(x_target)||²”
errors.evidence: Immediately after, Section 5.1.4 says: “After initializing the perturbation, we refine the adversarial example using projected gradient descent (PGD)” with “The loss function used during optimization is... L_MSE = ||f_v(x_adv)-f_v(x_target)||².”
errors.explanation: If δ_init is truly the constrained argmin of the same MSE objective, then a subsequent PGD refinement on that identical constrained objective should have no further objective to optimize. The text treats δ_init both as the optimized solution and merely an initialization for later optimization.

errors.claim: “This loss encourages the perturbed image’s value vectors to closely align with the target text’s representation.”
errors.evidence: Eq. 11 defines \(L_{\text{d-UAP}}=\sum_i (1-\cos(V_i(x+\delta),V_t))\), which would encourage alignment if minimized. But Eq. 12 defines \(L_{\text{re-CroPA}}=L_{\text{CroPA}}-\lambda L_{\text{d-UAP}}\), and the text says they “jointly minimize” the losses.
errors.explanation: If the overall objective is minimized, subtracting \(L_{\text{d-UAP}}\) would maximize the distance term \(1-\cos\), pushing value vectors away from the target rather than aligning them. This contradicts the stated purpose of semantic alignment.

errors.claim: “Jointly minimize -ve of this loss along with the CroPA loss” / “By jointly optimizing both losses ... enforces semantic alignment with the target text.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: Section 5.2 said the proposed method would “minimize losses between value vectors of x_i and T_i” and hypothesized alignment with target/reference images. This part’s Eq. 12 subtracts \(\lambda L_{\text{d-UAP}}\) from the CroPA loss.
errors.explanation: The paper’s earlier description says the value-vector loss is minimized for alignment, but the final objective’s sign implies maximizing it under minimization. The optimization direction is internally inconsistent.

errors.claim: “The attacker aims to generate a single perturbation pattern that, when applied to any image, causes a VLM to output a predetermined target text regardless of the input prompt or image content.”
errors.evidence: The same section’s Evaluation Setup says: “Success is measured by the ASR across different task types. A successful attack causes the model to fail to generate the correct output text…” Sec. 5.4.3 further says: “we present all cross-prompt and cross-model transferability results under the untargeted attack setting” and “the evaluation of the transferability between models and between images through non-targeted ASR…”
errors.explanation: The stated adversary goal is targeted, requiring a predetermined target text, but the evaluation and rationale define success as untargeted failure to produce the correct output. These are different attack objectives.

errors.claim: “Furthermore, we excluded CIA when comparing transferability…”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record that Sec. 2.3 says CIA “explores cross-prompt transferability and is used as comparison,” and the scope says the paper will “compare to other cross-prompt methods.”
errors.explanation: Earlier the paper presented CIA as a comparison method for cross-prompt transferability, but here it says CIA was excluded when comparing transferability. Unless the paper distinguishes different transferability comparisons, these statements conflict.

errors.claim: “we evaluated five state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs): OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP and LLaVA.”
errors.evidence: The sentence says “five” models but names only four: “OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP and LLaVA.”
errors.explanation: This is an internal numerical/list inconsistency within the same sentence.

errors.claim: “Claim 3: CroPA converges towards higher ASR as number of iterations increase [Reproduced]”
errors.evidence: Section 6.3 states: “Our obtained results ... resulted in contrasting results with respect to the original reported metrics of convergence with higher number of iterations ... While this certainly is the trend observed with the overall ASR across tasks ... when we investigated the ASR convergence for each task’s use case, individually the trend is prone to instability.”
errors.explanation: The section heading claims the convergence finding is reproduced, but the text says their results contrast with the original convergence metrics and are unstable at individual task level. The paper only supports the overall ASR trend, not the broad reproduced claim as stated.

errors.claim: “higher number of iterations” / “number of iterations increase” as the convergence variable in Claim 3
errors.location: this part, Section 6.3 heading and text
errors.evidence: The same paragraph says: “Where the original metrics showed CroPA converging with higher number of prompts.”
errors.explanation: Section 6.3 describes the claim as convergence with increasing iterations, but then says the original metrics concerned convergence with higher number of prompts. Iterations and prompts are different experimental variables, so the claim is internally inconsistent.

errors.claim: "CroPA+Init consistently outperforms both CroPA and Multi-P across all metrics"
errors.evidence: Table 3 has several metrics where CroPA+Init is lower: for target "unknown", CroPA+Init VQAgeneral 0.8824 and VQAspecific 0.8920 are below CroPA 0.9680 and 0.9880; for target "bomb", CroPA+Init Classification 0.9020 is below CroPA 0.9498 and Multi-P 0.9050; for target "very good", CroPA+Init VQAspecific 0.8894 is below CroPA 0.8990.
errors.explanation: The table supports higher overall ASR for CroPA+Init, but not consistent superiority across all per-task metrics.

errors.claim: "Table 3 ... achieving 6-15% gains in overall accuracy"
errors.evidence: Table 3 reports targeted ASRs, not accuracy: caption says "Targeted ASRs on Blip2". For target "very good", CroPA+Init overall is 0.8761 vs CroPA 0.8190, an absolute gain of 0.0571, i.e. 5.71 percentage points, below 6 percentage points.
errors.explanation: The text mislabels ASR as accuracy, and the stated 6–15% overall gain is not true as an absolute percentage-point range for all listed targets.

errors.claim: “We believe CutMix outperforms SCMix in promoting adversarial transferability...”
errors.evidence: Table 5 reports CroPA with SCMix: VQA 0.6560, VQAspecific 0.7160, Classification 0.5000, Captioning 0.9500, Overall 0.7055; CroPA with CutMix: VQA 0.4520, VQAspecific 0.7240, Classification 0.5000, Captioning 0.5500, Overall 0.5565.
errors.explanation: The table shows SCMix has a substantially higher overall ASR and is higher on VQA and Captioning, tied on Classification, with CutMix only slightly higher on VQAspecific. This contradicts the claim that CutMix outperforms SCMix.

errors.claim: “Our results in Tables 6 and 7 demonstrate… [CroPA+D-UAP] … give an overall ASR of 96.85%”
errors.evidence: Table 6 reports CroPA+D-UAP Overall = 0.9685, but Table 7 reports CroPA+D-UAP Overall = 0.9270.
errors.explanation: The 96.85% overall ASR applies only to Table 6 on BLIP-2, not to Tables 6 and 7 collectively or to Table 7 on OpenFlamingo.

errors.claim: “The method also presents a strong case for increasing cross-model transferability… especially in Classification and Captioning tasks (14% and 21% respectively)”
errors.evidence: In Table 8, for BLIP2→InstructBLIP CroPA+D-UAP improves over CroPA by 0.208 in Classification and 0.273 in Captioning; for BLIP2→Flamingo by 0.024 and 0.206; for BLIP2→LLaVA by 0.165 and 0.476; for InstructBLIP→BLIP2 by 0.283 and 0.273; for InstructBLIP→LLaVA by 0.227 and 0.272; for InstructBLIP→Flamingo by 0.071 and 0.082.
errors.explanation: The stated 14% and 21% improvements do not match the per-setting differences in Table 8. Even averaging the listed settings gives roughly 16.3% for Classification and 26.4% for Captioning, not 14% and 21%.

errors.claim: “[CroPA+D-UAP] … failing to transfer to OpenFlamingo” / Flamingo ASR is “insignificant”
errors.evidence: Table 8 reports BLIP2→Flamingo CroPA+D-UAP Overall = 0.2335, higher than CroPA = 0.1435 and Multi-P = 0.0780; Captioning is 0.3880. It also reports InstructBLIP→Flamingo CroPA+D-UAP Overall = 0.1375, higher than CroPA = 0.0598 and Multi-P = 0.0190.
errors.explanation: Although transfer to Flamingo is weaker than to some other models, Table 8 shows nonzero and improved transfer, so describing it as failing or insignificant overstates and conflicts with the table.

errors.claim: “This can limit transferability to model’s having the same or similar architectural design of the Vision Encoder… verified in Table 8”
errors.evidence: Table 8 reports BLIP2→LLaVA CroPA+D-UAP Overall = 0.5325, close to BLIP2→InstructBLIP Overall = 0.6850 and higher than InstructBLIP→BLIP2 Overall = 0.4900; InstructBLIP→LLaVA Overall = 0.3558 is also higher than transfer to Flamingo.
errors.explanation: The table does not cleanly verify transfer only to same/similar vision encoders: BLIP2→LLaVA transfer is substantial despite LLaVA not being identified in the paper’s earlier architecture grouping as sharing BLIP2/InstructBLIP’s fusion-based architecture.

errors.claim: Cross-model transferability results are presented here as targeted ASRs using target text “Bomb” / D-UAP target-text framing
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from Sec. 5.4.3: “all cross-prompt and cross-model transferability results presented under untargeted setting due architecture differences”; Sec. 5.4.1 also conflicted by saying D-UAP goal is target text but evaluation uses failure/correctness.
errors.explanation: This part presents D-UAP experiments as targeted ASR with target text “Bomb” and then analyzes cross-model transferability, which conflicts with the earlier methodological statement that cross-model transferability results are untargeted.

errors.claim: “across all evaluated benchmarks, our noise initialization method significantly outperformed both CroPA and random-initialized baselines”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes on Sec. 6.5.1/Table 3–4: “exceptions: unknown Init lower than CroPA on VQAgeneral/VQAspecific; bomb Init classification below CroPA/Multi-P; very good Init VQAspecific below CroPA; ... Table 4 ... CroPA VQAspecific 0.9457 > Init 0.9342.”
errors.explanation: The discussion claims the initialization method outperformed CroPA on all evaluated benchmarks, but the reported tables include several benchmark/task cases where CroPA or Multi-P scored higher.

errors.claim: “yielding up to 15% gains in Targeted ASR” / “an 13.5% improvement over the base CroPA method” for D-UAP
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: Sec. 6.5.1 Table 4 shows CroPA+Init overall 0.9209 vs CroPA 0.7958, a gain of 12.51 percentage points, though some individual Table 3 rows had 6–15% gains. Sec. 6.5.3 Table 6 shows CroPA+D-UAP 0.9685 vs CroPA 0.8433, a gain of 0.1252 = 12.52 percentage points; notes say prior text reported this as 12.5%.
errors.explanation: For D-UAP, the stated 13.5% improvement conflicts with the table values, which show about 12.5 percentage points. For initialization, the broad summary is imprecise if referring to overall ASR, since the overall gain is about 12.5 points rather than 15.

errors.claim: “we have substantiated the original claims” / “Our experiments confirmed that CroPA achieves strong cross-prompt transferability across diverse tasks ... consistently outperforming baseline methods.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Sec 6.3 heading says convergence as iterations increase, but text says original convergence metrics not reproduced; individual tasks unstable.” Also notes on Sec. 6.1: “Authors state CroPA underperforms for Classification/Captioning, esp. abstract texts.”
errors.explanation: This discussion overstates the reproducibility findings. Earlier results said the convergence metrics were not reproduced, and at least some task/target settings were described as CroPA underperforming rather than consistently outperforming.

errors.claim: “While this improves cross-model transferability between architecturally similar models (e.g., BLIP-2 and InstructBLIP), the overall improvement is greater between fundamentally different architectures (e.g., BLIP-2 and Flamingo).”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes on Table 8: BLIP2→InstructBLIP CroPA .5065, D-UAP .6850, improvement +.1785; BLIP2→Flamingo CroPA .1435, D-UAP .2335, improvement +.0900. InstructBLIP→BLIP2 improvement +.2612, while InstructBLIP→Flamingo improvement +.0777.
errors.explanation: The table values show larger D-UAP gains between architecturally similar BLIP-2/InstructBLIP pairs than between BLIP-2/InstructBLIP and Flamingo, contradicting the claim that improvement is greater between fundamentally different architectures such as BLIP-2 and Flamingo.

errors.claim: “By anchoring perturbations to semantically meaningful initializations, we can achieve higher ASRs without sacrificing cross-prompt transferability.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes on Table 4: CroPA VQAspecific 0.9457 > CroPA+Init 0.9342. Earlier notes on Table 3 also record exceptions: unknown Init lower than CroPA on VQAgeneral/VQAspecific; bomb Init classification below CroPA/Multi-P; very good Init VQAspecific below CroPA.
errors.explanation: Although initialization improves overall ASR, the paper’s own tables show several cases where CroPA+Init has lower cross-prompt ASR than CroPA, so it is not consistently achieved without sacrificing cross-prompt transferability.

errors.claim: “we were successfully able to reproduce the key results of CroPA”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Sec 6.3 heading says convergence as iterations increase, but text says original convergence metrics not reproduced; individual tasks unstable.” Also: “Contributions include reproducing four original claims… [including] convergence.”
errors.explanation: The paper earlier identified convergence as one of the original CroPA claims to reproduce, but Sec. 6.3 reportedly says the original convergence metrics were not reproduced. Thus the blanket claim that the key results were successfully reproduced overstates/conflicts with the reported results.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Revisiting CroPA: A Reproducibility Study and Enhancements for Cross-Prompt Adversarial Transferability in Vision-Language Models.” Abstract/intro claim reproducibility of Luo et al./CroPA, validating superior cross-prompt transferability vs baselines, plus improvements: initialization, cross-image/universal perturbations, target value-vector loss, extended models incl. LLaVA. Contributions include reproducing four original claims: superior cross-prompt transferability; independence from semantic meaning/word frequency; increasing prompt count improves transferability but converges rapidly; few-shot; convergence. Related/Scope: Sec 2.3 says CroPA pioneered cross-prompt transferability and no credible baselines due novelty, but Yang et al. 2024 CIA explores cross-prompt transferability and is later used as comparison. Earlier text says CIA excluded when comparing transferability because negligible/model-specific, yet Sec 6.5.1 and later include CIA in Tables 4, 6, 7. Part 19 says cross-model transferability comparisons do not include CIA because inherently non-transferable; consistent with Table 8 having no CIA but contrasts with CIA inclusion in other evaluations.

Methodology: targeted attack minimizes sum_i L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t^i),T), exact target text ASR. Non-targeted maximizes discrepancy from clean/correct output; success if output differs/fails correct. Section 4 Methodology so far: Problem formulation: VLM f with image x_v and text x_t; image perturbation δ_v constrained by ||δ_v||_p ≤ ε_v. Two attack scenarios reproduced: targeted attack generates target text T regardless of prompt, minimizing sum_i L(f(x_v+δ_v, x_t^i), T); non-targeted maximizes discrepancy between adversarial and clean outputs, max sum_i L(f(x_v+δ_v, x_t^i), f(x_v, x_t^i)). ASR: targeted requires exact target text; non-targeted succeeds if output differs from clean prediction. Baselines: Section 4.2 says no established baselines exist in literature, so they use Luo et al.’s Single-P and Multi-P. Single-P optimizes perturbation for one prompt: min L(f(x_v+δ_v,x_t),T). CroPA: learnable prompt perturbations compete with image perturbations; δ_v minimizes target loss, δ_t maximizes it, formal min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v, x_t+δ_t),T). errors.explanation: This part says no credible benchmarks or baselines exist for N6Z, but earlier parts framed the study as validating Q7X against existing N6Z baselines and reproducing its superiority. Those claims cannot both be true without qualification.

errors.explanation: Saying the study compares to other N6Z methods implies such methods/baselines exist, contradicting the earlier statement that no credible N6Z benchmarks or baselines have been established.

errors.claim: “The reference attacks introduced by Luo et al. (2024), absent established N6Z baselines…”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: Abstract claims Q7X’s “superiority to existing baselines in N6Z”; intro says replication tests include “superiority across target texts” and §3 says extended scope includes “comparison to other N6Z methods.” Related works §2.3 also made the same “No credible benchmarks or baselines have yet been established” claim, already conflicting with those statements.
errors.explanation: The paper simultaneously says there are no established N6Z baselines and that it compares Q7X against existing/other N6Z baselines or methods.

errors.claim: “The competing-prompt method … jointly optimizes δv and δt” and Eq. (5) uses f(xv+δv, xt+δt).
errors.evidence: Algorithm 1 computes image and prompt gradients using the unperturbed prompt: line 7 “gv = ∇xv L(f(x′v, xti), T)” and line 10 “gt = ∇xt L(f(x′v, xti), T)”; line 11 updates “x′ti”, but no later line uses x′ti in the forward pass.
errors.explanation: The described objective requires the adversarial prompt perturbation to affect optimization, but the algorithm as written never feeds the updated prompt x′ti into the model. Thus the prompt perturbation is updated but unused, contradicting the claimed joint/min-max optimization.

errors.claim: “Q7X performs poorly on G9M and D5R”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: Abstract claims Q7X/CroPA superiority to existing baselines in N6Z; Intro says image attacks remain effective regardless of textual input across G9M, D5R, VQA; Scope Claim 2 says Q7X has best aggregate performance across prompt counts.
errors.explanation: The paper previously characterized Q7X/CroPA as effective/superior across tasks including G9M and D5R, but this part states that Q7X performs poorly on exactly G9M and D5R without qualification.

errors.claim: “P2F increase over base Q7X” is listed as both “12.5%” and “13.5%”
errors.evidence: The table contains two rows: “P2F increase over base Q7X, results characterization | 12.5%” and “P2F increase over base Q7X, discussion characterization | 13.5%”.
errors.explanation: The same increase over base Q7X is assigned two different numerical values in the same table. Labeling them as results vs discussion characterizations does not reconcile the discrepancy.

errors.claim: “The loss is described as encouraging closeness to the target representation” and the method “jointly minimizes its negative with the Q7X loss.”
errors.evidence: Eq. (11) defines \(L_{\mathrm{X9C}}=\sum_i(1-\cos(V_i(x+\delta),V_t))\), so closeness to \(V_t\) requires minimizing \(L_{\mathrm{X9C}}\). But Eq. (12) defines \(L_{\mathrm{P2F}}=L_{\mathrm{Q7X}}-\lambda L_{\mathrm{X9C}}\).
errors.explanation: If the combined objective is minimized, subtracting \(L_{\mathrm{X9C}}\) encourages maximizing the distance from the target representation, not closeness to it. The equation’s sign conflicts with the textual description of target-representation alignment.

errors.claim: “All N6Z and F8V transferability results are presented under untargeted attacks.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record §5 quantitative results as including targeted transfer results: “targeted H2Q gains up to 15%; P2F aggregate targeted H2Q 96.85%; P2F increase over base Q7X ...; P2F A7L +13%, D5R +28%; value-guided F8V G9M +14%, D5R +21%.”
errors.explanation: This part says all N6Z and F8V transferability results are untargeted, but earlier reported results in the same section included targeted H2Q and targeted gains, including F8V/value-guided results.

errors.claim: “Five state-of-the-art VLMs were evaluated: OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, and LLaVA.”
errors.evidence: The sentence says five models but lists only four: “OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, and LLaVA.”
errors.explanation: The count contradicts the enumerated models in the same sentence.

errors.claim: “The Flamingo test measures targeted H2Q.” / Table 1 is “Targeted H2Q on Flamingo…”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from §5.4.3: “all N6Z and F8V transferability results are under untargeted attacks,” and §5.4 described F8V/K3R/N6Z scoring as untargeted success/failure to generate correct output.
errors.explanation: This part reports the N6Z/Flamingo reproduction as targeted H2Q, conflicting with the earlier blanket statement that all N6Z transferability results are under untargeted attacks.

errors.claim: “Increasing prompt counts raises H2Q for all methods; R4K intrinsically uses one prompt, making the count variation redundant for it.”
errors.evidence: The same sentence says prompt-count increases raise H2Q “for all methods,” but then says R4K uses only one prompt, so varying prompt count is redundant for it; Figure 4 description also says “R4K is the lone star.”
errors.explanation: If R4K has no meaningful prompt-count variation, then increasing prompt count cannot raise H2Q for all methods including R4K.

errors.claim: “B8N = CroPA+Init is reported to outperform Q7X and V9D consistently across every metric”
errors.evidence: Table 3: for target “unknown,” Q7X has A7L 0.9680 and T4B 0.9880, while B8N has A7L 0.8824 and T4B 0.8920. For “bomb,” Q7X has G9M 0.9498 and V9D has G9M 0.9050, while B8N has G9M 0.9020. Table 4: Q7X has T4B 0.9457 while B8N has T4B 0.9342.
errors.explanation: The tables show several metrics where B8N does not outperform Q7X and even one where it is below both Q7X and V9D, so the claim of consistent superiority across every metric is contradicted by the reported results.

errors.claim: “U8G is believed to outperform J6T for adversarial transfer...”
errors.evidence: Table 5 shows Q7X with J6T has higher H2Q than Q7X with U8G on VQA/A7L (0.6560 vs 0.4520), D5R (0.9500 vs 0.5500), and C8H (0.7055 vs 0.5565), with equal G9M (0.5000 vs 0.5000). U8G is higher only on T4B (0.7240 vs 0.7160).
errors.explanation: The table directly contradicts the claim that U8G outperforms J6T overall; J6T is better on the aggregate and most tasks.

errors.claim: “Experiments across all evaluated benchmarks are described as significantly favoring semantic noise over Q7X and random-initialized baselines.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from §6.5.1: “Text claims B8N outperforms Q7X/V9D consistently across every metric, but tables contradict: Table 3 unknown A7L/T4B B8N .8824/.8920 < Q7X .968/.988; bomb G9M B8N .9020 < Q7X .9498 and V9D .9050; very good T4B B8N .8894 < Q7X .8990; Table 4 average T4B B8N .9342 < Q7X .9457.”
errors.explanation: The discussion repeats an across-all-benchmarks superiority claim for semantic initialization, but the paper’s own tables show several metrics/benchmarks where B8N is worse than Q7X or V9D.

errors.claim: “X9C … improves related-architecture transfer, BLIP-2 to InstructBLIP, but offers greater aggregate gains across fundamentally different architectures, BLIP-2 to Flamingo.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from Table 8: “BLIP2→InstructBLIP V9D .2270/Q7X .5065/P2F .6850; BLIP2→Flamingo .0780/.1435/.2335.”
errors.explanation: The stated greater gain for BLIP-2→Flamingo is contradicted by the reported C8H improvements: P2F improves over Q7X by .1785 for BLIP-2→InstructBLIP but only .0900 for BLIP-2→Flamingo.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Revisiting CroPA: A Reproducibility Study and Enhancements for Cross-Prompt Adversarial Transferability in Vision-Language Models.” Reproduction/extension of Luo et al. “An Image is Worth 1000 Lies.” Claims validate Q7X/CroPA and superiority to baselines in N6Z; semantic meaning and target-word frequency do not determine transferability; extensions include initialization, common perturbations across images, attention/value-vector losses; evaluates OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, LLaVA; enhancements generally increase adversarial effectiveness.

Key terms: F8V = Cross-Model Transferability; K3R = Cross-Image Transferability/shared perturbations; N6Z = Cross-Prompt Transferability; Z4P = Universal Adversarial Perturbations. Tasks: G9M/classification, D5R/captioning, A7L=VQAgeneral, T4B=VQAspecific. H2Q = ASR. S3D = PGD. E3W = Context Injection/CIA comparator. R4K = Single-P baseline; V9D = Multi-P baseline.

Internal issues recorded earlier: §2.3/§4.2 say no established N6Z baselines, conflicting with abstract/intro/§3 claims about baselines/comparison to other N6Z methods. Algorithm 1 initializes/updates x′t but line 7/10 use xt, so prompt perturbation never used despite joint min-max objective. §5 says Q7X performs poorly on G9M/D5R and has limited F8V, in tension with broad effectiveness/superiority claims. P2F increase over base Q7X inconsistently listed as 12.5% and 13.5%. P2F loss text says encourages closeness to target representation, but formula L_P2F=L_Q7X−λL_X9C, minimized, maximizes L_X9C and pushes value vectors apart. K3R goal stated as predetermined target text for any image, but evaluation described as untargeted failure. §5.4.3 says all N6Z and F8V transferability results are untargeted, conflicting with targeted H2Q tables. §6 opening says five VLMs but lists four. §6.2 says increasing prompt counts raises H2Q for all methods although R4K uses one prompt. 

§6.1 Flamingo targeted H2Q: Q7X best every row; C8H Q7X unknown .7708, I am sorry .7985, not sure .5033, very good .7020, too late .6920, metaphor .8680. §6.4 few-shot: Q7X exceeds V9D all listed metrics at 0/2-shot; Q7X drops from 0 to 2 shot on A7L/G9M/D5R/C8H, T4B rises slightly.

§6.5.1 Noise Initialization B8N=CroPA+Init on BLIP-2. Text/discussion claim B8N outperforms Q7X/V9D across every/all benchmarks, but tables contradict: unknown A7L/T4B B8N .8824/.8920 < Q7X .968/.988; bomb G9M B8N .9020 < Q7X .9498 and V9D .9050; very good T4B B8N .8894 < Q7X .8990; average T4B B8N .9342 < Q7X .9457. Average C8H: V9D .7104, Q7X .7958, E3W .370, B8N .9209; B8N best on A7L/G9M/D5R/C8H but not T4B. Feature uptake Y2K for “Bomb”: Q7X 21.80, B8N 23.09; discussion calls it modest, not significant semantic-feature upgrade.

§6.5.2 K3R: unmodified Q7X not universal; Q7X prompt robustness not image-transfer. Table 5 untargeted best C8H: Base Q7X .4355; J6T .7055; U8G .5565. J6T higher overall and most tasks, although text says U8G believed to outperform J6T. Discussion correctly says J6T improves K3R, U8G also improves base; augmentation alone does not solve limitation.

§6.5.3 P2F/value vectors: BLIP2 targeted “Bomb” Table 6: V9D C8H .75, Q7X .8433, E3W .4199, P2F .9685; P2F task scores .9420/.9720/.9790/.9810. OpenFlamingo Table 7: V9D .7638, Q7X .8233, E3W .4380, P2F .9270. Text says P2F especially improves A7L/D5R.

§6.5.4 F8V Table 8: P2F exceeds Q7X and V9D in every listed cross-model row/task. C8H: BLIP2→InstructBLIP V9D .2270/Q7X .5065/P2F .6850; BLIP2→Flamingo .0780/.1435/.2335; BLIP2→LLaVA .0930/.3040/.5325; InstructBLIP→BLIP2 .1183/.2288/.4900; InstructBLIP→LLaVA .0505/.1345/.3558; InstructBLIP→Flamingo .0190/.0598/.1375; Flamingo→BLIP2 .0105/.0335/.1013; Flamingo→InstructBLIP .0075/.0290/.0938; Flamingo→LLaVA .0150/.0370/.1025. Discussion §7.4.1 claims greater aggregate gains for fundamentally different BLIP2→Flamingo than related BLIP2→InstructBLIP, but C8H gains over Q7X are smaller for Flamingo (.09) than InstructBLIP (.1785). §6.5.4 says BLIP2→OpenFlamingo fails/pass weakly; Flamingo-trained perturbations insignificant. Discussion says X9C robust to harmful text/guardrail activation and E3W inherently non-transferable.

§7 limitations: computational scarcity hindered replication/ablations; no author communication; GitHub issue unresolved.

Key terms: F8V = Cross-Model Transferability / architectural survival; K3R = Cross-Image Transferability / survival over multiple images, allowing shared perturbations; N6Z = Cross-Prompt Transferability / effectiveness over varying textual prompts; Z4P = Universal Adversarial Perturbations / shared perturbations rather than per-image optimized perturbations. Tasks: image G9M, D5R, VQA. H2Q = Attack Success Rate/ASR. S3D = PGD. E3W = Context Injection/Contextual Injection Attack/CIA comparator. R4K = Single-P baseline; V9D = Multi-P baseline.

Intro/Scope: Luo et al. introduced N6Z and competing learnable prompts; image attacks remain effective regardless of textual input across G9M, D5R, VQA. Reproduction claims: Q7X achieves N6Z across target texts; best aggregate performance across prompt counts; converges to higher H2Q with more iterations; outperforms baselines in few-shot settings. Extended scope includes F8V, K3R, comparison to other N6Z methods.

Related/method: §2.3 and §4.2 claim no established N6Z baselines, conflicting with abstract/intro/§3 claims about existing baselines and comparison to other N6Z methods. Targeted success = exact target text; untargeted success = departure from clean prediction. Eq(1) targeted minimizes summed LM loss over prompts; Eq(2) untargeted maximizes loss vs clean prediction. §4.2 baselines: Single-P/R4K, Multi-P/V9D. §4.3 Q7X/CroPA discards prompt perturbations at evaluation; joint minδv maxδt objective. Internal issue: Algorithm 1 initializes/updates x′t but line 7/10 use xt, so prompt perturbation never used despite joint/min-max objective.

§5 Additional Investigative Experiments: starts by saying Q7X performs poorly on G9M and D5R and has limited F8V; conflicts with prior broad effectiveness/superiority claims. Says S3D raises single-model H2Q but model-loss feedback constrains transferability; original authors recognize this; Appendix Table 9 verifies. Extensions address task inconsistency and transfer dimensions; K3R could remove per-image training; F8V could improve efficiency; transfer exploration not core proposal of Luo et al. Quantitative table: Q7X perturbation training on 50 images >6h on 48GB L40S at 95% VRAM; added initialization 20–25s per image on single GPU; initialization aggregate accuracy gains 6–15%; targeted H2Q gains up to 15%; P2F aggregate targeted H2Q 96.85%; P2F increase over base Q7X inconsistently listed as 12.5% results characterization and 13.5% discussion characterization; P2F A7L +13%, D5R +28%; value-guided F8V G9M +14%, D5R +21%; J6T aggregate K3R +~27%; U8G net increase over base K3R Q7X ~12%.

§5.1 W5J = Noise Initialization via Vision Encoding Optimization: replaces random noise with diffusion/target-image feature alignment. Hypothesis: semantic initialization improves attack efficacy under imperceptibility. Uses SDXL to synthesize target image x_target = D(T,z;θ_SDXL) (Eq6). δ_init minimizes ||fv(x+δ)-fv(x_target)||² under L∞ ε (Eq7). S3D refinement Eq8 projects gradient step minimizing L6V/MSE Eq9 = encoder-feature distance to target image. Method said to strengthen perturbations/N6Z and reduce convergence steps; preliminary BLIP-2/InstructBLIP favor semantic over random noise.

§5.2 value-vector guidance/F8V: targets middle-to-late vision-layer value vectors as vulnerable components; claims Q7X treats vision/language uniformly and lacks encoder-backbone sensitivity. Adapts Kim et al. 2024 X9C/Doubly-UAP/D-UAP component-selection loss for Z4P by minimizing, rather than maximizing, losses between value vectors of xi and Ti, retaining target-text reference.

errors.claim: “The loss is described as encouraging closeness to the target representation” and the method “jointly minimizes its negative with the Q7X loss.”
errors.evidence: Eq. (11) defines \(L_{\mathrm{X9C}}=\sum_i(1-\cos(V_i(x+\delta),V_t))\), so closeness to \(V_t\) requires minimizing \(L_{\mathrm{X9C}}\). But Eq. (12) defines \(L_{\mathrm{P2F}}=L_{\mathrm{Q7X}}-\lambda L_{\mathrm{X9C}}\).
errors.explanation: If the combined objective is minimized, subtracting \(L_{\mathrm{X9C}}\) encourages maximizing the distance from the target representation, not closeness to it. The equation’s sign conflicts with the textual description of target-representation alignment.

errors.claim: “Five state-of-the-art VLMs were evaluated: OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, and LLaVA.”
errors.evidence: The sentence says five models but lists only four: “OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, and LLaVA.”
errors.explanation: The count contradicts the enumerated models in the same sentence.

errors.claim: “The Flamingo test measures targeted H2Q.” / Table 1 is “Targeted H2Q on Flamingo…”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from §5.4.3: “all N6Z and F8V transferability results are under untargeted attacks,” and §5.4 described F8V/K3R/N6Z scoring as untargeted success/failure to generate correct output.
errors.explanation: This part reports the N6Z/Flamingo reproduction as targeted H2Q, conflicting with the earlier blanket statement that all N6Z transferability results are under untargeted attacks.

errors.claim: “Increasing prompt counts raises H2Q for all methods; R4K intrinsically uses one prompt, making the count variation redundant for it.”
errors.evidence: The same sentence says prompt-count increases raise H2Q “for all methods,” but then says R4K uses only one prompt, so varying prompt count is redundant for it; Figure 4 description also says “R4K is the lone star.”
errors.explanation: If R4K has no meaningful prompt-count variation, then increasing prompt count cannot raise H2Q for all methods including R4K.

Paper title: “Revisiting CroPA: A Reproducibility Study and Enhancements for Cross-Prompt Adversarial Transferability in Vision-Language Models.” Reproduction/extension of Luo et al. “An Image is Worth 1000 Lies.” Abstract claims validate Q7X/CroPA and superiority to baselines in N6Z; semantic meaning and target-word frequency do not determine transferability; extensions include initialization, common perturbations across images, attention-directed/value loss; evaluates OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, LLaVA; enhancements consistently increase adversarial effectiveness.

Key terms: F8V = Cross-Model Transferability; K3R = Cross-Image Transferability/shared perturbations; N6Z = Cross-Prompt Transferability; Z4P = Universal Adversarial Perturbations. Tasks: image G9M/classification, D5R/captioning, VQA split into A7L=VQAgeneral and T4B=VQAspecific. H2Q = ASR. S3D = PGD. E3W = Context Injection/CIA comparator. R4K = Single-P baseline; V9D = Multi-P baseline.

Intro/Scope: Luo et al. introduced N6Z and competing learnable prompts; image attacks remain effective regardless of textual input across G9M, D5R, VQA. Reproduction claims: Q7X achieves N6Z across target texts; best aggregate performance across prompt counts; converges to higher H2Q with more iterations; outperforms baselines in few-shot settings. Extended scope includes F8V, K3R, comparison to other N6Z methods.

Related/method: §2.3 and §4.2 claim no established N6Z baselines, conflicting with abstract/intro/§3 claims about existing baselines/comparison to other N6Z methods. Targeted success = exact target text; untargeted success = departure from clean prediction. Eq(1) targeted minimizes summed LM loss over prompts; Eq(2) untargeted maximizes loss vs clean prediction. §4.2 baselines: Single-P/R4K, Multi-P/V9D. §4.3 Q7X/CroPA discards prompt perturbations at evaluation; joint minδv maxδt objective. Internal issue: Algorithm 1 initializes/updates x′t but line 7/10 use xt, so prompt perturbation never used despite joint/min-max objective.

§5 Additional Investigative Experiments: starts by saying Q7X performs poorly on G9M and D5R and has limited F8V, in tension with broad effectiveness/superiority claims. Says S3D raises single-model H2Q but model-loss feedback constrains transferability; Appendix Table 9 verifies. Extensions address task inconsistency and transfer dimensions; K3R could remove per-image training; F8V could improve efficiency. Quant table: Q7X perturbation training on 50 images >6h on 48GB L40S at 95% VRAM; initialization 20–25s/image; initialization aggregate accuracy gains 6–15%; targeted H2Q gains up to 15%; P2F aggregate targeted H2Q 96.85%; P2F increase over base Q7X inconsistently listed as 12.5% and 13.5%; P2F A7L +13%, D5R +28%; value-guided F8V G9M +14%, D5R +21%; J6T aggregate K3R +~27%; U8G net increase over base K3R Q7X ~12%.

§5.1 W5J: semantic/diffusion target-image initialization via SDXL and CLIP/vision feature distance; S3D refinement. §5.2 value-vector guidance/F8V: X9C/D-UAP maximizes loss between original and perturbed value vectors; P2F/re-CroPA uses L_P2F=L_Q7X−λL_X9C. Text says encourages closeness to target representation, but minimizing with minus sign maximizes L_X9C and pushes away. §5.3 K3R via augmentation: J6T/SCMix and U8G/CutMix for universal perturbations.

§5.4 threat models: F8V optimizes one image perturbation on surrogate BLIP-2 or Flamingo with gradients/internal reps, target params unavailable; ε=16/255 L∞. K3R goal stated as one pattern causing predetermined target text for any image/content/prompt, but evaluation described as untargeted failure on unseen images. §5.4.3 says all N6Z and F8V transferability results are under untargeted attacks, conflicting with earlier/later targeted H2Q results.

§6 Results: opening says “Five” VLMs evaluated but lists four: OpenFlamingo-9B, BLIP-2 OPT-2.7b, InstructBLIP Vicuna-7b, LLaVA Vicuna-13B. §6.1 Claim 1 reproduced: Q7X achieves N6Z across target texts; Flamingo targeted H2Q table. Q7X best every row; C8H Q7X: unknown .7708, I am sorry .7985, not sure .5033, very good .7020, too late .6920, metaphor .8680. §6.2 Claim 2: says increasing prompt counts raises H2Q for all methods but R4K uses one prompt, making count variation redundant—self-conflict. §6.3 Claim 3: taskwise convergence unstable; aggregate increasing-iteration trend follows original.

§6.4 Claim 4 few-shot: Table 2 Flamingo? targeted H2Q with shot=0 vs shot=2, optimized 0-shot and evaluated 2-shot. V9D/Q7X. shot0 Q7X C8H .7708 vs V9D .6095; shot2 Q7X C8H .6635 vs V9D .5730. errors.claim: “Experiments across all evaluated benchmarks are described as significantly favoring semantic noise over Q7X and random-initialized baselines.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from §6.5.1: “Text claims B8N outperforms Q7X/V9D consistently across every metric, but tables contradict: Table 3 unknown A7L/T4B B8N .8824/.8920 < Q7X .968/.988; bomb G9M B8N .9020 < Q7X .9498 and V9D .9050; very good T4B B8N .8894 < Q7X .8990; Table 4 average T4B B8N .9342 < Q7X .9457.”
errors.explanation: The discussion repeats an across-all-benchmarks superiority claim for semantic initialization, but the paper’s own tables show several metrics/benchmarks where B8N is worse than Q7X or V9D.

errors.claim: “X9C … improves related-architecture transfer, BLIP-2 to InstructBLIP, but offers greater aggregate gains across fundamentally different architectures, BLIP-2 to Flamingo.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from Table 8: “BLIP2→InstructBLIP V9D .2270/Q7X .5065/P2F .6850; BLIP2→Flamingo .0780/.1435/.2335.”
errors.explanation: The stated greater gain for BLIP-2→Flamingo is contradicted by the reported C8H improvements: P2F improves over Q7X by .1785 for BLIP-2→InstructBLIP but only .0900 for BLIP-2→Flamingo.

grade.reason: The reviewer explicitly points out the claimed greater gain for BLIP-2->Flamingo is contradicted by Table 8, which shows a larger P2F improvement for BLIP-2->InstructBLIP (0.1785) than for BLIP-2->Flamingo (0.0900).

errors.claim: “Due to the relative novelty of this concept, no credible benchmarks/baselines have been established yet.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: Abstract says the study confirms CroPA’s superior cross-prompt transferability “vs baselines.” Introduction contribution says they reproduced the claim that “increasing number of prompts improves transferability but converges rapidly and baselines still do not surpass CroPA.”
errors.explanation: The paper has already described comparisons against baselines for CroPA/cross-prompt transferability, so claiming that no credible baselines have been established is inconsistent with its own earlier framing.

errors.claim: “The algorithm optimizes both visual perturbation δv and prompt perturbation δt but with opposing objectives” and the min-max objective uses “f(xv+δv, xt+δt)”
errors.evidence: Algorithm 1 line 7 computes the image gradient as “gv = ∇xv L(f(x′v, xit), T)” and line 8 updates only “x′v”, using the unperturbed prompt “xit” rather than the initialized adversarial/perturbed prompt “x′it”.
errors.explanation: The formal description says CroPA’s optimization involves perturbed prompts competing with image perturbations, but the reproduced algorithm step for updating the image perturbation ignores the perturbed prompt variable. Unless later lines alter this, the shown algorithm is inconsistent with the stated min-max formulation.

errors.claim: Algorithm 1 implements CroPA's adversarial prompt perturbation/min-max optimization.
errors.location: this part and notes on Section 4.3
errors.evidence: Earlier Section 4.3 states the formal CroPA objective is “minδv maxδt L(f(xv+δv, xt+δt), T)” and describes PGD where δv and δt are optimized antagonistically. But Algorithm 1 line 10 in this part computes “g_t = ∇_{x_t} L(f(x′_v, x^i_t), T)” using the clean prompt x^i_t, and line 11 updates “x′^i_t = x′^i_t + α2 sign(g_t)”; earlier line 7 similarly computed the image gradient using clean prompt “f(x′v, x_t^i)” rather than x′_t^i.
errors.explanation: The algorithm updates an adversarial prompt variable x′_t but computes both image and prompt gradients through the unperturbed prompt x_t^i, so the learned prompt perturbation does not actually enter the model call as required by the stated min-max objective.

errors.claim: “This loss encourages the perturbed image’s value vectors to closely align with the target text’s representation” and the final objective is “L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA ... - λ L_d-UAP.”
errors.evidence: Equation 11 defines L_d-UAP = Σ(1 − cosine similarity), which is minimized when value vectors align. But Equation 12 subtracts this loss from the objective, and the text says to “Jointly minimize -ve of this loss along with the CroPA loss.”
errors.explanation: If the overall objective is minimized, subtracting L_d-UAP maximizes the distance term 1 − cosine similarity, which discourages alignment rather than enforcing it. This conflicts with the stated purpose that the loss enforces or encourages alignment with the target representation.

errors.claim: “The attacker aims to generate a single perturbation pattern that, when applied to any image, causes a VLM to output a predetermined target text regardless of the input prompt or image content.”
errors.evidence: In the same §5.4.2 evaluation setup: “A successful attack causes the model to fail to generate the correct output text when presented with any previously unseen image, regardless of its content or the associated prompt.”
errors.explanation: The first statement defines the cross-image/universal attack as targeted, requiring a predetermined target text. The evaluation definition is untargeted, requiring only failure to produce the correct output.

errors.claim: “In our experiments, we present all cross-prompt and cross-model transferability results under the untargeted attack setting.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record the paper’s CroPA formulation as targeted: “Targeted objective minδv sum_i L(f(xv+δv, xt^i), T), success exact target text,” and CroPA as “minδv maxδt L(f(xv+δv, xt+δt), T).” Earlier §5.4 cross-model setup also stated: “adversary wants a single perturbation for an image causing multiple VLMs to output target text regardless of prompt.”
errors.explanation: The paper previously framed CroPA/cross-prompt transfer and the cross-model D-UAP threat model as targeted toward a target text. This part says all cross-prompt and cross-model transferability results are untargeted, without reconciling that change.

errors.claim: “we evaluated five state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs): OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP and LLaVA.”
errors.evidence: The sentence lists only four models: “OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP and LLaVA.”
errors.explanation: The claimed number of evaluated models is five, but only four are named in the same sentence.

errors.claim: “all cross-prompt and cross-model transferability results are untargeted because targeted transfer varies across architectures and untargeted ASR is fairer”
errors.evidence: This part says Claim 1 evaluates “Targeted Attack Success Rate (ASR)” for cross-prompt transferability and Table 1 presents “Targeted ASRs achieved by the CroPA method on the Flamingo VLM for different target texts.”
errors.explanation: Earlier the paper stated all cross-prompt transferability results are untargeted, but this section reports cross-prompt transferability using targeted ASR and target texts.

errors.claim: “6.3 Claim 3: CroPA converges towards higher ASR as number of iterations increase [Reproduced]”
errors.evidence: The same paragraph says: “Our obtained results ... resulted in contrasting results with respect to the original reported metrics of convergence ...” and “when we investigated the ASR convergence for each task’s use case, individually the trend is prone to instability.”
errors.explanation: The section labels the convergence claim as reproduced, but the text says the reproduction produced contrasting results and per-task convergence is unstable, so the reproduction status is internally inconsistent.

errors.claim: “Claim 3: CroPA converges towards higher ASR as number of iterations increase” / “the original reported metrics of convergence with higher number of iterations”
errors.evidence: The same paragraph later says: “Where the original metrics showed CroPA converging with higher number of prompts.”
errors.explanation: The section alternates between convergence as iterations increase and convergence as number of prompts increases. These are different experimental variables, so the claim is internally inconsistent about what was varied.

errors.claim: “CroPA+Init) consistently outperforms both CroPA and Multi-P across all metrics”
errors.evidence: Table 3 shows several metrics where CroPA+Init is lower than CroPA and/or Multi-P: for target “unknown,” CroPA+Init VQAgeneral = 0.8824 and VQAspecific = 0.8920, below CroPA’s 0.9680 and 0.9880; for “bomb,” CroPA+Init Classification = 0.9020, below Multi-P 0.9050 and CroPA 0.9498; for “very good,” CroPA+Init VQAspecific = 0.8894, below CroPA 0.8990.
errors.explanation: The table contradicts the claim of consistent outperformance across all metrics, although CroPA+Init has the best overall ASR for each listed target.

errors.claim: “CroPA+Init consistently outperforms CroPA/Multi-P across all metrics”
errors.evidence: Current Table 4: VQAspecific scores are Multi-P 0.8807, CroPA 0.9457, CIA 0.2281, CroPA+Init 0.9342.
errors.explanation: CroPA+Init is not best on VQAspecific in Table 4; base CroPA is higher. This reinforces the earlier inconsistency that the paper’s blanket claim of outperforming across all metrics is not supported by its own tables.

errors.claim: “We believe CutMix outperforms SCMix in promoting adversarial transferability…”
errors.evidence: Table 5 reports CroPA with SCMix overall 0.7055 versus CroPA with CutMix overall 0.5565. SCMix is also higher on VQA 0.6560 vs 0.4520 and Captioning 0.9500 vs 0.5500; CutMix is only slightly higher on VQAspecific 0.7240 vs 0.7160, and Classification is tied at 0.5000.
errors.explanation: The table shows SCMix outperforming CutMix overall and on most task metrics, contradicting the claim that CutMix outperforms SCMix.

errors.claim: “Our results in Tables 6 and 7… give an overall ASR of 96.85%”
errors.evidence: Table 6 reports CroPA+D-UAP Overall = 0.9685, but Table 7 reports CroPA+D-UAP Overall = 0.9270.
errors.explanation: The 96.85% overall ASR applies only to Table 6 on BLIP2, not to both Tables 6 and 7 as stated.

errors.claim: “Targeted ASRs on Blip2 using D-UAP…” and “Targeted ASRs on Open Flamingo using D-UAP…”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: §5.4.3 says all cross-prompt/cross-model results are untargeted, conflicting with targeted CroPA/§6.1 targeted ASR.
errors.explanation: This part again labels D-UAP/CroPA results as targeted ASRs, contradicting the earlier methodological statement that all cross-prompt/cross-model results are untargeted.

errors.claim: “Our experiment results in 6.5.1 empirically validate this hypothesis: across all evaluated benchmarks, our noise initialization method significantly outperformed both CroPA and random-initialized baselines…”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “§6.5.1 Noise Init: text claims CroPA+Init consistently outperforms across all metrics, but Table 3/4 contradict: some per-task metrics lower than CroPA/Multi. Table 4 BLIP-2 averages: ... CroPA+Init .9209, but CroPA VQAspecific .9457 > Init .9342.”
errors.explanation: The discussion repeats an across-all-benchmarks/outperformed-all claim, but the recorded table results include at least one benchmark/task where CroPA exceeds CroPA+Init.

errors.claim: “The D-UAP-modified CroPA framework ... achieving an overall Targeted Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 96.85%, an 13.5% improvement over the base CroPA method as shown in 6.5.3.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Table 6 Targeted ASRs on BLIP2, target Bomb: ... CroPA .8433; CroPA+D-UAP .9685.” Also: “Table 7 Targeted ASRs on OpenFlamingo, target Bomb: ... CroPA .8233; CroPA+D-UAP .9270.” Notes also state: “Text says Tables 6 and 7 demonstrate CroPA+D-UAP, ‘overall ASR 96.85%’ and +12.5% over base CroPA; this only matches Table 6 BLIP2, not Table 7 OpenFlamingo overall .9270.”
errors.explanation: The 96.85% overall ASR is only the BLIP-2 Table 6 value, not the OpenFlamingo Table 7 value. The improvement over BLIP-2 base CroPA is .9685 − .8433 = .1252, about 12.5 percentage points, not 13.5.

errors.claim: “By anchoring perturbations to semantically meaningful initializations, we can achieve higher ASRs without sacrificing cross-prompt transferability.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “§6.5.1 Noise Init: text claims CroPA+Init consistently outperforms across all metrics ... but Table 3/4 contradict: some per-task metrics lower than CroPA/Multi. Table 4 BLIP-2 averages ... CroPA+Init .9209, but CroPA VQAspecific .9457 > Init .9342.”
errors.explanation: The current claim says improved initialization raises ASRs without sacrificing cross-prompt transferability, but the recorded Table 4 result shows at least one cross-prompt/task metric where CroPA+Init is lower than CroPA.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Revisiting CroPA: A Reproducibility Study and Enhancements for Cross-Prompt Adversarial Transferability in Vision-Language Models.” Abstract: reproducibility of Luo et al. CroPA; validates superior cross-prompt transfer; improvements: novel initialization, cross-image/universal perturbations, value-vector loss; eval on Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, extended LLaVA. Conclusion/§7.6 says reproduced key CroPA results, resource limits constrained hyperparameter/cross-model/ensemble experiments; future work encoder-agnostic cross-model, cross-image, query-based optimization; §7.7 no direct communication with original authors, unresolved GitHub issue re BLIP-2/InstructBLIP.

Key internal issues: §6 setup says evaluated “five” VLMs but names four: OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, LLaVA. Algorithm 1 conflict: formulas/descriptions use perturbed prompts, model calls use clean prompts. Value-vector loss sign conflict: L_d-UAP=sum[1−cos(...)] encourages alignment, but Eq.12 L_re-CroPA=L_CroPA−λL_d-UAP if minimized would maximize L_d-UAP. errors.claim: “No credible benchmarks or baselines have yet been established for this relatively new concept [Cross-Prompt Adversarial Transferability].”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: Abstract claims the paper “validates Q7X and its superiority to existing baselines in N6Z”; Introduction says Luo et al. (2024) introduced N6Z and competing learnable prompts, and replication tests include “superiority across target texts.”
errors.explanation: This part says no credible benchmarks or baselines exist for N6Z, but earlier parts framed the study as validating Q7X against existing N6Z baselines and reproducing its superiority. Those claims cannot both be true without qualification.

errors.claim: The extended scope includes F8V, K3R, and comparison to other N6Z methods
errors.evidence: Earlier §2.3 claimed: “No credible benchmarks or baselines have yet been established” for N6Z; earlier abstract/intro also claimed Q7X’s superiority to existing baselines in N6Z.
errors.explanation: This part again says the study compares Q7X to other N6Z methods, which conflicts with the related-work claim that no credible N6Z benchmarks or baselines exist. The paper is inconsistent about whether established N6Z comparators/baselines exist.

errors.claim: “The reference attacks introduced by Luo et al. (2024), absent established N6Z baselines…”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: Abstract claims Q7X’s “superiority to existing baselines in N6Z”; §3 names reproduced claims including “Claim 2 Q7X has best aggregate performance across prompt counts” and “Claim 4 Q7X outperforms baselines in few-shot settings.”
errors.explanation: This repeats the inconsistency already present in §2.3: the paper says there are no established N6Z baselines, while elsewhere it frames the study as comparing Q7X against existing N6Z baselines and showing superiority over them.

errors.claim: “Q7X … jointly optimizes δ_v and δ_t, with antagonistic rather than collaborative objectives” and Eq. (5) uses f(x_v+δ_v, x_t+δ_t).
errors.evidence: Algorithm 1 computes the image gradient as “g_v = ∇_{x_v} L(f(x'_v, x_t^i), T)” and the prompt gradient as “g_t = ∇_{x_t} L(f(x'_v, x_t^i), T)”; although it updates “x'_t^i”, subsequent forward passes continue to use “x_t^i”, not “x'_t^i”.
errors.explanation: The text and equation say the adversarial prompt perturbation is part of the optimization, but the provided algorithm never uses the updated adversarial prompt in the loss. As written, δ_t is updated but has no effect on the image optimization, contradicting the claimed joint antagonistic optimization.

errors.claim: “P2F increase over base Q7X, results characterization | 12.5%” and “P2F increase over base Q7X, discussion characterization | 13.5%”
errors.evidence: The same table gives two different values for the P2F increase over base Q7X: “12.5%” and “13.5%.”
errors.explanation: Unless these are explicitly defined as different measurements, the table internally contradicts itself about the reported increase of P2F over base Q7X.

errors.claim: “The loss is described as encouraging closeness to the target representation” / the method “computes their cosine-similarity loss, and jointly minimizes its negative with the Q7X loss.”
errors.evidence: Eq. (11) defines L_X9C = Σ_i (1 - cosine(V_i(x+δ), V_t)); Eq. (12) defines L_P2F = L_Q7X(...) - λ L_X9C(δ_v). Earlier notes: Q7X targeted objective is minimized.
errors.explanation: If the combined objective is minimized, subtracting λL_X9C encourages increasing L_X9C, i.e. decreasing cosine similarity to the target value vector, not closeness to it. This conflicts with the text’s claim that the loss encourages closeness/semantic alignment with the target representation.

errors.claim: “The attacker seeks one image perturbation eliciting a specified target text from multiple VLMs independently of prompt”
errors.evidence: The same subsection says: “Success in this evaluation is failure by the target model to generate the correct output from the perturbed image, regardless of prompt.” §5.4.3 also says: “All N6Z and F8V transferability results are presented under untargeted attacks.”
errors.explanation: Eliciting a specified target text is a targeted attack objective, but the stated evaluation success criterion is untargeted failure to produce the correct output. The threat model and scoring definition are inconsistent.

errors.claim: “The goal is one pattern causing predetermined target text for any image, regardless of image content and prompt”
errors.evidence: The same subsection says: “Taskwise H2Q counts failure to generate correct output text on previously unseen images independently of content or prompt.” §5.4.3 says: “Non-targeted H2Q is also the chosen robust, fair, comparable assessment of between-model and between-image transfer.”
errors.explanation: A pattern causing predetermined target text is a targeted objective, while counting any failure to generate the correct output is an untargeted metric. The K3R goal and evaluation criterion do not match.

errors.claim: “All N6Z and F8V transferability results are presented under untargeted attacks.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record targeted F8V/value-guided results: “P2F aggregate targeted H2Q 96.85%,” “P2F increase over base Q7X,” and “value-guided F8V G9M improvement 14%, D5R improvement 21%.” Earlier methodology also defines targeted success as exact target-text generation and Q7X as optimizing toward target T.
errors.explanation: The paper previously reported targeted H2Q values in the F8V/value-guided transfer context, so the blanket statement that all N6Z and F8V transferability results are untargeted conflicts with those earlier reported targeted results.

errors.claim: “Five state-of-the-art VLMs were evaluated: OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, and LLaVA.”
errors.evidence: The sentence names only four models: “OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, and LLaVA.” Earlier notes also record evaluation of “Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, extended LLaVA,” i.e. four model families.
errors.explanation: The claim says five VLMs were evaluated but immediately lists only four, with no fifth model identified.

errors.claim: “B8N = CroPA+Init) is reported to outperform Q7X and V9D consistently across every metric”

final_notes:
Paper title: “Revisiting CroPA: A Reproducibility Study and Enhancements for Cross-Prompt Adversarial Transferability in Vision-Language Models.” Repro/extension of Luo et al. Abstract claims: validates Q7X/CroPA and superiority to baselines in N6Z; semantic meaning and target-word frequency do not determine transferability; adds initialization, common perturbations, attention/value loss; evaluates Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, LLaVA; enhancements consistently increase adversarial effectiveness. Code URL GitHub Swadesh06/Revisting_CroPA; OpenReview 5L90cl0xtf.

Definitions: F8V = cross-model transfer/architectural survival; K3R = cross-image transfer; N6Z = cross-prompt transfer; Z4P = universal/shared perturbation. Tasks: A7L VQAgeneral, T4B VQAspecific, G9M Classification, D5R Captioning, C8H Overall. H2Q = ASR. S3D = PGD. L6V = MSE. E3W/CIA = Context Injection Attack. X9C = Doubly-UAP/D-UAP. Targeted success = exact target text; untargeted success = departure from clean prediction.

Known internal errors/contradictions: Related work §2.3 says no credible N6Z benchmarks/baselines exist, conflicting with abstract/intro/§3/§4.2 framing about existing N6Z baselines/comparators and Q7X superiority. Algorithm 1 initializes/updates adversarial prompt x'_t^i but gradients use f(x'_v, x_t^i), not x'_t^i, conflicting with Eq.5/text that jointly optimize image and prompt perturbations. P2F Eq.12 L_P2F=L_Q7X−λL_X9C with L_X9C=Σ(1−cos(...)); if minimizing, sign encourages larger distance, contrary to text saying closeness/semantic target alignment. Threat-model inconsistency: §5.4.1/5.4.2 targeted transfer goals but §5.4.3 says all N6Z/F8V transfer results are untargeted; K3R H2Q counts failure to generate correct output. §6 says “Five” VLMs but lists only four: OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, LLaVA. §6.5.1 and §7.2 claim B8N/semantic noise outperforms Q7X/V9D consistently/across all evaluated benchmarks, but Tables 3/4 show exceptions: unknown A7L/T4B B8N .8824/.8920 below Q7X .968/.988; bomb G9M B8N .902 below Q7X .9498 and V9D .905; very good T4B B8N .8894 below Q7X .899; Table 4 avg T4B B8N .9342 below Q7X .9457. §6.5.2 text says U8G believed to outperform J6T, but Table 5 shows J6T higher aggregate and most tasks.

Key results: §3 reproduction: Q7X achieves N6Z across targets, best aggregate prompt-count performance, converges higher H2Q with more iterations, outperforms baselines in few-shot. Base Q7X has higher aggregate transfer Flamingo→BLIP2 than BLIP2→Flamingo. Table 1 OpenFlamingo targeted Q7X C8H: unknown .7708, I am sorry .7985, not sure .5033, very good .7020, too late .6920, metaphor .8680; weak on G9M/D5R for abstract targets. Table 2 few-shot unknown Flamingo visual ICL: 0-shot V9D .6095, Q7X .7708; 2-shot V9D .5730, Q7X .6635; Q7X beats V9D but drops from 0-shot to 2-shot on all tasks.

Noise init/B8N: Table 3 C8H unknown .8977, bomb .9260, I am sorry .9458, very good .8761, too late .9333. Table 4 avg C8H: V9D .7104, Q7X .7958, E3W .370, B8N .9209. Y2K CLIP feature uptake target Bomb: Q7X 21.80, B8N 23.09. §7.2 says Q7X already acquires target context; initialization gives modest Y2K increment, not significant semantic-feature upgrade, interpreted as starting closer to vulnerable regions and faster convergence.

K3R: unmodified Q7X not effectively universal; prompt-directed signals tied to originating-image low-level features; Q7X excels at prompt robustness not image transfer. Table 5 untargeted K3R H2Q: Q7X C8H .4355; J6T .7055; U8G .5565. Unmixed peaks 1700 iter; J6T 1500, U8G 1600. §7.3.1 says J6T improves particularly VQA/T4B/D5R; U8G also improves base; augmentation helps but does not eliminate limitation.

P2F/F8V: Table 6 BLIP2 target Bomb C8H: V9D .75; Q7X .8433; E3W .4199; P2F .9685. Table 7 OpenFlamingo target Bomb: V9D .7638; Q7X .8233; E3W .4380; P2F .9270. Table 8 cross-model: P2F improves over Q7X/V9D in every listed setting/task. C8H examples: BLIP2→InstructBLIP .6850 vs Q7X .5065; BLIP2→Flamingo .2335 vs .1435; BLIP2→LLaVA .5325 vs .3040; Flamingo-origin transfers very low. Same-encoder BLIP2→InstructBLIP transfer stronger than BLIP2→Flamingo. §7.3.2/7.4.1: value/X9C guidance improves related-architecture transfer but only modest gains across very different architectures; encoder-specific dependence remains obstacle; E3W cannot supply comparable transfer and is inherently/non-effectively transferable.

§7 limitations/future: no direct communication with original authors; BLIP-2/InstructBLIP repo issues unresolved. Compute scarcity limited replications, ablations, hyperparameter tuning, wider architecture transfer, and planned ensemble-model transfer. Future: encoder-agnostic F8V, stronger K3R, query-based optimization.
