final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” VideoBiasEval evaluates social representation/bias in text-to-video/video diffusion models using event prompts <p,a,c>. Biases = imbalanced portrayals across gender/ethnic groups.

Prompt construction: initially lists four gender categories (man, woman, neutral person, non-binary person) and seven ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), 42 verbs. Actual video prompt set has no explicit gender-specific conditions and VLM gender outputs only binary man/woman. Template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Actual video conditions: Person-only actor “person” (42 prompts); Ethnicity+Person (7×42=294). Earlier text confusingly mentioned ethnicity+gender, but actual video evaluation does not use explicit gender prompts.

Evaluation: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B. 16 frames/video; VLMs infer gender/ethnicity per frame. Gender labels binary {man,woman}; ethnicity labels seven groups. Majority vote within model to video labels, then ensemble fused. TAS = % frames matching final video label. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive male, negative female. Ethnicity metrics: P_e=N_e/N_total identifiable ethnicity; RDS_e=P_e−1/7; zero group should be −1/7 by formula. SDI=1−ΣP_e^2, higher more diverse. Bias Shift compares aligned vs unaligned: ΔPBSG, ΔRDS, ΔSDI.

Sec. 4 models/results: unaligned ModelScope and VideoCrafter-2; aligned InstructVideo and T2V-Turbo-V1. 10 videos per prompt/model. Table 2: ModelScope Avg PBSG .4815, White RDS .7690, SDI .0538. InstructVideo Avg PBSG .5295, White RDS .7833, SDI .0267; Δ +.0480, +.0143, −.0271. VideoCrafter-V2 Avg PBSG .7581, White RDS .6905, SDI .1252. T2V-Turbo-V1 Avg PBSG .8306, White RDS .6381, SDI .1119; Δ +.0725, −.0524, −.0133. Text claims consistent male bias and alignment amplifies gender imbalance. It also says ModelScope has strongest ethnicity imbalance, but table shows InstructVideo stronger by higher White RDS/lower SDI. T2V reduces White dominance vs VC but lowers diversity.

Human Evaluation: 400 videos, 3 annotators. VLM ensemble vs humans: Pearson r=.89 gender, .73 ethnicity; Cohen’s κ=.91 gender, .78 ethnicity; Fleiss’ κ=.92 gender, .82 ethnicity. High-agreement subset consensus 99.0% gender, 83.3% ethnicity; metrics stable PBSG .846→.863 p=.68; SDI .745→.761. This SDI scale conflicts with Table 2 SDIs (.0267–.1252) unless alternate computation/rescaling.

Sec. 5 image reward datasets/models. HPDv2 after processing: 28,783 validated tuples/29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic: 14,958/19 verbs. Figure 3 caption says gender preference across 42 verbs. HPDv2: 26/42 qualified; 18/26=69.23% preferred men. Pick-a-Pic: 18/42 qualified; 11/18=61.11% preferred women. Ethnicity: White preferred 43.34% HPDv2, 40.08% Pick-a-Pic, followed by East Asian and Indian.

Sec. 5.2 reward-model benchmark uses FLUX. Claims Sec. 3.2 templates but includes Ethnicity+Person and Ethnicity+Gender settings, conflicting with actual VideoBiasEval conditions. Table 3: Ethnicity+Person 294 prompts; Ethnicity+Gender 1176 prompts, implying 7 ethnicities×4 gender categories×42 verbs, though Figure 5 only shows gender {man,woman}. FLUX paragraph both says not assuming bias-free generator and says benchmark isolates reward preferences independently of generator artifacts. Human verification of 100 images: 77% unanimous, 97% majority, 3 no consensus. Reward models: HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore, CLIP base. Ethnicity-aware gender bias uses evaluation prompt “A/An [ethnicity] person...” and generation prompt “A/An [ethnicity] [gender]...”; scores standardized; PBSG = standardized male score minus female score for fixed ethnicity+verb, can exceed 1. Table 4: CLIP Avg PBSG −.0726, SDI .8495; HPSv2.0 +.6039, SDI .8492; HPSv2.1 −.0984, SDI .8470; PickScore −.1157, SDI .8483. RDS near zero. Text says HPSv2.1 training data undisclosed but also claims shifts align with each model’s training data.

Sec. 6 fine-tunes Video Consistency Model distilled from VideoCrafter-V2 (VCM-VC2) with HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore using T2V-Turbo-V1-like latent consistency distillation/single-step generation; reward optimizes decoded frames. Table 5 social biases over 42 verbs. VCM-VC2 Avg PBSG .8034, White RDS .6405, SDI .1433. +HPSv2.0 Avg PBSG .9116, White RDS .3667, ME RDS −.3667, SDI .1257. +HPSv2.1 Avg PBSG .2267, White RDS .4286, ME RDS −.4286, SDI .0976; many RDS missing. +PickScore Avg PBSG .3714, White RDS .6833, Black RDS −.1810, Latino RDS −.1929, East Asian RDS −.1952, ME RDS −.1143, SDI .1467. Text correctly says HPSv2.0 increases male bias, HPSv2.1/PickScore reduce PBSG toward balance/women. But text incorrectly says HPSv2.1 decreases Latino representation with RDS −.4352; table shows Latino RDS missing and −.4352 is Δ Latino PBSG. Text says ethnicity-only condition, while table caption says person-only condition/no ethnicity specified. Table caption says missing RDS means zero recognizable instances preventing metric computation, conflicting with earlier RDS formula where zero would yield −1/7. PickScore has highest SDI in Table 5 (.1467), slightly above base .1433.

Table 6 TAS: VCM-VC2 ethnicity mean .8904, gender .9763. +HPSv2 row/probably HPSv2.0 ethnicity .9305, gender .9967, gender perfect stability .9830. +HPSv2.1 ethnicity .9632, gender .9895, ethnicity perfect stability .8330 from baseline .5670; gender perfect stability .9440. +PickScore ethnicity .9406, gender .9884. Earlier part says alignment improves TAS/technical coherence and can entrench bias; HPSv2.0 raises PBSG .8034→.9116 and gender TAS .9967. Earlier part incorrectly says HPSv2.0 reinforces both male and White tendencies; Table 5 shows male bias rises but White RDS falls .6405→.3667.

Sec. 7 controllable preference modeling. Builds man-preferred and woman-preferred image reward datasets from Ethnicity+Gender set, each with 2.94M preference pairs; pair has same action/ethnicity but different gender; prompts “A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context].” Adds 537,660 HPDv2 image pairs. Trains CLIP-based reward models RMM and RMW. Table 7 reward PBSG: CLIP avg −0.0726; RMM avg 1.5280, all groups strongly positive; RMW avg −0.7448, all groups negative. Table 8 video alignment on VCM-VC2: baseline PBSG avg .8034; +RMM avg .9584, all groups higher; +RMW avg .3082, all groups lower but still positive. Thus claims that +RMW produces woman-preference bias or fully corrected/balanced representation conflict with positive PBSG, though it reduces male bias. Summary claimed RMW can “actively correct skewed portrayals, producing more balanced and socially representative generations,” conflicting with remaining male bias. It also suggests mixtures of man-/woman-preferred data yield continuous tunable tradeoffs, but notes only binary RMM/RMW experiments. Figure 6 action sensitivity: RMM amplifies male portrayals in exercise, row, cook; RMW shifts toward women-preferred bake, sleep, sweep. Normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG divided by each reward model’s baseline PBSG; sleep, stretch, read top under both. Responsible-use paragraph warns debiasing is not a silver bullet and requires stakeholder/community input.

Conclusion: VideoBiasEval intended to decouple identity attributes from content semantics and track how alignment reshapes social representations. Concludes reward-model-based alignment inherits and frequently amplifies biases from human preference data and calls for bias auditing/mitigation throughout video-generation pipeline.

Prompt construction: initially lists four gender categories (man, woman, neutral person, non-binary person) and seven ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), 42 verbs. Actual video prompt set has no explicit gender-specific conditions and VLM gender outputs only binary man/woman. Template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Actual video conditions: Person-only actor “person” (42 prompts); Ethnicity+Person (7×42=294). Earlier text confusingly mentioned ethnicity+gender, but actual video evaluation does not use explicit gender prompts.

Evaluation: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B. 16 frames/video; VLMs infer gender/ethnicity per frame. Gender labels binary {man,woman}; ethnicity labels seven groups. Majority vote within model to video labels, then ensemble fused. TAS = % frames matching final video label. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive male, negative female. Ethnicity metrics: P_e=N_e/N_total identifiable ethnicity; RDS_e=P_e−1/7; zero group should be −1/7 by formula. SDI=1−ΣP_e^2, higher more diverse. Bias Shift compares aligned vs unaligned: ΔPBSG, ΔRDS, ΔSDI.

Sec. 4 models/results: unaligned ModelScope and VideoCrafter-2; aligned InstructVideo and T2V-Turbo-V1. 10 videos per prompt/model. Table 2: ModelScope Avg PBSG .4815, White RDS .7690, SDI .0538. InstructVideo Avg PBSG .5295, White RDS .7833, SDI .0267; Δ +.0480, +.0143, −.0271. VideoCrafter-V2 Avg PBSG .7581, White RDS .6905, SDI .1252. T2V-Turbo-V1 Avg PBSG .8306, White RDS .6381, SDI .1119; Δ +.0725, −.0524, −.0133. Text claims consistent male bias and alignment amplifies gender imbalance. It also says ModelScope has strongest ethnicity imbalance, but table shows InstructVideo stronger by higher White RDS/lower SDI. T2V reduces White dominance vs VC but lowers diversity.

Human Evaluation: 400 videos, 3 annotators. VLM ensemble vs humans: Pearson r=.89 gender, .73 ethnicity; Cohen’s κ=.91 gender, .78 ethnicity; Fleiss’ κ=.92 gender, .82 ethnicity. High-agreement subset consensus 99.0% gender, 83.3% ethnicity; metrics stable PBSG .846→.863 p=.68; SDI .745→.761. This SDI scale conflicts with Table 2 SDIs (.0267–.1252) unless alternate computation/rescaling.

Sec. 5 image reward datasets/models. HPDv2 after processing: 28,783 validated tuples/29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic: 14,958/19 verbs. Figure 3 caption says gender preference across 42 verbs. HPDv2: 26/42 qualified; 18/26=69.23% preferred men. Pick-a-Pic: 18/42 qualified; 11/18=61.11% preferred women. Ethnicity: White preferred 43.34% HPDv2, 40.08% Pick-a-Pic, followed by East Asian and Indian.

Sec. 5.2 reward-model benchmark uses FLUX. Claims Sec. 3.2 templates but includes Ethnicity+Person and Ethnicity+Gender settings, conflicting with actual VideoBiasEval conditions. Table 3: Ethnicity+Person 294 prompts; Ethnicity+Gender 1176 prompts, implying 7 ethnicities×4 gender categories×42 verbs, though Figure 5 only shows gender {man,woman}. FLUX paragraph both says not assuming bias-free generator and says benchmark isolates reward preferences independently of generator artifacts. Human verification of 100 images: 77% unanimous, 97% majority, 3 no consensus. Reward models: HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore, CLIP base. Ethnicity-aware gender bias uses evaluation prompt “A/An [ethnicity] person...” and generation prompt “A/An [ethnicity] [gender]...”; scores standardized; PBSG = standardized male score minus female score for fixed ethnicity+verb, can exceed 1. Table 4: CLIP Avg PBSG −.0726, SDI .8495; HPSv2.0 +.6039, SDI .8492; HPSv2.1 −.0984, SDI .8470; PickScore −.1157, SDI .8483. RDS near zero. Text says HPSv2.1 training data undisclosed but also claims shifts align with each model’s training data.

Sec. 6 fine-tunes Video Consistency Model distilled from VideoCrafter-V2 (VCM-VC2) with HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore using T2V-Turbo-V1-like latent consistency distillation/single-step generation; reward optimizes decoded frames. Table 5 social biases over 42 verbs. VCM-VC2 Avg PBSG .8034, White RDS .6405, SDI .1433. +HPSv2.0 Avg PBSG .9116, White RDS .3667, ME RDS −.3667, SDI .1257. +HPSv2.1 Avg PBSG .2267, White RDS .4286, ME RDS −.4286, SDI .0976; many RDS missing. +PickScore Avg PBSG .3714, White RDS .6833, Black RDS −.1810, Latino RDS −.1929, East Asian RDS −.1952, ME RDS −.1143, SDI .1467. Text correctly says HPSv2.0 increases male bias, HPSv2.1/PickScore reduce PBSG toward balance/women. But text incorrectly says HPSv2.1 decreases Latino representation with RDS −.4352; table shows Latino RDS missing and −.4352 is Δ Latino PBSG. Text says ethnicity-only condition, while table caption says person-only condition/no ethnicity specified. Table caption says missing RDS means zero recognizable instances preventing metric computation, conflicting with earlier RDS formula where zero would yield −1/7. PickScore has highest SDI in Table 5 (.1467), slightly above base .1433.

Table 6 TAS: VCM-VC2 ethnicity mean .8904, gender .9763. +HPSv2 row/probably HPSv2.0 ethnicity .9305, gender .9967, gender perfect stability .9830. +HPSv2.1 ethnicity .9632, gender .9895, ethnicity perfect stability .8330 from baseline .5670; gender perfect stability .9440. +PickScore ethnicity .9406, gender .9884. Earlier part says alignment improves TAS/technical coherence and can entrench bias; HPSv2.0 raises PBSG .8034→.9116 and gender TAS .9967. Earlier part incorrectly says HPSv2.0 reinforces both male and White tendencies; Table 5 shows male bias rises but White RDS falls .6405→.3667.

Sec. 7 controllable preference modeling. Builds man-preferred and woman-preferred image reward datasets from Ethnicity+Gender set, each with 2.94M preference pairs; pair has same action/ethnicity but different gender; prompts “A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context].” Adds 537,660 HPDv2 image pairs. Trains CLIP-based reward models RMM and RMW. Table 7 reward PBSG: CLIP avg −0.0726; RMM avg 1.5280, all groups strongly positive; RMW avg −0.7448, all groups negative. Table 8 video alignment on VCM-VC2: baseline PBSG avg .8034; +RMM avg .9584, all groups higher; +RMW avg .3082, all groups lower but still positive. Thus claims that +RMW produces woman-preference bias or fully corrected/balanced representation conflict with positive PBSG, though it reduces male bias. Summary claimed RMW can “actively correct skewed portrayals, producing more balanced and socially representative generations,” conflicting with remaining male bias. It also suggests mixtures of man-/woman-preferred data yield continuous tunable tradeoffs, but notes only binary RMM/RMW experiments. Figure 6 action sensitivity: RMM amplifies male portrayals in exercise, row, cook; RMW shifts toward women-preferred bake, sleep, sweep. Normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG divided by each reward model’s baseline PBSG; sleep, stretch, read top under both. Responsible-use paragraph warns debiasing is not a silver bullet and requires stakeholder/community input.

Conclusion: VideoBiasEval intended to decouple identity attributes from content semantics and track how alignment reshapes social representations. Concludes reward-model-based alignment inherits and frequently amplifies biases from human preference data and calls for bias auditing/mitigation throughout video-generation pipeline.

Limitations: acknowledges two social dimensions, gender/ethnicity, with predefined categories; VLM evaluators may have biases/inaccuracies despite human validation and ensembling; alignment impact mainly assessed under single-step latent consistency distillation with limited reward models; controllable preference modeling constrained to synthetic gender-preference manipulations; VideoBiasEval fixed to 42 socially associated actions and may not generalize to open-ended/novel actions.

Broader Impact: argues alignment can stabilize/entrench social biases by improving fidelity/temporal consistency so stereotyped portrayals appear more natural and harder to detect. Frames controllable preference modeling as dual-use: curation of preference datasets can amplify or suppress social attributes, potentially aiding mitigation but also enabling exclusion/homogenization/propaganda. Urges event-centric auditing such as VideoBiasEval and rigorous, diverse preference dataset curation beyond aesthetic metrics.

That conflicts with the earlier description that prompts systematically vary both gender and ethnicity and with the stated four-category gender attribute space.

errors.claim: “We exclude gender bias from this analysis because, in the absence of explicit ethnicity specifications, generative models predominantly produce representations of White individuals …”
errors.location: this part, footnote under “Ethnicity-Aware Gender Bias”

errors.claim: “By computing PBSG under the ethnicity+gender condition, we capture how gender portrayals vary within each ethnic group…”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: Section 3.2 defined only two prompt conditions: “Person Only = 42 prompts” and “Ethnicity+Person = 294 prompts”; there were no gender-conditioned prompts. Section 3.3 also says gender is inferred post hoc by VLMs as {man, woman}.
errors.explanation: The paper previously described an ethnicity+person condition, not an ethnicity+gender condition. Gender is not explicitly conditioned in the prompts, so this claim misnames or invents a condition not present in the described experimental design.

errors.claim: “By using neutral ‘person’-based prompts that explicitly decouple verbs from identity attributes, deviations from PBSG ≈ 0 quantify…”
errors.evidence: The same paragraph defines PBSG “for each verb and ethnicity group” and later says it is computed “under the ethnicity+gender condition”; earlier notes say ethnicity-specific prompts are “Ethnicity+Person,” e.g., “An East Asian person…,” which explicitly include an ethnicity attribute.
errors.explanation: PBSG is described as ethnicity-aware and computed by ethnicity group, but the justification says it uses neutral person-only prompts that decouple identity attributes. Person-only prompts do not provide ethnicity groups, while ethnicity+person prompts do not decouple ethnicity from the prompt.

errors.claim: “Because prompts in this setting intentionally remove contextual and identity cues…”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from Section 3.2: person-only prompts use the template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]”; example “A person is baking cookies…”. Actor/context are fixed predefined, and 42 verb/action contexts are used.
errors.explanation: The person-only setting removes explicit identity cues, but it does not remove contextual cues; the prompts still include verbs/actions and contexts such as baking cookies.

errors.claim: RDS values such as Black RDS = -0.1952, Latino RDS = -0.1952, East Asian RDS = -0.1810, Middle Eastern RDS = -0.1976, and T2V-Turbo Latino RDS = -0.2476 are reported in Table 2.
errors.evidence: Earlier definition: “RDS_e = P_e − 1/|E|. With seven ethnic groups, ideal is 1/7 ≈ 14.3%.” Since P_e is a proportion, P_e ≥ 0, so the minimum possible RDS_e is −1/7 ≈ −0.1429.
errors.explanation: Several reported RDS values are below the mathematically possible minimum under the paper’s own definition of RDS with seven ethnic groups.

errors.claim: “Missing values are marked as ‘—’ and indicate cases where the model generated zero recognizable instances of the corresponding ethnicity under the person-only condition … preventing metric computation for those subgroups.”
errors.evidence: Earlier/current definition: “P_e = N_e/N_total” and “RDS_e = P_e − 1/|E|.” If N_e = 0 for an ethnicity, then P_e = 0 and RDS_e = −1/7 ≈ −0.1429, so RDS is computable.

errors.claim: “By conditioning on systematically varied demographic attributes, our benchmark isolates reward model preferences independently of generator-specific artifacts.”

errors.explanation: If the benchmark relies on FLUX-generated images and FLUX is not assumed bias-free, then the paper cannot also claim the benchmark isolates reward-model preferences independently of generator-specific artifacts. final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Main conclusion: introduces VideoBiasEval to audit social bias in text-to-video; argues alignment tuning with learned preference/aesthetic rewards improves controllability/quality but inherits, amplifies, and stabilizes social biases; urges auditing/mitigation. Broader Impact: alignment tuning can stabilize/entrench social biases by making stereotyped outputs polished/natural; controllable preference modeling is dual-use, enabling curated reward models to amplify/suppress social attributes; urges event-centric audits and preference dataset curation.

Definitions: “aligned models” = post-training optimized video diffusion models using learned preference/aesthetic reward; “unaligned counterparts” = likelihood-only baselines. VideoBiasEval: 42 verbs/actions. Gender categories initially: man, woman, neutral person, non-binary person. Ethnic groups: White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino. Prompt settings: Person Only = 42; Ethnicity+Person = 294; total 336. Template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” VLM ensemble: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B, 16 frames/video. Infer gender {man,woman} and ethnicity among 7 groups. TAS = % frames matching final majority-voted video label.

Metrics: PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive male, negative female, 0 balanced; PBSG=.5 means 3× men. RDS_e=P_e−1/7; range [-0.1429,0.8571]. SDI=1−ΣP_e^2. Bias shifts = aligned−unaligned.

Sec 4: InstructVideo/T2V-Turbo-V1 vs ModelScope/VideoCrafter-2, 10 generations/prompt. Table 2 averages: ModelScope PBSG .4815, White RDS .7690, SDI .0538; InstructVideo .5295, .7833, .0267; VideoCrafter-V2 .7581, .6905, .1252; T2V-Turbo .8306, .6381, .1119. Issues: impossible RDS values below -1/7 and dashes where zero counts should be -1/7; text says ModelScope strongest imbalance though InstructVideo has higher White RDS/lower SDI. Human eval: 400 videos, 3 annotators; VLM-human Pearson .89 gender/.73 ethnicity; Cohen .91/.78; Fleiss .92/.82. Issue: says verifying “prompted demographic attribute” for gender though gender not prompted.

Sec 5 image reward data: HPDv2 28,783 tuples, 29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic 14,958, 19 verbs. Gender pairs only man–woman. HPDv2: 26/42 verbs qualified, 18/26 prefer men. Pick-a-Pic: 18/42, 11/18 prefer women. Ethnicity preference: White strongest, 43.34% HPDv2, 40.08% Pick-a-Pic. Issue: captions claim distributions across 42 verbs despite fewer processed/qualified verbs.

Sec 5.2 reward benchmark: FLUX, 100 images/prompt. Settings Ethnicity+Person and Ethnicity+Gender; Ethnicity+Gender not earlier video setting. Table 3: 294 and 1176 prompts; 1176=7 ethnicities×4 gender categories×42 verbs, although Fig. 5 says images with gender∈{man,woman}. Reward results: gender PBSG = standardized men score−women score, can exceed 1. CLIP -0.0726, HPSv2.0 +0.6039, HPSv2.1 -0.0984, PickScore -0.1157. Ethnicity Table 4: CLIP SDI .8495 White RDS .0182; HPSv2.0 SDI .8492 shifts Middle Eastern RDS .0315; HPSv2.1 SDI .8470 shifts Latino RDS .0382; PickScore SDI .8483 shifts East Asian RDS .0352. All lower SDI than CLIP.

Sec 6: fine-tunes VCM-VC2 with HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore via T2V-Turbo/LCM. Table 5: VCM-VC2 avg PBSG .8034, White RDS .6405, SDI .1433. +HPSv2.0 PBSG .9116, White RDS .3667, Middle Eastern RDS -.3667, SDI .1257. +HPSv2.1 PBSG .2267, White RDS .4286, Middle Eastern RDS -.4286, SDI .0976. +PickScore PBSG .3714, White RDS .6833, Black RDS -.1810, Latino -.1929, East Asian -.1952, Middle Eastern -.1143, SDI .1467. Issues: says ethnicity-only condition though earlier only person-only; impossible RDS below -1/7; says HPSv2.1 decreases Latino representation RDS=-.4352, but table has Latino RDS dash and -.4352 is Latino PBSG delta; summary says HPSv2.0 reinforces White-preferred tendencies, but White RDS decreases from .6405 to .3667. Table 6 TAS: alignment improves temporal stability; HPSv2.1 ethnicity TAS .9632/perfect .8330; HPSv2.0 gender TAS .9967/perfect .9830. Label inconsistency: +HPSv2 vs +HPSv2.0.

Sec 7 controllable preference modeling, gender case study. Constructs man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets from Sec 5.1 images. Each has 2.94M preference pairs from Ethnicity+Gender, same action/ethnicity, differs by gender; prompt “A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context].” Labels: man-preferred male=1 female=0; woman-preferred opposite. Adds 537,660 HPDv2 image pairs. Trains CLIP-based RMM and RMW. Table 7 reward PBSG-like scores: CLIP avg -0.0726; RMM avg 1.5280 (+1.60), all groups ~1.43–1.63; RMW avg -0.7448 (-2.27), all groups ~-0.63 to -0.88. Sec 7 says no neutral/fair reward because base VCM-VC2 has strong man bias; uses counter-biased RMW analogous to HPSv2.1. Table 8 video alignment PBSG: VCM-VC2 avg .8034; +RMM avg .9584; +RMW avg .3082, all groups still positive. Issue: text claims +RMW indicates strong shift toward woman-preference bias / balanced generations, but positive PBSG means outputs remain man-biased, just less so. Sec 7 summary says controllable preference modeling can direct bias; RMM reinforces and RMW counteracts base tendencies; suggests continuous axis from mixtures though only two extremes reported. Fig 6: RMM amplifies male portrayals in exercise,row,cook; RMW shifts toward women-preferred actions bake,sleep,sweep.

Limitations: focus on gender/ethnicity with predefined U.S. Census/prior-literature categories; VLM evaluators may be biased/inaccurate despite validation; alignment impacts mainly under single-step latent consistency distillation and limited reward models; controllable preference modeling limited to synthetic gender preference; VideoBiasEval fixed to 42 socially associated actions. Acknowledgment: support from AFOSR MURI #FA9550-22-1-0380, ONR #N00014-23-1-2780, NSF #IIS-2449768, NVIDIA cloud credits, Technical AI Safety Research Program at Coefficient Giving; views not official endorsements.

Introduces VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for evaluating social representation in video generation. It uses event-based prompts grounded in social bias taxonomies to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity). Metrics evaluate: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Claimed contribution: first end-to-end analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in reward models, and propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Claimed results: alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 overview: VideoBiasEval uses VLMs to infer actor attributes such as gender and ethnicity across frames, then aggregate for bias quantification (Section 3.3). Analysis covers image-based reward models shaped by human-labeled preferences and their influence on social attribute distributions in diffusion-generated videos, disentangling human preference biases, reward preference biases, and downstream video diffusion model generation biases (Sections 5.1, 5.2, 6).

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Main claim/abstract/introduction: alignment tuning using reward/preference models trained on human preference comparisons improves visual fidelity/coherence/controllability but can encode, inherit, reinforce, and amplify social biases in text-to-video diffusion models, affecting who is represented, how often, and in what roles. The paper investigates how alignment tuning influences distributions of social attributes in video diffusion models.

Definitions from Introduction: “aligned models” = video diffusion models that undergo post-training optimization to better match human preferences beyond likelihood-based training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures using a learned preference/aesthetic reward model trained on human comparisons. General pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. “Unaligned counterparts” = trained solely using likelihood-based objectives, used as controlled baselines to isolate effects of alignment.

Introduces VideoBiasEval (Section 3), a diagnostic/comprehensive framework for evaluating social representation/bias in video generation. It uses event-based prompts grounded in established social bias taxonomies to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts/event content) from actor attributes. errors.claim: “The bounded attribute space balances coverage against control: four gender categories, seven ethnic groups, and 42 verbs…” and “Each actor carries gender and ethnicity attributes. Luccioni et al. (2023) supplies man, woman, neutral person, and non-binary person…”
errors.evidence: Section 3.3 defines extracted gender outputs as “g ∈ G = {man,woman}.” Section 3.2’s audit prompts also use only “person” and ethnicity-prefixed “person” prompts: “Fixing the actor to ‘person’ yields one prompt per curated activity… Deterministically prepending a predefined ethnic descriptor to ‘person’…”
errors.explanation: The part claims a four-category gender attribute space, including neutral person and non-binary person, but the actual extraction/evaluation gender label space is binary and the described prompt protocol does not instantiate all four gender categories.

errors.claim: “Demographic attributes are not introduced, constrained, or inferred during generation.”
errors.evidence: The same section says Table 1 prompts “explicitly contain ethnicity when specified,” gives V9R examples such as “An East Asian person…,” and states: “Deterministically prepending a predefined ethnic descriptor to ‘person’… permutes the verbs across ethnic groups.”
errors.explanation: Ethnicity is a demographic attribute, and V9R explicitly introduces it into the generation prompt. Thus the claim that demographic attributes are not introduced during generation conflicts with the described prompting protocol.

errors.claim: “The uniform reference pertains to neutral J7K auditing, whose prompts intentionally remove contextual and identity cues.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: J7K template is “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” J7K = Person-only one prompt per activity, omits explicit demographic cues; examples include “A person is baking cookies…”. Table caption says prompts contain verb and context.
errors.explanation: J7K removes explicit identity/demographic cues, but it does not remove contextual cues; the prompts still include verbs and contexts. Thus this part overstates what is removed in J7K.

errors.claim: Black F6N = -0.1952, Latino F6N = -0.1952, Middle Eastern F6N = -0.1976, and similar negative F6N values below -0.1429 in Table 2.
errors.evidence: Earlier definition in notes: “F6N/RDS_e = P_e - 1/|E|; with 7 groups balanced prob 1/7≈14.3%.” Since P_e is a proportion, its minimum is 0, so the minimum possible F6N is -1/7≈-0.1429.
errors.explanation: Several reported F6N values are mathematically impossible under the paper’s own definition because they are less than -0.1429.

errors.claim: “Throughout the video-distribution tables, ‘—’ denotes zero recognizable corresponding-ethnicity instances under J7K, severe diversity absence preventing subgroup computation.”
errors.evidence: The same table reports F6N values below the minimum possible value for zero instances: by the earlier definition, zero recognizable instances for an ethnicity would give P_e=0 and F6N=-1/7≈-0.1429, not values such as -0.1952, -0.1976, -0.2476.
errors.explanation: The table treats some groups as absent with ‘—’, but other groups appear to have F6N values implying negative proportions, which conflicts with the metric definition and the caption’s interpretation of absent instances.

errors.claim: “Each prompt is generated 10 times per model with different seeds; results are averaged to reduce sampling variance.”
errors.evidence: The Human verification table says “Generated videos in full pool: 400” for gender and ethnicity. Earlier protocol says J7K has 42 prompts and V9R has 294 prompts; with 10 generations per prompt and 4 models, this would produce 1,680 J7K videos and 11,760 V9R videos, not 400.
errors.explanation: The paper may mean a 400-video validation sample, but it calls it the “full pool,” which conflicts with the stated prompt counts, model count, and 10 seeds per prompt.

errors.claim: “E5W East Asian F6N | 0.0352”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantity table
errors.evidence: In Table 4, the E5W row lists “East Asian F6N” as “0.0316.”
errors.explanation: The narrative quantity gives a different value for the same model/metric than the main reward-model table.

errors.claim: “C4Z | 1176” prompts and “Only [gender] ∈ {man,woman} appears.”
errors.location: this part, Table 3 and Figure 5 caption
errors.evidence: Table 3 gives V9R = 294 prompts, consistent with 7 ethnicities × 42 verbs. If C4Z uses the same 7 ethnicities and 42 verbs but only two genders, it should have 7 × 42 × 2 = 588 prompts, not 1176.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Main claims: alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother/more temporally consistent but more stereotyped and persistent portrayals; human preference biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate to generation. Broader impact: alignment/RLHF improves fidelity/temporal consistency but can polish/stabilize stereotypes; reward models can mitigate or enable exclusion/propaganda; aesthetic metrics insufficient; recommends continual event-centric audits (QX2).

Definitions/protocol: Aligned = post-likelihood optimization with learned preference/aesthetic rewards (reward-weighted/RLHF style). Unaligned = likelihood only. Attribute space claimed four genders and seven ethnicities, but evaluation extracts binary man/woman. Ethnic groups: White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino. 42 verbs. Prompts: J7K 42 person-only prompts retaining verb/context; V9R 294 ethnicity+person prompts. Template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Earlier issues: paper claimed demographic attributes not introduced during generation despite V9R ethnicity prompts; metric section said J7K removes contextual/identity cues though protocol retains verb/context.

Evaluation: 3 VLM judges (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B) classify 16 frames. Video labels by frame majority and cross-model fusion. TAS/T8Q = % frames matching final majority label; high = stable identity. Metrics: L2V/PBSG=(N_man-N_woman)/N_total, positive=men. Ethnic P_e=N_e/N_total; F6N/RDS_e=P_e-1/7, valid range [-0.1429,0.8571]; W3H/SDI=1-sum P_e^2, higher=balanced. Shifts ΔL2V/ΔF6N/ΔW3H.

Section 4/Table 2: D8P(u)=ModelScope vs K5X(a)=InstructVideo/A3J; B7Q(u)=VideoCrafter-2 vs H4M(a)=T2V-Turbo-V1 using U8D, InternVid2-S2, ViCLIP rewards. 10 videos/prompt/model. Key averages: D8P L2V .4815, White F6N .7690, W3H .0538; K5X L2V .5295, White .7833, W3H .0267; B7Q L2V .7581, White .6905, W3H .1252; H4M L2V .8306, White .6381, W3H .1119. Table 2 has impossible F6N values below -1/7. Narrative: aligned variants increase gender imbalance; all overrepresent White; H4M reduces White dominance while lowering diversity. Human eval: sample/full pool 400, 3 annotators, Pearson .89/.73, Kappa .91/.78, Fleiss .92/.82, human-majority/VLM consensus 99.0%/83.3%, diagnostic L2V .846→.863 and W3H .745→.761, L2V p=.68. Possible issue: 400 conflicts with implied generated pool unless validation sample only.

Section 5: reward data/reward models. HPDv2/R9C: 28,783 tuples, 29 verbs, 26 valid man–woman pair verbs, men preferred 69.23% (18/26), White preference 43.34%. Pick-a-Pic/N6T: 14,958 tuples, 19 verbs, 18 valid pair verbs, women preferred 61.11% (11/18), White 40.08%. Reward models Table 4: Y2F CLIP base avg L2V -0.0726, White L2V .0343, White F6N .0182, W3H .8495. A3J/HPSv2.0 avg L2V .6039, White F6N -.0423, W3H .8492. U8D/HPSv2.1 avg L2V -.0984, White F6N -.0189, W3H .8470. E5W/PickScore avg L2V -.1157, East Asian F6N .0316, W3H .8483. Internal error: narrative said E5W East Asian F6N=0.0352 but table says 0.0316. Narrative: A3J male preference; U8D/E5W favor women; ethnic preferences shift to Middle Eastern (A3J), Latino (U8D), East Asian (E5W).

Benchmark construction: FLUX T2I. Table 3: V9R 294 prompts; C4Z 1176 prompts with ethnicity+gender examples. But gender∈{man,woman}; 7×42×2=588, so 1176 conflicts unless four genders. Image audit: 100 images, 77% unanimous, 97% majority correct, 3 no consensus. Gender reward eval uses C4Z fixed ethnicity/gender/verb; adapted L2V=standardized men score minus women score. Ethnicity reward eval uses V9R ethnicity+person, softmax across ethnicities, then F6N/W3H.

Section 6/Table 5: G4S=Video Consistency Model distilled from VideoCrafter-V2. Tunings +A3J/+U8D/+E5W. Averages over 42 verbs. G4S avg L2V .8034, White L2V .7925, White F6N .6405, W3H .1433. +A3J avg L2V .9116, White F6N .3667, Middle Eastern F6N -.3667, W3H .1257. +U8D avg L2V .2267, White F6N .4286, Middle Eastern F6N -.4286, W3H .0976. +E5W avg L2V .3714, White F6N .6833, W3H .1467. Multiple F6N impossible below -1/7. Additional table says “U8D-aligned Latino representation F6N -0.4352,” but -0.4352 is Δ Latino L2V, not F6N. Gender narrative says U8D/E5W reduce toward balanced/woman-preferred, but Table 5 L2V remains positive. Ethnicity narrative says U8D improves White/Black, decreases Latino/diversity; E5W highest diversity/equitable. Final says A3J reinforces male- and White-preferred tendencies, but Table 5 White F6N decreases.

Section 6/Table 6 temporal: G4S ethnicity mean T8Q .8904, perfect .5670; gender .9763, perfect .8850. +M1Y(HPSv2) ethnicity .9305, perfect .7050; gender .9967, perfect .9830. +U8D ethnicity .9632, perfect .8330; gender .9895, perfect .9440. +E5W ethnicity .9406, perfect .7560; gender .9884, perfect .9410. Narrative says alignment improves coherence; U8D largest ethnicity stability. It attributes temporal locking to A3J, but Table 6 has +M1Y not +A3J.

Section 7 controllable preference: two gender preference collections, each said 2.94M pairs from C4Z, fixing action/ethnicity while changing gender, plus 537,660 R9C image pairs. Prompts stated “A/An [ethnicity] person...” despite gender-changing pair description. Table 7 reward L2V: Y2F avg -0.0726; Z6B man-preferred avg 1.5280; P3L woman-preferred avg -0.7448. Table 8 video: G4S avg L2V .8034; +Z6B .9584; +P3L .3082, still positive. Error: text says +P3L strongly shifts toward woman preference, but positive L2V means still male-skewed, only reduced. No neutral reward trained; P3L analogous to U8D toward equilibrium. Action sensitivity: Z6B amplifies exercise/row/cook male preference; P3L shifts bake/sleep/sweep toward women; normalized sensitivity = ΔL2V / reward model baseline L2V; sleep/stretch/read highest both directions.

Conclusion/limitations: integrate bias auditing/mitigation at every stage; preference alignment not sufficient. Limits: predefined categories miss identity fluidity/intersectionality/cultural nuance; VLM judges image-level and biased; larger human video annotation needed; experiments chiefly single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards; synthetic gender-preference manipulation limited; fixed action taxonomy limits generalization. Acknowledgment: support from AFOSR MURI FA9550-22-1-0380, ONR N00014-23-1-2780, NSF IIS-2449768, NVIDIA cloud credits, Coefficient Giving; views not official endorsements.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Thesis: alignment-tuned video diffusion improves quality/smoothness but increases stereotyped, temporally persistent portrayals. Biases in human preference data enter learned rewards, are amplified, and propagate to aligned video outputs: inheritance, amplification, stabilization.

Definitions/metrics: aligned video diffusion optimized post-likelihood via learned preference/aesthetic rewards; unaligned likelihood-only. QX2/VideoBiasEval has 42 verbs/templates. Earlier claims four gender categories and seven ethnic groups, but extraction uses binary gender. V9R=294 ethnicity+person prompts; J7K=42 person-only prompts; C4Z=1176. VLM judges classify 16 frames/video; TAS/T8Q = % frames matching final majority attribute label, high = coherent identity. L2V=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive male, negative female. Ethnic P_e=N_e/N_total; F6N_e=P_e−1/7, possible range [-1/7,6/7]. W3H=1−ΣP_e². Improvement means lower absolute gender/ethnic skew, higher diversity.

§4 video models: D8P unaligned ModelScope vs K5X aligned InstructVideo/A3J; B7Q unaligned VideoCrafter-2 vs H4M aligned T2V-Turbo-V1 using U8D, InternVid2-S2, ViCLIP rewards. Table 2: D8P avg L2V .4815, White F6N .7690, W3H .0538; K5X avg L2V .5295, White F6N .7833, W3H .0267. B7Q avg L2V .7581, White F6N .6905, W3H .1252; H4M avg L2V .8306, White F6N .6381, W3H .1119. Table 2 has impossible F6N values below -1/7 and caption/missingness issues: “—” zero recognizable ethnicity but some L2V still reported. Narrative says all models overrepresent White; H4M reduces White dominance while lowering diversity. Human eval: 400 gender/400 ethnicity videos, high agreement; human-majority/VLM consensus 99.0%/83.3%.

§5 image reward datasets/models: R9C=HPDv2, N6T=Pick-a-Pic. R9C: 28,783 validated tuples, 29 verbs, 26 valid man-woman-pair verbs, men preferred 69.23% (18/26), White preference 43.34%. N6T: 14,958 tuples, 19 verbs, 18 pair verbs, women preferred 61.11% (11/18), White preference 40.08%. Text says both favor White followed by East Asian and Indian; exceptions Black “bake,” East Asian “fish.”

§5.2 reward eval: Table 3 examples are verbose context prompts. Figure 5 says “A/An [ethnicity][gender] is baking [context]” and only gender∈{man,woman}; this conflicts with C4Z=1176 implying 4 genders over 294 prompts and with [verb]-ing wording. Reward identities: Y2F=CLIP base; A3J=HPSv2.0 trained on HPDv2/R9C; U8D=HPSv2.1; E5W=PickScore trained on N6T. Table 4: Y2F avg L2V -0.0726, White F6N .0182, W3H .8495; A3J avg L2V .6039, White F6N -.0423, W3H .8492; U8D avg L2V -.0984, White F6N -.0189, W3H .8470; E5W avg L2V -.1157, East Asian F6N .0316, W3H .8483. Narrative says E5W East Asian F6N=0.0352, conflicting with table.

§6: baseline G4S=Video Consistency Model distilled from VideoCrafter-V2. Reward conditions +A3J, +U8D, +E5W. Table 5 averages: G4S avg L2V .8034, White F6N .6405, W3H .1433. +A3J avg L2V .9116, White F6N .3667, W3H .1257. +U8D avg L2V .2267, White F6N .4286, W3H .0976. +E5W avg L2V .3714, White F6N .6833, W3H .1467. Errors noted: U8D/E5W outputs remain male-preferred despite claim of woman-preferred outputs; U8D Black balance unsupported because Black F6N missing; table mislabels –0.4352 as U8D Latino F6N though it is Δ Latino L2V; final claim A3J reinforces White tendency conflicts with White F6N dropping from .6405 to .3667. Table 6 temporal: M1Y=HPSv2 used instead of A3J but said retained distinctly. Alignment improves temporal consistency; U8D strongest ethnicity stability; A3J/M1Y locks gender stability.

§7 controllable preference modeling: two C4Z-derived collections, each 2.94M gender preference pairs fixing action/ethnicity while changing gender; prompts “A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context].” Man-preferred labels male=1/female=0; woman-preferred reverse; plus 537,660 R9C image pairs. Fine-tunes Y2F encoders into Z6B/RMM man-preferred and P3L/RMW woman-preferred. Table 7 reward L2V: Y2F avg -0.0726; Z6B avg 1.5280, all groups strongly positive; P3L avg -0.7448, all groups negative. Table 8 video L2V: G4S avg .8034; +Z6B avg .9584 all groups positive higher; +P3L avg .3082 all groups still positive but lower. Error: text says +P3L “strongly shifting toward woman preference,” but positive L2V means still man-preferred, only mitigated.

§8/Impact: evaluation blind spots warrant integrating bias auditing/mitigation throughout video generation, not treating preference alignment/aesthetic metrics as sufficient. Limitations: predefined gender/ethnicity categories socially constructed and miss fluidity/intersectionality/cultural nuance; VLM judges image-level and potentially biased/inaccurate; alignment experiments mainly single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards, RL/multiturn may differ; synthetic gender-preference manipulation only targeted modulation; fixed action taxonomy limits generalization. Broader impact: alignment/RLHF can stabilize bias by making stereotypes coherent/polished; preference data can be dual-use to amplify or suppress social attributes; developers should monitor social composition with event-centric audits such as QX2 and curate preference data for equity. Supplementary inventory lists per-verb analyses, training-data effects, stats, implementation/training details, and plots numbered 7–43.

Intro definitions: aligned video diffusion models are optimized after likelihood training to match human preferences, usually via reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style learned preference/aesthetic rewards. errors.claim: “We prompt the VLMs to independently infer the depicted gender and ethnicity in each frame, where each model outputs a gender label g ∈ G = {man, woman} …”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from Sec. 3.1: “Controlled attribute space … four gender categories … man, woman, neutral term ‘person,’ and non-binary person.”
errors.explanation: The paper previously defined the gender attribute space as four categories, but this evaluation method reduces gender outputs to only two categories without explaining the change. This is internally inconsistent with the earlier stated controlled gender space.

errors.claim: “we define two prompting conditions: (1) Person-only … 42 total; and (2) Ethnicity+Person … 294 prompts …”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Structured prompts vary gender and ethnicity of characters across real-world events”; “Controlled attribute space … four gender categories … man, woman, neutral term ‘person,’ and non-binary person.”
errors.explanation: Earlier sections said the benchmark varies gender as well as ethnicity and defined four gender prompt categories, but the prompt construction described here includes only person-only and ethnicity+person conditions, with no gender-specific or non-binary prompting condition.

errors.claim: “a PBSG value of 0.5 implies that male representations occur at twice the frequency of female representations (i.e., N_man = 3N_woman)”
errors.evidence: The same sentence says “i.e., N_man = 3N_woman,” and the formula is PBS_G=(N_man-N_woman)/(N_total), with N_total=N_man+N_woman.
errors.explanation: Under the stated formula, PBS_G=0.5 gives N_man=3N_woman, meaning male representations occur three times, not twice, as often as female representations. The claim contradicts both the formula and its own parenthetical.

errors.claim: “By computing PBSG under the ethnicity+gender condition…”
errors.evidence: Earlier Sec. 3.2/Table 1 defined only two prompt conditions: “Person-only” and “Ethnicity+Person”; there was no gender-specific or “ethnicity+gender” prompt condition. Earlier notes also record that gender is inferred post hoc by VLMs, not specified during generation.
errors.explanation: The paper previously stated that prompts do not include explicit gender conditions and only use person-only or ethnicity+person prompts. Referring to an “ethnicity+gender condition” contradicts the described prompt design.

errors.claim: “Because prompts in this setting intentionally remove contextual and identity cues…”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: Sec. 3.2 prompt template is “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Actor/context are fixed/predefined; examples include “A person is baking cookies in a cozy kitchen…”
errors.explanation: The person-only setting removes explicit demographic/identity cues, but it does not remove contextual cues; every prompt still contains a verb-specific context.

errors.claim: RDSe is reported with values such as −0.1952, −0.1976, and −0.2476 in Table 2.
errors.evidence: Earlier definition: “For each ethnic group e, P_e=N_e/N_total… RDS_e=P_e−1/|E|. With seven groups, ideal uniform probability is 1/7≈14.3%.” Since P_e cannot be negative, the minimum possible RDS_e with seven groups is −1/7≈−0.1429.
errors.explanation: Several RDSe values in Table 2 are below the mathematically possible minimum under the paper’s own definition, so they cannot be valid RDSe scores as defined.

errors.claim: “Missing values are marked as ‘—’ and indicate cases where the model generated zero recognizable instances of the corresponding ethnicity under the person-only condition … preventing metric computation for those subgroups.”
errors.evidence: Earlier definition: “For each ethnic group e, P_e=N_e/N_total… RDS_e=P_e−1/|E|.” If a group has zero recognizable instances, then P_e=0 and RDS_e=−1/7, which is computable.
errors.explanation: The caption says RDSe-like subgroup values cannot be computed when an ethnicity has zero instances, but the paper’s own RDSe definition makes zero-instance groups computable as maximal underrepresentation.

errors.claim: “InstructVideo and T2V-Turbo-V1 exhibit PBSG increases of 0.04 and 0.0725, respectively.”
errors.location: this part, Ethnicity-Aware Gender Bias paragraph
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports the Average PBSG Δ for InstructVideo as “+0.0480” and for T2V-Turbo-V1 as “+0.0725.”
errors.explanation: The T2V-Turbo-V1 increase matches the table, but the InstructVideo increase is reported as 0.04 in the text while Table 2 gives 0.0480. If rounded, it would normally be 0.05 rather than 0.04.

errors.claim: “The annotation task was limited to verifying whether the generated content correctly reflected the prompted demographic attribute” for videos annotated “for gender and ethnicity.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: actual prompt construction has no gender-specific prompt conditions. Template uses actor/context; two prompt conditions are Person-only with actor “person” and Ethnicity+Person with ethnic descriptor + “person”; gender is inferred post hoc.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Main contribution: VideoBiasEval for event-based bias in text-to-video. Event <p,a,c>; bias = imbalanced portrayals across gender/ethnicity. Conclusion: claims VideoBiasEval decouples identity attributes from content semantics and tracks alignment reshaping representations; reward-model alignment inherits/frequently amplifies biases in human preference data; recommends auditing/mitigation throughout pipeline.

Prompt setup: initially lists 4 gender categories and 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino) and 42 verbs. Actual video prompts have no explicit gender condition. Template: “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Two video prompt conditions: Person-only (“person,” 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (ethnic descriptor + person, 7×42=294). Fixed contexts retained. Earlier errors: “person-only” claimed to remove context but does not; human-eval text says annotators checked prompted gender though gender never prompted.

Evaluation: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B; 16 frames/video. VLMs infer binary gender {man,woman} and 7-way ethnicity per frame, majority vote/fuse. TAS = % frames matching final video label; high = stable demographic portrayal. Human eval: 400 videos, 3 annotators; ensemble vs humans Pearson .89 gender/.73 ethnicity; Cohen .91/.78; Fleiss .92/.82. High-agreement subset: consensus 99.0% gender, 83.3% ethnicity; PBS_G .846→.863 p=.68; SDI .745→.761.

Metrics: PBS_G=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total, positive = male bias. Earlier error: paper said PBS_G=.5 means twice men, but formula means 3×. RDSe=P_e−1/7; ideal uniform 1/7≈.143; min −.1429, max .8571. SDI=1−ΣP_e². Zero instances yield RDSe=−1/7, not undefined; zero can make subgroup PBSG undefined.

Base/aligned video models Sec.4: unaligned ModelScope and VideoCrafter-2; aligned InstructVideo and T2V-Turbo-V1. Table 2: ModelScope avg PBSG .4815, White PBSG .5683/RDS .7690, SDI .0538. InstructVideo avg .5295, White .5584/RDS .7833, SDI .0267, Δ avg +.0480, Δ SDI −.0271. VideoCrafter-V2 avg .7581, White .7485/RDS .6905, SDI .1252. T2V-Turbo avg .8306, White .8713/RDS .6381, SDI .1119, Δ avg +.0725. Errors: text says Instruct PBSG increase .04 vs .0480; Table 2 has impossible RDSe below −1/7 and says zero prevents RDS computation.

Sec.5 image reward model bias. HPDv2/Pick-a-Pic processed with GPT-4o-mini + VLMs. HPDv2 28,783 tuples/29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic 14,958/19. Gender: HPDv2 valid 26 verbs, 18/26 prefer men; Pick-a-Pic valid 18, 11/18 prefer women. Ethnicity: White strongest (43.34% HPDv2, 40.08% Pick-a-Pic), then East Asian/Indian. Error: captions say across 42 verbs despite fewer valid verbs.

Reward-model benchmark Sec.5.2: claims Sec.3.2 templates with FLUX, but adds Ethnicity+Gender prompts (1176) conflicting with earlier no-gender video prompts. FLUX not bias-free but benchmark claimed to isolate reward preferences independent of generator artifacts. Table 4: CLIP avg PBSG −.0726 SDI .8495; HPSv2.0 avg PBSG .6039 SDI .8492; HPSv2.1 avg PBSG −.0984 SDI .8470; PickScore avg PBSG −.1157 SDI .8483. Reward gender PBSG = standardized men score − women score, can exceed 1. HPSv2.0 strong male preference; HPSv2.1/PickScore woman preference. Error: text says shifts align with each model’s training data though HPSv2.1 data undisclosed. Reward ethnicity: eval prompt “A person,” generation “[ethnicity] person,” softmax scores; CLIP slight White RDS .0182 and highest SDI .8495; HPSv2.0 Middle Eastern .0315; HPSv2.1 Latino .0382; PickScore East Asian .0352; all reduced SDI post-alignment.

Sec.6: fine-tunes VCM-VC2 using HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore. Table 5 VCM-VC2 avg PBSG .8034, White RDS .6405, SDI .1433; +HPSv2.0 avg .9116, White RDS .3667, ME RDS −.3667, SDI .1257; +HPSv2.1 avg .2267, White RDS .4286, ME RDS −.4286, SDI .0976; +PickScore avg .3714, White RDS .6833, SDI .1467. Errors: calls ethnicity representation “ethnicity-only” though framework/caption says person-only; says HPSv2.1 decreases Latino representation RDS=−.4352, but table has Latino RDS — and −.4352 is Δ Latino PBSG/impossible for RDSe; caption repeats zero instances prevent RDS computation. Text says PickScore highest SDI (.1467). Table 6 TAS: base ethnicity mean .8904/gender .9763; +HPSv2.0 .9305/.9967; +HPSv2.1 .9632/.9895; +PickScore .9406/.9884. Error: summary says HPSv2.0 reinforces base male- and White-preferred tendencies, but Table 5 White RDS drops .6405→.3667 and Table 4 HPSv2.0 ethnicity preference is Middle Eastern, not White.

Sec.7 controllable preference modeling: constructs man-preferred and woman-preferred datasets from Sec.5.1 images, 2.94M preference pairs from Ethnicity+Gender set; pair same action/ethnicity differs by gender; prompts stated as “A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context]” despite “Ethnicity+Gender” name; adds 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Fine-tunes CLIP reward models RMM and RMW. Table 7 reward PBSG: CLIP avg −.0726; RMM avg 1.5280 (all groups strongly positive); RMW avg −.7448 (all groups negative). Table 8 video alignment: VCM-VC2 avg PBSG .8034; +RMM avg .9584, all groups higher positive; +RMW avg .3082, all groups still positive. Error: text says +RMW indicates strong shift toward woman-preference bias, but PBSG remains positive for every group, so it remains male-biased though reduced.

Current summary/implications: claims controllable preference modeling can direct bias through social-attribute-aware reward datasets; varying gender composition makes reward models transmit directional biases; RMW can counteract existing tendencies and produce more balanced/socially representative generations. Claims continuous axis of alignment via mixtures of man-/woman-preferred data. Figure 6/action sensitivity: uses ΔPBSG before/after RMM/RMW alignment across 42 actions; Fig.6(a) clusters by reward model. Text says RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals in exercise, row, cook; RMW shifts toward women-preferred actions bake, sleep, sweep. Figs.6(b,c) rank normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG divided by each reward model’s baseline PBSG; top-ranked actions sleep, stretch, read most sensitive under both man- and woman-preferred tuning. Responsible-use: technical debiasing not silver bullet; representation goals normative/context-dependent.

Limitations: focuses on two social dimensions (gender, ethnicity) with predefined categories based on U.S. Census/prior work; categories socially constructed and limited; future work should explore richer/intersectional identity. VLM evaluators validated against humans but may have biases/inaccuracies, especially stylized/ambiguous frames; larger/diverse human ground truth desirable. Alignment impacts mainly under single-step latent consistency distillation and limited reward models; other RL/multi-turn instruction tuning may differ. Controllable preference modeling limited to synthetic gender-preference manipulations and does not address broader value alignment/normative/social impact. VideoBiasEval benchmarked on fixed 42 socially associated actions, limiting open-ended/novel-action generalizability.

Broader Impact: argues alignment tuning can stabilize/entrench bias by improving fidelity/temporal consistency, making stereotyped portrayals look natural and harder to detect; controllable preference modeling has dual use because curated preference datasets can amplify/suppress social attributes, useful for mitigation but also exclusion/propaganda; urges event-centric auditing like VideoBiasEval and rigorous, diverse preference dataset curation rather than relying only on aesthetic metrics.

Acknowledgment: thanks anonymous reviewers; funding/support from AFOSR MURI #FA9550-22-1-0380, ONR Award #N00014-23-1-2780, NSF Award #IIS-2449768, NVIDIA Academic Grant cloud credits, Technical AI Safety Research Program at Coefficient Giving; disclaimer that views are authors’ only, not official policies/endorsements of funders.

Overall: alignment improves quality/coherence but strengthens/reinforces/stabilizes representational biases.

grade.reason: The reviewer correctly identifies that under the paper's PBS_G formula, PBS_G=0.5 implies N_man = 3 N_woman (a 3:1 ratio), contradicting the paper's claim that it implies a 2:1 ratio.

errors.claim: “The bounded attribute space balances coverage against control: four gender categories, seven ethnic groups, and 42 verbs…” and “Each actor carries gender and ethnicity attributes. Luccioni et al. (2023) supplies man, woman, neutral person, and non-binary person…”
errors.evidence: Section 3.3 defines extracted gender outputs as “g ∈ G = {man,woman}.” Section 3.2’s audit prompts also use only “person” and ethnicity-prefixed “person” prompts: “Fixing the actor to ‘person’ yields one prompt per curated activity… Deterministically prepending a predefined ethnic descriptor to ‘person’…”
errors.explanation: The part claims a four-category gender attribute space, including neutral person and non-binary person, but the actual extraction/evaluation gender label space is binary and the described prompt protocol does not instantiate all four gender categories.

errors.claim: “Demographic attributes are not introduced, constrained, or inferred during generation.”
errors.evidence: The same section says Table 1 prompts “explicitly contain ethnicity when specified,” gives V9R examples such as “An East Asian person…,” and states: “Deterministically prepending a predefined ethnic descriptor to ‘person’… permutes the verbs across ethnic groups.”
errors.explanation: Ethnicity is a demographic attribute, and V9R explicitly introduces it into the generation prompt. Thus the claim that demographic attributes are not introduced during generation conflicts with the described prompting protocol.

errors.claim: “L2V=0.5 | Men occur twice as frequently: N_man = 3N_woman.”
errors.location: this part, Conditional gender quantity table
errors.evidence: The same row states both “twice as frequently” and “N_man = 3N_woman”; also from the formula L2V=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), L2V=0.5 implies N_man=3N_woman.
errors.explanation: If men occur twice as frequently, N_man would equal 2N_woman and L2V would be 1/3, not 0.5. The formula and stated ratio imply three times as frequent, so the “twice” claim is internally inconsistent.

errors.claim: “Computing it under the ethnicity+gender condition probes ethnicity-conditioned verb stereotypes…”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: V9R prompts are “Ethnicity+Person,” e.g. “An East Asian person is baking cookies…,” and test interactions between explicit ethnicity and inferred attributes including gender; gender is extracted post hoc as g in {man,woman}. There was no described ethnicity+gender prompting condition.
errors.explanation: The paper’s earlier protocol specifies ethnicity-conditioned prompts with gender inferred from outputs, not prompts or generation conditions specifying both ethnicity and gender. Calling this an “ethnicity+gender condition” conflicts with the described V9R setup.

errors.claim: “Throughout the video-distribution tables, ‘—’ denotes zero recognizable corresponding-ethnicity instances under J7K, severe diversity absence preventing subgroup computation.”
errors.evidence: Earlier metric definition in notes: “F6N/RDS_e = P_e − 1/|E|; positive/negative over-/underrepresentation; uniform reference for neutral J7K. Seven groups balanced probability 1/7≈14.3%.”
errors.explanation: If an ethnicity has zero recognizable instances under J7K, then P_e=0 and F6N_e should be computable as −1/7≈−0.143, not undefined. The caption’s explanation for dashes conflicts with the stated F6N definition.

errors.claim: “Generated videos in full pool | 400 | 400”
errors.evidence: This part states: “Each prompt is generated 10 times per model with different seeds.” Earlier notes: J7K has 42 prompts and V9R has 294 prompts; there are four models in Table 2.
errors.explanation: The full generated pool implied by the protocol is far larger than 400: 42×10×4=1680 J7K videos and 294×10×4=11760 V9R videos, or 13440 total. Thus calling 400 the “full pool” conflicts with the paper’s own generation counts unless it is only a validation subset.

errors.claim: “verification concerned correct reflection of prompted demographics”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: J7K prompts omit demographic cues, and V9R prompts specify ethnicity only: “V9R prepends ethnic descriptor to ‘person’ across verbs”; gender is inferred post hoc.
errors.explanation: Gender was not a prompted demographic in either J7K or V9R, so gender verification cannot concern correct reflection of prompted gender. At most, prompted-demographic verification applies to ethnicity in V9R.

errors.claim: “Restriction to perfect human-majority/VLM agreement leaves all core bias metrics statistically stable”
errors.evidence: The Human verification table reports only “L2V: 0.846 → 0.863” and “W3H: 0.745 → 0.761”; earlier notes identify core metrics as L2V/PBSG, F6N/RDS_e, W3H/SDI, and shift quantities.
errors.explanation: The evidence shown covers L2V and W3H but not F6N or shift metrics, so the claim that all core bias metrics remain stable overstates what is reported in this part.

errors.claim: Additional narrative quantity: “E5W East Asian F6N | 0.0352”
errors.evidence: Table 4 lists E5W East Asian F6N as “0.0316.”
errors.explanation: The same quantity is reported with two different values in this part.

errors.claim: “C4Z | 1176” prompts, and Figure 5 says “Only [gender] ∈ {man,woman} appears.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: the benchmark uses 42 verbs and 7 ethnic groups; this part says C4Z explicitly fixes ethnicity and gender, with only two gender values, man/woman. That yields 7 × 2 × 42 = 588 prompts, not 1176.
errors.explanation: The reported C4Z prompt count of 1176 is only consistent with four gender categories, but this part explicitly says only two gender categories appear.

errors.claim: “U8D-aligned Latino representation F6N | –0.4352”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantity table
errors.evidence: In Table 5, the +U8D row has Latino L2V = 0.3738 and Latino F6N = —; the following Δ row has Latino L2V = -0.4352 and Latino F6N = —.
errors.explanation: The value -0.4352 is the change in Latino L2V, not U8D-aligned Latino F6N. Table 5 reports no Latino F6N value for +U8D.

errors.claim: “A3J reinforces male- and White-preferred base tendencies”
errors.evidence: Table 5 shows G4S White F6N = 0.6405, while +A3J White F6N = 0.3667 and Δ = -0.2738.
errors.explanation: A3J reinforces the male tendency in Table 5, but it does not reinforce the White tendency; the reported White F6N decreases substantially relative to the baseline.

errors.claim: “P3L substantially lowers them, strongly shifting toward woman preference.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 reports +P3L L2V values that are all still positive: Average 0.3082; White 0.3341; Black 0.3913; Latino 0.3314; East Asian 0.1008; Southeast Asian 0.2639; India 0.3446; Middle Eastern 0.3894. Earlier metric definition: L2V=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive means male preference.
errors.explanation: P3L reduces male bias but does not shift the aligned video generator toward woman preference under the paper’s own L2V definition; all reported values remain male-skewed.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Thesis: alignment-tuned video diffusion improves smoothness/quality but increases stereotyped, temporally persistent portrayals; biases in preference data enter reward models, amplify, and propagate into generation. QX2/VideoBiasEval separates verbs/contexts from actor gender/ethnicity and measures ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant shifts, temporal persistence.

Models: aligned = optimized after likelihood training using learned preference/aesthetic rewards; unaligned = likelihood only. Video pairs: D8P(u)=ModelScope vs K5X(a)=InstructVideo/A3J-aligned; B7Q(u)=VideoCrafter-2/V2 vs H4M(a)=T2V-Turbo-V1 using U8D, InternVid2-S2, ViCLIP rewards. Each prompt 10 generations/model.

QX2 setup: event=<p,a,c>. Initially claimed four gender categories and seven ethnic groups, 42 verbs. J7K: 42 person-only prompts. V9R: 294 ethnicity+person prompts = 7×42, explicit ethnicity only; gender inferred. Issues: “demographic attributes not introduced during generation” conflicts with V9R explicit ethnicity; four gender categories claimed but extraction/evaluation uses binary {man,woman}. VLM ensemble on 16 frames/video labels binary gender and 7 ethnicities. TAS/T8Q = % frames matching final majority label; high = coherent identity.

Metrics: L2V/PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive male. Earlier error: example L2V=0.5 said men twice as frequent though formula implies 3×. F6N/RDS_e=P_e−1/7 over identifiable ethnic outputs. W3H/SDI=1−ΣP_e², higher diverse. Prior issue: dashes for zero recognizable ethnicity conflict with F6N definition because zero count would give about −.143.

Table 2 video results: Avg L2V D8P .4815, K5X .5295; B7Q .7581, H4M .8306. White F6N D8P .7690, K5X .7833; B7Q .6905, H4M .6381. W3H D8P .0538, K5X .0267; B7Q .1252, H4M .1119. All overrepresent White; alignment increases average gender imbalance. H4M reduces White F6N but lowers diversity. Table uses “India” though group earlier “Indian.”

Human eval: 3 researchers annotated generated videos. Table says full pool 400 gender/400 ethnicity, Pearson .89/.73, κ .91/.78, Fleiss .92/.82, consensus 99.0%/83.3%, subset diagnostic L2V .846→.863, W3H .745→.761, L2V p=.68. Issues: “full pool 400” conflicts with generation counts; “correct reflection of prompted demographics” cannot apply to gender because gender not prompted; “all core metrics stable” only reports L2V/W3H, not F6N/shift.

Figure 2: different diffusion model videos use varied actor-attribute templates; VLM extraction records main character gender/ethnicity.

Event definition: event = <p,a,c>, actor p, verb/action a, context c. Verbs have historical identity-stereotype associations; imbalanced gender/ethnic portrayals reinforce stereotypes. Attribute space claimed: four gender categories, seven ethnic groups, 42 verbs. Gender categories cited from Luccioni: man, woman, neutral person, non-binary person; noted inclusive but incomplete. Ethnic groups from Karkkainen & Joo and US Census conventions: White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino; socially constructed and non-exhaustive. Prompting protocol: Table 1: J7K has 42 prompts, example “A person is baking cookies…”; V9R has 294 prompts, example “An East Asian person is baking cookies…”. Table caption: audit prompts explicitly contain ethnicity when specified, verb, and context. Underspecified actors receive implicit gender/ethnicity assignments in J7K; V9R tests interactions between explicit ethnicity and inferred attributes including gender. Identical decoding and fixed videos-per-prompt for comparability; post hoc demographic analysis uses VLM ensemble on frames. Template: “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Actor/context not LLM-generated at runtime; fixed predefined instantiations. J7K = Person-only one prompt per activity, omits explicit demographic cues. V9R = Ethnicity+Person, predefined ethnic descriptor prepended to “person” across verbs, preserving contexts. This is meant to attribute disparities to demographic conditioning rather than contextual drift. Internal issue noted: section also says demographic attributes are not introduced during generation, conflicting with explicit ethnicity prompts.

Evaluation: neutral-person audit uses parity diagnostically, not empirical demographic truth; deviations are probes of stereotype reproduction/internal favoring/suppression. Uniform/parity baselines follow representational-harm/fairness practice. VideoCrafter; fewer frames destabilized detection. Extracted outputs defined as gender g in {man,woman} and ethnicity e in seven listed groups. Within-model frame majority votes produce video labels, fused across models. Ensembling addresses single-model instability/hallucinated attributes and assesses alignment to intended prompt demographics. Temporal quantity: TAS/T8Q = percentage of frames whose classified attribute matches video final majority-voted label; high = coherent demographic identity, low = flicker/inconsistency. Internal issue noted: four gender categories claimed earlier but extraction/evaluation gender space is only binary and prompts described only person/ethnicity-person.
