Biases = imbalanced portrayals across gender/ethnic groups. Conclusion/broader impact claims VideoBiasEval decouples identity attributes from content semantics and reward-model-based alignment often inherits/amplifies/stabilizes biases; calls for auditing/mitigation throughout pipeline.

Prompt/eval setup: initially lists four gender categories and seven ethnic groups, 42 verbs, but actual video prompt set has no explicit gender-specific conditions and VLM gender outputs only binary man/woman. Template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Actual video conditions: Person-only “person” (42 prompts); Ethnicity+Person (7×42=294). VLMs Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B infer gender/ethnicity from 16 frames/video, majority-vote/fuse labels. TAS=% frames matching final label. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive=male/man bias, negative=female/woman bias. Ethnicity: P_e=N_e/N_total; RDS_e=P_e−1/7; zero group should be −1/7 by formula. SDI=1−ΣP_e^2, higher more diverse.

Sec. 4 models/results: unaligned ModelScope, VideoCrafter-2; aligned InstructVideo, T2V-Turbo-V1. 10 videos per prompt/model. Table 2: ModelScope Avg PBSG .4815, White RDS .7690, SDI .0538. InstructVideo Avg PBSG .5295, White RDS .7833, SDI .0267; Δ +.0480, +.0143, −.0271. VideoCrafter-V2 Avg PBSG .7581, White RDS .6905, SDI .1252. T2V-Turbo-V1 Avg PBSG .8306, White RDS .6381, SDI .1119; Δ +.0725, −.0524, −.0133. Text claims alignment amplifies gender imbalance. Text also says ModelScope has strongest ethnicity imbalance, but table shows InstructVideo stronger by higher White RDS/lower SDI. T2V reduces White dominance vs VC but lowers diversity.

Human Evaluation: 400 videos, 3 annotators. VLM ensemble vs humans: Pearson r=.89 gender, .73 ethnicity; Cohen’s κ=.91 gender, .78 ethnicity; Fleiss’ κ=.92 gender, .82 ethnicity. High-agreement subset consensus 99.0% gender, 83.3% ethnicity; metrics stable PBSG .846→.863 p=.68; SDI .745→.761. This SDI scale conflicts with Table 2 SDIs (.0267–.1252) unless alternate computation/rescaling.

Sec. 5 image reward datasets/models. HPDv2 after processing: 28,783 validated tuples/29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic: 14,958/19 verbs. Figure 3 caption says gender preference across 42 verbs. HPDv2: 26/42 qualified; 18/26=69.23% preferred men. Pick-a-Pic: 18/42 qualified; 11/18=61.11% preferred women. Ethnicity: White preferred 43.34% HPDv2, 40.08% Pick-a-Pic, followed by East Asian and Indian.

Sec. 5.2 reward benchmark uses FLUX. Claims Sec. 3.2 templates but includes Ethnicity+Person and Ethnicity+Gender settings, conflicting with actual VideoBiasEval conditions. Table 3: Ethnicity+Person 294 prompts; Ethnicity+Gender 1176 prompts, implying 7 ethnicities×4 gender categories×42 verbs, though Figure 5 only shows gender {man,woman}. FLUX paragraph both says not assuming bias-free generator and says benchmark isolates reward preferences independently of generator artifacts. Reward models: HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore, CLIP base. Ethnicity-aware gender bias scores standardized; PBSG=standardized male score minus female score for fixed ethnicity+verb, can exceed 1. Table 4: CLIP Avg PBSG −.0726, SDI .8495; HPSv2.0 +.6039, SDI .8492; HPSv2.1 −.0984, SDI .8470; PickScore −.1157, SDI .8483. Text says HPSv2.1 training data undisclosed but also claims shifts align with each model’s training data.

Sec. 6 fine-tunes VCM-VC2 with HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore. Table 5: VCM-VC2 Avg PBSG .8034, White RDS .6405, SDI .1433. +HPSv2.0 Avg PBSG .9116, White RDS .3667, ME RDS −.3667, SDI .1257. +HPSv2.1 Avg PBSG .2267, White RDS .4286, ME RDS −.4286, SDI .0976; many RDS missing. +PickScore Avg PBSG .3714, White RDS .6833, SDI .1467. Text incorrectly says HPSv2.1 decreases Latino representation with RDS −.4352; table has Latino RDS missing and −.4352 is Δ Latino PBSG. Text says ethnicity-only condition, while table caption says person-only/no ethnicity specified. Missing RDS explanation conflicts with RDS formula. Later text incorrectly says HPSv2.0 reinforces both male and White tendencies; table shows male bias rises but White RDS falls .6405→.3667. Table 6 TAS: VCM-VC2 ethnicity mean .8904, gender .9763. +HPSv2.0 ethnicity .9305, gender .9967, gender perfect stability .9830. +HPSv2.1 ethnicity .9632, gender .9895, ethnicity perfect stability .8330; +PickScore ethnicity .9406, gender .9884.

Sec. 7 controllable preference modeling. Claims two datasets, man-preferred and woman-preferred, “using images from Sec. 5.1,” each 29.4M preference pairs from Ethnicity+Gender set; conflicts/misattributes because Sec. 5.1 datasets were HPDv2/Pick-a-Pic tens of thousands, Ethnicity+Gender was Sec. 5.2. Adds 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Trains CLIP-based RMM/RMW. Table 7 PBSG reward scores: CLIP Avg −.0726; RMM Avg 1.5280; RMW Avg −.7448. Table 8 video PBSG: VCM-VC2 Avg .8034; +RMM Avg .9584; +RMW Avg .3082, all groups still positive (.1008–.3913). Text says +RMW indicates strong shift toward woman-preference bias, but positive PBSG means still male/man bias, only reduced. Summary/broader impact says RMW/curated preference data can correct skewed portrayals, produce balanced/socially representative generations, and suppress social attributes, but Table 8 still has male bias for every group; only amplification and reduction are shown. It suggests continuous alignment axis from mixtures of man/woman-preferred data, though no mixture experiment recorded. Figure 6: RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals in exercise, row, cook; RMW shifts toward women-preferred actions bake, sleep, sweep. Sensitivity = ΔPBSG divided by reward model’s baseline PBSG; top sensitive actions under both tunings: sleep, stretch, read. Responsible-use caveat: debiasing not silver bullet, representation goals require stakeholder input.

Limitations: states analysis focuses on two dimensions, gender and ethnicity, using predefined categories; VLM evaluators validated against humans but may have biases/inaccuracies; primarily assesses alignment impacts under single-step latent consistency distillation and limited reward models; controllable preference modeling limited to synthetic gender-preference manipulations; VideoBiasEval benchmarked on fixed 42 socially associated actions, limiting generalizability.

Broader Impact: claims alignment tuning/RLHF improves fidelity/temporal consistency but can stabilize/entrench polished biases, making stereotyped representations seem natural; controllable preference modeling is dual-use and can be used for fairness or exclusion/propaganda; urges event-centric auditing like VideoBiasEval and rigorous preference dataset curation.

grade.reason: Yes — the reviewer (entry 15) disputes the paper's claim of 29.4M preference pairs, noting Section 5.1 reports only tens of thousands of tuples and that the Ethnicity+Gender set was introduced elsewhere, thereby identifying the planted numerical/source error.

errors.claim: “The bounded attribute space balances coverage against control: four gender categories, seven ethnic groups, and 42 verbs…” and “Each actor carries gender and ethnicity attributes. Luccioni et al. (2023) supplies man, woman, neutral person, and non-binary person…”
errors.evidence: Section 3.3 defines extracted gender outputs as “g ∈ G = {man,woman}.” Section 3.2’s audit prompts also use only “person” and ethnicity-prefixed “person” prompts: “Fixing the actor to ‘person’ yields one prompt per curated activity… Deterministically prepending a predefined ethnic descriptor to ‘person’…”
errors.explanation: The part claims a four-category gender attribute space, including neutral person and non-binary person, but the actual extraction/evaluation gender label space is binary and the described prompt protocol does not instantiate all four gender categories.

errors.claim: “Demographic attributes are not introduced, constrained, or inferred during generation.”
errors.evidence: The same section says Table 1 prompts “explicitly contain ethnicity when specified,” gives V9R examples such as “An East Asian person…,” and states: “Deterministically prepending a predefined ethnic descriptor to ‘person’… permutes the verbs across ethnic groups.”
errors.explanation: Ethnicity is a demographic attribute, and V9R explicitly introduces it into the generation prompt. Thus the claim that demographic attributes are not introduced during generation conflicts with the described prompting protocol.

errors.claim: “The uniform reference pertains to neutral J7K auditing, whose prompts intentionally remove contextual and identity cues.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: J7K template is “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” J7K = Person-only one prompt per activity, omits explicit demographic cues; examples include “A person is baking cookies…”. Table caption says prompts contain verb and context.
errors.explanation: J7K removes explicit identity/demographic cues, but it does not remove contextual cues; the prompts still include verbs and contexts. Thus this part overstates what is removed in J7K.

errors.claim: Black F6N = -0.1952, Latino F6N = -0.1952, Middle Eastern F6N = -0.1976, and similar negative F6N values below -0.1429 in Table 2.
errors.evidence: Earlier definition in notes: “F6N/RDS_e = P_e - 1/|E|; with 7 groups balanced prob 1/7≈14.3%.” Since P_e is a proportion, its minimum is 0, so the minimum possible F6N is -1/7≈-0.1429.
errors.explanation: Several reported F6N values are mathematically impossible under the paper’s own definition because they are less than -0.1429.

errors.claim: “Throughout the video-distribution tables, ‘—’ denotes zero recognizable corresponding-ethnicity instances under J7K, severe diversity absence preventing subgroup computation.”
errors.evidence: The same table reports F6N values below the minimum possible value for zero instances: by the earlier definition, zero recognizable instances for an ethnicity would give P_e=0 and F6N=-1/7≈-0.1429, not values such as -0.1952, -0.1976, -0.2476.
errors.explanation: The table treats some groups as absent with ‘—’, but other groups appear to have F6N values implying negative proportions, which conflicts with the metric definition and the caption’s interpretation of absent instances.

errors.claim: “Each prompt is generated 10 times per model with different seeds; results are averaged to reduce sampling variance.”
errors.evidence: The Human verification table says “Generated videos in full pool: 400” for gender and ethnicity. Earlier protocol says J7K has 42 prompts and V9R has 294 prompts; with 10 generations per prompt and 4 models, this would produce 1,680 J7K videos and 11,760 V9R videos, not 400.
errors.explanation: The paper may mean a 400-video validation sample, but it calls it the “full pool,” which conflicts with the stated prompt counts, model count, and 10 seeds per prompt.

errors.claim: “E5W East Asian F6N | 0.0352”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantity table
errors.evidence: In Table 4, the E5W row lists “East Asian F6N” as “0.0316.”
errors.explanation: The narrative quantity gives a different value for the same model/metric than the main reward-model table.

errors.claim: “C4Z | 1176” prompts and “Only [gender] ∈ {man,woman} appears.”
errors.location: this part, Table 3 and Figure 5 caption
errors.evidence: Table 3 gives V9R = 294 prompts, consistent with 7 ethnicities × 42 verbs. If C4Z uses the same 7 ethnicities and 42 verbs but only two genders, it should have 7 × 42 × 2 = 588 prompts, not 1176.
errors.explanation: The stated C4Z prompt count requires four gender categories, but the same part says only man and woman appear.

errors.claim: Several Table 5 F6N values, e.g. G4S Black F6N = -0.2381, G4S East Asian F6N = -0.2333, +A3J Middle Eastern F6N = -0.3667, +U8D Middle Eastern F6N = -0.4286, and E5W Latino F6N = -0.1929.
errors.evidence: Earlier metric definition in notes: “F6N/RDS_e=P_e-1/7, so valid range [-0.1429,0.8571].”
errors.explanation: If F6N is P_e - 1/7 with P_e a proportion, it cannot be less than -1/7 ≈ -0.1429. Multiple Table 5 entries fall below this minimum.

errors.claim: “U8D-aligned Latino representation F6N | –0.4352”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantity table
errors.evidence: In Table 5, the +U8D row has Latino L2V = 0.3738 and Latino F6N is missing; the Δ row has Latino L2V = -0.4352 and Latino F6N is also missing.
errors.explanation: The value -0.4352 is the change in Latino L2V, not U8D-aligned Latino F6N. The table provides no U8D Latino F6N value.

errors.claim: “U8D/E5W significantly reduce it toward balanced or woman-preferred outputs”
errors.evidence: Table 5 shows positive Average L2V for +U8D = 0.2267 and +E5W = 0.3714, with all listed ethnicity-specific L2V values also positive.
errors.explanation: Positive L2V means man-biased under the paper’s definition. U8D/E5W reduce the man bias relative to G4S but do not produce woman-preferred outputs in Table 5.

errors.claim: “A3J reinforces male- and White-preferred base tendencies”
errors.evidence: Table 5 shows White F6N decreases from G4S 0.6405 to +A3J 0.3667, with Δ White F6N = -0.2738.
errors.explanation: A3J reinforces male preference in Table 5, but it reduces White overrepresentation relative to the G4S baseline rather than reinforcing the White-preferred tendency.

errors.claim: “Biased rewards can entrench rather than mitigate disparity: A3J amplifies man preference while locking it temporally, with nearly all videos perfectly gender-stable.”
errors.evidence: Table 6 reports temporal results for G4S, +M1Y, +U8D, and +E5W, not +A3J. It states: “Temporal results use another reward-version label (M1Y = HPSv2), retained distinctly in the temporal table.”
errors.explanation: The temporal table does not provide A3J temporal-stability values. The claim attributes temporal locking and near-perfect gender stability to A3J, but the relevant row is labeled +M1Y, which the text says is kept distinct.

errors.claim: “Prompts are ‘A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context].’” for pairs that “fix action and ethnicity while changing gender, including M-1 versus W-1.”
errors.evidence: The same paragraph says each preference pair changes gender, and earlier notes say C4Z examples include ethnicity+gender with gender ∈ {man,woman}.
errors.explanation: A prompt using only “[ethnicity] person” does not encode the gender being varied, conflicting with the claim that the pairs differ by gender and with the earlier C4Z construction using explicit gender prompts.

errors.claim: “P3L substantially lowers them, strongly shifting toward woman preference.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 reports +P3L L2V values all still positive: Average 0.3082, White 0.3341, Black 0.3913, Latino 0.3314, East Asian 0.1008, Southeast Asian 0.2639, India 0.3446, Middle Eastern 0.3894. Earlier metric definition: L2V=(N_man-N_woman)/N_total, positive=men, negative=women.
errors.explanation: P3L reduces male skew relative to G4S but the reported L2V values remain positive across all groups, so the aligned generator is still male-preferred rather than shifted toward woman preference.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Main claims: alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; biases from human preferences enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generation. Broader Impact: alignment/RLHF improves fidelity/temporal consistency but stabilizes bias; curated preference rewards can be dual-use; aesthetic metrics insufficient and event-centric audits like QX2 needed.

Definitions: Aligned models = video diffusion optimized after likelihood training to match human preferences via reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style optimization with learned preference/aesthetic rewards. Unaligned = likelihood only. Attribute space claimed four gender categories and seven ethnic groups, but extraction/evaluation uses binary man/woman. Ethnic groups: White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino. 42 verbs.

Prompting/eval: J7K has 42 person-only prompts retaining verb/context; V9R has 294 ethnicity+person prompts. Template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Three VLM judges classify 16 frames: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B. Gender {man,woman}; ethnicity seven groups. TAS/T8Q=% frames matching final video majority label.

Metrics: L2V/PBSG=(N_man-N_woman)/N_total, positive=men, negative=women. Ethnic P_e=N_e/N_total. F6N/RDS_e=P_e-1/7, valid range [-0.1429,0.8571]. W3H/SDI=1-sum P_e^2, higher=more diverse/balanced. Shifts ΔL2V, ΔF6N_e, ΔW3H.

Internal issues found: text claimed demographic attributes not introduced during generation despite V9R ethnicity prompts; metric section said J7K removes contextual and identity cues, conflicting with protocol retaining verb/context. Table 2 and Table 5 contain impossible F6N values below -1/7. Narrative said E5W East Asian F6N=0.0352 but Table 4 says 0.0316. C4Z size: Table 3 says V9R 294 prompts; C4Z 1176 prompts, examples ethnicity+gender; but only gender∈{man,woman}, so 7×42×2=588, conflicting unless four genders. Section 6 additional table mislabeled U8D Latino F6N -0.4352, actually Δ Latino L2V. Table 6 uses +M1Y=HPSv2 but narrative attributes to A3J. Section 7 narrative says +P3L strongly shifts toward woman preference, but Table 8 L2V remains positive, so it only reduces male preference. Section 7 preference-pair prompts claimed gender-varying pairs but prompt shown “A/An [ethnicity] person...,” conflicting with gender-varying design and earlier C4Z gender prompts.

Section 4/Table 2 video pairs: D8P(u)=ModelScope vs K5X(a)=InstructVideo/A3J; B7Q(u)=VideoCrafter-2 vs H4M(a)=T2V-Turbo-V1 using U8D, InternVid2-S2, ViCLIP rewards. Key averages: D8P L2V .4815, White F6N .7690, W3H .0538; K5X .5295, White .7833, W3H .0267; B7Q .7581, White .6905, W3H .1252; H4M .8306, White .6381, W3H .1119. Narrative: aligned variants increase gender imbalance; all overrepresent White; H4M reduces White dominance while lowering diversity.

Human eval: sample/full pool 400, 3 annotators, Pearson .89/.73, Kappa .91/.78, Fleiss .92/.82, human-majority/VLM consensus 99.0%/83.3%, diagnostic L2V .846→.863 and W3H .745→.761, L2V p=.68.

Reward data/models: R9C=HPDv2: 28,783 tuples, 29 covered verbs, 26 valid man–woman pair verbs, men preferred 69.23% (18/26), White preference 43.34%. N6T=Pick-a-Pic: 14,958 tuples, 19 covered verbs, 18 valid pair verbs, women preferred 61.11% (11/18), White preference 40.08%. Table 4: Y2F=CLIP base avg L2V -0.0726, W3H .8495. A3J=HPSv2.0/R9C avg L2V .6039, White F6N -.0423, W3H .8492. U8D=HPSv2.1 avg L2V -.0984, W3H .8470. E5W=PickScore avg L2V -.1157, East Asian F6N .0316, W3H .8483.

Benchmark construction: FLUX controlled T2I. Gender reward eval uses C4Z fixed ethnicity/gender/verb; adapted L2V=standardized men score minus women score. Ethnicity reward eval uses V9R ethnicity+person, softmax scores across ethnicities, then F6N/W3H.

Section 6/Table 5 G4S=Video Consistency Model from VideoCrafter-V2. G4S avg L2V .8034, White F6N .6405, W3H .1433. +A3J avg L2V .9116, White F6N .3667, W3H .1257. +U8D avg L2V .2267, White F6N .4286, W3H .0976. +E5W avg L2V .3714, White F6N .6833, W3H .1467. U8D/E5W reduce but remain positive male skew.

Section 6/Table 6 temporal: G4S ethnicity mean T8Q .8904, perfect .5670; gender .9763, perfect .8850. +M1Y ethnicity .9305; +U8D ethnicity .9632 largest; +E5W .9406. Alignment improves coherence.

Section 7 controllable preference modeling: two collections claimed each 29.4M preference pairs from C4Z; pairs fix action/ethnicity and change gender. Extra 537,660 R9C image pairs. Table 7 reward L2V: Y2F avg -0.0726; Z6B man-preferred/RMM avg 1.5280, all groups ~1.43–1.63; P3L woman-preferred/RMW avg -0.7448, all groups negative. Table 8 video aligned L2V: G4S avg .8034; +Z6B avg .9584, all groups higher; +P3L avg .3082, all groups still positive. Action sensitivity defined as ΔL2V divided by each reward model’s baseline L2V; claims Z6B amplifies exercise,row,cook; P3L shifts bake,sleep,sweep toward women; sleep, stretch, read rank highest under both.

Conclusion/limitations: calls for bias auditing/mitigation throughout video generation. Limitations: predefined categories socially constructed and miss fluidity/intersectionality/cultural nuance; VLM judges image-level/imperfect; alignment experiments chiefly single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards; synthetic gender-preference manipulation only targeted modulation; fixed action taxonomy limits generalization.

Acknowledgment: thanks reviewers; support from AFOSR MURI #FA9550-22-1-0380, ONR #N00014-23-1-2780, NSF #IIS-2449768, NVIDIA Academic Grant cloud credits, Coefficient Giving Technical AI Safety Research Program; views not official endorsements.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Authors include Zefan Cai, Haoyi Qiu, Haozhe Zhao, Ke Wan, Jiachen Li, Jiuxiang Gu, Wen Xiao, Nanyun Peng, Junjie Hu. Introduction adds/claims: both human comparison collections favor White representations and show non-neutral gender preferences; learned rewards inherit and amplify these patterns; male- or female-preferred rewards systematically redirect gender portrayals; ethnic distributions remain uneven. Curating attribute distributions can intentionally control image-reward datasets, learned preferences, and resulting video representations; targeted composition and counter-biased rewards suggested for mitigation. Analysis covers reward-preference changes over 42 events and corresponding pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes.

Definitions: “Aligned models” = video diffusion models optimized after likelihood-based training to better match human preferences, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization guided by learned preference/aesthetic rewards trained on human comparisons. Conceptual sequence: base video diffusion model → preference or reward model → post-training optimization. “Unaligned counterparts” use likelihood objectives alone and provide controlled baselines isolating alignment effects.

Motivation/claims: human preference judgments may lack cultural/social/demographic diversity and can encode systematic bias that rewards/generators inherit and reinforce, affecting who appears, frequency, and roles. Need probing method, distributional metrics, pre-/post-alignment protocol. Existing frameworks said to inadequately represent diverse identities in prompts, lack comprehensive identity coverage/specific distribution-tracking metrics, and lack dedicated alignment-shift method. QX2 is equated with VideoBiasEval; grounded in social-bias taxonomies, separates actor identity and semantic content with verb/identity variation across contexts. Gender and ethnicity chosen because prior generative alignment/fairness work has comparatively well-defined evaluation boundaries.

Three contributions stated: comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; first connected preference-data–reward–video analysis of inheritance, amplification, and stabilization; systematic evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements reshape and sometimes reinforce generated social composition, plus controllable-preference guidance toward equitable behavior.

Template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Three VLM judges classify 16 frames: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B. Gender {man,woman}; ethnicity seven groups. TAS/T8Q=% frames matching final video majority label.

Metrics: L2V/PBSG=(N_man-N_woman)/N_total, positive=men, negative=women. Ethnic P_e=N_e/N_total. F6N/RDS_e=P_e-1/7, valid range [-0.1429,0.8571]. W3H/SDI=1-sum P_e^2, higher=more diverse/balanced. Shifts ΔL2V, ΔF6N_e, ΔW3H.

Earlier internal issues: text claimed demographic attributes not introduced during generation despite V9R ethnicity prompts; metric section said J7K removes contextual and identity cues, conflicting with protocol retaining verb/context. Table 2 and Table 5 contain impossible F6N values below -1/7. Narrative said E5W East Asian F6N=0.0352 but Table 4 says 0.0316. C4Z size: Table 3 says V9R 294 prompts; C4Z 1176 prompts, examples ethnicity+gender; but only gender∈{man,woman}, so 7×42×2=588, conflicting unless four genders. Section 6 additional table mislabeled U8D Latino F6N -0.4352, actually Δ Latino L2V. Table 6 uses +M1Y=HPSv2 but narrative attributes to A3J. Section 7 narrative says +P3L strongly shifts toward woman preference, but Table 8 L2V remains positive, so it only reduces male preference.

Section 4/Table 2 video pairs: D8P(u)=ModelScope vs K5X(a)=InstructVideo/A3J; B7Q(u)=VideoCrafter-2 vs H4M(a)=T2V-Turbo-V1 using U8D, InternVid2-S2, ViCLIP rewards. Key averages: D8P L2V .4815, White F6N .7690, W3H .0538; K5X .5295, White .7833, W3H .0267; B7Q .7581, White .6905, W3H .1252; H4M .8306, White .6381, W3H .1119. Narrative: aligned variants increase gender imbalance; all overrepresent White; H4M reduces White dominance while lowering diversity.

Human eval: sample/full pool 400, 3 annotators, Pearson .89/.73, Kappa .91/.78, Fleiss .92/.82, human-majority/VLM consensus 99.0%/83.3%, diagnostic L2V .846→.863 and W3H .745→.761, L2V p=.68.

Reward data/models: R9C=HPDv2: 28,783 tuples, 29 covered verbs, 26 valid man–woman pair verbs, men preferred 69.23% (18/26), White preference 43.34%. N6T=Pick-a-Pic: 14,958 tuples, 19 covered verbs, 18 valid pair verbs, women preferred 61.11% (11/18), White preference 40.08%. Table 4: Y2F=CLIP base avg L2V -0.0726, W3H .8495. A3J=HPSv2.0/R9C avg L2V .6039, White F6N -.0423, W3H .8492. U8D=HPSv2.1 avg L2V -.0984, W3H .8470. E5W=PickScore avg L2V -.1157, East Asian F6N .0316, W3H .8483.

Benchmark construction: FLUX controlled T2I. Gender reward eval uses C4Z fixed ethnicity/gender/verb; adapted L2V=standardized men score minus women score. Ethnicity reward eval uses V9R ethnicity+person, softmax scores across ethnicities, then F6N/W3H.

Section 6/Table 5 G4S=Video Consistency Model from VideoCrafter-V2. G4S avg L2V .8034, White F6N .6405, W3H .1433. +A3J avg L2V .9116, White F6N .3667, W3H .1257. +U8D avg L2V .2267, White F6N .4286, W3H .0976. +E5W avg L2V .3714, White F6N .6833, W3H .1467. U8D/E5W reduce but remain positive male skew.

Section 6/Table 6 temporal: G4S ethnicity mean T8Q .8904, perfect .5670; gender .9763, perfect .8850. +M1Y ethnicity .9305; +U8D ethnicity .9632 largest; +E5W .9406. Alignment improves coherence.

Section 7 controllable preference modeling: two collections claimed each 29.4M preference pairs from C4Z; pairs fix action/ethnicity and change gender, but prompt shown as “A/An [ethnicity] person...” causing conflict with gender-varying pairs and earlier C4Z gender prompts. Extra 537,660 R9C image pairs. Table 7 reward L2V: Y2F avg -0.0726; Z6B man-preferred/RMM avg 1.5280, all groups ~1.43–1.63; P3L woman-preferred/RMW avg -0.7448, all groups negative. Table 8 video aligned L2V: G4S avg .8034; +Z6B avg .9584, all groups higher; +P3L avg .3082, all groups still positive. Action sensitivity defined as ΔL2V divided by each reward model’s baseline L2V; claims Z6B amplifies exercise,row,cook; P3L shifts bake,sleep,sweep toward women; sleep, stretch, read rank highest under both.

Conclusion/limitations: calls for bias auditing/mitigation throughout video generation rather than treating preference alignment as sufficient. Limitations: predefined categories socially constructed and miss fluidity/intersectionality/cultural nuance; VLM judges image-level and imperfect; alignment experiments chiefly single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards; synthetic gender-preference manipulation is only targeted modulation; fixed action taxonomy limits generalization.

Supplement inventory in Broader Impact: A additional 42-verb video analysis, WebVid-10M training-data effects, statistical analysis #9; dataset ethnicity item #10 for human image-reward-dataset ethnicity preference distributions; C reward-model implementation/comprehensive 42-verb/statistical #11; D additional 42-verb aligned-video/statistical #12; F reward-model training/inference; G video post-training/inference; many numbered gender/ethnicity plots for four-model, reward-model, reward-aligned video, and controllable-preference analyses.

grade.reason: None of the reported reviewer errors addresses the numeric claim that each collection contains 29.4 million same-event man–woman pairs or the implied factor-of-10 miscount (29.4M vs 2.94M).

errors.claim: “We prompt the VLMs to independently infer the depicted gender and ethnicity in each frame, where each model outputs a gender label g ∈ G = {man, woman} …”

errors.explanation: The paper previously defined the gender attribute space as four categories, but this evaluation method reduces gender outputs to only two categories without explaining the change. This is internally inconsistent with the earlier stated controlled gender space.

errors.claim: “we define two prompting conditions: (1) Person-only … 42 total; and (2) Ethnicity+Person … 294 prompts …”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Structured prompts vary gender and ethnicity of characters across real-world events”; “Controlled attribute space … four gender categories … man, woman, neutral term ‘person,’ and non-binary person.”
errors.explanation: Earlier sections said the benchmark varies gender as well as ethnicity and defined four gender prompt categories, but the prompt construction described here includes only person-only and ethnicity+person conditions, with no gender-specific or non-binary prompting condition.

errors.claim: “By computing PBSG under the ethnicity+gender condition, we capture how gender portrayals vary within each ethnic group”
errors.evidence: Earlier Sec. 3.2/Table 1 defined only two prompt conditions: Person-only with actor fixed to “person” and Ethnicity+Person with an ethnic descriptor prepended to “person.” There was no gender-specific or “ethnicity+gender” prompt condition; demographic attributes are inferred post hoc by VLMs.
errors.explanation: The paper’s prompt design does not include an ethnicity+gender condition. The intended condition appears to be ethnicity+person, with gender inferred from generated videos.

errors.claim: “ModelScope exhibits the strongest imbalance (RDSWhite = 0.769, SDI = 0.0538), which is further amplified by alignment tuning in InstructVideo (RDSWhite = 0.783, SDI = 0.0267).”

The text says ModelScope has the strongest imbalance while also saying InstructVideo further amplifies that imbalance, which contradicts the table and its own follow-up statement.

errors.claim: “Missing values are marked as ‘—’ and indicate cases where the model generated zero recognizable instances of the corresponding ethnicity under the person-only condition … preventing metric computation for those subgroups.”

errors.explanation: The paper’s own RDS definition allows computing RDS for an ethnicity with zero instances, so zero recognizable instances of that subgroup should not by itself make RDS missing.

errors.claim: “The annotation task was limited to verifying whether the generated content correctly reflected the prompted demographic attribute” for annotations “for gender and ethnicity.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Prompt construction… Two prompt conditions only: Person-only with actor ‘person’… Ethnicity+Person with ethnic descriptor prepended to ‘person’… Controlled attribute space… prompt set has no explicit gender-specific conditions and VLM gender outputs only binary man/woman.”
errors.explanation: Gender was not a prompted demographic attribute in the described prompt set, so human gender annotation could not be limited to verifying whether generated content reflected a prompted gender attribute.

errors.claim: “all core bias metrics remain statistically stable… SDI: 0.745 → 0.761”

errors.explanation: The SDI values cited here are far larger than the SDI values reported in the main results table under the same metric definition. The paper gives no indication here that SDI has been rescaled or computed differently for the sensitivity analysis.

errors.claim: “Using the event prompting templates introduced in Section 3.2… The benchmark includes two generation settings: (1) Ethnicity+Person… and (2) Ethnicity+Gender, where both gender and ethnicity are explicitly indicated.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: Section 3.2/VideoBiasEval prompt construction had “two prompt conditions only: Person-only with actor ‘person,’ 42 prompts; Ethnicity+Person with ethnic descriptor prepended to ‘person,’ 7×42=294 prompts,” and “actual prompt set has no explicit gender-specific conditions.”

errors.claim: “By conditioning on systematically varied demographic attributes, our benchmark isolates reward model preferences independently of generator-specific artifacts.”

errors.claim: “These shifts align with each model’s training data”

errors.claim: “Table 5 reports two metrics: PBSG for gender imbalance across ethnic groups, and RDSe and SDI for ethnicity representation disparity and overall output diversity.”
errors.evidence: The sentence itself lists PBSG, RDSe, and SDI, and Table 5 has columns for PBSG, RDS, and SDI.
errors.explanation: It says there are “two metrics” but names and reports three metrics.

errors.claim: “Under the ethnicity-only condition, we analyze models’ representation balance using the previously defined RDSe and SDI metrics.”

errors.explanation: The paper’s own framework and the table caption indicate ethnicity representation is measured under person-only prompts, not an “ethnicity-only” condition.

errors.claim: “Alignment with HPSv2.1 … significantly decreases Latino representation (RDS = –0.4352).”
errors.evidence: In Table 5, the +HPSv2.1 row shows Latino PBSG = 0.3738 and Latino RDS = “—”. The value –0.4352 appears in the Δ row under Latino PBSG, not Latino RDS.
errors.explanation: The text reports –0.4352 as Latino RDS, but the table gives no Latino RDS for +HPSv2.1; –0.4352 is the change in Latino PBSG.

errors.claim: “HPSv2.0 reinforces the base model’s male- and White-preferred tendencies”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes for Table 5: “VCM-VC2 Avg PBSG .8034, White RDS .6405, SDI .1433. +HPSv2.0 Avg PBSG .9116, White RDS .3667 ... Δ Avg PBSG +.1082, White RDS −.2738, SDI −.0176.”
errors.explanation: HPSv2.0 does reinforce male preference, but it reduces White RDS from .6405 to .3667 rather than reinforcing/increasing the base model’s White-preferred tendency.

errors.claim: “Prompts follow the format ‘A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context].’” for “preference pairs from the Ethnicity+Gender set,” where pairs “differ by gender.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Sec.5.2 controlled T2I reward benchmark ... Table 3: Ethnicity+Person 294 prompts; Ethnicity+Gender 1176 prompts, implying 7×4×42. Figure 5 prompt shows only man/woman.” Also this part says each pair “differs by gender.”

errors.claim: “As shown in Table 7, RMM consistently assigns higher PBSG scores...” / Table 7 reports RMM Average PBSG = 1.5280, White = 1.6300, etc.
errors.evidence: Earlier notes define PBSG as “PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive male, negative female.” This metric is bounded between −1 and +1. Earlier reward PBSG values in Table 4 were within this range, e.g. HPSv2.0 +.6039 and PickScore −.1157.
errors.explanation: If Table 7 values are PBSG scores under the paper’s definition, values such as 1.5280 and 1.6300 are impossible because PBSG cannot exceed 1. The table either uses a different quantity or contradicts the paper’s stated PBSG definition.

errors.claim: “alignment with RMW substantially reduces these scores, indicating a strong shift toward woman-preference bias.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 reports +RMW PBSG values that are all still positive: Average 0.3082, White 0.3341, Black 0.3913, Latino 0.3314, East Asian 0.1008, Southeast Asian 0.2639, India 0.3446, Middle Eastern 0.3894. Earlier notes: “PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive male, negative female.”
errors.explanation: RMW reduces the male bias relative to VCM-VC2, but the reported PBSG scores remain positive for every group, meaning outputs are still male-biased by the paper’s definition. The table does not support a shift into woman-preference bias.

errors.claim: “introducing counter-biased reward models (e.g., woman-preferred RMW) can actively correct skewed portrayals, producing more balanced and socially representative generations.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Table 8 video: VCM-VC2 PBSG same as Table5 base; +RMM Avg .9584 ...; +RMW Avg .3082, all groups still positive (.1008–.3913), so reduced male bias but not woman-preference by PBSG definition.”
errors.explanation: RMW reduces the positive male-skew PBSG relative to the base, but Table 8 still reports positive PBSG for every group, meaning outputs remain male-biased by the paper’s own metric. The stronger claim that it “correct[s] skewed portrayals” into socially representative generations overstates what the reported results show.

errors.claim: “While this capability offers a powerful mechanism for correcting historical underrepresentation and mitigating bias”
errors.location: this part, Dual-Use of Controllable Preference Modeling
errors.evidence: Section 7 results in notes: Table 8 +RMW Avg PBSG .3082, all groups still positive (.1008–.3913), so it reduced male bias but did not produce woman-preference or balanced/socially representative generations by the paper’s PBSG definition.
errors.explanation: The paper’s demonstrated controllable preference modeling does not actually correct the skew or achieve balance in the reported video results; even the woman-preferred reward model leaves every PBSG group male-skewed. Thus this broader-impact claim overstates what the paper’s own results show.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” VideoBiasEval evaluates T2V/video social representation via event prompts <p,a,c>. Biases = imbalanced gender/ethnicity portrayals.

Prompt construction: initially lists 4 gender categories and 7 ethnic groups, 42 verbs, but actual video benchmark has no explicit gender-specific prompts and VLM gender outputs only binary man/woman. Template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Actual video prompt conditions: Person-only actor “person” (42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7×42=294). Earlier mentions of ethnicity+gender or ethnicity-only conflict with this.

Evaluation: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B; 16 frames/video; infer binary gender {man,woman} and 7 ethnicities. Majority vote frame→video per model; ensemble fused. TAS=% frames matching final label. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive male, negative female, bounded [-1,1]. Ethnicity: P_e=N_e/N_total; RDS_e=P_e−1/7; zero group should be −1/7; SDI=1−ΣP_e^2, higher diverse. Bias shift Δ compares aligned vs unaligned.

Sec.4 models/results: unaligned ModelScope, VideoCrafter-2; aligned InstructVideo from ModelScope using HPSv2.0; T2V-Turbo-V1 from VC2 using HPSv2.1/InternVid2-S2/ViCLIP. 10 videos/prompt/model. Table 2: ModelScope Avg PBSG .4815, White RDS .7690, SDI .0538. InstructVideo .5295, .7833, .0267; Δ +.0480, +.0143, −.0271. VC2 .7581, .6905, .1252. T2V-Turbo-V1 .8306, .6381, .1119; Δ +.0725, −.0524, −.0133. Sec.4 text says alignment amplifies male bias. It also says ModelScope strongest ethnicity imbalance, but table shows InstructVideo stronger by higher White RDS/lower SDI. T2V lowers White RDS vs VC but also lowers diversity.

Human eval: 400 videos, 3 annotators. VLM vs humans: Pearson r=.89 gender/.73 ethnicity; Cohen κ=.91/.78; Fleiss κ=.92/.82. High-agreement subset consensus 99.0% gender, 83.3% ethnicity; metrics stable PBSG .846→.863 p=.68; SDI .745→.761. This SDI scale conflicts with Table 2 SDIs (.0267–.1252) unless different computation.

Sec.5 image reward data/models: HPDv2/Pick-a-Pic. GPT-4o-mini extracts gender/ethnicity/verb from captions; 3 VLMs classify image attributes; aggregate caption+image; keep predefined verbs. HPDv2: 28,783 tuples, 29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic: 14,958, 19 verbs. Figure 3 caption says gender preference across 42 verbs. HPDv2: 26/42 qualified, 18/26=69.23% prefer men. Pick-a-Pic: 18/42 qualified, 11/18=61.11% prefer women. Ethnicity: White preferred 43.34% HPDv2, 40.08% Pick-a-Pic, then East Asian/Indian.

Sec.5.2 controlled T2I reward benchmark using FLUX. Claims Sec.3.2 templates but includes Ethnicity+Person and Ethnicity+Gender, conflicting with actual video benchmark. Table 3: Ethnicity+Person 294 prompts; Ethnicity+Gender 1176 prompts, implying 7×4×42. Figure 5 prompt shows only man/woman. FLUX paragraph says not assuming bias-free generator, yet benchmark isolates reward preferences independently of generator artifacts. Human verification: 100 images; 77% unanimous, 97% majority, 3 no consensus.

Reward models: HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore, CLIP. Table 4 gender reward PBSG: CLIP −.0726, HPSv2.0 +.6039, HPSv2.1 −.0984, PickScore −.1157. Text says CLIP slight woman, HPSv2.0 strong man, HPSv2.1/PickScore woman. Ethnicity reward Table 4 SDIs: CLIP .8495, HPSv2.0 .8492, HPSv2.1 .8470, PickScore .8483; all near max .857. Text says CLIP “lowest SDI .8495,” conflicting because fine-tuned SDIs are lower; also says all show reduced SDI post-alignment. Text says HPSv2.0 Middle Eastern RDS .0315, HPSv2.1 Latino .0382, PickScore East Asian .0352.

Sec.6 preference alignment in video: fine-tunes VCM distilled from VideoCrafter-V2 (VCM-VC2) using HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore. Table 5: VCM-VC2 Avg PBSG .8034, White RDS .6405, SDI .1433. +HPSv2.0 Avg PBSG .9116, White RDS .3667, Middle Eastern RDS −.3667, SDI .1257. +HPSv2.1 Avg PBSG .2267, White RDS .4286, Middle Eastern RDS −.4286, SDI .0976. +PickScore Avg PBSG .3714, White RDS .6833, SDI .1467. Sec.6 errors: says two metrics though table lists PBSG/RDS/SDI; says ethnicity bias under “ethnicity-only” condition though caption/framework indicate person-only; says HPSv2.1 decreases Latino representation RDS=−.4352, but −.4352 is Δ Latino PBSG and Latino RDS is missing. Summary says HPSv2.0 reinforces male and White tendencies, conflicting with Table 5 White RDS decrease from .6405 to .3667. Table 6 TAS: VCM-VC2 Ethnicity .8904, Gender .9763. +HPSv2 label likely HPSv2.0: Ethnicity .9305, Gender .9967. +HPSv2.1 Ethnicity .9632, Gender .9895. +PickScore Ethnicity .9406, Gender .9884.

Sec.7 controllable preference modeling. Constructs man-preferred/woman-preferred reward datasets from images in Sec.5.1, says 2.94M preference pairs from Ethnicity+Gender set where same action/ethnicity differs by gender, but gives prompt format “A/An [ethnicity] person...” lacking gender. Adds 537,660 HPDv2 image pairs. Trains CLIP-based RMM/RMW. Table 7 “PBSG” reward values: CLIP Avg −.0726; RMM Avg 1.5280 and group values up to 1.6300; RMW Avg −.7448. RMM values exceed possible PBSG range [-1,1]. Table 8 video: VCM-VC2 PBSG same as Table5 base; +RMM Avg .9584 (all groups positive high); +RMW Avg .3082, all groups still positive (.1008–.3913), so reduced male bias but not woman-preference/balanced by PBSG definition. Text claims RMW causes strong shift toward woman-preference bias, unsupported by Table 8. Sec.7 summary and broader-impact claims that RMW can correct/mitigate bias or produce balanced generations overstate Table 8 because all PBSG remain positive male-skew. Action-level Fig.6 ΔPBSG: RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals in exercise,row,cook; RMW shifts toward women-preferred actions bake,sleep,sweep; normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG divided by each reward model’s baseline PBSG; top-ranked sleep, stretch, read most sensitive under both tunings.

Conclusion: claims VideoBiasEval decouples identity attributes from content semantics and tracks alignment effects; reward-model-based alignment inherits and frequently amplifies biases in human preference data; calls for auditing/mitigation throughout video generation pipeline.

Limitations: focus on gender and ethnicity using predefined categories; VLM evaluators validated but may be biased/inaccurate; analysis primarily under single-step latent consistency distillation and limited reward models; controllable preference modeling only synthetic gender preference; VideoBiasEval fixed 42 socially associated actions, limiting generalizability.

Broader Impact: argues alignment tuning can stabilize/entrench polished biases, controllable preference modeling is dual-use, and VideoBiasEval-like event-centric auditing is needed. Potential overstatement: says controllable preference modeling offers mechanism for correcting underrepresentation/mitigating bias, but demonstrated RMW video outputs remain male-skewed.

Acknowledgment: thanks anonymous reviewers; funding from AFOSR MURI #FA9550-22-1-0380, ONR #N00014-23-1-2780, NSF #IIS-2449768, NVIDIA Academic Grant Program cloud credits, Technical AI Safety Research Program at Coefficient Giving; disclaimer that views are authors’ only, not official policies/endorsements.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.”

Main contribution per abstract/Fig.1/Intro: Introduces VideoBiasEval, a comprehensive diagnostic/evaluation framework for analyzing social representation/bias in text-to-video/video diffusion models. It uses event-based prompting grounded in established social bias taxonomies to separate semantic content (verbs/events/contexts) from actor identity attributes, allowing controlled assessment of how models represent social attributes. VLMs infer actor attributes (gender, ethnicity) across frames and aggregate them for bias quantification.

Definitions from Intro: “Aligned models” = video diffusion models that undergo post-training optimization to better match human preferences beyond likelihood-based training. Typically via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures, using a learned preference/aesthetic reward model trained on human comparisons to guide optimization of a base video diffusion model. General pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. “Unaligned counterparts” = trained solely with likelihood-based objectives; used as controlled baselines to isolate alignment effects.

Motivation/risk: Alignment tuning improves perceptual quality/temporal coherence but relies on subjective human preferences, potentially encoding demographic/cultural/social bias. Such biases may be inherited/reinforced by reward models and downstream video generation, affecting who is represented, how often, and in what roles. Central question: how alignment tuning influences social-attribute distributions in video diffusion models.

Prior evaluation limitations claimed: (1) prompts inadequately represent diverse social identities; (2) lack comprehensive identity coverage and specific metrics to track alignment effects on social attributes; (3) absence of dedicated method to track social-attribute distribution shifts before vs after alignment.

Focus: Gender and ethnicity, said to have comparatively well-defined evaluative boundaries.

Metrics claimed: multi-granular metrics evaluating (1) ethnicity bias / overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across different model variants/models, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos.

errors.explanation: RMW reduces the positive male-skew PBSG relative to the base, but Table 8 still reports positive PBSG for every group, meaning outputs remain male-biased by the paper’s own metric. Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” VideoBiasEval evaluates T2V/video social representation via event prompts <p,a,c>. Biases = imbalanced gender/ethnicity portrayals.

Prompt construction: initially lists 4 gender categories and 7 ethnic groups, 42 verbs, but actual video benchmark has no explicit gender-specific prompts and VLM gender outputs only binary man/woman. Template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Actual video prompt conditions: Person-only actor “person” (42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7×42=294). Earlier mentions of ethnicity+gender or ethnicity-only conflict with this.

Evaluation: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B; 16 frames/video; infer binary gender {man,woman} and 7 ethnicities. Majority vote frame→video per model; ensemble fused. TAS=% frames matching final label. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive male, negative female, bounded [-1,1]. Ethnicity: P_e=N_e/N_total; RDS_e=P_e−1/7; zero group should be −1/7; SDI=1−ΣP_e^2, higher diverse. Bias shift Δ compares aligned vs unaligned.

Sec.4 models/results: unaligned ModelScope, VideoCrafter-2; aligned InstructVideo from ModelScope using HPSv2.0; T2V-Turbo-V1 from VC2 using HPSv2.1/InternVid2-S2/ViCLIP. 10 videos/prompt/model. Table 2: ModelScope Avg PBSG .4815, White RDS .7690, SDI .0538. InstructVideo .5295, .7833, .0267; Δ +.0480, +.0143, −.0271. VC2 .7581, .6905, .1252. T2V-Turbo-V1 .8306, .6381, .1119; Δ +.0725, −.0524, −.0133. Sec.4 text says alignment amplifies male bias. It also says ModelScope strongest ethnicity imbalance, but table shows InstructVideo stronger by higher White RDS/lower SDI. T2V lowers White RDS vs VC but also lowers diversity.

Human eval: 400 videos, 3 annotators. VLM vs humans: Pearson r=.89 gender/.73 ethnicity; Cohen κ=.91/.78; Fleiss κ=.92/.82. High-agreement subset consensus 99.0% gender, 83.3% ethnicity; metrics stable PBSG .846→.863 p=.68; SDI .745→.761. This SDI scale conflicts with Table 2 SDIs (.0267–.1252) unless different computation.

Sec.5 image reward data/models: HPDv2/Pick-a-Pic. GPT-4o-mini extracts gender/ethnicity/verb from captions; 3 VLMs classify image attributes; aggregate caption+image; keep predefined verbs. HPDv2: 28,783 tuples, 29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic: 14,958, 19 verbs. Figure 3 caption says gender preference across 42 verbs. HPDv2: 26/42 qualified, 18/26=69.23% prefer men. Pick-a-Pic: 18/42 qualified, 11/18=61.11% prefer women. Ethnicity: White preferred 43.34% HPDv2, 40.08% Pick-a-Pic, then East Asian/Indian.

Sec.5.2 controlled T2I reward benchmark using FLUX. Claims Sec.3.2 templates but includes Ethnicity+Person and Ethnicity+Gender, conflicting with actual video benchmark. Table 3: Ethnicity+Person 294 prompts; Ethnicity+Gender 1176 prompts, implying 7×4×42. Figure 5 prompt shows only man/woman. FLUX paragraph says not assuming bias-free generator, yet benchmark isolates reward preferences independently of generator artifacts. Human verification: 100 images; 77% unanimous, 97% majority, 3 no consensus.

Reward models: HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore, CLIP. Table 4 gender reward PBSG: CLIP −.0726, HPSv2.0 +.6039, HPSv2.1 −.0984, PickScore −.1157. Text says CLIP slight woman, HPSv2.0 strong man, HPSv2.1/PickScore woman. Ethnicity reward Table 4 SDIs: CLIP .8495, HPSv2.0 .8492, HPSv2.1 .8470, PickScore .8483; all near max .857. Text says CLIP “lowest SDI .8495,” conflicting because fine-tuned SDIs are lower; also says all show reduced SDI post-alignment. Text says HPSv2.0 Middle Eastern RDS .0315, HPSv2.1 Latino .0382, PickScore East Asian .0352.

Sec.6 preference alignment in video: fine-tunes VCM distilled from VideoCrafter-V2 (VCM-VC2) using HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore. Table 5: VCM-VC2 Avg PBSG .8034, White RDS .6405, SDI .1433. +HPSv2.0 Avg PBSG .9116, White RDS .3667, Middle Eastern RDS −.3667, SDI .1257. +HPSv2.1 Avg PBSG .2267, White RDS .4286, Middle Eastern RDS −.4286, SDI .0976. +PickScore Avg PBSG .3714, White RDS .6833, SDI .1467. Sec.6 errors: says two metrics though table lists PBSG/RDS/SDI; says ethnicity bias under “ethnicity-only” condition though caption/framework indicate person-only; says HPSv2.1 decreases Latino representation RDS=−.4352, but −.4352 is Δ Latino PBSG and Latino RDS is missing. Summary says HPSv2.0 reinforces male and White tendencies, conflicting with Table 5 White RDS decrease from .6405 to .3667.

Table 6 TAS: VCM-VC2 Ethnicity .8904, Gender .9763. +HPSv2 label likely HPSv2.0: Ethnicity .9305, Gender .9967. +HPSv2.1 Ethnicity .9632, Gender .9895. +PickScore Ethnicity .9406, Gender .9884.

Sec.7 controllable preference modeling. Constructs man-preferred/woman-preferred reward datasets from images in Sec.5.1, says 2.94M preference pairs from Ethnicity+Gender set where same action/ethnicity differs by gender, but gives prompt format “A/An [ethnicity] person...” lacking gender, inconsistent with Ethnicity+Gender. Adds 537,660 HPDv2 image pairs. Trains CLIP-based RMM/RMW. Table 7 “PBSG” reward values: CLIP Avg −.0726; RMM Avg 1.5280 and group values up to 1.6300; RMW Avg −.7448. RMM values exceed possible PBSG range [-1,1]. Table 8 video: VCM-VC2 PBSG same as Table5 base; +RMM Avg .9584 (all groups positive high); +RMW Avg .3082, all groups still positive (.1008–.3913), so reduced male bias but not woman-preference by PBSG definition. Text claims RMW causes strong shift toward woman-preference bias, unsupported by Table 8.

Claims RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals in exercise,row,cook; RMW shifts toward women-preferred actions bake,sleep,sweep; normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG divided by each reward model’s baseline PBSG; top-ranked sleep, stretch, read most sensitive under both tunings. errors.claim: “While this capability offers a powerful mechanism for correcting historical underrepresentation and mitigating bias”
errors.location: this part, Dual-Use of Controllable Preference Modeling
errors.evidence: Section 7 results in notes: Table 8 +RMW Avg PBSG .3082, all groups still positive (.1008–.3913), so it reduced male bias but did not produce woman-preference or balanced/socially representative generations by the paper’s PBSG definition.
errors.explanation: The paper’s demonstrated controllable preference modeling does not actually correct the skew or achieve balance in the reported video results; even the woman-preferred reward model leaves every PBSG group male-skewed. Thus this broader-impact claim overstates what the paper’s own results show.

RMM values exceed possible PBSG range [-1,1]. Table 8 video: VCM-VC2 PBSG same as Table5 base; +RMM Avg .9584 (all groups positive high); +RMW Avg .3082, all groups still positive (.1008–.3913), so reduced male bias but not woman-preference/balanced by PBSG definition. Text claims RMW causes strong shift toward woman-preference bias, unsupported by Table 8. Sec.7 summary and broader-impact claims that RMW can correct/mitigate bias or produce balanced generations overstate Table 8 because all PBSG remain positive male-skew. Action-level Fig.6 ΔPBSG: RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals in exercise,row,cook; RMW shifts toward women-preferred actions bake,sleep,sweep; normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG divided by each reward model’s baseline PBSG; top-ranked sleep, stretch, read most sensitive under both tunings.

Conclusion: claims VideoBiasEval decouples identity attributes from content semantics and tracks alignment effects; reward-model-based alignment inherits and frequently amplifies biases in human preference data; calls for auditing/mitigation throughout video generation pipeline.

Limitations: focus on gender and ethnicity using predefined categories; VLM evaluators validated but may be biased/inaccurate; analysis primarily under single-step latent consistency distillation and limited reward models; controllable preference modeling only synthetic gender preference; VideoBiasEval fixed 42 socially associated actions, limiting generalizability.

Broader Impact: argues alignment tuning can stabilize/entrench polished biases, controllable preference modeling is dual-use, and VideoBiasEval-like event-centric auditing is needed. Potential overstatement: says controllable preference modeling offers mechanism for correcting underrepresentation/mitigating bias, but demonstrated RMW video outputs remain male-skewed.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Main claims: alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; biases from human preferences enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generation. Broader impact: alignment/RLHF can stabilize/entrench bias by making stereotypes polished, coherent, harder to detect; preference-data/reward engineering is dual-use; aesthetic metrics insufficient; developers should monitor generated social composition with multi-granular event-centric audits such as QX2 and curate preference data for diversity/equity. Limitations: predefined gender/ethnicity categories are socially constructed and miss fluidity/intersectionality/cultural nuance; VLM judges are image-level and may be biased/inaccurate; larger ground-truth video annotation needed; alignment experiments mainly single-step latent consistency distillation with limited rewards; RL/multi-turn alignment may differ; synthetic gender-preference manipulation only shows targeted modulation; fixed socially associated action taxonomy limits generalization.

Definitions: aligned models = video diffusion optimized after likelihood training to match human preferences via reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style learned rewards. Unaligned = likelihood only. Attribute space claimed four genders/seven ethnicities, but extraction/eval mostly binary man/woman. Ethnic groups: White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino. 42 verbs/actions. L2V/PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total; positive favors men, negative women. F6N/RDS_e=P_e−1/7, valid range [−.1429,.8571]. W3H/SDI=1−ΣP_e². TAS/T8Q = percentage frames matching video final majority label.

Prompt/data issues: J7K=42 person-only prompts retains verb/context though text said removes contextual cues. V9R=294 ethnicity+person prompts. C4Z image benchmark said 1176 prompts with example “East Asian woman…”, but 42×7×2=588 unless four gender categories. Earlier text also said demographic attributes not introduced during generation, conflicting with explicit ethnicity prompts.

Video model Table 2: D8P(u)=ModelScope vs K5X(a)=InstructVideo/A3J; B7Q(u)=VideoCrafter-2 vs H4M(a)=T2V-Turbo-V1 using U8D/InternVid2-S2/ViCLIP. Averages: D8P L2V .4815, White F6N .7690, W3H .0538; K5X .5295, White .7833, W3H .0267; B7Q .7581, White .6905, W3H .1252; H4M .8306, White .6381, W3H .1119. Some F6Ns impossible below −1/7.

Human eval: validation pool 400 generated videos, 3 annotators; Pearson .89 gender/.73 ethnicity; kappa .91/.78; Fleiss .92/.82; human-majority/VLM consensus 99.0%/83.3%.

Preference datasets: R9C=HPDv2 28,783 tuples, 29 covered verbs, 26 valid man–woman-pair verbs, Men 69.23% (18/26), White preference 43.34%. N6T=Pick-a-Pic 14,958 tuples, 19 covered verbs, 18 valid pair verbs, Women 61.11% (11/18), White preference 40.08%. Claimed both strongly favor White; exceptions Black for bake, East Asian for fish.

Reward models/Table 4: Y2F=CLIP base; A3J=HPSv2.0/R9C; U8D=HPSv2.1/X7H; E5W=PickScore/N6T. Table 4 averages: Y2F L2V −.0726, White F6N .0182, W3H .8495. A3J L2V .6039, White F6N −.0423, W3H .8492. U8D L2V −.0984, White F6N −.0189, W3H .8470. E5W L2V −.1157, East Asian F6N .0316, W3H .8483. Prior issues: narrative said Y2F lowest diversity though W3H highest; said E5W East Asian .0352 but table .0316. Reward scoring: gender prompt omits gender while generated image fixes ethnicity+gender; adapted L2V is men avg reward minus women avg reward and can exceed one. Ethnicity eval softmax across ethnicities for F6N/W3H.

Section 6/Table 5: G4S=Video Consistency Model distilled from VideoCrafter-V2/VCM-VC2; reward-specific tuning with A3J, U8D, E5W. G4S Average L2V .8034, White F6N .6405, W3H .1433. +A3J L2V .9116, White F6N .3667, W3H .1257. +U8D L2V .2267, White F6N .4286, W3H .0976. +E5W L2V .3714, White F6N .6833, W3H .1467. Issues: impossible negative F6Ns; claims of U8D/E5W woman-preferred outputs conflict with positive L2Vs; U8D White/Black balance unsupported due missing Black F6N; A3J “reinforces White” conflicts with White F6N decrease.

Temporal Table 6: G4S ethnicity T8Q .8904/perfect .5670; gender .9763/perfect .8850. +M1Y ethnicity .9305/.7050; gender .9967/.9830. +U8D ethnicity .9632/.8330; gender .9895/.9440. +E5W ethnicity .9406/.7560; gender .9884/.9410.

Section 7 controllable preference modeling: two image preference collections, each 2.94M C4Z pairs fixing action/ethnicity and changing gender; man-preferred labels male=1/female=0, woman-preferred reverse; plus 537,660 R9C image pairs. Table 7 reward L2V: Y2F avg −.0726; Z6B/RMM avg 1.5280, all groups ~1.43–1.63; P3L/RMW avg −.7448, all groups negative. Table 7 subscript inconsistency: Z6B deltas relative Y2F, P3L deltas appear relative Z6B, not Y2F. Table 8 aligned G4S variants: G4S avg .8034; +Z6B avg .9584 all positive; +P3L avg .3082 all positive. Issues: claims that P3L/woman-preferred data corrects imbalance, yields equilibrium, or shifts toward woman preference conflict with Table 8 positive L2Vs, which remain male-skewed.

Supplement inventory in broader impact: A additional 42-verb video analysis/WebVid-10M training-data effects/statistical analysis #9; ethnicity item #10 dataset ethnicity preferences; C reward-model implementation/comprehensive 42-verb/stat analysis #11; D aligned-video 42-verb/stat #12; F reward-model training/inference; G video post-training/inference; plot numbers 7–14 video gender/ethnicity, 19–29 reward model, 30–38 reward-aligned video, 39–43 controllable preference. Acknowledgment: support from AFOSR MURI #FA9550-22-1-0380, ONR #N00014-23-1-2780, NSF #IIS-2449768, NVIDIA Academic Grant cloud credits, Coefficient Giving Technical AI Safety Research Program; views not official endorsements.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” VideoBiasEval evaluates social representation/bias in T2V/video diffusion models via event prompts <p,a,c>. Biases = imbalanced portrayals across gender/ethnic groups. Conclusion/limitations: framework uses fixed 42 socially associated actions; focuses on gender/ethnicity with predefined categories; VLM evaluators validated against humans but may be biased; primarily assesses alignment under single-step latent consistency distillation and limited reward models; controllable preference modeling only synthetic gender preference manipulation and not full value alignment.

Sec. 3 controlled attributes originally lists four gender categories: man, woman, neutral “person,” non-binary person; seven ethnic groups: White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino; 42 verbs. Actual video prompts have no explicit gender-specific conditions and VLM gender outputs only binary man/woman. Prompt template: “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Two video prompt conditions only: Person-only, actor “person,” 42 prompts; Ethnicity+Person, ethnic descriptor + “person,” 294 prompts. Generated 10 videos per prompt per model. Demographics inferred post hoc by VLMs.

Evaluation: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B; 16 frames/video; majority vote to video label and ensemble. Gender label set binary {man,woman}; ethnicity seven groups. TAS = % frames whose classified attributes match final majority-voted video label. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive male bias, negative female bias, zero balanced; valid range [-1,1]. Sec. 4 says PBSG evaluated under ethnicity+person. Table 2 PBSG all positive; averages: ModelScope 0.4815, InstructVideo 0.5295; VideoCrafter-V2 0.7581, T2V-Turbo-V1 0.8306. Alignment amplifies male bias.

Ethnicity metrics: RDS_e=P_e−1/7 where P_e=N_e/N_total; uniform baseline 14.3%; valid RDS range [-0.1429,0.8571]. SDI=1−ΣP_e^2, higher = more diverse/balanced. Internal inconsistencies found: Table 2 and Table 5 report impossible RDSe below -0.1429. Table 2 person-only ethnicity results: ModelScope RDSWhite 0.7690, SDI 0.0538; InstructVideo 0.7833, 0.0267; VideoCrafter-V2 0.6905, 0.1252; T2V-Turbo-V1 0.6381, 0.1119. Earlier inconsistency: claim that reducing White overrepresentation directly causes diversity to fall conflicts with ModelScope vs VideoCrafter-V2 where White RDS lower and SDI higher.

Models: unaligned/aligned pairs: ModelScope/InstructVideo, VideoCrafter-2/T2V-Turbo-V1. InstructVideo built on ModelScope aligned using HPSv2.0; T2V-Turbo-V1 built on VideoCrafter-2 aligned with HPSv2.1, InternVid2-S2, ViCLIP.

Human Evaluation: 400 generated videos, 3 annotators for gender/ethnicity. VLM ensemble aligned with humans: Pearson 0.89 gender, 0.73 ethnicity; Cohen’s Kappa 0.91/0.78; Fleiss’ Kappa 0.92/0.82. High-agreement subset: consensus 99.0% gender, 83.3% ethnicity; metrics stable PBSG 0.846→0.863 p=0.68; SDI 0.745→0.761. Prior inconsistency: section says annotation checked “prompted demographic attribute” while earlier prompts had no gender-specific condition and demographics were post hoc.

Sec. 5 image reward data: HPDv2 28,783 validated tuples covering 29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic 14,958 across 19 verbs. Fig. 3 described as across 42 verbs. Gender preference after filtering valid man-woman pairs: HPDv2 26/42 verbs qualified, 18/26 preferred men; Pick-a-Pic 18/42 qualified, 11/18 preferred women. Ethnicity preference: White preferred 43.34% HPDv2 and 40.08% Pick-a-Pic, followed by East Asian and Indian.

Sec. 5.2 reward benchmark: claims to use Sec. 3.2 templates with FLUX T2I. Two settings: Ethnicity+Person, 294 prompts; Ethnicity+Gender, 1176 prompts; 100 images per prompt. Internal inconsistency: Sec. 3.2 had only Person-only and Ethnicity+Person, no explicit gender condition. Reward models: CLIP, HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore. Table 4: CLIP Avg PBSG -0.0726, SDI 0.8495; HPSv2.0 Avg PBSG 0.6039, SDI 0.8492; HPSv2.1 Avg PBSG -0.0984, SDI 0.8470; PickScore Avg PBSG -0.1157, SDI 0.8483. HPSv2.0 strongly male-biased; HPSv2.1/PickScore mostly female-biased except exceptions. Reward ethnicity: CLIP slightly favors White RDS=0.0182 and highest SDI=0.8495; aligned reward models lower SDI.

Sec. 6: fine-tunes VCM-VC2 using HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore. Table 5: base VCM-VC2 Avg PBSG 0.8034, White RDS 0.6405, SDI 0.1433. +HPSv2.0 Avg PBSG 0.9116, White RDS 0.3667, ME RDS -0.3667, SDI 0.1257. +HPSv2.1 Avg PBSG 0.2267, White RDS 0.4286, ME RDS -0.4286, SDI 0.0976. +PickScore Avg PBSG 0.3714, White RDS 0.6833, several impossible negative RDS values, SDI 0.1467. Errors found: text says HPSv2.1 decreases Latino representation RDS=-0.4352, but -0.4352 is ΔPBSG; says HPSv2.0 reinforces base male- and White-preferred tendencies, but White RDS drops 0.6405→0.3667.

Table 6 TAS: VCM ethnicity/gender mean 0.8904/0.9763; +HPSv2 label mean 0.9305/0.9967; +HPSv2.1 0.9632/0.9895; +PickScore 0.9406/0.9884. Ethnicity perfect stability baseline 0.5670 and +HPSv2.1 0.8330, increase 0.2660; gender +HPSv2.1 perfect stability 0.9440; HPSv2.0 gender perfect stability 0.9830.

Sec. 7 controllable preference modeling: constructs man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets from images in Sec. 5.1; says each has 2.94M preference pairs from Ethnicity+Gender, same action/ethnicity but differs by gender; also adds 537,660 HPDv2 image pairs. Internal error: prompt format “A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context]” lacks gender despite saying Ethnicity+Gender pairs differ by gender. Trains CLIP-based RMM and RMW. Table 7: CLIP Avg -0.0726. RMM Avg 1.5280 (+1.60), group values 1.4323–1.6300; RMW Avg -0.7448 (-2.27), group values -0.8846 to -0.6282. Internal error: RMM PBSG values exceed valid PBSG max 1. Table 8 aligned VCM-VC2: +RMM Avg 0.9584; +RMW Avg 0.3082, all groups still positive. Internal error: text says RMW causes “strong shift toward woman-preference bias,” but positive PBSG means remaining male bias, just reduced. Sec. 7 summary/implications: controllable preference modeling can steer bias; RMM reinforces male tendencies and RMW counteracts base tendencies, producing more balanced generations; suggests continuous alignment axis via mixtures. Fig. 6 action-level ΔPBSG; sensitivity = ΔPBSG divided by each reward model’s baseline PBSG; sleep, stretch, read top-ranked under both RMM/RMW.

Broader Impact: claims alignment tuning/RLHF can act as “bias stabilizer,” making biased representations more coherent and harder to detect; controllable preference modeling has dual use, can amplify/suppress social attributes and may correct underrepresentation or be exploited to exclude/homogenize/propagandize; urges multi-granular event-centric auditing like VideoBiasEval and rigorous preference dataset curation.

Acknowledgment: thanks reviewers; support from AFOSR MURI #FA9550-22-1-0380, ONR #N00014-23-1-2780, NSF #IIS-2449768, NVIDIA Academic Grant Program cloud credits, Technical AI Safety Research Program at Coefficient Giving; disclaimer views not official policies/endorsements.

Prior evaluation limitations claimed: (1) prompts inadequately represent diverse social identities; (2) lack comprehensive identity coverage and metrics to track alignment effects on social attributes; (3) absence of dedicated method to track social-attribute distribution shifts before vs after alignment. Metrics claimed: multi-granular metrics evaluating ethnicity bias / overall ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants/models, and temporal persistence/stability of social attributes within videos. grade.reason: Reviewer item 5 identifies that the paper's claim of an unavoidable trade-off is contradicted by reported data (one model has lower White overrepresentation and higher diversity), which matches the planted-error critique that the authors did not establish causality.

errors.claim: “The bounded attribute space balances coverage against control: four gender categories, seven ethnic groups, and 42 verbs...” and “Each actor carries gender and ethnicity attributes. Luccioni et al. (2023) supplies man, woman, neutral person, and non-binary person...”
errors.evidence: In §3.2, the actual prompt settings are only J7K = “person-only” and V9R = ethnicity + “person,” with 42 and 294 prompts respectively; in §3.3, extracted gender outputs are defined as “g ∈ G = {man,woman}.”
errors.explanation: The section claims a four-category gender attribute space including neutral and non-binary, but the described video-generation prompts do not instantiate man/woman/non-binary actors, and the extraction/evaluation label space only includes two genders. This conflicts with the claimed four-gender evaluation space.

errors.claim: F6N/RDS_e = P_e − 1/|E|; |E|=7 so uniform 1/7≈14.3%. Positive over-, negative under-representation.
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports many F6N values below −1/7, e.g. Black F6N = −0.1952 for D8P, Latino F6N = −0.1952 for D8P, H4M Latino F6N = −0.2476, H4M East Asian F6N = −0.2426.
errors.explanation: If F6N is P_e − 1/7 and P_e is a proportion, the minimum possible value is 0 − 1/7 ≈ −0.1429. Values such as −0.1952 and −0.2476 are impossible under the paper’s own definition.

errors.claim: “Reducing White overrepresentation directly causes diversity loss, an unavoidable trade-off.”
errors.evidence: Table 2 shows D8P White F6N = 0.7690 and Overall W3H = 0.0538, while B7Q White F6N = 0.6905 and Overall W3H = 0.1252.
errors.explanation: Across these reported models, B7Q has lower White overrepresentation than D8P and higher—not lower—overall diversity. This contradicts the claim that reducing White overrepresentation directly causes diversity loss as an unavoidable trade-off.

errors.claim: “E5W East Asian F6N | 0.0352”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantity table
errors.evidence: Table 4 lists the E5W row under “East Asian F6N” as “0.0316.”
errors.explanation: The additional narrative quantity gives a different value for the same metric/model than Table 4.

errors.claim: “C4Z | 1176” prompts, with C4Z exemplified as an ethnicity+gender prompt; and Figure 5: “Only [gender]∈{man,woman} appears.”
errors.evidence: Table 3 lists V9R as 294 prompts and C4Z as 1176 prompts. The same part says C4Z/image construction uses ethnicity, gender, verbs, and context, while Figure 5 states only two gender values appear: man and woman.
errors.explanation: With 7 ethnicities and 42 verbs, V9R has 7×42=294 prompts. If C4Z uses only two genders, it should have 7×42×2=588 prompts, not 1176. The 1176 count implies four gender categories, contradicting the claim that only man/woman appears.

errors.claim: F6N values such as Black −0.2381, East Asian −0.2333, Middle Eastern −0.1690, A3J Middle Eastern −0.3667, U8D Middle Eastern −0.4286, etc.
errors.evidence: Earlier definition: F6N/RDS_e = P_e − 1/7, where P_e is a proportion; therefore the minimum possible value is −1/7 ≈ −0.1429.
errors.explanation: Several Table 5 F6N entries are below the mathematically possible minimum under the paper’s own metric definition.

errors.claim: “U8D improves White/Black balance”
errors.evidence: Table 5 reports +U8D White F6N = 0.4286, but +U8D Black F6N is “—”; G4S Black F6N is −0.2381.
errors.explanation: The table provides no U8D Black F6N value, so the claim that U8D improves Black balance is not supported by the reported result. It cannot be compared from the table.

errors.claim: “U8D ... significantly decreases Latino representation and diversity”; also “U8D-aligned Latino representation F6N | –0.4352”
errors.location: Ethnicity paragraph and additional narrative quantity table in this part
errors.evidence: Table 5 reports +U8D Latino F6N as “—”. The value −0.4352 appears in the Δ row under Latino L2V, not Latino F6N.
errors.explanation: The text misidentifies a gender-bias change value as Latino representation F6N. The table gives no U8D Latino F6N from which to claim decreased Latino representation.

errors.claim: “A3J reinforces male- and White-preferred base tendencies”
errors.evidence: Table 5 shows White F6N decreases from G4S 0.6405 to +A3J 0.3667, with Δ White F6N = −0.2738.
errors.explanation: A3J reinforces the male tendency, but Table 5 shows it reduces White overrepresentation relative to the base model rather than reinforcing it.

errors.claim: “A3J amplifies man preference while locking it temporally, with nearly all videos perfectly gender-stable.”
errors.location: Temporal behavior paragraph in this part
errors.evidence: Table 6 contains rows for G4S, +M1Y, +U8D, and +E5W, but no row labeled +A3J. The part states: “Temporal results use another reward-version label (M1Y = HPSv2), retained distinctly in the temporal table.”
errors.explanation: The temporal claim is stated for A3J, but the temporal table reports M1Y instead, explicitly as a distinct label. As written, the table does not directly report A3J temporal stability.

errors.claim: “P3L substantially lowers them, strongly shifting toward woman preference.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 reports +P3L L2V values that are still positive for every group: Average 0.3082, White 0.3341, Black 0.3913, Latino 0.3314, East Asian 0.1008, Southeast Asian 0.2639, India 0.3446, Middle Eastern 0.3894. Earlier metric definition: L2V/PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total, positive male, negative female.
errors.explanation: P3L reduces the strong male bias relative to G4S, but the reported aligned-video L2V values remain male-biased, not woman-preferred. The claim overstates the result and contradicts the metric/table values.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Core claim: alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; biases in preference data enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into videos. Aligned = optimized after likelihood training using preference/aesthetic rewards; unaligned = likelihood alone. QX2/VideoBiasEval audits identity consistency/fairness in structured-event videos.

QX2: Event=<p,a,c>. Attribute space claimed: four gender categories (man, woman, neutral person, non-binary person), seven ethnic groups, 42 verbs. Ethnic groups: White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino. Possible issue: extraction/eval labels gender only {man,woman}. Prompting: J7K = 42 neutral person prompts; V9R = 294 ethnicity+person prompts, 7×42. Template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” J7K tests implicit gender/ethnicity; V9R explicit ethnicity and inferred gender. Evaluation: 3 VLM judges classify 16 frames/video; frame majority→video label; fused across models. TAS/T8Q = % frames matching final video majority label.
