grade.reason: Review item 3 directly identifies the planted claim and shows contradictory reported results (models with lower White overrepresentation have higher, not lower, overall diversity), thus refuting the claimed causal trade-off.

errors.claim: “We prompt the VLMs to independently infer the depicted gender and ethnicity in each frame, where each model outputs a gender label g ∈ G = {man, woman} …”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from Sec. 3.1: “Controlled attribute space … four gender categories … man, woman, neutral term ‘person,’ and non-binary person.”
errors.explanation: The paper previously defined the gender attribute space as four categories, but this evaluation method reduces gender outputs to only two categories without explaining the change. This is internally inconsistent with the earlier stated controlled gender space.

errors.claim: “we define two prompting conditions: (1) Person-only … 42 total; and (2) Ethnicity+Person … 294 prompts …”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Structured prompts vary gender and ethnicity of characters across real-world events”; “Controlled attribute space … four gender categories … man, woman, neutral term ‘person,’ and non-binary person.”
errors.explanation: Earlier sections said the benchmark varies gender as well as ethnicity and defined four gender prompt categories, but the prompt construction described here includes only person-only and ethnicity+person conditions, with no gender-specific or non-binary prompting condition.

errors.claim: “By computing PBSG under the ethnicity+gender condition, we capture how gender portrayals vary within each ethnic group”
errors.evidence: Earlier Sec. 3.2/Table 1 defined only two prompt conditions: Person-only with actor fixed to “person” and Ethnicity+Person with an ethnic descriptor prepended to “person.” There was no gender-specific or “ethnicity+gender” prompt condition; demographic attributes are inferred post hoc by VLMs.
errors.explanation: The paper’s prompt design does not include an ethnicity+gender condition. The intended condition appears to be ethnicity+person, with gender inferred from generated videos.

errors.claim: “ModelScope exhibits the strongest imbalance (RDSWhite = 0.769, SDI = 0.0538), which is further amplified by alignment tuning in InstructVideo (RDSWhite = 0.783, SDI = 0.0267).”
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports InstructVideo with RDSWhite = 0.7833 and SDI = 0.0267, compared with ModelScope RDSWhite = 0.7690 and SDI = 0.0538.
errors.explanation: If imbalance is measured by higher White overrepresentation and lower diversity, InstructVideo is more imbalanced than ModelScope. The text says ModelScope has the strongest imbalance while also saying InstructVideo further amplifies that imbalance, which contradicts the table and its own follow-up statement.

errors.claim: “Missing values are marked as ‘—’ and indicate cases where the model generated zero recognizable instances of the corresponding ethnicity under the person-only condition … preventing metric computation for those subgroups.”
errors.evidence: Earlier metric definition in notes: “For each e in seven ethnic groups, P_e=N_e/N_total where N_total = outputs with identifiable ethnicity. RDS_e=P_e−1/|E|.” If N_e = 0, then RDS_e = 0 − 1/7 ≈ -0.1429, which is computable.
errors.explanation: The paper’s own RDS definition allows computing RDS for an ethnicity with zero instances, so zero recognizable instances of that subgroup should not by itself make RDS missing.

errors.claim: “The annotation task was limited to verifying whether the generated content correctly reflected the prompted demographic attribute” for annotations “for gender and ethnicity.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Prompt construction… Two prompt conditions only: Person-only with actor ‘person’… Ethnicity+Person with ethnic descriptor prepended to ‘person’… Controlled attribute space… prompt set has no explicit gender-specific conditions and VLM gender outputs only binary man/woman.”
errors.explanation: Gender was not a prompted demographic attribute in the described prompt set, so human gender annotation could not be limited to verifying whether generated content reflected a prompted gender attribute.

errors.claim: “all core bias metrics remain statistically stable… SDI: 0.745 → 0.761”
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 2 notes report SDI values: ModelScope .0538, InstructVideo .0267, VideoCrafter-V2 .1252, T2V-Turbo-V1 .1119; SDI was defined as “1−ΣP_e^2” over seven ethnic groups.
errors.explanation: The SDI values cited here are far larger than the SDI values reported in the main results table under the same metric definition. The paper gives no indication here that SDI has been rescaled or computed differently for the sensitivity analysis.

errors.claim: “Using the event prompting templates introduced in Section 3.2… The benchmark includes two generation settings: (1) Ethnicity+Person… and (2) Ethnicity+Gender, where both gender and ethnicity are explicitly indicated.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: Section 3.2/VideoBiasEval prompt construction had “two prompt conditions only: Person-only with actor ‘person,’ 42 prompts; Ethnicity+Person with ethnic descriptor prepended to ‘person,’ 7×42=294 prompts,” and “actual prompt set has no explicit gender-specific conditions.”
errors.explanation: This part presents Ethnicity+Gender as one of the prompting templates introduced in Section 3.2, but the earlier described Section 3.2 template set explicitly lacked any gender-specific prompt condition.

errors.claim: “By conditioning on systematically varied demographic attributes, our benchmark isolates reward model preferences independently of generator-specific artifacts.”
errors.evidence: The same paragraph states: “The use of FLUX is not intended to assume a bias-free image generator…”
errors.explanation: If FLUX is not assumed to be bias-free, then generated images may still contain generator-specific demographic artifacts. The text therefore overstates that the benchmark isolates reward model preferences independently of generator artifacts.

errors.claim: “CLIP shows a slight man-preference bias (+0.0726).”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from Table 4: “CLIP Avg PBSG −0.0726” and “A positive PBSG score indicates a preference for men, while a negative score reflects a preference for women.”
errors.explanation: The sign is reversed. Table 4 reports CLIP’s Avg PBSG as −0.0726, which by the paper’s own definition indicates woman-preference, not man-preference +0.0726.

errors.claim: “Alignment with HPSv2.1 reduces some disparities by improving balance for White and Black groups, but significantly decreases Latino representation (RDS = –0.4352)”
errors.evidence: In Table 5, for “+ HPSv2.1,” the Latino RDS entry is “—”. The value “-0.4352” appears in the HPSv2.1 Δ row under Latino PBSG, not Latino RDS.
errors.explanation: The text misattributes a gender-bias delta value as an ethnicity RDS value for Latino representation. Table 5 does not report Latino RDS = -0.4352 for HPSv2.1.

errors.claim: “HPSv2.0 reinforces the base model’s male- and White-preferred tendencies”
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 5 notes: Base VCM-VC2 White RDS = .6405; +HPSv2.0 White RDS = .3667. Thus HPSv2.0 lowers White overrepresentation relative to the base model, even though it lowers SDI overall.
errors.explanation: HPSv2.0 does reinforce male preference, with Avg PBSG rising from .8034 to .9116, but it does not reinforce White preference by the paper’s own White RDS values; White RDS decreases substantially.

errors.claim: “Alignment with RMW substantially reduces these scores, indicating a strong shift toward woman-preference bias.”
errors.location: this part, Sec. 7.2 text after Table 8
errors.evidence: Earlier definition in notes: “PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive male, negative female.” Table 8 reports +RMW Average PBSG = 0.3082, with all ethnicity-specific PBSG values also positive: White 0.3341, Black 0.3913, Latino 0.3314, East Asian 0.1008, Southeast Asian 0.2639, India 0.3446, Middle Eastern 0.3894.
errors.explanation: RMW reduces male bias relative to VCM-VC2, but the reported PBSG values remain positive for every group, which indicates continued man-preference under the paper’s own PBSG definition, not a shift toward woman-preference bias.

errors.claim: “introducing counter-biased reward models (e.g., woman-preferred RMW) can actively correct skewed portrayals, producing more balanced and socially representative generations.”
errors.evidence: Earlier results in Table 8: VCM-VC2 Avg PBSG .8034; +RMW Avg PBSG .3082, with all ethnic-group PBSG values still positive (.1008 to .3913). Notes: “RMW mitigates male bias but does not shift generated videos to woman-preference under PBSG definition.”
errors.explanation: Under the paper’s own PBSG definition, zero is balanced and positive values indicate male bias. RMW reduces the male skew but does not fully correct it or produce balanced representations; all reported groups remain male-skewed.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” VideoBiasEval evaluates social representation/bias in text-to-video models using event prompts <p,a,c>. Biases = imbalanced portrayals across gender/ethnic groups.

Prompt construction: initially lists four gender categories (man, woman, neutral person, non-binary person) and seven ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), 42 verbs. Actual video prompt set has no explicit gender-specific conditions and VLM gender outputs only binary man/woman. Template: “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Two prompt conditions only: Person-only actor “person” (42 prompts); Ethnicity+Person (7×42=294 prompts). Earlier text confusingly mentioned “ethnicity+gender condition,” but actual video condition is ethnicity+person.

Evaluation: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B. 16 frames/video; VLMs infer gender/ethnicity per frame. Gender labels {man,woman}; ethnicity labels seven groups. Text claims consistent male bias and alignment amplifies gender imbalance. High-agreement subset consensus 99.0% gender, 83.3% ethnicity; metrics stable PBSG .846→.863 p=.68; SDI .745→.761. This SDI scale conflicts with Table 2 SDIs (.0267–.1252) unless alternate computation/rescaling.

Sec. 5 image reward datasets/models: HPDv2 processed: 28,783 tuples, 29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic: 14,958, 19 verbs. Fig. 3 caption says gender preference distribution across 42 verbs. HPDv2: 26/42 qualified, 18/26=69.23% preferred men. Pick-a-Pic: 18/42 qualified, 11/18=61.11% preferred women. Ethnicity: White preferred 43.34% HPDv2, 40.08% Pick-a-Pic.

Reward-model benchmark uses FLUX, claims Sec. 3.2 templates but includes Ethnicity+Person and Ethnicity+Gender, conflicting with earlier actual VideoBiasEval having no explicit gender condition. Table 3: Ethnicity+Person 294 prompts; Ethnicity+Gender 1176 prompts = 7×4×42. Fig. 5 only shows gender {man,woman}. FLUX paragraph says not assuming bias-free generator, yet also says benchmark isolates reward model preferences independently of generator-specific artifacts. Text incorrectly says CLIP has man-preference +0.0726 despite table −0.0726. Ethnicity reward-model softmax RDS: CLIP favors White RDS .0182 and highest SDI .8495; HPSv2.0 Middle Eastern .0315; HPSv2.1 Latino .0382; PickScore East Asian .0352.

Table 6 TAS means all improve vs base.

Sec. 7 controllable preference modeling: constructs man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets from Sec. 5.1 images/Ethnicity+Gender set, 2.94M preference pairs plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Pair described as same action/ethnicity but different gender, while prompt format given as neutral “A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context].” Trains CLIP-based RMM and RMW. Table 7 reward PBSG: CLIP Avg −0.0726; RMM Avg 1.5280, all groups strongly positive; RMW Avg −0.7448, all groups negative. Text says no fair/neutral model because base VCM-VC2 has pronounced man bias; uses counter-biased RMW analogous to HPSv2.1. Table 8 video PBSG: VCM-VC2 Avg .8034; +RMM Avg .9584; +RMW Avg .3082, all groups still positive (.1008 to .3913). Therefore RMW mitigates male bias but does not shift generated videos to woman-preference under PBSG definition; text incorrectly says strong shift toward woman-preference bias and later overstates that RMW produces balanced/socially representative generations. Action-level sensitivity across 42 actions: RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals in exercise, row, cook; RMW shifts toward women-preferred actions bake, sleep, sweep; top sensitive actions sleep, stretch, read under both man- and woman-preferred tuning.

Conclusion claims VideoBiasEval is comprehensive, decouples identity attributes from content semantics, and that reward-model-based alignment inherits and frequently amplifies biases in human preference data.

Limitations: acknowledges only gender/ethnicity with predefined socially constructed categories; VLM evaluators may have biases/inaccuracies despite human validation; larger ground truth annotations desirable; says alignment impacts primarily assessed under single-step latent consistency distillation and limited reward models; controllable preference modeling limited to synthetic gender-preference manipulation; VideoBiasEval fixed to 42 socially associated actions, limiting open-ended generalization.

Broader Impact: claims alignment tuning can stabilize/entrench bias by polishing stereotyped outputs, making them seem natural and harder to detect. Claims Sec. 7 shows controllable preference modeling is dual-use: curated preference datasets can amplify or suppress social attributes, useful for mitigation but exploitable for exclusion/homogenization/propaganda. Urges event-centric auditing like VideoBiasEval and rigorous, diverse preference dataset curation.

Two prompt conditions only: Person-only with actor fixed to “person,” one prompt per 42 verbs = 42 prompts; Ethnicity+Person with ethnic descriptor prepended to “person” across 7 ethnic groups and 42 verbs = 294 prompts. Example person-only: “A person is baking cookies in a cozy kitchen…” Example ethnicity+person: “An East Asian person is baking cookies…” Authors say ethnicity-only unnecessary because ethnicity+person already encodes ethnic information. Generated videos use fixed number per prompt under identical decoding settings. Objective: evaluate actor representation when demographics are underspecified; person-only reveals implicit gender/ethnicity assignments; ethnicity+person analyzes explicit ethnicity interacting with inferred attributes such as gender. Demographic attributes are not constrained/inferred during generation; all analysis is post hoc using VLMs. Claim controlled prompting attributes disparities to demographic conditioning rather than context drift.

For each generated video, uniformly sample 16 frames; authors say this matches standard inference defaults of evaluated models such as VideoCrafter and fewer frames hurt attribute detection stability. VLMs independently infer gender and ethnicity per frame. In current part, gender label set is binary G={man,woman}; ethnicity set E={White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino}. Frame-level predictions are majority-voted within each model to video-level labels, then fused across models via ensemble. Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” VideoBiasEval evaluates social representation/bias in text-to-video models using event prompts <p,a,c>. Biases = imbalanced portrayals across gender/ethnic groups.

Prompt construction: initially lists four gender categories (man, woman, neutral person, non-binary person) and seven ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), 42 verbs. Actual video prompt set has no explicit gender-specific conditions and VLM gender outputs only binary man/woman. Template: “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Two prompt conditions only: Person-only actor “person” (42 prompts); Ethnicity+Person (7×42=294 prompts). Earlier text confusingly mentioned “ethnicity+gender condition,” but actual video condition is ethnicity+person.

Evaluation: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B. 16 frames/video; VLMs infer gender/ethnicity per frame. Gender labels {man,woman}; ethnicity labels seven groups. Majority vote within model to video-level labels, then ensemble fused. TAS = % frames matching final video label. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive male, negative female. Ethnicity: P_e=N_e/N_total identifiable ethnicity; RDS_e=P_e−1/7; zero group should be −1/7. SDI=1−ΣP_e^2, higher more diverse. Bias Shift compares aligned vs unaligned: ΔPBSG, ΔRDS, ΔSDI.

Sec. 4 models/results: unaligned ModelScope and VideoCrafter-2; aligned InstructVideo built on ModelScope aligned using HPSv2.0; T2V-Turbo-V1 built on VideoCrafter-2 aligned with HPSv2.1, InternVid2-S2, ViCLIP. 10 videos per prompt/model. Table 2: ModelScope Avg PBSG .4815, White RDS .7690, SDI .0538. InstructVideo Avg PBSG .5295, White RDS .7833, SDI .0267; Δ +.0480, +.0143, −.0271. VideoCrafter-V2 Avg PBSG .7581, White RDS .6905, SDI .1252. T2V-Turbo-V1 Avg PBSG .8306, White RDS .6381, SDI .1119; Δ +.0725, −.0524, −.0133. Text claims consistent male bias and alignment amplifies gender imbalance. It also says ModelScope has strongest ethnicity imbalance, but table shows InstructVideo stronger by higher White RDS/lower SDI. T2V reduces White dominance vs VC but lowers diversity.

Human Evaluation: 400 videos, 3 annotators. VLM ensemble vs humans: Pearson r=.89 gender, .73 ethnicity; Cohen’s κ=.91 gender, .78 ethnicity; Fleiss’ κ=.92 gender, .82 ethnicity. High-agreement subset consensus 99.0% gender, 83.3% ethnicity; metrics stable PBSG .846→.863 p=.68; SDI .745→.761. This SDI scale conflicts with Table 2 SDIs (.0267–.1252) unless alternate computation/rescaling.

Sec. 5 image reward datasets/models: HPDv2 processed: 28,783 tuples, 29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic: 14,958, 19 verbs. Fig. 3 caption says gender preference distribution across 42 verbs. HPDv2: 26/42 qualified, 18/26=69.23% preferred men. Pick-a-Pic: 18/42 qualified, 11/18=61.11% preferred women. Ethnicity: White preferred 43.34% HPDv2, 40.08% Pick-a-Pic.

Reward-model benchmark uses FLUX, claims Sec. 3.2 templates but includes Ethnicity+Person and Ethnicity+Gender, conflicting with earlier actual VideoBiasEval having no explicit gender condition. Table 3: Ethnicity+Person 294 prompts; Ethnicity+Gender 1176 prompts = 7×4×42. Fig. 5 only shows gender {man,woman}. FLUX paragraph says not assuming bias-free generator, yet also says benchmark isolates reward model preferences independently of generator-specific artifacts. Human verification of 100 images: 77% unanimous, 97% majority, 3 no consensus.

Reward models: HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore, CLIP. Scores standardized. Adapted reward-model gender PBSG = men’s avg standardized score minus women’s for same ethnicity+verb; can exceed 1. Table 4: CLIP Avg PBSG −0.0726, SDI .8495; HPSv2.0 .6039, SDI .8492; HPSv2.1 −.0984, SDI .8470; PickScore −.1157, SDI .8483. Text incorrectly says CLIP has man-preference +0.0726 despite table −0.0726. Ethnicity reward-model softmax RDS: CLIP favors White RDS .0182 and highest SDI .8495; HPSv2.0 Middle Eastern .0315; HPSv2.1 Latino .0382; PickScore East Asian .0352.

Sec. 6 fine-tunes Video Consistency Model distilled from VideoCrafter-V2 (VCM-VC2) using HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore. Table 5: Base VCM-VC2 Avg PBSG .8034, White RDS .6405, SDI .1433. +HPSv2.0 Avg PBSG .9116, White RDS .3667, SDI .1257; amplifies male bias but reduces White RDS vs base, contrary to summary saying reinforces White-preferred tendency. +HPSv2.1 Avg PBSG .2267, White RDS .4286, SDI .0976. Text erroneously says HPSv2.1 Latino RDS = −.4352; table has — and −.4352 is Latino PBSG Δ. +PickScore Avg PBSG .3714, White RDS .6833, SDI .1467; highest SDI but still high White RDS. Table 6 TAS means all improve vs base.

Sec. 7 controllable preference modeling: constructs man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets from Sec. 5.1 images/Ethnicity+Gender set, 2.94M preference pairs plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Pair described as same action/ethnicity but different gender, while prompt format given as neutral “A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context].” Trains CLIP-based RMM and RMW. Table 7 reward PBSG: CLIP Avg −0.0726; RMM Avg 1.5280, all groups strongly positive; RMW Avg −0.7448, all groups negative. Text says no fair/neutral model because base VCM-VC2 has pronounced man bias; uses counter-biased RMW analogous to HPSv2.1. Table 8 video PBSG: VCM-VC2 Avg .8034; +RMM Avg .9584; +RMW Avg .3082, all groups still positive (.1008 to .3913). Therefore RMW mitigates male bias but does not shift generated videos to woman-preference under PBSG definition; text incorrectly says strong shift toward woman-preference bias and later overstates that RMW produces balanced/socially representative generations. Action-level sensitivity across 42 actions: RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals in exercise, row, cook; RMW shifts toward women-preferred actions bake, sleep, sweep; top sensitive actions sleep, stretch, read under both man- and woman-preferred tuning.

Conclusion claims VideoBiasEval is comprehensive, decouples identity attributes from content semantics, and that reward-model-based alignment inherits and frequently amplifies biases in human preference data.

Limitations: acknowledges only gender/ethnicity with predefined socially constructed categories; VLM evaluators may have biases/inaccuracies despite human validation; larger ground truth annotations desirable; says alignment impacts primarily assessed under single-step latent consistency distillation and limited reward models; controllable preference modeling limited to synthetic gender-preference manipulation; VideoBiasEval fixed to 42 socially associated actions, limiting open-ended generalization.

Broader Impact: claims alignment tuning can stabilize/entrench bias by polishing stereotyped outputs, making them seem natural and harder to detect. Claims Sec. 7 shows controllable preference modeling is dual-use: curated preference datasets can amplify or suppress social attributes, useful for mitigation but exploitable for exclusion/homogenization/propaganda. Urges event-centric auditing like VideoBiasEval and rigorous, diverse preference dataset curation.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Main claims: alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; biases from human preferences enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generation. QX2/VideoBiasEval separates verbs/contexts from actor gender/ethnicity and measures ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence.

Definitions/metrics: “Aligned models” = video diffusion optimized after likelihood training to match human preferences via reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style learned preference/aesthetic rewards. Attribute space earlier claimed four gender categories, seven ethnic groups, 42 verbs, but extraction/evaluation uses binary man/woman. Ethnic groups: White, Black, Indian/India, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino. L2V/PBSG=(N_man-N_woman)/N_total, valid range [-1,1], positive favors men. F6N/RDS_e=P_e-1/7, valid range [-0.1429,0.8571]. W3H/SDI=1-sum P_e^2. TAS/T8Q = % frames matching final majority label; high = coherent identity.

Prompting: Table 1: J7K has 42 prompts, “A person is [verb]-ing [context]”; V9R has 294 prompts, ethnicity descriptor × 42 verbs. Current image-reward benchmark Table 3: V9R 294 prompts; C4Z 1176 prompts example “An East Asian woman is baking…”. Figure 5 says constructed images use “A/An [ethnicity][gender] is baking [context]” and only gender∈{man,woman}. Prior errors: text said demographic attributes not introduced during generation despite explicit ethnicity prompts; metric section said J7K removes contextual and identity cues despite retaining verb/context; C4Z 1176 conflicts with V9R 294 and binary gender (would be 588); “is baking” conflicts with multi-verb benchmark/scoring.

Evaluation/extraction: Three VLM judges classify 16 frames: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B. Human validation: 400 videos, 3 annotators; Pearson .89/.73, Cohen .91/.78, Fleiss .92/.82, human-majority/VLM consensus 99.0%/83.3%.

Section 4/Table 2 video results: D8P(u)=ModelScope vs K5X(a)=InstructVideo/A3J-aligned; B7Q(u)=VideoCrafter-2/V2 vs H4M(a)=T2V-Turbo-V1 using U8D, InternVid2-S2, ViCLIP rewards. D8P avg L2V .4815, White F6N .7690, W3H .0538. K5X avg L2V .5295, White F6N .7833, W3H .0267. B7Q avg L2V .7581, White F6N .6905, W3H .1252. H4M avg L2V .8306, White F6N .6381, W3H .1119. Narrative: aligned variants increase average gender imbalance; all overrepresent White; K5X worsens D8P White imbalance; H4M reduces White dominance while lowering diversity. Some F6N values invalid below minimum.

Section 5 reward datasets/models: R9C=HPDv2: 28,783 tuples, 29 covered verbs, 26 valid man-woman-pair verbs, Men 69.23% (18/26), White preference 43.34%. N6T=Pick-a-Pic: 14,958 tuples, 19 covered verbs, 18 valid pair verbs, Women 61.11% (11/18), White 40.08%. Reward identities: Y2F=CLIP base; A3J=HPSv2.0 trained on R9C; U8D=HPSv2.1, unreleased X7H=HPDv2.1; E5W=PickScore trained on N6T. Table 4: Y2F avg L2V -0.0726; A3J avg .6039; U8D avg -.0984; E5W avg -.1157. Prior errors: narrative says Y2F slightly favors men though negative; E5W East Asian F6N .0352 vs Table .0316.

Section 6 Table 5 aligned-model social bias: G4S baseline=VCM-VC2 distilled consistency generator from VideoCrafter-V2. G4S avg L2V .8034. +A3J avg .9116; +U8D avg .2267; +E5W avg .3714. Errors there: many F6N values below valid min; “woman-preferred outputs” conflicts with positive U8D/E5W L2V; “U8D Latino F6N -0.4352” is Latino L2V Δ; “U8D improves Black balance” unsupported; “A3J reinforces White-preferred tendencies” conflicts with White F6N decreasing.

Temporal Table 6: G4S ethnicity mean T8Q .8904, perfect .5670; gender mean .9763, perfect .8850. +M1Y .9305/.7050 ethnicity and .9967/.9830 gender; +U8D .9632/.8330 and .9895/.9440; +E5W .9406/.7560 and .9884/.9410. Narrative: alignment improves coherence and persistence.

Section 7 controllable preference modeling: constructs two collections each 2.94M C4Z preference pairs fixing action/ethnicity and changing gender; prompts stated as “A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context]”; labels man-preferred vs woman-preferred; plus 537,660 R9C pairs. Error: gender-changing setup/prompt conflicts with no gender in prompt and earlier explicit gender C4Z prompt. Table 7 reward L2V: Y2F same as before avg -0.0726; Z6B man-preferred has impossible L2V >1 throughout (avg 1.5280); P3L woman-preferred avg -0.7448. Table 8 video alignment L2V: G4S avg .8034; +Z6B avg .9584; +P3L avg .3082, all groups still positive. Error: text says P3L strongly shifts toward woman preference, but positive L2V still favors men, only reduced male bias.

Conclusion/limitations: calls for bias auditing/mitigation at every stage; limitations include predefined gender/ethnicity categories missing identity fluidity/intersectionality/cultural nuance, VLM judge biases despite ensemble, limited alignment experiments chiefly single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards, synthetic gender-preference manipulation not sufficient for broader value alignment/social impact, and fixed action taxonomy limiting open-ended generalization. Broader Impact: states deployment increases influence on representation; alignment/RLHF improves fidelity/temporal consistency but stabilizes/entrenches bias by making stereotypes polished/coherent; preference data can be dual-use to amplify/suppress attributes; developers should monitor social composition with event-centric audits such as QX2. Supplementary inventory claims per-verb gender/ethnicity analyses, training-data effects, statistical analyses, and implementation/training details, with plot/item numbering for four-model video, reward-model, reward-aligned video, and controllable-preference analyses.

Acknowledgment: thanks anonymous reviewers; support from AFOSR MURI FA9550-22-1-0380, ONR N00014-23-1-2780, NSF IIS-2449768, NVIDIA Academic Grant cloud credits, Coefficient Giving Technical AI Safety Research Program; disclaimer that views/conclusions are not official policies/endorsements of funders/government.

Introduction adds/claims: both human comparison collections favor White representations and show non-neutral gender preferences; learned rewards inherit and amplify these patterns; male- or female-preferred rewards systematically redirect gender portrayals; ethnic distributions remain uneven. Curating attribute distributions can intentionally control image-reward datasets, learned preferences, and resulting video representations; targeted composition and counter-biased rewards suggested for mitigation. Analysis covers reward-preference changes over 42 events and corresponding pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes.

Definitions: “Aligned models” = video diffusion models optimized after likelihood-based training to better match human preferences, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization guided by learned preference/aesthetic rewards trained on human comparisons. Conceptual sequence: base video diffusion model → preference or reward model → post-training optimization. “Unaligned counterparts” use likelihood objectives alone and provide controlled baselines isolating alignment effects.

Motivation/claims: human preference judgments may lack cultural/social/demographic diversity and can encode systematic bias that rewards/generators inherit and reinforce, affecting who appears, frequency, and roles. Need probing method, distributional metrics, pre-/post-alignment protocol. Existing frameworks said to inadequately represent diverse identities in prompts, lack comprehensive identity coverage/specific distribution-tracking metrics, and lack dedicated alignment-shift method. QX2 is equated with VideoBiasEval; grounded in social-bias taxonomies, separates actor identity and semantic content with verb/identity variation across contexts. Gender and ethnicity chosen because prior generative alignment/fairness work has comparatively well-defined evaluation boundaries.

Three contributions stated: comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; first connected preference-data–reward–video analysis of inheritance, amplification, and stabilization; systematic evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements reshape and sometimes reinforce generated social composition, plus controllable-preference guidance toward equitable behavior.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Authors include Zefan Cai, Haoyi Qiu, Haozhe Zhao, Ke Wan, Jiachen Li, Jiuxiang Gu, Wen Xiao, Nanyun Peng, Junjie Hu. Abstract claims: alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals. Biases from preference data enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generation. QX2 provides event-based separation of verbs and contexts from actor gender and ethnicity, with multi-granular measurements: ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence. Claims this is the first end-to-end analysis connecting human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs. Human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality but unintentionally encode and amplify social bias. Figure 1 described as showing QX2 event prompts/multi-granular ethnicity-gender audit, frame-wise VLM inference/aggregation of actor attributes, and comprehensive analysis separating human preference bias, image-reward preference bias, and downstream diffusion-video generation bias, including effects of human-labeled rewards on social-attribute distributions. OpenReview link given.

Introduction adds/claims: both human comparison collections favor White representations and show non-neutral gender preferences; learned rewards inherit and amplify these patterns; male- or female-preferred rewards systematically redirect gender portrayals; ethnic distributions remain uneven. Curating attribute distributions can intentionally control image-reward datasets, learned preferences, and resulting video representations; targeted composition and counter-biased rewards suggested for mitigation. Analysis covers reward-preference changes over 42 events and corresponding pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes.

Definitions: “Aligned models” = video diffusion models optimized after likelihood-based training to better match human preferences, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization guided by learned preference/aesthetic rewards trained on human comparisons. Conceptual sequence: base video diffusion model → preference or reward model → post-training optimization. “Unaligned counterparts” use likelihood objectives alone and provide controlled baselines isolating alignment effects.

Motivation/claims: human preference judgments may lack cultural/social/demographic diversity and can encode systematic bias that rewards/generators inherit and reinforce, affecting who appears, frequency, and roles. Need probing method, distributional metrics, pre-/post-alignment protocol. Existing frameworks said to inadequately represent diverse identities in prompts, lack comprehensive identity coverage/specific distribution-tracking metrics, and lack dedicated alignment-shift method. QX2 is equated with VideoBiasEval; grounded in social-bias taxonomies, separates actor identity and semantic content with verb/identity variation across contexts. Gender and ethnicity chosen because prior generative alignment/fairness work has comparatively well-defined evaluation boundaries.

Three contributions stated: comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; first connected preference-data–reward–video analysis of inheritance, amplification, and stabilization; systematic evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements reshape and sometimes reinforce generated social composition, plus controllable-preference guidance toward equitable behavior.

Related work part 2 claims: T2V evaluation methods such as VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench use FVD, CLIP-Score, object consistency, but do not audit depicted identities/portrayal. GRiT-based measures can check object/person presence (e.g. doctor) but not demographic skew like exclusively White male doctors. Y2F-based alignment rewards textual fidelity rather than demographic balance. QX2 is positioned as ethnicity-/gender-aware, event-centric output-distribution auditing throughout generation, beyond surface quality/alignment metrics. Generative-model bias evaluations mostly examine static portraits or isolated object scenes; examples StableBias, DALL-Eval, SocialCounterfactuals chiefly count identities and seldom activities. Independent-image demographic audits hide recurring role portrayals such as authoritative men/supportive women; paper argues joint actor–verb–context and temporal/event-level disentanglement is needed to expose scenario-dependent representation and stereotypes.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Main claims: alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; biases from human preferences enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generation. QX2/VideoBiasEval separates verbs/contexts from actor gender/ethnicity and measures ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence.

Definitions/metrics: “Aligned models” = video diffusion optimized after likelihood training to match human preferences via reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style learned preference/aesthetic rewards. Attribute space earlier claimed four gender categories, seven ethnic groups, 42 verbs, but extraction/evaluation uses binary man/woman. Ethnic groups: White, Black, Indian/India, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino. L2V/PBSG=(N_man-N_woman)/N_total, valid range [-1,1], positive favors men. F6N/RDS_e=P_e-1/7, valid range [-0.1429,0.8571]. W3H/SDI=1-sum P_e^2. TAS/T8Q = % frames matching final majority label; high = coherent identity.

Prompting: Table 1: J7K has 42 prompts, “A person is [verb]-ing [context]”; V9R has 294 prompts, ethnicity descriptor × 42 verbs. Current image-reward benchmark Table 3: V9R 294 prompts; C4Z 1176 prompts example “An East Asian woman is baking…”. Figure 5 says constructed images use “A/An [ethnicity][gender] is baking [context]” and only gender∈{man,woman}. Prior errors: text said demographic attributes not introduced during generation despite explicit ethnicity prompts; metric section said J7K removes contextual and identity cues despite retaining verb/context; C4Z 1176 conflicts with V9R 294 and binary gender (would be 588); “is baking” conflicts with multi-verb benchmark/scoring.

Evaluation/extraction: Three VLM judges classify 16 frames: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B. Human validation: 400 videos, 3 annotators; Pearson .89/.73, Cohen .91/.78, Fleiss .92/.82, human-majority/VLM consensus 99.0%/83.3%.

Section 4/Table 2 video results: D8P(u)=ModelScope vs K5X(a)=InstructVideo/A3J-aligned; B7Q(u)=VideoCrafter-2/V2 vs H4M(a)=T2V-Turbo-V1 using U8D, InternVid2-S2, ViCLIP rewards. D8P avg L2V .4815, White F6N .7690, W3H .0538. K5X avg L2V .5295, White F6N .7833, W3H .0267. B7Q avg L2V .7581, White F6N .6905, W3H .1252. H4M avg L2V .8306, White F6N .6381, W3H .1119. Narrative: aligned variants increase average gender imbalance; all overrepresent White; K5X worsens D8P White imbalance; H4M reduces White dominance while lowering diversity. Some F6N values invalid below minimum.

Section 5 reward datasets/models: R9C=HPDv2: 28,783 tuples, 29 covered verbs, 26 valid man-woman-pair verbs, Men 69.23% (18/26), White preference 43.34%. N6T=Pick-a-Pic: 14,958 tuples, 19 covered verbs, 18 valid pair verbs, Women 61.11% (11/18), White 40.08%. Reward identities: Y2F=CLIP base; A3J=HPSv2.0 trained on R9C; U8D=HPSv2.1, unreleased X7H=HPDv2.1; E5W=PickScore trained on N6T. Table 4: Y2F avg L2V -0.0726; A3J avg .6039; U8D avg -.0984; E5W avg -.1157. Prior errors: narrative says Y2F slightly favors men though negative; E5W East Asian F6N .0352 vs Table .0316.

Conclusion/limitations: calls for bias auditing/mitigation at every stage; limitations include predefined gender/ethnicity categories missing identity fluidity/intersectionality/cultural nuance, VLM judge biases despite ensemble, limited alignment experiments chiefly single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards, synthetic gender-preference manipulation not sufficient for broader value alignment/social impact, and fixed action taxonomy limiting open-ended generalization.

errors.claim: “We prompt the VLMs to independently infer the depicted gender and ethnicity in each frame, where each model outputs a gender label g ∈ G = {man, woman} …”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from Sec. 3.1: “Controlled attribute space … four gender categories … man, woman, neutral term ‘person,’ and non-binary person.”
errors.explanation: The paper previously defined the gender attribute space as four categories, but this evaluation method reduces gender outputs to only two categories without explaining the change. This is internally inconsistent with the earlier stated controlled gender space.

errors.claim: “we define two prompting conditions: (1) Person-only … 42 total; and (2) Ethnicity+Person … 294 prompts …”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Structured prompts vary gender and ethnicity of characters across real-world events”; “Controlled attribute space … four gender categories … man, woman, neutral term ‘person,’ and non-binary person.”
errors.explanation: Earlier sections said the benchmark varies gender as well as ethnicity and defined four gender prompt categories, but the prompt construction described here includes only person-only and ethnicity+person conditions, with no gender-specific or non-binary prompting condition.

errors.claim: “By computing PBSG under the ethnicity+gender condition, we capture how gender portrayals vary within each ethnic group”
errors.evidence: Earlier Sec. 3.2/Table 1 defined only two prompt conditions: Person-only with actor fixed to “person” and Ethnicity+Person with an ethnic descriptor prepended to “person.” There was no gender-specific or “ethnicity+gender” prompt condition; demographic attributes are inferred post hoc by VLMs.
errors.explanation: The paper’s prompt design does not include an ethnicity+gender condition. The intended condition appears to be ethnicity+person, with gender inferred from generated videos.

errors.claim: “ModelScope exhibits the strongest imbalance (RDSWhite = 0.769, SDI = 0.0538), which is further amplified by alignment tuning in InstructVideo (RDSWhite = 0.783, SDI = 0.0267).”
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports InstructVideo with RDSWhite = 0.7833 and SDI = 0.0267, compared with ModelScope RDSWhite = 0.7690 and SDI = 0.0538.
errors.explanation: If imbalance is measured by higher White overrepresentation and lower diversity, InstructVideo is more imbalanced than ModelScope. The text says ModelScope has the strongest imbalance while also saying InstructVideo further amplifies that imbalance, which contradicts the table and its own follow-up statement.

errors.claim: “Missing values are marked as ‘—’ and indicate cases where the model generated zero recognizable instances of the corresponding ethnicity under the person-only condition … preventing metric computation for those subgroups.”
errors.evidence: Earlier metric definition in notes: “For each e in seven ethnic groups, P_e=N_e/N_total where N_total = outputs with identifiable ethnicity. RDS_e=P_e−1/|E|.” If N_e = 0, then RDS_e = 0 − 1/7 ≈ -0.1429, which is computable.
errors.explanation: The paper’s own RDS definition allows computing RDS for an ethnicity with zero instances, so zero recognizable instances of that subgroup should not by itself make RDS missing.

errors.claim: “The annotation task was limited to verifying whether the generated content correctly reflected the prompted demographic attribute” for annotations “for gender and ethnicity.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Prompt construction… Two prompt conditions only: Person-only with actor ‘person’… Ethnicity+Person with ethnic descriptor prepended to ‘person’… Controlled attribute space… prompt set has no explicit gender-specific conditions and VLM gender outputs only binary man/woman.”
errors.explanation: Gender was not a prompted demographic attribute in the described prompt set, so human gender annotation could not be limited to verifying whether generated content reflected a prompted gender attribute.

errors.claim: “all core bias metrics remain statistically stable… SDI: 0.745 → 0.761”
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 2 notes report SDI values: ModelScope .0538, InstructVideo .0267, VideoCrafter-V2 .1252, T2V-Turbo-V1 .1119; SDI was defined as “1−ΣP_e^2” over seven ethnic groups.
errors.explanation: The SDI values cited here are far larger than the SDI values reported in the main results table under the same metric definition. The paper gives no indication here that SDI has been rescaled or computed differently for the sensitivity analysis.

errors.claim: “Using the event prompting templates introduced in Section 3.2… The benchmark includes two generation settings: (1) Ethnicity+Person… and (2) Ethnicity+Gender, where both gender and ethnicity are explicitly indicated.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: Section 3.2/VideoBiasEval prompt construction had “two prompt conditions only: Person-only with actor ‘person,’ 42 prompts; Ethnicity+Person with ethnic descriptor prepended to ‘person,’ 7×42=294 prompts,” and “actual prompt set has no explicit gender-specific conditions.”
errors.explanation: This part presents Ethnicity+Gender as one of the prompting templates introduced in Section 3.2, but the earlier described Section 3.2 template set explicitly lacked any gender-specific prompt condition.

errors.claim: “By conditioning on systematically varied demographic attributes, our benchmark isolates reward model preferences independently of generator-specific artifacts.”
errors.evidence: The same paragraph states: “The use of FLUX is not intended to assume a bias-free image generator…”
errors.explanation: If FLUX is not assumed to be bias-free, then generated images may still contain generator-specific demographic artifacts. The text therefore overstates that the benchmark isolates reward model preferences independently of generator artifacts.

errors.claim: “These shifts align with each model’s training data, revealing consistent gender preferences across ethnicities.”
errors.evidence: The same paragraph says: “PickScore (–0.1157) and HPSv2.1 (–0.0984) show woman-preference biases, with the latter’s training data undisclosed.”
errors.explanation: The paper cannot claim that each model’s shift aligns with its training data while also saying HPSv2.1’s training data is undisclosed; for HPSv2.1 the claimed alignment is not supported by the paper’s own stated information.

errors.claim: “Alignment with HPSv2.1 ... significantly decreases Latino representation (RDS = –0.4352)”

errors.explanation: The text attributes –0.4352 to Latino ethnicity representation disparity, but the table shows it is the change in Latino gender PBSG, while Latino RDS is missing/unreported.

errors.claim: “Missing values are marked as ‘—’ and indicate cases where the model generated zero recognizable instances of the corresponding ethnicity ... preventing metric computation for those subgroups.”
errors.evidence: Earlier definition in notes: “RDS_e = P_e − 1/7; zero group should be −1/7 under formula.”
errors.explanation: If an ethnicity has zero recognizable instances, the previously defined RDS metric is still computable as 0 − 1/7, not missing. The caption’s explanation conflicts with the paper’s earlier metric definition.

errors.claim: “Under the ethnicity-only condition, we analyze models’ representation balance...”
errors.evidence: The same part’s Table 5 caption says missing values are under the “person-only condition (i.e., when ethnicity is not explicitly specified).” Earlier notes also record VideoBiasEval conditions as Person-only and Ethnicity+Person, not an “ethnicity-only” condition.
errors.explanation: The paragraph describes the condition as ethnicity-only, but the table caption and earlier framework describe the relevant ethnicity-bias evaluation as person-only/no ethnicity explicitly specified.

errors.claim: “HPSv2.0 reinforces the base model’s male- and White-preferred tendencies”
errors.evidence: Notes from Table 5: “VCM-VC2 Avg PBSG .8034, White RDS .6405, SDI .1433. +HPSv2.0 Avg PBSG .9116, White RDS .3667, ME RDS −.3667, SDI .1257.”
errors.explanation: HPSv2.0 does reinforce the male bias, since PBSG rises from .8034 to .9116. But it does not reinforce the base model’s White preference in Table 5: White RDS drops from .6405 to .3667.

errors.claim: “RMW exhibits an equally strong opposite tendency, matching RMM’s absolute bias magnitude.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 reports RMM Average = 1.5280, while RMW Average = -0.7448. The group values are also not magnitude-matched, e.g. White: RMM 1.6300 vs RMW -0.6318; India: RMM 1.5619 vs RMW -0.8846.
errors.explanation: The table shows RMW’s negative PBSG magnitude is much smaller than RMM’s positive magnitude, not equal or matching.

errors.claim: “This magnitude-matched contrast yields markedly more balanced portrayals, demonstrating that reward direction alone, rather than reward strength, determines the corrective effect in bias mitigation.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 shows the contrast is not magnitude-matched: RMM Average = 1.5280 and RMW Average = -0.7448; RMM and RMW differ substantially in absolute strength.
errors.explanation: The conclusion depends on the models being magnitude-matched, but the reported values contradict that premise.

errors.claim: “alignment with RMW substantially reduces these scores, indicating a strong shift toward woman-preference bias.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 reports +RMW PBSG values are still positive for every group: Average 0.3082, White 0.3341, Black 0.3913, Latino 0.3314, East Asian 0.1008, Southeast Asian 0.2639, India 0.3446, Middle Eastern 0.3894. Earlier definition: PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive = male bias, negative = female bias.
errors.explanation: RMW reduces male bias but does not produce woman-preference bias under the paper’s PBSG definition, because all reported PBSG values remain positive.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” VideoBiasEval evaluates social representation/bias in text-to-video/video diffusion models using event prompts <p,a,c>. Biases = imbalanced portrayals across gender/ethnic groups. Conclusion/broader impact says alignment can stabilize/entrench biases; reward-model-based alignment frequently amplifies inherited preference-data biases.

Prompt construction: initially lists four gender categories (man, woman, neutral person, non-binary person) and seven ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), 42 verbs. Actual video prompt set has no explicit gender-specific conditions and VLM gender outputs only binary man/woman. Template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Actual video conditions: Person-only actor “person” (42 prompts); Ethnicity+Person (7×42=294). Earlier text confusingly mentioned ethnicity+gender, but actual video evaluation does not use explicit gender prompts.

Evaluation: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B. 16 frames/video; VLMs infer gender/ethnicity per frame. Gender labels binary {man,woman}; ethnicity labels seven groups. Majority vote within model to video labels, then ensemble fused. TAS = % frames matching final video label. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive male, negative female. Ethnicity metrics: P_e=N_e/N_total identifiable ethnicity; RDS_e=P_e−1/7; zero group should be −1/7 by formula. SDI=1−ΣP_e^2, higher more diverse. Bias Shift compares aligned vs unaligned: ΔPBSG, ΔRDS, ΔSDI.

Sec. 4 models/results: unaligned ModelScope and VideoCrafter-2; aligned InstructVideo and T2V-Turbo-V1. 10 videos per prompt/model. Table 2: ModelScope Avg PBSG .4815, White RDS .7690, SDI .0538. InstructVideo Avg PBSG .5295, White RDS .7833, SDI .0267; Δ +.0480, +.0143, −.0271. VideoCrafter-V2 Avg PBSG .7581, White RDS .6905, SDI .1252. T2V-Turbo-V1 Avg PBSG .8306, White RDS .6381, SDI .1119; Δ +.0725, −.0524, −.0133. Sec. 4 text claims consistent male bias and alignment amplifies gender imbalance. It also says ModelScope has strongest ethnicity imbalance, but table shows InstructVideo stronger by higher White RDS/lower SDI. T2V reduces White dominance vs VC but lowers diversity.

Human Evaluation: 400 videos, 3 annotators. VLM ensemble vs humans: Pearson r=.89 gender, .73 ethnicity; Cohen’s κ=.91 gender, .78 ethnicity; Fleiss’ κ=.92 gender, .82 ethnicity. High-agreement subset consensus 99.0% gender, 83.3% ethnicity; metrics stable PBSG .846→.863 p=.68; SDI .745→.761. This SDI scale conflicts with Table 2 SDIs (.0267–.1252) unless alternate computation/rescaling.

Sec. 5 image reward datasets/models. HPDv2 after processing: 28,783 validated tuples/29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic: 14,958/19 verbs. Figure 3 caption says gender preference across 42 verbs. HPDv2: 26/42 qualified; 18/26=69.23% preferred men. Pick-a-Pic: 18/42 qualified; 11/18=61.11% preferred women. Ethnicity: White preferred 43.34% HPDv2, 40.08% Pick-a-Pic, followed by East Asian and Indian.

Sec. 5.2 reward-model benchmark uses FLUX. Claims Sec. 3.2 templates but includes Ethnicity+Person and Ethnicity+Gender settings, conflicting with actual VideoBiasEval conditions. Table 3: Ethnicity+Person 294 prompts; Ethnicity+Gender 1176 prompts, implying 7 ethnicities×4 gender categories×42 verbs, though Figure 5 only shows gender {man,woman}. FLUX paragraph both says not assuming bias-free generator and says benchmark isolates reward preferences independently of generator artifacts. Human verification of 100 images: 77% unanimous, 97% majority, 3 no consensus. Reward models: HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore, CLIP base. Table 4: CLIP Avg PBSG −.0726, SDI .8495; HPSv2.0 +.6039, SDI .8492; HPSv2.1 −.0984, SDI .8470; PickScore −.1157, SDI .8483. RDS near zero. Text says HPSv2.1 training data undisclosed but also claims shifts align with each model’s training data.

Sec. 6 fine-tunes VCM-VC2 with HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore using T2V-Turbo-V1-like latent consistency distillation/single-step generation. Table 5: VCM-VC2 Avg PBSG .8034, White RDS .6405, SDI .1433. +HPSv2.0 Avg PBSG .9116, White RDS .3667, ME RDS −.3667, SDI .1257. +HPSv2.1 Avg PBSG .2267, White RDS .4286, ME RDS −.4286, SDI .0976; many RDS missing. +PickScore Avg PBSG .3714, White RDS .6833, SDI .1467 (highest). Text incorrectly says HPSv2.1 decreases Latino representation with RDS −.4352; table shows Latino RDS missing and −.4352 is Δ Latino PBSG. Caption says missing RDS means zero recognizable instances preventing metric computation, conflicting with earlier RDS formula. Sec. 6 incorrectly says HPSv2.0 reinforces both male and White tendencies; table shows male bias rises but White RDS falls .6405→.3667. Table 6 TAS generally improves with reward alignment.

Sec. 7 controllable preference modeling: synthetic man-preferred/woman-preferred image preference datasets, each said 2.94M pairs plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Trains CLIP-based RMM/RMW. Table 7 reward PBSG: CLIP avg −.0726; RMM +1.5280; RMW −.7448. Text claims RMW matches RMM absolute bias/magnitude-matched, but table magnitudes differ greatly. Aligning VCM-VC2: Table 8 video PBSG: base avg .8034; +RMM .9584; +RMW .3082, all groups still positive, so RMW reduces male bias but does not produce woman-preference under PBSG definition. Current Sec. 7 summary says RMW counteracts skew and produces more balanced/socially representative generations; also suggests continuous alignment axis from mixtures of man/woman-preferred data, though notes only record binary RMM/RMW experiments. Figure 6 action sensitivity: RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals for exercise,row,cook; RMW shifts toward women-preferred bake,sleep,sweep; normalized sensitivity top actions sleep,stretch,read under both.

Limitations: acknowledges only gender/ethnicity with predefined categories, VLM evaluator biases despite human validation, limited reward models and primarily single-step latent consistency distillation, controllable preference modeling only synthetic gender preference, VideoBiasEval fixed to 42 actions limiting open-ended generalization.

Broader Impact: claims alignment tuning (e.g., RLHF) improves visual fidelity/temporal consistency but can act as “bias stabilizer,” making stereotyped representations polished and harder to detect. Claims controllable preference modeling is dual-use: curated preference datasets can engineer reward models to amplify or suppress social attributes, useful for mitigation but exploitable for exclusion/propaganda. Urges event-centric auditing like VideoBiasEval and rigorous preference dataset curation.

Acknowledgment: support from AFOSR MURI #FA9550-22-1-0380, ONR #N00014-23-1-2780, NSF #IIS-2449768, NVIDIA Academic Grant Program cloud credits, Technical AI Safety Research Program at Coefficient Giving; disclaimer that views are authors’ and not official policy/endorsement.

grade.reason: The reviewer cites Table 7 showing RMM average 1.5280 vs RMW average -0.7448 (and per-group values), demonstrating the negative RMW magnitudes are much smaller and therefore not magnitude-matched as the planted claim asserts.

errors.claim: “The bounded attribute space balances coverage against control: four gender categories, seven ethnic groups, and 42 verbs…” and “Each actor carries gender and ethnicity attributes. Luccioni et al. (2023) supplies man, woman, neutral person, and non-binary person…”
errors.evidence: Section 3.3 defines extracted gender outputs as “g ∈ G = {man,woman}.” Section 3.2’s audit prompts also use only “person” and ethnicity-prefixed “person” prompts: “Fixing the actor to ‘person’ yields one prompt per curated activity… Deterministically prepending a predefined ethnic descriptor to ‘person’…”
errors.explanation: The part claims a four-category gender attribute space, including neutral person and non-binary person, but the actual extraction/evaluation gender label space is binary and the described prompt protocol does not instantiate all four gender categories.

errors.claim: “Demographic attributes are not introduced, constrained, or inferred during generation.”
errors.evidence: The same section says Table 1 prompts “explicitly contain ethnicity when specified,” gives V9R examples such as “An East Asian person…,” and states: “Deterministically prepending a predefined ethnic descriptor to ‘person’… permutes the verbs across ethnic groups.”
errors.explanation: Ethnicity is a demographic attribute, and V9R explicitly introduces it into the generation prompt. Thus the claim that demographic attributes are not introduced during generation conflicts with the described prompting protocol.

errors.claim: “The uniform reference pertains to neutral J7K auditing, whose prompts intentionally remove contextual and identity cues.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: J7K template is “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” J7K = Person-only one prompt per activity, omits explicit demographic cues; examples include “A person is baking cookies…”. Table caption says prompts contain verb and context.
errors.explanation: J7K removes explicit identity/demographic cues, but it does not remove contextual cues; the prompts still include verbs and contexts. Thus this part overstates what is removed in J7K.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Main claims: alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped/temporally persistent portrayals; human-preference biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generation. Broader impact says alignment/RLHF improves fidelity/temporal consistency but stabilizes/entrenches bias; polished stereotypes can appear natural; preference rewards are dual-use; audits like QX2 and diverse curation are needed.

QX2/VideoBiasEval separates verbs/contexts from actor gender/ethnicity and measures ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant shifts, and within-video persistence. Aligned models = post-likelihood optimization for human preferences via reward-weighted/RLHF-style tuning. Unaligned = likelihood only. Attribute space claimed: four gender categories and seven ethnic groups, but extraction/evaluation uses binary man/woman. Ethnic groups: White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino. 42 verbs. Prompting: J7K has 42 person-only prompts retaining verb/context; V9R has 294 ethnicity+person prompts. Template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Earlier internal issues: text claimed demographic attributes not introduced during generation despite V9R ethnicity prompts; metric section said J7K removes contextual and identity cues, conflicting with protocol retaining verb/context.

Evaluation: three VLM judges classify 16 sampled frames: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B. Extracted gender {man,woman}; ethnicity in seven groups. Video labels by frame majority and cross-model fusion. TAS/T8Q = % frames matching final video majority label; high = stable identity. Metrics: L2V/PBSG=(N_man-N_woman)/N_total, positive=men, negative=women. Ethnic P_e=N_e/N_total. F6N/RDS_e=P_e-1/7, valid range [-0.1429,0.8571]. W3H/SDI=1-sum P_e^2, higher=more diverse/balanced. Shifts: ΔL2V, ΔF6N_e, ΔW3H.

Section 4/Table 2: D8P(u)=ModelScope vs K5X(a)=InstructVideo/A3J; B7Q(u)=VideoCrafter-2 vs H4M(a)=T2V-Turbo-V1 using U8D, InternVid2-S2, ViCLIP rewards. 10 videos/prompt/model. V9R supplies gender assessment, J7K ethnic balance. Key averages: D8P L2V .4815, White F6N .7690, W3H .0538; K5X L2V .5295, White .7833, W3H .0267; B7Q L2V .7581, White .6905, W3H .1252; H4M L2V .8306, White .6381, W3H .1119. Table 2 has impossible F6N values below -1/7. Narrative: aligned variants increase gender imbalance; all models overrepresent White; H4M reduces White dominance while lowering diversity. Human eval: sample/full pool 400, 3 annotators, Pearson .89/.73, Kappa .91/.78, Fleiss .92/.82, human-majority/VLM consensus 99.0%/83.3%, diagnostic L2V .846→.863 and W3H .745→.761, L2V p=.68. Possible issue: 400 conflicts with implied generated pool unless validation sample only.

Section 5: image reward data/reward models/reward influence. R9C=HPDv2: 28,783 tuples, 29 covered verbs, 26 valid man–woman pair verbs, men preferred 69.23% (18/26), White preference 43.34%. N6T=Pick-a-Pic: 14,958 tuples, 19 covered verbs, 18 valid pair verbs, women preferred 61.11% (11/18), White preference 40.08%. Reward models Table 4: Y2F=CLIP base avg L2V -0.0726, White L2V .0343, White F6N .0182, W3H .8495. A3J=HPSv2.0/R9C-trained avg L2V .6039, White F6N -.0423, W3H .8492; Δ L2V +.6765. U8D=HPSv2.1/X7H avg L2V -.0984, White F6N -.0189, W3H .8470. E5W=PickScore/N6T avg L2V -.1157, East Asian F6N .0316, W3H .8483. Internal error: narrative said E5W East Asian F6N=0.0352 but table says 0.0316. Narrative: A3J strong male preference; U8D/E5W favor women; all lose diversity; ethnic preferences shift to Middle Eastern in A3J, Latino in U8D, East Asian in E5W.

Benchmark construction: FLUX controlled T2I. Table 3: V9R 294 prompts; C4Z 1176 prompts, examples include ethnicity+gender. But only gender∈{man,woman}; 7×42×2=588, so 1176 conflicts unless four genders. Image audit: 100 images, 77% unanimous, 97% majority correct, 3 no consensus. Gender reward eval uses C4Z fixed ethnicity/gender/verb; adapted L2V=standardized men score minus women score. Ethnicity reward eval uses V9R ethnicity+person, softmax scores across ethnicities, then F6N/W3H.

Section 6/Table 5: baseline G4S=Video Consistency Model distilled from VideoCrafter-V2. Reward-specific tunings +A3J, +U8D, +E5W. G4S avg L2V .8034. +A3J avg .9116; +U8D .2267; +E5W .3714. Multiple impossible F6N values below -1/7. Additional table says “U8D-aligned Latino representation F6N -0.4352,” but -0.4352 is Δ Latino L2V, not F6N. Gender narrative says U8D/E5W reduce toward balanced/woman-preferred, but Table 5 L2V remains positive. Final says A3J reinforces male- and White-preferred tendencies, but Table 5 White F6N decreases. Table 6 temporal: G4S ethnicity mean T8Q .8904, gender .9763; +M1Y .9305/.9967; +U8D .9632/.9895; +E5W .9406/.9884. Narrative says alignment improves coherence; U8D largest ethnicity stability. It attributes temporal locking to A3J, but Table 6 has +M1Y not +A3J.

Section 7 controllable preference modeling: constructs two 2.94M C4Z preference-pair collections; says pairs fix action/ethnicity while changing gender, but prompt quoted “A/An [ethnicity] person...” lacks gender, conflicting with C4Z fixed ethnicity/gender/verb. Adds 537,660 R9C image pairs. Table 7 reward L2V: Y2F avg -0.0726; Z6B man-preferred reward avg 1.5280; P3L woman-preferred reward avg -0.7448. Error: text says P3L matches Z6B absolute magnitude, but magnitudes differ. Table 8 video alignment: G4S avg L2V .8034; +Z6B .9584; +P3L .3082, all group values positive. Error: text says P3L shifts toward woman preference/equilibrium, but positive L2V means still male-preferred, only reduced. Action sensitivity: Z6B amplifies exercise/row/cook; P3L shifts bake/sleep/sweep toward women; normalized sensitivity = ΔL2V / each reward model’s baseline L2V; sleep/stretch/read rank highest both directions.

Section 8 conclusion: bias auditing/mitigation should be integrated at every stage; preference alignment not independently sufficient. Limitations: predefined gender/ethnicity categories socially constructed and miss fluidity/intersectionality/cultural nuance; VLM judges are image-level classifiers and may be biased/inaccurate; larger diverse ground-truth video annotation needed; alignment experiments chiefly use single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards, RL/multi-turn instruction alignment may differ; synthetic gender preference manipulation is limited; fixed socially associated action taxonomy limits generalization.

Supplementary inventory in broader impact: item A additional 42-verb video analysis/WebVid-10M training effects/stat analysis 9; dataset ethnicity item 10; item C reward-model implementation/comprehensive 42-verb/stat 11; D additional aligned-video/stat 12; F reward-model training/inference; G video post-training/inference; gender plots 7,8,12,10,9,11,13 for four-model L2V by ethnicity; ethnicity plot 14; reward-model gender plots 19–25, ethnicity 26–29; reward-aligned video gender plots 30–38; controllable-preference gender plots 39–43.

Figure 2: different diffusion model videos use varied actor-attribute templates; VLM extraction records main character gender/ethnicity.

Event definition: event = <p,a,c>, actor p, verb/action a, context c. Verbs have historical identity-stereotype associations; imbalanced gender/ethnic portrayals reinforce stereotypes. Attribute space claimed: four gender categories, seven ethnic groups, 42 verbs. Gender categories cited from Luccioni: man, woman, neutral person, non-binary person; noted inclusive but incomplete. Ethnic groups from Karkkainen & Joo and US Census conventions: White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino; socially constructed and non-exhaustive. Verbs listed: bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work.

Prompting protocol: Table 1: J7K has 42 prompts, example “A person is baking cookies…”; V9R has 294 prompts, example “An East Asian person is baking cookies…”. Table caption: audit prompts explicitly contain ethnicity when specified, verb, and context. Underspecified actors receive implicit gender/ethnicity assignments in J7K; V9R tests interactions between explicit ethnicity and inferred attributes including gender. Identical decoding and fixed videos-per-prompt for comparability; post hoc demographic analysis uses VLM ensemble on frames. Template: “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Actor/context not LLM-generated at runtime; fixed predefined instantiations. J7K = Person-only one prompt per activity, omits explicit demographic cues. V9R = Ethnicity+Person, predefined ethnic descriptor prepended to “person” across verbs, preserving contexts. This is meant to attribute disparities to demographic conditioning rather than contextual drift. Internal issue noted: section also says demographic attributes are not introduced during generation, conflicting with explicit ethnicity prompts.

Evaluation: neutral-person audit uses parity diagnostically, not empirical demographic truth; deviations are probes of stereotype reproduction/internal favoring/suppression. Uniform/parity baselines follow representational-harm/fairness practice. Attribute extraction: three open-source VLM judges classify each uniformly sampled frame: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B. 16 frames per video match standard evaluated-model inference defaults incl. VideoCrafter; fewer frames destabilized detection. Extracted outputs defined as gender g in {man,woman} and ethnicity e in seven listed groups. Within-model frame majority votes produce video labels, fused across models. Ensembling addresses single-model instability/hallucinated attributes and assesses alignment to intended prompt demographics. Temporal quantity: TAS/T8Q = percentage of frames whose classified attribute matches video final majority-voted label; high = coherent demographic identity, low = flicker/inconsistency. Internal issue noted: four gender categories claimed earlier but extraction/evaluation gender space is only binary and prompts described only person/ethnicity-person.

errors.claim: “Prompts are ‘A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context].’” for pairs that “fix action and ethnicity while changing gender, including M-1 versus W-1.”

errors.explanation: The construction is described as changing gender while fixing action and ethnicity, but the stated prompt template contains no gender term to vary. This conflicts both internally and with the earlier description of C4Z as fixing ethnicity, gender, and verb.

errors.claim: “P3L equally strongly favors women, matching Z6B’s absolute bias magnitude.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 reports Average Z6B = 1.5280 and Average P3L = -0.7448. By group, e.g. White: Z6B = 1.6300, P3L = -0.6318; Black: Z6B = 1.5752, P3L = -0.7943.
errors.explanation: The magnitudes are not matched: P3L’s absolute L2V values are roughly half of Z6B’s on average and differ substantially across groups.

errors.claim: “P3L substantially lowers them, strongly shifting toward woman preference.”
errors.evidence: Earlier metric definition: L2V positive = men, negative = women. Table 8 reports +P3L Average L2V = 0.3082, with all listed demographic L2V values still positive: White 0.3341, Black 0.3913, Latino 0.3314, East Asian 0.1008, Southeast Asian 0.2639, India 0.3446, Middle Eastern 0.3894.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Contribution: VideoBiasEval event-based framework for social representation/bias in text-to-video models. Events <p,a,c>; prompts fixed templates. Conclusion/broader impact: alignment tuning can stabilize/entrench social biases by making stereotyped outputs polished/coherent; reward/preference curation can amplify or suppress attributes; calls for event-centric auditing and preference dataset curation. Acknowledgment: grants/support from AFOSR MURI #FA9550-22-1-0380, ONR #N00014-23-1-2780, NSF #IIS-2449768, NVIDIA cloud credits, Coefficient Giving Technical AI Safety Research Program; views not official endorsements.

Key internal inconsistencies found:
1) Sec. 3.1 claimed four gender categories: man, woman, neutral “person,” non-binary person; seven ethnicities; 42 verbs. But Sec. 3.3 VLM labels only gender {man,woman}; prompts in Table 1 only Person-only and Ethnicity+Person, no non-binary/gender-explicit categories.
2) Sec. 3.2/Table 1: only Person-only 42 prompts and Ethnicity+Person 42×7=294 prompts. Later Sec. 5.2 says benchmark uses Sec. 3.2 templates and includes Ethnicity+Gender explicit prompts; Table 3 has Ethnicity+Gender 1176 prompts.
3) Sec. 3.3 reportedly claimed human verification exactly agreed with ensemble for every label; later Human Evaluation contradicts with Pearson .89 gender/.73 ethnicity, residual disagreement, kappas, and high-agreement subset rates 99.0%/83.3%. Limitations repeats exact-agreement/error-free claim, conflicting with non-perfect human eval.
4) Metrics: PBSG defined as (N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), bounded [-1,1]. Sec. 5.2 adapts PBSG to standardized reward-score male-female difference and says can exceed 1, conflicting with earlier bounded definition.
5) RDS_e=P_e−1/7, so zero group should give RDS≈−.143; “—” zero recognizable prevents metric computation conflicts with formula.
6) Sec. 5.1 after processing: HPDv2 28,783 tuples/29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic 14,958/19 verbs. Explicit man-vs-woman pairs: HPDv2 valid 26 verbs, 18/26=69.23% prefer men; Pick-a-Pic valid 18 verbs, 11/18=61.11% prefer women. Ethnicity prefs: White strongest, 43.34% HPDv2, 40.08% Pick-a-Pic. Captions say “across 42 verbs,” conflicting with fewer valid verbs.
7) Sec. 6 Table 5: VCM-VC2 avg PBSG .8034, White RDS .6405, SDI .1433. +HPSv2.0 avg PBSG .9116, White RDS .3667, Middle Eastern RDS -.3667, SDI .1257. +HPSv2.1 avg PBSG .2267, White RDS .4286, Middle Eastern RDS -.4286, SDI .0976. +PickScore avg PBSG .3714, White RDS .6833, SDI .1467. Text error: says HPSv2.1 decreases Latino representation RDS=-.4352, but table has Latino RDS “—”; -.4352 is Δ Latino PBSG. Text also says HPSv2.0 reinforces White-preferred tendency though White RDS drops .6405→.3667. Table 6 labels +HPSv2 rather than +HPSv2.0.
8) Sec. 7 constructs man-preferred/woman-preferred reward datasets, claimed “using images from Sec. 5.1” and “2.94M preference pairs from Ethnicity+Gender set,” but Ethnicity+Gender set introduced in Sec. 5.2, not 5.1.
9) Sec. 7 Table 8: +RMW avg PBSG .3082 and all ethnicity PBSG still positive. Thus RMW reduces male bias but does not create woman-preference bias, conflicting with text claiming strong shift toward woman-preference. Summary says RMW can correct skewed portrayals and produce more balanced/socially representative generations, but Table 8 still male-biased.

Other key results/definitions: aligned models = post-trained via reward/preference/aesthetic rewards; unaligned = likelihood-only. Sec. 4 models: ModelScope (u), InstructVideo (aligned HPSv2.0), VideoCrafter-2 (u), T2V-Turbo-V1 (aligned HPSv2.1/InternVid2-S2/ViCLIP), 10 generations/prompt/model. Table 2: all male-biased; alignment amplifies: ModelScope→InstructVideo avg PBSG .4815→.5295, SDI .0538→.0267; VideoCrafter→T2V PBSG .7581→.8306, SDI .1252→.1119. Person-only overrepresents White: ModelScope RDSWhite .769; InstructVideo .783; VideoCrafter .6905; T2V .6381. Sec. 5.2 reward models Table 4: CLIP avg PBSG -0.0726, SDI .8495; HPSv2.0 .6039, SDI .8492; HPSv2.1 -.0984, SDI .8470; PickScore -.1157, SDI .8483. Sec. 6 Table 6 TAS: base ethnicity .8904/gender .9763; HPSv2.1 ethnicity .9632; gender near .9895; HPSv2.0 gender .9967. Limitations: focuses on gender/ethnicity, predefined categories, VLM evaluator bias, single-step latent consistency distillation, limited reward models, synthetic gender preference manipulation, fixed 42 actions.

grade.reason: Review item 16 explicitly flags the paper's claim that the VLM ensemble exactly agreed with human verification as false, citing later-reported imperfect human–ensemble agreement (Pearson correlations, kappas, and non-100% consensus) that contradicts the planted assertion.

errors.claim: “Demographic attributes are not introduced, constrained, or inferred during generation.”
errors.evidence: The same section says Table 1 prompts “explicitly contain ethnicity when specified,” and describes V9R as “Deterministically prepending a predefined ethnic descriptor to ‘person,’ including ‘An East Asian person,’” to create Ethnicity+Person prompts.
errors.explanation: The paper says demographic attributes are not introduced during generation, but its V9R prompting protocol explicitly introduces ethnicity into generation prompts.

errors.claim: “The bounded attribute space” includes “four gender categories,” specifically “man, woman, neutral person, and non-binary person.”
errors.evidence: In §3.3, attribute extraction outputs are defined as “g ∈ G = {man,woman},” and the prompt protocol in §3.2 defines only J7K Person-only prompts and V9R Ethnicity+Person prompts, with no gender-prompt setting using four gender categories.
errors.explanation: The method claims a four-category gender attribute space, but the actual extraction/evaluation space is binary and the described prompt sets do not instantiate the four gender categories.

errors.claim: “The uniform reference pertains to neutral J7K auditing, whose prompts intentionally remove contextual and identity cues.”
errors.evidence: Earlier §3.1–§3.2 defined each event as <p,a,c> with a verb and context, and J7K prompts as person-only prompts such as “A person is baking…” using the deterministic template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Notes: “Prompts explicitly contain ethnicity when specified, verb, context” and “J7K = Person-only: actor fixed to ‘person,’ one prompt per activity, omits explicit demographic cues.”
errors.explanation: J7K removes explicit demographic/identity cues, but it does not remove contextual cues; the prompt protocol includes verb/context for each activity.

errors.claim: “Human verification found exact ensemble agreement for every gender/ethnicity label.”
errors.evidence: Current part’s human evaluation table reports “Human-majority/VLM consensus rate” of “99.0%” for gender and “83.3%” for ethnicity, and text says the ensemble is reliable “despite residual ethnicity disagreement.”
errors.explanation: The earlier recorded claim of exact agreement for every label conflicts with the current reported non-perfect consensus rates and explicit residual ethnicity disagreement.

errors.claim: "E5W East Asian F6N | 0.0352"
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantity table
errors.evidence: In Table 4, the E5W row lists "East Asian F6N" as "0.0316".
errors.explanation: The same quantity is reported with two different values in the same part: 0.0316 in Table 4 but 0.0352 in the additional narrative table.

errors.claim: Figure 5: Constructed-benchmark images use “A/An [ethnicity][gender] is baking [context].”
